17817-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
Dated New York, December 24, 1881, this is number 312 of the Scientific American Supplement, the weekly extra to a journal founded in 1845. The Supplement cost five dollars a year, and it gave readers longer technical pieces than the main paper could hold.

This issue covers a fifteen-ton traveling crane for Port Alfred Harbor, a new steam boiler, New York's elevated railways, and a long survey of mechanical engineering in the past fifty years. Electric light, brakes, and phone systems also appear. It is a fine snapshot of late Victorian craft, for readers who like to see how the machine age talked about itself.
20891-itinerary-of-provence-and-the-rhon:
Plain, practical questions guide the Itinerary of Provence and the Rhone, made in the year 1819. Travellers with scant time can plan what to see and do with its help. Costs, roads, and sights are weighed for active use on the road.

John Murray's handbooks taught the British how to tour the Continent with sense. This tour down the Rhone covers towns, ruins, inns, and views in order. Provence's Roman stones and bright towns fill its pages. The book shows early guide writing at its most useful: exact, thrifty, and built for the hand, not the shelf.
24815-translations-of-german-poetry-in-a:
Edward Ziegler Davis wrote this study at the University of Pennsylvania, published in 1905 in the Americana Germanica series. It traces translations of German poetry in American magazines from 1741 to 1810, with other Teutonic verse and home-grown poems about German lands beside them.

Davis began from his doctoral thesis and reprints many pieces from rare, near-unique magazines so scholars could read them at all. Some verses trace back to Campbell, Scott, Wordsworth, and Gray. The book remains a key source for how early Americans first met German poetry in their own periodicals.
26178-the-mirror-of-taste-and-dramatic-c:
The Mirror of Taste and Dramatic Censor for March 1810, volume one, number three, is a journal of stage history and criticism. Its history of the stage compares Aeschylus, called father of Greek drama, with Shakespeare, called father of English drama. Aeschylus laid the plan of tragedy, while Shakespeare raised his country's stage at once to perfection.

The chapter moves to Sophocles, who beat his master as a rival at twenty-five, and to Euripides and Dionysius. Later pages print verses on the death of Mrs. Warren, once Mrs. Merry of the London theatre. The issue mixes scholarship, biography, and elegy, and it shows how early American readers studied the old stage.
26954-the-mirror-of-taste-and-dramatic-c:
The April 1810 number of The Mirror of Taste and Dramatic Censor, an early American periodical, opens with a history of the stage. Its fourth chapter traces comedy from its rough beginnings to Aristophanes and the death of Socrates. Its history notes that tragedy first covered comic shows too, before the two branches split.

The issue also weighs why audiences enjoy watching staged suffering in tragedy and folly in comedy, a question its writers admit few have answered well. The number mixes stage history with essays on drama and taste, showing how early American critics thought about the theater of their day.
8195-scientific-american-supplement-no-2:
The Scientific American Supplement, number 275, dated New York, April 9, 1881, gathers the week's news on new tools and trades for readers who followed invention and craft. Its notes on machines continue Arthur Archard's account of sending power over a distance, by air pressure, water pressure, and wires. They also describe the Hotchkiss revolving gun and an improved floating pontoon dock. Other parts cover craft and chemicals, in the issue's usual wide range.

The issue captures American skill in the early 1880s, when air, water, and wires vied to move power and win wars. Its notes, written for keen general readers, explain machines in clear and hopeful terms. For those who love old gear and gadgets, this issue sums up an inventive age well, and this number is a typical sample.
8296-scientific-american-supplement-no-3:
On October 22, 1881, the Scientific American Supplement packed a week of invention and industry into one issue. Engineers could study a giant eighty-ton steam hammer at work in France. They could compare the great Atlantic steamers Servia, City of Rome, Alaska, and Great Eastern, and read how American mills were changing their methods. A road locomotive and a machine for dotting light fabrics also got full illustrated treatment.

The chemistry pages covered photographic negatives, gelatine emulsion, and pottery, while natural history and miscellany filled out the rest. With its diagrams and workshop detail, the issue shows what counted as progress in 1881: bigger machines, faster ships, and finer craft. It reads today as a snapshot of the industrial age at full steam.
8297-scientific-american-supplement-no-2:
June 25, 1881, brought readers a thousand-horsepower Corliss engine, drawn to scale in five figures, and the opening of the Stevens Institute's new workshop, with speeches by Professor Raymond and Horatio Allen. A light steam engine built for a Russian naval officer's flying experiments shared the engineering pages with a cure for boiler scale and the progress of Eddystone Lighthouse.

Railway turntables, corrugated iron mills, and pleasure cars filled out a practical issue aimed at working engineers. The Supplement's mix of drawings, speeches, and shop notes shows a magazine speaking directly to builders. For modern readers, it is a window onto an age when steam power was still the measure of progress.
8391-scientific-american-supplement-no-2:
July 9, 1881, brought engineers a dry-air refrigerating machine, drawn in five figures, and Thomas's improved steam wheel, alongside an address to the American Society of Civil Engineers at Montreal. The chemistry pages ranged from alcohol found in snow water and rain to the heat value of fuels and the dangers of explosions, with carbon treated at length.

Natural history, notes on the water power of the United States, and miscellany filled the rest of the issue. The Supplement's blend of illustrated machines and laboratory reports shows a magazine serving both workshops and curious readers. For modern eyes, it is a snapshot of 1881 science, practical, confident, and fond of diagrams.
8408-scientific-american-supplement-no-2:
September 24, 1881, brought readers the progress of the marine engine, with boilers, corrosion, fuel use, and screw propellers treated at length. Steam ferry boats at Marseilles, a new English dock, grain elevators, dredgers, and a railway alarm whistle shared the engineering pages. A furnace for sulphide of carbon and a dry inscribing manometer added workshop detail.

Centrifugal casting of metals and wood pulp apparatus rounded out an issue aimed at practical engineers. The Supplement's illustrated, shop-floor reporting shows a magazine in close touch with builders and works. For modern readers, it captures the steam age's late prime, when ships, docks, and mills were still being remade year by year.
a-general-history-and-collection-of-voya: Volume fourteen of Robert Kerr's voyages prints James Cook's voyage toward the South Pole and round the world. Performed in the Resolution and Adventure from 1772 to 1775, the voyage passes from Dusky Bay to Queen Charlotte's Sound. Cook commands the Resolution and records southern seas with care. Kerr's volume brings Cook's great southern voyage to general readers.
abbott-primitive-industry-1881:
Charles Conrad Abbott, a doctor and keen digger in New Jersey, wrote this book on the Trenton gravels in 1881. He had found rough stone tools in the gravel beds near the Delaware River. The finds led him to a bold claim for the age of man in America.

Abbott held that the tools came from a true stone age race in America, as old as Europe's. His claim was the first of its kind for the New World, made in full print. Later men, led by Hrdlicka, took his proof apart stone by stone in the years that came.
actions-and-reactions-pg2381:
Rudyard Kipling gathers stories and poems under a title that promises causes and their costs. The contents list An Habitation Enforced, The Recall, and Garm — A Hostage. They list The Power of the Dog, The Mother Hive, and With the Night Mail. A Deal in Cotton, The New Knighthood, The Puzzler, and Little Foxes follow, with songs between them.

The first story drops a broken New York financier into an English village that quietly rebuilds him. Others fly the night mail of a future air age or follow bees, dogs, and soldiers through small crises with long echoes. Kipling's late manner is dense and allusive, and the verse frames each tale. The collection shows his mature range, from Sussex lanes to imperial air routes.
an-historical-account-of-the-rise-and-pr: Alexander Hewatt continues his historical account of South Carolina and Georgia in volume two, opening at chapter seven and carrying the story forward. The later chapters treat wars, politics, and the colonies' maturing institutions. Together the volumes form a full early history of the lower South. The second book keeps the same steady, source-based pace.
anania-de-natura-daemonum-latin-1581:
Gian Lorenzo Anania, an Italian priest, published De natura daemonum in 1581. The Latin work runs to four books on the nature, orders, and operations of demons. It belongs to the Counter-Reformation, the Catholic answer to Protestant reform, and it sums up demon lore in scholastic order.

Anania sorts demons by rank and task, as a naturalist sorts beasts. He explains how they act on bodies, minds, and the weather. Scripture and the church fathers supply his evidence throughout. The tone is calm, learned, and certain. Readers meet demons catalogued like specimens, in the most orderly demonology of its Italian moment.
annulus-platonis-oder-physikalisch-chymi:
Annulus Platonis, issued in a newly improved edition in 1781, offers a physico-chemical explanation of nature according to its origin, preservation, and destruction. The title page credits a society of true natural researchers. The editors of this edition attributed the work to Herwerd von Forchenbrunn. He was a member of a Rosicrucian society under the name Homerus. Hermann Kopp, in his studies of the Golden Chain of Homer, ascribed it instead to Anton Joseph Kirchweger of Gmunden, who died in 1746.

The book belongs to the nature philosophy that grew around the Aurea Catena Homeri, the golden chain linking all levels of creation. Its ring of Plato stands for that circle of generation and decay in nature. This edition adds many important notes, presenting the work afresh to German readers of the late Enlightenment.
arxiv-2412-03181:
Hafiz Faheem Shahid and Erkki Harjula set out a smart way to place the small services of web-linked things on the best nodes, from edge to cloud, with low energy use. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four.

Such apps strain compute and network as they grow. Edge-cloud mixes can lift their quality, but the right node for each part is a hard pick. The team's plan breaks each app into tiny parts, called nanoservices. It then places them by slices of both network and compute, in an energy-aware way. The joined scheme aims to meet each app's needs while it spends less. The work is a plan and a first test of the thought.
arxiv-2412-05581:
Markov and Markova wrote this plasma physics paper, published in two thousand twenty-four, on the hot matter called quark-gluon plasma. Inside it, soft collective waves, or plasmons, bounce off fast, hard particles, and tracking that dance needs a clean mathematical frame.

The authors show that a Hamiltonian frame they built earlier for soft modes alone carries far more than they first thought. They extend its bracket structure to mix soft waves with the hard particles' charges and momenta. From it they write the interaction terms to third and fourth order in full generality. They then set out the rules for clean changes of variables across both kinds of modes. The work ends with kinetic equations of Boltzmann type that track how a hard particle's mean color charge evolves. The frame aims to ground kinetic theory of the plasma in one consistent scheme.
arxiv-2412-06781:
Nicolas Dufour and three co-authors locate photos generatively in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Global visual geolocation guesses where on Earth an image was taken. Some images can be pinned tightly, others only loosely. That built-in ambiguity is usually ignored by deterministic models that output one point.

Their approach is the first generative one for this task. Diffusion and Riemannian flow matching drive it, with denoising done directly on Earth's surface. It reached state-of-the-art results on three benchmarks. They also introduce probabilistic geolocation, predicting a distribution over locations instead of a point. New metrics and baselines support that richer task. Readers get a locator that can honestly say: somewhere in this region, most likely.
arxiv-2412-12481: Shahzad Ahmad Butt and seven co-authors accelerate zero-knowledge proofs on FPGA hardware in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Zero-knowledge proofs let a prover convince a verifier of a statement while revealing nothing else. The succinct variant, zk-SNARKs, fixed older scalability problems and now serves blockchains and voting systems. Most prover time goes into multi-scalar multiplication. The authors present a scalable FPGA architecture that targets exactly that computation. Their design aims to make proof generation fast enough for wider practical use.
arxiv-2412-16081:
Robert Ott and five colleagues blueprint a quantum computer built from fermionic atoms, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Fermions are particles that refuse to share quantum states. Neutral atoms in optical traps can simulate fermionic systems efficiently, with the right statistics built into the hardware.

Error correction in such machines faces a quirk of atomic physics. Atom number cannot be put into coherent superposition, which blocks standard tricks. The authors design a fermionic reference using extra ancillary modes. Referenced fermions can then be superposed across different counts. Logical fermionic modes built this way admit error correction. The blueprint stays within current experimental capabilities, the authors argue. It maps a route to fault-tolerant fermionic processors.
arxiv-2412-19381:
David Broadway, Mykhailo Flaks, Adrien Dubois, and Patrick Maletinsky teach a neural network to turn pictures of magnetic stray fields back into pictures of the magnetization that made them. Microscopes can image the field above a magnetic film. But to invert that image is ill-posed, and standard reconstructions leave artifacts. Those artifacts limit what physicists can conclude about exotic spin textures.

The network fitting approach suppresses those flaws. Unlike classical methods, it lets extra physical models and bounds be folded in. Patterns whose magnetization points in varying directions, in the past out of reach, could be reconstructed. The team shows this skill on a range of topological spin textures in thin films.
arxiv-2501-00781:
Jonas Fransson explains what must hold for chiral molecules to sort electrons by spin. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The effect, called chiral induced spin selectivity, is well observed. Its origin has stayed an open question. Chiral molecules lack mirror symmetry, like a screw or a hand. Electrons passing through them come out spin-polarized.

Fransson shows two needs must be met together. First, chirality itself breaks the tie between spin states in light molecules. Heavy elements are not required for that split. Second, the molecule must lose energy to its surroundings. Without dissipation, no lasting polarization can form. Examples in the paper show each need at work. The theory gives chemists a clearer target when designing spin-selective materials.
arxiv-2501-01281:
Shunxing Yang and a team of co-authors use deep reward learning to place fluid antennas in a system that both talks and senses. Their paper, from two thousand twenty-five, aims for smart placement.

A fluid antenna can slide to a new spot, which opens fresh ways to lift both talk and sense work. Past work used that for talk alone, or to sense one target. Many targets at once were left bare. Joint choice of beams and spots is a hard, bent task, worse as antennas grow. The team sets out a frame that splits the task in blocks. A reward-taught agent picks spots in it. The aim is strong joint work at a cost that scales.
arxiv-2501-06381:
Mark van der Laan and Susan Gruber present a technical note on transporting a treatment effect from one population to another. Their estimator targets the average treatment effect that a clinical outcome would have shown in a new target population. Only baseline covariates are observed in that target population, while the conditional treatment effect is learned in the source population.

The note allows for the case where only a subset of covariates is measured in the target population, while all covariates are measured in the source. It also handles outcomes subject to missingness, and time-to-event outcomes subject to right-censoring. The authors derive the canonical gradients for both cases and present the corresponding targeted maximum likelihood estimators. The note serves statisticians who must generalize study results to populations that differ from the one studied.
arxiv-2501-07781:
Yuji Hirono, Kohei Kamada, Naoki Yamamoto, and Ryo Yokokura show how a broad kind of symmetry can drive turbulence. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, studies flows where energy moves to larger scales. Classic work ties such inverse cascades to conserved totals over all space. The new charges here live on slices of space, not the whole.

Their test case is an axion-based theory of electric and magnetic fields. The slice-based charge pushes the system toward big, smooth structures. The growth follows a self-similar pattern with exact scaling numbers. The authors suggest such symmetries may order many restless systems. That idea could reach from plasmas to the early universe.
arxiv-2501-09281:
Haobin Qin and colleagues built a synthetic dataset in 2025 for detecting soccer players in video. Player detection underpins event spotting and tactical analysis, but real match footage is scarce because of copyright limits, crowded scenes, and constant blocking of one player by another. The few existing real datasets lack variety, so detection models adapt poorly to new footage.

Their dataset, SoccerSynth-Detection, renders artificial players under randomized lighting and textures and adds simulated camera motion blur. They tested it with a standard detection model against two real datasets. Models transferred from the synthetic data matched real-data performance overall and did clearly better on blurred images. Used as pre-training before fine-tuning, the synthetic data also improved overall detection results.
arxiv-2501-10181:
Marius Potfer and four co-authors sharpen how fast a bidder can learn in a sale where many units go at one price, round by round. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The case in mind is power firms in a day-ahead market. The foe's bids are not known. The team gives a new form of the bid space, which holds the shape of the task. A learner that uses that shape cuts its loss at a rate they prove, which beats the past best and is tight but for log terms. A next feed form, from reserve markets, shows all won bids. It sits between full facts and bare win-or-lose. Their learner does well there too.
arxiv-2501-11781:
Andrei Asinowski and Michaela Polley wrote this math paper in two thousand twenty-five. It starts a planned study of pattern avoidance in rectangulations, ways to cut a rectangle into smaller rectangles.

The authors first define what a pattern means in this setting, then study those that shun a T-like pattern and its turns. For each set of banned turns they count the shunning layouts, in both weak and strong senses. T-shunning weak layouts are counted by the Catalan numbers, with neat swaps to known Catalan objects. Strong ones match set classes of inversion sequences, which settles a guess that two such classes count the same. A last link ties one class to rushed Dyck paths.
arxiv-2501-12381:
Hongjun Wang and eight co-authors present a new attention scheme that reads images as true two-dimensional scenes instead of flattening them into lines. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Transformers and their kin force pictures into one-dimensional order. That loses the layout of the scene and wastes compute.

Their network, GSPN, links every point to others through a line-scan that respects the grid. A stability rule keeps the signal flow steady and context-aware. For a square image, the effective path shrinks to the square root of the pixel count. Weights are learned from the input itself, with no position stamps needed. Tests top charts in image sorting and both kinds of image generation. It also sped up a big text-to-image model hugely at very high resolutions.
arxiv-2502-00581:
Luca Morando, Sanket Salunkhe, and six co-authors steer fixed-wing drones with math that flattens their motion. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, exploits differential flatness. In coordinated flight, a fixed-wing craft's whole path follows from a few chosen curves. That shortcut allows fast, feasible route building in real time.

The planner replans continuously as the aircraft advances. Replanning helps respect the tight turning limits of small wings. Simulations and real flights both test the system. Wind gusts are thrown at it in the harder trials. Trajectories stay smooth and flyable throughout. Small drone missions gain a nimble autopilot core.
arxiv-2502-04281:
Ashwin Kumar and William Yeoh present DECAF, a reinforcement learning approach to fair resource allocation among many agents, in a two thousand twenty-five artificial intelligence paper. A central arbitrator divides constrained resources while agents report their preferences.

The authors formalize this family as distributed evaluation, centralized allocation problems. They propose three methods built on double deep Q-learning: joint weighted optimization of fairness and utility, split optimization with separate estimators, and online perturbation steering an existing utility maximizer toward fairness. All three beat prior fair multi-agent methods across several allocation domains and fairness measures. The design also lets operators trade utility against fairness flexibly online.
arxiv-2502-15181:
Zhao, Su, Yang, Yu, Koutris, and Zhang ask why SQL queries can run far too slow when tables are joined in a bad order. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Even after long study, query tools can still pick plans that are far slower than the best plan. Past fixes for this risk often lack proof or cost speed.

The team reworks a method called Predicate Transfer and adds two new steps, LargestRoot and SafeSubjoin. The full method is proved safe for a broad class of queries. Built into DuckDB and tested on three known test sets, it cuts the spread in run time a great deal. It also speeds up most runs as a whole.
arxiv-2502-18281:
Kun Gao and eight co-authors ask how high the switch-on heat can go for standard superconductors at normal air pressure. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. They draw on computed data for more than twenty thousand metals. A superconductor carries current with no loss below its switch-on heat, and a room-heat version would change power and tech in large ways.

The data show a trade-off at the core of the hunt. Metals with the fastest lattice shakes tend to grip charge weakly, and strong grip comes with slow shakes. Two lithium compounds sit near the best mix the team found. The authors judge room-heat standard superconductors at normal pressure to be very unlikely.
arxiv-2502-19781:
Aayush Dhakal and colleagues improve the learned numeric fingerprints that represent places on Earth for prediction tasks. Such geo-embeddings feed models that classify species, estimate population density, or label biomes from location. Recent systems learn them by matching coordinates with photos taken there, but the authors argue, with information-theoretic backing, that this contrastive training throws away visual detail that later tasks need. Writing in twenty twenty-five, their fix is retrieval: estimate a place's visual features by blending the features of several similar-looking places found in a database.

Across a wide battery of tasks the retrieval-augmented embeddings beat the strongest previous models, often by wide margins, with sizable gains in both classification accuracy and regression fit. Code and models are promised on a public repository. The work speaks to geographers and ecologists who build maps from machine-learned location features.
arxiv-2503-03981:
Zehan Wu and Dehua Wen tighten universal relations among neutron star properties in a 2025 astrophysics study. The matter inside a neutron star is too dense to test on Earth, so its governing equation is deeply uncertain. Universal relations sidestep that problem: certain combinations of mass, spin, and tidal response follow patterns nearly independent of the unknown interior physics.

Astronomical observations can then constrain hard-to-see properties through easy-to-see partners. The authors push the precision of those relations further. Sharper relations mean telescope and gravitational wave data yield tighter limits on how stiff or soft dense matter can be.
arxiv-2503-08381:
Benjamin Kempinski and Tal Kachman introduce InfluenceNet in this two thousand twenty-five paper on measuring influence in voting games. Power indices such as the Banzhaf and Shapley values quantify how much each agent matters in a coalition. Computing them exactly or by estimation gets expensive for coalitions of ten or more members. That cost has limited how thoroughly researchers can study large multi-agent systems.

InfluenceNet replaces the heavy computation with trained neural networks that estimate the indices quickly. The authors report accuracy comparable to, and often better than, existing tools, at much greater speed. Faster estimates open the door to analyzing larger and more realistic coalitions. The approach is meant as a scalable, accessible tool for multi-agent system research.
arxiv-2503-14281:
Adam Štorek and six co-authors attack AI coding assistants in twenty twenty-five. Assistants gather context automatically from files, projects, and contributors. That large, mixed context feeds the model's prompt. It also opens a door: an attacker can poison one origin and sway outputs everywhere.

Their attack, XOXO, plants adversarial code changes that keep the same meaning. Because the code is semantically correct, it looks legitimate to reviewers. Traditional program analysis struggles to spot such perturbations for the same reason. The poisoned context can push the assistant toward vulnerable code or critical errors. Readers in software security get a stealth threat model for tools that read everything in a repository.
arxiv-2503-17681:
Joshua Hammond, Tyler Soderstrom, Brian Korgel, and Michael Baldea present a method for keeping neural network models accurate as the systems they describe drift over time, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Retraining from scratch is expensive, and plain finetuning needs much tuning.

Their Subset Extended Kalman Filter updates only the weights that matter. Parameters to change are picked by the gradient of the loss function, and the filter revises just that subset online. Four dynamic regression case studies with systemic drift compare the approach against finetuning. The filter matched or beat finetuning accuracy while taking significantly less time per iteration and needing less hyperparameter tuning.
arxiv-2503-21281:
Chengyi Wang and Ji Wang design a controller to calm vibrations in slender beams in a 2025 engineering study. Turbine blades in aircraft engines face extreme heat and fast airflow, which excite bending and twisting that can damage the blade. The beam model rotates and couples thermal and aerodynamic loads through a mixed system of equations.

Control acts only at the boundary, using measured outputs rather than the full internal state. That output-feedback design matches what real sensors and actuators allow. Hamilton's variational principle supplies the model, including non-local terms inside the hyperbolic part. Suppressing such vibrations extends blade life and engine safety margins.
arxiv-2503-22581:
The ATLAS Collaboration searches for hypothetical heavy cousins of the leptons in proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. These vector-like leptons appear in an extension of the Standard Model nicknamed the 4321 model.

In that model, the new leptons decay into a third-generation quark and a leptoquark, which itself decays into heavy fermions. The hunting ground is therefore final states rich in tau leptons and b-jets. The team uses the full Run 2 dataset, recorded at thirteen tera-electron volts. No significant excess over the Standard Model background showed up. So the collaboration sets limits: vector-like leptons lighter than about nine hundred ten giga-electron volts are excluded at ninety-five percent confidence. Null results like this steadily fence in where new particles can still hide.
arxiv-2504-03981:
Wen-Tao Hou, Zhuoxian Xiang, Yizhou Liu, and Jiadong Zang showed in twenty twenty-five how to build crystals out of hopfions. A hopfion is a three-dimensional knot-like swirl in a field, marked by a whole-number index. Single hopfions have been studied for years across physics, but no one had a recipe for arranging them into ordered arrays.

Their method blends the Hopf map with rational mapping tricks, stacking helical waves in four dimensions to set the pattern. They produce simple cubic, face-centered, and body-centered hopfion crystals, with the index open to tuning. The same tools build arrays of tori, torus links, and torus knots with higher indices. The work lays groundwork for hunting hopfions in real materials and studying how they act as a group.
arxiv-2504-05481:
Ryan O'Loughlin extends a classic theorem about the numerical range of matrices, the set of values a matrix produces under a certain lens. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. For two-by-two matrices that set is an ellipse, a fact known as the Elliptical Range Theorem. O'Loughlin asks what happens inside a restricted subspace of three-by-three matrices.

He characterizes the numerical range for matrices in such a subspace, generalizing the ellipse picture. A fresh proof of the classic theorem follows from a deep result on when two matrices are the same up to a unitary change. He also describes a weighted cousin, the C-numerical range, in full. That description covers all two-by-two matrices and all rank-one matrices of any size. The results tidy a corner of matrix analysis used in quantum theory.
arxiv-2504-06181:
Counsell, Gittins, Andersson, and Tews propose a gravitational-wave smoking gun for quark matter inside neutron stars. At crushing densities, matter may jump in a first-order transition to deconfined quarks. Masses, sizes, and tidal softness hint at such jumps only indirectly. Many detections would be needed to settle the question that way.

An interface mode offers a sharper tell. Where the two phases meet, a special vibration lives. As two neutron stars spiral together, tides can ring that mode resonantly. The team models the effect with relativistic perturbation theory and equations of state guided by chiral theory. The resonance may be audible to next-generation detectors. Even the upgraded current detector could catch it in loud events. One clean signal could prove the transition outright.
arxiv-2504-08781:
Xu-Xiang Zhong, Chao Yi, and Han-Jia Ye cut the cost, in a 2025 preprint, of grading large language models on big test sets. Benchmarks hold thousands of questions, and each model answers slowly. Running every model on every item burns time and money. The authors ask whether a model's full score can be estimated from a small slice of the test. They borrow a tool from shopping sites: collaborative filtering, which predicts a user's taste from other users.

Here models play the role of users and test items the role of products. Stage one picks items that best separate strong models from weak ones. Stage two predicts how the target model would do on the items it never saw. Tests show the estimates track the true scores closely. The trick slashes the number of costly model calls. Benchmark runners could screen new models far more cheaply this way.
arxiv-2504-08881:
Simon Weng and ten colleagues present a fresh harvest of data on the bright radio sources that the ALMA telescope uses as calibrators, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The ALMACAL survey has logged thousands of hours watching these calibrator sources across a wide band of frequencies.

Out of more than a thousand calibrators, nearly seven hundred now have spectroscopically confirmed redshifts, plus fifty featureless blazars. The distances peak around redshift one and stretch from nearby galaxy cores to a quasar at redshift three point seven. The paper adds seventy new spectra taken with the X-Shooter instrument on the Very Large Telescope, spanning ultraviolet to near-infrared light. Those spectra will feed future searches for cold gas around galaxies. Infrared data suggest most sources are quasars or blazars. The authors also fit the radio spectra of the sample, turning a calibration byproduct into a sky survey.
arxiv-2504-11781:
Guanchun Wang and six co-authors spot anomalies in hyperspectral images with a lean state space model called ACMamba. Their paper from twenty twenty-five serves earth monitoring, where unknown targets must stand out from background. Dense pixel sampling makes training slow and costly on such rich spectra. Their key note is waste: samples from one uniform zone teach the same lesson many times over.

Their design swaps pixels for region-level cases, a cheaper stand-in. A Mamba module reads each region's global context, which reconstruction needs. A consensus scheme then pulls two ways at once: rebuild the background well, and squeeze the anomalies down. Theory and tests on eight benchmarks agree. Speed and accuracy both beat the state of the art in their runs.
arxiv-2504-12781:
Hao Li, Xinyi Chen, and Hao Liu derive spectra for hexagonal graphs in two thousand twenty five. Each edge of a base graph is replaced by paths. One path has length one, others have length five. Repeating the swap builds iterated k-hexagonal graphs.

Linear equations from the graph structure yield the full spectrum. The normalized Laplacian spectrum is solved for k equal one and beyond. Clean formulas follow for Kemeny's constant of the graphs. The multiplicative degree Kirchhoff index gets a formula too. Spanning tree counts complete the set of uses.
arxiv-2504-12881:
Ryo Hamano and Masahito Mochizuki present a study from twenty twenty-five on how light can flip the magnetic state of a material in theory. Their model is the Kondo lattice on a cubic grid. In its ground state the material is ferromagnetic, with spins aligned. Light pulses stir the electrons, which then settle in a new pattern.

They show the lit system settles into a three dimensional antiferromagnetic state, with spins opposed. The shift comes as the lower band fills in a near even, half full way after the light hit. On the way, two named kinds of opposed spin patterns flash by. Wave spectra of spin ripples show a softening that seeds the flip. The path of the flip shifts with the light's angle.
arxiv-2505-00781:
Leonardo Badurina and others calculate what proposed atom gradiometers could learn about dark matter purely from its gravity. These instruments compare the ticking of separated atomic clouds, sensing spacetime delays with extreme precision. The dark matter targets span an enormous range, from ultralight waves to ultraheavy compact clumps. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team models kilometer-scale ground detectors and space concepts. Finds the atom instruments parametrically out-sense laser interferometers for fast-oscillating spacetime ripples driven by ultralight dark matter.

Under reasonable background assumptions, the most ambitious space design could detect a clumped component making up about a tenth of the local dark matter, in a mass window no experiment has touched. It could also probe local overdensities of ultralight matter well above the average. The study hands detector builders concrete discovery targets.
arxiv-2505-01481:
Zongxia Li and eight co-authors build a test of fake videos to see whether vision-language models truly grasp physics and common sense. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Most tests use real footage much like training data. High scores there may reflect pattern matching, not understanding.

Their set, VideoHallu, holds scenes made by top video generators that break physics or logic. Experts wrote question-answer pairs across four kinds of violation. Leading models that shine on standard benches missed many of these breaks. That gap exposes shallow visual reasoning. Fine-tuning with reward learning on the new set sharpened violation spotting. Standard bench scores did not drop. The data are shared in public. The work argues for negative controls in judging machine sight.
arxiv-2505-02281:
Amir Ali Farzin, Yuen-Man Pun, Philipp Braun, and Iman Shames study how to minimize a broad class of functions with no slope data at hand. Their paper from twenty twenty-five covers quasar-convex functions, which bend in a weak way around their low point. Only function values can be probed, through a noisy oracle. Their method smooths the function with random Gaussian noise.

For the free case, they prove the method reaches the global low point and bound its cost. For the boxed case, they define a new near form of the bend property. The method then lands near the low point. A variance-cutting trick lets users shrink that gap. Tests cover tasks where this bend shape arises in the wild. These include finding system parameters and fitting broad linear models.
arxiv-2505-03081:
Mikhailo Dokuchaev, Farangis Johari, and José L. Vilca-Rodríguez introduce inverse semialgebras in a two thousand twenty-five algebra paper. The idea grows out of partially defined operations, such as derivations or linear maps that are only defined on part of an algebra.

The authors define partial actions of a Lie algebra on a non-associative algebra and build a Lie inverse semialgebra that governs those actions. They prove a Lie version of classical inverse semigroup results. In particular, partial representations in meet semilattices correspond exactly to a category of F-inverse Lie semialgebras. An adjunction with the category of Lie algebras completes the picture.
arxiv-2505-05181:
Bojian Yin and Federico Corradi put forth a way in place of backpropagation in this two thousand twenty-five machine learning paper. Backpropagation trains networks but needs gradient synchronization and memory. Local learning rules cost less, yet lose the cross-layer fit that makes learning hang as one. Stochastic Layer-wise Learning threads the needle. It splits the goal into layer-local updates that stay in line through the form of the network.

The method draws on the evidence lower bound under a Markov claim across layers. A divergence term that can not be tracked is swapped for a Bhattacharyya surrogate, worked out from categorical posteriors through geometry-preserving projections. Dropout can be added for regularization. Tests ran from MNIST to ImageNet, spanning connected, convolutional, and transformer forms. The method beat local methods and matched backpropagation. Memory use stayed flat as depth grew, a win for models and neuromorphic hardware.
arxiv-2505-10881:
Donghyeon Ki, JunHyeok Oh, Seong-Woong Shim, and Byung-Jun Lee work on teaching agents from fixed past data. Their paper from twenty twenty-five sits in offline reinforcement learning, where no live trial and error is allowed. A common plan uses diffusion models, which build action paths step by step. Past ways to steer these models were slow or drifted off course.

The team offers a new steering method called Prior Guidance. It swaps the plain starting noise of the model for a learned start shaped by past good acts. Training keeps the model close to sound past conduct in a hidden space. Tests on long task suites show the method beats prior top methods. It also skips the slow step of sampling many paths to pick one.
arxiv-2505-13781:
Chun and co-authors recast the Erdős-Hajnal problem inside finite projective geometries, with colored points. The multicolored version says a coloring that avoids a small fixed pattern must hold a large subspace missing some color. The subspace size should grow as a polynomial in the dimension.

The smallest case colors a three-point triangle over the field with two elements. Three cases arise, and the team resolves all of them. Two follow from a recent Kelley and Meka breakthrough in additive combinatorics. The rainbow case falls to a structure theorem: such colorings split into two-colored pieces. Existing results also settle certain cases over three elements.
arxiv-2505-15881:
Trainor and co-authors chart the glowing hydrogen halos around galaxies when the universe was young. The data come from the Keck Baryonic Structure Survey at redshifts two to three. Lyman-alpha light spreads far beyond each galaxy's visible body. Profiles were traced out past 50 kiloparsecs from the center. The team measured how quickly the glow fades with distance. That fade length is the halo's scale length.

Scale length barely tracked the central galaxy's traits. Brightness and emission strength showed little grip on halo size. One weak trend ran against past claims: faint, high-emission galaxies may hold larger halos. The result steadies models of gas around young galaxies.
arxiv-2505-18581:
Wentao Hu and co-authors wrote this machine learning paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on a failure mode of retrieval-augmented generation. Such systems fetch facts before writing, but bad fetches can mislead the writer and stack new errors on old ones, a loop the authors name hallucination on hallucination.

Their fix, Debate-Augmented RAG, makes software agents argue the case at both stages. In retrieval, backers, skeptics, and a judge hash out which documents to trust. In writing, agents hold uneven information and debate, which hardens the reasoning. No training is needed; the debate runs on top of existing models. Across several tasks, the method improved retrieval quality and cut the stacked errors. Factual accuracy rose overall. The team has released its code in public.
arxiv-2505-19681:
Bo-Ren Shen and six co-authors simulate light-driven electron release from neon with tied control. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Two-tone ultraviolet pulses strike the atom, one at a base tone and one at twice that tone. The base tone is picked to match the gap between two inner shells of neon.

That match lets both shells release electrons at the same energy, one fed by each tone. Rabi coupling between the shells then ties the two electron waves into one coherent pair. The first-principles runs back a past theory built on a simpler states model. The laser settings used are within reach of free-electron lasers today, so lab tests could chase this linked state.
arxiv-2505-21881:
Rui Guan, Junjie Liu, and Jian-Hua Jiang find a duality of control cost in two thousand twenty five. Multipartite quantum systems serve many information tasks in modern labs. Steering them costs energy that lacks a full theory. Weak coupling to a thermal bath frames their analysis.

Universal relations link global and local control costs exactly here. Multipartite correlation shapes those costs at finite times. Neither global nor local cost is always the larger one. That ambiguity complicates cost management in real devices. Multi qubit reset experiments back the theory numerically.
arxiv-2505-23381:
Bowen Ping and four co-authors built AutoGPS in twenty twenty-five, a system that solves geometry problems with readable, reliable proofs. Geometry demands both reading a diagram and reasoning rigorously; neural methods can be unreliable, symbolic ones brittle. AutoGPS pairs the two in a neuro-symbolic loop.

A multimodal formalizer translates the problem, diagram included, into a structured formal language, guided by feedback from the reasoner. The deductive reasoner then treats solving as expanding a hypergraph of facts, producing minimal step-by-step derivations a human can audit. On benchmark data sets it reached top performance. Human judges of the reasoning steps found ninety-nine percent stepwise logical coherence. The authors pitch the system as a model for trustworthy AI mathematics.
arxiv-2505-23681:
Bo Zhao, Nima Dehmamy, Robin Walters, and Rose Yu explain a curious fact about neural networks: their good solutions connect. Different training runs land in different valleys, yet low-loss paths link them. That linkage powers tricks like merging models, but its cause was murky. The team blames symmetry in the space of weights.

Many weight settings compute the same function, and those symmetries shape the valleys' layout. For linear networks the authors count exactly how many separate pieces the solution set has. Skip connections shrink that count. They then map when straight-line links between solutions hold, fail, or nearly hold, using the bend of explicit connecting curves. Symmetries account for much of the observed connectedness. The work gives model merging a firmer theoretical footing.
arxiv-2505-24581:
Nacar and co-authors build GATE, a text code set tuned for Arabic sense match. Sense match scores how close two texts sit in what they mean. It backs hunt, group, and sense work in word tools. Arabic work in that vein lags for lack of good sets and models. Thin stock has held back both tests and gains in the field. GATE codes use nest-style learn, where codes hold codes in size steps.

A mixed loss plan trains the codes on Arabic triple sets. Those sets come from sense-draw tasks that need fine splits. GATE tops the MTEB sense match tests in the team's runs. It beats more big models, OpenAI's in the mix. Gains of 20 to 25 percent show on those test sets. Fine traits of Arabic sense come through in the codes.
arxiv-2506-00081:
Aditya Naik, Jovi Thomas, Teja Sree Mandava, and Himavanth Reddy Vemula study how people use AI chatbots for mental health support in a 2025 study. Many people with mental health struggles never reach professional care, and chatbots have become an easy first stop. The authors surveyed past chatbot users and ran scenario-based tests of large language model chatbots.

Participants mostly treated the bots as a brief, non-judgmental companion, a kind of five minute therapist. Anonymity and the absence of judgment were prized. The findings, presented by the authors from their tests, show both the comfort such tools offer and the care needed around their limits.
arxiv-2506-03981:
Francesco Giannino, Annalisa Iuorio, and Cinzia Soresina build a vegetation model around a newer ecological idea in this two thousand twenty-five paper, published in Physica D. Most pattern-formation models for dryland vegetation rest on competition for scarce water. Autotoxicity, where plants poison their own soil and suppress their own growth, has recently emerged as another key driver, especially by raising mortality. In a standard reaction-diffusion model, biomass-toxicity feedback alone cannot create stable patterns.

The authors derive a cross-diffusion model as the fast-reaction limit of a three-species system with separated time scales. Besides growth inhibition and extra mortality, the derivation yields a third effect, propagation reduction, where toxicity slows vegetation spread. Linear analysis, simulations, and continuation then map the pattern-forming regime. Thanks to cross-diffusion, stable Turing patterns arise from biomass and toxicity alone across wide parameter ranges, with no explicit water dynamics.
arxiv-2506-05981:
Qingbin Zeng and five co-authors simulate city crime with language model agents that can see their surroundings. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Rule-based agent models explain mechanisms but predict poorly. Deep learning predicts better yet stays opaque and data hungry. Neither adapts well when the city changes. Their CrimeMind framework aims for all three virtues.

Routine Activity Theory structures how the agents act. Offenders, targets, and guardians meet in simulated urban scenes. Visual, social, and cultural cues feed the agents' choices. The agents reason flexibly as conditions shift. City simulations gain a cognitive layer over classic agent models. Urban safety research gets a new sandbox.
arxiv-2506-07681:
Dutra and a team of ten co-authors study a magnetic crystal with the formula EuZn2P2 in a twenty twenty-five paper. The crystals were grown by a tin-flux method and order in an antiferromagnetic pattern at low temperature. The team probed both spin behavior and how the crystal acts under light.

A Mossbauer test confirmed the europium sits in one charge state only. Resonance tests showed the spin rest time is set by spin-to-spin links, and that trapped magnetic polarons form and raise the electrical resistance. Light tests found a small change in the resonance and a photovoltaic effect. The team reads this as a good sign for future light-based devices.
arxiv-2506-08481: Enrico Bernardi and Tatsuo Nishitani exhibited a group of wave-like differential operators in 2025 whose basic forecasting problem breaks down in a precise sense. For their second-order hyperbolic operators, the Hamilton map that governs wave propagation changes its spectral character. And the operators can all possess characteristic curves tangent to the set where the equation degenerates. As a consequence, the authors prove the Cauchy problem for these operators is not locally solvable near the origin within Gevrey regularity classes above a certain order. A sharp form of ill-posedness.
arxiv-2506-10081:
Eugenio Bianchi and Mauricio Gamonal sharpened predictions of Starobinsky inflation in twenty twenty-five. This model of the early universe adds a squared curvature term to Einstein's gravity and fits current observations with one parameter. But an honest effective theory at the same order must also include the Weyl-squared term, usually dropped.

The authors include it self-consistently, expanding in the ratio of the two couplings and reducing the order of the equations. Cosmic perturbations then travel with distinct sound speeds for scalar and tensor modes, linked by a simple ratio during inflation. They compute the main observables — the tensor-to-scalar ratio, the tensor tilt, and the running of the scalar tilt — to very high order, all expressed through the measured scalar tilt. The corrections are small but now firmly quantified.
arxiv-2506-10281:
Xinmin Fang, Lingfeng Tao, and Zhengxiong Li argued in twenty twenty-five that AI is best seen as a cognitive engine. It is closer to written language than to steam power. The industrial revolution mechanized muscle. This wave, they claim, boosts intellect itself. Their work builds a frame in theory. It weighs the rise of AI next to past leaps in information technology.

Cases from several fields show AI lifting productivity in knowledge work. The authors blend computer science with economics and sociology. They trace how AI reshapes jobs, firms, and society at large. Diagrams chart the shift from manual work to cognitive productivity. Their end claim is clear. The promise of AI lies in how it helps human thought. To ride the shift, skills, firms, and policy all need fresh thought.
arxiv-2506-18781:
Zhenru Lin and co-authors tested whether today's language models agree with themselves in 2025, and found they often do not. Self-consistency, never contradicting one's own earlier statements, is basic to trustworthy thinking. Yet on on purpose simple tasks, weighing points on a line or a plane, or tracing a group tree, every smaller model tested was highly inconsistent. And even the strongest thinking models were not fully self-steady.

To move beyond anecdotes, the authors introduce metrics that quantify inconsistency and propose two automatic repair plans, one based on graphs and one on energy functions. Both fixes help, but only partially. The gap that remains is the paper's point: even elementary coherence is unsolved, and checking it exactly is a prerequisite for building language models whose thinking users can rely on.
arxiv-2506-21581:
Sarthak Chaturvedi and five co-authors at a national lab test how well dense search models hold up across mixed fields. How a test set is built can change how much gain fine tuning seems to give. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The team fine tuned a ColBERT model on federal reports that judge the impact of projects on nature. On a test set with clear topic lines, the gain was tiny. On a test set with blurred topic lines, the same models showed a gain more than three times as large. The authors link the gap to how spread out and how tangled the topics are in each test set.
arxiv-2507-06381:
James Hazelden, Laura Driscoll, Eli Shlizerman, and Eric Shea-Brown dissect how gradient descent reshapes the internal activity of recurrent networks, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. As these networks train, their dynamics can collapse onto simple patterns and form latent representations that seem to support strong generalization.

Neuroscientists use the shape of such representations to compare artificial and biological learning. Yet rigorous theory for finite, nonlinear models has lagged behind the observations. The authors take an operator view of the gradient flow, the continuous process that tracks how training changes the model. They show this flow splits into a product of two operators, one acting on parameters and one on the network's activity patterns. The split, which they call KPFlow, exposes the mechanism behind dynamic collapse. The work gives a sharper tool for explaining why trained recurrent systems organize themselves the way they do.
arxiv-2507-09581:
Sourish Wawdhane, Sashwat Anagolum, Poulami Das, and Yunong Shi design a compact language for whole families of quantum circuits. New quantum tasks, from error checks to device tests, run many near-identical circuits. Today's tools list each circuit out in full, which bloats files and loads. Their format, Ensemble-IR, writes the family once instead.

One shared program holds the common structure of the family. Symbols mark the points that vary: gate kinds, placements, values, or qubit choices. A device can then rebuild each member circuit on the fly at run time. The team rewrote eighteen real workloads from past papers in the format. Each shrank to a single concise file. The work aims to make large quantum workloads easier to move, store, and run.
arxiv-2507-15081:
Qi Gong and four co-authors made a collaborative storytelling experience in twenty twenty-five. They study how people adapt to social isolation. Isolation breeds anxiety and loneliness. Most fixes aim at the body or at logistics. Exercise and video calls are two of them. They do not aim at imagination. Their probe put people in quarantine in social virtual reality. The group made up a space journey. It was a metaphor for their confinement.

In real quarantine, eighteen people designed spaceship rooms. They role-played as a group in them. Study of the designs, transcripts, and interactions brought out creative adaptation strategies. The act itself changed how the group coped. The study argues that playful narrative design can reveal how people get through isolation. The lesson can shape kinder aid for quarantines to come and for long missions.
arxiv-2507-16181:
Syed Emad Uddin Shubha and Tasnuva Farheen simulate attacks on quantum hardware in twenty twenty-five. Superconducting quantum computers are increasingly shared between tenants. Hardware crosstalk lets one tenant's signals leak into another's qubits. An adversary can craft pulses to induce targeted errors across that boundary.

The study works at the pulse level, where real control signals live. A three-qubit system is modeled in the rotating frame, with always-on couplings and injected drives. Two attack orders are tested: attacker first and victim first. The team varies pulse timing, shape, amplitude, and coupling to find the most damaging settings. Protocol tests on a quantum coin flip and a classification circuit showed uneven vulnerability. Some protocols proved highly exposed.
arxiv-2507-19481:
Byungjun Kim and six co-authors present HairCUP, a prior model for 3D head avatars that treats hair as its own part. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that past priors fuse face and hair into one block. That fusion blurs the split between them, more so when training data is scarce. Swaps of face or hairstyle then turn clumsy.

HairCUP learns face and hair codes in split spaces. A made-up hairless data pipeline makes this split training possible. It strips hair from studio captures using shape and texture guessed by a diffusion prior. Paired sets of hair and hairless heads train the two priors. Face and hair parts can then move between avatars while identity holds. A few shots of a new person suffice to fit a fresh avatar.
arxiv-2507-19581:
Sahil Hegde and Steven Furlanetto wrote this astrophysics paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on modeling the first stars. Population III stars formed from pristine gas in the universe's first billion years, and where and when they lit up shapes everything after.

Their model, called abcd, is a semi-analytic bathtub: fast equations that track gas, stars, and metals in dark matter halos over time. It follows pristine and enriched star formation side by side, with the latest physics for molecular cooling halos and metal mixing folded in. Under plausible conditions, pristine star birth stays strong alongside later generations down to fairly late times, but only in the biggest halos. The authors map how shaky physics inputs widen the forecast range. Early predictions cover galaxy brightness counts, burst rates, and the global radio signal.
arxiv-2507-22281:
Minsoo Kim and Seung-won Hwang present CoEx, an agent whose world model grows as it explores. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. Language model agents plan with an inner world model learned in training. That model is fixed, so plans drift from the true state as new facts arrive.

CoEx plans in layers of subgoals, steered by the model's reason. Each subgoal trial feeds a lasting world model held as text notes plus code-based memory, a paired belief state. Across game-like and plan test worlds, CoEx beats past agent designs at both plan and search tasks.
arxiv-2507-22481:
Tianyi Liu and five colleagues tackle recovery of videos whose bitstreams have been corrupted. Even slight bitstream damage can badly degrade the pixels viewers see. Earlier recovery methods need laborious manual annotation of corrupted regions in every frame, and leftover information in damaged frames can mislead reconstruction.

Their framework is the first blind approach, needing no hand-labeled masks. A Detect Any Corruption model uses a visual foundation model's priors plus bitstream knowledge to localize damage. A corruption-aware feature completion module then weighs residual information adaptively inside a mixture-of-experts structure. Evaluations show strong recovery performance across corruption types, pointing toward more reliable multimedia storage and communication.
arxiv-2507-22881:
Sandra Robles, Drona Vatsyayan, and Giorgio Busoni revisited in 2025 a dramatic way to hunt dark matter: watching whether old neutron stars still exist. Asymmetric dark matter. This has no antimatter counterpart to annihilate with, can be caught by a neutron star's gravity as the star sweeps through space, sinking to the core and piling up. Pile up enough. And the dark core exceeds its balance limit, collapses into a small black hole. And eats the star from inside, so every ancient neutron star still shining is evidence about dark matter's traits.

Earlier constraints from this argument leaned on simplifying approximations. The authors rework the whole chain with boosted treatments of catch, thermalization, black hole formation, growth, and evaporation, across a class of fermionic dark matter models. Their conclusion relaxes previous limits on the particle's mass and its scattering strength off neutrons by several orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2508-00981:
Anna Ivleva and co-authors modeled a birth story in 2025 for odd radio circles, a puzzling class of enormous faint radio rings found in deep sky surveys. Nobody knows what makes them, and their odd traits strain current accounts of diffuse radio sources. One likely cause is a major merger inside a galaxy group, whose shocks might light up a ring in the gas between galaxies.

The team ran a magnetohydrodynamic zoom-in model of a massive group assembling, with cosmic rays tracked on the fly. So X-ray and radio release could be worked out every time from the same virtual object. The modeled group's X-ray appearance matched real groups of similar mass, licensing the radio contrast. Inside, a major galaxy merger fired a series of strong shocks into the surrounding medium that trace a ring from the right viewing angle, supporting the merger-shock account as feasible.
arxiv-2508-01281:
Yui Kasagi and a large team unveil the atmosphere of HR 7672 B in two thousand twenty-five. The target is an L type brown dwarf companion. Data come from REACH at the Subaru Telescope. The spectrograph works at very high resolution in near infrared bands.

Their model, built on the ExoJAX code, handles clouds and starlight spill. Telluric absorption from Earth's own air is modeled too. Water and iron hydride emerge as the main absorbers. A thick cloud layer fits the spectra well. Cloud top heat hints at titanium, aluminum, or iron clouds. The run is REACH's first science demonstration.
arxiv-2508-02681:
Julius Herb and Felix Fritzen present UNO-CG, a hybrid solver for physics problems in materials, in a twenty twenty-five paper. The problems ask how a mixed material behaves as a whole, given its fine structure. Classic solvers are trusted but slow, since they loop many times to converge.

UNO-CG speeds the classic conjugate gradient solver with a learned helper, a unitary neural operator. The helper acts as a preconditioner, a reshaping that makes each loop count more. Safety is kept: the solver still converges by construction. On tests with millions of unknowns, the hybrid cut the loop count a lot and stayed competitive with pure learning methods.
arxiv-2508-08681:
Kaixi Tian, Shengjia Zhao, Yuhan Zhang, and Shan Yu wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It tackles brain-computer links that read many motion traits at once from one batch of brain cells, not just one trait at a time.

Reading direction, place, speed, and acceleration together is hard, since the traits share brain ground and can clash, and the fit can fail on new days or new subjects. Their frame, OrthoSchema, keeps the trait codes at right angles to each other so they do not clash. It also reuses set features with care to adapt with few new samples. Tests on macaque motor cortex data show clear gains, above all when new samples are scarce.
arxiv-2508-11281:
Axel Delaval, Shujian Yang, Haicheng Wang, Han Qiu, and Jialiang Lu build ToxiFrench, a large resource for catching toxic French comments. English toxicity detection is mature; French lags for want of culturally grounded, human-checked data. Their set holds over fifty-three thousand online comments, with a balanced benchmark split. A semi-automated pipeline kept hand labeling near ten percent of the total.

Large models pre-labeled the confident cases, humans verified, and statistics confirm alignment with fully human annotation. Benchmarking many models produced a surprise: small models often beat larger ones on robustness and generalization. The team then fine-tuned with chain-of-thought reasoning and a loss that shifts weight toward the final decision. Their tuned four-billion-parameter model topped the benchmark, beating famous large models while keeping cross-lingual skill. Faithfulness of the reasoning improved as well.
arxiv-2508-13081:
Simran Chowdhry and Nuno Loureiro model how thin sheets of electric current form in magnetized plasma when the plasma also loses energy by radiation. Current sheets are the sites of magnetic reconnection, the explosive reshaping of magnetic fields behind solar flares. Their model follows the collapse of an X-shaped magnetic crossing point and can be solved on paper, which is rare in plasma physics. Writing in twenty twenty-five, they add optically thin radiative cooling to the classic picture and track how cooling changes the collapse along and across the flow.

Cooling speeds the inward collapse but can stall or reverse the lengthening of the sheet. Their updated steady model then finds that when cooling beats the heating from compression, the sheet stays shorter than the system and reconnection runs faster than the classic rate. Groundwork is laid for a fuller theory.
arxiv-2508-17681:
Robert Yang wrote this position paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on a hard question about AI and science: do language models create new knowledge, or only remix what they memorized? The paper proposes a test rather than reporting results.

The test borrows unlearning, a tool usually meant for privacy or copyright. Here the point is ablation: delete a target result and everything that props it up, then see whether the model can rebuild the result from allowed basics alone. Success would signal real constructive power; failure would mark its limits. Yang sketches a small pilot in math and algorithms and notes the same probe could later reach physics or chemistry. The paper aims to spark debate about falsifiable tests for AI-driven discovery.
arxiv-2508-17881:
Sergey Meliakov and eight co-authors probe how confined electrons in CsPbI3 nanocrystals couple to nuclear spin swings, using time resolved Faraday ellipticity. The crystals sit in glass, about eleven nanometers wide. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The electron spin precession rate grew in line with the field, giving a g factor just over two. Even at zero field a small split remained, which the team traces to hyperfine coupling with nuclear spin swings. Model fits split the coupling between lead and iodine orbitals, with iodine in the lead. A density based check backs that split, and an atomic hyperfine constant for iodine follows.
arxiv-2508-18081: The LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA teams jointly authored a 2025 methods paper for the fourth version of their gravitational-wave transient catalog. The catalog gathers candidate signals from ripples in space-time, found and characterized by the three detector collaborations working together. A byline of hundreds of names reflects the scale of the shared observing effort behind each release.
arxiv-2508-20581:
Hirak Kumar Koley, Subikash Choudhury, Argha Deb, and Mitali Mondal simulate particle making in small collision systems with the EPOS4 event generator, in a two thousand twenty-five nuclear physics paper. Proton-proton and proton-lead collisions unexpectedly show collectivity and boosted strangeness.

The study covers collisions at a nucleon-nucleon energy of 5.02 TeV. EPOS4's core-corona setup reproduces several seen trends: spectra hardening with multiplicity, hierarchical strangeness enhancement, and shifting yield ratios. Its microcanonical treatment of the core fits small systems better than grand-canonical methods. Number-based gaps remain, and the authors suggest refinements such as improved core-corona balance and split freeze-out settings for multi-strange hadrons.
arxiv-2509-00081:
Luca Cotti, Anisa Rula, Devis Bianchini, and Federico Cerutti combine language models with domain ontologies for clearer cyber threat intelligence in 2025. Threat work needs facts drawn from security logs in a strict, shared form. Logs are often messy or vague, so current tools extract facts in ways that are hard to trust or check.

An ontology is a formal map of concepts and their links in a field. SHACL rules, which state what a valid graph must look like, guide the model's output form and enforce sense. Drawn facts are stored in a graph database enriched by the ontology for later search and analysis. The design aims for extraction that is both more accurate and open to audit.
arxiv-2509-00181:
Megan Delamer and nine co-authors present POKEMON in 2025, print methods to align microlenses with thousands of fibers for a new telescope array. Modern astrophysics needs huge light-collecting area, but giant mirrors cost billions. The Large Fiber Array Spectroscopic Telescope instead arrays many smaller mirrors, each feeding its own fiber to shared spectrometers.

Joining each fiber bundle to the spectrometer slit must be precise to keep the light gain. Two-photon polymerization printing now makes optical-quality microlenses and nanostructures that can align each fiber. The paper reports optimization of that print step for kilo-fiber experiments. Cheap, precise coupling could make array telescopes rival far costlier giants.
arxiv-2509-00481:
Anton Wolter joins four co-authors, Georgios Vidalakis, Michael Yu, Ankit Grover, and Vaishali Dhanoa, in building a multi-agent system for data charts and stories. Several AI agents split the work from exploring data to writing a clear visual narrative, a chart sequence that explains what the data show.

Wolter and his co-authors mix agent steps with fixed, rule-based parts that keep key logic outside the language models, for clarity and trust. Outputs come in small modules, so users can change one part without redoing all of it. Tests on four varied datasets show strong narrative quality and low resource use, pointing to a practical way for people and agents to build data stories together.
arxiv-2509-00581:
Saumya Chaturvedi, with two co-authors, Aman Chadha and Laurent Bindschaedler, builds SQL-of-Thought, a system that turns plain questions into SQL, the language used to query databases. Better text-to-SQL widens access to data for people who do not write code.

Chaturvedi and her co-authors split the task among agents for schema linking, matching words to tables, subproblem finding, query planning, SQL writing, and a guided correction loop. Unlike systems that only fix errors by running the query, theirs uses a taxonomy, a classified list of error types, to guide dynamic fixes, with in-context learning and chain-of-thought reasoning, step-by-step thinking. The method reaches leading results on the Spider dataset and its variants.
arxiv-2509-00781:
Haomiao Tang leads a team of five authors on secure face retrieval. Face retrieval is often outsourced to third parties. That outsourcing risks the privacy of user portraits. Homomorphic encryption allows computing on encrypted data. It is secure but too slow for real-time use. The team seeks a faster path to the same safety.

They propose Cancelable Product Quantization for the task. The framework works in two stages. A fast indexing module first filters likely candidates. A cipher-space module then ranks the final faces precisely. Product quantization compresses face features into short codes. A tailored protection scheme secures the indexing stage. Templates can be revoked and replaced if leaked. Tests on benchmarks show a decent balance of speed, accuracy, and security.
arxiv-2509-00881:
Ingvar Ziemann, writing alone, gives a simpler proof of the Hanson-Wright inequality. This result in probability bounds how quadratic forms concentrate. A quadratic form wraps a random vector around a matrix. The vector has independent sub-Gaussian entries. Those are variables with tails like a Gaussian curve. Parameters in the bound depend on norms of the matrix.

The best prior proof still used a convex decoupling step due to Bourgain. It then used Gaussian comparison to finish. Ziemann sidesteps that decoupling step entirely. He uses only basic properties of sub-Gaussian variables. He also uses Gaussian rotational invariance, the uniform spread of Gaussian direction. As a bonus, his proof yields improved constants in the bound.
arxiv-2509-00981:
Liancheng Zheng leads a team of seven authors on mean field games for self-driving cars. The framework supports interactive choices among many vehicles. Vehicles vary in style, which the framework must capture. A style scheme maps traits to concrete parameters. Those parameters include speed, safety factors, and reaction time.

Style parameters enter the game through a spatial influence field. A safety-critical lane-change method guards dense traffic. It uses dynamic safety margins and time-to-collision checks. Several layers of constraints add further protection. Real-world NGSIM data calibrates styles and validates the system. Tests show zero collisions across six style combinations. Two fifteen-vehicle scenarios and NGSIM trials also pass safely. The approach beats standard game-theoretic baselines throughout.
arxiv-2509-01481:
Making fractional quantum Hall states, exotic phases where electrons act collectively, inside cold atomic gases is a long-standing aim of quantum simulation. Ophelia Evelyn Sommer and Nigel R. Cooper present a new way to build optical flux lattices that support such phases with only two internal atomic states. Older routes suffered low interaction energies, small energy gaps, or uneven fields.

Adding a scalar potential gives a general mechanism for bands that are both nearly flat and ideal, traits that favor the desired phases. Tuning the lattice to special flat manifolds produces those bands, and the simplest case shares its origin with magic-angle conditions known from layered materials. A dark-state lattice design is a central result. Sommer and Cooper argue this simpler setup could make robust fractional phases reachable in the laboratory.
arxiv-2509-01581:
Complex adaptive systems, from markets to ecosystems, resist simple global models. Their order grows from local interactions. Gueorgui M. Mihaylov and Sergio L. Cacciatori build a gauge field theory for such systems. They borrow the geometry physicists use for basic forces. Their build starts from a discrete geometry of small blocks. It keeps the key traits of the smooth classical case.

In this frame, bundles attach data to each point of a space. They become non-trivial in a natural way, through local links between agents. Tools for measuring that twisting are defined for the setting. Complexity itself is modeled as the result of local and spatial blocks to flatness. The theory offers a geometric language for emergence.
arxiv-2509-01681:
Mohamed Ilyes Lakhal and Richard Bowden present GaussianGAN, a method that builds moving digital people who look real in real time. Past avatar tools often blur fine detail. Their system places small soft blobs, called Gaussian splats, on tube shapes around the limbs of a skeleton pose. A camera based step then maps what each body part is in the view.

A neural network merges the splat data and the part maps into the final life like image. The system runs at seventy-nine frames per second, fast enough for live use. On two motion capture test sets it beats older methods on image quality scores. The work offers a path to crisp avatars for games, calls, and virtual sets.
arxiv-2509-02381:
Mengyuan Zhao, Maël Le Treust, and Tobias J. Oechtering wrote a 2025 information theory paper revisiting the Witsenhausen counterexample, a famous control problem where two decision makers act without full shared information. They study how the best strategy changes when power is scarce.

Their low-power estimation strategy makes the first decision maker quantise the source state in steps. The resulting system state then follows the source in sloped pieces. Classic two-point strategies can win on accuracy but demand large power budgets. The authors show the binary version of their approach is first-order optimal when power is tiny. The analysis also explains the known sawtooth-shaped solutions as a blend of low-power and high-power behaviour.
arxiv-2509-02481:
Aishwarya Sarkar and six co-authors wrote a 2025 hydrology paper on forecasting floods with a graph-based model that respects river structure. Flood prediction needs local runoff drivers plus flow routing across a whole basin network.

Their HydroGAT model builds a basin graph whose nodes are individual land and river pixels, linked by physical flow directions and catchment relations. An attention transformer then learns which past times and upstream places matter most. Tests in two Midwestern basins beat five rival architectures on standard accuracy scores, with low bias in hourly discharge. Attention maps stayed sparse and readable, showing which catchments influence each other. A distributed training pipeline scaled the work across many GPUs on a supercomputer.
arxiv-2509-02581:
Azanzi Jiomekong and fifteen co-authors wrote a 2025 community perspective paper on using AI to organise scholarly knowledge. Publication volume keeps rising, yet many researchers still extract and structure knowledge by hand, unaware of existing tools or lacking field-specific versions.

Different research communities have built their own knowledge base tools in isolation. That separation slows the sharing of methods, models, and good practice. The authors map shared challenges across these groups and suggest ways to open cross-disciplinary dialogue. Collaboration routes and future research directions are categorised for the field. The piece is a position paper rather than a system report: its goal is to connect scattered efforts toward reliable, queryable scholarly knowledge bases that update over time.
arxiv-2509-02781:
Simon May, Neal Dalal, and Andrey Kravtsov present a 2025 cosmology paper tightening bounds on ultra-light dark matter using the smallest known galaxies. Ultra-faint dwarfs are sensitive to fuzzy dark matter, whose wave behaviour heats stars and puffs galaxies up.

Earlier bounds used a perturbative estimate of that heating. The authors check it against full Schrödinger-Poisson simulations, which evolve the wave dark matter directly. Heating in the simulations runs stronger, because a dense central soliton forms and fluctuates, so the older mass bound was conservative. Tidal stripping cannot rescue lighter masses, and self-interactions are blocked by large-scale structure limits. A possible new tiny galaxy, Ursa Major III, would push the mass floor up by more than tenfold if confirmed as a galaxy.
arxiv-2509-02881:
Richard Ninness wrote a 2025 probability paper on a deformed version of the discrete Whittaker processes. Those processes track random arrays of whole numbers whose shape follows set drift parameters, numbers that bias how entries grow.
