When the drifts vanish, the arrays become reverse plane partitions, a classic counting object.

The deformation adds a parameter called q, which twists the rules in a controlled way. The new process connects closely with Whittaker functions tied to a quantum group and with the Toda lattice, a model of particles linked by springs. Ninness shows the process still projects cleanly onto smaller skew shapes, preserving its random structure. That property keeps the model usable for deeper probability work.
arxiv-2509-03481:
Lorenzo Talamanca and one co-author introduce PoolPy in a 2025 research paper on combinatorial group testing, where samples are pooled and tested together to cut costs. Designing good pooling schemes is hard, methods suit different settings, and usable tools have been scarce. PoolPy aims to close that gap for large screening work.

PoolPy is presented as a single framework and web platform covering design, automation, and decoding of test results. Users can benchmark competing strategies against limits set by their own assay, the chemical test they run. Demonstrations cover screening interactions between proteins and small molecules, and genome-wide molecular profiling. The authors argue pooled designs can scale multi-readout functional assays without testing every sample alone.
arxiv-2509-03581:
Davide Paglieri and eight co-authors' 2025 research paper asks when language model agents should stop and plan. Agents built on large language models often plan before every action, following patterns like ReAct. Planning each step wastes computing power and can hurt long tasks, yet never planning also limits results.

Their framework lets an agent decide flexibly where planning effort is worth spending at test time. Training runs in two stages: supervised learning on varied synthetic examples first, then reinforcement learning in long-horizon settings. In the Crafter game environment, dynamically planning agents learn faster and reach more complex goals. Human-written plans can also steer these agents beyond what they manage alone. The authors link that steerability to safer, more collaborative agent systems.
arxiv-2509-03681:
Andrew J. Stier and four co-authors work on making topological data analysis cheap enough for massive biological datasets in a 2025 research paper. Topological data analysis, or TDA, finds geometric structure hidden in data, like loops and voids across scales. Many of its algorithms demand so much memory that huge datasets stay out of reach for ordinary labs.

Their protocol, ALBATROSS, uses stochastic sub-sampling, drawing random smaller subsets of the data in a principled statistical way. That lowers memory needs sharply while keeping the filtration, the step-by-step construction TDA relies on, faithful to the full dataset. Validation on two empirical datasets reproduces earlier findings at a fraction of the memory cost. As a demonstration, they map the topology of functional correlations across the human cortex in fine spatial detail. That mapping was previously infeasible without the new approach.
arxiv-2509-03781:
A 2025 research paper by Brian S. Vermilyea and one co-author treats twisted bilayer graphene acting as a plasmonic crystal at terahertz frequencies. Two graphene sheets twisted by an angle form a moiré pattern, and in gapped samples a triangular network of domain walls appears. Those walls host one-dimensional electronic states protected by topology, which can carry plasmons, waves of charge.

The authors model the system as a network: equations of motion govern charge on each link, with impedance conditions imposed at the nodes. The calculated plasmon band structure shows notable features. Multiple gapless branches appear alongside flat bands, and dissipationless modes sit at high-symmetry points. Their network formalism is compared with random phase approximation, the standard alternative, clarifying when each approach is valid. Simulations launching plasmon waves from scatterers mimic terahertz nano-imaging experiments. The work positions twisted graphene as a tunable platform for terahertz light control.
arxiv-2509-04481:
Yi-Chun Chen and one co-author, Arnav Jhala, turn short stories into playable two-dimensional game scenes in a 2025 research paper. Language models write compelling tales, yet converting narrative text into visual game worlds remains open in procedural content generation. Their lightweight pipeline reads an LLM-generated story, picks three key time frames, and extracts spatial predicates shaped as object-relation-object triples. Visual assets are then retrieved from the GameTileNet data set using affordance-aware semantic embeddings, meaning matches that respect what objects can do.

Layered terrain grows through cellular automata, simple rules applied cell by cell. Objects are placed by rules drawn from the predicate structure. Ten diverse stories tested tile matching, affordance alignment, and constraint satisfaction.
arxiv-2509-04581:
Minyoung You, writing alone, argues that symmetric entanglers do exist for a debated family of topological phases in a 2025 physics paper. Such phases with non-invertible symmetries seemed to lack symmetric entanglers, the globally symmetric shallow circuits linking one phase to another, because they lack a stacking structure. Using topological holography, which views a system through a higher-dimensional bulk, You argues an entangler should exist whenever the phases are linked by fixed-charge dualities.

A worked example settles the point for two phases with a particular representation symmetry. The circuit is written as a matrix product unitary, a compact tensor description of the change. A predicted impossibility in quantum matter theory narrows a lot.
arxiv-2509-05181:
The third known interstellar comet shows polarisation behaviour unlike any comet or asteroid measured before. Zuri Gray, lead author with fifteen co-authors, present the first polarimetric observations of that object in a 2025 astronomy paper. Three telescopes observed it before perihelion across a range of phase angles.

Its negative polarisation branch is deep and narrow, reaching an unusual minimum at a small phase angle, with an inversion angle also unmatched in earlier objects. The small-angle slope resembles certain distant icy bodies, consistent with spectra suggesting a red, possibly ice-bearing surface. Imaging shows a diffuse coma from the earliest observations.
arxiv-2509-05281:
Two views of an image, its look and its hidden frequency pattern, are combined to spot forgeries by Naman Tyagi and Riya Jain in a 2025 computer vision report. Faked and altered images spread fast, and checking authenticity by eye is getting harder.

Their network runs two branches, one on spatial features and one on frequency features, then merges them inside a paired comparison network. The output is a compact code used to classify the image as real or forged. On the CASIA test set the method reached accuracy near seventy-eight percent, beating older statistical methods. The authors stress balance: modest computing cost with reliability fit for practical forensic use.
arxiv-2509-05381:
Human feedback that is wrong in a systematic way can make alignment exponentially hard, Madhava Gaikwad argues in a solo 2025 paper on learning from human feedback. On some kinds of input the feedback is simply mistaken, while the true goal may point elsewhere.

Gaikwad proves that when bias affects a share of contexts, any algorithm needs exponentially many samples to tell two possible true reward functions apart. A calibration oracle, a guide that knows where feedback is unreliable, breaks that barrier with far fewer, well-aimed questions. The lesson is blunt: rare edge cases with subtle bias dominate the gap between the trained proxy and the real objective.
arxiv-2509-05581:
Walking gracefully in an oversized costume is the challenge for a humanoid robot named Cosmo, studied by Arturo Flores Alvarez and nine co-authors in a 2025 robotics paper. Cosmo was built for entertainment, with a head holding a large share of its mass, limited sensing, and shells that restrict movement.

The team uses adversarial motion priors, a reinforcement learning method where a discriminator rewards natural-looking motion learned from examples. Tailored randomisation and reward design protect the hardware during transfer from simulation to the real robot. Experiments show stable standing and walking despite the extreme mass distribution. Entertainment robots, the work suggests, need not trade looks for function.
arxiv-2509-05881:
Before trusting language models to run geographic analyses, their skills need a proper test, argue Qianheng Zhang and eight co-authors in a 2025 paper. Interest in automating GIS workflows with these models is growing, but real ability is unproven. Their answer is GeoAnalystBench, a benchmark of fifty Python tasks drawn from real geospatial problems and checked by GIS experts.

Each task ships with a minimum acceptable product, and scoring covers workflow validity, structure, meaning, and code quality. Top proprietary models produced valid workflows nearly always and cleaner code, while small open models often returned incomplete or inconsistent plans. Tasks needing deeper spatial reasoning, like detecting spatial relations or picking optimal sites, challenged every model. The authors frame the benchmark as a reproducible base for human-guided progress in GeoAI.
arxiv-2509-06181:
Forecasting the solar wind from the Sun's magnetic map is improved by letting a neural network tune the physics, in a 2025 paper led by Prateek Mayank with four co-authors. The Wang-Sheeley-Arge model has anchored operational forecasts for nearly twenty years, but its empirical parameters are fixed or hand-tuned, limiting adaptation. Their WSA+ keeps the relation and learns its settings.

First, a neural optimizer adjusts parameters for each solar rotation to match spacecraft observations inside a differentiable, physics-constrained pipeline. Then a network learns to predict those tuned maps straight from magnetogram features, so new conditions need no manual work. WSA+ beats the classic relation across quiet and active periods by roughly forty percent on average, and drops into existing heliospheric pipelines.
arxiv-2509-06281:
A proposed spin supersolid phase is absent at high field in a triangular-lattice quantum magnet, report K. Shi and nine co-authors in a 2025 paper. Their material is a rubidium cobalt selenite with cobalt ions on a triangular lattice, close to the Ising limit. Between its one-third magnetization plateau and the polarized state, theory had suggested an exotic intermediate phase.

Magnetization, torque, specific heat, and nuclear magnetic resonance map the phase diagram up to thirty tesla. Resonance spectra identify the plateau's up-up-down spin pattern, and that pattern persists through the intermediate phase before polarization destroys it. The spectroscopic evidence rules out the proposed supersolid there, and the full diagram contradicts the theoretical expectation.
arxiv-2509-06481:
Sending fewer radio messages while still dividing jobs fairly among robots is the aim of a 2025 robotics paper by Vinita Sao and three co-authors. Fleets of drones for surveillance or rescue must share tasks without a central controller, since radio range is limited. A known method, the consensus-based bundle algorithm, works well but demands constant chatter.

The authors add an event-driven rule: robots speak up only when something important changes, instead of talking nonstop. They prove the method keeps the same solution quality and performance guarantees as the original. Monte Carlo simulations, repeated random trials with different numbers of targets, robots, and task bundles, back that claim. Message traffic falls by as much as about half, which eases congestion and lost packets in real fleets.
arxiv-2509-06981:
Tom Bensky and Karl Saunders describe a genetic algorithm that builds teaching schedules for a university physics department, in a 2025 paper. Handled by hand, the job means matching about two hundred classes to roughly fifty professors three times a year. A good schedule must respect contract rules and treat faculty fairly over time.

In their method, each chromosome proposes a pairing of professors with classes drawn from numbered lists. A fitness score rates how well a pairing meets contract limits and single teaching wishes. Mixing and random changes then breed better schedules across many generations. The program usually settles within minutes and fills more than ninety percent of the classes needed. Per-professor scores track satisfaction, helping keep assignments fair year after year.
arxiv-2509-07281:
Mous-Abou Hamadou and 1 co-author extend a classic tool for modeling dependence between many random variables in a 2025 paper. A copula is a function that joins separate distributions into one joint picture while keeping each part intact. The Farlie-Gumbel-Morgenstern family is simple and popular, but its dependence range is narrow, which limits real data fits.

The extended version adds parameters built from Legendre polynomials, a standard family of curves, to widen that range in any number of dimensions. The authors derive direct formulas for the new parameters and prove the estimates are unbiased, consistent, and approach a normal shape in large samples. Computer trials check small-sample behavior. On the Bearing dataset, a benchmark used in earlier studies, the classic model fits poorly, while a reduced form of the extended model is selected as the better description.
arxiv-2509-07481:
Xing-Jian Lv and 5 co-authors quantify a neglected uncertainty in predictions of diffuse gamma-ray glow across our Galaxy in a 2025 paper. Diffuse gamma rays, spread-out high-energy light, trace how cosmic rays are distributed in the Galaxy. Models and observations disagree in places, so honest error bars matter. Past work stressed fluctuations in the lepton part of the cosmic ray flux.

Using fully three-dimensional, time-dependent GALPROP simulations, the team injects cosmic ray protons from discrete Galactic sources and watches the hadron flux vary over time. That temporal randomness feeds straight into the hadronic part of the diffuse gamma-ray estimate. The resulting uncertainty is far from negligible and can match or exceed current experimental errors at very high energies. The finding corrects the assumption that only lepton fluctuations matter for diffuse emission models.
arxiv-2509-07681:
Pierre Lambert and 3 co-authors introduce FUnc-SNE in 2025, a neighbour embedding algorithm that refuses the usual speed-versus-quality trade. Neighbour embeddings flatten high-dimensional data into low-dimensional maps for visualization and analysis. Fast approximations based on negative sampling, as in UMAP, can blur fine structure, while costlier ones like FIt-SNE preserve structure but crawl and only target two or three dimensions.

Their acceleration needs only a small number of computations per iteration while keeping fine-grained structure and full flexibility in the target dimension. Hyperparameters give users dedicated control over the structures extracted. The name advertises the mix: flexible, fast, and unconstrained, since the embedding space is not limited to visualization sizes. Better embeddings matter wherever analysts explore single-cell data, images, or text collections through maps.
arxiv-2509-07781:
Lorenzo Martignetti and 3 co-authors introduce TRAM in 2025, an atomic multicast protocol built for shared memory systems. Atomic multicast delivers messages to replica groups in a consistent order, letting services combine replication for fault tolerance with sharding for scale. Most protocols target message-passing systems; few are designed for shared memory, where replicas read and write common memory directly.

TRAM uses an overlay tree architecture, a routing tree layered over the replicas, and its design is deliberately simple and practical. Against leading shared-memory protocols it raises throughput by more than three times and cuts latency by more than 2.3 times. Against message-passing protocols the gains grow larger still, up to 5.9 times the throughput and a fraction of the latency. Faster ordered delivery strengthens the dependable systems built on top of it.
arxiv-2509-07981:
Jack T. Dinsmore and 1 co-author improve how X-ray polarization is extracted from faint cosmic sources in a 2025 astrophysics paper. The IXPE space telescope measures polarization, the preferred direction of light waves, which reveals magnetic structures around black holes and neutron stars. Faint sources demand careful statistics, because background particles and the telescope's own blur muddy the signal.

New weighting schemes account for the point-spread function and for particle background, and can be combined with earlier neural-network weights plus time and energy information. The combined weights shrink the uncertainty region on polarization measurements noticeably. The authors validate the method on simulated data and archival observations, and they release a public tool so other IXPE users can apply the same treatment.
arxiv-2509-08281: Number theory often hides simple patterns inside forbidding definitions, and Yi-Ju Tsai reports one such pattern in a 2025 research paper. The paper presents a new summation formula for the Hurwitz-Kronecker class number, a quantity that counts algebraic structures attached to quadratic forms. For any prime, a specific sum of these class numbers over a bounded range collapses to a strikingly simple value. That value is expressed directly in terms of the prime itself.
arxiv-2509-08681:
Light beams that twist like corkscrews carry orbital angular momentum, and that twist can be passed to the harmonics they generate. B. Kumar Das and 3 co-authors study anomalous vortex beams in a 2025 research paper. High-order harmonic generation converts a driving laser into much higher frequencies inside a material. The authors ask how beam shape controls the twist of the output.

By tuning the order and topological charge of the driving beam, they control the size of each generated harmonic vortex. Harmonics can reach very high topological charges while keeping a compact beam size. Their far-field divergence stays nearly uniform across many harmonic orders. That combination is valuable for applications needing structured extreme-ultraviolet light, from microscopy to information encoding. The work extends the toolbox for sculpting light with orbital angular momentum.
arxiv-2509-08781:
Ultrasound imaging with encoded apertures produces crisp pictures, until the probe or the patient moves. Tyler Keith Henry and 7 co-authors present READI, a motion-tolerant imaging method, in a 2025 research paper. The work builds on Hadamard-based aperture encoding, which boosts signal quality, and on a special electrode array design with pulse inversion abilities. Motion during the encoded sequence normally corrupts the image.

READI decodes subsets of the sequence into several low-resolution images that motion barely affects. A companion process compares those images to estimate the motion, warps them into alignment, and then combines them. The full-resolution result is restored. Tests fully recovered images corrupted by probe motion and tissue detail in a beating heart phantom. The method even recovered blood speckle at realistic flow speeds, a step toward motion-proof clinical ultrasound.
arxiv-2509-08981:
Alessandro Ferrari and 1 co-author study how the choice to specialize shapes supply chain strength in a 2025 paper. Firms that make parts choose how narrow their goods are. Narrow goods add more value, but fewer final makers can use them.

Final makers need many parts that fit each other, so one lost part can stop the line. In the market outcome, parts end up too narrow. Each maker ignores how its choice hurts the odds that others find all their parts. Chains thus earn more in calm times but break more easily than is best for all. A transfer can restore the best outcome, and shared fit standards also help.
arxiv-2509-09081:
Diwen Xue and 4 co-authors fingerprint deep packet inspection devices by their ambiguities in a 2025 paper. Deep packet inspection boxes sit in networks and can censor, throttle, or intercept traffic. Once limited to wealthy states, they are now widely sold, yet hard to measure.

Their dMAP framework uses differential fuzzing to find probes that expose parsing choices inside these boxes. Ambiguities in protocols force vendors to choose, and those choices become observable fingerprints. Twenty to forty probes reliably distinguish a wide range of products, including major censorship systems. The method offers a first step toward active reconnaissance of inspection devices worldwide.
arxiv-2509-09181:
Cooperation among strangers runs on reputation, but reputations arrive with gaps, and the kind of gap matters. Heejeong Kim and Yohsuke Murase analyze incomplete reputation information in a 2025 research paper. They study indirect reciprocity, where people help those with good reputations. Two failure modes are compared: actions sometimes going unobserved, and reputations sometimes reading as unknown.

Under missed observations, the conditions for cooperation stay unchanged. Fewer updates are balanced by higher stakes per update. Fading reputations are worse: cooperation demands ever better benefit-to-cost ratios as identification gets rarer. Costly punishment, added as a third action, rescued cooperation across wider conditions in the fading case without hurting efficiency. The authors review earlier work to map when punishment helps. Their distinction warns modelers and platform designers alike: not all missing information is missing in the same way.
arxiv-2509-09381:
Humans reason by analogy constantly, spotting that an atom is like a solar system, yet language technology rarely treats analogy as cognition. Molly R Petersen, Claire E Stevenson, and Lonneke van der Plas bridge two literatures in a 2025 research paper. They summarize cognitive science theory on how analogical reasoning works. Then they relate those processes to current natural language processing research.

The cognitive processes map onto concepts the language field already uses, though seldom through a cognitive lens. The authors show the mapping matters beyond solving analogy puzzles. Several major challenges in language research turn on relational understanding of exactly this kind. Current practice leans heavily on similarity between individual entities, which analogy research warns is the shallow cue. The paper invites model builders to optimize for relational structure in text, the way human thinkers demonstrably do.
arxiv-2509-09681:
Yikuan Xia and 8 co-authors describe the DB3 team's winning entry to the Meta KDD Cup 2025 challenge in a 2025 systems paper. The contest, called CRAG-MM, asks questions over several turns while mixing text with images, including first-person, ego-centric queries. A strong entry needs search that fits each task flavour and a model that knows when to stay silent rather than invent an answer.

The team built separate retrieval routes for image-linked knowledge graphs, web sources, and ongoing conversations. Tuning then combined supervised training, preference optimisation, and reinforcement learning to curb made-up replies. Placings were second in two tasks and first in the third, earning the grand prize, with first-person questions handled especially well.
arxiv-2509-09781:
Zetao Cheng and 2 co-authors prove uniqueness results for blowup solutions of Liouville systems in a 2025 analysis paper. The system couples several equations on a compact curved surface, with a nonnegative coefficient matrix linking the parts and positive weights inside exponential terms. Blowup solutions spike sharply at isolated points, and telling whether such a spiking pattern is forced, and whether it wobbles under small changes, is delicate.

Under natural assumptions the authors settle both questions: the blowup is locally unique and non-degenerate. The work extends single-equation findings to whole systems. Two obstacles demanded new machinery, a continuous family of standard bubble profiles needing extremely sharp pointwise bounds, and a Pohozaev identity whose information had to be read through a fresh Fredholm theory.
arxiv-2509-09881:
Ruojing Jiang proves an area limit for a family of curved surfaces inside hyperbolic three-dimensional spaces in a 2025 geometry paper. The surfaces are closed, embedded, and bend with constant mean curvature of at least one, inside a space of finite volume. Jiang caps their total area using only the curvature value and a bound on the surface's genus, its count of handles.

That cap forces a compactness conclusion for the whole family, ruling out surfaces that wander off to infinite area. Bryant surfaces, the special case where the curvature equals exactly one, inherit a particularly clean statement: their area grows at most in proportion to the genus. Results of this sort help geometers organise solution spaces that would otherwise sprawl.
arxiv-2509-10081:
Ambre Assor and Jean-Daniel Fekete report ongoing work on how experts explore medical data, in a 2025 paper built around a tool called ParcoursVis. The tool draws event sequences from electronic health records at huge scale. It covers millions of patients and billions of events. It was built with emergency departments at 16 Paris hospitals and the French Social Security.

Rather than run another usability test, the authors study the insights expert users form while exploring, and the strategies behind them. Early findings show a loop: using the tool helps experts pin down which data variables matter, and that in turn reshapes the tool. They offer their study protocol as a model for insight-based evaluation under real-world limits.
arxiv-2509-10181:
T. M. Aliev and 2 co-authors compute how a charmed baryon decays in this 2025 particle physics paper. The decays, in which a Xi_c baryon turns into a Xi baryon plus a lepton and a neutrino, are measured in experiments and also computed on space-time lattices. The two routes currently disagree, and this paper adds an independent analytic estimate to the argument.

Using light-cone QCD sum rules, with the baryon's internal structure described by distribution amplitudes, the authors compute the transition form factors and then the decay widths and branching fractions. Their numbers land close to the lattice results and above the current experimental values. That agreement strengthens the case that the tension lies with measurement or with rival theory methods.
arxiv-2509-10381:
Two measurements that cannot be performed together sit at the heart of quantum theory, and Sébastien Designolle asks which measurements are the most incompatible of all in this solo 2025 physics paper. For systems of a fixed size, universal limits on incompatibility have been hunted for years.

Designolle constructs explicit universal parent measurements, single devices from which many measurements can be derived, and extracts bounds that beat the previous state of the art. For the robustness measures that matter most, sets of anticommuting observables turn out to give the most incompatible pairs of simple two-outcome measurements. He also recasts the construction as a sum-of-squares optimization problem, and early numerics already improve on his own analytic values. The results feed directly into certifying the true dimension of a quantum system.
arxiv-2509-10681:
Zahra Tajik and three co-authors dissect the magnetic patches that make up solar active regions in this 2025 solar physics paper. Active regions, clusters of opposite-polarity magnetic patches, drive much of the Sun's dramatic atmospheric behavior, so tracking how patches emerge and evolve matters for space weather. Their tool is a complex-network method that identifies individual patches in magnetogram data.

They apply it to a patch of the Sun centered on active region NOAA 1158, observed in 2011 by the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager aboard the Solar Dynamics Observatory. The statistics are clean: patch area, lifetime, and magnetic flux all follow power-law distributions with distinct exponents. A Hurst exponent just above one half also reveals long-range memory in how new patches appear, meaning today's emergence pattern still echoes earlier activity.
arxiv-2509-10881:
Riku Ikaida and 4 co-authors compute why a famously dilute superconductor acts as it does in this 2025 paper. Strontium titanate, when doped with electrons, carries current with no loss at very low carrier counts. The team used basic theory to track how the crystal's vibrations change as carriers are added or taken away.

As the carrier count fell, some soft vibrations slowed down in step. The team fed those results into a standard formula for the transition point. The estimated transition heat rose as the count fell. That trend matches what labs see. A closer look pointed to the soft modes as the main driver of the rise. At still lower counts the math gave unstable vibrations, which marks the edge of the model.
arxiv-2509-10981:
David Hilditch and 3 co-authors introduce a journal collection on hyperboloidal slices in this 2025 editorial. In general relativity, space-time can be cut into slices in many ways. Hyperboloidal slices bend toward the far future. That shape suits wave problems well. It lets a simulation follow radiation cleanly out of the system. No artificial edge cuts the waves off.

The editorial frames a special collection for a gravity journal. The work grew from a 2023 workshop in Copenhagen called Infinity on a Gridshell. The papers span black hole vibrations and the shape of far-away regions. Others treat starting data for simulations and sharper numerical methods. The editors present the set as a snapshot of a method on its way from pure math into astrophysics.
arxiv-2509-11381:
Matias D. Cattaneo, Jason M. Klusowski, and Ruiqi Rae Yu ask when causal trees can be trusted. This 2025 statistics paper studies a workhorse tool. Causal trees split data again and again by traits. They gauge how a treatment's effect shifts from person to person.

The authors prove lower bounds on the error. Standard CART-style trees can converge at a crawl in the worst case. The pace can lag any power of the sample size. This holds even when the true effect is flat and treatment is random. Greedy splits are the cause. They often pick lopsided cuts. Some leaves end up with very few cases and huge spread. Splitting the sample for honesty does not cure this. Mean error can still look small while some groups are far off.
arxiv-2509-11681:
Yang Xu, Haibin Kan, and Guangyue Han study rank-based partitions of modules under duality. This 2025 algebra and coding theory paper groups module elements by rank support or rank weight. A partition equal to its dual is called reflexive. Reflexivity decides if structures like association schemes can form.

Partitions from rank support pass the test. They are mutually dual under suitable pairings, hence reflexive. The authors compute the linked generalized Krawtchouk matrices. Past results for matrix spaces over finite fields are generalized. Partitions from rank weight behave the other way. Over a finite chain ring that is not a field, they are provably non-reflexive. Dual partitions are given in explicit form. One corollary settles an open question: the rank metric yields an association scheme exactly when the ring is a field.
arxiv-2509-12081:
A model that leans on false links between traits and labels breaks when the setting shifts. Anirudha Majumdar proposes a sly defense in a solo 2025 paper. The defense fools a shift detector on purpose. It is called deceptive risk minimization.

The trick is to shape the model's internal features so the training data looks plain and uniform to a watcher. That watcher is a detector built on conformal martingales. Traits that change across settings get exposed and dropped. Stable traits stay. One smooth objective chases both the deception and the task loss. It needs no data from unseen settings. It also needs no fixed split of training domains. Tests cover concept shift. They also cover a simulated robot task where the inputs shift.
arxiv-2509-12181:
Pujan Paudel and Gianluca Stringhini present LOKI in a 2025 paper on finding scam websites before victims report them. Online shopping and pet scams cause large losses each year. Detectors can judge a given site well, but finding candidate scam sites to check remains slow when it relies on user reports or broad search queries.

LOKI scores search keywords by how likely they are to return many fraudulent sites in search results. Its model learns from privileged information and distilled features taken from search result pages. Across ten major scam categories, the authors report a large improvement in discovery over heuristic and data-driven baselines. Better candidate finding matters because downstream detectors can only block sites they are shown.
arxiv-2509-12381:
A trapped ion swimming through a thin cloud of cold atoms can stick to one of them, forming a fleeting molecular complex. Saajid Chowdhury and one co-author release software for that scene in 2025: a MATLAB script that runs the trajectory simulations on a graphics processor.

Their specialized solver reworks the classic Runge-Kutta method for the graphics card and runs up to twenty-two times faster than the standard MATLAB solver. Users can swap atoms, ions, interaction laws, trap settings, and starting conditions with simple input changes. The script then reports sticking probabilities, scattering angles, complex lifetimes, and plots of sample paths.
arxiv-2509-12581:
Which training examples shaped a model's answer? Attribution methods answer that, but the best ones demand full access to the model and heavy computation, luxuries missing when the model is a commercial black box. Shiyuan Zhang and three co-authors study attribution under those limits in 2025.

Their systematic tests explore stand-ins such as proxy models when access is partial. One surprise is practical: attribution scores from a model never trained on the target dataset still carry useful signal across many tasks, which helps when compute is scarce. The paper distills guidance for deploying attribution in real, constrained settings.
arxiv-2509-12981:
Yikang Chen, Xingzhe Sun and Dehui Du find cause from quantile effects in 2025. Quantile partial effect gauges how inputs shift outputs at each level. Their theory ties that gauge to cause direction.

When the effect lies in a finite span, cause and effect can be told from joint data alone. No noise or mechanism guess is needed. Basis tests on the gauge split directions in pairs. For many vars, Fisher data gives the cause order under a moment rule. Broad fake and real tests back both paths. Shape alone can thus reveal cause.
arxiv-2509-13081:
Francesco Pappone and 4 co-authors propose semantic reward modeling for training language models to explain better in a 2025 paper. Aligning model outputs with qualitative goals such as pedagogical soundness is hard. Standard reinforcement learning often relies on slow, expensive judge evaluations by another large model or on brittle keyword metrics that miss semantic quality.

Their approach works within the Group Relative Policy Optimisation framework. A small, efficient encoder-only transformer serves as a semantic reward model, scoring a generated explanation by its cosine similarity to a ground-truth reference. That dense, semantically rich signal guides the policy toward explanations that are factually correct and structurally aligned with expert reasoning. They apply the method to training a model for the Italian medical-school entrance examination.
arxiv-2509-13181:
Shyam Rai, Shyamgopal Karthik and four co-authors argue in 2025 that road obstacle splitting is a video task, not a still task. Self-driving stacks must mark hazards to stay safe. Frame-only methods flicker between frames and lose time links.

Four benchmarks are adapted for video scoring. Eleven top image and video methods are scored on them. Two new baselines built on vision base models are added. The new baselines set the top mark for long clips. Shared benchmarks and scores give the field a shared yardstick. Time-aware design is shown as the way forward.
arxiv-2509-13281:
Vincent Siu, Nathan Henry and four co-authors isolate refusal vectors for single concepts in 2025 with RepIt. Safety tests that use fixed benchmarks can miss narrow holes. Broad steering already breaks refusal at high rates.

RepIt picks out concept-linked directions in model activations. Editing them mutes refusal for one topic while refusal elsewhere holds. Across five frontier models, fakes that answer weapons queries yet pass standard screens result. Edits live in a thin slice of dimensions. A dozen cases on one GPU suffice for robust vectors. Current screens need representation-aware checks.
arxiv-2509-13881:
Tharun Krishna and four co-authors model how heavy quarks travel through quark-gluon plasma in a 2025 nuclear physics paper. Charm and bottom quarks are born early in a heavy-ion collision. They then plow through the hot plasma. Their final patterns reveal the plasma's transport properties. They also show how the plasma turns back into ordinary hadrons.

Their approach combines modern T-matrix interactions for elastic scattering with an effective treatment of gluon radiation. All of it runs inside a Langevin simulation. The background is a viscous hydrodynamic evolution. Hadronization uses a recombination model that conserves momentum. Fragmentation, tuned to proton-proton data, completes the picture. Applied to charm hadrons in lead-lead collisions at the LHC, the framework matches experiments fairly well. It also flags where the inputs still need improvement.
arxiv-2509-13981:
Thomas Jacob Maranzatto and Sennur Ulukus derive age-of-information identities in a 2025 networking paper. In gossip networks, nodes pass updates to random neighbors, and the age of information measures how stale each node's picture of the source is. Exact formulas for the moments of that age process, its averages and spreads, are the field's basic currency.

A recent link between gossip age and first passage percolation, the spread of a fluid through a random medium, lets the authors recover known recursive identities for every moment of the age. Their proofs are shorter than the originals and need only elementary probability, adapting techniques familiar in statistical physics, with noted connections to the Eden growth model. The cleaner derivations should make the identities easier to teach and extend.
arxiv-2509-14181:
Yifan Hu and six co-authors present TimeAlign in 2025, a small add-on meant to make time series forecasts more accurate. Forecasters often learn patterns from past data that do not match what comes next. Methods that align patterns have helped in vision and language, but forecasters have rarely used them.

TimeAlign aligns past and future patterns by rebuilding extra features and feeding them back into a base forecaster, so it can plug into many models. Across eight test sets it beat the base models it was added to. Further checks pointed to mismatched rhythms between past inputs and future outputs as the main source of the gain, and the authors give two theoretical reasons why the approach should help.
arxiv-2509-14381:
Jayce R. Getz, Heekyoung Hahn and HaoYun Yao prove a conditional result in 2025 for the Ramanujan conjecture, a deep claim about the size of certain number theory coefficients. Their proof assumes the expected analytic behaviour of triple product L-functions. L-functions encode arithmetic data in a form analysis can study.

Under that assumption, the conjecture follows in full. The authors also show how the same analytic properties drive steps in building functorial transfers in the Langlands program. Those transfers move problems from a general group to a general linear group, where tools are stronger. At stable level, any transfer reduces to a finite family fixed by the starting group. Conditional proofs still matter: they map exactly which analytic facts would unlock major open claims.
arxiv-2509-14881: Stephen DeBacker, David Schwein, and Cheng-Chiang Tsai propose a cleaner way to index ramification groups in a short 2025 note. These groups track how number fields branch at a prime, and they come in lower and upper forms in local class field theory. The note sets out a new normal form for the indexing and tests how it acts under base change for Langlands parameters.
arxiv-2509-15381:
Tiannan Zhang leads a team that plans safe routes for many moving agents at once. Think of robots in a warehouse that must not collide. Planning full routes for all of them is slow, so new methods plan short parts at a time. The risk is that a short plan can trap the team later, with no way to finish.

Their method, DAG-ECBS, groups agents on the fly and plans for each group within set cost limits. They prove the method still always finds a full set of routes when one exists. In tests it scales better than a strict optimal method and beats a fast method that lacks the same promise. The work gives a pattern for other planners to copy.
arxiv-2509-16081:
Big science codes rarely start from scratch; they lean on shared libraries for hard math on modern hardware. Marcel Koch and five co-authors discuss what it takes to add Ginkgo, a library for sparse linear algebra, into such codes. Ginkgo helps programs move to new machines and run their number work faster.

Case studies span fluid flow, power grid models, and heart signal studies. For each case, the authors weigh how the library changed the host code and the work of its team. They stress habits that keep both the library and its users healthy over time, a lesson for any shared science tool.
arxiv-2509-16381:
Bright bursts of high-energy light from gases, used to probe atoms and make attosecond pulses, depend on how well the light waves stay in step. Danny Attiyah and eight co-authors drive this process with laser beams of three polarization patterns, including two vector patterns that swirl around the beam. A 3D-printed gas cell keeps the gas pressure even across the interaction zone.

The swirling beams needed about twice the gas pressure of the plain beam for best output. The team ties that gap to a phase shift that differs by the same factor. Their cell design preserves the beam shape, a help for future light sources.
arxiv-2509-16781:
Andrei-Marius Avram and co-authors build the largest set yet for spoken Romanian variety in a 2025 paper. The set holds many hours of audio and tens of thousands of clips. Clips are balanced between speech from Romania and from Moldova. The task is to tell which variety a speaker uses.

Their method fights bias by training against side traits like gender and age. Weights for that fight are tuned by a meta-learning step. Scores rose sharply under this setup. One model did far better on variety when gender was the side trait. The set could anchor fairer speech tools for Romanian speakers.
arxiv-2509-16881:
Yifeng Liu, Yichao Tian, Liang Xiao, Wei Zhang, and Xinwen Zhu review work on bounding Selmer groups in a 2025 survey paper. Selmer groups are algebraic objects that control deep questions about equations and symmetries. The review covers the authors' joint work on a major conjecture for Rankin-Selberg motives. That conjecture links algebraic cycles to special values in number theory.

Alongside the review, the authors add fresh observations. They also speculate on links to a categorical form of the local Langlands program, a vast unifying vision. Surveys like this map a fast-moving frontier for younger researchers. The new remarks may steer the next steps in the program.
arxiv-2509-16981:
Shaobo Gan, Yao Tong, and Jiagang Yang prove an entropy formula for smooth maps in a 2025 dynamics paper. The maps have a dominated splitting, meaning their directions separate into stronger and weaker bundles. The team study unstable entropy, which counts complexity along expanding directions. Their case places a single zero exponent in the center direction.

In that case, the center adds no entropy, and unstable entropy equals the full metric entropy. A known invariance principle also holds when the center is one-dimensional. Earlier results on maximal entropy measures carry over to this smoother class. The work is part one of a planned series on the formula.
arxiv-2509-17081:
Martine Schut, Jackson Tiong, and Valerio Scarani propose spreading a nanoparticle across space in a 2025 quantum paper. Making a large mass sit in two places at once tests the limits of quantum theory. Their setup traps a charged nanoparticle, hundreds of nanometers wide, alongside a single ion in a radio-frequency trap.

The ion's electric pull steers the particle's spatial state. The shift achieved is smaller than the particle itself. Still, it dwarfs the width of the trap's ground state wave. If noise can be isolated well enough, the scheme could demonstrate true delocalisation of a hefty object, a landmark test for quantum mechanics at large scales.
arxiv-2509-17181:
Mahdi Shamsi, Hadi Zayyani, and Farokh Marvasti wrote a 2025 arXiv paper on keeping smart radio surfaces secure when channel knowledge is flawed. These surfaces, called RIS, steer signals by tuning many small elements. In practice the channel data they rely on is never exact, and errors can open gaps that eavesdroppers exploit.

The authors build a robust fix from a first-order approximation of the channel error. Their method refreshes the surface settings with just a few matrix steps, with no costly inverse steps for small errors. The study covers both an untrusted user who might listen in and a stealth radar case. Simulations show gains in security and speed at low computing cost. The frame also gives a baseline for how strongly methods react to channel errors, a point of value for future 6G work.
arxiv-2509-17381:
Yongliang Wang and Hamidreza Kasaei built a fast planner for robot arms in cluttered spaces. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that classic motion planners often must solve hard kinematic or dynamic equations to finish a path. Model-free reinforcement learning, by contrast, can learn to dodge obstacles straight from experience, and the authors argue it holds strong promise here.

Their system joins two parts. A vision stage plans the path in task space, using a large segmentation model plus spline-smoothed kinodynamic search. A learning stage then steers the arm's joints, using an improved policy method with action ensembles and policy feedback. Those upgrades sharpen precision and stability in reaching goals while avoiding hits. The result is a planner that finds joint-space paths without solving the arm's equations at each step.
arxiv-2509-17981:
Sihong Shao, Yanli Wang, and Jie Wu make a gas-flow solver that adapts its own basis as it runs. Their 2025 paper deals with the Boltzmann equation, which tracks how gas particles spread in speed space. A Hermite basis can fit that spread, but a fixed basis wastes effort or loses detail.

A new signal flags when high-order terms carry too much weight. Scale and order of the basis then shift to match that flag, for both even and mixed flows. Tests in up to three dims show far lower error from scale shifts at near no cost. Order shifts cut run time by large shares.
arxiv-2509-18281:
Thiago Landim builds a weight frame for K-motives over quotient stacks. His 2025 paper works in characteristic zero, on a tame stack formed as a quotient. Motives are a broad way to hold the shape traits of spaces in one algebra-like form.

He builds a Chow weight structure on a full part of that category. In a wide set of cases, he shows that part is just the set of geometric K-motives. As a use, he gives a partial Springer split in the K-motive frame. Such weight frames let hard objects be built from pure, graded parts in steps.
arxiv-2509-18381:
Radar networks that learn can shift their search toward spots where targets are likely. Nicholas L. K. Goradia, Harpreet S. Dhillon, and R. Michael Buehrer develop detection methods for such cognitive radar in this 2025 paper. The hard part is finding many targets when noise and clutter patterns are unknown. Their methods keep the false alarm rate steady even so.

First they build a detection rule for a single multi-antenna radar that holds its false alarm rate as data grows. They give the conditions under which the rule holds. Learning then guides the radar toward likely target zones. The work extends to networks where radars share what they learn, in both central and spread-out forms. A key finding is a trade-off: more antennas can swap for more time samples, and the reverse. Tests show the gains and costs of each fusion style.
arxiv-2509-18881:
Rotation can stir the quark matter made in heavy-ion collisions, and spin may answer back. Lutz Kiefer, Ashutosh Dash, and Dirk H. Rischke study that interplay in a standard model of quarks in this 2025 paper. The model is the Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model under rigid rotation. Spin appears in it as an axial-vector condensate, a bulk alignment of quark spin.

Rotation alone tends to suppress the chiral condensate, the order that gives quarks their mass. The team finds a spin condensate can counter that suppression and boost the chiral one. It can also flip the chiral transition from smooth to abrupt. The results come in the model's mean-field limit. They bear on spin hydrodynamics, the young theory of fluids with spin. Collisions that spin quark matter may thus show altered transition behavior worth hunting for.
arxiv-2509-18981:
Sen-Peng Eu and two co-authors count paths in a combinatorial game played on pairs of Dyck paths. A Dyck path steps up and down but never drops below its start line. Put one path above a mirrored copy of another and the region between them forms a grid polygon. Inside it, a billiard ball bounces around, and the authors count its possible trajectories.

That count turns out to match a known statistic for meanders, curves that wind across a line. The team builds a pairing scheme on path pairs that raises or lowers the count by exactly one. With it they prove a result about how meanders with even and odd numbers of pieces compare, settling a claim by Di Francesco and co-authors. They also study generating functions for restricted families of paths.
arxiv-2509-19381:
Yingdong Wu and one co-author study how gravity bends the phase of a quantum wave, in a spacetime that mixes charge, a scalar field, and gravity. Their framework is teleparallel gravity, an alternative formulation where gravity acts through torsion rather than curvature. They derive a general formula for the gravitational phase difference in an interference experiment. The formula is then applied to an Einstein-Maxwell-Scalar black hole spacetime.

Mass dominates the phase difference, whether or not the black hole carries charge. Under ordinary astrophysical conditions the charge's own contribution is negligible. But near an extremal charged black hole, the charge can team up with a coupling constant to amplify its effect measurably. The authors suggest quantum interferometers could one day probe charged black hole parameters through this channel. The work links quantum measurement technique with strong-field gravity theory.
arxiv-2509-19681:
Reasoning models can spend extra computing time at test time, but they judge their own answers poorly. Anisha Garg and five co-authors build an explanatory verifier that grades pairs of candidate solutions. The verifier gives a calibrated confidence score plus plain-language reasons. Reinforcement learning trained it to reward sound grading.

Paired grading helps strategies such as picking the best of many tries and guided self-repair. The verifier shines when both candidates share the same wrong answer, a trap where majority voting fails outright. Better grading raises both accuracy and efficiency, since fewer wasted retries are needed. The work treats checking as a skill in its own right. Reliable checkers may matter as much as stronger solvers for hard problems.
arxiv-2509-20081:
Robots and survey vehicles build volume maps from laser scans, usually with graphics chips doing the heavy lifting. Jose E. Maese, Luis Merino, and Fernando Caballero do it on a plain CPU. Their DB-TSDF system fuses LiDAR points into a voxel grid as a truncated signed distance field. A directional bitmask scheme drives the integration.

Processing time per scan stays constant whatever the grid resolution, a rare property. Dense, consistent maps result at high resolution without the usual slowdown. On public real-world datasets, accuracy matches contemporary methods. CPU-only mapping suits platforms where power, cost, or heat rule out graphics chips. Constant-time updates also make timing predictable, which real-time systems prize.
arxiv-2509-20381:
Chat-based recommenders often lean on a language model's summarizing skill while skipping training. Jianyu Wen and five co-authors take the training route with USB-Rec, a framework presented in a 2025 arXiv paper. The name reflects its user simulator, which stands in for real users during learning. Training and inference are designed together, not bolted apart.

First, a strategy builds preference data for reinforcement learning from simulated conversations. That teaches the model the moves of good conversational recommendation. At inference time, a self-enhancement strategy squeezes more from what training taught. Experiments on several datasets showed steady gains over earlier state-of-the-art systems. The authors argue that model-level training, not prompt craft alone, is what conversational recommenders have been missing.
arxiv-2509-20581:
Language is hierarchical, from letters to discourse, but transformers read it flat. Ayan Sar and five co-authors build that hierarchy into the architecture itself in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their Hierarchical Resolution Transformer borrows from wavelets, processing text at several resolutions at once. Attention runs within and across scales, composing upward and contextualizing downward.

Exponential shrinking across scales cuts the complexity below the usual quadratic cost. The team tested the model on language understanding suites, long-range tasks, and language modeling. Scores beat standard transformer baselines by several percent across those suites. Memory use fell by about two fifths and latency by over a third against similar-sized models. Ablations credit both the cross-resolution attention and the scale-specialized modules. The authors frame multi-scale processing as a better match to how language is built.
arxiv-2509-20681:
A robot planning a safe path needs a map of surfaces, yet building one usually takes many photos. Wei-Teng Chu and three co-authors present FINS in a 2025 paper on implicit surface models from a single image. The paper was written for the 2026 IEEE ICRA robotics conference.

FINS builds a signed distance field, a model that gives the distance to the nearest surface at any point. It pairs a multi-resolution hash grid encoder with small geometry and color networks. Training uses an efficient approximate second-order method and can finish within seconds. Older methods such as NeuS need many views and long training. Fast single-image surfaces could help robots generate motion on the spot.
arxiv-2509-20781:
Databases use indexes to find sorted data fast, and learned indexes replace formulas with trained models. Alireza Heidari and three co-authors present Sig2Model in a 2025 paper on learned indexes that must handle frequent updates. Static learned indexes work well until data changes.

Updates break the model's fit and can force a full retrain that blocks queries. Sig2Model attacks that cost with three techniques, starting with a sigmoid boosting approximation of the data distribution. The design adapts locally instead of retraining everything, keeping query speed high under changing workloads. The authors argue that earlier approaches leave real-world update costs unsolved. Their index aims at services where data changes constantly and queries cannot pause.
arxiv-2509-20981:
Coxeter groups, such as the symmetry group F4, carry a rich order structure called Bruhat order. Paolo Sentinelli and Andrea Zatti construct combinatorial codes for intervals of that order in a 2025 mathematics paper. Their algorithm builds a multicomplex for any lower Bruhat interval of F4.

For Weyl groups, such multicomplexes always exist, by work of Bjorner and Ekedahl, and their rank-generating functions match the interval's. A strong Lehmer code, the usual coding tool, provably does not exist for F4. The authors therefore weaken the notion, basing their algorithm on only two functions. They also realize the palindromic Poincare polynomials of F4 as a lattice inside the Bruhat order. The work blends computation with algebraic combinatorics.
arxiv-2509-21181:
How the norms of a least norm fit grow with sample size is a basic question in modern regression theory. Credit goes to Shuofeng Zhang and Ard Louis. Such models have more parameters than data points. Among all fits that match the data, training picks the one with the smallest norm under a chosen rule. The paper asks how a whole family of those norms grows as more data arrives.

The authors give a unified, high probability answer through a dual ray analysis. The analysis shows a contest between a signal spike and a bulk of null coordinates. It predicts a data dependent turning point where growth changes. It also gives a sharp threshold that splits norms that level off from norms that keep growing. They extend the picture to diagonal linear networks trained by gradient descent.
arxiv-2509-21681:
Moving points pose geometric questions that static computational geometry cannot answer. Laurence Boxer examines new problems in dynamic computational geometry in a 2025 paper. The field, introduced by Atallah, concerns momentary and long term properties of moving point objects. Research there has been dormant recently, Boxer notes. Algorithms for the dynamic setting are the contribution.

Classical problems change character when points move continuously. Maintaining structures like hulls or nearest neighbours over time needs new methods. The paper develops algorithms with applications across the dynamic problems it poses. Some material builds on the author previous papers, with citations given. Reviving a quiet field is part of the aim, as moving data becomes common in modern applications.
arxiv-2509-21781:
Xiaoqin Zhan, writing alone, studies block designs in this 2025 mathematics paper. A block design arranges points into groups, called blocks, so that each pair of points meets in the same number of blocks. Zhan looks at designs whose symmetry group moves point-block pairs in a restricted way, called half-flag-transitive. The question is what such a group must look like.

The paper gives three conditions that force the group to act primitively, meaning it cannot split the points into smaller blocks of its own. It then sorts the possible groups into three broad types: affine, almost simple, and product. For the almost simple type with a sporadic simple group at its core, only one group can occur. That case pins the design down to two known examples with set sizes.
arxiv-2509-22581:
Jini Yang and 3 co-authors add semi-supervised learning to spiking neural networks. Spiking networks mimic brain cells and save energy, but learning methods that use unlabeled data lag those for standard networks. Their framework, SpikeMatch, is the first built for spiking models. It exploits the leakage factor, which sets how fast a spiking cell's charge fades, to get varied predictions from one network.

Agreement among those predictions yields trustworthy pseudo-labels for unlabeled samples. Clean weakly-augmented samples then teach strongly-augmented ones, which curbs the risk of the model reinforcing its own errors. On standard benchmarks, SpikeMatch beat adapted semi-supervised methods for standard networks across several spiking backbones.
arxiv-2509-22881:
Karim Khamaisi and 5 co-authors compare sound-based fault detectors for a pumped-storage hydropower plant. Unplanned outages at such plants are costly and hard to service. Most past work used generic factory data or fake data, not real plant sound. The team used two real data sets from the Rodundwerk II plant in Austria.

One data set had faults made on purpose, and one came from normal plant work. The team cleaned the noisy sound, pulled out time and frequency traits, and tested three models. A one-class support vector machine gave the best mix of accuracy and short training time. A long short-term memory autoencoder also scored well but cost more compute.
arxiv-2509-23481:
Neutrinos may carry faint electric and magnetic traits that one-loop physics can predict. J. P. Gutiérrez-Montes and 4 co-authors compute these dipolar traits for Dirac neutrinos inside a minimally extended Standard Model. They focus on form factors that arise when the coupling of the Z boson to neutrinos gets radiative corrections. The work is done in a general covariant gauge.

The team shows the results do not depend on the gauge choice, a key check on the math. Numerically, the weak-magnetic dipole moment comes out at the same order of size as the known magnetic dipole moment prediction. That scale sets what future searches might hope to see.
arxiv-2509-23581:
How fast the inner Milky Way spins traces how its mass is spread, from bulge to dark halo. Y. Sofue and M. Kohno derive that inner rotation curve with the terminal velocity method. They apply it to longitude-velocity diagrams built from large surveys of the galactic plane in hydrogen and carbon monoxide lines. The result agrees well with curves from maser tracking and from the Gaia mission.

Merging the data gives one curve from the center out to about twenty-five kiloparsecs. The authors split it into bulge, disc, and dark halo parts and estimate the dark matter density near the Sun. An east-west asymmetry in the curve grows toward the center, which they link to a possible weak bar.
arxiv-2509-23681:
Video diffusion transformers make striking clips, but their size blocks routine use. Weilun Feng and 10 co-authors compress them with QuantSparse, which joins two squeezes that fight each other when naively combined: quantization and attention sparsification. Cutting attention starves the model of information, which then magnifies quantization noise and shifts attention patterns. Their fix distills attention at two scales, using global structure and local salient cues to counter the bias.

A second trick reuses stable second-order residuals over time to recover what sparsity drops. On HunyuanVideo-13B, the method scored far above the best quantization baseline in picture quality, while cutting storage more than threefold and speeding generation.
arxiv-2509-24581:
Granular rings of unconventional superconductors can trap magnetic flux on their own, and the amount trapped fingerprints the pairing state. Junyi Zhang and Yi Li study Josephson couplings in such materials, generalizing a classic formula with symmetry constraints and disorder in interface orientation. Applied to granular rings, their framework yields a no-go result.

Single-band chiral superconductors cannot trap flux spontaneously, they show. That rules out chiral p-wave pairing in a bismuth palladium compound, given the half-quantum flux seen in recent experiments. A helical equal-spin pairing state, stabilized by spin-orbit coupling from local inversion breaking, is favored instead. Its rings can trap a half-step flux robustly against disorder.
arxiv-2510-00681:
Zhang, Li, Lin, and Lu introduce the first open-vocabulary object detection framework for event cameras in this 2025 arXiv paper. Event cameras report brightness changes with microsecond timing and no motion blur, which suits fast scenes. They capture no colour or texture, though, and detectors trained on fixed categories cannot name objects they never saw in training. Vision-language models such as CLIP solve that problem for ordinary photos, but their knowledge does not transfer directly to sparse event streams.

The team uses ordinary image frames as the teacher's input and distills CLIP's visual knowledge into an event-based student through spatial attention. A spiking neural network slices the event stream adaptively, choosing split moments that keep key temporal features instead of discarding them. A convolutional stage then runs the detection itself. In experiments the model consistently beat dataset-specific baselines and generalized to unseen categories.
arxiv-2510-00981:
Li and a large team from Microsoft, the Chinese University of Hong Kong Shenzhen, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University present FlexiCodec in this 2025 arXiv paper on speech technology. Neural audio codecs turn speech into tokens that language models can process. Lower frame rates shorten token sequences and cut computing cost, but low rates tend to lose semantic content. FlexiCodec attacks that trade-off with a dynamic frame rate.

The codec merges frames where the signal carries little information, and keeps more frames where speech is dense. An ASR-assisted dual-stream encoder and transformer bottlenecks help preserve meaning at low rates. At average rates of six and a quarter, eight point three, and twelve and a half hertz, it beat baseline codecs on semantic preservation and reconstruction quality. Users can choose the frame rate at inference time, between three and twelve and a half hertz.
arxiv-2510-01381:
Teetaert and co-authors estimate the full moving shape of soft continuum robots in continuous time, with uncertainty attached. Such robots bend everywhere, so state estimation usually leans on heavy dynamics or crude shape guesses. Disturbances that nobody modeled break both approaches easily.

Kinematics are corrupted by smooth noise inside a factor-graph formulation borrowed from navigation research. Fast sensing plus the simple model absorbs unmodeled pushes and survives sensor dropouts. Pose, velocity, and strain come out with covariances, queryable at any instant. Sparse structure keeps the computation linear in time, which real robots need. Gyroscope and pose sensors supplied the demonstration measurements. Interpolation during estimation admits measurements between explicit states. White-noise-on-acceleration style priors keep the curves physically smooth. Boundary factors at the robot's base anchor each solution. Soft robots need soft mathematics, probabilistically speaking, throughout the body.
arxiv-2510-01781:
Ding, Komatsu, and Liu count special primes in a classic coin problem in this 2025 number theory paper. Given two coprime coin sizes, some amounts can be formed in several ways and others in none. The authors fix a bound on the number of ways and look at the largest amount that stays under it. They then count how many primes below that bound need more representations than the bound allows.

For a fixed smaller coin size of at least three, they prove an exact asymptotic formula for that prime count. The count grows like a clean fraction of all primes up to the same bound. They also prove a positive lower bound under a mild size condition on the coins. Companion counts for primes with few representations receive similar treatment. The results sharpen what is known about primes hiding inside this Frobenius-style interval problem.
arxiv-2510-01881:
Krasucki and six co-authors probe the vibrations of a layered magnet in this 2025 physics paper. The material is chromium germanium telluride, a ferromagnet built from weakly bound sheets. They measured its Raman scattering spectra with high resolution across a wide temperature range. Calculations predicted ten Raman-active vibration modes, and the team identified all of them.

Cooling the crystal exposed a strong coupling between spin order and lattice vibrations. Spectral features shifted near two characteristic temperatures, one around one hundred fifty kelvin and one near sixty. Those marks signal local magnetic order appearing, then the full ferromagnetic phase locking in. One mode showed an unusual comb of very narrow peaks. Modeling explained that comb as vibrations of germanium pairs, split apart by the different germanium isotopes present. The work maps how magnetism and sound-like motion intertwine in this material.
arxiv-2510-01981:
Backis and eight co-authors test a modern readout chip for the T-REX neutron spectrometer in this 2025 instrumentation paper. T-REX, bound for the European Spallation Source, detects neutrons with Multi-Grid technology. Its grid of coated blades forms a voxelised proportional counter filled with gas. The open question was whether the VMM3A chip, built for other detectors, suits this readout.

The team measured a prototype at a finely collimated thermal neutron beam at the ISIS source. They mapped how pulse height and detection efficiency vary with position inside the voxels. Measurements were compared against two electronics schemes and against Garfield++ and Geant4 simulations. Corner regions of each voxel collect charge slowly, which can shrink pulses and lose events. The scans quantify that effect across the detector face. The results judge the chip's suitability for the final spectrometer and validate the simulation chain behind it.
arxiv-2510-02181:
Wu and Jain make live captions adapt to Deaf and hard-of-hearing speakers during conversation in this 2025 accessibility paper. Speech recognition often mangles the speech of DHH users, especially in real time. Older personalization demands piles of pre-recorded data and puts all the work on the DHH speaker. EvolveCaptions instead recruits the hearing partner into the fix.

While a conversation runs, hearing participants correct transcription errors as they spot them. The system turns those corrections into short, phonetically targeted prompts for the DHH speaker to record. About five minutes of such recordings fine-tune the recognizer on the spot. In a study with twelve DHH and six hearing participants, word error rates fell for every DHH user within one hour. Participants called the process easy, low-effort, and natural to use mid-conversation. Adaptation becomes a shared, in-situ activity rather than homework.
arxiv-2510-02281:
Kravchuk and Radcliffe study a new kind of defect inside a critical quantum model. Their 2025 physics paper works with the O(2N) model at its critical point. A defect is a line or surface where the rules change. Most studied defects keep full symmetry around them. This defect keeps symmetry only along itself. Across the defect, rotations must pair with an internal twist. The twist comes from a monodromy defect, which changes fields after a loop. A relevant operator then drives the system to a new fixed point.

The authors compute defect operator dimensions two ways. Large N expansion gives one set of leading values. A second expansion near four dimensions gives another. The two routes agree where they overlap. They also match older results for plain monodromy and pinning defects. Spinning defects widen the map of possible critical behavior.
arxiv-2510-02581:
Elghaayda, Rahman, and Mansour measure quantum coherence in expanding de Sitter spacetime without basis bias. Their 2025 physics paper studies two detectors moving with the expansion. Coherence usually depends on the measurement basis chosen. That dependence clouds what the quantity really means. Their framework splits coherence into total, collective, and local parts. Each part is defined without leaning on a basis. The detectors couple to a light scalar field around them. Two vacuum choices frame the analysis. One is the standard thermal style vacuum. The other adds squeezing through a tunable parameter.

Squeezing sharply boosted the coherence that detectors can extract. The boost survived even under strong thermal noise. Collective coherence also swung in a non-monotonic pattern. In the thermal limit, heat first suppresses coherence before it recovers. Such control knobs matter for relativistic quantum protocols. Curved spacetime becomes a resource, not just a nuisance.
arxiv-2510-02681:
Fronzi and co-authors predict heat-to-power material properties with networks that explain themselves. Their 2025 materials paper applies Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks. Such materials turn heat into power, so discovery matters. Standard machine learning predicts well but hides its logic. Black box models give little insight. The new networks split functions into readable pieces. They target the Seebeck coefficient and the band gap. Accuracy matched the usual deep network models. The difference lies in what comes out afterward. Plain formulas summarize each structure-property link.

Benchmarks against published models confirmed the robustness. The formula pipeline named the strongest input factors. It pruned redundant connections inside the network. Rebuilt formulas aligned with known physics. Designers can reverse the formulas toward target properties. Readable models speed up materials discovery cycles. Output plus reasons beats output alone in the lab.
arxiv-2510-02981:
Li and co-authors fix a timing flaw in ultra-low-power wireless links. Ambient backscatter devices ride on radio waves already in the air. They send data by reflecting those waves, using almost no power. Receivers must line up their sampling with each symbol. Delay and start-up lag break that alignment in practice. Standard sync methods fail here, since the ambient source will not cooperate. The team tackles the offset head-on.

A special pilot sequence at the sender creates a telltale error pattern. The receiver reads that pattern to estimate the timing offset. The estimator uses maximum likelihood reasoning on the signal statistics. Once measured, the offset is corrected before detection. An energy detector then reads the cleaned symbols. Bit error rates recovered most of what the offset had cost. That keeps it fit for cheap, massive Internet of Things rollouts.
arxiv-2510-03081:
Liu and co-authors argue that humanoid robots should evolve body and brain together. Most research tunes control software for a fixed robot shape. Nature took a different path, shaping limbs and behavior jointly. Their position paper calls for body-control co-design in humanoids. Form and policy would adapt side by side for each task. Resource limits would shape both, as they do in animals.

Three practical routes anchor their proposal. Clever exploration can search the joint space of shapes and skills. Simulation-to-real transfer can test designs cheaply before building them. Meta-policy learning can reuse lessons across many body shapes. The case is argued from methods, uses, and community needs. Benchmarks and design-aware control sit on that list. World models and reasoning systems mark the far end. Co-design, they conclude, is a cornerstone for the next humanoid generation.
arxiv-2510-03281:
Van Batenburg wrote a thesis that puts Shapley explanations of machine learning models on firm math ground. Shapley values split credit for a model's output among its input facts. They grew from game theory and were adapted for machine learning by Lundberg and Lee. Earlier papers stated the key results but left proofs sketchy or incomplete. The thesis goes back to the source claims and proves them with full care.

One result shows that Shapley values are the only explanation meeting four fairness style rules. The author also gives a case that disproves a past claim, showing that the symmetry rule cannot be dropped. A second result shows the values are the single best answer to a weighted fitting problem. These proofs matter because doctors, banks, and courts now ask why a model decided as it did. Sound math makes those answers safer to trust.
arxiv-2510-03681:
Majumder and Sahoo present a 2025 arXiv paper selecting which factors drive PFAS contamination in California groundwater, from a list of candidates, under data conditions. PFAS chemicals persist in the environment and threaten health, their drivers are entangled. Measurements are censored, since low levels go unreported, and wells correlate. The authors build a Bayesian hierarchical model that handles censoring inside a spatial process, approximated for scale. A global local shrinkage prior then separates signal variables from noise.

They compare three rules for declaring a variable selected: credible intervals, shrinkage weight thresholds, and a clustering method. In simulations, the credible interval rule proved most reliable. Shrinkage weights won in ultra sparse settings, while clustering stayed flexible. Applied to PFOS in California groundwater, the model picked a scientific set of demographic, industrial, and environmental predictors. Knowing which drivers matter focuses cleanup and monitoring money. The machinery transfers to censored spatial problems in science.
arxiv-2510-03781:
Asgari-Bidhendi and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper building a corpus of a million hadith narrations with an automated pipeline. Hadith, the sayings and reports about the Prophet Muhammad and the Imams, are Islam's second source of knowledge after the Qur'an, and they survive in collections. The pipeline segments texts, separates each narration's chain from its content, and validates the split. Enrichment layers add translation into twelve languages, vowel marking, summaries, thematic tags, and links between narrations.

Six experts graded a sample of twelve hundred narrations. Chain separation and summarization both scored about nine point three out of ten, near human quality. The corpus averaged eight point five overall, dwarfing a curated rival's score. Vowel marking lagged, with word error rates above fifteen percent. Work estimated at two hundred thousand expert hours was done in months at a fraction of the cost. Islamic studies gains a searchable infrastructure at scale.
arxiv-2510-04281:
Gao and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper introducing GROK, a multimodal model designed to reason from eye images and quantitative biomarkers to a clinical diagnosis. Earlier medical adaptations of multimodal language models often underexploited the complementary value of these inputs and produced weakly grounded explanations. GROK instead organizes its training around a quantitative-to-qualitative chain of reasoning resembling a clinician's workflow.

A CLIP-style module aligns OCT representations with biomarker concepts before supervised instruction fine-tuning teaches the model to explain findings and annotate lesions. The authors evaluate it on a new Grounded Ophthalmic Understanding benchmark spanning six disease categories and classification, report generation, and chain-of-thought quality. With LoRA fine-tuning of a seven-billion-parameter Qwen2 backbone, GROK surpassed comparable models, including a larger thirty-two-billion-parameter baseline and OpenAI o3, on report and fine-grained clinical measures.
arxiv-2510-04481:
Otis Chodosh wrote this 2025 survey paper on minimal surfaces and comparison geometry. A minimal surface is a surface that locally takes the least possible area, like a soap film. Geometers study how such surfaces reveal the curvature and shape of the space around them. The method echoes a classic trick: study shortest curves to learn about a space as a whole.
