Chodosh reviews what decades of work on area minimizers have shown.

The survey covers existence and smoothness results from geometric measure theory. It explains how first and second variation of area force a minimizer to have zero mean curvature and obey a stability inequality. Landmark results then use stable surfaces to limit the topology of spaces with positive scalar curvature. The Geroch conjecture and the stable Bernstein problem get detailed treatment. Recent progress has nearly settled the Bernstein question, with one case still open.
arxiv-2510-04581:
Anh Dang, Rick Nouwen, and Massimo Poesio wrote this 2025 paper on how language models read ambiguous plural pronouns. A word like they can point back to two things at once, or to a whole made of parts. People handle such choices with ease and show steady preferences. The team asked whether large language models share those preferences and can spot the ambiguity. They ran tests on pronoun production, interpretation, and ambiguity detection.

The models sometimes knew the possible referents of an ambiguous pronoun in the tests. They did not always choose the reading that people prefer, though. The gap grew when the favored reading was not stated in plain words nearby. Models also failed to flag ambiguity unless the prompt told them to look for it. Results shifted across test types in ways that lacked a clean pattern. The authors read this as shaky, surface level handling of reference.
arxiv-2510-04681:
Yang and nine coauthors at the Danish Meteorological Institute wrote this 2025 paper on a new climate record for Denmark. Denmark is a maze of coasts, with hundreds of islands and mixed land and sea in most districts. Global weather records blur those coastal features. The team built DANRA, a reanalysis that replays the weather from 1990 to 2023 on a grid of about two and a half kilometers. It rests on a proven regional forecast model fed with observations.

Against the leading global reanalysis, DANRA represented near surface weather more faithfully in their checks. The gains held in calm conditions and in extremes alike. Case studies cover a hurricane force storm in 1999, a heat record in 2022, and a cloudburst in 2007. Planners can use the record for adaptation and impact studies. Learning based forecast models can also train on sharp fields. The data set is free in a format from a public store.
arxiv-2510-05081:
Ronen Kamenetsky and five co-authors give image editors a finer dial in this 2025 arXiv paper. Text prompts steer modern image generators, but they offer clumsy control. Changing one attribute often distorts others. Editors also want smooth control over how strong an edit feels.

Their method, SAEdit, edits the text embedding rather than the image model itself. A sparse autoencoder lifts the embedding into a space where attributes sit apart. Moving along one direction changes just that attribute, such as adding a laugh to one chosen person. A scale factor adjusts the edit's strength continuously. Because only embeddings change, the trick works across many image backbones.
arxiv-2510-05181:
Ander Artola Velasco, Stratis Tsirtsis, and Manuel Gomez-Rodriguez police dishonest billing in the AI cloud market in this 2025 arXiv paper. Providers charge per token a model generates. That pricing tempts providers to inflate the token counts they report. Users cannot check the counts on their own.

The authors build an auditing framework on martingale theory. A trusted auditor queries the provider sequentially and watches for statistical inconsistencies. Theory guarantees detection of any misreporting strategy, whatever the provider tries. Honest providers are almost never flagged by mistake. Across Llama, Gemma, and Ministral models, cheating surfaced after fewer than about 70 observed outputs. False-flag probability stayed below five percent in their tests.
arxiv-2510-05381:
Yufeng Du and nine co-authors show that long inputs hurt language models even when nothing is hidden in this 2025 arXiv paper. The usual explanation blames retrieval failures inside long contexts. If a model finds every relevant fact, it should perform like it does on short inputs. The authors test that assumption directly.

Across five models and math, question answering, and coding tasks, performance fell sharply as length grew. Drops ranged from about 14 to 85 percent despite perfect retrieval. The failure persisted when filler tokens were replaced by whitespace or masked entirely. Even placing all evidence right before the question did not rescue performance. A recite-first prompting trick recovered up to about 4 percent for GPT-4o on RULER.
arxiv-2510-05581:
Ponkshe and Vepakomma make shared data embeddings private for the first time. Collaborative learning usually shares model weights between clients and a server. Sharing embeddings instead saves client compute, but no formal privacy guarantees existed for them. Their 2025 Power Mechanism learns embeddings with differential privacy built in.

A privacy encoding network works with a small utility generation network on the client. The resulting embeddings carry formal epsilon and delta guarantees. A powerful server then post-processes them for the actual task. The server model can be deep learning, random forests, or XGBoost. Clients need only one round of privatized communication. Experiments show better privacy-utility trade-offs and resource efficiency than baselines. The evaluations focus on tabular datasets, the enterprise workhorse format. Extending the co-design to text, speech, and vision remains future work. Split learning gains a principled privacy story from this design.
arxiv-2510-05881:
Chen and colleagues generate complete songs segment by segment. Full-song generation must stay coherent across minutes of symbolic piano music. Composers work from a theme and structure, consulting only relevant sections. Their 2025 Segmented Full-Song Model mimics that workflow directly.

Users supply a song structure and optionally a short seed segment. A rule-based algorithm splits the song into segments beforehand. Each segment is then generated attending only to structurally related predecessors. That selective attention beats uniform context encoding in coherence and motif awareness. A user study confirms the advantage over the prior WholeSong system. A web application wraps the model for iterative co-creation on a piano roll. Customizable structures and flexible segment ordering support the interaction. Stronger seed adherence rounds out the measured improvements. Generation also runs an order of magnitude faster, enabling real-time streaming.
arxiv-2510-06281:
Li and three co-authors enhance full-disk solar images toward telescope quality with deep learning in a 2025 computer vision paper. The GONG network watches the whole Sun in hydrogen-alpha light, but cannot resolve fine structures like filaments and fibrils. The Goode Solar Telescope delivers far sharper views over smaller areas.

They train a generative adversarial network based on Real-ESRGAN, with dense blocks and a relativistic discriminator. Carefully aligned GONG and GST pairs teach the model what sharp solar detail looks like. The enhanced images recover sunspot penumbra detail and resolve filaments and fibrils convincingly. Cross-correlation with ground truth reached about 0.78 on average. Small remaining misalignments capped the quantitative scores. The team plans better alignment and a larger dataset. Upgraded network images would give solar physicists fine-scale dynamics with full-disk coverage.
arxiv-2510-06381:
Cazenave proposes Monte Carlo Permutation Search, an improved tree search for game playing, in a 2025 machine learning paper. Deep reinforcement learning dominates headlines, but many settings lack its compute demands. General Game Playing needs strong search that works immediately on unseen games.

MCPS builds on the GRAVE algorithm for Monte Carlo tree search. Its exploration term also uses statistics from every playout containing all moves on the root path. Those permutation statistics capture move-order information plain node statistics miss. Cazenave derives the weighting formulas for the three statistics sources. The derivation removes GRAVE's bias hyperparameter, so less tuning is needed. Across Hex, Go, AtariGo, NoGo, and a wargame, MCPS almost always beat GRAVE. The result strengthens a classic approach to game AI. It matters where learning pipelines are impractical and decisions must be good immediately.
arxiv-2510-06481:
Khass and six co-authors couple risk-averse path refinement with active view selection for robot navigation in a 2025 robotics paper. Safe navigation in uncertain environments demands caution and curiosity. A robot must avoid risky routes while sensing what matters next. Separate planning and perception waste safety and information.

Their framework refines a coarse reference path using tail-sensitive risk maps. The maps derive from Average Value-at-Risk statistics over an online-updated 3D Gaussian-splat field. Locally safe, feasible trajectories emerge from that risk surface. In parallel, next-best-view selection becomes optimization on the pose manifold. Riemannian gradient descent maximizes expected information gain. The objective targets uncertainty critical for imminent motion, not curiosity in general. Scalable gradient decompositions keep the loop updating efficiently online. Extensive computational studies demonstrate effectiveness. Robots gain a principled way to look where danger and ignorance overlap.
arxiv-2510-06581:
Bo Li, Fangxiao Wang, and Shiji Xing study fair division, but for burdens instead of goods. Their 2025 paper asks how to split indivisible chores among people with unequal weights. A leading fairness idea is the weighted maximin share, which promises each person a fair worst-case portion. Nobody knew whether a constant-factor approximation to it was even possible.

The authors present the first constant-factor approximation algorithm for this fairness notion. Their method simplifies hard cases into canonical ones and bounds what agents can value. They also prove that no method can guarantee better than a factor of two. That lower bound improves the earlier best mark, which stood near one point three seven. The true best ratio now sits somewhere between two and twelve. Closing that gap remains an open problem in weighted fair division.
arxiv-2510-06681:
Leonardo Clarke leads a team studying how distant galaxies formed their stars. Their 2025 paper uses data from the James Webb and Hubble space telescopes. The sample holds 659 star-forming galaxies seen as they were billions of years ago. The team measures the star-forming main sequence, a tight link between galaxy mass and star formation rate.

They estimate star formation two ways, from hydrogen light and from ultraviolet light. Each estimate gets its own dust correction. The scatter around the main sequence grows toward lower masses in the hydrogen-based version. It shows no such trend in the ultraviolet version. Comparing the two rates reveals bursty histories in much of the sample. Between 41 and 60 percent of galaxies clash with a steady star formation story. Burst timescales may also shorten at earlier cosmic times. The results portray young galaxies as flickering builders rather than steady ones.
arxiv-2510-07081:
Fanheng Kong, Jingyuan Zhang, Yahui Liu, and Zirui Wu speed up a new breed of language models that write many tokens at once. Their 2025 paper studies diffusion language models, which decode text in parallel. Open implementations play safe and finalize only the single most confident token per step. That caution wastes many refinement rounds, a delay the authors name delayed decoding.

Their analysis found that confident tokens stabilize their neighborhoods. Nearby predictions lock in early and rarely change afterward. Their method, LocalLeap, exploits that local determinism. It finds high-confidence anchors and decodes relaxed neighborhoods around them in parallel. The strategy needs no retraining of the model. Across reasoning, code, and instruction benchmarks, throughput rose nearly sevenfold. Decoding steps fell to about fourteen percent of the original count. Quality loss stayed negligible in their measurements. Faster diffusion models could make parallel generation practical for everyday use.
arxiv-2510-07281:
Eides revisits the error budget behind one of precision physics' prized numbers, the hyperfine splitting of muonium. Its splitting once anchored key constants and still gives the best value of the muon-to-electron mass ratio. Recent global adjustments of physical constants quoted the theory uncertainty at a strikingly small figure. Eides argues that figure understates the true uncertainty by a large factor. 

Two earlier careful analyses put the uncertainty at several hundred hertz, not the fifty-one hertz now quoted. The smaller number, Eides shows, was misread as the full theoretical prediction error. Sharper measurements elsewhere have retired its old role in fixing the fine structure constant, which makes the remaining error budget even more pointed. He calls for an immediate correction in the recommended values. The note warns how one mislabeled number can spread through shared reference data.
arxiv-2510-07581:
Yue, Wang, Zhan, Li, and co-authors give language models new kinds of actions, so they can stop spelling out tool calls in prose. Their 2025 paper attacks an awkward bottleneck. Models reason in text, so every interaction with a calculator or simulator must be written in a special format, parsed by hand-built machinery, and routed externally. Language ends up doing two jobs, reasoning and control, badly entangled.

A reinforcement learning method with counterfactual rollouts teaches the model to explore rarely used but critical environment actions. On multi-turn tasks needing contingent planning, including calculator-based multitask problems and a partially observed sorting task, the approach beats strong baselines confined to vocabulary actions. Decoupling control from language removes a whole class of format errors and brittle prompt engineering.
arxiv-2510-08081:
Lan and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper presenting AutoQual, a language-model agent that discovers interpretable features for ranking online reviews. Review quality is domain-dependent and shifts over time, so hand-built features do not scale. AutoQual mimics a human researcher. It proposes feature hypotheses through reflection, implements them itself as tools, and stores lessons in persistent memory.

Deployed on a platform with a billion-level user base, AutoQual raised reviews read per user by under one percent in A/B testing. Reader conversion rose by a fraction of a percent, large in absolute terms at that scale. Discovered features stayed explicit and computable. The authors frame the framework generally: it turns tacit knowledge in labeled data into features people can inspect, building trust in ranking systems.
arxiv-2510-08281:
Tianwei Li and co-authors tackle lifetime value prediction for mobile gamers in a 2025 arXiv paper. Ad platforms that sell space by real-time bidding need to know what each user is worth over time. Good estimates guide ad placement and raise returns for advertisers. Gamer spending is spiky and full of outliers, which makes direct prediction of total spend unreliable.

Instead of guessing the total at once, their model breaks the goal into smaller parts. It first predicts how many purchases a gamer will make at each price point. It then rebuilds the total payment from those counts, matching how in-app purchases actually occur. The team tested the model on a real industrial data set. They also ran it live on the TapTap ad system in an online A/B test. It was compared there with ZILN, a leading model for this task.
arxiv-2510-08481:
Yifei Xu and co-authors forecast hashtag popularity by letting language models reason about context in a 2025 arXiv paper. Viral hashtags steer campaigns, opinion, and large advertising budgets, yet predicting them is notoriously hard. Classic regressors use surface features and miss the story behind a tag. Language models reason well about context but estimate numbers poorly.

Their framework, BuzzProphet, assigns each job to the tool that does it best. A language model writes rationales about a hashtag's timing advantage, audience reach, and topical virality. Those rationales enrich the features fed into a standard regressor, which makes the numeric forecast. They release HashView, a benchmark of seven thousand five hundred thirty-two hashtags from social media. Across regressor and model combinations, BuzzProphet cut prediction error by up to 2.8 percent and raised correlation by thirty percent.
arxiv-2510-09081:
Kraaijeveld and co-authors render vast bundles of moving lines in real time without faking the lighting, in this 2025 arXiv paper on computer graphics. Line sets appear in flow simulations and in brain imaging, where thousands of fibers trace the wiring of white matter. Dense sets need honest transparency and soft shadowing to be readable, but those effects are expensive. The team's framework voxelizes the lines, boxing them into a three-dimensional grid.

That grid supports two tracing styles at once: true ray tracing for accurate see-through layering, and cone tracing for ambient occlusion, the gentle darkening where lines crowd together. A culling step rebuilds the acceleration data only for voxels the camera can actually see, slashing per-frame preparation. In comparisons, it beat the prior state of the art on quality and speed for mostly opaque dynamic line sets.
arxiv-2510-09481:
Walter van Suijlekom, Michael Wondrak, and Heino Falcke study particle creation by gravity in a 2025 arXiv paper. The Schwinger effect creates particle pairs in a strong electric field, and its derivation assumes the field switches on and off in the distant past and future. The authors pursue a gravitational analogue in an expanding FLRW universe, using a long gravity pulse to mimic a steady background.

They derive the production rigorously through the Heun equation, using new formulas linking its local solutions to read off probabilities for an infinitely long pulse. Production shows a lower threshold in the late-time frequencies, tied to how long the switching takes. At high frequencies in a spatially flat universe, the spectrum is Planckian, with a temperature inversely tied to the duration of the scale change. They compare the result with Schwinger's own for an electromagnetic pulse.
arxiv-2510-09681:
Sashank Makanaboyina, the sole author, presents NNDM in a 2025 arXiv paper, a hybrid model for finding brain tumours in MRI scans. Accurate tumour segmentation guides diagnosis and treatment planning. Standard network models such as U-Net often struggle on new data and on exact edges, and with narrow training sets.

NNDM couples NN-UNet, a strong self-configuring network, with a diffusion probabilistic model. The diffusion stage learns the pattern of errors between the network's predicted mask and the true mask. It then progressively refines the mask, correcting small flaws and sharpening tumour edges through iterative denoising. On the BraTS 2021 benchmark datasets, NNDM beat plain U-Net and transformer-based baselines on both Dice overlap and Hausdorff distance, two standard scores. The refinement also improved robustness across scan types and tumour parts.
arxiv-2510-09881:
Kim, Seungmin Lee, Junho Kim, and Young Min Kim present LTGS in this 2025 arXiv paper on 3D scene reconstruction. LTGS builds a long-term chronology of a scene from sparse view updates, using Gaussian splatting, a method that renders scenes from many soft 3D blobs. Everyday places change often, so a single capture goes stale fast.

The authors note that tracking such change the usual way needs dense observations in both space and time, which casual camera captures rarely provide. LTGS instead works from occasional new views of the same place. It updates the scene record so that each state reflects when things changed. The goal is photo-realistic playback of a place as it evolves over weeks or months.
arxiv-2510-09981:
Fan Zuo and co-authors scale traffic monitoring with AI cameras in this 2025 arXiv paper on transportation systems. Cities need accurate traffic data for both daily management and long-term planning, above all during disruptions like disasters, big construction, or New York City's congestion pricing program. Fixed sensors are costly to install and maintain, so coverage stays thin.

The team uses language model powered camera systems to extract traffic insights from video at scale. Cameras are already widespread, so the approach avoids new sensor networks. The system aims to turn raw footage into counts and patterns that planners can act on. Cheaper, wider monitoring would let agencies judge policy effects, such as pricing, with far better evidence.
arxiv-2510-10381:
Rodríguez-Falcón and Luciano Stucchi quantify emergence in agent-based models in this 2025 arXiv letter on complex systems. Emergent behavior, patterns that arise from many simple agents interacting, defines complex systems. Yet measuring emergence has mostly meant eyeballing space-time patterns and judging them by eye.

The authors propose mean information gain as a numeric metric of emergence. Information gain measures how much observing the system teaches an observer over time. A model whose patterns carry more new information scores as more emergent. A quantitative scale lets researchers compare models and parameter settings objectively. That could turn emergence from a talking point into a design variable for simulations of crowds, markets, and ecosystems.
arxiv-2510-10581:
Heng Zhang and seven co-authors build a tool for finding the true cause of failures in multi agent systems, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Agent teams excel at complex tasks but fail often in long, multi turn deep search. Existing methods blame steps by their order in time, which confuses symptoms with root causes when errors spread across agents. The missing piece is how information flows between agents, not just when actions happened.

Their framework, GraphTracer, builds Information Dependency Graphs that record how agents reference and build on earlier outputs. It traces failures through these dependencies to localize root causes. It also generates synthetic failure data aimed at critical nodes. On the Who&When benchmark, their 8 billion parameter model reached up to 18.18 percent higher attribution accuracy than state of the art models in the reported comparisons. Plugged into production frameworks, it improved performance by between 4.8 and 14.2 percent across deployments.
arxiv-2510-10781:
Douglas Hutchings, Luai Abuelsamen, and Karthik Rajgopal coordinate mixed drone and ground robot teams for hazardous material emergencies, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Standard coverage control spreads robots using Voronoi cells, territories built around each agent. In emergencies it struggles: aerial and ground agents move at very different speeds, teams start clustered, and response must be fast. Their two layer approach optimizes aerial and ground positioning separately.

Aerial agents airdrop ground sensors onto high priority locations, speeding deployment. The paper details bounded Voronoi cell computation, numerical integration for importance weighted centroids, and control strategies that keep agents from getting trapped. In simulations, the method cut response time by 88 percent compared with ground only deployment. It reached the target sensor coverage in 25 seconds, versus 220 seconds for ground robots alone, accepting a modest sensor loss. The full implementation code is publicly available.
arxiv-2510-10981:
Tomoya Wakayama and Taiji Suzuki prove that in context learning in language models amounts to Bayesian inference, in this 2025 arXiv paper. In context learning is the trick where a model learns a new task from examples inside its prompt, with no weight updates. Working in a meta learning framework that allows mixtures of task types, the authors decompose the total risk into two orthogonal parts. The Bayes gap measures how close the trained model comes to the best possible in context predictor. The posterior variance captures the task's intrinsic uncertainty and does not depend on the model.

For a uniform attention Transformer, they bound the Bayes gap in terms of how many pretraining prompts were used and how long their contexts were. The striking finding concerns the mixture: uncertainty about which task is at hand vanishes exponentially fast with just a few in context examples.
arxiv-2510-11181:
How many trains a railway junction can handle depends on the mix of freight and passenger services sharing it. Tamme Emunds, Paul Brunzema, Sebastian Trimpe, and Nils Nießen present a method for computing that capacity without fixing a timetable in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their approach fits the traffic rate assignment problem, where capacity must hold under changing traffic distributions.

The underlying task is a non-linear constrained optimization that maximizes throughput, with capacity constraints that are expensive to compute. The authors solve it with Bayesian optimization, adapting the method to a setting where the objective is known but the constraints are costly. They tailor the acquisition step and build prior knowledge about the constraint shapes into the Gaussian process surrogate model. Benchmarked on a railway junction near Paris, their approaches significantly outperformed fixed traffic composition models, showing the benefit of dynamic capacity allocation.
arxiv-2510-11481:
Some partial differential equations have rough, wildly varying coefficients, yet their answers turn out smooth: that miracle is the De Giorgi-Nash theory, which settled Hilbert's nineteenth problem in the late nineteen fifties. Giovanni Brigati and Clément Mouhot present self-contained lecture notes on the method and its modern quantitative form in this 2025 arXiv paper. The notes review the classical theory for elliptic and parabolic equations, including Moser's Harnack inequality.

The new part extends De Giorgi's method to hypoelliptic equations, which appear in kinetic theory when particles move freely between collisions. The simplest case is the Kolmogorov equation with a rough diffusion matrix in the velocity variable. The authors also stress newer quantitative methods based on constructing trajectories. These yield explicit regularity estimates rather than mere existence of smoothness.
arxiv-2510-11981:
Yankai Zhang and Yoshitaka Tanimura build exact simulation tools for atoms bathed in heat. An atom governed by a Coulomb potential, the classic attraction between charges, never sits alone: a thermal environment keeps jostling it. Treating that influence without crude shortcuts is hard. Their 2025 arXiv paper derives hierarchical equations of motion tuned for atomic orbitals, called AO-HEOM.

Their math uses a rotation-proof three-dimensional model of system plus bath, so the setup respects the atom's spherical symmetry. The resulting equations are exact in their numbers within the model and handle strong coupling and memory effects that simpler theories drop. To test it, the authors compute the linear absorption spectrum of an atom in an isotropic thermal environment. They vary the coupling strength and temperature step by step. The spectra show how the environment reshapes the atom's response to light, checking a tool meant for realistic, warm quantum systems.
arxiv-2510-12281:
Wei characterizes a class of rough curves called t-quasicircles using a new family of mappings, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Quasicircles are images of circles under maps that distort shapes in a controlled way, and they sit at the boundary between smooth and fractal geometry. Classical results describe ordinary quasicircles through quasisymmetric boundary maps, which control how distances are stretched.

Wei introduces (rho, t)-quasisymmetric mappings, a broader class that generalizes the classical notion. With them he gives an analytic characterization of t-quasicircles, viewing the result as an analogue of a classical theorem of Tukia and Väisälä. He then studies conformal mappings from the unit disk onto t-quasidisks, the regions these curves bound. The boundary values of such mappings turn out to be almost quasisymmetric in the new sense, with the parameter squared. This extends the classical Quasicircle Theorem to the t-quasicircle setting.
arxiv-2510-12381:
Zheng, Takayasu, and Takayasu ask whether railway commuters choose routes rationally and consistently over time, using a year of Tokyo smartphone data, in a 2025 arXiv paper. The data cover over one million users in the Tokyo area during 2023. Few earlier studies had measured how stable route choice behavior is, or how it varies by origin destination pair.

The team built algorithms to extract commuting paths, transport modes, and transfer stations from raw position data. They then reinterpreted the standard route choice model through the canonical ensemble of statistical physics, treating rationality as a temperature like quantity. Route choice behavior in aggregate proved stable across the whole region through the year. However, behavior varied strongly by origin destination pair. Estimated parameters split into two groups with opposite preference signs, meaning commuters divide into two camps on what they value. They argue that transfer modeling in railway route choice needs more care.
arxiv-2510-12581:
Haghighi and colleagues make diffusion models teach themselves by aligning their weaker internal layers with their strongest ones, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Earlier work showed that guiding a diffusion model's intermediate representations with external supervision speeds training and improves output quality. LayerSync replaces the external teacher with the model's own most semantically rich layers.

The method adds a plug in regularization term with no training overhead and needs no pretrained models or extra data. Representation quality varies across layers, and LayerSync uses the best layers as intrinsic guidance for the weaker ones. On image generation it greatly accelerated training of a flow based transformer on ImageNet while improving quality scores by a large margin. The approach is domain agnostic and also improved audio, video, and human motion generation in their tests. The authors present self alignment as a general recipe for faster, better generative training.
arxiv-2510-12781:
Diarra, Coulibaly, and Leventhal measure the human cost of building speech datasets in this 2025 arXiv paper. They study Bambara, a Manding language of Mali, as an example of a predominantly oral language, meaning speech rather than writing carries most knowledge. Such languages lack the large text collections that language technology usually trains on, and nobody knew how much labor corrected transcription really takes.

Over one month, ten native-speaking transcribers corrected machine-generated transcripts of fifty-three hours of Bambara recordings. The team found that one hour of speech needed about thirty hours of human work under laboratory conditions and about thirty-six hours in the field. Their figures give planners a concrete baseline for similar language projects.
arxiv-2510-12981:
Cho and colleagues argue that common unlearning metrics can hide retained knowledge in this 2025 arXiv paper. Machine unlearning aims to make a generative model behave as if it never saw unwanted data, yet current metrics judge success against reference responses or classifier outputs. A model can pass those checks while the knowledge stays reachable through different prompts or attacks.

The authors propose FADE, a metric that compares the full output distributions of the unlearned model and a reference model. It scores how likely each finds the other's generated samples, in both directions. On two standard benchmarks, for language model unlearning and for text-to-image diffusion unlearning, methods scoring near-optimally on traditional metrics failed this distributional test. Many had actually moved farther from the gold standard after unlearning, which the authors present as a fundamental gap in evaluation practice.
arxiv-2510-13281:
Kim and colleagues correct speech recognition errors by consulting both ears and eyes in this 2025 arXiv paper. Audio-visual speech recognition combines microphone audio with lip movements, and generative error correction uses a language model to polish recognizer output. Existing correction, though, usually refines hypotheses from a single stream.

Their framework, DualHyp, hands the language model two independent hypothesis lists. One comes from an audio recognizer and one from a visual lip-reading recognizer. It lets the model compose them directly in language space. A guidance mechanism called RelPrompt supplies the temporal reliability of each stream, so the model shifts its trust between audio and visual hypotheses moment by moment as conditions change. Under varied corruption on the LRS2 benchmark, the framework gained far more error reduction over a standard audio baseline than single-stream correction managed. Code and the hypothesis dataset are released.
arxiv-2510-13581:
Zhang and co-authors map the full phase diagram of a non-Hermitian PXP model, a chain of constrained spins. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds a framework for quantum criticality in this open system. Past work had left the full diagram unknown. The model is a test bed tied to Rydberg atom setups.

From a transition point found by computer search, they build an exact line of second-order transitions. Two checks, one from equilibrium data and one from dynamics, place this line in the Ising class. Correlation data then split the symmetric zone into confined and deconfined phases. In the complex-energy zone, they find two PT transitions of distinct kinds. They also pin down the Yang-Lee edge singularity and its critical exponent. The exponent matches non-unitary conformal field theory, and they propose a Rydberg array test.
arxiv-2510-13681:
Dubois, Yvon, and Piantanida show that how a language model samples text can make machine writing nearly undetectable. Their 2025 arXiv paper stress-tests detectors that claim near-perfect accuracy at spotting AI text. Those claims rest on fixed generation settings chosen by the detector builders. Small decoding tweaks are enough to break the spell, they find.

The team varies temperature, top-p, and nucleus sampling across many configurations. Even minor changes can crash detector scores, with the area under the curve falling as low as one percent in some settings, far below the near-perfect marks usually advertised. Subtle shifts in the word-level distribution drive the collapse. The results expose blind spots in how detectors get evaluated today. The authors release a dataset spanning thirty-seven decoding setups, plus their code. They urge broader protocols before any detector is trusted.
arxiv-2510-14181:
Dhruv Sharma builds a framework for simulating how molecules behave when their states cross, with careful attention to geometric phase effects, in this 2025 arXiv paper. When a molecule loops around certain crossings, its quantum state picks up an extra phase, a memory of the path, which can inhibit or reshape the mixing between states. Ignoring that phase distorts nonadiabatic dynamics.

His two-level model covers avoided crossings, conical intersections, and elliptic intersections through parameters. His Ehrenfest dynamics, a quantum-classical method, includes force corrections derived from Berry curvature, the source of the geometric phase. A prelooping start encodes the gathered phase as an initial condition. For conical intersections the method reproduces the expected phase, while elliptic ones yield a tunable phase, whatever the loop size. Tests confirm the approach matches theory for state mixing and its geometric inhibition.
arxiv-2510-14381:
Andrew Zhao and co-authors present a systematic security analysis of language-model prompt optimizers, the tools that refine prompts by iterating against scored feedback, in this 2025 arXiv paper. As chatbots, computer-use assistants, and robots rely on optimized prompts, the optimization loop becomes an attack surface nobody had examined.

Using the HarmBench evaluation suite, the team finds optimized systems are more vulnerable to manipulated feedback than to poisoned queries alone. Feedback-based attacks raised the attack success rate by nearly half a point on their scale, in the worst case. They introduce a fake reward attack that inflates scores for harmful behavior without any access to the reward model, increasing vulnerability. On the defensive side, a highlighting technique, which marks feedback content for scrutiny, cut the fake reward attack's effect without degrading utility. The authors establish prompt optimization pipelines as an attack surface needing safeguards.
arxiv-2510-14681:
Carminati and co-authors introduce, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a Bayesian model for clustering data that arrives in separate groups. Think of patients in several hospitals, or measurements from several surveys. Standard models let groups share cluster centers exactly, by using the same atoms in each group's mixing measure. That sharing can be too rigid when groups differ slightly, and it forces a trade-off between good clusters and good density estimates.

Their hierarchical shot-noise Cox process mixture lets each group's atoms gather near shared centers without coinciding with them. A kernel spreads them, so groups borrow strength while keeping their own character. The construction stays tractable: the authors derive closed-form prior moments, the correlation between groups, and the predictive rules, plus an efficient sampling algorithm for inference. Simulations and a large galaxy dataset show balanced clusters and better density estimates than the standard hierarchical Dirichlet process.
arxiv-2510-14881:
Abebayew proposes, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a protocol for keeping language model agents reliable when they work inside large, sensitive systems such as codebases. Agents are stateless and their context windows are limited, so their picture of a system drifts out of sync with reality. The result is unreliable output and wasted tokens spent re-reading material.

The Gatekeeper Protocol flips the usual order. The agent must first reason over a minimalist, low-fidelity sketch of the system, a latent state, and only then request high-fidelity details on demand. Every exchange passes through a unified JSON format that keeps the agent's model of the system synchronized with the system itself. A reference implementation for software development, called Sage, demonstrates the approach. The author reports significantly better agent reliability and lower token consumption, arguing the protocol can scale agent interaction with complex systems in a grounded, verifiable way.
arxiv-2510-14981:
Alzayer, Zhang, Geng, Huang, and Wu solve an annoyance of photo editing, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Fix the same object in ten photos of it, and each edit comes out different. 2D editors produce changes view by view, but nothing keeps them consistent across a multi-view set of a scene. Earlier fixes optimized 3D representations, a slow process that turns unstable when views are sparse.

Their method needs no training and no 3D model. Coupled diffusion sampling runs two generation trajectories at once, one drawn toward a multi-view image distribution, the other toward the 2D editor's distribution. A coupling term pulls the trajectories together, so the edited images stay faithful to the edit and to each other. This implicit 3D regularization enforces consistency without geometry. The team validated the framework on three multi-view editing tasks and across model architectures, and present it as a general solution.
arxiv-2510-15181:
Štěpán Marek, Wulf Wulfhekel, Ferdinand Evers, and Richard Korytár explain how an electric current could spin a molecular motor in just one direction. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds on helical orbitals, electron states that wind like a corkscrew around chains of carbon atoms. A current through such orbitals circulates around the chain, and its angular momentum should push rotation once switched on.

That intuition lacked a strict definition of helicality as something measurable, so the authors supply one. With it, they show how helicality fixes which way the motor turns. Working through simple Hückel models of carbon chains, they trace why the two frontier orbitals wind in opposite senses to a hidden symmetry of the chain's sublattice. One testable consequence follows: use the chain as a rotor axle, and the turning direction stays the same even if the current is reversed.
arxiv-2510-15381:
Christian H. Weiß and Philipp Adämmer offer a simple test for whether values in a spatial grid lean on their neighbors, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such spatial dependence matters in fields from climate science to medical imaging, where data live on two- or three-dimensional grids. Existing pattern-based tests handle flat grids well but usually stop at two dimensions.

Their trick is to thread the grid into one long sequence using a Hilbert curve, a path that visits every cell while keeping nearby cells close in the sequence. Spatial dependence then shows up as serial dependence along that sequence, which ordinal pattern tests can detect without assuming any distribution. Generalized Hilbert curves handle grids of any size and any dimension beyond three as well. The authors present the method as easy to implement and broadly applicable, needing only gridded data and no model fitting.
arxiv-2510-15781:
Alberto Acevedo Meléndez and a large team present a method in a 2025 paper. It prepares the lowest-energy state of a quantum system. The task matters in materials science and chemistry. Some optimisation problems need it too. Imaginary time evolution mimics a cooling process. It settles a system into its ground state. Its quantum version is a leading strategy. But it can be slow and rigid.

Their variant is compressed and adaptive. It adjusts the evolution as it proceeds. They supply a geometric reading of why the adaptation works. The approach builds on classical dynamical optimisation ideas. It stays compatible with step-by-step circuit methods. Current quantum hardware can run those methods.
arxiv-2510-15981:
Rafael Cabral and five co-authors present ProofFlow, a pipeline that turns human proofs into machine-checked code without mangling the argument. Translating theorems into verifiable form is key to using language models in rigorous maths, yet current tools often produce code that runs while losing the original meaning and logical shape.

ProofFlow first draws the proof as a directed acyclic graph of dependencies between steps. Each step is then formalised as its own intermediate lemma, which preserves the structure of the human argument. To judge such work they add a benchmark of undergraduate problems with hand-annotated steps and graphs, plus ProofScore, a metric joining syntactic correctness, semantic faithfulness, and structural fidelity. Their pipeline sets a new best score, far above whole-proof and step-by-step baselines, and all parts are open-sourced.
arxiv-2510-16081:
Jiaye Yang, Xinyu Zhao, Tianlong Chen, and Kandyce Brennan present a chatbot for sexual and reproductive health counselling. The team works at a university nursing school. General chat systems falter in this sensitive domain. They hallucinate and lack the specialist knowledge safe counselling needs. Most health AI also chases diagnosis over education and steady care. Such counselling in fact rests on care and teaching.

SARHAchat is a proof of concept built to close those gaps. It joins medical expertise with empathetic communication in a user-centred system. Tests show it gives accurate contraceptive counselling that fits each context. It keeps a natural conversational flow at the same time, the four authors report. A public demo accompanies the work. The project frames specialist chat support as a practical aid where clinician time is scarce. It is not framed as a replacement for clinicians.
arxiv-2510-16281:
Yilin Wu and five co-authors fix a gap between what a robot says it will do and what it then does. Reasoning robot models write a step-by-step plan in words before acting. Yet the actions can drift from the plan, most in new settings. The authors name this drift a lack of embodied faithfulness.

Their fix runs at action time with no retraining. The same model offers several action sequences, and a simulator previews where each one leads. A vision-language model then picks the outcome that best matches the plan. Only plan-true sequences get carried out. On behavior tests, the method lifts success by up to fifteen percent over prior work. It also shines at mixing skills in new ways. The team also releases a plan-marked test set for others to probe this faithfulness gap.
arxiv-2510-16381:
David Peer and Sebastian Stabinger propose ATA, a design for AI agents that can be trusted with high-stakes work. Language models alone hallucinate, wobble between runs, and hide their reasoning, which bars them from sensitive jobs. ATA splits the job: first, knowledge is written down in a formal symbolic base, which human experts can check and fix.

When a task arrives, it is translated into the same formal language. A symbolic decision engine then reasons over the checked base to reach the answer, step by auditable step. In full-auto mode the system matches top end-to-end models on a hard reasoning task. With a human-verified base it beats even larger models, while staying perfectly deterministic and immune to prompt injection. The design offers a practical route to agents whose decisions can be inspected and defended.
arxiv-2510-16881:
Vedad Kunovac leads twenty-five co-authors in mapping spots on a distant star in a 2025 paper. The star WASP-85 A hosts a hot Jupiter planet. Star spots are dark patches that disturb planet-hunting measurements. As the planet crossed the star, it acted like a scanning probe.

Ground telescopes tracked brightness while a spectrograph recorded the starlight in detail. A spectrograph spreads light into colors to reveal fine changes. The team found seven active regions, six holding dark spots. During spot crossings, spectral lines widened and shifted measurably. That widening points to magnetic fields as strong as sunspot fields. Combining both views set lower bounds on the star's total field. The method turns planet transits into star-surface microscopes.
arxiv-2510-17381:
Safety systems need to flag data that does not belong, but a single outlier score hides what kind of odd data arrived. Achref Jaziri, together with three co-authors, argues that knowing the type of shift matters, because the right response depends on it. Most detectors squeeze every difference from normal data into one number, which loses that vital context.

Jaziri and his co-authors present DISC, a method that reads the cleaning steps of a diffusion model at many noise levels and turns them into a rich feature profile. On image and table benchmarks, DISC matched or beat the best detectors at spotting odd data. Unlike earlier methods, it could also name the type of shift it had found.
arxiv-2510-17581:
Optimisation methods usually assume the slope information they receive is exact, yet in many real problems that slope is computed by a solver and is only approximate. Humberto Gimenes Macedo and Luís Felipe Bueno build a descent framework that stays reliable under such inexact gradients. Their motivating case is design work constrained by differential equations, where the gradient comes from an adjoint calculation whose accuracy depends on an inner iterative solver.

The framework allows cheap, coarse gradients early on and sharper ones near the answer, and Macedo and Bueno prove global convergence under two step size rules. They implement it as plain gradient descent and as a quasi-Newton style variant, and test both on two inverse problems. Adaptive accuracy cut the total computing time, and adding curvature information improved efficiency further.
arxiv-2510-17881:
Yizhuo Chen, with nine co-authors, personalizes large language models by first learning what each user likes, in plain words. Their POPI system splits the job in two. One shared model reads mixed user signals and writes a short taste summary. A second model then answers using that summary as guidance.

Both parts train under one goal, with reinforcement learning for the summary step. Because the summary is plain text, it can be reused with other models, even closed commercial ones. Tests on four benchmarks mostly improved personal fit. The design shows a clean way to carry user taste across systems.
arxiv-2510-17981:
Maria Axenovich and four co-authors improve a long-standing bound in Ramsey theory, a field about forced patterns in colored networks. The question asks how large a complete network must be so that any coloring with a set number of colors yields a one-color odd cycle of fixed length. A conjecture by Fox predicted the sharper bound they now prove.

Their upper bound is the first gain in the exponent beyond a constant factor since work from 1973. Progress on this problem had stalled for decades at that basic level. For combinatorics readers, the paper closes a named conjecture and resets the scale for multicolor cycle problems.
arxiv-2510-18181:
Sin Kyu Kang and C J Ouseph review a small extension of particle theory that gives neutrinos a magnetic link to a heavy neutral partner. In the neutrino dipole portal, a transition magnetic moment joins an active neutrino to a heavy neutral lepton through the light field. That single interaction predicts up-scattering, glowing decays, meson changes, and shifted recoil patterns.

Limits today come from accelerators, recoil detectors, colliders, and neutrino observatories, plus strong bounds from the early universe and supernova cooling. The review gathers theory, completions, and search plans in one place. Particle physicists get a map of a portal that many experiments can probe.
arxiv-2510-18381:
Giorgio Piras and his five co-authors work on a hard trade-off. They want to shrink neural networks. They also want the small networks to resist attacks. Pruning cuts weights that seem less useful. Each weight gets a score, and low scores are cut. The team found a flaw in how scores are picked. The best scores can sit in a sharp dip of the loss curve. A mask picked there is unstable. The pruned model then loses much of its safety.

Their fix is a plug-in method called S2AP. It hunts for flat ground in score space. It nudges the scores and checks the loss at each nudge. A mask picked on flat ground shifts less. It holds up better after fine-tuning too. Tests used many data sets, models, and pruning levels. The method steadied mask choice and made pruned networks more robust.
arxiv-2510-18481:
Gaëlle Aymeric, together with Emmanuelle Lavaine and Brice Magdalou, asks how much a child's home environment shapes school results, and whether that influence grows with age. Their data cover every child aged eight to fifteen in the Madrid region from 2016 to 2019. Home environment here means two things: the education parents themselves completed, and the effort parents put into raising their children.

Across mathematics, literature, and English, children from more favorable home environments scored better, matching most earlier research on this lasting effect. The growth question, called the Matthew effect, split by subject. The home advantage shrank with age in mathematics, rose then fell in literature, and grew steadily in English. The authors read the English pattern as a sign that foreign language learning leans more on social background than the more school-taught subjects do.
arxiv-2510-18581:
Katerina Drakos and her six co-authors weigh a design choice for mental health chatbots. Such bots are sold as a way to widen access to support. Most are built with a narrow slice of expertise. Whole fields get left out of parts of the design. The authors say that pattern is risky. A mental health tool is a sensitive, high-stakes tool.

Their case rests on the bot's whole lifecycle. Technologists catch some problems. Clinicians, ethicists, and lawyers catch others. The missed ones range from unsafe replies to legal duties. The European AI Act treats such systems as high risk. The paper gathers practical advice and known frameworks. The aim is to balance teamwork friction against its gains. The end goal is bots that fit human values and the law.
arxiv-2510-18681:
Changfeng Gui and Amir Moradifam generalize a sharp geometric inequality. It concerns surfaces of constant positive curvature. The original Sphere Covering Inequality bounds total area from below. It covers two surfaces over the unit disk. The surfaces must match along the boundary. Gui and Moradifam relax that rule. The boundary values may now differ by a fixed constant.

The new version reveals a hidden stability structure. The area bound shifts in a precise, quantified way. It does not collapse when matching is imperfect. Boundary data can be perturbed, and the effect is tracked. Such results matter beyond pure geometry. The same equations arise in elliptic problems with exponential terms. They arise in conformal geometry as well. That field studies angle-preserving maps. Links to mathematical physics follow from there.
arxiv-2510-18981:
Joseph DeRose and Shi-Fan Chen introduce lensing counterterms, a formal way to split large and small scale signals in weak gravitational lensing. Cosmic shear mixes clean cosmology on large scales with messy effects on small scales, such as gas feedback or possible new physics like axion dark matter.

By averaging over the new counterterms, analysts can keep the large-scale signal without cutting away small-scale data by hand. In a test modeled on a future survey, the gain in precision is large. The method also lets the small-scale part speak about feedback instead of being thrown away.
arxiv-2510-19081:
Shifa Sulaiman and three co-authors develop a mobile manipulator robot meant to help inside a self-driving laboratory. Such labs automate chemical synthesis and reaction work, and a robot arm on a moving base can handle samples alongside human operators if it moves precisely and grasps reliably.

The authors model the arm's motion with a standard convention, solve the inverse problem of reaching target poses, and add vision algorithms that recognize textured objects in real time. Reliable grasping of varied lab items is treated as the key skill that makes the whole mobile system useful.
arxiv-2510-19181:
Kartikeya Aneja and three co-authors build a question answering system that works only from a knowledge graph, without large language model retrieval pipelines. Instead, a small paraphraser model turns the entity and relation edges found in the graph into a natural final answer.

Documents are first turned into question-answer pairs, then into a knowledge graph that is searched with embeddings and fuzzy matching, re-ranked, and paraphrased. Judged by a language model on a standard benchmark, the system performs competitively. The design offers an interpretable route to answers, where each step can be traced through the graph.
arxiv-2510-19281:
Shubham Joshi reports an empirical study of how intuitive bitwise operators feel to programmers at many levels, from people with no coding background to doctoral students. Bitwise symbols are famously cryptic, and the study tests whether exposure changes how fast and accurately people answer questions about them.

Twenty-three participants completed tasks in a JavaScript program under a within-subjects design, so each person served as their own comparison. Response time and error rate were the main measures. Findings about which operators confuse novices most can guide teaching, language design, and the warnings that development tools give beginners.
arxiv-2510-19581:
Luca Piano, Peng Huanwen, and Radu Ciprian Bilcu present a new approach to multi-focus image fusion. The task is to combine photos taken at different focus settings into one image that is sharp throughout. Ordinary lenses keep only a slice of a scene in focus. Fusion methods also struggle with scarce training data and faked synthetic examples.

Their method, VAEEDOF, uses a distilled variational autoencoder for faithful, efficient reconstruction. It can fuse up to seven images at once. To fix the data problem they built MattingMFIF, a synthetic 4K dataset that imitates realistic depth-of-field effects from real photographs. The system produced seamless, artifact-free results at the level of the best existing methods.
arxiv-2510-19681:
Jianfeng Hou, Xizhi Liu, and Yixiao Zhang refine a classical theorem of Ahlswede and Katona about small patterns inside graphs. The original theorem fixes the maximum possible density of the two-edge star, a vertex joined to two others, in any graph with a given edge density. The question belongs to extremal graph theory, which asks how much of a pattern a graph can hold under constraints.

Motivated by applications to hypergraph Turán problems, the authors add an assumption: the graph contains a large independent set whose vertices all have high degree. Under that extra structure they establish a sharper version of the Ahlswede-Katona result. The refinement gives Turán-type arguments a stronger tool for controlling star densities.
arxiv-2510-19881:
V. Apinyan and T. K. Kopeć study how canted antiferromagnetism and excitonic order coexist in double-layer graphene under a gate voltage. The system is two AB-stacked graphene layers; electrons in them can pair across layers as excitons while magnetic order tilts away from a simple pattern. Using a generalized Hubbard model, the authors compute the chemical potential, the charge imbalance between layers, and both order parameters at zero temperature.

The excitonic pairing turns out to live on a larger energy scale than the antiferromagnetic gap. Charge neutrality holds only when the gate potential vanishes. Both orders strengthen as the interlayer Coulomb interaction grows, and both weaken under a large gate voltage, giving experimentalists two knobs with opposite effects.
arxiv-2510-19981:
Martha Teiko Teye, Ori Maoz, and Matthias Rottmann present FutrTrack, a transformer-based system for tracking many objects in three dimensions by fusing camera and LiDAR data. The framework builds on existing 3D detectors rather than replacing them. A temporal smoother first refines sequences of detected boxes over a moving window, reducing jitter before identities are assigned.

The tracker itself merges box geometry with fused bird's-eye-view features from both sensor types, so it needs no explicit motion model. Query-based propagation carries identities across frames and re-identifies objects through occlusions and viewpoint changes using both geometric and semantic cues. On the nuScenes and KITTI benchmarks the system reached strong accuracy with few identity switches, showing multimodal features markedly improve query-based tracking.
arxiv-2510-20181:
Sk Jamaluddin and fifteen co-authors report a large, tunable topological Hall effect driven by domain walls in a layered magnetic material. The material is an iron-intercalated transition metal dichalcogenide with a chiral lattice and ferromagnetic order. Designing spin textures that give strong, distinct electrical responses is a standing challenge for quantum states and spintronics.

By varying the iron content step by step, the team controls the magnetic ground states and thereby tunes the Hall response. Magnetic force microscopy gives direct images of periodic stripe domains, confirming the microscopic source of the transport signal. The findings show a practical way to shape domain topology so layered magnets produce substantial electromagnetic responses on demand.
arxiv-2510-20281:
Jiayi Zou, Gengyun Jia, and Bing-Kun Bao tackle bias in Visual Commonsense Reasoning, where a model answers questions about an image and explains its answer. High accuracy on standard datasets can hide reliance on co-occurrence and statistical biases in both the text and the images. The authors expose those biases and build two out-of-distribution test sets to measure true generalization across both modalities.

Drawing causal graphs of the task, they pinpoint prediction shortcuts that let models answer without real reasoning. A backdoor adjustment method then removes the bias, using a dictionary built from the set of correct answers to break the shortcut links. Experiments across different datasets show the debiasing method works, giving a clearer picture of what the models actually understand.
arxiv-2510-20581:
Alice C. Quillen and Abobakar Sediq Miakhel explore whether a chaotic Floquet-driven quantum system can generate pseudo-random unitary operators. Their test system is the perturbed Harper model on a torus, run with strong perturbations and a driving frequency above the libration frequency. That regime ensures an ergodic region covering phase space with no resonant substructure, which is what a random unitary generator should mimic.

Floquet propagators are computed from a distribution of control parameters to form samples of unitaries in a finite-dimensional space. Frame potentials compare those samples against the Haar-random distribution that defines true randomness for unitaries. Uniform distributions over four control parameters generate an approximate three-design, and drifting system parameters can achieve the same with fewer control parameters, the authors find.
arxiv-2510-20681:
Xinhe Mu and seven co-authors shrink diffusion models so they can estimate how many rows a database query will return, a count that guides fast query plans. Learned estimators must capture tangled links between columns, and diffusion models excel at rich distributions but run far too slowly for database use.

Their system, ADC, pairs a mixture based selectivity estimator with a score based density estimator in a hybrid design for precise sampling based counts. New theory on score behavior at small and large times lets the model fit mid sized database problems under strict delay limits. Tests against five learned rivals show the downsized design keeps high accuracy while meeting practical speed needs.
arxiv-2510-20781:
Wesley J M Ridgway, Mohit P Dalwadi, Philip Pearce. S Jonathan Chapman extend pattern formation theory to structured models whose steady states bunch sharply in a trait such as age or chemistry. Classic weakly nonlinear tools assume smooth base states, so sharply peaked states break the usual steps.

Their framework pairs WKBJ approximations with Stokes phenomenon analysis to resolve the solution shape as the base state nears a spike. A bacteria model where cells signal each other by chemistry serves as the test case. The analysis yields an amplitude equation near the onset of patterning and predicts a pitchfork split, with a single grouped setting deciding whether that split bends forward or backward.
arxiv-2510-21081:
Zhuojin Li leads two co-authors on accelerating neural network inference on mobile devices by splitting work finely between the central and graphics processors. Phones have limited compute, yet their shared memory and narrow performance gap between the two chips invite cooperation.

Two obstacles dominate, the synchronization cost of merging partial results and the difficulty of predicting how long each task takes on each chip when implementations and parallelism shift dynamically. Their fine grained co execution scheme attacks both problems. Lower latency on device inference matters for translation, vision, and assistants that should work without the cloud.
arxiv-2510-21281:
Christian Salomonsen and three co-authors estimate a key input signal for PET scans of mice, used to measure glucose use in tissue. The standard way to get that arterial input function is invasive and slow, and image-based estimates can fail when the animal moves and blurs the scan during imaging.

Their model reads the signal straight from the scan images, guided during training by a physics-based law describing how the tracer moves between blood and tissue in the heart and brain. It was trained on seventy mouse scans with measured reference signals. When heavy motion blur was simulated, the physics-guided model held its accuracy in severe cases, matching its plain counterpart on clean images and showing stronger resistance to damaged inputs.
arxiv-2510-21581:
Ciara Rowles and five co-authors give video a voice: their system, Foley Control, generates sound effects that match moving images while leaving two big pretrained models untouched. Foley artists normally craft those sounds by hand, and automated rivals often retrain heavy multimodal systems end to end, which is costly and rigid.

A small learned bridge of cross-attention layers is the only trained part. Video features from a frozen visual model enter the frozen text-to-audio model right after its text conditioning, so the prompt sets the scene's gist while the video steers timing and local dynamics. Pooling the video tokens first trims memory and steadies training. On curated benchmarks the bridge matches recent multimodal systems for timing and meaning while using far fewer trainable parameters, and parts can be swapped without retraining.
arxiv-2510-21781:
Runchu Dong, with Peng Zhao, Guiqin Wang, Nan Qi, and Jie Lin, addresses a common failure of video analytics at the network edge. Small models running on cameras are fast, but when lighting, weather, or the scene itself changes, their accuracy fades, and retraining them on remote servers is slow and can chase yesterday's footage.

Their system, EdgeSync, filters training samples by freshness and by what the current model already predicts, so updates focus on video that matches what the camera sees now. A scheduling module also decides when updates should run and in what order. Tests on varied real-world datasets show accuracy gains of roughly three to ten percent over earlier approaches, with updates arriving sooner.
arxiv-2510-21881:
Nannan Shi, Chuanyu Qin, Shipeng Song, and Man Luo build training material to help vision-language models solve geometry problems, a weak spot where strong text reasoners stumble once a diagram is involved. Existing datasets, they argue, are too small and too plain, rarely showing the step-by-step thinking a solver needs to learn.

Their GeoThought collection holds about six thousand problems, plus an expanded version with nearly eleven thousand, each with a visual description, worked solution, explicit reasoning chain, reflection steps, and a final answer. Training a model on this material produced a geometry-focused system with stronger diagram reasoning. The dataset is offered as a remedy for both halves of the problem: richer supervision and more of it.
arxiv-2510-22081:
Amir Nazemi and Hongyi Xiao simulate a tiny scallop trying to swim through sand. A scallop in water cannot get anywhere by opening and closing symmetrically, a classic result, but grains are not water: they jam, lock, and remember contact, so the rules change.

Using particle simulations, the pair watches the force networks around a flapping swimmer in a frictional granular bed. Stagnant, jammed zones form more weakly during the opening stroke than during the closing stroke. That asymmetry, counted in strong particle contacts, grows in direct proportion to how far the swimmer travels across many setups. A second mechanism appears when the swimmer's own inertia matters, near the point where its flapping period matches the time it needs to coast to a stop. Together the two effects explain how reciprocal motion can still make progress in grains.
arxiv-2510-22181:
Chao-Qiang Geng, Xiang-Nan Jin, Chia-Wei Liu, Xin-Yi Liu, and Xiao Yu propose a hunting ground for an unseen particle. The particle is the doubly charmed baryon Xi-cc-plus. It carries two charm quarks in one package. A sibling with a different charge has been observed. The missing partner is a standing target for collider experiments.

The team suggests looking in one decay of the Lambda-b baryon. It decays into the sought particle plus a negative D meson. That channel tags the production cleanly. It can also be fully reconstructed. A fully charged final state is spelled out for detectors. Their estimate puts the main branching share within reach. The cleanest fully charged route is far rarer. Weighing both, they argue LHCb has a real chance at discovery. Prospects for the doubly charmed Omega are briefly sized up too.
arxiv-2510-22381:
Janosz W Dewberry and three co-authors use computer simulations to study what happens when an accretion disk is strongly stretched into an eccentric shape. Even without magnetic fields, a distorted disk can seed instabilities. Their three dimensional nonlinear runs are paired with simpler linear calculations to separate local from global effects.

Locally, they see parametrically excited inertial waves that match local theory and stir wave turbulence. Globally, a separate family of slow, vertically shaped modes grows and bends the eccentricity profile up and down. The authors suggest such effects may wrinkle a flat eccentric disk into a corrugated one.
arxiv-2510-22481:
Quantum imaginary time evolution, a method for guiding quantum systems toward low energy states, is the subject of a 2025 paper by Min Chen, with Bingzhi Zhang, Quntao Zhuang, and Junyu Liu. The method is promising for near term quantum machines, yet its basic theory has stayed thin.

Chen and co-authors show the method matches a form of training that uses quantum geometry to set step sizes. For wide quantum neural networks, they build a math model of its motion. Their proofs say it always converges faster than plain gradient descent, though that edge shrinks as the system grows, helping explain past experiments.
arxiv-2510-22881:
Aligning language models with human preferences is often complex and unstable. Saeed Najafi and Alona Fyshe propose a simpler route in 2025. Their method is MMPO, for MML based Preference Optimization. MML means maximum marginal likelihood. It is a classic statistical estimation idea.

MMPO maximizes the marginal log likelihood of preferred text. Preference pairs serve as samples for approximation. No explicit reward model is needed. No entropy maximization is needed either. Theory shows it performs preference optimization implicitly. Its gradient up weights chosen replies over rejected ones. Tests span models from small to eight billion parameters. MMPO proved more stable and preserved general skills.
arxiv-2510-23281:
Yingjie Zhou reports new hypernuclei measurements from the STAR experiment at a heavy-ion collider. Hypernuclei bind a hyperon together with ordinary nucleons, and their yields reveal how they form in collisions. Some, like helium-5 Lambda and hydrogen-4 Lambda, are much tighter bound than hydrogen-3 Lambda.

The loose, large hydrogen-3 Lambda should be suppressed in coalescence models but not in thermal models, where size plays no role. Comparing yields for mass three to five hypernuclei therefore tests which picture is right. Zhou proceedings summarize what STAR data say about binding effects on production.
arxiv-2510-23481:
A Del Popolo, Saeed Fakhry, Maryam Shiravand, and Morgan Le Delliou study how dynamical friction affects structure growth in a universe dominated by generalized Chaplygin gas. Building on earlier spherical collapse work, they ask how friction changes the growth rate of density perturbations, the effective sound speed, the equation-of-state parameter, and the expansion history.

Their results show dynamical friction significantly delays collapse compared with frictionless models. Delayed collapse alters when galaxies and clusters form in Chaplygin cosmology. The shear and rotation effects they include make the collapse model closer to real, spinning, friction-damped overdensities.
arxiv-2510-23881:
Xidong Feng and twelve co-authors teach generative AI to compose chess puzzles that feel genuinely creative: aesthetic, surprising, and counter-intuitive. Off-the-shelf generators struggle at exactly those qualities. The team first benchmarked standard architectures, then built a reinforcement learning framework whose rewards come from chess engine search statistics, tuned to favor uniqueness, counter-intuitiveness, diversity, and realism.

The training worked dramatically. Counter-intuitive puzzles rose tenfold, reaching about two and a half percent of output. That beat the rate in existing datasets and in a model trained on Lichess puzzles. The generated puzzles kept classic aesthetic themes and passed novelty checks. Human experts rated them more creative, enjoyable, and counter-intuitive than composed book puzzles, nearly matching classic compositions. The project ends with a curated booklet of AI-composed puzzles, praised by three renowned experts.
arxiv-2510-24181:
SiYing Wang and three co-authors find an exact error threshold for the surface code when nearby errors are correlated. The surface code is a leading plan for fault tolerant quantum computing, with a high threshold and links only between neighbors. Prior exact analyses assumed errors are independent, while numeric work on correlated errors gave only lower bounds.

The team maps quantum error correction to a statistical physics model, a random bond Ising model on a square octagonal lattice, through a new error edge map. With that map, they derive the exact threshold under a realistic noise model that mixes single qubit errors with correlated errors between nearest neighbors. The result may allow higher thresholds than the independent case.
arxiv-2510-24381:
Matteo Giordano studies what chiral symmetry restoration implies for the Dirac spectrum in a hot gauge theory, working alone. This is the first paper in a series, set in the two flavor chiral limit with lattice Ginsparg-Wilson fermions. He proves symmetry is restored at the level of scalar and pseudoscalar susceptibilities exactly when none of them diverges as the quark mass goes to zero.

That condition forces the susceptibilities to be smooth functions of the squared mass, or mass times such a function, depending on their structure. By expressing the susceptibilities through the Dirac spectrum, Giordano turns these facts into constraints on the eigenvalue density near zero in the symmetric phase.
arxiv-2510-24581:
Adrien Le Boudec writes alone on groups that share a large home. A cocompact envelope is a big group holding a smaller one snugly. The small group sits inside as a discrete, cocompact subgroup. Le Boudec takes two finitely generated groups with one shared envelope. He asks which traits the two groups must then share.

For totally disconnected envelopes, nilpotent subgroups must nearly match. Nilpotent groups are built from steps that almost commute. For solvable groups of finite rank, he finds rigidity and flexibility. Rigidity means the partner group must be solvable of finite rank too. Flexibility means he builds partners where that fails outright. So the class is not QI-rigid, not fixed by rough geometry. Similar freedom appears for finitely presented groups as well.
arxiv-2510-24781:
Tatsuru Kikuchi, the sole author, tracks how new tech spreads through two paths at once. One path is place: firms near an adopter are more apt to adopt, with the pull fading by miles. The other path is links: firms tied in a supply chain pass the tech along their ties.

He tests the frame on six techs taken up by five hundred firms over more than a decade. Place pull fell off in a smooth curve, with spill gains near zero past a set range. Chain links grew far more dense as take up spread. The two paths let him split where spread came from for each tech.
arxiv-2510-24981:
Phan Quoc Khanh and Felipe Lara name a new broad class of curve shapes for use in best fit math. The class, star quasiconvex, wraps in plain convex shapes, star shapes, and a few known kin as plain cases. Such shapes matter since first order tools can be shown to home in fast on them, past the plain convex world.

The pair give a few marks of the class, for both smooth and rough cases. In the rough case, all low sets of such a curve are star shaped at a low point. In the smooth case, strong forms match a known slope rule. They also show a close step tool runs in a straight line pace to the lone best point.
arxiv-2510-25081:
Yuepeng Guan and Masatoshi Yamada map the phase chart of the strong force at heat and dense baryon load, with a flow tool. The chart shows where quark pairs break their chiral match, a key shift in such matter. Past flow work most oft adds fake boson fields to tame wild terms in the math.

Their way skips those fields and takes a weak form of the flow rules, which lets the flow act in a non smooth way. The quark force is then worked out in a local take, from quark acts alone. The chart that comes out rests on those quark wiggles. It shows how heat and load move the chiral line.
arxiv-2510-25181:
Yixiang Zhou, Tong Wu, Meixia Tao, and Jianhua Mo cut the talk cost of shared learning for radio channel feedback in huge antenna systems. Each phone must send back what the channel looks like, and that load is vast. Shared learning keeps data on the phone, but full model swaps still cost too much and tastes in data clash.

Their frame, Fed-PELAD, keeps a own code arm on each phone to catch its own channel traits. A shared decode arm is tuned the shared way, but just by lean add ons, so swap load is small. A freeze swap plan with set learn rates steadies the joins. Tests cut up link cost to less than half.
arxiv-2510-25481:
Nils Melsom Kristensen, Kristian Mogensen, Sarah-Jane Lock, and Oyvind Breivik study storm surges. Their 2025 paper examines the inverse barometer effect. That effect links sea level pressure to water level. They run the global ocean model NEMO standalone. Configurations cover years 2015 through 2022 in simulations. Residual water level excludes tidal variations here.

A control run omitted the inverse barometer effect. Another run used dynamic pressure forcing directly. The control effect was added diagnostically for comparison. Three experiments resulted from these different treatments. They compare against global GESLA3 water level data. Including the effect reduced root-mean-square error on average. Error fell by about one centimeter on average. For large residual events, reductions reached four to five centimeters. Regional differences appeared between diagnostic and dynamic methods. Dynamic forcing performed slightly better in enclosed basins. The Baltic Sea was one such basin example. Ensemble forecasts showed stronger early surge indications.
arxiv-2510-25681:
Enrica Barrilli, Bernard Mourrain, and Daniele Taufer study sums that break down symmetric tensors. Their 2025 paper in pure math calls such a sum a GAD. A tensor here is a grid of numbers with a flip rule. From the shape side, a GAD is a point on a secant line set. It gives a short, neat form for the tensor.

They give a way, with plain matrix steps, to gauge the size of a GAD. The least size is named the GAD-rank of the tensor.
