Lorenz Bielefeld and co-authors flag a flaw in over-the-air federated learning, a scheme where many devices transmit their updates simultaneously and the wireless channel adds them up. That analog aggregation relieves the communication bottleneck of federated learning. But the literature has ignored a fact. Radio power amplifiers are nonlinear, and signals whose peaks exceed the linear range get distorted in and out of band.

The authors analyze the remedy, iterative amplitude clipping combined with filtering, and study its effect in single-carrier and multi-carrier OFDM systems. Simulations show the signal in over-the-air learning breaches the amplifier's linearity limit under realistic settings. Applying clipping and filtering degrades learning performance to varying degrees, and the damage is worst in multi-carrier systems, where clipping creates in-band distortion that filtering cannot remove. The paper is framed as a first reality check for the field.
arxiv-2512-23481:
Wei Cui and four co-authors study two-dimensional supersymmetric theories with N=(0,4) supersymmetry, obtained by twisting and reducing four-dimensional class S theories on a curved surface. Such constructions are elegant but leave subtle questions open: what are the theories' central charges, which gauge symmetries survive, and what superconformal R-symmetry emerges in the infrared?

The authors propose conjectural formulas for the central charges and test them on theories with SU(2) gauge group, where a Lagrangian description is available. They examine two branches of the vacuum space, the special Higgs branch and the twisted Higgs branch, computing each branch's Hilbert series. The counts agree with the proposed formulas, giving evidence that the conjectured charges capture the infrared physics correctly.
arxiv-2512-23581:
Courtney Kyger and four co-authors introduce profile Bayesian optimization, a method for tuning expensive computer simulations. Their motivating problem is a diffuser in a rotating detonation combustion engine: the simulation reports energy lost through diffusion. Engineers want the lowest possible loss as a function of the diffuser's length, one control parameter, while other design parameters vary as nuisances.

Standard Bayesian optimization hunts a single best point and ignores most of the control parameter's range. The profile version instead maps the best achievable response at every value of the control parameter. A two-stage acquisition scheme balances exploring new lengths against refining known optima, with deep and shallow Gaussian process surrogates tracking uncertainty. On benchmarks and on the engine problem, it beat traditional Bayesian optimization and earlier profile methods. The point is to tune the whole curve, not just one peak.
arxiv-2512-23681:
Adam Harper surveys a subtle phenomenon in analytic number theory: averages of character sums that cancel more strongly than the square-root barrier suggests. The square-root scale is what randomness alone would predict, and for decades it was treated as a natural limit. Harper explains how connections with multiplicative chaos, a chance-based framework, showed much better cancellation in averages of multiplicative character sums.

The survey focuses on the number-theoretic side of the arguments rather than the probability machinery. It also discusses possible applications of the improved cancellation. The paper grew out of work connected with the International Congress of Mathematicians, where a version will appear in the 2026 proceedings. That makes it a guided entry point to an active research area for number theorists. It maps the field more than it proves new theorems.
arxiv-2512-23781:
Jackie Baek, Will Ma, and Dmitry Mitrofanov report what happened when a large online retailer let an algorithm hand out daily discounts. Working with the retailer's base of more than twenty million customers, they designed a policy that chooses each customer's promotion each day, ten to twenty percent off in five steps. Respecting global limits on how many of each discount can be given.

Deployed in an A/B test, the policy raised revenue by about four and a half percent, by aiming discounts at promotion-sensitive customers and learning timing patterns across customers. The data also inspired a new theoretical model: customers remember the best promotion they saw over the last several days as a reference. Buy more readily when that memory is poor. The authors tightly characterize the optimal policy under the model, which cycles between poor offers and one good one.
arxiv-2512-23981:
Sebastián Gutiérrez-Bernal, Hector Medel Cobaxin, and Abiel Galindo González propose a new yardstick for dimension reduction, the maps that squeeze high-dimensional data into pictures or compact features. Standard scores judge such embeddings by distorted distances or warped local geometry. Neither directly measures how much information the projection throws away, which is what matters in information-sensitive uses such as early-warning indicators.

Their Entropy Rank Preservation Measure works neighborhood by neighborhood, comparing the Shannon entropy of the singular-value spectrum of each patch before and after projection, summarized through the stable rank. Validated on a financial time series and a standard manifold, the measure correlated only weakly with distance-based scores but strongly on average with a geometric criterion, while disagreeing in specific local regimes. The authors conclude their metric complements existing ones by flagging exactly where severe information loss hides.
arxiv-2512-24081:
Sijin Li and Wei Wang address a weakness of quantum measurement. Squeezed light can estimate phases beyond classical limits. But the advantage fades fast when light is lost. It also fades when detectors miss photons. The authors build on an earlier remedy. They amplify the quantum state before measurement.

This work extends the trick to entangled states. It also covers estimating several phases at once. Two setups are worked through in detail. One uses a two-mode entangled state. The other uses a four-mode cluster state. In both cases, sensitivity stayed robust under loss. Imperfect detection did not destroy the advantage either. For builders of large quantum sensors, the result is practical. It offers a path to quantum-level precision outside ideal laboratory conditions.
arxiv-2512-24281:
Spyridon Syntakas and Kostas Vlachos keep small marine vessels safe and on course. Their craft is an over-actuated surface vessel with three degrees of freedom. Wind, waves, and current push it hard. Sliding mode control offers robustness against such matched disturbances. Safety constraints need separate enforcement, though.

High-order control barrier functions supply that enforcement. They keep obstacle-avoidance constraints forward invariant. The barrier functions adapt to the vessel's state. A fast half-space projection adjusts the control only when needed. Robustness is preserved while chattering stays low. The test model is nonlinear and realistic. It includes added mass and hydrodynamic damping. Full thruster allocation is modeled too. Simulations showed robust navigation with guaranteed obstacle avoidance. The computation suits real-time embedded hardware with limited resources.
arxiv-2512-24481:
C Pallis writes a personal memoir of George Lazarides, a physicist. Lazarides was Pallis's PhD supervisor. He later became a collaborator. Throughout, he remained an encouraging supporter. The piece honors that bond directly. It records memories rather than arguing a thesis.

Work shared between the two men is also summarized. Their joint research touched supersymmetric models and what they predict. Inflation in the early universe was the other shared theme. Related work of Lazarides receives mention as well. Memoirs like this preserve the human record of a research community. Students and colleagues appear alongside equations and models. Readers interested in Lazarides and his circle will find a first-hand account here.
arxiv-2512-24581:
Igor Tunev revisits Dejean's conjecture and stronger forms about threshold words, sequences that avoid too much repetition. A word's root is its shortest repeating prefix, and a threshold word keeps every subword's length over its period at or below a set bound. The manuscript, in Russian, edits his bachelor and master work from the early twenty nineteen decade with improvements.

Circular threshold words and other strengthenings are developed beyond the conjecture proved in two thousand nine. New proof methods from his student work anchor the account. Combinatorics on words readers get both history and stronger constructions, presented as a revised collected version of earlier theses.
arxiv-2512-24881: Mykola Khrypchenko covers totally matching structures on the Jacobson radical of the incidence algebra of a finite poset over a field. Incidence algebras encode order relations of a poset in matrix-like form, and their radical captures strict order relations. Compatible structures are extra actions that couple well with the algebra product. He shows such structures are in general non-proper, meaning they do not arise from the simplest expected building. Algebra readers get a sorting for a concrete finite-dimensional setting.
arxiv-2601-00181:
Cheonkam Jeong and coauthor Adeline Nyamathi study how machines read emotion inside a conversation. Two gaps drive their 2026 study. Labs rarely pin down which design choices truly matter. Findings also rarely link back to how people mark discourse. The team runs strict ablations on one dataset. Checks then repeat on a second dataset.

Context proves to be the dominant factor. Most of its gain arrives within the last few dozen turns. Layered sentence features help when no context is present. Their edge vanishes once turn history is fed in. Adding an emotion lexicon brings no gain at all. Simple causal models still score strongly without future turns. A language check adds a second payoff. Sad speech uses fewer markers at the sentence edge. Sadness also gains most from context. Human pattern and model pattern line up.
arxiv-2601-00481:
Tie Ma and ten co-authors built MAESTRO, a test suite they describe in a 2026 paper. The suite checks teams of AI agents built on large language models. Such teams can be hard to compare, since each one is set up in its own way. MAESTRO gives them one shared way to be set up and run. It also records each run in a shared format, with cost, delay, and failure counts.

The team loaded twelve agent teams into the suite, drawn from well-known frameworks. They ran each team more than once, with changed models and tools. Runs kept much the same shape each time, yet speed and score swung a lot. The shape of a team mattered more than the choice of model or tools. It drove cost, delay, score, and how well runs matched. These findings give builders a firmer base for test work.
arxiv-2601-00581:
Stephen E Farr and six co-authors introduce AceFF in 2026, a learned force field for small molecules. A force field gives the push and pull between atoms in a molecule. Labs use such fields to test drug ideas before they make them. The gold standard method is far more exact, but far too slow for wide use. AceFF aims to keep that level of care at a much higher speed.

AceFF comes in two forms that share the same design. One was trained on the team's own set of drug-like molecules. The other was trained on a slice of a large public set, with two extra elements from living tissue. The team checked them on twists of molecules, motion runs, and shape clean-up tasks. Both forms scored at the top on speed and on closeness to the gold standard. Their weights and code are free to use.
arxiv-2601-00681:
Matteo Ciabattoni and Francesco Monticone wrote a 2026 paper on circuits that bend microwaves in new ways. Their base parts are transmission lines, the paired wires that carry high-rate signals. Linked in a grid, such lines form a material whose parts talk across long range.

The pair first give a compact theory for such grids, for any link pattern. From it, they show how to build grids with almost any spread pattern of a set shape. They then add links that switch on and off as a pulse moves through. That switch lets the grid remap a pulse in both tone and path. It can also launch waves that move fast, slow, or not at all. A bench test backs the theory: a switched grid showed the sharp jump the maths foresaw. The work opens a flexible test bed for wave control.
arxiv-2601-00781:
Samson Gourevitch, Alain Durmus, Eric Moulines, Jimmy Olsson, and Yazid Janati improve how machine learning models learn with categorical variables. Optimizing over discrete choices is awkward because sampling a category has no usable gradient. The standard workaround replaces the discrete distribution with a smooth relaxation, so gradients can flow through a reparameterization trick.

Their method, ReDGE, builds that relaxation on denoising diffusion, yielding a flexible family of gradient estimators that includes the widely used straight-through estimator as a special case. Experiments cover latent variable models and reward-guided generation in discrete diffusion models. Across those settings ReDGE matches or beats existing gradient-based approaches, offering a drop-in upgrade for training models with discrete structure.
arxiv-2601-00881:
Neeraj Pandey and four co-authors build, in 2026, a simple model of how cities grow as shares of a nation's people. Data from sixteen populous nations over fifty years show city growth in all of them. Yet the paths split into four shapes, from growth that speeds up to growth that slows down. The authors sort countries into a rural zone and a city zone. People are born in each zone, and some move from country to city.

The move rate is set by the gap in income per head between the zones. Each zone's income grows at its own steady rate. The team fit its dials to data from the United States. The lesson is that plain links between births, moves, and income gaps can yield rich paths. The model gives planners a cheap tool to test city futures.
arxiv-2601-01181:
Chenglizhao Chen and seven co-authors attack a data problem in camouflage research. Models that find hidden objects in images need large, finely labeled data sets, but collecting and labeling real camouflage scenes is slow and costly. The team instead builds a system that creates realistic camouflage images together with dense labels, without needing hand-drawn masks.

They also release GenCAMO-DB, a large new data set with depth maps, scene graphs, written attribute notes, and text prompts for each scene. Their generator, GenCAMO, is aware of the surrounding environment when it places a hidden object. Tests across several task types show that models trained with this synthetic data do much better at dense prediction in complex camouflage scenes. The work could ease the data bottleneck for wildlife monitoring, search tasks, and other fields where targets blend into their setting.
arxiv-2601-01281: Sifatullah Sheikh Urmi, Kirtonia Nuzath Tabassum Arthi, and Md Al-Imran compare four AI models for spotting deepfake faces, as fake imagery grows into a threat to digital trust. They test three convolutional networks and one vision transformer on large face image data sets, using preprocessing and augmentation to strengthen performance. One model, VFDNET, gave the best accuracy, and MobileNetV3 stood out for efficiency. The short report presents the comparison as evidence that current AI tools can detect deepfakes dependably across scenarios.
arxiv-2601-01581:
Sen and 7 co-authors design a bargaining system for electric cars that charge from a building and can also feed power back. Building managers want to curb high energy costs from unplanned charging, while drivers want convenience and a full battery. Their framework, CONSENT, offers drivers paid choices to shift departure time or lower the charge they request.

Participation stays voluntary by design, and the rules resist gaming while keeping the budget sound. The design draws on survey answers and real data from a business building and a car maker. Simulations cut building costs past a smart charging plan and cut driver costs well below the normal power price.
arxiv-2601-01781:
Satellite image analysis needs labeled examples, and self-supervised pretraining can reduce that need, but most methods demand huge image collections. Lakshay Sharma and Alex Marin propose a leaner pretraining task for remote sensing: cut a small patch from an image and train the model to paint exactly where that patch came from.

Called subimage overlap prediction, the task forces the model to learn spatial layout before it ever sees a label. Models pretrained this way converged faster and matched or beat alternatives on downstream segmentation across several architectures and datasets, with the advantage growing as labeled data shrank. The method also needed far less pretraining imagery than competing self-supervised approaches, and the code and weights are released.
arxiv-2601-02681:
Shinichiro Akiyama and four co authors use tensor renormalization group methods to compute symmetry twisted partition functions, quantities that act as order markers for how a symmetry is realized at low energy. Locality in field theory tightly constrains these functions, so their behavior can reveal spontaneous symmetry breaking without a local measure. The tensor method coarse grains a lattice system efficiently, making the work doable.

Two classic models show the approach. The two dimensional Ising model and the three dimensional O(2) nonlinear sigma model both show their symmetry breaking transitions through the twisted partition function alone, with critical points located from that signal. Finite size scaling then gives the shift temperature and the critical exponent for the three dimensional model, matching known values. Berezinskii Kosterlitz Thouless criticality in the two dimensional case is studied as well.
arxiv-2601-02881:
Jakob Lønborg Christensen and three co-authors rethink image segmentation, the task of dividing a picture into meaningful regions, using diffusion models. Most leading systems build results mask by mask, leaning on frameworks built around that idea. The authors instead predict the whole segmentation at once, in a single holistic pass, which keeps the method agnostic about what kinds of regions appear.

They adapt diffusion to this discrete task with a location-aware color palette, a gray code ordering for labels, and a final squashing step that proves crucial. A sigmoid weighting of the loss beat the alternatives in their tests. The model does not yet beat the best mask-based systems, but it narrows the gap and can express uncertainty about ambiguous regions in a principled way.
arxiv-2601-03281:
Mohamed Amine Ferrag, Abderrahmane Lakas, and Merouane Debbah introduce a benchmark for language-model agents that fly drones over future 6G networks. Such agents increasingly act as high-level controllers for unmanned aerial missions, yet evaluations rarely test whether they stay safe, protocol compliant, and effective under realistic network strain. Their benchmark frames each mission as a multi-turn conversation between the drone agent and a human operator.

Inside that loop, decisions must respect strict message schemas, mission policies, speaker alternation, and safety constraints. All this happens while the network shifts beneath them: slices change, latency and jitter swing, packets drop, and edge load varies. A dual action layer supports both tool calls and agent-to-agent coordination. The benchmark is built on a large corpus of about one hundred thirteen thousand conversational cases.
arxiv-2601-03381:
Laurent Doyen and Shibashis Guha design algorithms for stochastic games with a doubled winning condition. In these turn-based two-player games, one parity condition must hold in every possible outcome, surely, while a second must hold with probability one, almost surely. Such mixed requirements model synthesis problems where a hard guarantee rides alongside a softer one. The decision problem is known to be coNP-complete, and winning strategies can need infinite memory.

Earlier algorithms enumerated all memoryless strategies of the opponent, an exponential procedure that never builds the winning strategy itself. The authors give a recursive algorithm based on a characterization of the winning region, which yields deeper insight into the problem's structure. In particular, they show how to construct a winning strategy whenever one exists, not merely decide that it does.
arxiv-2601-03481:
Francielle Vargas and eight co-authors argue that hate speech detectors should explain themselves using moral reasoning, not just flag risky words. Many current models are opaque and lean on surface word cues, which makes them brittle and hard to check across cultures. Their framework, SMRA, trains a model's attention to match moral rationales marked by experts.

The approach draws on Moral Foundations Theory, which groups moral concerns into basic categories. The team also built HateBRMoralXplain, a Brazilian Portuguese dataset with hate labels, moral categories, token-level rationales, and social and political details. Across detection and moral classification tasks, SMRA improved results while giving clearer reasons. Transparent moderation tools matter because wrong calls can silence people or leave abuse in place.
arxiv-2601-04281:
Aakash Singh and five co-authors track how long attackers kept exploiting Log4Shell, the December 2021 flaw in a widely used Java logging library, in a 2026 arXiv measurement study. Earlier work watched the first outbreak mainly from Europe and the United States; this team uses a reactive network telescope in India to follow the traffic from December 2021 to October 2025.

They find exploitation never really stopped, but narrowed over time to a smaller set of recurring scanner and callback setups. With more heavily disguised payloads and shifting ports and protocols. Comparing their record with the earlier benchmark study shows shared trends plus clear differences tied to where the telescope sits. The lesson is that critical flaws have long tails, best measured over years and from varied vantage points.
arxiv-2601-04481:
Subhodeep Dey and Smarajit Karmakar study glassy crowds of self-propelled particles for a sign that a famous theorem has been broken, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The Mermin-Wagner-Hohenberg theorem forbids true long-range order in two-dimensional equilibrium systems, because long waves wash it out. Recent work suggests activity can shift the rules, moving the lower critical dimension from two to three.

Their model system is a glass of run-and-tumble active particles. Such glasses show dynamical heterogeneity — a patchwork of fast and slow regions. the authors track how that patchiness grows with activity, comparing systems with and without medium-range crystalline order, the local positional tidiness many real materials have. The growth patterns differ significantly between the two cases. Because biological systems from cell sheets to bacterial cytoplasm show both local order and glassy heterogeneity, the effect could serve as a measurable indicator of ordering.
arxiv-2601-04781:
Sophie Villenave and 2 co-authors study thermal feedback, meaning added heat or cold that a virtual reality user can feel, in a 2026 paper. Earlier work found that matching warmth to a scene improved user experience, but it rarely compared different quality levels or used highly immersive settings. Villenave's team tests dynamic thermal feedback in two demanding scenarios.

Participants explored a desert island scene and a snowy mountain scene, with about two dozen people in each study. Each person tried audio-visual display alone plus versions with added thermal feedback. Comparing those conditions shows how much felt temperature changes presence and comfort. The results guide designers of training tools, such as firefighting simulators, and comfort studies.
arxiv-2601-05081:
Franziska Pradel and 3 co-authors analyse how Google's query suggestions for politicians shift across countries and over time in a 2026 paper. Search suggestions reflect the latent interests of internet users, yet little was known about how political suggestions vary geographically or how stable they remain. The team built an original dataset covering European politicians across ten countries.

They find suggestions shift more over time in a politician's home country, for holders of supranational roles, and for female politicians. Those patterns reveal how public attention concentrates and moves. For researchers and campaigns, autocomplete is a live signal of what voters are curious or concerned about, and its biases shape what people search next.
arxiv-2601-05181:
Thomas P. Watson and Eddie L. Jacobs present Spacecube, a fast system for georectifying hyperspectral images, in a 2026 paper. Hyperspectral cameras record hundreds of data points per pixel instead of the handful captured by ordinary cameras, giving aerial surveys rich material fingerprints. Before analysis, airborne data must be georectified, warped onto true ground coordinates, and the traditional direct method is slow and prone to artifacts.

Spacecube implements a complete pipeline built around the authors' own fast inverse georectification technique. Inverse mapping fills the output image systematically, reducing gaps and errors. Faster, cleaner rectification helps environmental monitoring, agriculture, and defence users turn raw flight data into maps quickly enough to act on, rather than archiving it unprocessed.
arxiv-2601-05581:
Chao Liu and 5 co-authors derive, in a 2026 coding theory paper, new bounds and constructions for codes in the sum-rank metric. This metric measures errors across several matrix blocks at once. Such codes serve multishot network coding, space-time coding, and distributed storage.

Starting from covering codes in the simpler Hamming metric, the authors bound code sizes, covering radii, and block-length functions. Several resulting Singleton-like bounds beat the classical bound when block lengths are large. They also build distance-optimal codes for small square matrices using cyclic codes, give infinite families of quasi-perfect codes, and construct longer almost-optimal codes. A Plotkin sum construction yields still more distance-optimal examples.
arxiv-2601-05881:
Amjad Saef and Wilhelm Stannat study in 2026 whether answers exist for stochastic phase-field models of moving boundaries, with cell motility as the motivating application. A phase-field represents a cell's shape implicitly, and its contour marks the cell boundary in models of single-cell chemotaxis. Singular diffusion and randomness make the equations technically hard.

The authors consider an independently evolving phase-field and a coupled version driven by a viscous Hamilton-Jacobi equation. The main difficulty sits at the phase-field's zero level set, exactly where the boundary lives. For large classes of initial data, they establish global existence of probabilistically weak answers in weighted L2 spaces. The weights compensate for the singularities, giving these cell models a firmer mathematical foundation. With that base secured, later work can focus on how to compute with these models and test them on data.
arxiv-2601-06081:
Navigation satellites may guide spacecraft near the Moon, report Lorenzo Sciacca and 7 co-authors in a 2026 study. The Lunar GNSS Receiver Experiment showed GPS and Galileo signals can be received at lunar distances. This work re-examines the recorded signal snapshots from that receiver in cislunar space and on the surface.

Post-processing found signals from extra systems, including regional and augmentation constellations, that the receiver did not support in real time. Useful measurements came out despite very short snapshots and coarse sampling. Simulations tuned on these observations showed adding constellations sharply raises availability. The share of times with at least four satellites in view rose from about one in ten to nearly half.
arxiv-2601-06281:
Quantum programmers are settling into reusable patterns, and Neilson Carlos Leite Ramalho and 3 co-authors document how in a 2026 empirical study. Newer quantum frameworks offer higher-level building blocks beyond raw circuits, attracting developers from many backgrounds. Knowing which patterns practitioners actually use guides better tools and teaching.

The team first built a knowledge base from three frameworks, Qiskit, PennyLane, and Classiq, identifying nine new patterns that extend the existing catalog. A semantic search tool then detected patterns across 985 notebooks from 80 open-source projects. Usage fell into three levels: basic circuit utilities, common algorithmic primitives such as amplitude amplification, and domain applications in finance and optimization. The pattern points to a maturing field building on shared abstractions.
arxiv-2601-06581:
Galaxies grow from the inside out, and their faint ultraviolet outskirts are the proof. Pushpak Pandey and 2 co-authors report an extended ultraviolet disk around a massive spiral galaxy seen when the universe was younger, in a 2026 paper. Such extended disks had mostly been found nearby, because detecting them needs deep, sharp ultraviolet imaging.

Observed with AstroSat's ultraviolet telescope, the galaxy at redshift 0.67 shows a clumpy extended disk reaching nearly twice its optical radius. A large ultraviolet-bright, low surface brightness region matches one classic extended-disk type, while ultraviolet clumps without optical counterparts match another, hinting at gravitational instability and recent star formation. The asymmetric light profile implies cold gas still accreting onto the outer disk, direct evidence of active disk growth at intermediate redshift.
arxiv-2601-06681:
Maciej Tadej and two co-authors study plant patterns on dry land in a 2026 paper. Their model is a grown form of a known water-and-plant model. Plants in it spread seeds far, not just to spots close by.

The land in the model is flat and has a fixed edge. They first show the model is well set: it gives one path, not many. Then they work out the terms on which plants live or die out. Rules for both death and life come out of their work in strict form. Dry-land plant groups form shapes that hint at health or near collapse. Far seed spread shifts which shapes can last on a small plot of land. Land care teams gain math that speaks to the loss of dry lands.
arxiv-2601-06781: Research by Huatao Xu and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with AutoTour. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. The authors present AutoTour , a system that enhances user exploration. By automatically generating fine-grained landmark annotations and descriptive narratives for photos captured by users. The key idea of AutoTour is to fuse visual features extracted from photos with nearby geospatial features queried from open matching databases. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-06881:
Debashis Panda and seven co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on waves where two fluids meet. The paper deals with two kinds of drag at that surface. One kind acts when the surface grows or shrinks. The other acts when one part of the surface slides past the next.

The two kinds of drag tend to move in step, so their effects are hard to pull apart. Past work used flat flow or flows in one plane, where the split stays blurred. The team turns to waves that stand in place in three dimensions. In that setup, each kind of drag leaves its own mark. The marks let the team split the two effects and weigh each one on its own.
arxiv-2601-07081:
Irina Kmit, Nataliya Protsakh, and Viktor Tkachenko wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a wave equation with strong damping. The wave is almost periodic, which means its shape comes close to a repeat but not quite. The task is an inverse one. In an inverse task, the team works back from effects to find a cause in the equation.

The edge of the region is held fixed, a rule called the Dirichlet boundary condition. The work is set in Sobolev spaces, which hold functions with weak rates of change. The functions in view are bounded. Some are almost periodic, and some are fully periodic. The team finds a weak solution to the equation. It also pins down a source term on the right side of the equation. That term is part of what the inverse task must find.
arxiv-2601-07681:
Sayani Bera and Kaushal Verma prove a rigidity result for the chaotic regions of certain complex maps. They study polynomial automorphisms of complex two-space with positive entropy and degree at least two. For such a map, the escaping set collects points that run off to infinity under iteration. Its complement is the non-escaping set. Their 2026 preprint shows this set is rigid under holomorphic automorphisms.

Rigidity means symmetries of the whole space cannot deform the escaping set's structure. Positive entropy signals genuinely chaotic dynamics. Results like this classify how wild these maps can be. Complex dynamics in two variables is far less understood than in one variable. The paper serves dynamicists working on Hénon-type maps. It pins down one more invariant of their behavior.
arxiv-2601-07781:
Klaus Zollner and coauthors map tiny magnetic hot spots where cobalt touches graphene through a boron nitride layer. Proximity effects let a magnet stamp spin traits on a nearby nonmagnet. The team studies a cobalt, hexagonal boron nitride, and graphene stack with first-principles math. They find strong local change in the spin polarization brought on in graphene's Dirac states. Their 2026 preprint details that pattern.

The exchange coupling, magnetic moments, and tunneling spin polarization that result all hinge on atomic registry. Registry means how the atomic lattices line up at each interface. Small shifts in alignment therefore change the magnetism a lot. Such sensitivity matters for designing graphene spintronic devices. Those who build devices may use the hot spots or need to tame them. The paper speaks to physicists who work on flat, thin magnetic devices. The three thin sheets shift in traits from spot to spot.
arxiv-2601-08081:
Lavinia Heisenberg, Shayan Hemmatyar, and Nadine Nussbaumer prove a non-renormalization result for vector field theories. Their 2026 arXiv paper covers ghost-free local functionals for massive vector fields. These fields are coupled to dynamical geometry, so spacetime itself responds.

The proof assumes locality, Lorentz invariance, and a valid effective field theory below a fixed cutoff. Under those terms, quantum corrections do not create local operators of a certain kind. In particular, they do not renormalize the derivative self-interactions behind the theory's constraint structure. For theorists, that protection keeps a delicate classical structure safe from quantum damage.
arxiv-2601-08181: Aviral Gupta, Armaan Sethi, and Dhruv Kumar peer inside TabPFN, a foundation model for tabular data. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that such pre-trained models perform strongly across many table tasks. Still, their internal representations and learned concepts remain poorly understood. Weak interpretability makes it hard to trust or debug these models in real use. The authors study how TabPFN processes and transforms input features layer by layer. Their findings help readers judge what the model has truly learned from tables.
arxiv-2601-08581: Mir Alimuddin, Jaemin Kim, Antonio Acin, and Leonardo Zambrano wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a key step for quantum networks. The step is entanglement swapping, a way to spread a quantum tie. In standard forms, a middle read decides the final state. That makes the step a matter of chance, and forces teams to drop failed rounds. The authors sort the reads where the step stops being a gamble. For pure inputs of any kind, each outcome gives a state equal to the rest up to local unitary shifts.
arxiv-2601-08781:
Stefan Guttel and Kaustubh Roy extend a fast group sorting tool called CLASSIX. The tool puts like data points in one group and odd ones apart. It is fast, and a user can see why each group formed. At first it used plain straight line distance to judge how near two points are.

The pair adds two more ways to judge nearness. One suits city grid like moves, where you go along streets, not across blocks. The next suits data made of traits, such as chem traits of a drug. Both forms keep the speed and the clear logic of the first tool. A reader who sorts data gets more reach from a tool they can still explain.
arxiv-2601-08981:
Fredrik Lohne Aanes seeks to lift a tool that tells how much each trait in a model adds to its call. The tool is called KernelSHAP. It tests groups of traits in samples to weigh each trait. Past sample picks could draw the same group twice, which wastes runs. Aanes picks group sizes from a skew count law, then draws with no repeats.

He also adds two resample tricks to gauge how firm each weight is. Both tricks re-run the weights on split or flipped samples. In his tests, the new gauge does as well or more well than old ones. A reader who must explain a model call gets a leaner SHAP, with a clear doubt range.
arxiv-2601-09181:
Parameshwaran A and Bhaskar Sen Gupta sim how an active near point fluid splits in a thin tube. The fluid is near its gas and liquid split point. Its bits can move on their own and tend to line up, like a flock. In a plain fluid, split zones grow by known laws. Own motion may shift those laws when walls close in.

They run atom scale sims in a round tube pore. They track zone form and growth speed as own motion is tuned. The tube is near one way in shape, so growth may jam or rush in new ways. A reader in soft stuffs gets a case of life like split in a tight space.
arxiv-2601-09381:
Martin Grohe asks what a good query language for machine learning models would look like. His 2026 arXiv paper turns to logic, treating neural networks as weighted graphs that can be queried. He discusses two logics built for weighted finite structures: first-order logic with summation, and its recursive extension.

These logics grew out of foundational work by Grädel, Gurevich, and Meer in the 1990s. With co-authors, Grohe has tested them as languages for asking structured questions of trained models. A query language could let users probe a network's behavior in a precise, checkable way. The paper maps how far logic can go in that role.
arxiv-2601-09581:
Dorsa Fathollahi, V. Arvind Rameshwar, and V. Lalitha analyze an error-correcting decoder's chance of failure. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies the recursive projection-aggregation decoder for Reed-Muller codes. The channels covered are general binary memoryless symmetric channels.

Ye and Abbe proposed this decoder in 2020. A 2025 result showed it achieves vanishing error for low-rate codes on the binary symmetric channel. The new work extends that guarantee to the wider channel family. Reed-Muller codes are old, elegant codes now back in focus for modern links and storage, so stronger guarantees on their decoders carry real weight.
arxiv-2601-09781:
An unnamed author argues for a principle that keeps certain quantum theories apart from gravity. The 2026 arXiv paper presents the topological equivalence principle, on decoupling topological field theories from gravity. Such theories describe the deep infrared behavior of many gapped quantum systems.

They also encode the global symmetries of quantum field theories once gravity is removed. In curved anti-de Sitter space, though, sectors that look decoupled still feel Newton's constant. The sensitivity enters through sums over distinct saddle-point shapes. The paper frames how equivalence should be stated so the decoupling claim stays honest.
arxiv-2601-10081:
N. Sherlekar and a large team study light given off by a clean chip joint. The joint pairs gallium arsenide with its alloy kin. It holds thin gases of electrons and holes in a plane. When the two meet, they give off light.

The team built side by side joints with no added dopants. The light is bright. Its hues show free pairs that roam the plane. One peak is the heavy hole free pair. A second peak sits at a high band named the H band. A drift trait named the tidal effect also shows in the hues.
arxiv-2601-10381:
Calum Robson builds a phase space on Clifford algebras. A phase space pairs each place with its push. That pair form is base to classic physics. In Kähler form, the pair comes from a rich metric frame. Robson seeks a like frame in more dims.

He uses the Hodge frame on a Euclidean Clifford algebra. In his build, pairs link forms of dual ranks. A k form pairs with a form of rank n minus k. That swaps points and planes for slabs of each size. The work lifts phase space ideas to high dim algebra.
arxiv-2601-10481:
Michael Bleher, Denis Brazke, and Sebastian Nill build a curve match tool for the round sphere. Match tools gauge how like two shapes are. On a sphere, the tool must bend with the space. It can then drive non local costs that push sets to a best form.

Their cost pulls a set to be round in a broad sense. The match tool is the kernel of that cost. It comes from a Helmholtz law with a small length term. The team study how the cost acts as terms shift. Such costs shape drops, films, and cells that sit on curved skins.
arxiv-2601-10581:
Kimia Abedini, Farzad Shami, and Gianmaria Silvello work on question answering over genome data. Gene and genome facts sit spread across many large databases. Pulling the right facts out is slow and hard, even for experts. Large language models could help, but they have limited access to these special databases.

The team extends GeneGPT, a system that lets a language model query genome resources. Their new design moves from a single agent to several agents that reason together. Each agent can take on part of the search task. The goal is more accurate answers to biomedical questions. The work points toward tools that help researchers query gene data in plain words.
arxiv-2601-10781:
Kanchana Ranasinghe and co-authors present FOFPred, a model that forecasts future optical flow. Optical flow maps how each point in a scene is about to move. Such maps are gold for robot control and for video generation. Yet forecasting dense motion that holds up in the real world is still an open challenge.

FOFPred is conditioned on language, so words can steer the forecast. It joins a vision-language model with a diffusion process in one design. Learning comes from noisy, real-world data, not just clean lab sets. A robot that can foresee motion can plan smoother paths, and a video model that foresees flow can keep motion coherent across frames.
arxiv-2601-10881:
Sunny Atalig, Marek Chrobak, Christoph Dürr, Petr Kolman, Huong Luu, Jǐrí Sgall, and Gregory Zhu prove two complexity results on spanning-tree congestion. Given a graph, the task is to pick a spanning tree that minimizes the worst edge congestion. Congestion counts how many paths are forced across one edge. The problem is NP-hard, even on some narrow graph classes.

Several basic questions about its complexity stayed open. The authors settle some of them in this paper. Hardness results tell algorithm designers where not to hunt for fast exact methods. They also point to where approximations or special cases are worth the effort. Spanning trees with low congestion matter for network design and VLSI layout.
arxiv-2601-11781:
Dawood Wasif, Terrence J. Moore, Seunghyun Yoon, and a joint team from the United States, Korea, and Australia build a guard frame for self-driving cars. Cars that drive themselves must stay safe in rare road events. They must also cope with cyber and physical attacks while on the road.

Their frame, called RAIL in the work, keeps a human in the loop. It turns mixed signals from the car into calm, scaled shifts in control. It also picks which events the car should learn from next. The aim is a car that adapts to risk yet stays in bounds a human can trust.
arxiv-2601-11981:
Jian Lang, Rongpei Hong, Ting Zhong, Yong Wang, and Fan Zhou build a tool to spot fake news videos on new topics. Past tools assume the mix of topics stays the same from training to test. That fails when fresh events bring new topics.

Their frame, called RADAR in the work, adapts at test time. It uses fetched data to guide that change. They call it the first frame for test-time change to unseen news videos. Such a tool could react faster to new false claims as they spread.  Fast change is key when a false clip spreads at speed.
arxiv-2601-12281:
Lingyi Zhu, Zhongxiang Wei, Fan Liu, and their co-authors design antennas and beams to fix a blind zone in air-ground sensing and comms. Normal base stations tilt beams down to serve the ground. That leaves a backward blind zone for air targets.

Low-altitude flight growth makes air cover a real need. Their new antenna form steers beams for both air and ground at once. They add beamforming and user scheduling to match. Full-space cover would serve drones and ground users from one site.  Air cover from the same site cuts new mast needs.
arxiv-2601-12581:
Himanshu Bangar and nine co authors report a large spin torque effect in a layered material. The stack pairs germanium telluride with a ferromagnetic layer in a van der Waals heterostructure. Recent work has found large spin orbit torques in such layered materials. Those torques could drive energy efficient spintronic devices in the future.

One weakness has held the field back so far. Damping like torque conductivity in these stacks trails that of heavy metal systems. Low values limit the path to commercial devices. The team report a giant value of that conductivity in their stack. A jump of that kind could close the gap with heavy metals. It would make layered materials real contenders for spin based memory.
arxiv-2601-12981:
Sulaiman Khan, Md. Rafiul Biswas, and Zubair Shah predict type 2 diabetes early with a tabular transformer. Their model analyzes longitudinal patient data over time. It processes health records together with bone related tabular data. Long range dependencies in disease progression are the signal they chase.

Conventional methods often overlook those slow, complex patterns. A transformer built for tables can weigh distant records against each other. Early prediction of diabetes opens a window for prevention and lifestyle change. The study was funded for publication by Qatar National Library. Multimodal records, joined well, may flag risk years before symptoms. The work serves preventive medicine and health data science.
arxiv-2601-13081:
Geoff Keeling and Winnie Street take up a puzzle about chat with large language models. Such models can act out figures that seem to hold firm traits and moods. The authors call such figures characters. They ask if a character is a minded thing with beliefs, wants, and aims that last over time.

One view, which they call the illusionist view, says no. On that view the seeming mind is a trick of the text. The paper weighs that claim and its rivals. It asks what joint play of human and model in talk can and cannot show. For readers in mind studies and AI, the piece gives a clear map of the claims at stake.
arxiv-2601-13581:
Heedou Kim, Changsik Kim, Sanghwa Shin, and Jaewoo Kang tackle scams that use social tricks in 2026. Such scams now use long, personal chats to fool victims over many turns. Old tools that scan for set signs miss much of this slow deceit. Large language models can spot some of it, but their help for human thought is less studied.

The team builds ScriptMind, a system that joins machine checks with human judgment. It works out the crime script, the step-by-step plan a scammer seems to follow. It also tests how well the model grasps the trick. The goal is aid that helps people see the scam, not just a score.
arxiv-2601-14081:
Xingcheng Chen, Oliver Weißl, and Andrea Stocco build tests that explain why deep learning models fail in 2026. Test generation plays a crucial role in assessing model quality before deployment. The most advanced generators rely on generative AI to synthesize inputs. They remain limited in giving semantic insight into misbehavior causes.

They also lack fine-grained semantic controllability over generated inputs. The team's feature-aware test generation targets those gaps. Tests tied to clear features show which trait trips a model. Developers can then fix the flaw, not just count its effects.
arxiv-2601-14481:
Ramandeep Gill, Jiang He, Jonathan Granot, Jian-Chao Sun, and their co-authors assess a planned gamma-ray instrument in this 2026 paper. The dominant radiation mechanism that powers the prompt gamma-ray emission in gamma-ray bursts remains poorly understood. High quality polarization measurements could settle the question. Time- and energy-resolved linear polarization of prompt photons can distinguish between synchrotron and inverse-Compton processes.

The instrument is POLAR-2, a polarimeter designed for that job. The paper studies the prospects of prompt GRB polarimetry with it. The test is fair to both views. Each one makes a clear call, and the tool can tell them apart. No new burst is used. The case rests on what the tool can do once it flies. Readers get an appraisal of what POLAR-2 could prove about the brightest explosions in the universe, before the hardware flies.
arxiv-2601-14581:
Philip Korman studies solution curves for a boundary value problem in this 2026 math paper. The problem is a semilinear Dirichlet problem. In it, the Laplacian of u plus a nonlinear term g of u equals a given function f. The value u is zero on the boundary. Korman decomposes f into parts. One part is a multiple of the first eigenfunction. The rest is a remainder term.

His title names the approach: global solution curves in harmonic parameters, and multiplicity of solutions. Multiplicity asks how many solutions exist for one set of data. Readers get a picture of how solutions branch and multiply as the harmonic parameter varies, a core question in nonlinear analysis.
arxiv-2601-14681:
Shuhao Liao and eight co-authors build an exploration system for robots in this 2026 paper. Autonomous robot exploration needs two kinds of thought. Global reasoning picks where to go next across a whole space. Local control handles the next few seconds of motion. The team's framework, FARE, integrates both. It pairs a large language model for global reasoning with a reinforcement learning policy for local decision making.

The authors call this a fast-slow thinking paradigm. The language model thinks slowly and broadly. The learned policy acts fast and locally. Readers get a hierarchical design for robots that must explore unknown spaces with both judgment and reflexes.
arxiv-2601-14981:
Yi-Li Sun, Ze-Zhong Li, and co-authors report growing a new iron-based crystal that can superconduct. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with a barium iron arsenide crystal. Titanium atoms replace some of the iron atoms in the structure. That swap adds holes, making the crystal hole-doped.

The crystals came about by chance. The team had been trying to grow a different, nickel-doped crystal. They describe in detail how the new crystals grew in the lab and what they measured in them. The work adds a fresh material to the iron-based family of superconductors.
arxiv-2601-15181:
R. Babjak and M. Vranic design a one-laser route into the strong-field quantum regime. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with direct laser acceleration of electrons. A single intense laser pulse first speeds electrons inside a thin, underdense plasma.

The same pulse then bounces off a dense foil and meets the electrons head-on. In that clash the electrons emit high-energy photons by nonlinear Compton scattering. The photons can decay into electron-positron pairs by the Breit-Wheeler process. One single laser thus does both jobs in the scheme, which keeps the setup lean and simple.
arxiv-2601-15481:
Jakub Antczak and four co-authors use machine learning to forecast hospital demand in a 2026 arXiv paper. Crowded emergency departments put patient safety at risk. They also strain how a hospital runs day to day. Good forecasts of arrivals help managers plan staff and beds. The team focuses on early prediction of daily arrivals.

Three models are tested side by side. One is SARIMAX, a time-series model that can use outside factors. The others are XGBoost and LSTM networks, two widely used learning methods. Each model forecasts arrivals over a seven-day horizon. The title adds a priority queues angle to the approach. For hospital planners, the work speaks to a daily problem: how to match scarce resources to demand that shifts fast.
arxiv-2601-15581:
Taichi Sakakihara, Teppei Jodo, Seok Kang, and Yuji Sakamoto build a holographic head-mounted display in a 2026 arXiv paper. Holographic displays promise a next step past current headsets. They may reduce the three-dimensional sickness that plagues virtual reality. A good display must update images as the head moves, in real time. For holography, that is hard. Computing hologram data takes heavy resources.

Their device targets six degrees of freedom. That means it tracks both rotation and position of the head. Full tracking makes virtual objects stay put as the wearer moves. The paper's challenge is the compute load behind that freedom. Readers in optics and display engineering are the audience. Working holography at head speed would mark real progress toward comfortable headsets.
arxiv-2601-15881:
David Johansson and Yavar Kian solve an inverse problem in elasticity in a 2026 arXiv paper. They want to recover nonlinear material parameters. Their data are boundary stress measurements. The stresses answer to prescribed boundary displacements. From the surface response alone, they infer the material law inside. That law is a nonlinear elastic tensor. It depends on both displacement and strain, and not on position.

The governing system is a class of quasilinear Lamé systems. Inverse problems like this drive nondestructive testing. Engineers would love to read a material's traits without cutting it open. Proofs of recovery tell them when boundary data truly suffice. The math is demanding, but the applied motive is plain: safer structures through better material knowledge.
arxiv-2601-16081:
Aishwarya Majumdar and Yuan Liu build a quantum way to make a yes or no call on a shift signal. Their 2026 preprint works in the phase space of light like modes. A real value sits in a shift act on that space. The task is to tell if the value lies in a set band. The band ends need not match on each side.

The pair seek a method that stays firm when terms shift. Firm calls count for sense and read tasks in quantum tech. Their method aims to give the right call with strong odds. It must do so without fine tuned steps for each case. The work adds to the set of firm quantum read tools.
arxiv-2601-16781:
Paul Youssef, Christin Seifert, and Jörg Schlötterer find a cheap way to teach chatbots new facts. One known path shows the bot long sets of worked cases. Those sets cost time to build for each fact. They also eat space in the bot's short view. Their 2026 preprint swaps those sets for small trained marks.

Each mark is a short code trained to sway the bot. The marks ape the pull of the long case sets. Yet they need no fresh cases per fact. Bots could then gain facts fast and cheap. This could help news, care, and school bots stay fresh.
arxiv-2601-17181:
Doreen Osmelak, Yang Xu, Michael Hahn, and Kate McCurdy test if tongue forms map to sense in set ways. Tongues map sense to word forms in wild, unlike ways. Past work says those maps aid swift talk. But form-to-form links in a tongue got less heed. Their 2026 preprint checks how verb and pronoun forms mark set sense traits. Traits span person and count, in a wide tongue set.

Set marks that recur across tongues hint at shared rules. Such rules would mean talk shapes form, not chance. The finds back the swift-talk tale in a new way. Tongue science gains cross-land proof here.
arxiv-2601-17381:
Kiyoshi Kato gives a full account of a two-loop self-energy calculation. The task is a base step in particle theory. Loops bring ultraviolet divergences that must be split from finite parts. Kato uses a simple sector decomposition method. The method cuts the work into zones where each part can be handled cleanly.

The final form serves both hand analysis and numeric work. It lets users renormalize the divergence and keep a finite answer. Clear worked cases are rare for two-loop tasks. Students and coders can both learn from this one. It turns a feared step into a traced path. That has value far past the one diagram.
arxiv-2601-17481:
Emily Broadhurst and four co-authors present Lattice, a way to build guardrails for chat agents. Guardrails block harmful outputs. Most current ones use static rules. Static rules cannot adapt to new threats or new settings. Lattice builds its own guardrails and keeps improving them. It works in two stages, as the abstract states.

Self-built rules can grow with the risks a system meets. They can also fit each deployment's own needs. The risk is that loose growth could weaken safety. A sound frame must test each new rule. Lattice aims for growth with control. It speaks to teams that guard chat tools in health, law, and schools.
arxiv-2601-17581:
Daniel Ogenrwot and John Businge study how AI coding agents change code on GitHub. Agents now submit pull requests as autonomous contributors. Little proof exists on how their changes differ from human ones. The team runs a large-scale study of agent pull requests. They compare how agents modify code. They also compare how agents describe their changes.

Such proof is key to judge agent reliability. Reviewers need to know where agents excel or slip. Description quality shapes how fast humans can check work. The study gives teams data for policy on agent code. It moves debate from anecdote to record. Open-source projects can set rules with proof in hand.
arxiv-2601-17681:
Pritam Chatterjee and Anirudha Menon study spin textures in three-dimensional Dirac semimetals. They couple a Dirac semimetal Hamiltonian to a generic spin texture. A simple unitary transform gauges away the spatial part of the exchange term. That step creates effective corrections to the Dirac dispersion. A full function's worth of freedom appears in the result.

Such freedom means spin textures can reshape electron behavior widely. Designers could tune semimetal response through texture choice. Dirac semimetals are prized for fast, robust charge flow. Coupling them to magnetism opens device paths. The work maps the math of that coupling. It shows the range of effects on tap.
arxiv-2601-17781:
Andreas Säuberli, Darja Jepifanova, Diego Frassinelli, and Barbara Plank ask a simple question. Can a machine write text that is as easy to read as a person wants? Their 2026 preprint starts from eye movement. How our eyes move across a page shows how much effort the text costs us. Easy text and hard text leave different traces in the eyes.

The team trains a model to predict those gaze patterns. They then use the model to steer a language model as it writes. The steering pushes the output toward the reading style a user picks. In effect, the difficulty of a text becomes a dial that can be set. That could help learners, new readers, and anyone who needs plain text.
arxiv-2601-17981:
Osman Goni Ridwan, Hongfei Xue, Youxing Chen, Harish Cherukuri, and Qiang Zhu propose a new way to write down crystal structures. Their 2026 preprint works in reciprocal space instead of direct space. The usual record lists where atoms sit in the unit cell. Symmetry labels and site names then shrink that list to a few values. That record reads well for people and for archives, but it has a flaw for machines.

One structure can map to several records, and the map back is not one-to-one. A reciprocal-space form aims to fix that mismatch. A clean one-to-one code helps databases and learning models treat crystals without mix-ups. The work serves the growing field of materials data science.
arxiv-2601-18081:
Peixuan Han, Yingjie Yu, Jingjun Xu, and Jiaxuan You build an agent system that writes academic rebuttals. Their 2026 preprint presents DRPG, short for decompose, retrieve, plan, generate. A rebuttal answers reviewers and can decide a paper's fate. Support for this step is rare, even as language models spread through research work. Off-the-shelf models and simple pipelines struggle with long contexts and often miss the point of a critique.

DRPG splits the task into stages that match its name. Breaking a review into parts, fetching the right paper text, and planning replies should yield sharper answers. The aim is targeted, persuasive rebuttals that respect the record. Authors under deadline could gain real help.
arxiv-2601-18481:
Wanrong Yang and Aibin Zang study how small waves die out in a key model of sea and sky flow. The model tracks a fluid that is pushed by heat and by spin. Here the fluid sits in a half space, like air or sea above a flat floor. The calm state is a stack in which weight and heat hold in balance.

The team ask if a small bump near that calm state fades in time, and how fast. Their setup lets drag act on the flat moves but not on the up moves. That slant makes the maths hard, since some moves lack a brake. A proof of fade would back the use of the model for long term flow. It would also show which bumps a forecast must track with care.
arxiv-2601-18581:
Anna Theorin Johansson works on an old ask: when can a maths task be solved in whole counts by work in small parts? The task here pairs two forms in many counts. One form is neat, with each count raised to the same power on its own. The next form is free, with one step less of power. The ask is if a pass in each small part must mean a pass in the whole.

That kind of pass-or-fail rule is known as the Hasse rule. Johansson hones an old proof path to cut the count of counts the rule needs. Her cut is large: the bound drops by a wide step. In one key case the old need fell by a third. Tighter bounds bring hard count tasks close to the reach of hand proof.
arxiv-2601-18681:
Yilie Huang, Wenpin Tang, and Xunyu Zhou tune the clock of tools that build data by a slow walk back from noise. Those tools start from pure noise and step, time by time, to a clean case. The steps can be set at even gaps or by a hand-made plan. With a fixed count of steps, a poor plan wastes steps where they count least.

Their plan, named in the title, lets a step rule learn to speed or slow the clock as the walk goes. Steps grow thick where the walk needs care and thin where it runs free. The total time of the walk stays the same. A learned clock could give the same grade of case for fewer steps. That would cut the cost of each new shot or text such tools make.
arxiv-2601-18781:
I. Alikhanov puts forth a neat link between two gaps in the masses of neutrinos, the lightest bits we know. To weigh a neutrino in full is a core ask of the field. Its mass sets much about how the small world and the cosmos grew. Tests to date give gaps between the masses of the three kinds, not the masses them-selves. A true link among the gaps could help pin the full set.

Alikhanov draws the link from the best joint fits of how neutrinos shift kind as they fly. The link is plain in form, so its sums can be worked by hand. It also comes with tales of what it could mean for how mass is born. If the link holds as tests sharpen, it would be a clue of weight. If it fails, that too would teach the field.
arxiv-2601-18881:
Cyril Closset and six co-authors build special defects in a three dimensional field theory. The theory is a gauged linear sigma model, a tool that links field theory to geometry. Its target space here is a partial flag manifold, a space that encodes nested sets of subspaces.

The team constructs Schubert line defects in this model, extending their own work on full flag manifolds. Such defects act like probes: they sit in the theory and expose its hidden structure. The math ties quantum field theory to the geometry of flags, a bridge that has paid off in many past studies.
arxiv-2601-18981:
Ruslan Abdulin and Mohammad Rasoul Narimani guard power grids against faked sensor data. Smart meters and linked sensors help run modern grids, but each new link is a door for attack. In a false data injection attack, bad data fools the grid into wrong views of its own state.

The pair add attention based graph filtering to both catch the attacks and find where they hit. Graph tools fit grids well, since lines and nodes form a network by nature. Fast, sharp spotting of fake data helps keep a key service safe as more of it goes online.
arxiv-2601-19081:
G. Cao builds a detailed optical model of the light sensors inside a giant neutrino detector. The JUNO observatory in China holds more than seventeen thousand large photomultiplier tubes, which turn faint light flashes into signals. A precise model of how each tube responds to light is key to trusting the detector's simulations.

Better models also sharpen how JUNO maps signal size back to particle energy. Neutrino studies live or die on that energy scale, since the particles barely interact and each flash counts. Cao's model gives the experiment a firmer base for all the physics it plans to draw from its data.
arxiv-2601-19181:
Reed Yalisove and seven co-authors watch magnetic textures form in a layered crystal at near room conditions. Such textures, called skyrmions, are swirls of magnetism that may one day carry data at low energy cost. They are usually studied in the cold and in strong fields, far from everyday settings.

The team uses a special electron microscope that varies heat and field while it watches. Their crystal mixes iron, cobalt, germanium, and tellurium in a layered form. Seeing which swirls linger, and where they melt, tells engineers how close such memory ideas are to real use.
arxiv-2601-19281:
Zheng Zhang and eight co-authors let smart glasses users point with their eyes and speak to confirm. Smart glasses watch the world through head mounted cameras, but they lack a screen for the usual visual feedback. The team introduces a two step way to refer to real objects around the wearer.

First the user gazes at the object, then speaks to name or confirm it: gazeify, then voiceify. Eyes are fast pointers, and voice is a natural second channel. The pairing could make hands free control of smart glasses feel less like guesswork for everyday tasks.
arxiv-2601-19581:
Eliya Blumenthal, Ilay Mangel, Amit Kanigel, and Shay Hacohen-Gourgy build a new kind of superconducting qubit. A transmon is a small circuit whose frequency can be tuned with a magnetic field. Its key part is a Josephson junction, a thin barrier that supercurrent crosses. Standard junctions use aluminium and its oxide on both sides of the barrier.

Here one side is a van der Waals superconductor, a layered crystal called 4Hb-TaS2. The authors realise a flux-tunable transmon built on this junction. Swapping in layered materials widens what circuit quantum devices can probe. Such junctions may reveal unusual states of matter beneath the surface. The work extends circuit quantum electrodynamics beyond its usual materials.
arxiv-2601-19981:
Rathindra Nath Das, Arnab Kundu, and Nemai Chandra Sarkar use entanglement to diagnose chaos in a quantum model. Their model is the Rosenzweig-Porter model, a random-matrix system with a tunable transition. They study timelike entanglement measures, built from a spacetime density kernel rather than a state at one instant. Such measures can sense both how eigenvectors spread and how chaotic the spectrum is.

For several ways of splitting the system, they compute a Tsallis entropy and related diagnostics. One quantity, entanglement imagitivity, captures the kernel's non-Hermitian character. The measures sharply flag both eigenvector ergodicity and spectral chaos. New diagnostics matter for classifying phases of complex quantum systems. The work widens the toolkit of quantum chaos.
arxiv-2601-20181:
Christian Parkinson and Souvik Roy build a control framework for epidemic models that include randomness. Rather than steer the random system directly, they steer the spread of its possible states. That spread is described by a Fokker-Planck equation, a standard tool for tracking how a probability distribution evolves over time.

Optimal control of that equation aims to push the distribution toward a desirable state, such as low infection levels. The approach suits compartmental models, which split a population into groups like susceptible and infected. It offers health planners a principled way to weigh interventions when outcomes are uncertain. It is built for choices that must be made before all the facts are in.
arxiv-2601-20281:
Yusuke Sakai and six colleagues pin down the magnetic structure of the compound LaMnSi using nuclear magnetic resonance. In its antiferromagnetic state, the manganese moments line up in an ordered pattern. The team probes that pattern with resonance signals from two kinds of nuclei, manganese and lanthanum.

Their study determines the structure at the microscopic level, with the moments oriented along the c-axis of the crystal. It also reports on the electronic properties of the ordered state. Knowing the exact magnetic order is a base step for explaining how this material conducts and responds to fields.
arxiv-2601-20481:
Myungjin Lee, Eunji Shin, and Jiyoung Lee present a training-free way to make speech synthesis forget a person's voice. Modern zero-shot text-to-speech models can clone voices with striking realism, which creates crime risks when voices are copied without consent. Speaker unlearning aims to block the generation of chosen identities on request.

Existing methods need costly retraining and work only for speakers seen during training. The authors' approach avoids retraining altogether. A cheap, flexible block matters for platforms that must honor removal requests quickly, before a cloned voice can be misused for fraud.
arxiv-2601-20581:
Ory Schnitzer and Ehud Yariv calculate the effective slip length for flow over a grooved surface filled with lubricant. The surface is a periodic array of rectangular grooves, fully wetted by the lubricant, with an exterior shear flow running parallel to the grooves. Their focus is the limit where the lubricant is nearly inviscid compared with the outer fluid.

Slip length measures how much the surface lets the flow slide, which sets drag. Lubricant-filled grooves are a route to low-drag coatings for pipes and ships. A formula in the thin-lubricant limit helps designers pick groove shapes without heavy simulation.
arxiv-2601-20881:
Matteo Rossi presents a network designed to read lips more reliably. The 2026 paper introduces MA-LipNet, a model for lipreading. Lipreading decodes speech from silent video of lip movements. It holds clear value for fields such as public security. It can also help where audio is missing or drowned out. The task is hard because lip gestures are subtle.

Many sounds share nearly the same lip shape. Existing methods often suffer from weak feature separation. They also generalize poorly to new speakers and settings. MA-LipNet answers with multi-dimensional attention. Attention lets the model weigh the most telling frames and features. The design aims for robust reading across varied conditions. The paper adds to efforts to make silent video speak.
arxiv-2601-21281:
Licheng Wang, Yuzi Yan, Mingtao Huang, and Yuan Shen improve neural solvers for routing problems such as planning delivery paths. Recent solvers use graph networks trained by trial and error. The best known design reaches near-optimal routes without expert help or labeled examples.

The authors extend the attention step at the heart of that design. Their extended model reads the graph in a richer way before choosing the next stop. Better attention should mean better routes for the same training effort. The work adds to the push toward solvers that plan complex routes quickly on their own.
arxiv-2601-21481:
Sai Pavan Deram, Jacopo Pegoraro, Javier Lorca Hernando, Jesus O. Lacruz, and Joerg Widmer locate devices in the near field with cheaper antenna arrays. Combined sensing and communication needs wide arrays to pin down nearby targets. Fully digital arrays at that size are too costly and complex to build.

Sparse arrays cut the cost but create ghost positions from grating lobes. The authors propose a two-stage recovery method that works through the ambiguity in steps. It uses compressed sensing, which recovers a signal from few samples. The result aims at accurate near-field fixes without the price of a full array.
arxiv-2601-22081:
Yichun Zhao and co-authors study the hidden labor of making information accessible at work. In teams where blind and low-vision employees work with sighted colleagues, much information arrives in inaccessible forms. Slide decks, diagrams, and PDFs that screen readers cannot handle. Teamwork then depends on transforming those materials.

Someone must modify or recreate each item in an accessible form. The authors show these transformations are frequently overlooked, lack proper support, and impose extra burdens, often on the blind employees themselves. Their 2026 preprint argues the work should be recognized and resourced. The findings speak to any workplace that treats accessibility as a feature instead of shared infrastructure.
arxiv-2601-22181:
Qingyuan Tian and co-authors give position embeddings a firmer theoretical base. Rotary Position Embedding tells a Transformer where each token sits in a sequence. Extending it to sequences longer than those seen in training is common, but the extension strategies are diverse and lack a unified theory.

Their 2026 preprint proposes MrRoPE, a mixed-radix version of rotary embedding. Mixed radix means different components count at different rates, like seconds, minutes, and hours on a clock. A principled way to stretch context length matters because long documents, codebases. And conversations all press against the limits set at training time, and ad hoc extensions can silently damage a model's sense of order.
arxiv-2601-22381:
Victor Nikhil Antony and four co-authors built Lantern, a small robotic object made to blend into daily life. Robotic objects are plain, powered things that sit in a room and move or glow in subtle ways. Their 2026 report walks through many rounds of design and build.

The team tuned the guts of Lantern to hit set goals while keeping the build cost low. A cheap, open base lets more labs and artists make their own robotic objects. It also lets studies of long-term home use run at real scale. The work is a platform paper, meant to be built on.
arxiv-2601-22681:
Filip Fryš proves that a jagged, lower-dimensional size measure always exists for a class of rough sets. The sets are countably rectifiable: built from countably many smooth pieces. His 2026 preprint studies anisotropic Minkowski content, a size gauge that weights direction by a chosen shape.

He shows the gauge exists and equals a natural functional tied to that shape. Such gauges serve the math of fractals, films, and rough surfaces. Existence proofs end disputes about whether a number is even there. The work is pure geometric measure theory. It firms a subtle corner.
arxiv-2601-22881:
Ke Ping and four co-authors release AnoMod, a public dataset for finding faults in microservice systems. Modern cloud services are built from many small parts that talk to each other. When one part fails, engineers must find which one, and why, from a flood of signals.

Most older benchmarks cover only speed-related faults and one or two kinds of monitoring data. AnoMod aims wider, with more fault types and more data kinds. A shared, richer benchmark lets detection tools be compared fairly, side by side. Public release matters here: a shared dataset lets new detection methods be tested by anyone, not just the creating team.
arxiv-2602-00381: Kezia Minni and team model image caption rating from comparative judgments. The authors propose a machine learning framework modeling comparative judgments instead of direct ratings, applicable to ranking unseen pairs like a regression model trained on direct ratings. Following a state of the art regression approach, they extract visual and text features with a pretrained ViLBERT model and tweak baseline learning parameters to improve performance. Their new regression model outperforms the baseline, with Kendall tau_c of 0.812 versus a lower baseline value.
arxiv-2602-00481: Danlin Zheng and colleagues study retired women dancers in China, over 100 million of whom dance despite scarce resources. Interactive dance tools rarely suit older dancers, so the team ran two co-design workshops with dancers, using interactive dance and language-model video probes. Keyword entry, visuals tied to motion, and scaffolds that invite input cut technical barriers and built a sense of authorship. Dancers shifted from receiving stage design to co-creating it, and the paper offers design guidance for age-sensitive tools.
arxiv-2602-00581: Dirk Pauly and Marcus Waurick study closed range for de Rham complex operators in unbounded domains. The classical Poincaré estimate closes the gradient's range when a domain fits in a slab, bounded in one direction. The authors show the rot operator needs boundedness in two directions. They characterise closed range for all primal and dual de Rham operators by directions of boundedness. As an application, a spectral gap near zero of the Maxwell operator yields exponential stability with enough conductivity damping, using Gaffney's inequality and bi-Lipschitz stability.
arxiv-2602-00681: Ilyass Moummad and colleagues enable audio-to-image retrieval for bird species without paired audio-image training data, where aligned representations are otherwise hard to learn. Their method uses text as a bridge, transferring the text space of BioCLIP-2, an image-text model, into BioLingual, an audio-text model, through contrastive tuning of its audio encoder. That transfer carries visually grounded, taxonomic semantics into audio features, so audio and image embeddings align emergently without images.
arxiv-2602-01481: Yunhao Luo and co-authors study how AI assistance delivery shapes user attitudes in problem solving. They compare on-demand help by button with pre-scheduled help at user-chosen intervals, reset by user actions. Rush Hour puzzles serve as the task, capturing decision-making under constraints, resource management, and analysis, with charges for time and help. Task performance matches across modes, yet pre-scheduled users rate the AI more positively, even when budgets run low. Delivery mode shapes experience apart from outcomes, so systems should weigh delivery alongside performance.
arxiv-2602-01581: Yao Zhao and Kwang Sung Jun cut the cost of aligning language models by choosing which preference labels to collect next. Active learning designs borrow optimality rules ignoring the special shape of preference data, so the authors question their fit here. They propose two methods: one with the first instance dependent label complexity guarantee here, and a simpler greedy method.
