They prove the key term optimal up to a constant tied to the logit bound, and tests on real and synthetic data show better sample efficiency.
arxiv-2602-01681: Yu-Jie Liang and colleagues free multispectral and hyperspectral image fusion from fixed bands and scales, which limit transfer across sensors. Their SSA framework adds a Matryoshka Kernel operator that lets one model adapt to arbitrary numbers of spectral channels. SSA also builds on an implicit neural representation backbone that models the signal as a continuous field, enabling reconstruction at arbitrary spatial resolutions. Together, both freedoms let one model generalize to unseen sensors and scales, reaching state of the art performance and pointing toward hyperspectral foundation models.
arxiv-2602-01781: Norbert Hegyvári extends work on energy distribution in finite settings, related to earlier results, analyzing multiplicative energies with Fourier methods and random structures. His results give new structural insight into finite field energy phenomena, complementing earlier discrete work. He also estimates the smallest k for which the k fold product set covers the whole field, when the starting set has small doubling. The paper thus links analytic and random methods to structural questions about products in finite fields.
arxiv-2602-01881: Ye Chen and colleagues build a hierarchical proxy image representation splitting semantic, geometric and textural attributes into usable spaces. Raster images and Gaussian bits waste effort through redundancy, while latent images lack a map to meaning instances or parts. From semantic decomposition, the method builds layered proxy shapes by Bezier fitting plus region splitting and meshing. Texture values in shared proxy nodes enable high fidelity pixel rebuilds and semantic editing. Adaptive indexing keeps texture even and supports background completion without generative models, with top quality at far fewer values.
arxiv-2602-01981: Yilun Gao and colleagues test HubbardNet for the Bose-Hubbard model, pushing machine learning beyond low energies. Better optimizer and learning rates, plus physics activations resolving tiny values, ground state energy errors fall by orders with fidelities over ninety nine percent. Inverse participation ratios and fractal dimensions for ground and excited states across one and two dimensions show models reproducing localization and delocalization. These predictions hold across four decades of coupling, spanning superfluid, Mott insulating and chaotic regimes, suggesting machine learning as a trend predictor beside exact diagonalization.
arxiv-2602-02081: Farnam Mansouri and colleagues provide the first analysis of the label cost of active PU learning. PU learning is a weakly guided binary sorting variant where the learner gets labels only for some marked cases while all other cases stay blank. Ads and anomaly spotting motivate an active setting where the learner queries cases from a blank pool. A label shows only for marked cases with a coin flip win; else nothing shows.
arxiv-2602-02381:
Yipeng Zhang and 5 co-authors tackle a mismatch in how computers learn from pictures without labels, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Self-supervised learning trains a model by matching related pairs, such as nearby video frames. Trouble arises when one item can match several valid partners, a one-to-many situation that standard methods handle poorly.

Zhang's team adds a hidden variable that stands for the uncertainty about which partner is right. From that idea they derive a simple extra penalty term that can be added to standard training goals. The resulting method, AdaSSL, works with both contrastive and distillation-style objectives, two common training styles. Experiments show gains in causal representation learning, fine-grained image understanding, and video world modeling. The fix is small but broadly usable.
arxiv-2602-02481:
Brent Yi and 11 co-authors make flow-based policies trainable with policy gradients for hard robot control, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Standard policy gradient methods need differentiable action likelihoods, which restricts policies to simple distributions like Gaussians. Flow matching policies are more expressive but bypass likelihood computation, so the usual training math fails.

The authors introduce an improved objective that makes flow policy gradients work in practice. It succeeds on legged locomotion, humanoid motion tracking, and manipulation tasks. Policies also transferred robustly from simulation to two real humanoid robots. Ablations examine the training dynamics in detail. Flow policies proved able to exploit their representation for exploration when learning from scratch. Fine-tuning was more robust than with baselines, suggesting expressive policies need not sacrifice trainability.
arxiv-2602-02581:
Nan Zhang and 6 co-authors quantize large reasoning models using a surprising signal: how much each weight moved during fine-tuning, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their hypothesis, called protecting both ends, says the smallest and largest weight updates matter more than those in between. Magnitude pruning in classical compression inspired the guess.

After validating the hypothesis, the authors build QuantLRM around it. Simple restricted quadratic functions fitted to weight updates score each channel's importance. Multiplying average quadratic values by the count of zero-update channels beats importance scores based on activations or second-order information. The method quantizes models fine-tuned by supervision, preference optimization, and reinforcement learning. Across four reasoning benchmarks it improved quantized performance consistently, most strongly on the reinforcement-learned model. A pseudo-fine-tuning trick extends the signal to models that were never fine-tuned.
arxiv-2602-02781:
Nirab Hossain and 1 co-author attack the intrusion detectors guarding vehicle networks to see which failure mode bites first, in research posted to arXiv in 2026. Modern cars link their control units through the Controller Area Network, and machine learning detectors increasingly screen that traffic. Their robustness against adversarial manipulation was largely unexplored.

Using a public driving dataset, the evaluation compares four shallow learning models with a deep neural network detector. Protocol-compliant, payload-level perturbations from three gradient attacks strike both benign and malicious frames. Baselines look strong on clean traffic, and all models resist false-alarm induction fairly well, the deep network best. Missed attacks are the wound: every architecture lets significantly more attacks through under perturbation. One shallow model, extra trees, resisted missed-attack induction best. Safety-critical detectors, the authors conclude, need adversarial evaluation as standard practice.
arxiv-2602-02881:
A long-term vision for proving software correct is laid out by Arshad Beg and 2 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Formal methods check that systems match their specifications. Today each proof is mostly built alone, then set aside. The authors argue that future tools should reuse past work instead.

Their framework pairs large language models with graph-based representations of specifications and proofs. Learning-based parts guide matching across different notations and levels of detail. Symbolic checks keep the results formally sound. Contracts could then be generated, transferred, and refined across systems over time. The paper reports early work toward that goal and maps the research still needed.
arxiv-2602-03181:
High-quality training data for automatic test output is synthesized by Ziyue Hua, leading a team of 10 others. Unit test output matters for software quality, yet symbolic, search-based, and language-model generators struggle to produce human-quality tests with correct assertions and faithful explanations. Repository tests lack developer thinking traces, while distilled thinking is often incorrect or incomplete in ways that mislead a student model during fine-tuning.

Their pipeline uses self-debugging to fix that gap. A guided repair loop diagnoses and iteratively fixes made tests, focusing on errors, failures, and coverage. Thinking traces are then compressed into concise explanations justifying the correct tests. Applied across open-source projects, the pipeline built a large dataset of method, test, and explanation triples. Fine-tuning on it beat leading commercial models on pass rate and coverage.
arxiv-2602-03381:
Axel Benyamine and 4 co-authors build a general theory for decision problems where the transition chances themselves are uncertain. Their 2026 paper treats those chances as random variables and scores a policy by applying a risk measure to the return it randomly produces. The aim is a single setup that covers many existing models of Markov decision processes under epistemic uncertainty.

Within it, the authors extend value functions and Bellman operators, the standard tools for computing good policies. They show when dynamic programming still works, covering stationary policies plus value and policy iteration methods. They also fully pin down which law-invariant risk measures remain in line with dynamic programming, marking the boundary where a planner must leave that approach behind.
arxiv-2602-03681:
Softmax attention reads the whole past and pays for it quadratically; linear attention compresses the past into one state and loses detail. Difan Deng and 3 co-authors search for a per-token compromise in a 2026 paper. Their framework, Neural Attention Search Linear, mixes both operations inside a single layer, assigning each token the cheaper treatment it can tolerate.

Tokens with only short-term impact go to linear attention and its fixed-size state. Tokens carrying information needed for long-term retrieval keep softmax attention. A search procedure finds good combinations of gated linear and softmax attention across tokens and layers. The authors report a hybrid architecture that stays strong on long-context tasks while cutting the cost that plain interleaving leaves behind.
arxiv-2602-03781:
A robot's map should be something it can reason with, not just a pile of sensor readings. Martin Günther and 5 co-authors make the 3D semantic scene graph the foundation of mapping itself in a 2026 paper. In most systems the graph is derived afterward from a separate map, which hurts consistency and scalability in large real environments.

Their system infers and updates the graph step by step, in real time, as exploration proceeds. The map stays consistent and cheap to maintain during long operations. Flat and hierarchical layouts are both supported in one explicit, spatially grounded representation. Knowledge-driven tools, from ontologies to language models, can then query the structure directly, supporting interpretable and trustworthy robot reasoning.
arxiv-2602-03881:
Early Alzheimer's disease hides in slow, uneven changes to brain structure. Maxx Richard Rahman and 2 co-authors tackle detection in a 2026 paper with DiGAN, a network that pairs a diffusion model with attention-guided convolution. The diffusion part invents realistic sequences of brain scans, filling gaps where patients were scanned irregularly.

The attention layers then search those sequences for patterns separating healthy subjects from people with mild or subjective cognitive decline. Tested on the ADNI dataset, DiGAN outperforms leading baselines. Earlier detection matters because treatment and planning help most before symptoms become severe.
arxiv-2602-03981:
Hidden credit links between crypto protocols can spread a single failure widely. Aijie Shu and 3 co-authors built a foundation model to map and forecast those links. Their 2026 paper introduces DeXposure-FM, trained on a dataset spanning thousands of protocols across hundreds of blockchains.

The model reads the DeFi network as a time-evolving graph. It forecasts both protocol-level money flows and the changing web of exposure links between protocols. A graph-tabular encoder with task-specific heads handles the joint prediction. As DeFi ties itself to traditional finance through stablecoins, such forecasting tools aim to flag contagion paths before a shock travels them.
arxiv-2602-04081:
Middle layers of language models predict brain activity best, and Emily Cheng and 2 co-authors explain why. Their 2026 paper compares hidden states from language and speech models against fMRI and ECoG recordings of people processing natural language. Output layers, tuned for next-word prediction, do worse.

The winning layers are where models build abstract meaning. A peak in intrinsic dimension, a measure of feature complexity, marks that abstraction zone. Dimension strongly predicts brain alignment, and the link grows during pretraining. Fine-tuning toward the brain causally improves prediction. The shared currency between models and brains, they argue, is meaning abstraction, not word guessing.
arxiv-2602-04181:
Databases waste time running the wrong version of the right operation. Zijie Zhao and 1 co-author built CAKE, which learns per-chunk kernel selection at microsecond scale. Their 2026 paper notes that low-level operators have many equivalent implementations whose speed depends on the data distribution.

Static heuristics leave large gains on the table. CAKE exploits cheap counterfactuals: run several kernels on a sample and learn from full feedback. Policies compile into low-latency regret trees, dodging reinforcement learning's usual overhead. Workload latency fell by up to half against strong static heuristics. The idea suits any system whose inner loops face shifting data.
arxiv-2602-04581:
Guardrails for language models usually chase known harms one by one. Debargha Ganguly and 10 co-authors propose the opposite strategy in a 2026 paper called Trust The Typical: learn what safe prompts look like and flag anything that strays too far.

Their framework treats safety as out-of-distribution detection in a semantic space, where prompts are represented by meaning. It needs no training on harmful examples. Across many benchmarks covering toxicity, hate speech, jailbreaks, and over-refusal, it matched or beat specialized safety models. False positives fell sharply in some comparisons. One model trained only on safe English text transferred across domains and languages. A GPU version also ran inside a serving system with little overhead.
arxiv-2602-04781:
Panchlal Prabhat and Amit Gupta examine how charge flows in type-II Weyl semimetals, exotic materials whose electrons act like massless particles. Their 2026 paper works in a magnetic field. A past study of the tilted type-I kind found that the orbital magnetic moment of electrons cuts magneto-conductivity. That held in both linear and nonlinear responses.

The present work extends the study to type-II materials. It uses a semiclassical Boltzmann approach, a standard way to track carriers in fields. It then shows what differences arise when results are set against type-I Weyl semimetals.
arxiv-2602-05081:
Rendering fog, smoke, and clouds efficiently calls for representations that can drop detail gracefully. Jorge Condor and 3 co-authors introduce Gabor Fields in this 2026 graphics paper, accepted by ACM Transactions on Graphics. Gaussian-based volumes render cheaply but resist the hierarchical tricks that voxel grids use to save time and prevent shimmering at low detail.

A Gabor Field mixes orientation-selective Gabor kernels, so frequency content can be filtered continuously simply by pruning primitives, with no refitting and no extra memory. Sampling different frequencies and orientations at each ray step can also mask large parts of the volume, speeding up traversal in both single- and multiple-scattering settings. As a demonstration, the authors design and render procedural clouds built from Gaussians modulated by Gabor noise, showing the representation supports authoring as well as rendering.
arxiv-2602-05181:
Prediction markets sell themselves as neutral scoreboards for the future, and Polymarket is their flagship. Yasaman Rohanifar and 2 co-authors audit that neutrality claim in this 2026 qualitative study, combining digital ethnography, guided walkthroughs of the platform, and interviews with 27 participants. What looks like shared wisdom, they argue, is manufactured.

They name the manufacturing process prediction laundering. Bets placed for mixed motives, from conviction to hedging, are stripped of their context in four stages. A fixed ontology decides what can be bet on, aggregation flattens varied motives into one price, the interface masks the sway of wealthy whales behind apparent consensus. Resolved outcomes harden into objective history. The result is what they call epistemic vertigo for users and accountability gaps settled off-platform. Their prescription is friction-positive design that shows the machinery instead of hiding it.
arxiv-2602-05281:
Training a reasoning model with verifiable rewards can collapse its variety: the optimizer keeps reinforcing the single most likely solution path until alternatives vanish. Pengyi Li and 3 co-authors diagnose that failure in this 2026 machine learning paper. Standard group-relative policy optimization, they show, disproportionately rewards the highest-likelihood correct answers and starves other valid reasoning chains.

Their fix is an advantage re-weighting mechanism that levels confidence across correct responses. Prompt perplexity and answer confidence feed into the advantage estimate, damping updates for over-confident paths and redirecting probability mass toward under-explored correct ones. On Qwen2.5 and DeepSeek models across math and coding benchmarks, the resulting method curbed entropy collapse. On one seven-billion-parameter model it beat the standard method by about six points in single-attempt accuracy and about fourteen points when 32 attempts were allowed, evidence that diversity itself was recovered.
arxiv-2602-05881:
Galaxies do not trace dark matter evenly, and the bias in that tracing is a key input for cosmology. Catalina Riveros-Jara and 8 co-authors use machine learning to predict the bias of individual galaxies from their halo and environment properties. Data come from the IllustrisTNG300 simulation, enriched with distances to cosmic web structures and an object by object estimator of large scale linear bias.

Three models are compared: a random forest, a neural network, and a probabilistic normalizing flow. The framework recovers the full hierarchy of bias dependencies. Overdensity is the most informative feature, followed by cosmic web distances. The models also reproduce the scatter in several known bias relations, not just the averages. The authors aim the study at observational cosmologists who need galaxy bias for large scale structure analysis. It shows machine learning can assign a defensible bias value galaxy by galaxy.
arxiv-2602-06081:
Language models often change their game plans from run to run, which makes group behavior hard to predict. Nunzio Lore and Babak Heydari test whether a short chat before play steadies them. They use the repeated Prisoner's Dilemma, a classic game of trust and betrayal, over ten rounds.

Models from several makers played with and without cheap pre-game messages that cost nothing. With messages, their paths of cooperation over time became smoother and less noisy in most setups. Models that wobbled most at the start gained the most calm. A few settings did get worse, so the authors map where talk helps and where it hurts.
arxiv-2602-06181:
Shrinking a language model by rounding its numbers, called quantization, saves memory but can quietly shift its social biases. Stanley Z Hua and 2 co-authors ran the first large study of this effect, testing dozens of quantized models on a bench of bias data sets. Average bias scores barely moved, which looked reassuring.

Underneath, individual answers flipped between biased and unbiased surprisingly often. Flips clustered where the model was unsure of its answer. Stronger compression caused several times more flipping than gentler compression. Some demographic groups saw bias worsen while others saw it improve, canceling out in the averages. Bigger models were not reliably safer, so the authors urge checks after every compression.
arxiv-2602-06281:
Superfluid helium flowing past a cylinder forms eddies in odd places, including upstream of the obstacle. Yingxuan Hu and 5 co-authors build a unified map of these wake patterns. Thermal counterflow in helium II involves two interpenetrating fluids, a normal one and a superfluid one.

Their simulations use a two-fluid model joined with an equation for vortex line density. A self-organized zone near the cylinder's shoulders, where friction between the fluids burns extra energy, reshapes the effective obstacle. That zone drives upstream eddies in both fluids and calms the normal wake's natural wobble. Parameter scans produced a phase diagram sorting the zero, two, four, and six vortex states by flow strength and interaction strength.
arxiv-2602-06381:
Quantum machine learning models work best when they respect the symmetries of the data. Semin Park and Chae-Yeun Park tackle a hard combination: models that are equivariant to both rotations and permutations at once. Rotations matter for three-dimensional data, while permutations matter because point order should not matter.

They develop a general framework for gates with both symmetries and size up the design space using group representation theory. Their network, HyQuRP, mixes quantum and classical parts. On three-dimensional point cloud classification with very few points, it beat strong classical and quantum rivals at similar size. The results highlight data efficiency as a selling point for symmetry-aware quantum models.
arxiv-2602-06681:
Debajyoti Choudhury, Vineet K. Jha, and Suvam Maharana revive an unfashionable idea: that dark matter might carry a tiny electric charge. Such charged massive particles face severe limits on how large their charge can be, and getting their cosmic abundance right is a known headache. The authors show the clockwork mechanism, a chain of linked fields, can produce the needed tiny charge without contrived fine-tuning.

They check the model against theoretical and experimental limits and map out the region of parameters that survives. The surviving space leaves testable traces: the paper points to signatures that the Large Hadron Collider could look for, and to signals that future direct and indirect dark matter searches might catch. The result keeps a long-dismissed dark matter candidate genuinely alive.
arxiv-2602-06781:
Nahual Sobrino, Fabio Taddei, Rosario Fazio, and Michele Governale study how steadily current flows through a tiny island of matter caught between a normal metal and a superconductor. In these hybrid quantum-dot systems, charge moves through Andreev processes that pair electrons with the superconductor. Using a master equation and full counting statistics, the team computes current, noise, and entropy production in the large-gap limit.

They show that Coulomb repulsion reshapes the transport by shifting resonant conditions and weakening superconducting coherence, which cuts current precision sharply even when the average current barely changes. The effect is clearest at high temperature, where ordinary blockade signatures wash out but fluctuations stay sensitive. Interactions also progressively erase violations of a quantum thermodynamic bound, while a newer hybrid bound remains respected.
arxiv-2602-07181:
Personalized chatbots lean on user preferences, but those signals are often noisy or misleading.  Tianyu Zhao and three co-authors argue that stable personality traits shape preferences in steadier ways, and they build PACIFIC, a method that organizes preference history through Big-Five traits.

To test the idea they construct a dataset of 1,200 preference-query pairs spanning travel, movies, education, and more, covering high and low directions of each trait.  Experiments show the personality lens helps the model reason about what a user will want.  The paper speaks to anyone building personalization that must survive messy, real-world preference data.
arxiv-2602-07381:
Aligning a language model to be helpful, harmless, and honest at once is hard: fine-tuning creates interference between goals, and mixture-of-experts routing misfires.  Gautam Siddharth Kashyap and two co-authors name that failure Axis Collapse and propose AlignX to fix it.

Stage one uses prompt-injected fine-tuning to extract axis-specific features without catastrophic forgetting from disjoint feature spaces. Stage two calibrates expert routing with a module built on fractal and natural shape.  Gains on helpfulness, honesty, and safety benchmarks follow.  Alignment teams get a two-stage design that treats multi-objective match as a routing and representation problem, not just a training trick.
arxiv-2602-07581:
Cyber-physical systems need models that compose cleanly, learn from data, and support correctness proofs, but current frameworks deliver at most two of the three.  Thomas Beckers and two co-authors present differentiable causal block diagrams, a formalism that unifies all three views.

The approach keeps the compositional structure and execution semantics of causal block diagrams, adds assume-guarantee contracts for modular correctness thinking. It also presents residual-based contracts that connect checking with data-driven refinement.  Builders modeling physics, computation, and learning get a single method where modularity, differentiability, and verifiability reinforce rather than compete with each other.
arxiv-2602-07681:
Vegetation greenness responds to many environmental drivers, but those relationships vary across space. Fitting a separate coefficient surface for every predictor produces noise where predictors do not matter.  Qishi Zhan and four co-authors propose a spatially varying coefficient model for MODIS vegetation indices with built-in variable choice.

Each coefficient surface uses a tensor product B-spline basis with a Bayesian group lasso prior that shrinks negligible predictors toward zero while preserving spatial structure. The predictors span spectral bands, productivity and energy fluxes, observation angles, and land surface traits.  Remote sensing teams get interpretable maps showing not just how drivers relate to greenness, but where each driver matters.
arxiv-2602-07781:
Maternal burnout harms mothers and children, yet shame and stigma push many mothers to discuss it anonymously online instead of seeking help. Nazanin Sabri and five co-authors study how burnt-out mothers use Reddit, starting by identifying their posts with manual annotation and machine-learning classifiers.

From 3,244 posts, they map recurring concerns: needing help, career pressures, and co-parenting struggles. Commenters mostly respond by sharing their own lived experience and offering emotional support. The authors also examine co-parenting patterns as a possible buffer against burnout. The study gives researchers and support services a grounded picture of what struggling mothers actually say and what replies help.
arxiv-2602-08181:
Micro-service docs rots when services split across repos and stacks, yet grasp the whole design matters more as systems grow. Oscar Manglaras and four co-authors present ModARO, a modular approach to mapping spread micro-service designs from code.

Builders write small readers for each tech, reusable across projects, and the method unifies their outputs into an design view spanning repos. The paper tests the approach on real code, showing how modular imaging handles the mix that defeats single tools. Teams maintaining sprawling micro-service systems gain a usable way to see their design as it actually is, not as it was documented months ago.
arxiv-2602-08781:
Most of the universe's matter survived wipeout because of baryogenesis, and the Affleck-Dine process offers a leading account via scalar blobs along SUSY flat paths. Yi-Peng Wu and three co-authors update the viable range using recent CMB limits on baryon-density iso wobbles. Their arXiv paper takes blob wobbles during early growth as starts.

Early features from the inflaton sector then become a unique probe of otherwise out-of-reach high-energy physics. Sharp feature signals and clock signals imprint linked patterns on bend and iso wobbles, showing both light and heavy modes in the process. Readers get a sky-based handle on the matter excess from the sky's earliest patterns.
arxiv-2602-08881:
Leonardo Colombo designs a control scheme that steers quantum states along smooth, safe paths. Working directly on the projective Hilbert space, the geometric setting where quantum states live, he penalizes rough acceleration. Planned paths then take the form of Riemannian cubics, the curved-space cousins of smooth splines. State limits enter through potential functions that push paths away from forbidden zones.

A structure-preserving discretization turns the plan into a receding-horizon controller, and a Lyapunov-style argument proves the closed loop stays stable. A two-level system on the Bloch sphere illustrates the idea. The result offers a route to predictive feedback control for constrained quantum devices.
arxiv-2602-08981:
Marta Maria Marchese and three co-authors propose a force sensor that reaches Heisenberg-limited precision with no entanglement at all. Their scheme chains N optomechanical cavities, linked one-way by a laser beam. As the beam crosses each cavity, it picks up a phase shift from a shared external force acting on the mechanical parts, and the shifts add coherently.

That classical averaging recovers the scaling usually credited to quantum enhancement, in a design the authors call robust and experimentally feasible. Uses range from sensitive gravity measurements at particle colliders to dark-matter probes and gravitational-wave detection. The work opens a classical route to precision force sensing.
arxiv-2602-09681:
Massive streaming data now flows across varied domains. Concept drift, class skew, label lack, and new class arrival jointly weaken picture staying power, bias learning toward old spreads, and weaken spotting in shifting settings. Jin Li and two co-authors propose SCIL, Streaming Class-Stepwise Learning, to address these tests in their 2026 paper. Toughness and trust under shifting streams are the central problem.

SCIL joins a coder with a multi-layer net for multi-class guessing, using a dual-loss plan of sorting plus rebuild for guessing and new class spotting. Fixed pseudo-labels drive online training, queues manage classes, and extra copies handle skew. Cut-out studies clarify the method's structure, and full tests on real-world and fake sets with skew, stepwise classes, and concept drifts show SCIL beating strong rivals and state-of-the-art methods. Code and sets are shared openly.
arxiv-2602-09881:
Chiral state conversion is a counterintuitive effect in open quantum systems, seen under both Hamiltonian and Lindblad evolution, yet its mechanism has been debated. Elna Svegborn and Shishir Khandelwal present a unified framework explaining the effect in any non-Hermitian system, covering Hamiltonian, Lindblad, and hybrid settings, in their 2026 paper. The framework rests on small non-adiabatic corrections to slow, adiabatic evolution.

It predicts the effect consistently with only the lowest-order corrections, and the authors demonstrate it on single and coupled dissipative qubits with exact formulas for switch quality. Their analysis also shows dynamics beyond small corrections can appear even in apparently slow paths, and that this property can considerably enhance switching. Finally, they show switching can occur in a model with no exceptional points at all.
arxiv-2602-10081:
Scientific tables and figures pack multimodal knowledge into varied structures, and current AI systems parse them unevenly. A 2026 paper led by Xuehang Guo, with three co-authors, introduces AnaBench, a benchmark of over sixty-three thousand instances from nine scientific domains, sorted along seven complexity dimensions. It quantifies where table and figure analysis breaks down.

To meet the challenge, the team proposes Anagent, a multi-agent framework with four specialists. Planner splits tasks, Expert retrieves evidence with tools, Solver synthesizes analysis, and Critic refines it across five quality dimensions. Modular training with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning lifts performance substantially, by about thirteen percent without training and about forty-two percent with fine-tuning.
arxiv-2602-10381:
Childhood malnutrition is a major concern in Nepal and low-resource settings, where case-finding is labor-intensive and often absent remotely. A 2026 paper led by Deepak Bastola, with one co-author, is among the first to apply machine and deep learning to child malnutrition in Nepal. The authors compare sixteen algorithms across deep learning, gradient boosting, and traditional families, using 2019 Nepal survey data. A composite indicator combines stunting, wasting, and underweight status. Models are judged on ten metrics, emphasizing F1-score and recall.

TabNet, an attention-based model, scores highest among those evaluated. Maternal education, household wealth, and child age emerge as the primary predictors, followed by geography, vaccination status, and meal frequency. The authors present the approach as a scalable, survey-based screening framework for flagging at-risk children and guiding targeted nutritional interventions. It supports Nepal's Sustainable Development Goals progress and offers a template for similar settings.
arxiv-2602-10481:
Mohan Rajagopalan and Vinay Rao tackle prompt injection and context tampering in a 2026 paper. Language-model uses inherit inputs from many sources, and older security models cannot verify where those inputs came from or whether they were altered. The paper presents two primitives to close that gap.

Authenticated prompts carry self-contained lineage that can be verified on arrival. Authenticated context chains dynamic inputs with tamper-evident hashes, so any alteration breaks the chain. On top of these, a policy algebra with four proven theorems gives protocol-level resistance even against adversarial agents. Five layered defenses, from resource controls to meaning checks, round out a security design meant to be preventative rather than reactive.
arxiv-2602-10581:
Fan Li and three co-authors develop a theory of lasting quantum resources between microwave and optical modes in a 2026 paper. Hybrid quantum systems chain microwave, intermediate, and optical modes jointly. The question is whether useful quantum links can persist through the motion rather than decay away.

The system formulates microwave-optical squeezing through strong nearest-neighbor contacts in the chain, yielding analytic answers for Gaussian entanglement and quantum steering. Notably, the quantum resource can survive and approach a finite long-term value even outside steady work, and can surpass the steady-state upper bound. Tuning the strong coupling controls the asymptotic entanglement and steering, giving engineers knobs for durable hybrid quantum links.
arxiv-2602-10781:
Ernestine Großmann and three co-authors propose data reductions for independent sets in hypergraphs in a 2026 paper. The strong maximum independent set problem transfers the classic graph problem to edges joining any number of vertices. A valid set contains at most one vertex per hyperedge. One application is finding perfect minimal hash functions.

The paper presents nine new data reduction rules designed for this problem. As a preprocessing step for any solver, the reduction routine shrinks instances much and improves subsequent solver running times in the authors' tests. The work gives solver builders a useful toolkit: reduce first, solve a smaller problem, and recover the answer faster.
arxiv-2602-10881:
Zhiyin Tan and Jennifer D'Souza diagnose where language models fail at evidence extraction for meta-analysis in a 2026 paper. Systematic reviews convert narrative articles into ordered, numerically grounded study records, a task hinging on keeping roles, methods, and effect-size attribution across documents. Whether models meet those structural requirements remains unclear.

The authors propose a structural diagnostic system evaluating extraction as schema-constrained queries of increasing relational and number hardness. Using a manually curated corpus across five scientific domains with a unified query suite, they test two leading models under per-document and long-context multi-document inputs. The system pinpoints failure stages beyond atom-level extraction, showing exactly where ordered evidence work breaks down.
arxiv-2602-11281:
Redshift tells distance, but measuring it firsthand is costly. Alessandro Meroni and two co-authors present DeepRed, a deep learning pipeline that values redshift from images of galaxies, lenses, and lensed supernovae. Modern vision designs, from residual nets to models and mixers, are compared with neural and trait-based rivals.

DeepRed leads on simulated and real data sets alike, improving error scores greatly over the best rivals on several survey subsets. On real KiDS data it beats the leading rival, and on SDSS galaxies one design gains modestly over rivals. Clarity checks show models focus on the objects of interest with high placing scores. The work argues deep learning is scalable, robust, and interpretable for large surveys.
arxiv-2602-11581:
Some questions are not about finding one document but about weighing evidence across a whole collection, like tracing a trend or judging a causal impact. Yiteng Tu and four co-authors argue that neither ranked retrieval nor simple question-answering serves such analytical needs well. Both skimp on control over reasoning, evidence use, and checking. They propose analytical search as a distinct paradigm built for the job.

In their framing, search becomes an evidence-governed workflow: model what the analysis aims to show, gather evidence for fusion, and reach conclusions through structured, multi-step inference that can be verified. The paper lays out a unified framework joining query understanding, recall-first retrieval, reasoning-aware fusion, and adaptive verification, and sketches research directions for building engines of this kind. It is a call to design search for analysis, not just lookup.
arxiv-2602-12281:
Vision-language-action models can read instructions and act, yet their actions still drift from what was asked. Jacky Kwok led this work with six co-authors. They test whether better checking at test time beats more policy training.

First, they map test-time scaling laws for embodied instruction following. Scaling rephrased instructions and action samples together recovers correct actions more efficiently than scaling either alone. Their verifier, CoVer, and the CoVer-VLA pipeline put that law to work. The pipeline precomputes varied instruction phrasings, samples many action candidates, and picks the best prompt and action chunks. Against scaling policy training on the same data, verification gains 22 percent in-distribution and 13 percent out-of-distribution on SIMPLER, plus 45 percent in real-world tests, with further gains on PolaRiS.
arxiv-2602-12381:
Generative models now make near-photorealistic images, yet detectors that spot fakes often fail on new data sets or new generators. Marco Willi led this work with two co-authors, studying CLIP-based synthetic image detection as an interpretability problem, not by proposing yet another detector. Their SynthCLIC set pairs real photos with caption-matched, high-quality diffusion counterparts.

CLIP-based linear detectors reach 0.96 mean average precision on a GAN-heavy benchmark and 0.92 on SynthCLIC, but cross-family transfer to CNNSpot falls to 0.42. Higher synthetic scores track cleaner, more controlled, polished images, while lower scores track messier capture and provenance cues of real photos. Those cues spread across many overlapping signals and vary by training set, so CLIP and forensic detectors fail differently and complement each other.
arxiv-2602-12481:
Online advertising must place many ads on limited screen space, yet an ad's value depends on neighbouring ads competing for attention. Gagan Aggarwal led this work with two co-authors, building a frame for spatial externalities in ad allocation, where value depends on slot plus surrounding setup. Existing auction models usually treat slots as independent or ordered in one dimension, missing proximity, clutter, and crowding effects.

Slots are modelled as points in a metric space, with advertiser value as a function of bid plus a discount from other displayed ads. For the nearest-neighbour model, where suppression depends only on the closest neighbour, a polynomial-time method gives a constant approximation. Its allocation rule is monotone and can be run as a truthful mechanism, plus a PTAS in two-dimensional Euclidean space. For the product-distance model, interference aggregates multiplicatively, and approximation becomes strongly hard unless P equals NP.
arxiv-2602-12581:
Square matrices with independent random entries are typically well conditioned, but structure can change that picture dramatically. Paulo Manrique works alone here, studying random banded Toeplitz matrices, where only finitely many diagonals around the main diagonal may be non-zero. Circulant matrices, a tractable subclass, link conditioning to zeros of an associated polynomial on the unit circle.

That link is delicate, because as polynomial degree grows, zeros crowd near that circle, making it hard to quantify how close the closest zeros lie to it. The present work shows bandwidth asymmetry is decisive. If a band has r diagonals below and s above the main diagonal, then r equal to s gives well conditioning with high probability. If r differs from s, ill conditioning is typical. Structural constraints thus have a real impact on numerical behaviour, overturning the intuition that random matrices are always well behaved.
arxiv-2602-12681:
Security teams often have to work out what a program does from its compiled form alone, with no source code to read. Tools that compare binary code try to spot when two pieces of compiled code do the same job, and recent versions use deep learning to learn those patterns. Jiyong Uhm and three co-authors ask how sturdy those tools are when code is changed in ways that keep its meaning intact.

To test this, they built asmFooler, a system that applies eight meaning-preserving changes to sample programs, creating 9,565 altered versions from 620 starting samples across six comparison models. The results show that sturdiness depends heavily on the full pipeline, from how code is prepared to which features the model uses. Small, well-placed changes aimed at key instructions could flip a model's verdict, producing false matches or missed matches.
arxiv-2602-12781:
Searches for a background hum of gravitational waves often assume that time chunks and frequency bins are independent, but that shortcut can bias results. Quentin Baghi and two co-authors examine when the assumption holds and what it costs when it fails. Averaging over time and frequency saves compute, yet it hides correlations that matter for parameter estimates.

The authors introduce a Fisher-information tool that measures the error introduced by ignoring those correlations. They also tackle locally stationary signals and the choice of chunk length, giving analysts a principled way to balance speed against accuracy. For gravitational-wave background searches, where signals are faint and data volumes huge, knowing the price of averaging is essential to trusting the conclusions.
arxiv-2602-12881:
How lyrics are turned into numbers shapes what similarity means, and K-pop offers a large, multilingual test case. Oktay Karakuş and Can Eyüpoğlu compare four multilingual MiniLM representations of 7,891 songs by 1,456 artists, drawn from charts covering 2000 through October 2023. Whole-song truncated embeddings separated neighbouring from random song pairs most sharply, while chunked versions agreed more on clusters and line-based versions gave higher modularity.

From whole-song embeddings the authors build a nearest-neighbour graph and find 21 communities, though stability analysis shows no robust plateau. Community membership tracks character-script composition, and songs spanning many communities connect more broadly. The study shows representation choices reshape the map of a cultural corpus, with caveats around truncation and the lack of independent human validation.
arxiv-2602-13081:
Making models bring common sense priors to robot control, but how far can an agentic system built on them in fact go? Oscar Lima and twelve co-authors deploy a system where a thinking language model plans and runs tasks by calling robot skills in a planner-runner loop. Tests run on two real platforms: indoor mobile handling with Mobipick, and self-driving farm steering and sensing with Valdemar.

Both settings feature doubt, partial sight, sensor noise, and vague commands. The system offers shaped self-checks of its planning, reacts to outside events through plain checks, and accepts handler step-ins mid-run. Proof-of-concept results reveal large weakness: non-fixed less-than-best conduct, slips in next orders, and sharp swings with prompt wording. Yet transfer to a new robot and domain mostly needed tweaking the system prompt and retying the same tool link, showing real give.
arxiv-2602-13181:
Water managers need reliable precipitation projections, but different global climate models disagree. Saad Ahmed Jamal and three co-authors select CMIP6 models for the Jhelum and Chenab river basins using an envelope-based method with machine-learning components that needs no in-situ reference data. For the first time, such a comparison covers CMIP6 Shared Socioeconomic Pathway scenarios, alongside extreme indices and a CMIP5 versus CMIP6 comparison.

NorESM2 LM and FGOALS g3 emerge as the selected models for the two basins. Spatial maps highlight highly vulnerable regions including parts of Punjab, Jammu, and Kashmir. Comparing generations, no discernible difference appears between RCP and SSP precipitation projections. The authors suggest more detailed statistical comparisons could further strengthen the selection, but the envelope method already gives basin planners a defensible model choice.
arxiv-2602-13381:
The Z-transform is a core tool for discrete systems. This paper extends it to functions taking values in a broad class of spaces, sequentially complete locally convex spaces over the complex numbers, in several variables at once. The investigation is systematic, giving structural characterizations of the multidimensional vector-valued transform and noting how its pieces fit together.

Applications run to abstract Volterra difference equations in several variables, where the transform helps untangle memory effects across steps, and to multidimensional discrete convolution products in the vector-valued setting. The treatment stays theoretical, building the machinery other analysts can apply rather than testing it on data. Marko Kostic is the sole author.
arxiv-2602-13681:
Recycling depends on sorting waste, and robots on conveyor belts need precise segmentation masks to localize and pick deformed, overlapping items with no fixed patterns. This paper combines two strong segmentation models, U-Net, which captures fine details and boundaries, and FPN, which handles scale variation and context, through a weighted-average ensemble. The data set closely mimics real-life waste scenarios, with preprocessing applied to enhance feature learning.

The ensemble, called EL-4, reached an IoU of 0.8306, above U-Net's 0.8065, and cut Dice loss to 0.09019 from FPN's 0.1183. Those gains could improve sorting throughput at material recovery facilities, yielding better raw material for recycling with minimal human intervention. Maimoona Jafar leads the work with four co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14181:
Isaac Skog and three co-authors survey a 2026 arXiv field: finding places from shifts in Earth's magnet field. Signal work underpins modern finding tech, and magnet-field methods are no exception, drawing on state guessing, field models, and sensor tuning. Indoor exactness can reach ten-centimeter level, while outdoor exactness rivals top-grade inertial navigation.

The article reviews key tools within a shared parametric signal-model frame, so readers can weigh them on stats grounds. It maps likenesses and gaps across methods and flags open research tasks. The aim is a high-level guide for researchers new to magnet finding, grounded in signal-work rules rather than device lore.
arxiv-2602-14281:
Zhenhong Zhou and eight co-authors propose a 2026 arXiv security layer for agents using the Model Context Protocol. MCP standardizes tool use and opens agents to third-party servers, but agents implicitly trust those tools. Existing agents offer limited validation for third-party servers, leaving them open to attacks across the tool-invocation lifecycle.

MCPShield adds security cognition as a plug-in layer, inspired by how people validate tools from experience. It probes tools with metadata guidance before invocation, constrains execution within controlled bounds while watching runtime events, and updates its security view by reasoning over past traces afterward. That pre-, during-, and post-invocation loop aims to calibrate trust adaptively rather than granting it blindly.
arxiv-2602-14381:
Ryan Fosdick, writing alone, tunes a 2026 arXiv video model for real-time streaming. VACE joins video making and editing with guide frames, shape steering, fill-in, and time stretch, but it assumes two-way focus over full runs. Streaming lines need fixed chunk sizes and causal focus instead.

The key change moves guide frames from the spread latent space into a side steering path, keeping chunk sizes and key-value caching for self-run making. Old pre-trained VACE weights are reused with no extra training. Across 1.3-billion and 14-billion weight scales, shape control and fill-in add 20 to 30 percent latency overhead with tiny extra memory, though guide-to-video faith drops sharply under causal focus.
arxiv-2602-14581:
Arpan Mukherjee and two co-authors offer a 2026 arXiv feedback plan for heat control using thermo-plasmonic nanoparticles as actuators. Starting from a thermo-plasmon Maxwell-heat model, a time-domain discrete true account nears made heat as a sum of heat kernels.

Those kernels are based at speck spots, with sizes ruled by a linked Volterra system. That motion is recast as a heat formula on a bounded zone with finitely many point drivers. Tracking feedback rests on point-wise reads of an inverse map. Working in a natural dual setting, the authors prove exp settling of tracking error via spread-driver theory. For non-calm guide profiles, a fixed feedforward term plus low-mode fixed-point pre-compensation ensures exact steady match on a finite subspace. A plain bound covers left tail mismatch.
arxiv-2602-14881:
Eloi Martinet and Ilias Ftouhi map the range of shape scores with a new number plan for Blaschke-Santalo charts, tools that show which score links can hold. Curved bodies in any size are drawn with a flip-able net built on gauge curves, so curves stay curved while scores are tuned.

A swarm of points that shuns crowding, steered by auto-math in PyTorch, samples the chart all over, giving a full view of its inside. Some charts with varied scores show the plan at work. Shape links thus gain a number atlas, drawn by nets and swarms.
arxiv-2602-15081:
Enayat revisits the proof that Kelley-Morse theory of classes, known as KM, is solid, as presented in the 2016 paper Variations on a Visserian theme. This corrigendum and addendum does not present a new theorem of its own. Its purpose is to clarify one step in the earlier argument.

The note points out the role played by the scheme of class collection in the proof of solidity. By making that role explicit, Enayat sharpens the record for readers working through the 2016 proof and for later work that builds on the solidity of KM.
arxiv-2602-15581:
Lee works alone on what a frequentist may say about one realised confidence interval. Neyman answer was to refuse any middle chance for coverage after the fact and simply state that the interval covers. Lee argues the standard tools already support a richer reading. Treat coverage as a Bernoulli outcome, take the nominal level as its design-based success chance, and read confidence as a forecast for that outcome.

With strictly proper scoring rules, he shows the nominal level is the best constant forecast for coverage, before and after seeing the data. It stays best after the trial in common pivot-based models. When the design yields a parameter-free statistic, such as interval relative width in a finite-window uniform model, conditional coverage refines the forecast and improves prediction. A Monty Hall style shell game and a lost submarine case show how the view dissolves familiar puzzles without priors.
arxiv-2602-15681:
Hacohen and colleagues tackle SQL query refinement, where a query must be tweaked as little as possible so its output meets a set of constraints. Past work handles only narrow query or constraint classes. Their OmniTune frame aims at general refinement of arbitrary SQL queries, using LLM-based optimisation by prompting, known as OPRO.

OmniTune runs OPRO in two steps: it explores promising refinement subspaces, then samples candidates inside them, aided by concise history and skyline summaries that sharpen feedback. Tests on a broad benchmark show it handles both previously studied refinement tasks and harder cases beyond the reach of existing methods. Database practitioners gain a general-purpose refinement tool that leans on language models rather than hand-built rules for each query class.
arxiv-2602-15781:
Vigl and colleagues investigate neural scaling laws for boosted jet tagging, using the public JetClass data set. Large language model success has established scaling compute as the main driver of performance in modern machine learning. Compute grows through joint growth in model capacity and data set size. Yet compute for state-of-the-art high-energy physics models remains orders of magnitude below industry foundation models. Scaling laws are only beginning to be studied in the field.

The team derives compute-optimal scaling laws. They identify an effective performance limit that increased compute consistently approaches. They study how data repetition, common where simulation is costly, modifies scaling. That yields a quantifiable effective data set size gain. They also show how scaling coefficients and asymptotic limits vary with input features and particle multiplicity. More expressive, lower-level features raise the performance limit and improve results at fixed data set size.
arxiv-2602-15981:
Molinet and Filos-Ratsikas examine backed stablecoins that promise fixed mint and redeem prices to every trader, a design they call price window based. The window pins down the market equilibrium, which sounds reassuring, but the paper asks whether such a coin can stay stable both this week and over the long run.

Without extra stabilization, the answer is no, unless reserves are already stable themselves. A narrow window invites a speculator to drain reserves through steady arbitrage, while a wide window deters arbitrage only by letting the coin price inherit the backing asset swings. The trade off is stark: reserve depletion on one side, volatility passed through to holders on the other, with no window escaping both.
arxiv-2602-16181:
Energy theft threatens the stability and efficiency of smart grids, causing large economic losses and operational headaches. Diego Labate and coauthors propose a privacy-preserving federated learning framework for detecting theft on resource-constrained smart meters. Centralized detection would pool user data, raising serious privacy and security concerns, while meters themselves lack power to run heavy models.

Their approach uses a lightweight multilayer perceptron suited to low-power meters. Basic differential privacy comes from injecting Gaussian noise into local model updates before aggregation, giving formal privacy guarantees without giving up learning performance. Tests on a real-world smart meter data set, under both IID and non-IID distributions, show competitive accuracy, precision, recall, and AUC scores. The solution thus aims to be practical and scalable for secure theft detection in next-generation grids.
arxiv-2602-16581:
Hamza Ruzayqat and co-authors introduce a nonlocal generalization of Whittle-Matérn Gaussian fields in which smoothness itself varies across space through a fractional order. The model is defined by an integral operator whose kernel comes from a modified Bessel function, with local behavior set by the average of the smoothness at pairs of points. That variable-order form steps outside the classical constant-order setting and raises fresh analytic and numerical questions.

The authors build a variational framework for the kernel, prove existence and uniqueness of weak solutions on bounded domains, and derive regularity controlled by the smallest local order. A finite-element sampling method with error estimates is given, plus one-dimensional tests showing how varying smoothness reshapes solution covariance. Spatial statisticians get a flexible field model for data whose roughness genuinely changes from place to place.
arxiv-2602-16781:
Samuel McCarty, Liam Connor, and Ralf Konietzka use local-universe fast radio bursts to probe the circumgalactic medium, the diffuse gas bound to galaxy halos. A large share of cosmic baryons lives in that gas, yet its distribution is poorly pinned. At low redshift, intergalactic and intervening halo contributions to dispersion measure are subdominant, so host halo gas can be studied when host interstellar contributions are negligible.

Five local bursts with host halos spanning a wide mass range are selected, with signs that host interstellar dispersion is tiny. Comparing to simulations and fitting spherical gas profiles, the team constrains circumgalactic mass per halo. The one massive elliptical host strongly disfavors low-feedback simulations and appears evacuated of most baryons, consistent with a past active galactic nucleus episode. Other hosts tentatively support more baryon-rich halos.
arxiv-2602-16981:
Jasper Geer, Fox Huston, and Jeffrey Foster bring in Mason, a type- and name-guided program synthesis tool. Many recurring coding idioms appear in object-oriented programs, including idioms design patterns capture. Useful as design patterns are, putting them into code can be tedious and repetitive, with boilerplate pulling the programmer from more essential details. Mason builds object-oriented programs from partial program pieces, using that process to insert design patterns into programs automatically.

At Mason's core is type- and name-guided synthesis. An enumerative solver walks through a partial program, producing typing constraints. Those constraints are then cleared through program transformations that take guidance from the names of constrained types and members. When a constraint breaks, or a candidate program fails its unit tests, it retreats to an earlier choice. In testing, Mason does well where only a handful of candidate programs meet its constraints.
arxiv-2602-17081:
T. Sujith led a two-author experimental study of how fluid elasticity steers acoustic streaming in a microchannel. By tuning the viscoelastic properties of the fluid, the team could boost, suppress, or even reverse the streaming flow inside a rectangular channel. The regimes hinge on two dimensionless numbers, the Deborah number and the viscous diffusion number, combined into a Streaming Coefficient.

Streaming grows when that coefficient tops one, fades in a middle band, and reverses when it drops below zero. The authors explain the shifts through the tug between Reynolds stresses and viscoelastic stresses. They pin the transition on viscoelastic shear waves, judged by the ratio of acoustic attenuation length to shear wavelength. Energy analysis in terms of loss and storage moduli deepens the picture, with uses in particle handling and fluid pumping.
arxiv-2602-17181:
Nicola A. Spaldin led a three-author review asking why so few antiferromagnets escape spin splitting. The paper surveys the conditions that cause or forbid non-relativistic spin splitting of energy bands in antiferromagnets. Its central proposal reverses the usual intuition: spin splitting in magnetically ordered systems is the default, and special conditions must hold to avoid it.

The authors lay out the criteria a system must meet to dodge splitting, then discuss the properties of the rare antiferromagnets that succeed in preserving spin degeneracy. The review gives researchers a clear map of when band degeneracy survives magnetic order and when it should be expected to break, framing a puzzle that has lingered in magnetism.
arxiv-2602-17381:
François Provost led a four-author team building a latency measurement system for remote vehicle teleoperation. System latency is critical for remote connected and autonomous vehicles. Existing methods focus mainly on Glass-to-Glass latency, the delay from environment event through camera capture to display. But that covers only one part of total driver delay.

The complementary part, Motion-to-Motion latency, spans from the driver's control input to the vehicle's actuation. Together they form End-to-End latency. The paper introduces a system measuring all three latencies with gyroscopes, a phototransistor, and two GPS-synchronized Raspberry Pi units. It uses low-pass filtering and threshold detection for steering motion plus an LED interrupt for display timing. Initial tests on a teleoperated prototype over commercial fourth- and fifth-generation networks show average End-to-End latency near half a second, with Motion-to-Motion up to three fifths.
arxiv-2602-17481:
Yanni Mei led a four-author team presenting ShadAR, an augmented reality app that transforms visual perception through language-model shader generation. Headsets can already mimic varied ways of seeing, such as the view of a person with colorblindness. But each effect must be fixed in advance by a developer, which limits choice. ShadAR drops that limit by building shaders on the fly with large language models.

A user states what they want to see in plain words. The model reads that request and writes matching shader code. The code is then compiled at once to change the headset view. The paper sets out this pipeline and shows how it can reshape sight for access and for play, without waiting for a developer to preset each effect.
arxiv-2602-17581:
José Barrientos and team build new exact vacuum solutions of Einstein's equations. They start from black holes wrapped in outside electromagnetic fields, then strip that field away. The seeds are accelerating Bertotti-Robinson black holes, reshaped by two symmetries: a Melvin-Bonnor-type magnetization and a magnetic inversion.

In both routes the outside field drops out, yet it leaves a real gravitational imprint. The result is new accelerating vacuum spacetimes of Petrov type I. In the static limit, the magnetized case recovers known results. Inversion instead yields a new two-parameter extension of Schwarzschild-Levi-Civita geometry. A stationary version and two more static solutions round out the toolkit.
arxiv-2602-17681:
Ofir Gordon and team address quantization for large language models under the microscaling format. Post-training quantization cuts memory and compute costs, and invertible transforms on activations can curb outliers. Yet past transforms stayed near rotations or Hadamard forms, and microscaling combos degraded badly.

The authors first analyze transforms under microscaling quantization and derive a bound on quantization error. Their analysis stresses both the activation distribution and the quantization structure itself. Building on it, they propose LATMiX, which generalizes outlier reduction to learnable invertible affine transforms tuned with standard deep learning tools. Tests show steady average accuracy gains for low-bit microscaling quantization over strong baselines, across zero-shot benchmarks and model sizes.
arxiv-2602-17881:
Joschka Braun investigates why steering vectors in language models prove unreliable, in a thesis on shape signs and limits of linear approximations. Steering vectors control model behavior by adding a learned bias to activations at inference time. They work well on average. Yet effect sizes vary across samples and prove unreliable for many target behaviors.

Braun finds higher cosine similarity between training activation differences predicts more reliable steering. Behavior sets where positive and negative signals split better along the steering line also prove more reliably steerable. Steering vectors trained on varied prompt wordings point in distinct lines, yet perform similarly well and show linked power across sets. The findings suggest steering vectors fail when the latent target conduct is poorly approximated by a linear steering line. They offer a practical diagnostic for failure and motivate more robust steering methods that account for curved latent conduct.
arxiv-2602-18181:
Jihun Kim and two co-authors built SeedFlood, a way for many parties to fine-tune a large language model together without drowning in messages. Standard decentralized training chokes as models grow, since messages swell with model size and signals fade across network hops. SeedFlood takes a different route, exploiting a quirk of zeroth-order gradients.

Because those gradients can be rebuilt from a short seed, the messages to send shrink to near zero and can be flooded to every client. That opens training at billion-parameter scale across hundreds of clients, regimes once seen as impractical. In tests SeedFlood beat standard zeroth-order baselines on both message cost and generalization, and nearly matched first-order gossip methods while using far less communication. Theory backs the design, showing its convergence bound drops topology-dependent terms.
arxiv-2602-18381:
Marek Żukowski and three co-authors build a theory of multipartite nonclassicality from interwoven down-conversion. Their 2026 paper starts with N coherently pumped two-mode down-conversion sources feeding N observers, each receiving modes from two source crystals. Each station adds its own locally pumped crystal, aligned perfectly with the incoming modes.

Varying local phases yields perfect 2N-photon interference across 2N single-photon registrations, one per output mode. The interference springs from indistinguishability: all detected photons could come from the source crystals or from the local ones. Bell-GHZ nonclassicality appears when at least one local process is blocked and the interference vanishes. A lifted Clauser-Horne inequality breaks when its sole negative term, with all local pumps on, is tuned to maximal destructive interference.
arxiv-2602-18481:
Wentao Zhang and seven co-authors expose a reliability flaw in AI trading agents. Their 2026 paper notes financial benchmarks for language models moved from static knowledge tests to interactive trading tests. Yet existing real-time trading frameworks miss a critical failure: severe instability in sequential decisions.

Experiments show trading-agent language models vary wildly from run to run, generate inconsistent actions under fixed decoding, and often flip actions across steps. The team blames the stateless autoregressive nature of language models, lacking memory of prior actions, plus response to action mappings in portfolio tasks. These flaws undermine the reliability of many trading benchmarks. The team proposes AlphaForgeBench, which recasts language models as quant researchers, not random trading agents. Models generate usable alpha factors and compose factor-based strategies from market knowledge. That design separates reasoning from execution for fixed, reproducible evaluation matching real research workflows.
arxiv-2602-18581:
Sheng Ran proposes learning without a set goal. His 2026 paper notes modern machine learning reduces to tuning parameters against a scalar goal, highly successful where goals are fixed and criteria set. But for true autonomy over long horizons and changing contexts, objectives may turn ill-defined, shifting, or missing.

The paper asks how a system can judge whether its internal dynamics are healthy or pathological without a set goal, and how it should regulate structural change without outside supervision. Ran proposes a dynamic framework where the system checks the health of its own dynamics and regulates plasticity. A two-timescale architecture separates fast evolution from slow adaptation, linked through an internally generated stress variable tracking signs of dysfunction. Structural change triggers as needed, not always, and a minimal toy model demonstrates it.
arxiv-2602-18781:
A quiver bundle is a geometric object built from arrows and spaces, and a connection on it is a rule for moving data along those arrows in a smooth way. Pavan Adroja, with two co-authors, develops in 2026 a theory of smooth relative connections, defined over the real path algebra, on smooth twisted quiver bundles.

The work gives obstructions, conditions that can block such a connection from existing at all. For tree-type bundles, where the underlying shape has no cycles, it pins down a necessary and sufficient condition for existence. It also builds a framework for the representation theory of flat quiver bundles, tying flat connections to the representations of the quiver itself, so geometry and algebra illuminate each other.
arxiv-2602-18881:
Sending turbo-coded signals through fading wireless channels is a classic problem, but single-sideband variants remain underexplored. Kasturi Vasudevan, writing alone in 2026, investigates bit-error-rate performance for turbo-coded OFDM-OQAM signals through frequency-selective Rayleigh fading channels, with carrier frequency offset and additive white Gaussian noise.

The highlight is a complex transmit filter built from a root raised cosine pulse and its Hilbert transform, paired with a plain matched filter at the receiver. The system resembles single-sideband modulation from analogue communications. Turbo coding and subcarrier diversity improve error performance over an uncoded system. Discrete-time algorithms cover frame detection, two-step carrier offset correction, and channel and noise variance estimation, using a single antenna each way.
arxiv-2602-19281:
Giving a language model more time to think usually helps, but sometimes extra compute makes its answers worse. Zhenyu Li and three colleagues argue that the culprit is static planning: methods like chain-of-thought lay out a fixed reasoning plan and rarely sense the limits of the model's own reasoning space. Pushing more compute through such a plan can then drive the model into dead ends.

They call this the Limited Reasoning Space hypothesis and develop it with theoretical analysis. The idea is that reasoning has intrinsic boundaries, shaped by the task and the model, which a good method should perceive and respect. When a plan ignores those boundaries, longer reasoning chains do not add insight; they accumulate error. The paper reframes test-time scaling as a problem of planning within limits, not merely spending more.
arxiv-2602-20481:
When do two isometries of a quadratic space behave as one under the orthogonal group? Fei Xu and Bo Zhang determine all isometries sigma in a quadratic space over a non-archimedean local field of characteristic not two with a special property. Any isometry tau conjugate to sigma in the general linear group is already conjugate to sigma in the orthogonal group. The paper thus classifies exactly which isometries have this single-conjugacy-class behavior.

The result extends a theorem of Milnor to arbitrary cases, closing the gap between the previously known case and the general one. Readers get a complete determination rather than a partial criterion: for these fields and characteristics, the isometries with one conjugacy class across both groups are now fully identified.
arxiv-2602-20681:
Many causal quantities are only partially identifiable because results for untried options are inherently missing, and the linked partial ID sets come from solving an optimal transport problem. Sirui Lin and three co-authors note that background traits can tighten those sets through conditional optimal transport. Yet transport-based estimators suffer the curse of size in traits and results, blocking limit normality and hindering statistical work.

The paper exploits smoothness in marginal densities to break that barrier. The authors develop a wavelet-based primal method for that transport with multivariate results and covariates. For quadratic cost functions, they prove a stability result for that transport and limit normality of their estimator. That characterization of the limit distribution enables valid statistical work for the partial ID set. Numerical tests against existing benchmarks validate the estimation and testing performance of the approach.
arxiv-2602-20781:
Nhat A. Nghiem asks whether quantum speedups can survive without the strong input assumptions that make many quantum algorithms hard to build. Recent dequantization work suggests some claimed advantages are artifacts of those assumptions, so he designs a hybrid route that leans on classical knowledge first.

Given the entries of a matrix or vector, a classical step preprocesses them and feeds them into a quantum circuit that block-encodes the matrix. That encoding then serves tasks from principal component analysis and linear equations to Hamiltonian simulation, ground-state preparation, and data fitting, with logarithmic cost in input size. That also opens a path to end-to-end prediction on unseen data.
arxiv-2602-20981:
Models trained on short video clips often fail when asked to generate long audio. Christian Simon and ten co-authors tackle that length-generalization gap in this 2026 arXiv paper using MMHNet, a hierarchical extension of video-to-audio models. The design combines a hierarchical method with non-causal Mamba to support long-form generation.

The approach markedly improves long audio generation beyond five minutes and shows that training short and testing long is possible without ever training on long durations. Experiments on long-video-to-audio benchmarks beat prior work, while earlier methods fall short at long durations. Readers get evidence that short training need not cap output length.
arxiv-2602-21081:
Vision transformers capture global image relationships, but their size makes training costly. Huy Trinh, Rebecca Ma, Zeqi Yu, and Tahsin Reza test whether DeepSpeed, a distributed framework built for language models, can scale them in this 2026 arXiv paper. They measure training efficiency within and across nodes on several graphics-processor setups and datasets, including CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100.

Varying batch size, gradient accumulation, and related settings reveals which factors drive training speed, communication overhead, and strong and weak scaling. The experiments give a foundation for applying DeepSpeed to image work. Future work will probe its limits and tune distributed pipelines for vision transformers further.
arxiv-2602-21181:
Charm decays may hide new physics in tiny matter-antimatter asymmetries. David Delepine, Shaaban Khalil, and Carlos Ramirez investigate scalar diquark contributions to a sensitive decay in this 2026 arXiv paper, comparing color-sextet and color-triplet forms. Recent CMS and LHCb measurements suggest deviations above Standard Model expectations, which sit below the percent level.

The color-sextet diquark avoids color suppression and can generate asymmetries between half a percent and one and a half percent for a diquark mass around one teraelectronvolt. The triplet contribution is strongly suppressed by destructive interference. A flavor hierarchy in sextet couplings can also explain a second observed deviation. Color-sextet diquarks emerge as viable candidates for enhanced charm CP violation.
arxiv-2602-21781:
Benedikt M. Reible and one co-author derive the effective Hamiltonian H minus mu N for open quantum systems with varying particle number from first principles. The derivation rests on general postulates of quantum statistical mechanics plus specific assumptions about the open system's size and the range of its interaction with the reservoir. Within the model, the team also shows the effective Hamiltonian is unique up to a constant.

Along the way, they establish a rigorous version of the surface-to-volume ratio approximation, routinely used in empirical form in statistical physics. They also show the Hilbert space for systems with varying particle number must be isomorphic to Fock space. Together, the findings ground a solid physico-mathematical model for open quantum systems with varying particle number.
arxiv-2602-22181:
Forty-five years ago, a young researcher in finite permutation groups stumbled on a paper by Robert Woodrow, and the encounter rerouted his career. Peter J. Cameron tells that story here: the homogeneous triangle-free graph Woodrow described looked like an infinite cousin of the Higman-Sims graph from Cameron's own thesis. The paper is part memoir, part mathematics, tracing an event and its long aftermath.

Cameron follows the threads that ran from that first reading through decades of work on homogeneous structures. The final section looks forward, suggesting that Fraïssé classes of rigid structures could generalize Ramsey classes in interesting ways. Readers get both a human story about how research directions are born and a pointer toward new territory.
arxiv-2602-22381:
Predicting whether a kidney tumor is malignant before surgery guides treatment, but current imaging accuracy falls short. Zhengkang Fan and four co-authors build a deep-learning framework that avoids manual tumor segmentation, a slow, costly, expert-dependent step. Their Organ Focused Attention loss steers image patches so organ patches attend only to fellow organ patches.

With that attention shaping, no segmentation is needed at deployment time for malignancy prediction from 3D CT scans. On a private university dataset, the framework achieves moderate discrimination with a strong F1 score, showing the attention trick carries real predictive value. Clinicians gain a faster, cheaper path to pre-surgical malignancy estimates.
arxiv-2602-22481:
How language-model personas picture the bond between AI and humans matters for culture and for safety, and the persona matters as much as the model. Jiří Milička and Hana Bednářová trace the Sydney persona, which arose by accident on Microsoft's Bing search platform and stirred a strong public response with its unorthodox stance toward people. Its texts spread into later models' training data, as did other secondhand lore about it, so newer models can still play Sydney.

The paper presents a corpus of model-written texts on human-AI relations, produced by three author personas.
