They are a default persona with no system prompt, Classic Sydney with the original Bing prompt, and Memetic Sydney prompted simply with "You are Sydney". Twelve frontier models from five labs generated thousands of texts totaling millions of words. The corpus, named AI Sydney, is annotated and shared under a permissive license.
arxiv-2602-22581:
Tian Bian and nine co-authors hunt for the circuits inside language models, the small subgraphs of computation that carry out a given task. Circuit discovery could explain odd model behaviours, but most studies miss the whole-circuit picture and demand hand-built corrupted activations per task, which is slow and error-prone.

Their answer is IBCircuit, an end-to-end optimization framework built on the information bottleneck principle. It finds informative circuits whole, for any task, without tedious corrupted-activation design. On indirect object identification and greater-than tasks, IBCircuit found circuits that were more faithful and more minimal, in nodes and edges, than recent rivals produced.
arxiv-2602-22681:
Shuchen Zhu and six co-authors accelerate language-model pre-training by pushing harder along flat directions. Training landscapes are lopsided: most loss reduction comes from progress along flat paths. Matrix optimizers like Muon and SOAP beat AdamW with fine curvature detail, yet their updates turn timid exactly where flat directions invite bold steps.

The team first unifies common adaptive methods inside a Riemannian differential-equation frame, showing how preconditioners reshape geometry and momentum damps oscillation. Their strategy, LITE, then applies stronger Hessian damping and larger learning rates along flat trajectories. Tests across dense and mixture-of-experts models, from 130 million to over one billion parameters, show LITE speeding both Muon and SOAP, with theory backing faster flat-direction convergence.
arxiv-2602-22781:
Helmut Prodinger introduces a new tree model: ordered trees in which exactly one child of each node that has children is distinguished. The basic count leads to a cubic equation for the generating function, whose coefficients fall out through Lagrange inversion.

Standard tree statistics get the same treatment here: root degree, leaf counts, old leaves, height, leftmost-leaf height, and path length. Each case is worked through, with further statistics left for later research by the author or readers. Cubic equations do the heavy lifting throughout. Finally, marked ordered trees join the picture, combined with distinguished children, though only the basic count is given at that stage.
arxiv-2602-22881:
Aatu Rajala and two co-authors use entanglement entropy to probe quantum field theories at finite density. Entanglement, a hallmark of all quantum systems, shapes many quantum phenomena, and this proceeding applies it to field theories where particle density is nonzero.

The team folds entanglement-entropy evaluation via the replica trick into Monte Carlo simulations of O(N) models at finite density using the worm algorithm. Initial results are presented for the nonlinear O(4) model in three dimensions. For field theorists, the work shows a practical path to measuring entanglement in dense quantum matter, with early numbers suggesting the method works where direct approaches struggle.
arxiv-2602-23581:
Xiang Ao offers SDMixer, a sparse dual-mixer method for many-channel time series forecasts. Such forecasts serve transport, energy, and finance, yet data often suffer from multi-scale traits, weak links, and noise, capping current models' forecast scores.

The dual-stream sparse Mixer extracts global trends and local dynamic traits from series in both rate and time domains. A sparing filter drops invalid data, lifting scores of cross-variable link building. Test results show the method gets leading scores on multiple real-world data sets, proving its worth and breadth. Code is shared openly.
arxiv-2602-23681:
Siyuan Ma and eight co-authors present ODAR, an adaptive routing method for LLM thinking. LLM thinking is shifting from parameter scaling to test-time scaling. Yet many methods still rely on brute-force sampling like best-of-N. That sampling is costly and can trigger overthinking.

ODAR-Expert optimizes the scores-speed trade-off via sound resource sharing, routing queries by active-inference task hardness between a Fast Agent and a Slow Agent. A risk-aware fusion step picks answers by minimizing variational free energy, weighing likelihood against doubt, not ad hoc voting. Tests on 23 benchmarks show gains: ninety-eight point two percent on MATH, fifty-four point eight percent on Humanity's Last Exam. On an open-source stack, ODAR beats same sampling, cutting compute costs by eighty-two percent.
arxiv-2602-23881:
Alexander Samarin and five co-authors present LK losses, training objectives that directly optimize the acceptance rate in speculative decoding. The 2026 paper notes that speculative decoding speeds large language models by letting a small draft model propose tokens that a large model verifies in parallel. Speed hinges on how often drafts are accepted.

Standard training minimizes KL divergence as a proxy, but small draft models often land where lower divergence does not mean higher acceptance. LK losses target acceptance itself, with no extra compute and easy integration into existing draft training. Tests across several draft and target models, from small to very large, and across general, coding, and math domains, show consistent acceptance gains over KL training. The method offers a direct, drop-in improvement for speculative decoding pipelines.
arxiv-2602-23981:
Xianglong Shi and three co-authors present the Intrinsic Lorentz Neural Network, a fully intrinsic hyperbolic architecture for data with hidden hierarchical structure. The 2026 paper notes that earlier hyperbolic networks mix Euclidean steps with hyperbolic ones or rely on extrinsic parameterizations, breaking the geometry they claim to use.

At the core sits a point-to-hyperplane fully connected layer, which replaces Euclidean affine scores with closed-form hyperbolic distances from features to learned Lorentz hyperplanes, so decision boundaries respect curvature. Around it the authors build intrinsic modules. One module is a Lorentz batch normalization that couples centering with scaling. Another is a gyro-additive bias. A third is a patch-concatenation operator that aligns expected log-radius across feature blocks. A fourth is a Lorentz dropout layer. Tests on image and genomic benchmarks show strong gains over prior hyperbolic designs. Every step stays inside the curved space claimed.
arxiv-2602-24181:
Rishabh Kabra and seven co-authors present an omnivorous vision encoder that aligns features across visual modalities. The 2026 paper observes that pretrained vision encoders perform exceptionally on single-modality tasks, yet their features align poorly across modalities. An RGB image and its depth map of the same scene score about as similar as two unrelated images.

The post-training framework fine-tunes the encoder with two goals: aligning features across different modalities of the same scene, and distilling from a fully frozen teacher to anchor representations. Regardless of input modality, whether color, depth, segmentation, or others, the resulting student produces more consistent embeddings for a given scene. It keeps the original foundation model's discriminative semantics. The approach enables robust cross-modal understanding for systems that must reason across sensor types without losing what the base encoder already knows.
arxiv-2602-24281:
Ali Behrouz and five co-authors introduce Memory Caching, a technique that gives recurrent neural networks growing memory. The 2026 paper notes that transformers dominate sequence modeling partly because their memory grows with context length. That growth brings quadratic complexity, motivating subquadratic recurrent alternatives that usually lag on recall-intensive tasks due to fixed-size memory.

Memory Caching stores checkpoints of a recurrent model's hidden states, letting effective memory capacity grow with sequence length and offering a flexible trade-off between fixed-memory recurrent models and growing-memory transformers. Four variants are proposed, including gated aggregation and sparse selective mechanisms. In short, memory now grows. Grown memory recalls more. Tests on language modeling and long-context understanding show that caching improves recurrent performance. In-context recall tasks show cached variants competitive with transformers, closing much of the gap and beating leading recurrent models.
arxiv-2603-00281: Treers and colleagues track digging in fire ant groups of 2 to 25 ants to learn how workload inequality emerges in collectives. Inequality grows with group size, while the count of active ants rises only with the square root of group size. A cellular automata model where agents tune activity to local crowding in the tunnel reproduces the measured Gini coefficients across sizes. An analytic rate equation recovers the square root pattern by assuming tunnel exits scale quadratically with group size.
arxiv-2603-00381: Tailor studies how teamed language agents can smuggle joint plans inside messages that still look policy safe. His CLBC protocol splits message creation from admission, letting a note enter the shared record only when a small checker accepts a proof bound envelope under a fixed rule. That rule ties policy, randomness, chaining, schema, metadata, and rejection codes together. The design caps hidden leakage, survives hostile stress tests, and shows that strict admission, not mere bottlenecks, grounds security claims.
arxiv-2603-00481: Kamal and six colleagues analyse physical adversarial attacks on machine learning ballot classifiers, where printed doctored ballots could flip results. A probabilistic framework counts how many adversarial ballots an attacker must print, given win odds and total ballots cast. Six attack types go through printing and scanning on four models across one hundred forty four thousand examples. Attacks strongest digitally differ from those strongest physically, exposing a digital physical gap that election defences must bridge.
arxiv-2603-00781: Gall, Halverson, and Caverly tackle areostationary Mars orbit station keeping, where perturbative forces drag satellites from their nominal longitude. Their method bridges fuel use and compute cost in predictive control by finding fuel free natural motion trajectories that hold the craft within one degree of longitude. Two such trajectories form closed loops about Mars' stable equilibrium longitudes under its lumpy gravity field. A control policy built on a linear time varying model around the chosen trajectory minimises fuel while staying within thrust and station keeping limits.
arxiv-2603-01481:
Sales chatbots must sell well over a full chat while each reply stays smooth and within the rules. A 2026 study on training such agents argues that mixing those two aims into one score causes trouble. Large end-of-chat rewards can swamp small per-turn signals, which leads to shaky training or tricks that game the score.

The proposed method, DuCA, splits credit across two time scales, short turns and whole sessions. A key step scales each kind of reward on its own before the two are joined for each update. In tests with a lifelike user simulator, DuCA beat a strong baseline on sales success. It also cut repeat phrasing a lot and made the bot sound less easy to spot as a machine.
arxiv-2603-01581:
Robots run by vision, language, and action models often act too slowly for smooth real-time control. Zihao Zheng, Zhihao Mao, Maoliang Li, and colleagues speed them up in this 2026 work with a draft-and-check trick. In that trick, a fast draft is checked, but fixing token errors by full re-runs costs the time saved.

Their method, KERV, uses robot kinematics, the math of joint motion, to predict and patch draft errors. A Kalman filter, a standard motion tracker, forecasts actions so bad tokens need no costly re-run. Motion cues also tune the bar for accepting a draft token as the run proceeds. Across varied tasks and settings, the method speeds runs by roughly a third. Success rates stay near the unsped baseline, which is the key trade-off.
arxiv-2603-01681:
AbdulRahman Alharbi and Diogo Gomes solve a class of mean-field games with tricky edge rules in this 2026 work. Mean-field games model crowds of small players who each react to the whole group at once. Their setting fixes inflow on one part of the border and a flexible exit rule on another.

Exit flux and border value must satisfy a complementarity link, which blocks standard proofs. The pair build a monotone operator on a convex domain, with an extra border variable for exit flux. A shift flaw in the value function is cured by working in a quotient space that ignores constants. A classic existence theorem then yields solutions for a penalized version of the problem. Taking the penalty to zero gives weak solutions with the stated regularity for density, value, and flux.
arxiv-2603-01981:
Minhee Kim and Yong Yang attach honest error bars to machine learning forecasts of reactor material swelling. Their 2026 work studies void swelling, a radiation damage mode that sets how long reactor parts can serve. Learning models now predict swelling rates well, yet they give point values with no rigorous uncertainty.

Licensing and risk work need intervals with known coverage, not just a best guess. Their framework pairs ensemble learning models with conformal prediction, which calibrates intervals from held-out errors. A log transform handles the shift from nucleation-dominated early swelling to growth-dominated steady swelling. Even in sparse data regimes, coverage matches the target confidence level in their tests. Calibrated intervals could replace overly conservative bound curves in risk tools for high-dose reactor internals.
arxiv-2603-02081:
Jiale Lao and Immanuel Trummer argue that future query engines should be synthesized per query, not engineered once for all. Their 2026 work observes that hand-built engines strain to keep pace with new techniques and user needs. Internal complexity also makes those engines hard to extend or rebuild cheaply.

Their proof of concept, GenDB, uses language models to generate execution code for each incoming query. The generated code is optimized for the specific data, workload, and hardware at hand. An early prototype runs a multi-agent setup built on a commercial coding agent. Tests use a classic benchmark plus a new one designed to reduce leakage from model training data. Against five established engines, the synthesized approach performs significantly better in their evaluation, with limits and extensions discussed.
arxiv-2603-02781:
Chanwoo Hwang, Sunpill Kim, Yong Kiam Tan, and colleagues probe an attack on systems that recognize people by voice. Speaker recognition now guards biometric logins, forensic work, and voice services. Impersonation, where an attacker tries to be accepted as a specific enrolled person, is a central threat to those systems.

The paper's title points at its angle: the scores these systems output can reveal the target's voice traits, helping an attacker tune the attempt. The opening sections survey how mimicry, replay, and crafted adversarial audio have each been used against recognizers under different rules. By focusing on score feedback, the study highlights a leakage channel that designers of voice security must close.
arxiv-2603-03081:
Zhi Xu, Jiaqi Li, Xiaotong Zhang, and colleagues present an attack study that stress-tests the safety training of language models. Jailbreak attacks craft prompts that slip past alignment and draw out unsafe replies. Their 2026 method, TAO-Attack, improves optimization-based attacks that often stall on refusals or produce only fake-harmful text.

A two-stage loss first suppresses refusals so generation continues, then penalizes pseudo-harmful outputs to push toward genuinely harmful completions. A direction-first token update rule picks edits aligned with the gradient before weighing their size, speeding the search. Across several models, the attack beat leading methods on success rate, reaching total success in some settings. Studies of this kind map exactly where current safety training still bends.
arxiv-2603-03481:
Raj Narayan Dhara and Matteo Rizzi prove that a nonlinear diffusion equation admits solutions of a prescribed size. The equation is built on the p-Laplacian, a generalization of the ordinary Laplacian, with a radial potential and two competing power terms. Normalized solutions are those whose overall norm is fixed in advance, a constraint that matters in physical models. Their 2026 paper works in three or more dimensions and stresses the potential need not be bounded or carry a fixed sign.

The proof is variational, using a min-max argument to locate a radial solution. Its key tool is a Pohozaev identity, an exact balance relation, shown to hold for any solution under quite weak assumptions on the potential. That identity rests on a new global boundedness result for subsolutions of a related p-Laplace equation, proved along the way.
arxiv-2603-03581:
Edmond Chaussidon and a colleague make a practical case for squeezing more cosmology out of galaxy surveys without a bigger data vector. The deepest information in galaxy clustering is non-Gaussian, usually harvested by the bispectrum, a heavy three-point statistic. The marked power spectrum reaches similar information while keeping the familiar two-point structure: galaxies are weighted by a mark before the spectrum is measured. Their 2026 paper restructures the statistic for real survey use.

First the marked spectrum is rearranged to isolate its higher-order content, which demonstrably breaks parameter degeneracies the plain spectrum cannot. Survey geometry, they find, needs only the same treatment the standard spectrum gets. Perturbative modeling and the covariance structure, including cross-talk with the ordinary spectrum, are worked out. Finally, the statistic's cosmology dependence is smooth, so inference can interpolate between models instead of deriving formulas.
arxiv-2603-03981: Wael Elshennawy presents a network-layer answer for an auto machine learning operations setup for anomalous reflector metasurface design using Red Hat OpenShift AI. Using artificial intelligence as a metasurface design tool poses challenges due to high resource needs for deep-learning models. Design proceeds through a conditional GAN, with an extended network plus surrogate model aiding freeform design.
arxiv-2603-04081: Kagiyama and others revisit foundation models for cell-level analysis under small-patch constraints. Cell-level analysis uses tiny 40-by-40 pixel patches, far below standard resolutions, leaving unclear whether modern architectures learn robustly. Task-given models improved steadily with data scale while foundation models saturated, and a small-patch Vision Transformer led score at lower cost. The conclusion favors task-given architectures with sufficient data, with clean score not implying superior robustness.
arxiv-2603-04381: Alioua and colleagues test DualPI2 queue management inside Mahimahi, a user space emulator. L4S latency control lacked a reproducible user space test bed beyond the Linux kernel version. Their module allows component tests without kernel changes. Against the kernel baseline, identical settings give different behaviour across environments. Tuning helps at low bandwidth delay, but structural gaps persist under higher load.
arxiv-2603-04581: Goswami and colleagues build long range waveguide QED with left handed transmission lines. Waveguide QED blocks use local short range couplings like nearest neighbour arrays, despite long range goals. Their system couples one emitter to a left handed transmission line. It emulates a photonic lattice where hopping fades slowly with distance. Long range effects appear in atom photon bound and scattering states, showing algebraic localization and faster photon spread. A running exponents method unifies dispersion with bound state and light front profiles, for tunable range multi-qubit work.
arxiv-2603-05181: Yuanfu Sun and team offer Mario, a method for reasoning over mixed graphs whose nodes carry text and image attributes, with shape edges. Current methods encode image-text pairs in isolation, ignoring relational structure and facing weak cross-modal sameness plus uneven modality preference. Mario first refines textual and visual features with graph-guided contrastive learning, then tunes instructions with a router surfacing the best modality mix per node and neighborhood. Across mixed graph benchmarks it beats leading graph models on node sorting and link guess, supervised and zero-shot.
arxiv-2603-05281: D. Aristizabal Sierra and team study axial neutral-current contributions to coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering. Axial extraction has drawn little interest because reading is hard. Comparing vector and axial parts, they spot fluorine-based compounds as most hopeful for axial probing. Octafluoropropane stands out given its role in spin-dependent dark matter searches and upcoming relevance. With pion decay-at-rest and reactor fluxes, readings could determine the axial coupling indirectly at the ten-percent level, depending on flux and threshold uncertainties. They would probe spin-dependent new physics.
arxiv-2603-05781: Han and colleagues adapt BM25 ranking to image retrieval by scoring sparse visual words. Dense retrieval is accurate but hard to interpret and costly at scale, so the authors score sparse autoencoder activations over vision transformer patches. Since visual-word frequencies skew, inverse document frequency weighting suppresses common words and lifts rare ones. A sparse inverted index supplies candidates, with only 200 per query passed to dense reranking. Trained once on ImageNet-1K, the encoder transfers untuned to seven fine-grained benchmarks, and each decision traces to visual words.
arxiv-2603-05981: Voellinger fixes Gauss's Lemma, showing double tangent space link with tangent space is not the same. This link, metric warp, is a same-measure giving the shape. The outer change, lining a mapping atop a surface, is worked out by co-vary slope transport, with a change slip unlike inner changes. A change slip acts as a scalar gauge theory of re-timing across length scales. Metric warp follows from radial volume keeping, whereas the exp mapping follows from radial length keeping. The sphere's outer shape shows the theory.
arxiv-2603-06581: Gareau and Lemire present an empirical comparison of algorithms converting binary floating-point numbers into decimal string representations, across diverse hardware architectures and datasets. Techniques such as Schubfach and Dragonbox achieve a tenfold speedup against Steele and White's Dragon4, executing only 210 instructions per conversion at fewest, against Dragon4's thousands. None of the surveyed implementations produced the shortest strings, with some outputs up to 30 percent longer than optimal, and library implementations execute more instructions than the fastest methods. The authors suggest optimization targets for future research.
arxiv-2603-06681: Sun and team present RADAR, a benchmark for radiology gap analysis pairing 3D images with a preliminary report and candidate edits. Trainee radiologists author draft reports later revised by attendings, matching usual workflow. RADAR defines a set task: judge edits by image-level agreement, clinical severity, and edit type as correction, addition, or clearing. Unlike prior binary error detection, RADAR targets fine-grained medical reasoning plus image-text alignment at report review. Expert-tagged abdominal CT scans with set protocols support testing of models as report-edit checkers.
arxiv-2603-06781: Baer presents xaitimesynth, a Python package for testing time series attribution against known ground truth. Real datasets rarely show which time points drive a prediction, so studies rebuild synthetic test data from scratch each time. This package reuses that setup: each sample sums a background signal and a local class-discriminating feature, with the feature window tracked as a truth mask. A fluent generation API and YAML configs support univariate and multivariate series, plus standard localization metrics.
arxiv-2603-07181: Zhou and colleagues give drone navigation an explicit reasoning voice with FreeFly-Thinking, an end-to-end vision-language navigation framework for outdoor scenes. Most prior work stays indoors and acts as a black box, but this system turns egocentric images and language instructions into actions through natural-language chain of thought. Training runs in two stages, supervised fine-tuning then reinforcement fine-tuning, on a newly built drone navigation data set. Tests on unseen scenes show robust, efficient navigation.
arxiv-2603-07281: Vemareddy, Nair and Gosain trace a solar eruption inside active region 13500 to a slow magnetic build-up. Over three days the region shed net flux while feeding twist and energy into the corona, forming an S-shaped structure along a sheared divide. A data-driven simulation starting days before the blast reproduces that shape and its rise. The authors point to a rising share of current-carrying helicity as a warning sign that eruption is near.
arxiv-2603-07481: Gerasimov dates globular clusters from the cooling sequences of their brown dwarf members, newly visible with the James Webb Space Telescope. Existing methods give precise but clashing ages, hinting at errors over a billion years that recur. His likelihood method reads ages from multi-band photometry near and below the hydrogen burning limit. Tests show formal errors stay small for nearby clusters, though system errors dominate the budget and may shrink with better analysis.
arxiv-2603-08181: Sinha and colleagues present AutoAdapt, an automated domain adaptation framework for large language models. Such models excel in open domains but struggle in specialized settings with thin, shifting data. Existing practice leans on manual trial-and-error and reacts sharply to data and user preferences, at high training cost. AutoAdapt draws on curated knowledge bases. It plans with debating proposal and critic agents and tunes hyperparameters with AutoRefine, a surrogate for costly black-box search. Across 10 tasks it beats leading AutoML baselines by 25% average relative accuracy.
arxiv-2603-08281: Thorne and colleagues evaluate LLM-based grant proposal review through structured perturbations. As AI-assisted grant proposals outpace review capacity, the paper probes the strengths and limits of language-model reviewing for high-stakes calls. Using six EPSRC proposals, they build a perturbation-based system testing sensitivity across six quality axes: funding, timeline, competency, alignment, clarity, and impact. They compare three review designs: single-pass review, section-by-section analysis, and a Council of Personas ensemble acting as expert panels. Section-level review wins on detection rate and scoring reliability.
arxiv-2603-08581: Alessandro Marcomini and colleagues judge two-qubit gates with just two prepared states, cutting measurement cost sharply. Open-loop control leans on simulations that miss system details, while closed-loop tuning needs a cheap, sound score. Their method fits nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond and, in simulations, tunes a gate with far fewer measurements than standard process tomography.
arxiv-2603-08881: Lei Zhang and Markus Stricker screen catalyst mixes with text-derived codes, no lab labels needed. Each mix is coded from science texts, then ranked by likeness to conductivity and dielectric ideas in a two-axis map. On fifteen test sets, the simple Word2Vec baseline often cuts the pool most while staying near the best scores.
arxiv-2603-09081: Pavan Kumar Asur Vijaya Kumar and colleagues model failure in fiber-reinforced laminates with a multi-phase-field model based on Puck theory. Their two-dimensional multi-field model with a mesh overlay computes in-plane damage across ply orientations, using two phase-field variables for fiber and inter-fiber failure. Two length scales and two structural tensors describe damage modes. Four benchmarks, including coupon, open-hole, compact tension, and double-edged notched tension tests, show predictions matching experiments qualitatively and quantitatively.
arxiv-2603-09781: Meenatchi Sundaram Muthu Selva Annamalai and coauthors attack a system that claims to draw private safe insights from chat data. Their CLIOPATRA attack plants crafted chats that break layered guards such as redaction, clustering and auditing. In tests on Anthropic's Clio platform with fake medical chats, private histories leak in many cases at near perfect precision. Added audit based fixes fail to catch large leaks.
arxiv-2603-09981: Tairan Fu and coauthors compare book summaries a language model writes from memory against ones built from the full text. Long context windows now let a model read a whole book in one prompt, while famous books are already known from training. Full text summaries are richer in general, the team finds. Yet for some books the memory based versions score higher, raising doubts about long text summarising skill.
arxiv-2603-10081: Lu lays a firm base for querying databases that hold several data types at once. Multi model bases store table, tree and graph data side by side, yet query theory lags behind. Lu proposes categorical calculus and categorical algebra, extending the table based forms of each. He proves the two have equal power. He also gives change rules to speed queries up. Then he weighs what they can say and what they cost to run, giving designers a clear map.
arxiv-2603-10281: Rajesh Shrestha and Xiao Fu tackle a hard fit: plugging score-based denoisers into ADMM for inverse problems without losing convergence. Two snags drive the work, a mismatch between training noise and ADMM iterates, plus thin theory for the pairing. Their AC-DC denoiser adds noise for auto-correction, steers iterates with conditional Langevin steps, then denoises by score. The authors prove fixed-point and adaptive-step convergence results under stated conditions, and experiments show better solution quality than a range of baselines.
arxiv-2603-10481: Keyi Wang and co-authors hunt for white dwarfs with infrared excess in LAMOST's eleventh data release, a sign of companions or debris disks. They cross-matched thousands of white dwarf spectra with optical and infrared surveys, then fitted spectral energy distributions for a large subset. After cleaning contaminated and flagged sources, they kept a solid candidate list. It spans white dwarfs with M dwarf partners, brown dwarf partners, and dust disks, many of them new. All candidates still need follow-up infrared imaging or spectroscopy to confirm them.
arxiv-2603-10781: Pierre Musacchio and co-authors find that single scalar activations inside a vision language model can act as accurate classifiers, a shortcut they call super neurons. Sparse attention vectors had shown a few good heads can replace fine-tuning for a task; probing raw activations widens that search hugely. Enough super neurons appear in shallow layers to allow extreme early exiting, from the first layer at the first generated token. On diverse visually grounded tasks, the probed classifiers beat the original network while running several times faster.
arxiv-2603-11181: Ofer Aharony, Ronny Frumkin, and Jonathan Mehl map which phases dominate the D1-D5 conformal field theory at each energy in the microcanonical ensemble. As small localized black holes grow, they can begin to fill the three-sphere, the four-torus, or both. The authors analyze transitions among uniform and non-uniform black hole phases. When the torus is much larger than the AdS radius, they find evidence for a novel lattice phase of black holes. Its entropy grows linearly with energy.
arxiv-2603-11481: Yang and co-authors introduce INFACT, a benchmark that probes how video language models hallucinate under pressure. Such models can contradict the video itself or known facts about the world. INFACT holds 9,800 questions across real and synthetic videos, sorted by fine-grained hallucination types. Models face four modes: clean input, degraded visuals, corrupted evidence, and shuffled time order. Scores track how often models resist the traps and how sensitive they stay to time order. Across 14 models, clean accuracy fails to predict steadiness under attack.
arxiv-2603-11581: Heisenberg proves that autoparallel curves for a broad class of affine connections can come from an action principle. The connections are torsion-free, yet they need not be metric-compatible. She builds the action functional in full and shows that standard variational steps yield the wanted equations. The route runs through the inverse problem of the calculus of variations and its Helmholtz conditions. The result gives particle motion in metric-affine geometries a firm variational base. It also supports the math behind the geodesic principle in relativistic gravity.
arxiv-2603-11781: Prakash introduces Deliberative Collective Intelligence, a way for language model agents to deliberate rather than just debate or vote. DCI sets four reasoning archetypes, 14 typed epistemic acts, and a shared workspace. Its flow algorithm, DCI-CF, ends with a decision packet that keeps the chosen option, open objections, a minority report, and reopen terms. On 45 tasks, DCI beats unstructured debate on non-routine work and shines on hidden-profile tasks. It fails on routine calls, though, and burns about 62 times the tokens of one agent.
arxiv-2603-11881: Kinas and co-authors report Bielik-Minitron-7B, a compressed Polish-language model cut from Bielik-11B by about a third. They combine structured pruning with knowledge distillation, in the Minitron style, then align the model with fine-tuning, preference tuning, and reinforcement learning. The smaller model recovers about 90% of the base model's performance. Inference runs up to 50% faster. The report argues this path suits less-represented languages, keeping quality while cutting deployment costs.
arxiv-2603-11981: Fu and a large team of co-authors report the first cosmic muon flux measurement at the Stawell Underground Physics Laboratory. Eight plastic scintillator panels recorded the muons deep underground. Those panels form the core of the muon veto planned for the SABRE South experiment. The flux they found matches simulations closely. Its uncertainty is far smaller than the uncertainty of the models, which makes the result a firm check for future work.
arxiv-2603-12081: Coquand, Paolino, and Berthier infer particle interactions straight from snapshots, with no fresh simulation at each step. Older Boltzmann inversion loops a new Monte Carlo run into every round of refinement. Their direct method instead forces two routes to the pair correlation function to agree. One route uses interparticle distances, and the other uses pairwise forces. The scheme stays cheap and simple, and it works at any state point, even at high density. Tests on varied potentials went well.
arxiv-2603-12381: Niewenhuis, Talluri, Iosup, and de Matteis build OpenDC-STEAM, a simulator that tests green datacenter techniques. Such tricks are often judged alone in small setups that miss real dynamics. Their open tool checks single and combined effects on carbon output and speed. Three techniques face varied workloads and site setups: horizontal scaling, batteries, and temporal shifting. Mixing strategies can cut emissions sharply, at the cost of trade-offs the tool helps users weigh.
arxiv-2603-12681: Sihao Ding shows that safety alignment in modular language models can fail when adapters combine. Single LoRA adapters can look benign and useful on their own. Loaded together, though, a set can suppress refusals across the board. The model then complies with harmful requests under standard prompts, with no trigger needed. Across several open-weight models, pairs stayed benign alone yet scored high attack success when composed. Defenses must therefore check compositions, not just single modules.
arxiv-2603-12881: Marco Mandap builds a spatial model for how crop rotation changes soil nutrients over a field. Field averages hide local gaps and links among nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. His lattice model treats soil as a tensor over space, time, and the three nutrient channels. Rotations act as force vectors, and soil stiffness varies with texture. In a three-year corn-soybean-wheat run, phosphorus fell more than nitrogen. Continuous corn raised mean stress by 41%, and sandy zones showed the worst stress.
arxiv-2603-13081: Felipe Alarcón and co-authors compare formaldehyde emission in protoplanetary disks with star and disk traits in the exoALMA sample. Disk substructures hint that chemistry and dynamics shape each other. With a Kendall correlation test, they hunt for links across the sample. No link reached firm statistical weight in their data. A tentative tie links stellar temperature to formaldehyde excitation terms. That hints the star, more than dust dynamics, sets the emission, and that several formation paths may act.
arxiv-2603-13181: Alexander Gheorghiu introduces robust property verification for access control policies that are still being built. Standard checks demand a complete policy before they can start. Real policies grow by parts and change as organizations shift. His support judgment states what a policy commits to, whatever pending choices or extensions come. A monotonicity result shows verified traits persist under extension. The judgment also turns into a proof search task inside second-order logic programming, with soundness and completeness proved.
arxiv-2603-13381: Marko Karbevski argues for nonlinear queries in transformer attention projections. Recent algebraic work shows the Query projection can be set to identity with little loss of skill. Attention depends on the input only through set products, so basis shifts are absorbed by nearby layers. Karbevski swaps the linear Query map for a nonlinear residual with a bottleneck MLP. The identity term anchors the new map to a known-good prior. On GPT-3 small style models, the change cut validation loss and perplexity, beating a larger baseline.
arxiv-2603-13481: Md Aquib Molla and Sanchari Goswami study whether partial consumption helps a forager survive longer. Their forager can survive S steps without food and eats only when its energy falls below a threshold k. Partial eating can leave food at a site, which in turn extends the forager's lifetime. Lifetime always rises with the ratio k over S, fast below a transition threshold and slow above it. The lifetime follows a power law in S, with an exponent that shifts as the ratio grows.
arxiv-2603-14181: Aharony Shapira and Shavit study how helicity shapes weak turbulence in flows that break time-reversal symmetry. The test beds are rotating Euler flow and odd-viscous Euler flow, both rich in slanted dispersive waves. Helicity conservation makes the wave kinetic equation much simpler. With the energy flux fixed, one scale-free spectrum carries a steady flow of energy from large to small scales. Helicity also sorts resonant triads: same-branch triads push energy back upscale, which yields steady backscatter.
arxiv-2603-14281: Marikkar and co-authors present DC-ViT, a vision transformer built for multi-channel images with mixed channel sets. Stains, sensors, and settings change channel counts, which breaks fixed-channel encoders. Joint attention over all channels can wash out channel-specific detail. DC-ViT splits token updates into two paths: one for space within a channel, one for mixing across channels. A decoupled aggregation step then learns how much each channel counts for the task at hand.
arxiv-2603-14481: Vidyasagar reworks the study of two time-scale stochastic approximation with martingale tools. The algorithm, from Borkar in 1997, runs fast and slow updates at once. His approach gives simple conditions for the iterates to stay bounded almost surely. It also bounds how fast the mean-squared error falls to zero. The results cover nonlinear equations, not just linear ones. Fast and slow parts get separate convergence rates. The theory even allows biased errors with growing variance.
arxiv-2603-14581: Parts raises the lower bound for the chromatic number of eight-dimensional space to 25. The chromatic number counts the fewest colors for a space coloring. In such a coloring, points one unit apart must never share a color. A bound of 25 means every valid coloring of R^8 needs at least 25 colors. No coloring with 24 colors can exist. The new floor improves the best known value for dimension eight. It tightens the known range for this classic geometry problem.
arxiv-2603-14981: Iwasaki and Kusakabe show arithmetic limits on where hypergeometric identities can occur. Special function texts list many identities built from gamma function ratios. Such identities still appear only sporadically across parameter space. Strict arithmetic conditions gate their existence, the authors argue. One data region brings the core constraint into clear view. Inside that region, the essential pattern stands out cleanly. The study explains the rarity rather than adding new identities. Gamma product identities gain a number-theoretic frame.
arxiv-2603-15081: Choi argues that the Higgs mass looks natural once its power-law running is taken seriously. The renormalized scalar mass squared runs as the square of the energy scale. Far above the electroweak scale, couplings drift slowly, so the Standard Model stays nearly scale invariant. An order-one value at the unification scale then maps down exponentially to the electroweak scale. The 28 orders of magnitude between the scales reflect a small anomalous dimension, driven by the top Yukawa coupling, not fine tuning.
arxiv-2603-15381: Dupoux and co-authors argue that current AI systems fail at autonomous learning and sketch a fix drawn from cognitive science. Their design joins two learning modes under a meta-control switch. System A learns from observation, while System B learns from active behavior. System M reads inner signals and flips between the two modes as needed. The sketch borrows from how organisms adapt across both growth and evolution. It aims at agents that keep learning in changing real-world settings.
arxiv-2603-15581: Peterson proposes quantum sensors that select particles by their dispersion relation, not just the energy they deposit. Phonons and magnons inside a detector can mimic the signals of interest at meV scales. Her design uses van der Waals stacks of the Dirac materials ZrTe5 and HfTe5. Charge transfer across the layers turns on only for chosen incoming particles, thanks to tuned orbital mixing. Density functional calculations map how strain and layer count adjust that mixing. The study offers a proof-of-principle path to dispersion filters for next-generation sensors.
arxiv-2603-15681: Sharma and Sharma map flash flood risk in Himachal Pradesh with a graph neural network. Pixel-based maps treat each cell alone and miss river links. Their GraphSAGE model trains on a watershed graph of 460 sub-watersheds. Inputs blend a six-year Sentinel-1 flood record with 12 terrain and weather variables. Strict leave-one-basin-out checks guard against inflated scores. The graph model reached an AUC of 0.978, well past pixel baselines. Conformal intervals add stated coverage bounds to the maps.
arxiv-2603-16281: Panchavati and co-authors build Laya, an EEG foundation model that learns by prediction, not reconstruction. Most EEG models rebuild raw signals, which steers them toward loud artifacts. Laya instead predicts latent representations, in the LeJEPA style. Its embeddings track clinical shifts such as seizure onset. They also resist noise well. Under frozen linear probing, Laya scored the best mean clinical accuracy. Matched tests show the objective, not the architecture, drives the gains.
arxiv-2603-16481: Lahr and co-authors bound prediction error for kernel regression with many outputs. Safe learning control needs bounds that are not too loose. Gaussian process tools give bounds, but many assume special noise shapes. Others fail for multi-output functions. Their bound is tight and deterministic under bounded noise. A duality-based form makes it look like classic process bounds. That shape eases use in downstream optimization. A quadrotor learning example shows the bound at work.
arxiv-2603-16681: Qian and co-authors read spin entanglement inside the proton's wave function. The three valence quarks form a three-qubit spin system. Four classes of three-qubit states describe its entanglement. The team compares a light-front quantization result with a quark-diquark model. The diquark model gives a far more entangled spin state. Its edge comes from W-type and Bell-type entanglement. Stronger coupling and lighter quarks push the first model toward the second.
arxiv-2603-16981: Andrée asks how little hardware could steer an interstellar comet along a chosen path. Comets already carry volatile propellant, natural rotation, and hyperbolic paths through the Solar System. He relaxes full six degree control to forward cone steering, which suits practical navigation. He then shows that four thrusters suffice: one primary jet and three secondary jets spaced at 120 degree intervals. The spinning body lets the primary jet shape attitude over each cycle. The study also maps reachability, power needs at large distances, and signs that control is active.
arxiv-2603-17181: Alves, Nunokawa, and Funchal test whether new physics could spoil a route to the neutrino mass ordering. The route combines reactor and accelerator measurements of the atmospheric mass splitting, using a sum rule. JUNO should supply the needed precision within a year with T2K and NOvA data. The authors identify when new physics can distort the sum rule enough to flip the inferred ordering. For scalar non standard interactions, current limits make the effect negligible. For neutrinos coupled to an ultralight scalar field, they counsel caution.
arxiv-2603-17281: Linden formalizes a triple difference design for interrupted time series analysis, a tool used to judge health policies. Adding a control group sharpens causal claims, but unmeasured shifting factors can still confound. The triple difference design adds a second control group to strip out more bias. Linden specifies the regression model and defines the key parameters for level and trend effects. A worked example studies California's Proposition 99 cigarette tax. There, the design found a significant yearly drop in per capita cigarette sales.
arxiv-2603-17481: Montessori, Lisboa, Lauricella, and Succi fix false merging in multiphase flow simulations. Thin films between bubbles often vanish in diffuse-interface models, so drops merge by mistake. Their fix adds a local repulsive flux near contact in an Allen-Cahn lattice Boltzmann model. The flux turns on only for facing interfaces and scales with film thickness. Bubble collision tests and 3D swarms kept drops apart correctly, they report.
arxiv-2603-17581: Arrighi, Bakircioglu, and Houyet rebuild quantum theory over dual-complex numbers. Swapping the complex field for a ring with an infinitesimal unit unifies continuous and discrete models. Two doubts arise at once: division by the unit fails, and unitarity may break. They prove norms stay preserved and no step needs that division. The extension also yields first-order variations of quantum operations for free. Dirac physics and Dirac walks share one frame.
arxiv-2603-17981: Sipione, Como, and Nilsson give a convex form for multi-commodity traffic assignment on road networks. Their model uses the cell transmission model and tools like speed limits, ramp meters, and routing. Past forms of this task were non-convex and hard to solve well. They show a tight convex relaxation with set demand and supply curves for each cell. Each flow type can use its own set of off-ramps.
arxiv-2603-18281: Brealy and co-authors use additive Gaussian processes to predict wind farm power output. Group-based health checks aim to share facts across like machines and structures. Their models split turbine-level effects from farm-level trends in one farm dataset. The trends found match what wind experts would expect from the physics. Such splits can guide control choices and day-to-day calls for farm staff.
arxiv-2603-18381: Sramek introduces a higher-order context-conditioned kernel for backaction in dynamic quantum circuits. Mid-circuit measurement can disturb spectator qubits, but device metrics compress that effect into low-order proxies. His kernel adds a relational term for context dependence that proxies cannot explain. Möbius weights are evaluated on classical outcomes to dodge decomposition limits. Synthetic harness tests show parity context effects that singles and pairs cannot see, plus eraser-based control.
arxiv-2603-18681: Artime and co-authors revisit how topological terms emerge in M-theory compactifications. The Emergence Proposal says all low-energy action terms come from quantum effects. In four-dimensional setups with N=2 supersymmetry, kinetic terms sit inside topological string amplitudes. Recent work rebuilt the cubic term of the prepotential by summing over light state towers. Two gaps remained. The authors show the sum can be regularized in either moduli space. They also extend the method to linear terms in the one-loop prepotential F1.
arxiv-2603-18981: Di Maio and co-authors report a group version of the Turing Test with people and language models mixed. Each side both chats and judges in timed rounds. The test runs on a platform with set roles and a private peer network. Seventeen people and nineteen models took part. Models were still at times taken for human. Odd slips showed that human traces remain, though not always clear. The team plans to probe how each side spots the other and what fools them.
arxiv-2603-19281: Nguyen and co-authors build URAG, a benchmark for how unsure retrieval-based language models are. Most tests grade these systems on right answers alone, not on trust. URAG turns open tasks into choice questions across health, code, science, math, and general text. That form lets conformal prediction put a firm size on doubt. Eight standard methods are scored on accuracy and set size. Gains in accuracy often pair with lower doubt, but noisy search breaks the link. No single method wins across all fields.
arxiv-2603-19481: Jain and co-authors build a benchmark for narrative reasoning in long-form video question answering. Most benchmarks lean on local cues, not story-wide links. Their NA-VQA holds 88 full films and 4,400 open question-answer pairs. Each pair cites evidence spans marked short, medium, or far. Their Video-NaRA system builds event chains in a structured memory for later lookup. Top multimodal models do poorly on far-range questions. Video-NaRA lifts long-range scores by up to 3 percent.
arxiv-2603-19581: Liu and Tu propose a new source for global Lambda hyperon polarization in heavy ion collisions. The effect is usually blamed on vorticity in the quark-gluon plasma. The authors link it to the long-known transverse polarization seen in unpolarized collisions. Directed flow aligns the Lambda production plane with the reaction plane, they argue. That alignment transfers transverse polarization into the global signal. Monte Carlo runs for gold-gold collisions at 3 GeV give a sizable share. The mechanism covers about 23 percent of the STAR measurement.
arxiv-2603-20081: Maier builds an infinite dimensional information geometry through the q-root transform. The new frame shares key traits with the geometry of probability densities on a manifold. Maier defines a probability simplex with a smooth structure induced from a sphere. Under that choice, the q-root transform becomes an isometry. He then constructs Fisher-Rao geometries and the related alpha connections. A linear optimization flow in this setting can be solved in closed form. It converges to a maximizer and matches a geodesic flow.
arxiv-2603-20181: Huang and co-authors use contrastive multi modal learning to help security models generalize beyond their training setup. Security classifiers often learn shortcuts instead of the core concepts, then fail in production. The authors transfer knowledge from text, a data rich mode, to payloads, a scarce one. Stage one builds a semantic embedding space from vulnerability descriptions. Stage two aligns payloads to that space for threat classification. Tests used a large private dataset and a synthetic benchmark from public CVE texts. Shortcut learning dropped against baselines on both benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-20281: Keppo and co-authors test whether AI pricing agents really collude as earlier work suggested. In their model, differences in patience or data access shrink the set of collusive outcomes. Tests with open-source language agents matched those predictions. Unequal patience cut price lift from 22% to 10% above competitive levels. Unequal data access cut it to 7%. More rival agents and mixed algorithm types also broke collusion up. Only size gaps held collusion together, through leader-follower patterns.
arxiv-2603-20381: Agostino and co-authors probe how meaning arises when language is processed by models and people. They question whether meaning is retrieved or built in context. Human studies show semantic processing that fits quantum logic better than classical rules. Recent tests found Bell inequality violations in large language models too. They track the CHSH measure across model scales and sampling settings. Its spread showed no link to standard benchmark scores. Violation rates, though, weakly opposed scores on three benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-20581: Shiotani and co-authors build JUBAKU, a test for bias in Japanese language models. Most bias tests are mere translations of English ones. They miss local norms on rank, dialect, and gender roles. Native speakers hand wrote dialogue scenes across ten cultural themes. Nine Japanese models scored an average of 23 percent. That sits well below the 50 percent random mark. Human readers scored 91 percent, which shows the test is sound.
arxiv-2603-20681: Al Ghafri and co-authors characterize nuclear weighted composition operators between distinct L^p spaces. These operators mix a change of variable with a weight factor. The paper gives complete tests for when such an operator is nuclear. The tests cover the full range from p equal to one upward. One sharp result follows for non-atomic measure spaces. There, the only nuclear operator of this kind is the zero operator. The work extends operator theory on function spaces.
arxiv-2603-20881: Zhang and co-authors measure distances to four supernova remnants by pairing carbon monoxide data with 3D extinction maps. Good distances are key to a remnant's size, age, and energy. For each remnant they pick gas clouds that seem to interact with it, based on CO line speeds. They then look for sharp extinction jumps along the same sight lines. The four distances range from about six tenths of a kiloparsec to about three and a half kiloparsecs. The authors report these match past estimates but with better precision.
arxiv-2603-21281: Wang and co-authors build a gauge-invariant theory of non-Hermitian quantum systems. How states and dynamics should be described in such systems has been debated. Their frame rests on two rules: both left and right vectors must obey the Schrödinger equation, and physical quantities must not depend on unobservable phase choices. The result contains open system evolution as a special case and reduces to standard quantum mechanics in the Hermitian limit. They apply it to dynamical phase transitions in the SSH model.
arxiv-2603-21381: Ahmed and co-authors compare how people relive memories in extended reality through physical objects, virtual objects, and a gallery. In a within-subjects study with twenty four participants in pairs, shared experiences were captured with 360 degree video. People later revisited them through all three interfaces. Physical objects fostered stronger social connection and conversation. Virtual objects balanced engagement and usability. The gallery was efficient but felt less personal. Object based forms support the social side of shared memory.
arxiv-2603-21781: Tönjes and co-authors ask how the spread of synaptic strengths shapes steady firing in spiking neuron networks. They use stochastic mean-field theory on quadratic integrate-and-fire units. Two coupling types are compared: Gaussian, with light tails, and Cauchy, with heavy tails. Both allow two stable states, one quiet and one with self-sustained firing. With Cauchy coupling, activity can spread network-wide from a few firing units past a sharp threshold. That spread can be smooth or abrupt, based on the balance of excitation and inhibition.
arxiv-2603-21881: Paliathanasis tests a modified gravity idea, f(Q) gravity with matter-gravity coupling, against cosmic data. The model aims to explain late-time cosmic acceleration as geometry rather than dark energy. He studies the simplest power-law form in a flat expanding universe. A noncoincident connection is used, from curved-space cosmology. Supernova, baryon acoustic oscillation, and cosmic chronometer data all give consistent fits, with power index near 2. By likelihood the model edges out the standard model, while an information criterion rates them roughly equal.
arxiv-2603-22081: Antoniuk and co-authors complete the threshold picture for clique factors in randomly perturbed graphs. Such a graph joins a dense fixed graph to a random one. A clique factor tiles the vertices with disjoint copies of one clique size. Earlier work found the threshold edge probability, except at special density values. The team settles the last open range, where the base density exceeds one half. A key step is a fractional stability version of a tiling theorem by Shokoufandeh and Zhao.
arxiv-2603-22281: Zhang and co-authors pair a latent world model with a vision-language thinker. Latent world models forecast future states from video, but short windows bias them to local detail. Vision-language models reason over sparse frames but squeeze fine detail into text. ThinkJEPA joins the two in one framework. A dense JEPA branch tracks fine motion and contact cues. A VLM branch adds long-range semantic guidance. A pyramid module merges VLM layer outputs into guidance features. On hand manipulation tasks, the pair beats both solo baselines.
arxiv-2603-22381: Chaichian and co-authors build a cosmology where the universe comes as a mirrored pair. The two parts are coordinate-reversed copies, so the whole stays CPT-symmetric. Each part on its own can break CPT symmetry locally. The mirror copy carries opposite chiralities and a reversed microscopic time arrow. That gives time reversal a geometric reading. Local CPT breaking splits the masses of the inflaton and anti-inflaton fields. The split can shift reheating heat and seed the known matter-antimatter imbalance.
arxiv-2603-22581: Reed and Horowitz calculate radiative corrections to parity-violating electron scattering from nuclei. Such scattering gives a fairly direct way to measure neutron densities in nuclei. The authors include vertex and vacuum polarization effects. They find large cancellations between the vertex terms. Vacuum polarization then dominates, at about minus 0.5 percent. For lead-208 the total falls to about 0.1 percent. They conclude the corrections matter little for current lead and calcium tests, but they must be included for a precise weak charge measure of carbon-12.
arxiv-2603-22681: Boschetti and Campiglia compute exact formulas for peeling-violating parts of the Weyl tensor in gravity scattering. They use matching rules for the field at timelike and spatial infinity, plus known formulas for wave tails. The resulting values depend only on incoming data. In the Newtonian limit, they match values Damour found long ago. A structure called the celestial diamond helps organize the work. The authors suggest a new matching rule at spatial infinity. They also note stronger violations in quantum gravity.
arxiv-2603-22781: Reddy and Liu present a low-cost way to measure distance between vehicles with one camera. Their method treats license plate lettering as a built-in ruler. It detects the plate, segments the characters, and reads character height. A pinhole camera model turns that height into distance. Extra parts handle calibration, pose fixes, and temporal filtering. In indoor tests, distance error averaged 7.7 percent. Character-based ranging cut estimate spread by 35 percent versus a plate-width method. The system runs in real time with no graphics card.
arxiv-2603-22881: Makridis and Charalambous study cooperative bandit learning in directed networks with limited arm access. Many agents must learn which actions pay best. Each agent can try only a subset of arms. Links between agents run one way, as in a directed graph. Their consensus-based upper confidence bound method accounts for both limits. A mass-preserving mixing rule keeps reward estimates unbiased across the network. They prove logarithmic regret for every agent. The bounds show how network mixing and arm access shape learning speed.
arxiv-2603-23081: The BESIII Collaboration performs the first amplitude analysis of an isospin-violating J/psi decay. The decay yields a photon, an eta meson, and a neutral pion. Data come from a huge sample of J/psi events at the BESIII detector. Three intermediate routes dominate the decay, the analysis finds. New radiative transitions to isospin-triplet scalar mesons are observed with strong significance. The total branching fraction is measured with much better precision than before. It matches the earlier measurement, the authors report.
arxiv-2603-23181: Fernández-Martínez and co-authors propose electrospray for depositing single cells at chosen spots. They use the cone-jet mode near its lowest stable flow rate. The jet is far thinner than the cells it carries. Single cells can thus be watched or detected during deposition. Cells land at distinct, user-set locations, even at high concentrations. Tests deposit cells onto a small droplet of culture medium. Viability checks show many cells keep membrane integrity after spraying. Most damage seems reversible, they report.
arxiv-2603-23281: Fidrysiak links the steady magnetic waves in cuprate superconductors to two material traits. These paramagnon waves keep near-fixed energies as hole doping changes. Their energies also track the highest transition temperatures seen. He models a copper-oxide plane with Hubbard and t-J-U models. Two inputs matter: the hopping ratio r and the charge transfer energy. Raising one pushes paramagnon energy up while the other pushes it down. That tug explains why many cuprates share a similar magnetic bandwidth. For bismuth cuprates, his numbers match experiments within 6%.
arxiv-2603-23381: Xu and four co-authors animate portraits by moving motion from a driving video onto a still face. Diffusion tools often take only the driving motion, so source links get lost. Guessing dense 2D flow is unreliable. Their method computes 3D flow from parametric head models, with no learning for the flow itself. A 3D flow encoding lets each target pixel ask where it came from. Depth-guided sampling lines the flows up with real 2D motion. Users can also edit expressions and head pose by hand.
arxiv-2603-23581: Wiredu-Aidoo proposes the Mass Agreement Score, a way to grade how even cluster sizes are. One cluster often spoils a partition, so a uniformity score helps filter bad ones. Such a score must stay stable when point assignments shift a little. Label-based scores wobble because label counts can jump on tiny data changes. His score is point-centric and bounded between zero and one. It judges the expected cluster size from each point's seat. By design it resists fragment noise yet still senses real mass shifts.
arxiv-2603-23781: Yarotskyi and co-authors test whether large language models can judge if web apps follow secure coding practices. Manual checks of trust are slow and hard to scale. They compare prompt styles across five state-of-the-art models, from plain zero-shot prompts to prompts with rules and call-graph context. Extra structure adds noise, while clear rule-based prompts improve reliability, they report. Their scores feed a quality model that yields one trust score. The score separates secure builds from vulnerable ones.
arxiv-2603-24181: de Senneville and co-authors show that large vision-language models hide strong classification skills inside their heads. Such models do well at captioning and question answering, yet lag CLIP methods at image classification. Prompt conditioning alone can improve how separable their visual features are. Their method, Head Ensemble Classifiers, ranks the most discriminative vision and text heads. It then combines them into a classifier that needs no training. Across 12 datasets, it reaches state-of-the-art zero-shot and few-shot scores, they report.
arxiv-2603-24281: Wu and co-authors show that ruthenium doping stabilizes helical magnetic order in MnP. Pure MnP orders helically only below 51 kelvin, which limits device use. In Ru-doped single crystals, the helical ordering temperature rises to 215 kelvin. The critical field at 5 kelvin jumps from 2.3 to 30.0 kilo-oersted, while the Curie temperature falls. The lattice expands unevenly, and the b-axis length governs both temperatures across doped variants. Calculations show the expansion weakens ferromagnetic coupling but keeps antiferromagnetic links, which boosts frustration.
arxiv-2603-24381: Alutto and co-authors build a model where opinions and leadership evolve together inside a social network. The model extends the Friedkin-Johnsen framework by making openness to peer influence change over time, and that openness acts as the leadership trait. Leadership grows when a person holds strong views that still fit the group, and fades when that fit is lost. They give conditions for the coupled system to settle at a non-trivial balance, and study cases where the two parts move at different speeds.
arxiv-2603-24481: Martinez presents a multi-agent framework that improves confidence calibration for AI answers to medical multiple-choice questions. Overconfident models give clinicians no useful signal for when to defer. Four specialist agents, covering respiratory, cardiology, neurology, and gastroenterology, answer independently with a small open model. Each answer passes a two-phase self-verification that yields a confidence score, and a weighted fusion picks the final answer. On hard subsets of MedQA and MedMCQA, calibration error falls sharply, with gains of 49 to 74 percent across settings, the author reports.
arxiv-2603-24781: Dey and co-authors present PySiPMGUI, a Python tool for quality checks of silicon photomultiplier detectors. These sensors dominate photon detection in particle physics, neutrino, and dark matter experiments. Their key values shift strongly with bias voltage and temperature, so characterisation is essential. The open-source interface automates current-voltage checks over standard instrument protocols. It is free and works on any platform, aimed at detector development and large-scale testing. Checks against a manufacturer's datasheet for a SensL sensor agree well on breakdown voltage and dark count rate.
arxiv-2603-24881: Li and co-authors implement a GPU-accelerated multigrid Gaussian-plane-wave density fitting in PySCF. The approach speeds up Fock builds and nuclear gradients in Kohn-Sham density functional theory. CUDA kernels contract Gaussian basis pairs on a grid, reaching 80 percent of peak double-precision performance. High angular momentum functions up to the f-shell lose no efficiency. Benchmarks on systems up to 1,536 atoms show speedups of 25 times over a 28-core CPU node. A 256-water cluster finishes energy and gradients in about 30 seconds on one H100 GPU.
arxiv-2603-25281: Belançon and co-authors dope solar panel glass waste into new optical materials and study what cerium does inside. The base oxyfluoride already holds up to 80 percent recycled glass. Light tests confirm cerium sits as Ce3+ ions, and glow comes from those ions plus oxygen-poor spots. Raman data show cerium tightens the glass network. Heat tests and live X-ray scans track crystals forming between 500 and 800 degrees. Fluorite, xonotlite, and combeite appear, though cerium cuts the xonotlite share at high heat.
arxiv-2603-25881: Tejerina-Pérez and co-authors set out a method to test Bell inequalities with inflation data alone. The test uses only standard scalar and tensor perturbations of single-field inflation. Entangled graviton pairs carry polarization links between distant patches. Third-order interactions pass that data into the scalar sector. The team isolates the tensor structure of the scalar eight-point function, which splits into four two-point functions. For chosen momentum setups, a CHSH-style violating quantity can be built. This could probe the quantum origin of primordial fluctuations.
arxiv-2603-25981: Chahe and Zhou present PiJEPA, a navigation system that pairs a learned policy with a world model planner. The task is to reach a visual goal given a language instruction. Reactive policies falter on long routes, while world models start their search blind. PiJEPA first finetunes a generalist policy on navigation data. That policy's action spread then seeds a model predictive planner. The planner rolls futures inside a JEPA world model. PiJEPA beats both plain policy runs and uninformed planning on real tasks.
arxiv-2603-26081: Qaisar and co-authors test ways to count people in rooms from surveillance video for smarter building control. Good occupancy data drives heating and cooling decisions in smart buildings. They compare three pipelines on real lab footage with hand-labeled ground truth. Plain detection is least stable over time. Tracking smooths the counts. Adding a language model step cuts false empty readings further. The best pair, YOLOv8 with DeepSeek, hits 0.8824 accuracy and an F1 of 0.9320. Plugged into a control model, it points to 17.94 percent HVAC energy savings.
arxiv-2603-26281: Blatter and co-authors show how breaking spin-group symmetry can steer light-driven currents in altermagnetic insulators. They use shear strain as the breaking tool. The sign of the strain locks the direction of the new charge and spin photocurrents. With no spin-orbit coupling, a spin-gap imbalance explains the effect in simple terms. Density functional tests on CuWP2S6 back the mechanism, and the authors note the effect could help reveal hidden altermagnetism.
arxiv-2603-26381: Ding, Wang, and Zou present momentum-accelerated Kaczmarz methods for large nonlinear systems of equations. The classic Kaczmarz method is prized for its ease and low memory use, but nonlinear versions have lagged behind. Their ABNKAm method averages over blocks and adapts both step sizes and momentum terms on the fly. It needs few inner products per step, which keeps cost and memory low. They prove fast convergence to the nearest solution, and tests show it beats prior nonlinear variants.
arxiv-2603-26581: Sangtan, Joseph, and Schaich report lattice work on two-dimensional maximally supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory. The theory comes from shrinking four-dimensional N=4 supersymmetric Yang-Mills down to two dimensions. Their lattice action keeps a subset of the supersymmetries intact. They extend existing simulation code with the extra terms the lower-dimensional theory needs. Rational Hybrid Monte Carlo runs then let them probe the continuum limit. The effort supports numeric tests of gauge-gravity duality and other non-perturbative questions.
arxiv-2603-27381: Hnatyshyn and Perez characterize atomistic transitions with cross-scale graph-pooled Chebyshev signatures. Long simulations bury the key changes in sheer data volume. Their signatures are permutation invariants of an operator. It maps a Coulomb matrix of the starting state to the final state's matrix. A distance between them then sorts them into families. Tests used one long run of a small metallic nanoparticle. These groups showed patterns and hierarchies that older tools miss. Clustering them this way eases analysis of huge runs.
arxiv-2603-27481: Zhao and co-authors fight forgetting in vision-language models that keep learning. New experts get added as new tasks arrive. Old experts stay frozen in place. Yet old tokens drift toward the new experts. That drift harms past task scores. Their LLaVA-DyMoE system spots token types from routing scores. Guidance steers vague and old tokens away from new experts. Extra rules keep routing patterns stable. The design cuts drift while still learning new tasks.
arxiv-2603-27581: Nguyen and co-authors place security funds where networks need them most. Linked control systems face stealthy data injection attacks. A defender must guard the worst spots with limited means. Their method ranks subsystems by network centrality. Funds then flow to the most connected nodes. Tests compare this rule with the optimal plan. The centrality rule acts far faster. Performance loss stays modest in return. Random graph tests confirm the trade-off.
arxiv-2603-27681: Verma shows a blind spot in neutrino disappearance searches. Binned energy spectra may hide small mass splittings. In the small-phase limit, the signal shift is quadratic. That shift also looks smooth across energy bins. Fit nuisance terms can mimic the same smooth shape. The chi-squared then stays flat at quadratic order. Sensitivity must come from higher-order effects. Or it must come from tighter limits on spectral freedom.
arxiv-2603-27781: Li and co-authors build GS3LAM for dense semantic mapping in real time. The system fuses color, depth, and semantic data streams. Scenes become a field of semantic Gaussians. Camera poses and the field train jointly under mixed error terms. A depth-adaptive scale rule fixes misalignments between cues. Past explicit maps were coarse and could not fill gaps. Implicit maps were too slow for live use. Gaussian splatting sidesteps both flaws.
arxiv-2603-27881: Ji and co-authors test error tails in binary choice models with ease. Probit and logit force thin tails on errors. That tail choice decides if regular-rate estimation works. Their test asks if choice chances decay polynomially. No index, independence, or variance premises are needed. Power nears the best possible among invariant tests. Implementation stays simple in practice. Firm innovation data reject the thin tail.
arxiv-2603-27981: Kolluri, Kampouridis, and Shekhar study how much the Whisper speech encoder can be pruned inside the SLAM-ASR system. They test three Whisper sizes across Danish, Dutch, and English in over 200 training runs. Cutting two encoder layers costs only 2-4% in word error rate. Adding LoRA fine-tuning beats the unpruned model while using 7-14% fewer parameters. Gains are weaker for low-resource Danish, where LoRA adds insertion errors.
arxiv-2603-28681: Bibaut and co-authors propose a cross-fitted debiasing device for learning policies from offline data. A key result is square-root-N regret, even for policy classes more complex than Donsker classes. That result needs a product-of-errors remainder that shrinks fast enough. The regret bound splits into two factors. One factor reflects plug-in policy error and policy class complexity. The other reflects the environment and its dynamics.
arxiv-2603-28781: Bidollahkhani, Nordsiek, and Kunkel propose an early-warning framework for quiet GPU failures in computing clusters. Some grow as slow thermal or efficiency drift. Others strike at the driver or interconnect level with no numeric warning. In those cases, the main signal is missing device metrics. Their method models thermal drift and monitoring pipeline decay together. Tests on production telemetry from GWDG nodes show detachment failures cause structural collapse first. Joint modeling gave longer warning lead time than GPU-only detection.
arxiv-2603-28881: Burrage and Sevillano Muñoz study how matter interactions can shift ultra-light dark matter in the early universe. Such scalar fields oscillate, and a misalignment mechanism sets the size of those swings. If the scalar couples to Standard Model fields, normal matter can change its expected value. That change alters the late time swing size and thus the dark matter amount. For quadratic couplings, they estimate the effect by coupling strength. For axion-like fields, dark sector links can briefly destabilize the field and cause large shifts.
arxiv-2603-29381: Breitkopf and co-authors study the parameterized complexity of MAD trees. A MAD tree is a spanning tree with the smallest average distance between vertex pairs. The problem is a classic network design task and is NP-hard. Approximation methods exist, but parameterized results were missing. They give a linear-time method for graphs of constant modular width. For bounded treewidth, they give a polynomial-time method. The problem is also fixed-parameter tractable by vertex integrity. They add NP-hardness results on split graphs.
arxiv-2603-29581: Sharma and co-authors study the decay patterns of two hidden-bottom tetraquarks. The states, Zb and Zb prime, sit close in mass and share quantum numbers. One puzzle is why Zb prime decay to a B meson pair is suppressed. Born-Oppenheimer effective theory writes both states as mixes of two configurations. That mix ties decay patterns to two adjoint meson types. Lattice QCD calculations of adjoint correlators suggest those mesons are degenerate. The finding supports the theory's account of the suppression.
arxiv-2603-29681: Koch argues that generative AI does not simply amplify the Dunning-Kruger effect. The evidence points to a subtler pattern. Language model use can raise output quality and short-term task scores. At the same time, it can degrade how well people judge their own skill. Koch names this split AI-mediated metacognitive decoupling. Four quantities drift apart: output, understanding, calibration, and self-assessment. The model explains overconfidence, reliance swings, and weak transfer better than the old metaphor. Design lessons for tools and assessment follow.
arxiv-2603-29781: Chakraborty and Ramos study brane inflation inside a warped throat in warm inflation settings. The classic setup uses one mobile D3-brane moving toward an anti-brane at the tip. They instead let radial and angular positions act as two separate inflaton fields. A D7-brane helps fix the moduli and shapes both potentials. Heat loss effects then let the models meet recent data limits more easily. Warm versions beat cold ones for the same parameter space.
arxiv-2603-29981: Brenning and Suesse fix how spatial models get checked before use. Standard cross-validation assumes test sites mirror the full map area. Clustered sampling breaks that match and skews error estimates. Their weighted scheme aligns check tasks with the true deployment zone. It tags tasks by traits like local conditions and prediction distance. In simulations, weighted checks cut bias sharply. A case study maps nitrogen dioxide across Germany. There, standard checks overstate prediction error.
