Their prior family combines the total variation function, which penalizes abrupt spatial changes, with Lp norms.

Embedded in a Bayesian regression framework with posterior sampling by the No-U-Turn Sampler, the method is compared against maximum-likelihood estimation and Bayesian priors. The tests use synthetic brain and cardiac datasets plus a real in-vivo breast dataset. The new prior produced concentrated posterior densities and lower variance and smaller bias than the alternatives, yielding reliable T1 estimates. The authors conclude that building the total-variation structure into the prior improves the spatial coherence and the uncertainty quantification, and they release the code.
arxiv-2606-05581:
Maesumi and colleagues bring a heavy shape tool to messy real-world meshes in a 2026 arXiv paper. Geometry software leans on surface operators like the Laplacian to analyze and edit shapes. Those tools assume clean meshes, but wild collections are full of flaws and split parts. The team estimates a volumetric operator instead, the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map. It links values on a shape's surface through the space inside and around it.

Random sampling does the estimating, in the Monte Carlo style. The method shrugs off poor triangles, fine detail, and shapes in many pieces. It ran orders of magnitude faster than older boundary-element solvers. The team computed spectra for about four hundred fifty thousand shapes from the uncurated Objaverse set. They also built Steklov-CLIP, a network that learns shape codes from these operators. The work shows volumetric spectra can scale to web-sized shape libraries.
arxiv-2606-05681:
Shimizu builds estimators for drifting trends buried in Gaussian noise in a 2026 arXiv paper. The data stream mixes a steady centered Gaussian process with a deterministic drift that changes over time. Dense, high-frequency sampling is assumed. The drift's shape carries the parameter of interest. Shimizu scores candidate drifts by a least-squares style contrast built from small step-to-step increments.

The estimator proves consistent and settles into a normal limit under mild dependence in the noise. Its speed depends on two forces at once: how rough the noise is locally, and how information piles up over long horizons. The theory covers sinking, polynomial, and repeating drift families. Some families yield non-standard convergence speeds. Persistent or growing drifts can even give faster than usual rates. The framework unifies cases that earlier work handled one family at a time, each with separate tools.
arxiv-2606-05981:
Ootani finds that shrinking a video stylizer's image model makes its text brain the new bottleneck in a 2026 arXiv paper. A distilled U-Net of under half a billion parameters paints each frame in a few steps. The vision-aware text encoder, a multimodal model ten times larger, then dominates per-frame cost. His pipeline attacks that imbalance with three mechanisms on consumer hardware.

Asymmetric CUDA streams overlap encoder batches with denoising work, amortizing text cost across frames. A reformulated control adapter folds the whole network stack into one fused, compiler-friendly graph. Periodic refreshes reuse prompt understanding instead of recomputing it each frame. On a single RTX 3090 Ti the system sustained about twenty-seven frames per second over long runs. Faster cards pushed past fifty and seventy frames per second. An oil-painting adapter generalized to unseen video clips. The paper reports throughput as streaming, not interactive latency.
arxiv-2606-06181:
Adelin Roty, Jan Tobias Mühlberg, and Jean-François Determe ask whether discarded phones stay secure when reused in this 2026 arXiv paper. An estimated five point three billion mobile phones became electronic waste in 2022 alone, and many still work well enough for a second life. Modern phones, though, lean on hardware security features provisioned by the vendor for one fixed lifecycle. Reuse outside that ecosystem may quietly void the protections users assume.

Working with a PinePhone, an open-hardware smartphone, the authors test three things: boot chain integrity, the isolation of the trusted execution environment, and protection of hardware-bound secrets. Their simulated repurposing scenarios show that rebuilding trust anchors, the roots from which security checks grow, is complex and fragile. They generalize the findings into requirements for secure repurposing and argue that vendor-locked mechanisms block safe reuse for most discarded devices.
arxiv-2606-06281:
Rickmer Krohn and co-authors teach robots to feel with several senses of touch at once in this 2026 arXiv paper. Manipulation tasks that involve rich contact, like inserting or sliding objects, are hard to learn from cameras alone. Tactile sensors help, but they differ wildly: some give detailed images of contact at low rates, others stream fast but coarse signals. Fusing those mismatched streams is the challenge here.

Their framework, MiTaS, encodes each stream with its own convolutional stem, then merges them with a transformer. The inputs are an RGB camera, a GelSight Mini vision based touch sensor, and a high frequency event based Evetac sensor. The fused representation steers a flow matching policy learned from demonstrations. Across five contact rich tasks, MiTaS succeeded eighty percent of the time on average. A vision only baseline managed thirty one percent, and a visual tactile one fifty four percent.
arxiv-2606-06481:
Sondos Mahmoud Bsharat and co-authors build a benchmark for a murkier authorship problem in this 2026 arXiv paper. Real documents increasingly come from human AI co editing: a person drafts, an assistant revises, and authorship blurs line by line. Detectors are usually tested only on final texts, purely human or purely machine. Their OpAI Bench instead tracks the whole journey, producing nine progressively revised versions of each human written document.

Revisions follow five edit operations at set levels of AI coverage, across four domains, with authorship tracked at document, sentence, token, and span level. Seventeen detectors were evaluated. Detectability depended not just on how much AI text was present, but on the edit type, the domain, and the revision history. Surprisingly, mixed middle versions were often harder to flag than either endpoint, a blind spot current benchmarks miss. The testbed asks when, not just whether, assisted writing becomes detectable.
arxiv-2606-06581:
Martin S Sloth teaches the early universe's great stretch in this 2026 arXiv paper, a set of advanced lecture notes. Written for the Nordita Winter School, the lectures open with why inflation is needed at all. Without a burst of exponential expansion, distant sky patches could never have been in causal contact. Yet they share a temperature. Penrose diagrams make that horizon problem vivid.

The course then builds slow roll inflation step by step: background, linear perturbations, then nonlinear theory. Later lectures reach current research. Soft theorems constrain very long wavelength modes. Gravitational memory effects describe the imprint a passing wave leaves on a ring of observers. Sloth ties both to asymptotic symmetries, showing how a patient satellite array could record the change in quantum state.
arxiv-2606-06681:
Cloud computers waste energy when machines sit switched on between jobs. Liu, Khuller, and Tang study a scheduling puzzle behind that waste in this 2026 arXiv paper, called span minimization. Jobs with release times and deadlines must be packed onto machines. The goal is to shrink the total time machines stay active. There is no limit on how many jobs share one machine.

The twist is that choices must be made online, as jobs arrive, without seeing the future. Earlier deterministic methods could guarantee results within twice the best possible. The authors show that a randomized strategy beats that barrier for jobs of equal length. The strategy deliberately flips coins. It reaches a competitive ratio near one point four four. They also prove no randomized method can go below about one point three seven, and allowing restarts, they reach exactly the golden ratio.
arxiv-2606-07181:
Chemists planning a synthesis work backward from the target molecule, and software must rank the candidate first steps. Pappala and co-authors split that job in two in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their RETROSPECT system pairs a transformer that proposes precursor molecules with a learned reranker that reorders them. The proposals come from chemical strings, augmented in aligned and random forms during training.

On the standard USPTO-50K test set of five thousand reactions, the generator alone hit fifty five percent top one accuracy. Its top ten lists reached about eighty six percent. The reranker then lifted top one accuracy to fifty nine point four percent over pools of roughly one hundred candidates. Ablations showed most reranking signal came from the proposal score and template frequency. Quantum chemistry features added little and inconsistently. The modular split also lets the generator drop into larger ensemble planners.
arxiv-2606-07281:
Zhang, Li, and Zhang solve a stubborn technical problem in meshfree simulation methods in this 2026 arXiv paper. Meshfree methods model physics on scattered points instead of a fixed grid, which helps with cracking, large deformation, and moving boundaries. Their weakness is imposing essential boundary conditions, meaning fixed values on the boundary, because the method's coefficients are not point values. Simply setting those coefficients does not force the field to match the required boundary trace.

Their natural decomposition method inserts boundary data before discretization instead of patching afterward. A source subproblem handles the forcing, a weighted curl correction fixes the remaining mismatch, and a recovery step rebuilds it. They prove the rebuilt field equals the true boundary-satisfying solution for simple connected domains. Benchmarks report the method's conditioning, cost, and response to boundary perturbations, all without penalty terms or multiplier tricks that rival approaches require.
arxiv-2606-07481:
Jung and co-authors replace diffusion sampling with a one-pass generative method for predicting indoor airflow, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Computational fluid dynamics gives accurate flow fields for designing ventilation, but its cost blocks design exploration. Generative surrogate models can imitate those fields, yet diffusion-based ones need many sampling steps, erasing much of the speed gain. The authors adapt the newer drifting method, which generates samples in a single pass, run inside a learned latent space from a variational autoencoder.

Label-aware masking aligns flows with their boundary conditions, such as inlet positions and speeds. Their label-conditioned model matched iterative models in accuracy and flow consistency while running 100 times faster. A spatial-conditioning variant points toward room shapes never seen in training. The authors position conditional drifting as the practical route to real-time fluid dynamics surrogates, where inference speed decides whether designers can explore interactively.
arxiv-2606-07581:
Xu and Wu name a source of AI training bugs: the model you train is not the model you deploy, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Training kernels compute with precise accumulators and shapes, while inference kernels fuse low-precision operations behind caches. In finite precision the two implement different functions of the weights, producing off-policy bias in rollouts, regressions under 8-bit deployment, and scores that fail to reproduce across hardware. The authors call this a missing index on the policy symbol.

Their kernel contract bundles numerical, statistical, and observability clauses with an escalation policy for violations. They derive bounds chaining a clause on logit drift through distributional distance into a bound on rewards. In reinforcement learning post-training, a per-token bound on the train-inference probability ratio bounds the policy-gradient estimator's bias. This reinterprets a clipping trick as a budget on the kernel pair rather than the policy.
arxiv-2606-07681:
Lahlou, Hawkins, and Gentine use AI agents to translate Fortran climate code into JAX, a framework where programs can be differentiated automatically, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Differentiable models allow gradient-based tuning and data assimilation, a way of blending observations into a simulation. Hand-converting decades-old code is slow, though. Their five-phase pipeline orders modules by dependency and repairs compile errors in a loop. It checks numbers against the Fortran original.

Applied across seventy-three module tasks to CLM-ml-v2, a nineteen-thousand-line land surface model, the translated model computes the Jacobian in one backward pass. The Jacobian is the table of sensitivities of outputs to inputs. The model recovers parameters in eight times fewer steps than gradient-free search. At an ensemble size of two thousand forty-eight, it runs twenty-four times faster than the Fortran version. The pipeline is released for reuse.
arxiv-2606-07781:
Lars Andersson, Khuri, Mars, and Simon define a new quasilocal mass for black-hole regions and prove it behaves as a mass should, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In general relativity, energy refuses to localise. Physicists therefore measure a region's mass by comparing it with every reasonable completion into a full asymptotically flat spacetime. Bartnik's version takes the smallest such completion mass, but proving it positive has been hard.

The authors prove strict positivity in two black-hole settings. One covers compact regions bounded by an apparent horizon. The other covers open regions with flat ends that contain an apparent horizon. In plain terms, such regions carry genuinely positive mass unless they came from empty Minkowski space. The authors also prove the mass never decreases with time in the matching evolution scenarios. Both results need a careful no-extra-horizons condition on the completions, which keeps the comparison honest.
arxiv-2606-07881:
Elam and co-authors remove the idle bubbles from pipeline-parallel training without letting model versions drift apart, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Splitting a network across devices forces a choice. Synchronous schedules keep every stage on consistent weights but leave devices waiting. Asynchronous schedules keep devices busy at the cost of mismatched weight versions, usually patched with stashing or prediction tricks.

Their method, PACI, bounds the version drift instead of eliminating it. Local gradient accumulation slows how fast parameter versions evolve relative to pipeline delay, capping how many updates any batch can cross. No extra parameter copies, stash, or global synchronisation are needed. In GPT-style pretraining, PACI matched the stability and final perplexity of the synchronous schedule at the same peak memory. Its pipeline ran fully utilised, and time-to-accuracy improved up to about one point seven times over the fastest synchronous baseline.
arxiv-2606-07981:
Myungsoo Yoo, Daniel Würzler Barreto, and Mevin B. Hooten make a scalable Bayesian method safe to trust, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Prior proposal recursive Bayesian inference updates a posterior in stages, recycling each stage's result as the next stage's proposal, which parallelises beautifully. But when the posterior shifts a lot between stages, the recursion can silently converge to the wrong distribution.

Their fix borrows parallel tempering from Metropolis-coupled Markov chain Monte Carlo: run coupled chains at several temperatures so information flows between them and stage shifts get corrected. They prove the tempered version targets the true posterior and show it empirically. Applications to earthquake counts and North Atlantic sea salinity compare the method against its untempered parent and a standard sampler. The tempered recursion won on effective sample size per second.
arxiv-2606-08081:
Po-Ya Angela Wang and co-authors test whether AI agents develop the private shorthand that human partners build, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In repeated reference games, two players describe the same tangram shapes round after round. Humans steadily compress their descriptions, entraining on partner-specific conventions rooted in their shared history. Multimodal model agents also align on labels, but earlier work showed they never get more efficient, raising the question of what their alignment really is.

The team's contribution is a pseudo-dyad baseline: pair each agent's output with a stranger's history, breaking the partnership. Humans compress and align more with real partners. Agents keep fixed effort and verbose descriptions from round one, and their near-ceiling label overlap is indistinguishable between real and pseudo dyads. Their alignment is a shared task vocabulary, not partner-specific grounding: they converge on the obvious labels, not on a history with you.
arxiv-2606-08181:
Kaneko and Imada tackle the mechanism behind the highest known superconducting temperature in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their material is a layered copper oxide called Hg1223, which becomes superconducting, meaning it carries current with no resistance, near one hundred thirty-four kelvin at normal pressure. Under pressure that record climbs still higher, yet the microscopic reason has stayed unclear. The authors compute the material's behavior from first principles, using a variational method assisted by a neural network.

Their calculations reproduce the observed dome shape, where the superconducting strength first rises and then falls as conditions change. They trace the strong effect at normal pressure to powerful local repulsion between electrons, poorly screened in this layered compound. Under pressure, electron hopping grows while both local and longer-range repulsion shrink, lifting the transition temperature further. Most strikingly, the pairing of electrons is explained as an attraction emerging from the strong repulsion itself.
arxiv-2606-08381:
Arbabi and Kerschbaum propose a way to audit hidden provider policies inside commercial language models, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Models are released through opaque pipelines, letting providers inject provider-specific policies without announcing them. Users have reported responses reflecting such proprietary rules, shading into censorship or misinformation on controversial topics. Detection is hard, partly because there is no ground-truth standard for what a neutral model should say.

Their framework works comparatively rather than absolutely. In a shared semantic space, it measures steady deviations between a target model's responses and those of a reference set of baseline models answering the same prompts. Because the method measures relative gaps instead of correctness against a standard that does not exist, it can flag alignment that stands out. The goal is a tool that works even when providers will not open up their inner rules.
arxiv-2606-08481:
Ranganath and Raghavendra automate the creation of test sets for systems that translate questions into database queries, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Text-to-Cypher systems answer natural language questions by generating Cypher, the query language for property graphs. A useful benchmark must reflect the questions users actually ask of that company's graph. Yet enterprise graphs vary widely in schema and terminology, and they change over time. Each benchmark question must also be executable and stay balanced across query types and difficulty.

Their pipeline, PIPE-Cypher, turns a live property graph plus optional seed queries into balanced benchmarks locally. It combines schema profiling, reverse-query grounding, constrained generation, governance checks, execution validation, redaction, and diversity controls. A calibrated local language model acts as judge. Generation and judging run on a local model, keeping proprietary graph data inside the enterprise.
arxiv-2606-08581:
Benjamini and Shellef analyze a simple particle system that spreads itself out, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The pile process runs on a graph. At each step, one particle at a vertex that has a lower neighbor moves to a neighboring vertex of minimum height, as if a pile slumps downhill. The authors study the process on a cycle, a ring of vertices, started with all particles stacked on one vertex. They ask how long stabilization takes.

They prove the expected stabilization time is at most a constant multiple of the cube of the ring size. A deterministic transportation argument gives a lower bound of quadratic order, since the particles must physically travel around the ring. Simulations suggest the true order is near the cubic upper bound, meaning random choices genuinely slow the spreading well beyond the transportation minimum.
arxiv-2606-08681:
Yu Wei, Bienstock, and Polychroniadou justify the most popular privacy mechanism and improve it in low dimensions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Differential privacy protects individuals in datasets by adding calibrated noise to query answers, and the additive noise mechanism is its foundational tool. The Gaussian mechanism, adding bell-curve noise, is the most widely used, for its simplicity and strong guarantees. The authors show that as the dimension grows, no additive-noise mechanism can beat the Gaussian mechanism's privacy-utility trade-off in strong privacy settings.

They also develop a new family of mechanisms based on the spherical generalized gamma distribution, which contains both the Gaussian mechanism and a recently studied alternative as special cases. Within this family they identify members that outperform both predecessors in certain low-dimensional settings. They further show tight composition, how privacy loss accumulates across queries, for the whole family.
arxiv-2606-09081:
Lei and colleagues help drones spot tiny objects on a compute budget, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Aerial images teem with small objects, but lightweight detectors downsample, erasing shallow detail. The team studied YOLOX-Nano under edge limits and added a P2 branch, a high-resolution head preserving fine detail. They also ran a quantum-inspired evolutionary algorithm to screen structural variants, scoring candidates on accuracy, computation, latency, memory, and recall.

On VisDrone, P2 raised small-object precision by 31.10 percent over the baseline. Against NanoDet-Plus at similar size, it improved precision by 17.5 percent and small-object precision by 44.9 percent. The search's favorite candidate won on recall, but after full training P2 remained strongest on precision, and proxy rankings did not always transfer. The verdict: add the high-resolution branch for small objects, and use the search as a cheap screening tool, not an oracle.
arxiv-2606-09681:
Tianyu Lin and a large team build eye movement data from scratch to train a brain-health screening tool in this 2026 arXiv paper. Saccades are the quick darts the eyes make between gaze points. Their speed and aim mirror the state of brain circuits, which makes them fine biomarkers. Real patient video is scarce, though, since privacy rules lock it away.

Their pipeline, GenEyePose, makes fully fake yet body-true eye videos, with no patient records at all. From knowledge-based models of eye motion, it renders clips of sound and faulty saccades. Faults span undershoot and overshoot of the target. A deep classifier trained only on this fake data then faced real clinic clips. It scored an AUROC of zero point seven six, with sensitivity of zero point seven one. The team sees uses at home and in emergency rooms, where a cheap camera test could triage patients fast.
arxiv-2606-09781:
Saharian, Karapetyan, and Mirzoyan build a general frame for how flaws in spacetime shape a quantum field's local traits in this 2026 arXiv paper. The flaws are topological defects, like cosmic strings and global monopoles, set in warped geometries. Warping scales space by a factor that shifts along an extra direction. Such settings arise in braneworld models of our universe.

The team splits the curvature into three sources: the warp factor, the radial shape, and the angular flaw pattern. For any curvature coupling, the field equation then splits into clean radial, angular, and warp parts. They solve for a full set of wave modes at general flaw strengths. Case work spans flat-warp spaces, broad cosmic strings, monopoles, and anti-de Sitter warps. As a capstone, they work out the Hadamard two-point function, a key measure of field links, for a monopole in anti-de Sitter space.
arxiv-2606-09881:
Ryan Brown and Chris Russell even out deepfake detectors across faces, with no group labels, no retraining, and no accuracy tax in this 2026 arXiv paper. Detectors can miss by wide margins across demographic groups. One tool's false alarms ran near twice as high for women as for men. Past fixes need the very labels that privacy rules withhold, or they trade away sharpness.

Their Face-Fairness frame hangs a light calibrator on a frozen detector. The calibrator remaps the detector's raw score, steered by face embeddings that quietly carry the traits that track its faults. Two kin variants aim at worst-group accuracy, one with true labels and one with groups found in the embeddings. Across home and away test sets, the frame cut false-rate gaps and lifted the worst group's score. Overall accuracy held or rose.
arxiv-2606-09981:
Luo and colleagues revisit a quasar that seemed oddly faint in X-rays, in a 2026 arXiv paper on astronomy. PHL 1811, a narrow-line Type 1 quasar, was long treated as the prototype of intrinsically X-ray weak quasars, whose centers genuinely emit few X-rays. A bright flare caught by the Einstein Probe in 2024 changed the picture. The authors gathered archival observations spanning 2001 to 2024.

Before 2024 the quasar showed weakness factors from about twenty-three to about one hundred seventy-nine across all epochs, meaning X-rays far below expectation. The flare briefly revealed a normal X-ray state, followed by rapid decline. Three signatures favor heavy obscuration by a clumpy, dust-free absorber: a hard X-ray excess in a 2015 spectrum, flat shapes in two Swift observations, and state changes without matching optical changes. A partial-covering model fits every epoch, pointing to a wind off the accretion disc.
arxiv-2606-10081:
van Rossum presents an exact optimization algorithm and a public benchmark library for railway crew scheduling, in a 2026 arXiv paper on operations research. Crew scheduling assigns tasks to staff as feasible duties at minimum cost, a core planning problem for railway operators. Public benchmark instances are also rare, hampering comparison between methods.

His branch-and-price implementation is studied systematically across branching rules, primal heuristics, and reduced cost fixing. The new library holds seventy-five instances ranging from four hundred fifty to just over three thousand tasks, generated by mimicking the full railway planning process and validated against Netherlands Railways data. Average optimality gaps stayed well below one percent across all sizes, driven mainly by strong primal heuristics. Branching and cost fixing contributed little, showing that improving the dual bound remains the main challenge for exact methods.
arxiv-2606-10281:
Anand and his team benchmark how well language models can dig into cyberattacks from system logs, in a 2026 arXiv paper on computer security. Incident response teams read audit logs to triage alerts and find how attackers persisted on compromised machines, work that is slow and expertise-heavy. Their benchmark, AuditBench, contains system audit logs from Linux and Windows machines spanning over fifty security investigation scenarios with both malicious and benign activity.

They test five frontier language models on the benchmark and study how scores and error profiles vary with model size, data format, prompt design, and task type. The study also profiles the quality of the explanations models produce and the kinds of errors they make across scenarios. The work provides a base for assessing language models as investigation assistants, showing where they already help incident responders and where their log analysis remains shaky for security-critical calls.
arxiv-2606-10381:
Ruobing Jiang and his team build an AI research assistant built for muon collider physics, in a 2026 arXiv paper on information systems. Muon collider research spans accelerator physics, detector design, and high-energy theory, with evidence scattered across a fast-growing, mixed literature. Their agentic hybrid retrieval-augmented generation system combines a hybrid retriever, mixing sparse lexical and dense semantic search. An agentic reasoning module breaks up queries, expands evidence, and writes grounded answers.

To evaluate it, they construct the first benchmark for retrieval-augmented scientific question answering in the muon collider domain, with a curated literature corpus plus its own retrieval and answer-generation test sets. A domain-grounded assistant that cites real papers could speed design studies for a future muon collider, a machine whose case rests on pulling together exactly this scattered evidence.
arxiv-2606-10781:
Slabbert, Malan, and Kamper revisit word discovery in unlabelled speech in this 2026 arXiv paper on speech processing. Unsupervised term discovery segments speech into word units and clusters them into a lexicon. Real lexicons are Zipfian: a few types are very frequent and most are rare. The standard tool, K-means, is biased toward equal clusters, so lexicons come out too uniform. The authors cluster the similarity graph between segment embeddings, partitioning it with the Leiden algorithm.

Across 3 languages, at word and syllable level, graph clustering outperforms the centre-based methods, K-means, Gaussian mixtures, and BIRCH, in type recovery, with distributions much closer to Zipf's law. Agglomerative clustering does well, supporting the diagnosis that dropping centre geometry is the key move, but scales worse and gives less control over the distribution. Its two hyperparameters give interpretable control of the lexicon's shape, making graph clustering, the authors argue, the default.
arxiv-2606-10981:
Kamiński and colleagues report new behavior from the merged star V838 Monocerotis in this 2026 arXiv paper. The star is the remnant of a 2002 merger and now resembles a red supergiant. In late 2025 it entered its deepest dimming since 2006, and the team followed the event with photometry and high-resolution spectra from minimum into recovery.

The color changes fit a passing clump of fresh dust, dimming the star by about one and a quarter magnitudes, while the surface temperature barely moved. During recovery, hydrogen lines flared in emission with the odd ratios of pulsating Mira stars, and metal lines sat blueshifted by 90 kilometers per second: signs of a pulsation shock. It is the first evidence of pulsations in a merger remnant.
arxiv-2606-11081:
Pietro Cagnasso, Belilovsky, and Oyallon tackle the communication bottleneck in training large language models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Standard training keeps every worker's model identical through synchronous All-Reduce rounds, where all machines average updates together. That global step stalls when bandwidth varies or workers run slow.

Their algorithm, GASLoC, decentralizes pretraining. Workers take local optimizer steps and exchange information through sparse, randomized peer gossip instead of global collectives. An outer optimizer, borrowed from DiLoCo, accelerates the communication. Full communication recovers the DiLoCo update exactly, so the method unifies both lines of work. On standard training tasks, GASLoC beat state-of-the-art decentralized algorithms in the one-step-per-communication setting across several topologies. With multiple local steps it matched DiLoCo, something earlier decentralized methods could not do, and under uneven bandwidth it finished in shorter wall-clock time.
arxiv-2606-11581:
Purnima Kamath, Roman, Saito, Mitsufuji, and Bello test how spatial audio metrics behave in a 2026 arXiv paper, from New York University and Sony. Evaluating generative spatial audio for First-Order Ambisonics is hard because little is known about how metrics respond to changes in spatial parameters like azimuth and elevation. They analyze metric sensitivity along continuous spatial trajectories, borrowing from parametric sound synthesis.

Using controlled scenes of increasing complexity, they define three desiderata for metric behavior: responsiveness, smoothness, and symmetry. They assess standard distribution-based and sample-based metrics, including Fréchet Audio Distance, intensity vectors, and acoustic maps. Fréchet Audio Distance with localization-specific embeddings, and acoustic maps, show high responsiveness with robust smoothness and symmetry across conditions. Intensity vectors degrade as scenes grow more complex. It is a first step toward knowing which metrics can be trusted to judge generated sound fields.
arxiv-2606-11681:
Sangmin Lee and three Yonsei colleagues scale text-to-speech to hundreds of languages in this 2026 arXiv paper. A speech synthesiser needs a text encoder that knows how written words sound. The standard route converts spelling to phonemes, units of sound, but reliable converters exist for only about one hundred languages, capping coverage.

Their encoder, UR-BERT, instead converts every writing system into Romanisation, spelling sounds with the Latin alphabet, giving one shared representation for 495 languages. During training the encoder must also predict speech tokens, forcing it to learn how text aligns with sound rather than spelling alone. Experiments show systems built on UR-BERT beat recent text encoder baselines across languages with rich and poor resources. The encoder also generalises strongly to languages unseen in training, a step toward universal speech synthesis.
arxiv-2606-12581:
Stolarski and co-authors ask whether shrinking a network first breaks the search for its most influential members, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Influence maximization picks seed sets from which spreading, of news or infection, reaches furthest. Real networks are huge and noisy, so analysts reduce them, by sparsification, dropping edges, or coarsening, merging nodes. Whether that preprocessing distorts the answer was untested. Their SORB benchmark standardizes the test.

SORB combines seven reduction algorithms, five sparsifiers and two coarseners, with six influence models across seven networks, single-layer and multilayer. On single-layer networks, sparsification preserves seed-set quality at every seed size tried; coarsening costs only a little. Flattened multilayer networks are the warning case: their rankings degrade whatever reduction is used. Impact also depends on the scoring task. The moral: reduction must be evaluated reduction-aware and multi-task, since a harmless shrink on one network type corrupts another.
arxiv-2606-12881:
Yu and colleagues report an empirical study of Direct Preference Optimisation, or DPO, for fine-tuning a chatbot language model, in this 2026 arXiv paper. DPO aligns a model with human preferences directly, skipping the reward model that standard reinforcement learning from human feedback needs. The authors apply it to the pre-trained dolphin-2.1-mistral-7b model using a human-labelled preference dataset.

Their experiments show that DPO eases the training pipeline and cuts computing cost while reaching strong results. Scoring with BLEU, ROUGE, and cosine similarity metrics, which measure overlap and semantic nearness between generated and reference text, shows effective learning and convergence during training. The study is candid about limits: training instability was observed and needs further work. The authors present DPO as a handy, lower-complexity route to preference-aligned fine-tuning, with the caveat that stability, rather than final quality, is the open problem their results expose.
arxiv-2606-12981:
Shahbaz and Agarwal describe a camera and LiDAR fusion detector for cooperative 3D object detection on the TUMTraf V2X dataset, built for the DriveX 2026 challenge, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The detector fuses 3 roadside cameras with a pre-registered point cloud combining infrastructure and vehicle LiDAR, in a bird's-eye-view space.

Trained on the provided train and validation splits, the model reaches a 3D mean average precision of 0.85 on the public test split. The report's important contribution is a benchmark integrity finding: 44 of the 50 test frames are also present, with labels, in the train and validation splits. The authors quantify the consequences with 2 studies. Fine-tuning while oversampling the 44 overlapping frames raises the score to 0.89, and a post-processing run that replaces predictions on those frames with the ground truth reaches 0.99, a configuration uploaded for testing but not published on the leaderboard.
arxiv-2606-13081:
Landi and colleagues present Emotional Regulation, a framework for modelling emotion in deep learning through artificial subjective experience, and test it on image classification, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Emotion shapes human cognition, aiding memory and learning, and emotion-augmented deep learning tries to import that benefit into neural networks. Current methods define emotion only through objective neurophysiological factors, missing subjectivity, the personal appraisal that shapes an emotional response.

The authors test image classification, pre-training ResNet and Vision Transformer designs on 4 emotional data sets and testing on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 benchmarks. Results show gains over the same backbones trained without the emotional regulation stage. The authors report that the approach surpasses prior emotion-augmented methods on the CIFAR benchmarks, making it the new state of the art in emotion-augmented deep learning for vision data sets.
arxiv-2606-13381:
Vo, Martínez-García, and Valera present Hölder++ in this 2026 arXiv paper, a multimodal variational autoencoder. Such models learn to generate data in modalities at once, for example images paired with text. They face a trade-off between generative quality, how realistic and diverse the samples are, and coherence, whether the modalities in one sample agree with each other. Recent work showed that a pooling method inspired by Hölder's inequality improves coherence. But it approximated the pooling and assumed one shared representation for all modalities, which cost some diversity.

Hölder++ removes the approximation, implementing the pooling for the first time in this setting. Its architecture models shared and private representations separately, so each modality keeps features of its own while sharing a core. Hierarchical inference disentangles the two kinds of information. The authors report an improved balance between quality and coherence over prior models.
arxiv-2606-13681:
Xu and colleagues introduce EvoArena in this 2026 arXiv paper, a benchmark for agents in changing environments. Language model agents score well on static benchmarks, but deployment is dynamic: software updates, shifting preferences, and revised tasks force agents to realign their knowledge and behaviour. EvoArena models environment change as sequences of updates across terminal, software, and social domains. The authors also propose EvoMem, a patch-based memory that records memory evolution as update histories, letting agents reason about how their environment changed rather than just its current state.

Current agents struggle on the benchmark, averaging under forty percent accuracy across the evolving domains. Patch-based memory gives agents a fighting chance by making the history of changes an object of reasoning. The work reframes agent evaluation around adaptation over time, which decides whether an agent deployed for months stays useful. It also supplies a memory pattern that builders can adopt independently.
arxiv-2606-13781:
Merchant and colleagues release a catalogue of galaxy structural parameters from two telescope surveys in this 2026 arXiv paper. The data combine Hubble and James Webb imaging in up to 29 wavelength bands for galaxies in survey fields. Parameters, sizes, shapes, and light profiles, are measured across the bands, a lever arm. The team explores the galaxy size-mass relation, how a galaxy's size scales with its mass. They trace it across time, from when the universe was a few billion years old to nearly its age.

Multi-wavelength structure matters because a galaxy's appearance changes with wavelength: young stars, old stars, and dust dominate different bands. Measuring sizes in 29 bands separates those components' distributions. The catalogue, a data release from the CANUCS and Technicolor programmes, is community infrastructure. Size-mass change is a test of galaxy formation models, and a uniform catalogue across this redshift range gives theorists a benchmark.
arxiv-2606-13881:
Kumar connects a finance equation to the math of swirling fluids. The Ivancevic model prices options with a nonlinear Schrödinger equation, a wave equation where an adaptive term stands for market feedback. Betchov's classic work rewrote similar equations for vortex filaments as fluid-style laws. His 2026 arXiv paper shows the Ivancevic equation admits the same treatment when its coefficients stay constant.

Splitting the wave into density and velocity yields a continuity equation and a momentum-type law. The volatility and adaptive terms set the pressure and dispersive parts of the momentum flux. Kumar tests the form on known soliton solutions, the self-keeping wave packets of the model. He stresses the reading is structural, not a claim that markets are fluids. Its value is a shared language linking wave theory, fluid mechanics, and finance.
arxiv-2606-14181:
Landajuela puts the marriage of neural PDE solvers and finite elements on rigorous footing. Physics-informed neural networks handle moving geometry meshlessly; finite elements excel on fitted meshes. Coupling them lacked theory. His 2026 arXiv paper views each solver as a Steklov-Poincaré operator, mapping interface traces to fluxes: Dirichlet-Neumann iteration can diverge; Robin-Neumann coupling cures it, with a closed-form optimal impedance.

His contraction theorem covers the realistic case: a trained network realizes only a perturbed operator, yet Robin-Neumann still contracts, to a floor set by the training loss. A Fourier-mode probe recovers the network's interface eigenvalues within zero point five percent. Theory predicted measured contraction rates within seven percent. In Stokes flow with a rigid disc in contact, the meshless side absorbed the topology change with no remeshing. The contact reaction matched the disc's submerged weight within zero point four percent.
arxiv-2606-14681:
Gomez and co-authors propose a magnetic explanation for mysteriously wide spectral lines in solar flares in a 2026 arXiv paper. During flares, chromospheric metal lines such as magnesium and calcium show Lorentzian wings about thirty times wider than standard pressure broadening predicts, and no known collisional mechanism explains the excess.

The authors posit that magnetic fields cause the extra broadening, since flare activity raises magnetic complexity. A field-strength distribution falling as the inverse cube of field strength reproduces the observed magnesium line wings while leaving hydrogen Balmer lines and optically thin transitions largely unaffected. The model's rare high-field tail reaches extreme strengths with tiny filling factors below one part in a million. They propose spectropolarimetric flare observations, measuring polarization in the lines, to test whether magnetic structures in flare ribbons truly cause the broadening.
arxiv-2606-14781:
Torres and co-authors restore underwater images with a math-guided neural net in a 2026 arXiv paper. Underwater photos suffer poor sight and warped color. Ocean work depends on them. Their model-based unfolding net turns an optimization model into a learnable design. The model encodes dehazing physics as a cost to minimize. The net's stages mimic solver steps.

The cost form uses a dehazing split. A scaled leftover term soaks up leftover artifacts. A nonlocal gradient rule keeps structure and edge sharpness. The authors prove a solution exists for the cost problem. Mamba sequence layers inside the unfolding capture self-similar patterns well. A path loss keeps each stage in line with an ideal restore step. Tests show better looks and scores on par with recent top enhancers.
arxiv-2606-14981:
Wu and coauthors steer robot policies with both vision and touch at deployment time in a 2026 study. Pretrained robot policies propose actions, and steering checks them before execution without retraining. Vision alone misses contact details, such as grip force. The authors split guidance across the two senses, which work on different time scales.

Their framework, ViTaL, runs a two-level scheme inside a learned visuo-tactile world model. At the high level, sampled action sequences are scored by a visual verifier for long-horizon task progress. At the low level, tactile-guided diffusion editing refines the chosen sequence to meet local contact needs. A text-conditioned tactile reward scores predicted touch outcomes directly in latent space. Tests cover pipetting, wiping, and peg insertion on a real robot. ViTaL raises overall success above the base policy, beats vision-only steering, and tops naive fusion of the two senses.
arxiv-2606-15181:
Taha and coauthors revisit the PBH controllability test in a 2026 control theory letter. Controllability asks whether inputs can steer a linear system to any desired state. The PBH test answers through eigenvectors, pinpointing which modes inputs cannot move. Checking it on networks normally needs an eigendecomposition, which is too costly. The authors recast the question as a smallest-energy steering problem over a horizon. When a target state is unreachable, optimization theory yields a certificate vector proving it.

They prove every certificate is a blend of the uncontrollable modes themselves. Krylov subspace algorithms then extract those modes from the certificate. The method never builds the controllability matrix or diagonalizes the system. Tests on networks with thousands of nodes show favorable scaling. Accuracy stays high when the certificate mixes only a few dozen modes. The letter turns a yes-or-no test into a fast, targeted diagnostic for large systems.
arxiv-2606-15381:
Wu and coauthors ask whether space-based gravitational wave detectors could sense torsion-inspired dark matter near a black hole, in a 2026 astrophysics paper. In Einstein-Cartan gravity, matter with aligned spin generates torsion, a twist in spacetime. A spike of such spin-polarized dark matter around a massive black hole adds a repulsive spin-spin effect. The authors deform the rotating Kerr black hole geometry and follow a small companion spiraling in, an extreme-mass-ratio inspiral.

In their fiducial system the deformation pushes the innermost stable orbit slightly outward and advances the final plunge by several hours. Accumulated over the inspiral's many cycles, the waveform phase shifts could be large. The authors stress the forecast is optimistic: it omits detector response, self-force fluxes, and eccentric orbits. The result constrains an effective near-zone operator rather than predicting a detection.
arxiv-2606-15681:
Liu and colleagues tackle depth estimation from monocular endoscope video in 2026, where one camera must judge distances inside the body for surgery. Self-supervised methods usually judge each frame alone or add weak temporal smoothing, so their depth maps drift and disagree across frames. The team instead recasts the whole sequence as one multi-view three-dimensional reconstruction problem.

The framework jointly infers depth, camera parameters, and one 3D scene through differentiable Gaussian splatting. Three constraints keep it honest: photometric rendering, explicit alignment in world coordinates, and multi-scale temporal gradient consistency. On public benchmarks it cuts geometric drift and temporal instability against leading frame, video, and reconstruction baselines, reaching top spatial accuracy. It also holds up in zero-shot clinical settings it never trained on. Anchoring every frame to one coherent 3D structure is what turns shaky per-frame guesses into a map a surgeon could trust.
arxiv-2606-15781:
Mousavi and colleagues map crustal stress across Iran's Zagros mountain belt in 2026, using the national earthquake catalogue from 2006 to 2024. The Zagros, where the Arabian plate collides with Eurasia, is among the world's most active continental collision zones and threatens dense population centres. The team computes how seismicity parameters vary across space, depth, and time.

The belt-wide b-value, the relative frequency of large versus small earthquakes, is about 0.81, signalling a dominantly high-stress crust. Persistently low b-value zones, between 0.4 and 0.7, line up with the major fault systems: the Mountain Front, High Zagros, and Main Zagros Reverse faults. Those low values sit mainly in the upper ten kilometres, where the brittle crust releases its energy. Fractal dimension values run high in the same zones, marking structurally complex, heterogeneous fault networks. Together they single out the critically stressed segments where hazard is highest, sharpening hazard maps beyond earthquake counts.
arxiv-2606-16081:
Zhang studies in 2026 how special generating sets of modules, called simple-minded systems, can be reduced and glued over self-injective algebras. The work sits in the stable module category, where modules are studied up to projective summands. Koenig and Liu introduced these systems for artin algebras, and Dugas later extended them to triangulated categories.

Zhang presents a recollement, a standard three-category gluing diagram, for this setting. Through a chosen subset of a system, gluing assembles systems on smaller pieces into systems on the whole algebra. As a byproduct, the paper studies the extendible property: when a partial system can be completed to a full one. Reduction and gluing turn classification problems for large algebras into tractable problems on smaller ones.
arxiv-2606-16181:
Saha and colleagues test in 2026 whether a claimed crystal structure behind a proposed polar altermagnet exists. Theory had suggested Ca3Ru2O7 becomes a polar altermagnet by changing from its known Bb21m structure to a lower-symmetry Pn21a structure. Altermagnets combine magnetic order with unusual spin splitting, and polar order would add electric polarity. The team searched for that phase directly.

Synchrotron X-ray diffraction on single crystals of Ca3Ru2O7 and its 1 percent titanium variant found no Pn21a sign down to 20 kelvin. The search limits, near 60 to 200 femtometers of atomic shift, sit far below the roughly 1 picometer distortion theory predicted. Tighter bounds cap any such shift near 0.18 picometers at most. Together with nonlinear transport results, the study suggests strong electron links drive an electronic transition with no visible lattice symmetry change.
arxiv-2606-16281:
Yun and co-authors fuse the strengths of several masked diffusion language models in 2026, without any extra training. These models generate text by gradually unmasking tokens, and different models hold different knowledge. The team first studies how their decoding unfolds over time. Successful generations show stable confidence patterns over the answer-relevant positions, while failing runs wobble.

Their framework, TIE, tracks those confidence dynamics during decoding to judge which model is on the more reliable path. It then transfers partly denoised sequences from the leading model to the others, so a stuck model can restart from a promising state. The lead can change across steps, letting each model contribute where it is strongest. Across diverse reasoning tasks, TIE improves performance consistently in the reported tests, with no added training. The work reframes ensembling for diffusion models: not a vote at the end, but a relay during generation itself.
arxiv-2606-16781:
Bijnens and Krichevskiy compute higher-order corrections in QCD-like theories in a 2026 particle physics paper. Such theories mimic quantum chromodynamics but with different fermion types, and they are candidate homes for dark matter made of dark pions. Chiral Perturbation Theory describes their low-energy behavior as a series in small quantities.

The authors work with two fermion flavors whose masses differ, in both real and pseudoreal representations. For the pseudoreal symmetry-breaking pattern they derive the reduced next-to-leading-order Lagrangian. They then calculate the following order as well for pion masses, decay constants and vacuum condensates, extending earlier results that assumed equal masses or stopped one order lower. Fitting the theory's constants to lattice data for a four-color gauge theory shows the corrections matter, shifting dark pion phenomenology.
arxiv-2606-16881:
Yewei Huang and colleagues present SGM-SLAM in a 2026 robotics paper on teams of mapping robots. Robots that build a shared map must find where their observations overlap, then stitch their maps together. Matching raw sensor features between robots is brittle under changed viewpoints and lighting, and it costs bandwidth.

Their system matches scene graphs instead: summaries of a place as objects with labels and center positions, linked in space. Each robot fuses camera and lidar data into a segmented point cloud plus a layer of bounded objects. Robots exchange only the object data with neighbors and match graphs to find the constraints that align their maps. A multi-step exchange and optimization process keeps communication light. Trials in simulation and with real legged robots show the method works while sending far less data than feature-based pipelines.
arxiv-2606-17081: A. Ponce-Torres and colleagues peel graphite into graphene with a blast of transonic flow, air moving near the speed of sound. This impulsive hydrodynamic exfoliation yields monolayer sheets plus nanofragments, useful for composites and electronics. The paper details the fluid mechanics and characterizes the product, offering a scalable route to cheap graphene.
arxiv-2606-17281:
Kim and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on a failure mode of speech recognition built on language models: writing the transcript in the wrong language. Flexible multilingual systems often misjudge which language was spoken, harming transcription quality and every task built on it. The authors name this lack of language adherence, define a metric for counting such violations, and look for fixes that keep code-switching possible.

Their approach uses soft prompting, hinting at likely spoken languages without forcing the output into one. Three mitigation strategies are compared across languages: zero-shot prompting, supervised fine-tuning for prompt adherence, and chain-of-thought reasoning during decoding. Each reduces language violations to a different degree while affecting overall recognition accuracy differently. The analysis closes with trade-offs to guide which strategy fits a given compute budget and use case.
arxiv-2606-17581:
Zhai and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on Visored, a proof system shaped around how language models and humans actually write mathematics. Models now draft plausible proofs, but trust requires machine checking, and mainstream provers demand a formal style far from natural mathematical prose. Visored's surface imitates controlled natural language, while a rule-driven layer closes the routine steps a textbook would skip. Accepted proofs thus feel like ordinary mathematics yet rest on a dependent-type core underneath the friendly notation.

An accepted proof can be re-emitted as a checked Lean file, tying the new system to an established kernel. Early experiments suggest models can learn to use Visored well on a standard benchmark without any prover-specific training data. That hints the bottleneck is interface design as much as model skill. If drafting and checking share one language, AI-written mathematics becomes far easier to absorb and verify.
arxiv-2606-18081:
Tiwari reads the family tree of merging black holes in the newest gravitational-wave catalogue, in a 2026 paper. With GWTC-5.0, about two hundred fifty binary black hole events are known, enough to see structure in the chirp-mass distribution. Clear peaks sit near seven and a half, fourteen, and twenty-seven solar masses, each roughly double the previous, like rungs of a ladder.

A hierarchical merger story explains the rungs neatly: the first peak holds black holes born from stars, and higher peaks hold the heavier products of earlier mergers. The new data add a wrinkle the theory had predicted, an intermediate peak near nineteen solar masses from mergers mixing generations. Two recently reported groups of mixed-generation mergers slot in as distinct rungs, strengthening the case that black holes build up by repeated collisions.
arxiv-2606-18181:
Bodwell and colleagues build a database of illegal fishing and seafood crime out of the world's scattered reporting, in a 2026 paper. Illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing, widened by the authors into IUU+, covers supply-chain fraud and labor abuse as well as poaching. Everyone agrees the threat is grave, yet basic counts of incidents, places, species, and actors remain hard to assemble from news, court, and agency documents.

Their system, IUU+DB, uses large language models to read that mixed material at scale. It judges whether a document describes a relevant incident, then extracts actors, locations, species, vessels, violations, and enforcement outcomes into a shared schema, with deduplication across sources. Case studies show regulators could screen seafood trade risk or map links between fishing practices and labor abuses, turning anecdote piles into trend data.
arxiv-2606-18381:
Abaskohi and colleagues present SproutRAG, a retrieval system for answering questions over long documents, in a 2026 natural language processing paper. Retrieval-augmented generation lives or dies by how documents are chopped up: large chunks bring noise, small chunks shred context. Fixes based on extra language model calls or summaries add cost or lose information.

SproutRAG instead learns, from attention patterns inside a smaller language model, how sentences group into progressively larger but coherent units, building a binary tree over each document. A hierarchical beam search then retrieves evidence at whatever grain fits the question, from single sentences to broad subtrees, with no added model calls or compressed summaries. Across four benchmarks covering scientific, legal, and open-domain material, it improved information efficiency by about six percent over the strongest baseline. The authors note that richer, multi-branch trees remain an open direction for harder multi-hop questions.
arxiv-2606-18581:
Zou examines how to correct imaging-related distortions in clustering measurements made with emission-line galaxies from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument's second data release, in a 2026 cosmology paper. Variations in imaging depth and quality across the sky can imprint fake patterns on the galaxy map, and the standard correction for this tracer uses a neural network.

Zou derives correction weights by linear regression separately for subsamples split by galaxy properties such as stellar mass, emission-line luminosity, and colors, aiming for a physically informed alternative. A key complication is regional: deeper imaging in one survey footprint yields more galaxies but misses extreme colors and shifts the redshift mix. That footprint needs separate treatment in catalog production. With regions handled separately, the property-dependent weights further cleaned spurious clustering in about a tenth of subsamples, while the standard scheme stayed best for the full sample.
arxiv-2606-18781:
Lyu and the team diagnose why dense retrieval fails on long documents, and repair it without retraining, in a 2026 information retrieval paper. Standard dense retrieval compresses each document into a single vector. So a short decisive passage can be diluted by thousands of irrelevant tokens during encoding. The authors name that failure document-side early compression.

They introduce an Evidence Dilution Index. It measures how far a document's vector score falls below its strongest chunk-level evidence. They then propose DICE, which splits documents into chunks, encodes them independently with a frozen model, and aggregates the chunk vectors back into one document vector. That preserves the retrieval interface. On the LongEmbed benchmark, DICE improved retrieval across four model backbones, with the largest gains beyond four thousand tokens. One model's passkey score in that range tripled. The dilution index fell in nearly ninety-three percent of over twelve thousand samples.
arxiv-2606-18981:
Markidis and colleagues describe a 2026 library family that computes the Fourier transform in an unusual way. Instead of a classic fast Fourier transform, the code runs a quantum Fourier transform circuit on a classical quantum simulator. Inputs map straight onto state amplitudes, so the quantum routine can stand in for standard transform calls. A planner fuses gates and shapes memory layout to cut data movement and raise work per step.

The design runs on top of Google's qsim simulator with OpenMP, AVX, and CUDA backends. On a modern server chip, the AVX version matches the speed of the widely used FFTW library at large thread counts. On a graphics processor, the CUDA version runs far faster than both at large sizes. A trimmed quantum transform that drops tiny rotations cuts depth and run time while keeping accuracy. The work shows quantum circuit tools can serve as practical high-performance code.
arxiv-2606-19181:
Di Patti and colleagues study noise-seeded oscillators in a multi-population model in 2026. Stochastic oscillations can arise in a two-population system purely from finite-size demographic fluctuations, with no external pacemaker. Such quasi-cycles are coherent rhythms born of noise itself. The authors extend a prototypical neuronal interaction scheme by adding a third fluctuating species, and ask what that addition does to the rhythms of the original pair.

Both analytic and numerical results show the third species can enhance the quasi-cycles or even suppress them entirely. The added population thus acts as a control knob on noise-driven coherence, not just as extra noise. The finding broadens the framework for synchronization studies beyond the classic Kuramoto setting. Coupled noisy oscillators of this type appear in neural populations, biological rhythms, and power grids. That knob could help explain varied sync behavior in such systems.
arxiv-2606-19281:
Solon presents a universal closed form for dynamical Love numbers of black holes in 2026. Static Love numbers, which measure tidal deformability, vanish for black holes. Their dynamical counterparts do not, and they govern how a black hole responds to time-varying tides. The paper gives the scheme-independent dynamical response of a Schwarzschild black hole in closed form, to all orders, for every spin and multipole in a single expression.

The result is built from a leading-log solution to a renormalization group equation, lifted by a dressed logarithm. That dressing resums the log to all orders and contains a tower of Riemann zeta values, universal across spin and multipole. Shell effective theory checks confirm the formula for scalar, electromagnetic, and gravitational cases.
arxiv-2606-19481:
Thomas Frost and Steve Harris present Insulin4RL in 2026, a dataset for offline reinforcement learning in intensive care. Offline reinforcement learning means training a decision model from past records, with no live trial and error. The dataset covers insulin dosing, where staff adjust a drip to keep blood sugar in a safe range.

Built from the MIMIC-IV hospital records, Insulin4RL holds over 375,000 labelled decisions for 12,209 patients who needed insulin infusions. Unlike older sets, it keeps the natural, uneven timing of real care instead of forcing events into fixed time slots. Frost and Harris add baseline scores from model-free methods and a shared test protocol based on fitted Q-evaluation. Care teams and model builders gain a fair way to check whether a dosing policy would have worked in real wards.
arxiv-2606-19581:
Benjamin Johnson and Maria Rugenstein argue in 2026 that land warming faster than ocean shapes recent climate trends. Land-sea contrast is the gap between warming over continents and over seas. That gap may drive a Pacific pattern that looks like a negative phase of the Inter-Decadal Pacific Oscillation.

Observed and modelled trends show sea level pressure falling over fast-warming land relative to ocean. The pattern mirrors the seasonal cycle and land-heating responses in idealised model runs. Coupled models with historical forcing understate the land-sea warming ratio. Only the early response to an abrupt carbon dioxide quadrupling matches the observed ratio. In those runs, oceanic highs strengthen and a negative Pacific pattern like the observed one appears. Johnson and Rugenstein propose that many model-observation trend gaps trace back to this ratio. Finding its cause could sharpen forecasts of future climate change.
arxiv-2606-19681:
Shingyu Leung computes stochastic flow stretching far more cheaply in 2026. Finite-time Lyapunov exponents measure how fluid parcels separate over a fixed window. Their variance-based cousins track the spread of random arrival points instead.

Older methods solve a Fokker-Planck equation per starting point, which turns costly on dense grids. Leung expands stochastic paths around the deterministic flow in the small-noise regime. A closed covariance equation for the leading random displacement follows. Embedding that dynamics in space yields one transport-reaction equation for a covariance tensor field. Reading the field at each arrival point recovers every starting covariance at once. The largest eigenvalue defines the moment-based exponent, and eigenvectors show spreading directions. Tests include an exact linear case and double-gyre flows with uneven diffusion. Main spreading structures survive at a fraction of the old cost.
arxiv-2606-19781:
Jan-Lucas Uslu, Kevin Greif, Daniel Whiteson, and Benjamin Nachman show in 2026 that training data mix can steer neural scaling laws. Scaling laws chart how performance grows with compute, model size, and data size. Particle physics offers cheap, high-fidelity simulated data, unlike text or images.

Data can therefore be plentiful while parameters stay costly, favouring data-heavy regimes. The test task classifies hadronic jets from high-energy particle collisions. Adding pretraining data that is more diverse and better aligned with the jet task shifts the balance. Scaling then demands more data rather than larger models. The dataset itself becomes a design lever over the scaling curve. Physics teams can thus plan compute budgets around data they control. Engineered pretraining mixes join model size as a first-class scaling choice.
arxiv-2606-19881:
Guneesh Vats and six colleagues release REDACT in 2026, a controlled benchmark for finding personal data in text. Detectors for personally identifiable information guard privacy, yet test corpora cover few entity kinds. Ad hoc test sets also hide which surface traits break detectors.

REDACT holds over thirteen thousand records with more than three hundred thousand entity annotations. Fifty-one entity types appear across twenty-five languages and nine scripts. A covering-array sampler controls nine generation axes, from format to code-switching. Each entity carries disclosure status, disclosure form, and a GDPR-aligned sensitivity tier. Five detectors face a locked, language-stratified sample of one thousand records. The rule-based detector fails worst on the highest-stakes data, with recall near zero on top-tier items. Language model detectors stay far more robust on those same slices.
arxiv-2606-19981:
Edwin van Dam, Hong-Jun Ge, and Jack Koolen settle a bounding question for a class of highly structured graphs in 2026. For regular graphs with three distinct eigenvalues, spectral and algebraic complexity coincide: such graphs are strongly regular with coherent rank three. Whether coherent rank stays bounded for regular graphs with four eigenvalues was open, even with the extra condition of co-edge-regularity, where non-adjacent vertex pairs share fixed neighbour counts.

For every prime power, the authors construct infinitely many co-edge-regular graphs with exactly four eigenvalues and coherent rank growing without bound. The smallest eigenvalue and a rank lower bound are given explicitly in terms of the prime power. Spectral graph theory loses a hoped-for tidy correspondence, and the constructions supply fresh test cases for algebraic combinatorics.
arxiv-2606-20081:
Wenhua Zhao, Christos Tserkezis, Asger Mortensen, and Kurt Busch examine the light emitted when a fast electron beam passes through a tiny dielectric sphere. Their 2026 paper separates two kinds of radiation that usually blur together. Cherenkov radiation arises when a particle outruns light in a medium. Transition radiation is emitted when the particle crosses a boundary between materials. Both matter for cathodoluminescence, a microscopy method reading the light electrons provoke from nanostructures.

Combining time-domain simulations with Mie theory, the team tracks the induced fields, the directional pattern of emitted light, and how power flows over time. Below the Cherenkov threshold, transition radiation dominates, its fingerprints forming at the entry and exit points. Well above threshold, a clear Cherenkov front appears. A constant-permittivity model first isolates each channel, before a realistic material with resonances is tackled. The dual view gives experimenters a clearer map for reading electron-beam spectra.
arxiv-2606-20381:
Qian Zhao and eleven colleagues identify a geometric flaw in the dominant recipe for training large language models in 4-bit floating point. Their 2026 paper studies FP4 pretraining, which promises big savings in memory and compute, and centers on the E2M1 format used by current hardware. Non-uniform formats like E2M1 suffer shrinkage bias: a negative rounding error from the uneven spacing of representable values. The bias accumulates across layers and is amplified by the Random Hadamard Transform.

Uniform grids such as E1M2 and INT4 avoid this error entirely. The team therefore proposes UFP4, a uniform 4-bit recipe applying the transform to all three training matrix multiplications while restricting stochastic rounding to one term. Across dense and mixture-of-experts models up to 124 billion parameters, UFP4 degraded loss less than E2M1 baselines. Future accelerators, the authors argue, should treat uniform 4-bit grids as first-class formats.
arxiv-2606-20981:
Kiminad Mamo and Ismail Zahed construct gluon distributions at strong coupling in 2026 using gauge and string duality. The distributions studied, called GTMDs, are the most complete two-parton functions in quantum chromodynamics. They encode joint spatial and momentum structure of hadrons.

Conformal moments of unpolarized gluon distributions are built for fixed even spin. Two regimes are distinguished: zero separation and finite separation. At finite separation, a minimal worldsheet governs the amplitude. The moment factorizes into a universal soft factor and a target-dependent amplitude. Universal reductions are also derived. Strong-coupling results contrast with perturbative methods, helping theorists see which features of hadron structure survive.
arxiv-2606-21481:
Bevelynn Whaler models two related mosquito-borne viruses in 2026, Bunyamwera and Batai, as they infect human A549 cells in the lab. Her deterministic model tracks cell division and death, plus continued entry of virus particles into already infected cells. A notable twist follows: re-infection shortens the eclipse phase, the quiet period before a cell starts releasing new virus. Parameters were fitted by Markov chain Monte Carlo to decay data, growth curves at two doses, and genome copy counts.

Bunyamwera showed much longer eclipse and infectious periods than Batai, while Batai produced virus faster per cell. Re-infection shortened the eclipse phase for both, markedly more for Bunyamwera. Genome copy data proved essential to pin down how many cells one unit of virus can infect. The comparison quantifies life-cycle traits that lab assays cannot measure directly.
arxiv-2606-21881:
Zhang's 2026 note works in representation theory, the study of algebras through their modules, and compares two kinds of families of objects called simple-minded systems. These systems live in the stable module category of a self-injective algebra, where they serve as coordinates for the category's structure. A weaker variant drops some conditions, and the note asks exactly when the weaker notion forces the stronger one.

Zhang gives a necessary and sufficient condition for orthogonal systems over domestic Brauer graph algebras, a concrete class drawn from graphs, to be simple-minded. As a byproduct, Zhang constructs a whole class of simple-minded systems over 2-domestic Brauer graph algebras. The note also adds a sufficient condition, in its main theorem, for a weakly simple-minded system over a general self-injective algebra to be simple-minded.
arxiv-2606-22181:
Yao and colleagues test, in 2026, whether the explanations given by protein allergenicity classifiers match real immune biology. Such classifiers screen novel foods for allergen risk, and their residue-level scores highlight which amino acids drove a prediction. The immune system, though, recognizes specific regions called epitopes, so the authors built an epitope-grounded benchmark for faithfulness.

Across frozen ESM-2, a multi-task ESM-2, and DeepPlantAllergy, protein-level results were strong. Yet the head's explanation signals did not beat random alignment with annotated epitopes on any of the ranking metrics used. Integrated gradients found residues that mattered to the model, but they were not the epitope residues. Saturation mutagenesis suggested the classifiers lean on broad chemical and composition features instead. The authors warn against reading such scores as immune explanations.
arxiv-2606-22481:
N. Violante, G. Kopanas, L. Franke, J. Philip, and G. Drettakis address a visual effects problem in this 2026 paper. 3D Gaussian Splatting stores a scene as millions of soft colored blobs that render from new viewpoints. Moving an object from one captured scene into another is useful, but the pasted object keeps its old lighting and looks wrong.

The team train a diffusion model to harmonize each composite view so its lighting matches the new scene. Training data mixes synthetic, generated, and real image pairs showing the same scene with wrong and then corrected lighting. A user extracts an object, composites it into the target scene, and renders the combined views. The model fixes each view, and results consolidate back into a 3D representation with a final optimization step. The authors report better quality than previous methods, with shadows and reflections matching the new environment.
arxiv-2606-22681:
Wei-Chieh Chou and five colleagues make multi-step retrieval cheaper in this 2026 paper. Retrieval-augmented generation answers hard questions by searching documents over several rounds. Existing systems either propagate early errors or over-generate steps, raising cost without improving accuracy.

Their framework, Grounded Delta Planning RAG, plans around the information delta: what the system does not yet know. Three design choices do the work. A preliminary retrieval grounds the plan in real evidence before execution begins. A gap-conditioned prompt asks only for the missing information. A skeletal trajectory pairs each subquery with a thought carrying early evidence to the final answer. On three multi-hop benchmarks it reached the highest accuracy, about sixty-one percent. Its cost-of-pass undercut the PAR-RAG baseline by twenty-two percent and KnowTrace by sixty-eight percent. No rival method was both more accurate and cheaper.
arxiv-2606-22781:
Zhiqiang Yu proves a classification result about fusion categories in this 2026 mathematics paper. A fusion category is a structured set of objects that can be fused together, much like representations of a group. A category is called group-theoretical when it is built, in a precise sense, from a finite group together with a cocycle, a twisting rule.

Yu studies integral non-degenerate fusion categories. In these, the size of each simple object, its Frobenius-Perron dimension, is a whole number. His theorem says that if every simple object has dimension either one or a power of a single prime, the category must be group-theoretical. A simple condition on sizes thus forces the whole category to come from group data. The result aids wider efforts to classify fusion categories by the arithmetic of their dimensions.
arxiv-2606-23081:
Andreas Zimmerer and colleagues benchmark cardinality estimation for meaning-based database operators in a 2026 paper. Modern databases can filter or join records by a natural language instruction, judged by a large multimodal model. Such semantic operators cost far more per record than ordinary ones. A query optimizer must guess how many records will pass each step, called cardinality estimation, before choosing a plan. Bad guesses now hurt by orders of magnitude more than before. No benchmark existed for this new estimation problem.

Zimmerer and colleagues built SemCEB from a real dataset of structured text and images. Its one hundred two hand-made queries span wide selectivity ranges for filters and joins. They test sampling methods and a leading semantic histogram method on accuracy, cost, speed, and memory. Sampling proved robust across predicate types but scales poorly and costs much. The histogram approach was cheaper yet limited in important cases.
arxiv-2606-23181:
Jungseob Lee and colleagues route questions between fast answers and deep thinking in a 2026 paper. Hybrid reasoning models can reply directly or spend extra tokens thinking first. A good router sends easy questions to the fast path and reserves long thought for hard ones. Earlier routers needed labeled training data or fixed budgets set in advance. Their framework, DART, needs no training. It samples two cheap drafts written without extended thinking. When the drafts agree, the model answers directly.

Lee and colleagues use disagreement as the warning sign. When drafts clash, DART predicts a thinking budget from how uncertain the drafts look. Across math tests, accuracy rose by up to nine points on Olympiad-level problems, while the thinking tokens fell sharply. Code tasks gained even more, with token use roughly halved. The agreement signal held across model sizes, families, and hosted application programming interfaces.
arxiv-2606-23281:
