Pritom Sarma and Krishnendu Paul model the timing of rainfall-triggered landslides in Mizoram, India, in a 2026 geoscience paper. Mizoram records the highest landslide frequency of any Indian state, yet no physics-based failure timing model existed for it. The team applies a rate-and-state friction block-slider framework to nineteen rainfall-triggered events around Aizawl from 2016 to 2025. Satellite rainfall estimates feed a one-dimensional infiltration model that pushes water down to failure depth, under three conductivity scenarios. Friction parameters are then fitted to reproduce each observed failure date.

Sarma and Paul find the events split cleanly into two regimes by a normalized pore-pressure measure. Synchronous failures fire at peak pore pressure, like the eight-event cluster during Cyclone Remal. Delayed failures lag by hours to ten days, governed jointly by pore pressure and a friction ratio. The study then scales toward future extreme rainfall under climate projections.
arxiv-2606-23481: This paper derives continuity equations in the generalised Lagrangian mean theory. The deriving derives. Their equations are continuity. The theory is generalised Lagrangian mean. It is fluid dynamics. The deriving is continuity. The Lagrangian continuity aids ocean modeling. The derived equations conserve mass and momentum.
arxiv-2606-23581:
Ma, Eitzinger, Köstler, and Wellein make cached attention memory reusable anywhere in a sequence, in a 2026 machine learning systems paper. Multimodal agents keep re-examining the same video frames and screenshots as their context window slides. Standard caches store key-value pairs, the attention memory of a language model, tied to fixed positions. So every fresh look triggers a full re-encoding, wasting most of the compute budget on repeats.

The authors pinpoint what naive reuse loses: conditioning that a chunk of content absorbs from its neighbors. A small low-rank patch, a compact correction, stored beside each chunk restores exactly that missing part. Reuse then needs only a rotation of position codes plus the patch, with no retraining. A patch recovers full accuracy on benchmarks that bind information across chunks, where blind reuse halves multi-hop accuracy. The method also reconstructs production cache data to within rounding error.
arxiv-2606-23781:
Zhang and colleagues, together with the Roman HLIS Cosmology Project Infrastructure Team, stress test three common shortcuts in the joint analysis of galaxy surveys, in a 2026 paper on cosmology. A 3x2pt analysis combines galaxy clustering with weak lensing, the subtle bending of light by matter, to measure cosmic structure. The coming Roman and Rubin surveys will reach precision where casual approximations distort answers. The team validates its pipeline against an established code.

All three shortcuts prove dangerous. The Limber approximation can bias the inferred cosmology. Ignoring redshift space distortions, the squashing of galaxy maps by galaxy motions, also biases results. So does a sloppy nonlinear power spectrum model. Biases approach or exceed one standard deviation, passing two for Rubin in several cases.
arxiv-2606-23881:
Ma, Wu, Zhou, and Ma simplify how multimodal AI answers questions that require outside knowledge about what an image shows, in a 2026 paper on visual question answering. Knowledge based VQA asks about entities in an image whose facts live in sources like Wikipedia, not in the pixels. Standard systems retrieve articles and re-rank their sections in one tangled step. The authors observe a useful asymmetry: multimodal models often fail to name an entity freely, yet pick the right name reliably from a short candidate list.

Their framework, identify before answer, exploits that asymmetry with no training. The model first selects high confidence entities from candidate names alone. A text re-ranker then chooses the supporting evidence sections. On two benchmarks, the method beats fine tuned multimodal baselines while cutting training and inference complexity.
arxiv-2606-23981:
George takes on a hard equation at the heart of complex geometry, the study of shapes described with complex numbers. Dinew and Popovici had used a Monge-Ampère-type equation for forms of positive degree to prove part of Demailly's Morse inequality. Their proof, though, assumed the equation could be solved. George's 2026 paper removes that assumption and proves the result outright.

One obstacle comes first. The trace condition proposed at first turns out too rigid to allow any solutions at all. George swaps it for a flexible gauge-fixing, which yields a family of equations with two free parameters. Careful advance estimates then show solutions exist for varied parameter values. At one setting the framework collapses to the classic complex Monge-Ampère equation, which recovers the inequality for higher-degree forms. Uniqueness of solutions also strengthens under an added kernel condition.
arxiv-2606-24081:
Sheng and colleagues build PixJail, a system that automatically rebuilds published jailbreak attacks on text-to-image generators so results can be compared fairly. Attack methods evolve quickly, and judging one involves a whole pipeline: rewriting the prompt, generating the image, passing safety filters, and scoring the output with another model. Reproducing a paper's pipeline by hand is slow, and mismatched setups make cross-paper comparisons unreliable.

Given a jailbreak paper and any available code, PixJail builds a matching attack module plus a runnable evaluation pipeline that both obey one shared contract. A memory bank stores paper summaries, attack patterns, reusable templates, and past failures, so later reproductions can reuse earlier experience and the system improves over time. Sheng's team reproduces eleven representative methods, including papers with no released code, recovering the original results with small average error and zero median error under the original settings in 2026 tests.
arxiv-2606-24281:
Finlay and colleagues argue that a reasoning model's confidence means two different things, before and after it thinks. Before thinking, a confidence estimate should forecast the chance of solving the prompt at all. After answering, it should judge whether this particular realised answer is correct. Existing practice asks only once, conflating the two targets and supervising both with the wrong labels.

CALIBER elicits both estimates. Each is supervised with the target matching its information state: prompt-level success rates for the early estimate, per-answer correctness for the late one. Under this unified protocol, expected calibration error falls by more than half against the strongest single-confidence baseline, on a digit-arithmetic benchmark for the mid-size model tested. Finlay's 2026 message for builders of reasoning systems is simple. When you ask a model how sure it is determines what its answer can honestly mean.
arxiv-2606-24481:
Tang refines how badly a Kähler-Einstein potential can behave near a singular variety's bad points. Kähler-Einstein metrics, whose curvature is proportional to the metric itself, exist even on mildly singular varieties from the minimal model program. Their potentials may blow up or vanish near the singular locus, though. Bounding that behaviour from above and below is the L-infinity estimate problem.

Iterated logarithmic functions are built from a defining function of the non-klt locus, the bad set where singularities worsen. They yield refined lower bounds, improving earlier estimates by Di Nezza, Guedj, and Guenancia and by Datar, Fu, and Song. Proofs build explicit subsolutions and supersolutions for degenerate complex Monge-Ampère equations, alongside refined integrability estimates from pluripotential theory. Writing alone in 2026, Tang sharpens control over canonical metrics on singular spaces.
arxiv-2606-24581:
FitzGreen brings lensing, Einstein's bending of light by mass, onto a student lab bench. Acrylic lenses machined to the right curvature deflect light the way a galaxy's gravity does. The phenomenon is simulated with tabletop optics. The fabricated lenses reproduce the key features of strong lensing. The simulation extends into the weak and microlensing regimes, with images analogous to modern observations.

Analysis of the lensed images in each regime measures, on its own, the simulated mass of the lens. Those separate measurements agree with each other, and with the value predicted from the machined curvature. The loop between fabrication, observation, and theory closes. Writing alone in 2026, FitzGreen presents the exercise as a complete hands on arc for students. Build the analogue, photograph the Einstein ring like distortions, and weigh spacetime curvature with a ruler and a camera. That is how astronomers measure masses of objects they can never touch.
arxiv-2606-24681:
Domenico Compagnini and six colleagues demonstrate a quantum buffer built entirely from optical fibre. A quantum internet must hold light signals briefly so asynchronous signals can be aligned. Matter based memories store light long, but have narrow bandwidths and need cryogenic cooling. All optical memories run at room temperature, yet they suffer high input and output losses. Most also handle only one kind of photonic encoding. The new device aims to remove both limits.

The buffer uses an actively switched dual Sagnac cavity driven by cross phase modulation. It achieves input and output loss of only 0.46 decibels. Storage time exceeds 18 microseconds. Bandwidth tops 12.5 terahertz, covering the full telecom C band. Over 200 temporal modes can be buffered at once and addressed singly or together. They store time bin, frequency bin, and polarisation qubits with high fidelity. Entanglement survives storage too, which the team reads as true universality.
arxiv-2606-24981:
Wei-Cheng Lee and Francesco Orabona prove that one stepsize schedule is enough for temporal difference learning. TD(0), a reinforcement learning algorithm, runs on data from a Markov trajectory. Their version is plain: no projection step, with Polyak Ruppert averaging of the iterates. The stepsize shrinks like one over the square root of time, adjusted by the chain's mixing time and a log factor. Crucially, it needs no knowledge of the curvature parameter that earlier analyses used.

Two results follow with high probability. The iterates stay bounded, with no projection and no stability argument based on curvature. The averaged estimate then converges at the better of two rates: a curvature free rate, and a faster one when curvature is favourable. A Poisson equation toolkit for mixing chains does the work, splitting Markov noise into a martingale part plus a remainder, and a self bounding induction gives pathwise stability.
arxiv-2606-25181:
Spotting speech sound errors in children early is hard where specialists are scarce. Milosz Dudek and eleven colleagues build a screening pipeline for Polish speaking children, aimed at sibilant substitutions, that can run outside the clinic.

A wav2vec2 based recogniser reads phoneme sequences from the child's speech, and an alignment step types the errors. On held out recordings from ten unseen children, 559 utterances, the recogniser matches the exact target sequence in close to nine cases out of ten. Flagging segments where the system emits substitution evidence gives precision near seventy three percent and recall near sixty one, with a false alarm rate under three percent. A template grounded assistant explains results to caregivers, framed strictly as screening, not diagnosis.
arxiv-2606-25381:
Some crystals host surface electrons whose existence is guaranteed by symmetry, and warming the crystal can switch that phase off. Jingwen Li and colleagues watch the lattice respond in 2026, probing a lead tin selenide crystal with terahertz pulses. One low energy surface vibration softens markedly as the material crosses its topological transition. In ferroelectrics such a dip warns of structural collapse, but here the crystal structure stays put.

The team attributes the softening to a Kohn anomaly, a dip caused by strong coupling between the vibration and the Dirac like surface electrons of the topological phase. The vibration's linewidth also departs from the usual thermal pattern, backing the coupling story. Phonon softening thus becomes a spectroscopic fingerprint that can tell the two phases apart without contacting the surface electrically.
arxiv-2606-25781:
Two populations share one space. They diffuse under a common pressure set by their total density. But each drifts under its own external potential. Charles Elbar and Guy Parker study this cross diffusion system in 2026. Start the populations segregated, meeting at a single interface. Push the drifts toward each other at that interface. What happens next, the authors show, is not decided by the equations alone. It depends on what you accept as a solution.

One accepted route adds a whisper of viscosity and removes it. That limit produces overlap: the populations mix at the interface. Another route keeps a segregated weak solution, with the phases staying apart. Both solve the same problem, so the problem has no unique weak solution. The pair prove this first for an explicit stationary case. Then they extend the non uniqueness to general segregated starting data. Modelling choices, in short, can change predicted physics.
arxiv-2606-26081:
Max Hörmann gives an analytic account of superradiance in Dicke models with interacting matter. A Dicke model couples one cavity light mode to many matter units at once. Integrating out the cavity leaves an exact self-consistent energy formula. The photon contributes only a scalar field in that formula. A classical penalty term balances the bare matter energy. No phase can appear that the matter alone does not already allow.

One curve organizes the whole phase diagram. Candidate states trace a single connected curve. First-order superradiant transitions become folds of that curve, not crossings of separate sheets. A fold can even straighten into a continuous transition line. The onset of superradiance reads off the bare matter susceptibility. Its leading singularity sets the threshold, which can be finite, zero, or approached gradually. The analysis starts with the Dicke-Ising model and extends to other cavity-coupled magnets.
arxiv-2606-26181:
Mario Brcic and Stjepan Frljic argue that schools ask the wrong question about AI. Allow it or ban it is a false choice, they say. Placement is the real design question. AI in the wrong spot replaces the mental work learning needs. Students then feel masterful while learning little, an illusion that collapses on unaided tests. Their essay assembles the strongest causal evidence on both sides. One unguarded helper left students measurably worse on an unaided exam. Rebuilding that same model to withhold answers erased the harm.

Six moves structure their frame for learning something new: Prime, Probe, Point, Attach, Strengthen, and Test. Guard the first hard attempt and the last unaided check. Let scaffolded AI help in the middle moves. One diagnostic rules placement: if AI makes the task feel effortless, it sits in the wrong place. Classic teaching moves map onto each step.
arxiv-2606-26281:
Clara Briand, Leonie Kayser, and Julian Weigert find the polar degrees of reciprocal linear spaces, which arise when each coordinate of a linear subspace is replaced by its inverse. These numbers from projective geometry turn out to be written inside a polynomial that belongs to combinatorics.

Their proof links the geometry of conormal varieties to the conormal fan of the matroid attached to the subspace: substituting into the matroid's reduced characteristic polynomial yields exactly the polar degrees. As a bonus, the result settles two open conjectures about matroid discriminants, quantities used to tell when special configurations degenerate.
arxiv-2606-26881:
Benedict Leimkuhler and Peter A. Whalley speed up Langevin sampling, a workhorse for exploring chance distributions in physics and statistics. Sampling with fixed steps wastes effort: stiff regions need small steps, easy regions tolerate large ones. Their combined method pairs two devices. SamAdams adapts the step size automatically using a relaxed stiffness monitor. Position-adaptive dynamics concentrates friction along the local force direction.

The combined scheme still samples the exact target distribution. A symmetric integrator design needs only one force evaluation per step, keeping costs low. Tests covered four model problems, from classic test landscapes to a a data problem with a sparsity prior. Mixing improved several-fold on the stiff landscapes. Other examples gained more than tenfold efficiency.
arxiv-2606-26981:
Xiaomeng Fu and six colleagues generate human motion from text by coupling a language model planner to physics checks. Language models read open-ended instructions well and sketch plausible action plans. Their raw motions, though, often break physics. Physics-based controllers are realistic but choke on complex or novel instructions. Their framework runs the two in a predictive loop.

A planner module breaks each command into pieces and drafts candidate motions from motion tokens. A second module scores the candidates in simulation. It combines physical success with match to the text's meaning. The best candidate guides the next stretch of generation, like model predictive control in robotics. The loop keeps semantic freedom while discarding motions the body could not perform.
arxiv-2606-27081:
How do proteins pass protons, the hydrogen ions behind much cell energy flow? A team whose contact authors include Cao and Guo sorts the twenty standard amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, by a hidden talent. Some blocks can relay a proton by switching a covalent bond, a shared-electron link, at their tip. Simulations that swap single blocks at a key channel site test each of the twenty in turn. During 2026, only thirteen pass that bond-switching test.

Active blocks share clear signs: a negative electric potential dip at the atom that receives the proton, plus low energy barriers for the relay. The seven inactive blocks end in carbon-hydrogen bonds of a saturated kind and face much higher barriers. Inside channels, active blocks cluster near the pore to carry protons along. Inactive ones gather at the edges and hold the structure steady.
arxiv-2606-27281:
Ramírez and Alvarez test a neuro-symbolic pipeline that lets small local language models reason without repeated sampling. Their pipeline has the model translate a problem into typed finite-domain rules. A symbolic layer checks traceability and consistency. In the 2026 resource-aware study, a deterministic solver then performs the actual reasoning step, run through LM Studio on Apple Silicon.

On generated precedence problems, the pipeline reaches near-perfect accuracy with one model call, where self-consistency needs five calls for far lower accuracy. A harder logical deduction set shows an even wider gap. A stronger adaptive baseline trims sampling cost but not the accuracy gap. Results vary by model: one rival reproduces the same boundaries, another fails on typed constraints. Bounded logic can replace repeated sampling for some structured tasks, saving calls and delay.
arxiv-2606-27481:
Vega and El-Khadra teach a diffusion model to sample lattice field configurations while respecting gauge symmetry exactly. Lattice simulations of quantum fields slow critically near the continuum limit, and samples can freeze into one topological sector. Their test bed is the Schwinger model, two-dimensional quantum electrodynamics with two fermion flavours. A score-based generative model, built equivariant under the theory's U(1) gauge symmetry, learns to draw gauge link configurations directly. Model likelihoods then convert samples into unbiased estimates of observables in this lattice physics paper from 2026.

The estimates closely match those from standard Markov chain simulations. Near critical parameters, topological freezing visibly eases compared with hybrid Monte Carlo in the reported comparisons. Generative sampling thus survives contact with an exactly symmetric gauge theory. The study is a first step, and the authors frame it as such. Symmetry-aware generative models earn a place in the lattice toolbox.
arxiv-2606-27581:
Humanoid robots learn control through reinforcement learning. That means the controller improves by trial and error. Such robots move well in open space. They falter when tasks involve touching objects or crossing rough ground. Sirui Chen and five colleagues present SceneBot in 2026. SceneBot is a single policy for free movement, uneven terrain, and whole-body manipulation.

The policy reads reference motions plus per-link contact labels. These labels state which body parts should touch the world at each moment. Labelled interaction data barely exists, though. So Chen's team rebuilt scenes after the fact from retargeted human motion. They inferred which objects and surfaces each motion involved. Training used seven and a half hours of this rebuilt data. The policy then generalised to motions and settings it had never seen. In one test it carried a box upstairs. That task mixes climbing with holding.
arxiv-2606-27681:
World models summarise interaction history in a latent state. In many language-model architectures, predictions can bypass that state and peek at raw history. The state then becomes unidentifiable, and good scores say nothing about representation quality. Xiang Gao and four colleagues enforce strict mediation in 2026 to fix this. Under strict mediation, predictions may depend only on the latent state and the action.

Text makes enforcement hard. Textual states are discrete and non-differentiable, and strong decoders ignore bottlenecks. The authors introduce textual latent states that are discrete, readable, and variable in length. A tree-structured reinforcement learning method, factorized GRPO, enforces the mediation during training. Experiments ran on TextWorld and ScienceWorld. One-step prediction accuracy was preserved. Representation quality rose by up to fifty-seven percent. Rollout performance improved by up to ninety-eight percent. Gains grew with task complexity and prediction horizon.
arxiv-2606-27881:
Named entity recognition struggles with historical texts. Names drift in form and prominence across centuries. Language models still reason weakly about such drift over time. Emanuela Boros studies how to add time information to recognition models in 2026. Lightweight fusion strategies inject temporal metadata into Transformer-based models. Both absolute and relative time forms are tested. Fusion happens early or late, through cross-attention, adapters, or simple concatenation.

Tests use French and German historical datasets. Late fusion proves more robust overall. It also generalises better across periods. Its edge is largest in the early, noisy stretches of the corpora. Other placements fare worse by comparison. The lesson is that time information helps only when fused at the right depth. Care matters here, because names change in both form and salience as centuries pass.
arxiv-2606-28481:
Thomas Bouley, Xucheng Gan, Hailin Xu, and Tien-Tien Yu calculate a force that dark matter itself exerts. Quadratically coupled ultralight scalar dark matter forms a coherent field washing over Earth, and it can push different materials differently, a composition-dependent force that equivalence-principle experiments hunt for.

Earlier calculations assumed Earth was a perfect sphere. Using a partial-wave treatment of dark matter scattering, the team derives how the force varies with angle. They also give an analytic form valid even when the dark matter's wavelength is far smaller than Earth. Screening by Earth splits the signal into a characteristic band of frequencies, whose sidebands wax and wane annually as Earth moves through the halo. Re-evaluating the MICROSCOPE mission's limits and forecasting proposed space experiments, they show the full band structure sharpens sensitivity a lot.
arxiv-2606-28781:
Halaharvi proposes HyphaeDB, a memory system for groups of AI agents that shares knowledge by itself instead of waiting to be asked. Today's vector databases, which store text as numbers for similarity search, treat memory as passive storage that agents must query one by one. Halaharvi reuses the graph inside those databases, called HNSW, as a communication fabric linking the agents.

Agents hold fixed positions in that graph, and knowledge spreads between neighbours through a gossip protocol, meaning each holder passes items onward while their strength fades with distance. From those local rules, the design aims for contradiction warnings, pattern formation and agreement across agents to emerge naturally. The system rests on knowledge nodes, topology edges and memory updates, with a reference version built on PostgreSQL. A multi-agent software method called Swarm-Driven Development serves as the test deployment.
arxiv-2606-29081:
Nguyen and Zhu propose a safety measure for language models facing attacks hidden inside input embeddings, the numeric vectors representing text. Their measure is the worst-case divergence, a statistical distance, between the output distributions of the clean model and the attacked model, subject to a stealthiness limit on the attack. The limit rests on a neat equivalence: transformer attention behaves like rational inattention, an economics model of costly focus.

The authors analyse perfectly undetectable attacks within this framework and derive an upper bound on the measure through a Bregman-divergence argument. They then apply the measure to GPT-2 and GPT-Neo-125M. Both showed non-trivial output shifts under attack, and the measure separated their safety profiles. The contribution is a principled yardstick: it quantifies how far an attacker can move a model's behaviour while staying hidden.
arxiv-2606-29181:
Balapour and Hach present Anomaly Factory 3D, a tool that fabricates fake defects to train 3D anomaly detectors. Detecting defects in point clouds, sets of points mapping an object's surface, is hard because abnormal samples are scarce and varied, while training data is usually all normal. Detectors that learn from synthetic pseudo-anomalies need a rich supply of them.

Their framework makes diverse fake defects from normal point clouds. A deformation model, defined in local frames from principal component analysis, warps the surface with controlled falloff, direction gating and separate normal and sideways shifts. That yields a broad set of defect presets, from dents to bumps. The authors plug the tool into two detectors, one predicting offsets and one based on reconstruction, showing it transfers across detection styles. On two benchmarks it improved object-level and point-level detection and localisation, with ablations confirming the value of the preset groups.
arxiv-2606-29481:
Lin, Zhang, and Feng tackle a quiet flaw in reinforcement learning for language models, the training method that rewards good answers. Training data often overlaps text the model saw earlier. A model can then recall a memorized answer and fabricate reasoning that merely looks like deduction. Scores rise, yet the reasoning skill itself stays hollow.

Their framework, HIPPO, injects hints on purpose to trigger that shortcut behaviour. The traces produced become anchors for pairwise comparison, where a light judge model weighs two attempts side by side. A tailored pairwise reward model learns to tell genuine deduction from shortcut-driven rationalization, meaning reasoning invented after the answer. Experiments show clear gains over standard baselines. Gains also carry to out-of-distribution tasks, tasks unlike the training set. The authors argue the method extracts transferable reasoning rather than surface patterns.
arxiv-2606-30181:
Adrián Irles reports, on behalf of the FCAL Collaboration, beam tests of a compact silicon-tungsten calorimeter. Such calorimeters are planned for the LUXE experiment at DESY. They also suit future colliders. Thin silicon pad sensors sit between tungsten absorber plates. The stack resolves nearby showers in crowded environments.

The basic unit is called a Compact Silicon Sandwich module. Each module integrates sensor, signal routing, voltage distribution, and support. A dedicated facility assembles these modules into full detectors. A partly instrumented prototype entered an electron beam in twenty twenty-five. Beam energies ran from one to six GeV. First results include sensor calibration with minimum-ionizing particles. Event displays show shower development inside the granular detector. The campaign validates the technology for LUXE and future colliders.
arxiv-2606-30281:
Ben Foxman and four colleagues build a tool that mimics random objects for quantum algorithms. Researchers often study algorithms given oracle access to a random function, permutation or unitary. An oracle is a black box the algorithm may question but not inspect. Classically, lazy sampling answers such questions on the fly. The quantum analogue, called a compressed or recording oracle, is harder because queries can arrive in superposition.

The team define a path-recording oracle that stores superpositions of input-output pairs. This openly records what an algorithm could have learned from its queries. It simulates, perfectly, random elements drawn from any closed subgroup of the unitary group. Their update rule is described through the commutant, the operations that commute with the group's action. Comparing oracles for permutations and unitaries then yields a simple route to pseudorandom unitaries. The recipe multiplies a pseudorandom permutation by a random Clifford operation.
arxiv-2606-30381:
Santiago Camara and Sanaa Latif trace how news about Canadian bank profits moves the whole economy. Banks' balance sheets can amplify or dampen business cycles. When bank net worth rises, credit supply expands. Borrowing spreads fall as lending gets easier. The hard part is isolating that credit-supply news. Stock prices react to many kinds of information at once.

The authors build high-frequency shocks from earnings announcement days. Six large Canadian banks anchor the identification strategy. Co-movement with corporate spreads purges contaminating information from raw surprises. The cleaned shocks are then traced through the economy. Favorable shocks lower corporate spreads, as the model predicts. Bank values and broader equity prices rise together. The Canadian dollar appreciates after such shocks. Real activity increases over the medium run. Results hold across specifications, samples, and extra outcomes.
arxiv-2606-30781:
Dorian Amaral and four colleagues present a force sensor built from a magnet floating inside a superconductor trap. The sensor hunts for exotic spin-dependent interactions, hypothetical forces between spins that new particles beyond the Standard Model could carry. Such forces push in directions set by the spins' arrangement, which makes them hard to isolate with ordinary sensors.

A levitated ferromagnet answers pushes along different axes with different vibration modes, each at its own resonance frequency. Directional signatures therefore land in separate channels of one device. The team work through one example: a parity-violating interaction carried by a proposed spin-one boson between two levitated ferromagnets. A matched-filter analysis shows a setup modelled on an already demonstrated experiment could probe electron couplings at force ranges below a centimetre. That range, tied to mediator masses above a tiny threshold, was closed off before.
arxiv-2606-31281:
Waalkes and twelve colleagues report the Hubble transmission spectrum of AU Mic b, a young sub-Neptune planet. At about twenty million years old and 9.7 parsecs away, the planet is a prime test case for how such worlds form. Earlier density and escaping hydrogen data point to a thick early atmosphere worth probing directly.

Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 scanned unsteadily, which shifted the instrument profile and the baseline between orbits. Spectral binning eased but could not remove the effect. The host star's strong magnetic activity added spot crossings and a transit light source effect, where starspots distort the measured spectrum. The team pin down spot coverage near one third of the surface, and retrievals show the spectrum is dominated by that stellar contamination.
arxiv-2606-31581:
Levene and Harris measure how robust a trained neural network stays when its inputs are perturbed by random noise. Users need to know how much error a network will make on noisy data before it fails in the field. Their robustness measure is simple, fast, and treats the network as a black box, needing no access to its weights.

With high probability the measure bounds the network's mean squared error for a given input perturbation size. Tests on several real-world datasets show the bound is useful in practice. The pair also introduce robustness curves, which plot that behaviour across perturbation levels and let users compare robustness within one dataset and between datasets. The tools give practitioners a cheap pre-deployment check on noise tolerance.
arxiv-2606-31681:
Ranney, Makaram, Ding and Fei test how well hardware implementations of ML-KEM, the new post-quantum key encapsulation standard, resist side-channel attacks that read secrets from power use or electromagnetic emissions. The weak point is the Fujisaki-Okamoto verification step inside decapsulation, where a re-encryption comparison can leak enough to recover the long-term secret key.

Three verification designs, unprotected, hash-based first-order protection, and higher-order masking, are evaluated on both a microcontroller and an FPGA chip. Field-programmable chips run faster but often leak more, especially in high-bandwidth parallel configurations. Even the higher-order masked designs leak through hardware-level effects. Their parallel processing exposes enough first-order leakage for full secret-key recovery. This shows how hard protected post-quantum hardware remains.
arxiv-2606-31781:
Bui and four colleagues present SpikeLogBERT, a log parser designed to use far less energy than dense neural models. Log parsing turns raw system messages into structured event templates for monitoring and anomaly detection. Standard neural parsers rely on heavy matrix multiplication, which costs power when parsing runs around the clock.

SpikeLogBERT combines a spiking transformer, whose neurons fire sparsely and only when needed, with knowledge distillation from a BERT teacher. Sparse, event-driven computation cuts the number of active operations sharply. On the HDFS dataset it reaches a parsing accuracy of 0.99997 in the reported tests, beating neural rivals. Estimated energy use falls by up to 62.6 times under standard chip assumptions.
arxiv-2606-31881:
Huang and Wen present stratified counterpossible logic, a system for conditionals whose if-parts are impossible. Standard Stalnaker-Lewis semantics makes every counterpossible true for no reason, so it cannot tell a sensible impossible supposition from an absurd one. Current non-vacuist fixes still blur two grades of impossibility: metaphysical impossibility and outright logical contradiction.

Their systems, SCP and SCP1, split worlds into logic-normal worlds and anti-logic worlds, with a metaphysical accessibility relation nested inside the normal layer. Reasoning stays intact even when what metaphysics says must hold fails. SCP1 adds a non-empty constraint on the selection function, so counterpossibles turn on the link between antecedent and consequent instead of coming out true for free. Soundness, completeness and decidability are proved for both.
arxiv-2606-31981:
Li and eight others present LUNA, a neural model that animates 3D human avatars without linear blend skinning. Photorealistic animatable avatars usually depend on parametric body models and skinning, which cap expressivity and inject fitting artifacts. LUNA instead maps 2D controls, such as images, keypoints or sketches, straight into deformations of 3D Gaussians.

A transformer-based motion regressor separates global rigid motion from fine local dynamics, capturing coherent movement plus subtle non-rigid effects. Hybrid supervision distills soft structural priors from a skinning teacher while letting training use unlabeled in-the-wild video. Visual fidelity rivals skinning-based approaches in their tests. Zero-shot generalization across identities and driving modalities is a highlighted strength of the system.
arxiv-2608-00081:
Yashunsky and Tabalin study value distributions of read-once polynomials over finite fields. In such expressions, each variable occurs at most once. Inputs are drawn independently and uniformly. The value distribution has k atoms for a field of order k. Their main result places every such distribution in a set B_k.

The set is defined by a relation on the sorted distribution atoms. Its key bound links the smallest atom to the second-largest one. The body is stable under convolutions tied to field operations. More broadly, any quasigroup operation on k points preserves it. The body is full-dimensional and holds the uniform law and every point mass. Its volume comes from an exact one-dimensional integral. The k-th root of that volume tends to 0.2183305369. The full development is formalized in Lean 4.
arxiv-2608-00181:
Mehta and co-authors ask whether long-horizon agent training builds transferable skill. In self-contained RL settings, a policy can exploit local quirks. Tool schemas, grader parsing, and task templates can carry rewards. An in-distribution holdout shares those same quirks. Cross-benchmark transfer is the sharper place to look, they argue.

They post-train an open mixture-of-experts model on 363 MCP tasks. Training ran in two stages: supervised fine-tuning, then RL. No external benchmark task or score entered training. The trained model beat its base on five external tests at greedy pass-at-one. Gains reached 9.6 points on Toolathlon. Both software benchmarks improved, though training held no software tasks. Paired trajectory analysis found four recurring behavioural shifts behind the transfer.
arxiv-2608-00381:
Pei and Su advance RDMFT for molecules and periodic solids. RDMFT treats strong electron correlation in a rigorous frame. Use in solids was long blocked by two snags. Good transferable functionals were lacking. Tuning orbital occupations was slow as well. They show both snags can fall together.

Their build tunes natural orbitals and occupation numbers at once. That coupled scheme needs far fewer steps than split routes. Short-range screening makes the Power functional transferable across molecules and solids. Screening also reshapes the tuning landscape toward robust step sizes. Convergence speeds up sharply as a result. The screened functional beats semilocal and hybrid density functionals on surface reaction barriers.
arxiv-2608-00481:
Mishra introduces F-WANDA, a Fisher-reweighted twist on one-shot pruning for large language models. One-shot post-training pruning is the most energy-frugal compression route. Existing tools trade quality for cost: WANDA is cheap, SPARSEGPT is stronger but pricier. F-WANDA reallocates the per-row keep budget across output neurons. The budget follows the empirical Fisher information of each pre-activation.

That Fisher signal takes one extra backward pass over WANDA's own calibration corpus. No weights are updated in the process. On LLAMA-2-7B at 50 percent unstructured sparsity, perplexity on WikiText-2 hits 6.85. Five-shot MMLU improves by 1.6 points over WANDA and 1.1 over SPARSEGPT. Pruning wall-clock and energy run at one third of SPARSEGPT's. No extra calibration data or fine-tuning is needed.
bjornson-arne-anderson-1881:
Rasmus B. Anderson translated Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson's Arne and early tales for Houghton Mifflin in 1881 and 1882. Bjørnson, later a Nobel laureate, built modern Norwegian prose from peasant life. Arne, the title tale, follows a crofter's son torn between his father's violence, his mother's songs, and his own longing to leave the valley.

Other sketches in the volume give brides, fishermen, and small farms in Bjørnson's fresh, direct manner. He wrote against the stiff book language of his day, close to living speech. Anderson, himself of Norwegian stock, made these tales a bridge between Norway and America. The volume helped found a national literature and export it at once. Bjørnson's peasants entered world reading through doors like this one.
bodin-de-magorum-daemonomania-latin-1581:
Bodin's Démonomanie reached learned Europe in this Latin translation, printed at Basel in 1581. The translator worked under the pen name Lotarius Philoponus. Latin carried Bodin's legal demonology to judges and scholars who read no French, greatly widening the book's power.

The four books define sorcery, weigh evidence, and prescribe punishments with a lawyer's care. Bodin's rigor answered Weyer's doubts and hardened witchcraft theory into law. This complete Latin text spread that theory far beyond France. It belongs beside the French original of 1580 in any serious study. Together they show how one jurist's book could steer trials across a continent.
bracton-de-legibus-twiss-vol4-1881:
The fourth volume of Twiss's Bracton came out in 1881, continuing the Rolls Series text of the great thirteenth-century treatise. Bracton wrote as a royal justice who knew the courts from inside. His book ordered the whole of English law, and Twiss's edition spread that order across six volumes.

Volume 4 takes up the criminal side of the law, the pleas of the crown. It covers felonies such as homicide, theft, and arson, and how the king's justice pursued them. Trial by jury was still young, and Bracton shows older proofs giving way to newer practice. The common law appears here at its sternest, with death or outlawry waiting for many offenses. The volume is a prime source for the birth of English criminal law.
cia-0000007481:
Winter 1962 brought volume 6, number 1 of Studies in Intelligence, the CIA's internal journal for working officers. One named piece, Anatomy of Spying, signals the issue's focus on how espionage actually works. The journal circulated inside the agency rather than to the public.

Inside, practitioners wrote for each other about tradecraft, analysis, and the hard parts of secret work. Such writing helped a young agency turn field experience into shared lessons. Released decades later, the issue lets outsiders watch that training process. It is primary evidence for how the early Cold War CIA understood its own trade.
cia-0000008381:
Plans for the Tan-Zam Railway drew CIA attention in an October 1965 paper on the project's prospects. The line was meant to link landlocked Zambia to the sea through Tanzania, easing its reliance on routes south. China backed the scheme, which made it a Cold War contest as well as a railway.

The paper weighs whether the line would be built and what it would change. Railways in such studies stand for trade, loyalty, and reach, not just track and trains. Readers see Beijing's growing role in Africa judged from Washington. The file captures development politics at an early Cold War turning point.
cia-0000008881:
Iran's current crisis, as of February 1951, is the subject of a CIA paper from the oil dispute's first heat. Iran's parliament was moving to take over the British-owned oil industry, and nationalist feeling ran high. The shah's authority and the government's stability both looked shaky.

The paper weighs the players: court, parliament, street, and foreign powers with oil at stake. Two years later, a coup backed by Washington and London would end the crisis by force. Reading the 1951 analysis shows the problem as first framed. It is a prelude written before anyone in the file names the ending.
cia-0000009081:
Peru's prospects came before CIA analysts in a paper dated June 1965. President Fernando Belaunde's government was pushing reforms while facing economic strain and stirrings of guerrilla unrest in the Andes. Washington watched Peru as one front in a wider Latin American contest.

The paper weighs the government's strength, the opposition, and the chances of upheaval. Country studies like this one tried to warn of crises before they broke. Peru did fall to a military coup three years later, which gives the analysis edge. Readers can measure the analysts' judgment against what actually followed in Lima.
cia-0000009681:
Two American prisoners held by the North Vietnamese Army were sighted in the Prey Ve area, a May 1972 report states. The place name is cut short in the heading, which places the sighting in the Cambodian border region. North Vietnamese units operated widely inside Cambodia by 1972.

Prisoners in NVA hands inside Cambodia fell between two countries' records. Officials in Saigon and Washington both had reason to track them, and neither had easy access. A dated sighting at least fixed the men's survival to that spring. The file preserves it as one more point in the borderland captivity record of the war.
cia-0000009981:
An American pilot died in the crash of an L-19 reconnaissance plane in Vinh Binh province, an October 1972 report states. The L-19 Bird Dog was a small, slow spotter plane whose crews flew low over battlefields. Vinh Binh lies in the Mekong Delta's flat, wet south.

Bird Dog crews directed artillery and strikes, work that kept them over enemy guns daily. Their losses were steady and their planes left little wreckage to find. A confirmed death in a Delta crash closed one such crewman's case. The file honors the spotter war's risk with a plain provincial record.
cia-0000010581:
North Africa's current situation is surveyed in an August 1952 CIA paper. France then ruled Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia as protectorates or territory, and nationalist movements pressed in all three. Egypt, newly under its Free Officers after the July 1952 revolution, watched from the east.

The survey weighs French control against rising demands for independence across the Maghreb. Washington was torn between its French ally and the region's clear direction. Within a decade every territory named was independent, Algeria through a brutal war. This file catches the old order's last calm, surveyed whole in the summer of 1952.
cia-0000010881:
In February 1951 the CIA judged how three Southeast Asian lands might stand up to communist pressure: Thailand, Burma, and Malaya. China had just fallen to Mao's forces, and Washington feared the region could topple country by country. Malaya was already fighting a communist revolt under British rule, while Burma faced revolts of its own.

The paper grades each country's will and strength to resist, one by one. It treats their governments, armies, and rebel movements as the front line of a wider contest. Written before America's deep plunge into Vietnam, it shows the early map of fears that shaped later policy.
cia-0000012281:
Ed Proctor and Jack Smith, two American officials, talked over the use of material called Chickadee in May 1961, and a CIA record preserves their conversation. Chickadee was a cover name for sensitive source material in the Penkovsky case. The question before the men was how such material could be used without exposing the man who supplied it.

The record shows the home front's paperwork: coordination, caution, and argument inside the government. Running a great source took as much care in Washington as in Moscow. For readers, the page reveals the handling rules that protected secrets and source alike.
cia-0000012381:
Military Thought, the Soviet armed forces' journal, might be declassified, and an October 1965 paper weighs the considerations. The agency had gathered the journal's issues through channels tied to the Penkovsky years. Its articles, written by Soviet generals for each other, had been mined in secret for what they revealed about doctrine and plans.

Releasing such material meant judging what secrecy still protected. The paper balances the gains of openness against the habits of classification. For readers, it shows open-source gold being weighed: the foe's own words, and the question of who else might read them.
cia-0000012481:
Six American pilots were held in a two-story building in Sam Neua, Laos, and a CIA report from July 1967 records the fact in detail. Sam Neua was the Pathet Lao's stronghold country in the northeast. The report describes the captives' circumstances: the building's layout, the guards' routines, and the conditions the men lived under, as sources on the ground reported them.

Such detail made the intelligence believable and usable. Rescue planning and family accounting both began from facts like these. For readers, the report is architectural witness: a prison's address, known and written down.
cia-0000014781: Communist reaction to the Rosenberg execution in Uruguay fills a CIA file dated July 1, 1953. The executions had taken place on June 19 in New York. Reaction files flowed in from capitals around the world that summer. Uruguay's entry shows the case echoing even in countries far from the main stage. The Uruguay reaction file rests in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015281: Unknown flying objects were seen over Budapest, in a CIA report dated March 1, 1957. Budapest had risen in revolt the fall before and been crushed. Reports from a watched capital carried weight beyond the sighting itself. The file adds Hungary's sky to the eastern bloc sightings the agency gathered. The Budapest report is now held in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015381: An interview with a deleted name fills a CIA file dated September 4, 1955. No topic survives in the clipped title at all. Such a file can be logged but barely described from outside. It stands in the record as proof a talk took place, with its heart cut away by the censor's hand.
cia-0000037481:
American prisoners and missing men in Laos are the subject of a CIA record dated June 2, 1968, tied to the JPRC. The JPRC was the Joint Personnel Recovery Center, which worked to rescue and account for men in Southeast Asia. Laos was its hardest field, since the war there was secret.

Inside, the file concerns the center's Laos cases: who was held, who was missing, and what was known. Recovery work in Laos faced jungles, enemy forces, and official silence at once. The record shows the organization built for that work, and the scale of the task it faced in a country where little could be said aloud.
cia-0000041181:
Talks to prisoners of war, attributed to Jane Fonda, were broadcast from North Vietnam, in a CIA record dated June 5, 1972. The broadcasts aimed her words at the men held in Hanoi's prisons. Speaking to prisoners was the most charged part of her whole visit.

Inside, the attributed talks are preserved as the monitors heard them. Prisoners who heard such broadcasts faced them from inside cells and camps. The file records how the visit reached its sharpest point. A famous American voice was carried into the prisons, and the men there had no choice about hearing it from their captors.
cia-0000042781:
Further reportage on the Jesuit assassinations fills a CIA record dated November 3, 1989. The November date places this file weeks into the case's public life. By then the murders had become a fixed point in the war's story.

Inside, the reporting continues, with the case still drawing daily coverage. Sustained reportage kept pressure on every party to the war. Governments could outwait a single headline. They could not so easily outwait a story that returned each day with fresh detail and fresh anger. The file preserves that persistence, which helped make the priests' case the best known crime of the Salvadoran war.
cia-0000042881:
El Salvador faced human rights concerns, in a CIA record dated October 2, 1989 in the catalog. The title ties the account to the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front. Concerns was the polite word for a grim and growing list.

Inside, the pressures on the country over its rights record are surveyed. Reports from churches and rights groups fed the case against it. American aid debates turned on those reports each session. The file shows a small country cornered by its own record. The autumn's killings were about to make that record far harder to defend.
cia-0000045981: Handwriting specialists weighed in on the claimed prisoner photograph and on samples of writing, and a CIA item dated June 1, 1991, kept their comments. Graphology, the study of handwriting, was one of several tests thrown at the evidence that summer. The item shows the missing-men hunt reaching for any tool that might settle a claim.
cia-0000049281: A status report on El Salvador from 1980 fills a CIA item kept with the Truth Commission records. Status reports were the baseline genre: where the country stood, in the writer's judgment, that season. This one catches the country in the civil war's first year, before the lines hardened into a decade's shape.
cia-0000049381: The Situation in Central America is the broad heading of declassified CIA document 0000049381, dated February 5, 1989. Marked for the Truth Commission, the paper surveys the region as a whole. Its generality is the point to note: It is a single dated overview item rather than a country study. The agency kept it as part of its closing-years reporting on Central America.
cia-0000096481: An untitled document about no independence for British Guiana is declassified CIA document 0000096481, dated September 5, 1964. The record admits it has no title and gives the stance instead. Readers find a brief declassified item arguing the colony should not become independent, preserved under a descriptive heading supplied by the catalog rather than the author.
cia-0000097981: Memorandum titled What Should We Do About the Russians? is declassified CIA document 0000097981, dated May 4, 1984. The heading poses its subject as a direct question. The brief file is a memorandum record whose interrogative title stands out among declarative agency headings, preserved as evidence of the question being asked in that form.
cia-0000105881: Loss of Indonesian Air Force Transport Over Malaysia is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000105881, dated August 6, 1964. The heading records a loss: one Indonesian air force transport, over Malaysia. It gives no crew, cause, or outcome in the title itself. The brief record is an incident item, dated in the summer of 1964 as released.
cia-0000107981: Weekly Surveyor Article re Pakistan's Predictions That It Can Operate the Karac is the heading, cut off mid-name, on declassified CIA document 0000107981, dated January 1, 1977. The title reports a prediction: Pakistan could run a plant whose name breaks off at Karac. The claim belongs to Pakistan, as the heading states it. The brief record preserves the break exactly as released.
cia-0000108081: Capture of Two U.s. Pilots During Three Day Air Attack in the Dan Neua Area Of is the heading, cut off mid-phrase, on declassified CIA document 0000108081, dated February 4, 1969. The title records two American pilots captured during a three day air attack. The province name breaks off after the word Of in the heading. The brief record is a capture item from 1969.
cia-0000108481: Weekly Situation Report International Terrorism - 29 April 1981 is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000108481, dated March 3, 1981. The title dates its week to April 29, 1981, weeks after the March file date. That gap stands on the face of the record itself. The brief record is one weekly issue in the terrorism series from 1981.
cia-0000118681: Probable Reactions to Various Courses of Action with Respect to North Vietnam is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000118681, dated January 4, 1964. The heading asks how others would react to varied courses of action on North Vietnam. Probable reactions is the forecast phrase at the front of the title. The brief record is a reactions study item from the first week of 1964.
cia-0000119581:
A November 1964 CIA special report describes Czechoslovakia trying a new role inside the Soviet bloc. Prague was testing how much room Moscow would grant a loyal ally. That question would return with far higher stakes four years later.

The report follows the early stages of that experiment. Small shifts in a satellite state's foreign and economic policy mattered to Washington because they hinted at looseness in Soviet control. For readers, the paper shows the long buildup to 1968. The Prague Spring did not appear from nowhere. Analysts had been tracking Prague's search for room to move since the mid-1960s.
cia-0000126881: A September 1968 CIA report covers the treatment of Czechoslovak leaders during their forced stay in Moscow. Dubcek and his colleagues had been summoned to the Kremlin and pressed into submission after the invasion. The paper documents that strong-arming as the agency learned of it. The Moscow meetings ended with the Czechoslovak leaders signing terms they had crossed a border hoping to refuse, the hinge on which the Prague Spring closed.
cia-0000132481: A widening rift between Venezuela and Cuba is forecast in item 6 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated April 5, 1960. Caracas and Havana were drifting apart month by month. Within two years Venezuela would break relations with Cuba entirely. The short item records the state of the quarrel that spring, well before the final break made headlines across the hemisphere.
cia-0000132581: Brazil's president-elect possibly trying to mediate fills item 12 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated September 3, 1960. Its headline breaks off after the word between, leaving the parties unnamed. Brazil's incoming leader was placing himself as a peacemaker in the hemisphere's quarrels. The short item reports the possible mediation effort.
cia-0000132681:
Only two days after a March 1 companion, this CIA briefing on Cuba is dated March 3, 1961. The Bay of Pigs landing was about six weeks away. Updates were coming fast enough that a two-day gap merited a fresh paper.

That pace is the story here: by March, Cuba reporting had become a near-daily service for a government closing in on an invasion decision. Each short paper refreshed the last, tracking an island whose defenses and politics decided the plan's odds. The declassified text survives via the CIA Reading Room mirror at the Internet Archive.
cia-0000132781:
Election season colors this Cuban Developments entry of September 4, 1960. In the United States, Kennedy and Nixon were campaigning for the presidency, and Cuba had become one of their issues. The CIA's running series kept reporting through the contest.

The paper belongs to the pre-election file both campaigns argued over: how the revolution had happened and what to do about it. Its September date places it two months before voters decided. For readers, the briefing links intelligence reporting to a famous campaign, in which Cuba's fate at home and abroad were debated together.
cia-0000135681: Brigade 2506's Spanish files include this document dated 1 March 1961, the start of the brigade's last full month before the April landing in Cuba. The force of anti-Castro exiles had been built and trained by the CIA over the previous year. The catalog records no subject for this item. It remains a primary source in Spanish, dated and placed within the brigade's papers, and its contents are for the reader of the text to establish.
cia-0000135881: Routing sheet in the declassified files, dated 2 January 1954, covers briefing notes tied to the name Calibaris, routed through the office with a memo attached. The paper sits inside the CIA drive against President Arbenz, run under the code name PBSUCCESS and crowned by the June 1954 coup. Its worth is in the detail it pins down, one dated piece of a covert war fought largely on paper.
cia-0000136081: Dated 3 March 1954 and now declassified, a CIA cable records closing down SARANAC, ending a coded project whose work was done, or whose cover was blown. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000136381: Castillo must be contacted, Washington agrees in this March 1952 cable, two years before he led the Guatemala invasion. The contact should learn the opposing forces, the opportunity for buying support among the army, Guardia Civil, and key officials, and how unbuyable forces might be immobilized through student or labor action. All details needed to estimate the proposed movement's success are requested, with a full report to follow. Signed by J. C. King, it is an early seed of PBSUCCESS.
cia-0000136981: Spares and supplies are moving on the most urgent basis. This late June 1954 status report tells LINCOLN so. Spares for P-51s will arrive 29 and 30 June. Three P-51s will proceed on 28 June. Headquarters is recruiting up to twenty cargo handlers. They will travel on supply flights from 28 June. A supply officer and two technicians are also sought. They will inventory the huge stock of spares. Some spares may later be repacked for onward shipment.
cia-0000139481: Filed in 1988 under Project SUN STREAK, document 0000139481 comes from the last phase of the government's remote viewing work. Viewers in the program sat with little more than map references and tried to report what stood at the target, while monitors logged each claim. The record does not mark this file as special within the series. Declassified along with the program's other papers, it is part of the fullest public account of official psychic spying.
cia-06828481:
Menu sheet for the OHB Main Cafe covers the week of 15 January 2018, opening with a closed day. The Monday line reads that the cafe is closed, and wishes readers a good holiday. On Tuesday, January 16, three teas are featured at one dollar and twenty-nine cents a cup. They are organic mint melange, organic blood orange, and Indian masala chai.

Recurring plates that week are a Cuban panini, Vietnamese-style banh mi burgers, and ropa vieja. Tuesday mains are citrus marinated pork tenderloin and cod with Mediterranean salsa. Wednesday brings Argentinian flank steak with quinoa primavera. Thursday lists brown sugar glazed pork loin and rosemary chicken. Friday closes with orange glazed salmon and eggplant with chickpeas, plus clam chowder. Second-page Tuesday entrees range from Szechuan beef and lamb curry with pumpkin to carnita tacos and saag paneer.
coke-institutes-part2-1681:
The Second Part of Coke's Institutes appeared in print in 1681, decades after its author's death in 1634. Coke had written it as an exposition of the great statutes of England. Parliament ordered the later parts published during the civil war era, when his authority served the cause against the crown.

Above all, the volume expounds Magna Carta clause by clause, treating the charter as England's fundamental law. Coke reads old words broadly, finding in them guards for liberty, property, and fair trial. His commentary became the arsenal from which seventeenth-century lawyers drew their arguments against royal power. American founders later drank from the same source. The book taught generations that even kings stand under a law they did not make.
cyril-five-tomes-against-nestorius-pusey:
Cyril, patriarch of Alexandria, led the attack on Nestorius, the patriarch of Constantinople who split Christ into two sons in his preaching. His Five Tomes Against Nestorius answer the rival book by book. Edward Bouverie Pusey translated them for the Library of the Fathers in 1881, with Cyril's Scholia on the Incarnation and other pieces.

Cyril defends one Christ, true God and true man in a single person, and the title Mother of God for Mary. The fight came to a head at the Council of Ephesus in 431, which cast Nestorius out. Pusey's volume gives the winning side in its own strong words. It is a core text of the Christological debates.
darwin-vegetable-mould-1881:
Charles Darwin spent his last years studying small things close to home at Down House in Kent. His final book, published in 1881, reports forty years of watching earthworms turn soil. He had first read a short paper on worms to a learned society back in 1837. Few readers expected worms to fill a bestseller, yet the book sold fast.

Darwin shows that worms drag leaves below ground, swallow earth, and cast it up as fine mould. Inch by inch, he argues, they bury stones, ruins, and whole fields under new soil. The book is a quiet proof that slow, small forces can reshape the land.
dryden-absalom-achitophel-1681:
John Dryden, England's poet laureate, wrote Absalom and Achitophel in 1681 during a fight over the royal succession. Catholics were barred from the throne, and some Protestants wanted the king's son Monmouth to inherit instead. Dryden answered with a satire in biblical dress, published anonymously.

King Charles becomes David, Monmouth becomes his beloved son Absalom, and the scheming Earl of Shaftesbury becomes the tempter Achitophel. Dryden praises his friends and shreds his enemies in polished heroic couplets. The poem is a masterclass in political satire: elegant, funny, and ruthless. It helped define the form for the next century of English verse.
europmc-pmc10266981:
Pang and co-authors argue that the physical shape of the brain strongly constrains how it works, in a 2023 study. The classic view holds that brain activity flows through networks of specialized cell groups wired together. Pang's team asks how much of that activity can be explained by the brain's geometry alone, through waves traveling across its folded surface.

They model brain activity as waves shaped by the cortex's form. The model matches observed activity across many tasks at least as well as wiring-based models. The study reframes how shape and function relate in the brain.
europmc-pmc10310781:
Zhang and co-authors published a 2023 review on drugs that target amyloid beta in Alzheimer's disease. Amyloid beta is a small protein that builds up in clumps in the brain. Many scientists have blamed those clumps for driving the loss of memory and thinking in this illness.

The review traces the amyloid idea over 30 years of work. It notes that many trials of anti-amyloid drugs failed, which raised real doubt about the idea. It then notes that some recent trials did succeed. Zhang weighs open questions about current drugs and sets out ways to build better ones for care and for prevention.
europmc-pmc10364581:
The GBD 2021 Diabetes Collaborators measured the world burden of diabetes from 1990 to 2021. Diabetes is a long-term illness in which blood sugar runs too high. The study spans 204 nations and areas, split by age and sex. It also forecasts how common the disease will be through 2050.

In 2021, 529 million people lived with diabetes across the globe. The team split cases into type 1 and type 2 forms. Type 2 is the far more common form, tied to weight, diet, and low activity. The study weighed 16 risk factors for the type 2 burden. Lost healthy years were counted as deaths plus years lived with the illness. Forecasts used social and weight trends to project the rise.
europmc-pmc1054881:
Hauf and co-authors studied in 2005 how a protein ring lets go of chromosomes as cells divide. The ring, cohesin, holds twin copies of each chromosome side by side. At division, most of the ring leaves the arms of chromosomes early, well before the twins split. Two kinases, enzymes that add phosphate tags, drive that exit.

The team hunted tag sites on all four cohesin parts with a mass tool. Hauf found that tags on one part, Scc1, were not needed for the early exit. Tags on a second part, SA2, proved vital for it. Cells with a tag-proof SA2 kept cohesin stuck on the arms. The work pins SA2 as the key target of the kinase Plk1 in this path.
europmc-pmc10857981:
Xue and colleagues review a signal path that helps cancers spread in this 2024 paper. Spread, called metastasis, causes about nine in ten cancer deaths. One driver is a change called EMT, where anchored cells loosen and gain the power to move. The Wnt and beta-catenin path, a chain of signals inside cells, is a key switch for that change.

When the path switches on, beta-catenin builds up and moves into the cell nucleus, the control centre, where it turns on spread genes, the review says. This axis is overactive in many cancers of organs and blood. It also helps tumours resist drugs. Small RNA pieces and plant-based chemicals can damp the path in lab studies. The authors present the axis as a target worth aiming drugs at.
europmc-pmc11223881:
Bugnon and colleagues present the 2024 release of a free web docking service in this paper. Molecular docking predicts how a small drug molecule binds a protein target. It can speed drug screening by ranking candidates before lab tests. SwissDock, first released in 2011, prepares molecules and targets automatically for users.

The old docking engine was replaced by two state-of-the-art programs, the authors report. AutoDock Vina gives faster predictions, while Attracting Cavities gives more accurate ones. Molecules can be imported as files, as SMILES text strings, or as sketches drawn on screen. Targets come from uploaded files or a database ID. The interface was fully redesigned for interactive submission and analysis. Advanced search options link users to widely used databases for both molecules and targets.
europmc-pmc11226681:
O'Leary and a large team describe a US resource for fetching sequence data across the tree of life in this 2024 paper. NCBI Datasets is run by the National Center for Biotechnology Information. It gives simple, direct access to sequences, annotations, and metadata covering many species. Public repositories struggle to keep growing data discoverable and usable.

Data arrive as packages of sequences plus metadata, which aids sharing and reuse, the authors report. Access comes through web pages, command-line tools, and documented program interfaces. The resource follows the FAIR principles: data should be findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable. The paper outlines the current scope of data on offer. It also explains the options for exploring and downloading packages. Proper delivery, they note, supports credit for data producers.
europmc-pmc11252281:
Liu, Zhou, Tan, Siu, and Guan survey the modern menu of cancer treatments in this 2024 review. Classic chemotherapy and radiation burden patients with heavy physical and mental strain. Care has since been transformed by more precise options. Small molecule targeted agents, antibody-drug conjugates, cell-based therapies, and gene therapy now lead the new wave.

Antibody-drug conjugates pair a homing antibody with a toxic payload. The review works through five classes: small molecule drugs, antibody drugs, peptide drugs, gene therapy, and cell therapy. For each it explains the method, development status, clinical challenges, and potential. These modalities target tumours personally and precisely, the authors say, and can improve patient comfort. Untapped headroom remains in all of them. The authors frame the comparison as a guide for both clinic and lab.
europmc-pmc1190181:
Shiffman and colleagues built a scoring tool for medical guidelines in 2005. Guidelines tell doctors what best care looks like. Many still fail to change daily practice. A guideline that is hard to apply will often sit unused.

Their tool, called GLIA, rates how easy a guideline is to use. It has 31 items grouped in ten areas. Clear wording, clear actions, and clear outcomes count as core areas. Shiffman tested the tool with expert review and trial use. Spotting barriers early can save costly failed rollouts. Clear actions are the Decide and Execute dimensions in GLIA.
europmc-pmc11926181:
Vogler and co-authors reviewed a protein family that controls cell death. The family is called BCL2, named after a blood cancer gene. Its members govern whether a cell releases a signal to self-destruct. That signal comes from mitochondria, the cell power stations.

Drugs that mimic natural blockers can free that death signal in cancer. Venetoclax, the first such drug, changed care for several blood cancers. Newer drugs and guided carriers are now in trials. Vogler also covers roles beyond cancer and newer drug designs. The review links basic cell biology to bedside use.
europmc-pmc1240281:
Meerts and co-authors tested flame retardant chemicals for hormone action in 2001. The chemicals, called PBDEs, are added to plastics and fabrics. They persist in nature and had turned up in human fat and blood. Their hormone effects were largely unknown.

Cell tests measured estrogen-like activity with a glowing reporter gene. Eleven PBDE types showed estrogen-like effects in breast cells. One altered form beat the natural hormone in strength, at far higher doses. Related bisphenol compounds varied with their bromine load. Meerts flags a hormone concern for this chemical family.
europmc-pmc1315281:
Stranger and co-authors mapped DNA variants that alter gene expression in humans in 2005. Medical genetics hunts variants behind complex traits. Reliable assays and maps are prerequisites for that hunt. The team analyzed 630 genes in 60 unrelated Utah residents.

Genes sat in high-interest regions, including the ENCODE pilot areas. Of the genes, 374 were expressed in the test cells. Many regions showed significant links between single variants and expression levels. Three correction methods were applied to guard against false hits. Stranger proves expression itself can be mapped like a trait. The genes sat on chromosome 21, chromosome 20, and in ENCODE zones.
europmc-pmc1413581:
Could eating blueberries slow aging? Wilson and co-authors tested that idea in 2006 using a tiny worm, Caenorhabditis elegans, a common lab stand-in for aging work. They fed worms a mix of blueberry polyphenols, plant compounds often praised as health aids.

Worms on the mix lived longer and kept moving better as they aged. The mix also helped worms survive heat stress, but not a chemical stress test. Wilson split the mix into three parts. Only the part rich in one compound class gave the gain. The effect needed a gene pathway tied to salt stress defense, not the usual stress routes.
europmc-pmc1552081:
Reviews of test accuracy studies had no software of their own. Zamora and co-authors built one in 2006, called Meta-DiSc. Such reviews pool studies of how well a medical test spots disease. Analysts had to borrow general stats tools.

Meta-DiSc checks why results differ between studies and pools sensitivity and specificity, the two core accuracy measures. It handles both fixed and random effects models and draws forest plots and summary curves ready for papers. Its math was checked against other tools and published reviews. Zamora offers the Windows program free for academic use.
europmc-pmc1626481:
Meta-analysis software can be pricey and hard to learn. Bax and co-authors built a free alternative in 2006, called MIX. It pools results across studies to judge therapies and disease causes. Their target users were students and researchers new to the method.

MIX runs inside Excel, using its sheets for calculation and Visual Basic for the interface. Built-in tutoring tools guide users, and the design pairs with standard textbooks. To validate it, Bax re-ran eight published meta-analyses and matched outputs against two reference programs, STATA and Comprehensive Meta-Analysis. The results agreed, supporting MIX as a teaching-friendly tool.
europmc-pmc1634881:
Oceans swarm with viruses, most of them unknown to science. Angly and co-authors surveyed them in 2006 across four ocean regions, from 184 viral samples at 68 sites gathered over a decade.

Most sequences matched nothing in current databases. Global diversity ran to several hundred thousand species by their estimate. Richness varied with latitude, richer toward the south in their gradient. The Sargasso Sea teemed with cyanophages, while Arctic samples held many prophage-like sequences. Yet most species appeared in many regions. Angly concludes local conditions enrich common types rather than excluding others outright.
europmc-pmc2062481:
Bhattarai and co-workers measured malaria trends in Zanzibar in 2007 after two major control measures began. Zanzibar introduced artemisinin-based combination therapy, the strongest drug mix, for free in late 2003. Long-lasting insecticide-treated nets followed in early 2006 for young children and pregnant women. The team ran child surveys in North A District in 2003, 2005 and 2006, and reviewed all 13 public clinics there.

Parasite prevalence in children under five fell sharply, with an odds ratio of 0.03 by 2006, a ten-fold drop after nets arrived. Under-five deaths fell 52 percent between 2002 and 2005. Malaria admissions fell 77 percent, blood transfusions 67 percent, and malaria deaths 75 percent. Weather stayed favourable for malaria throughout, so the gains were not a climate effect.
europmc-pmc2125481:
Russell L. Cecil of Columbia's Presbyterian Hospital clinic injected rabbits repeatedly with non-hemolytic streptococci from human cases of infectious endocarditis and rheumatic fever in 1916. He dyed the animals alive with trypan blue to mark the wandering cells. The rabbits develop an acute arthritis resembling acute rheumatism's in most respects.

Joint sections carry the inflammation from a fresh outpouring through to advanced repair. Heart involvement comes with it: endocarditis and pericarditis in a small share of cases, and, frequently, focal patches of death and cell infiltration in the heart muscle, differing considerably from Aschoff's nodules. Kidney and liver lesions occur but show nothing characteristic. In two cases streptococci were recovered from the joint fluid itself. Readers get rheumatic fever rebuilt in rabbits, with its telling cells traced by dye.
europmc-pmc2128381:
G. O. Broun opened his blood destruction series by following a single day of exercise in dogs, hour by hour. His paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1922, from the Rockefeller Institute. Rous and Robertson had shown that red cells normally break up by fragmentation in the bloodstream, possibly from mechanical wear, and hard exercise should speed that wear.

Early in exercise, the share of cells and hemoglobin in the jugular vein blood rose. That first change probably reflects a reshuffling, with more red cells pushed into the outer circulation. As exercise continued, the plasma volume itself grew by a definite amount. Then both the total cell volume and the pigment volume fell together during prolonged work. That paired fall, Broun argues, is the signature of actual blood destruction taking place. The day's arc thus runs from reshuffling, to dilution, to real loss of red cells.
europmc-pmc2128581:
Ernest G. Stillman asked whether breathing pneumococci can vaccinate a mouse through its own airways. His paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1924, from the Rockefeller Institute hospital. Earlier work had shown inhaled virulent germs vanish from normal mouse lungs within hours and rarely infect, so he tested repeated inhalation as training.
