Repeated inhalation of live pneumococci induced a definite degree of active immunity in the mice. Repeated inhalation of killed organisms induced only slight immunity by comparison. The living germ, arriving by the natural road and cleared by the lung's own defenses, teaches the body far better than the dead one. The result matters beyond the laboratory trick: it shows the respiratory surface is not merely a gate for infection. It is also a place where protection can be built, dose by breathed dose.
europmc-pmc2131581:
Drury described a surgical method in a 1929 paper from The Rockefeller Institute: the total removal of the liver in rabbits. Removing the liver kills fast if blood flow through the portal and caval veins is blocked. No clean rabbit method had been reported, though the operation was wanted for studies of sugar metabolism. Drury sets out his technique step by step.

A first operation coaxes side channels, collaterals, to grow around the portal and caval veins. With those in place, the liver can come out without circulatory trouble. Given glucose, liverless rabbits lived up to forty hours. Before death they showed the same disturbances as liverless dogs: without sugar they died early from low blood sugar.
europmc-pmc2140481:
Jacques Loeb opened a Donnan equilibrium series in 1921, on membrane potentials in protein solutions. A gelatin chloride solution in a collodion bag, set against plain water, reaches an equilibrium with an electric potential difference across the bag wall. Part one measures that voltage and how a neutral salt changes it.

Adding neutral salt depresses the potential difference, much as it depresses the osmotic pressure of the gelatin solution. The depression can be computed fairly well from Nernst's formula, taking the voltage to arise from the unequal hydrogen ion levels on the two sides. That inequality is itself the Donnan membrane equilibrium at work. A solid block of gelatin chloride shows the same voltage behavior against its surrounding water.
europmc-pmc2140981:
Liver catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide, and John Williams measures how fast that reaction runs when enzyme amount, peroxide amount, acidity, and temperature each change. His 1928 study tries to tie those variables together rather than treat each one alone.

Williams concludes the peroxide first sticks to the catalase surface, a step called adsorption. He splits the process into two linked reactions: the breakdown itself, fastest near pH 6.8 to 7.0, and a wearing-out of the enzyme caused by fresh oxygen clinging to its surface. That second claim departs from the usual view blaming the peroxide itself. The paper also reworks Yamasaki's equation and links it with Northrop's, giving enzyme workers a fresh frame for older data.
europmc-pmc2292181:
Sunkar and co-workers hunted new microRNAs in rice in 2008 using deep sequencing of small RNA libraries. MicroRNAs are tiny RNAs that switch genes off, and rare ones escape conventional sequencing. The team built libraries from normal rice seedlings and from seedlings stressed by drought or salt, then used pyrosequencing, a high-throughput method reading many fragments at once. They matched tens of thousands of unique small RNAs to the rice genome.

Most known conserved microRNAs were confirmed. Twenty-three genuinely new microRNAs were found, mostly each from a single genome locus. Six of them are conserved in other grass crops. Forty further candidates await confirmation. Using loose matching rules, the team predicted twenty target genes for nine of the new microRNAs. Deep sequencing thus uncovers low-abundance regulators, including candidates tied to drought and salt responses in a staple crop.
europmc-pmc2361981:
Hamaguchi and co-authors tested a new delivery form of the cancer drug paclitaxel in 2005. Paclitaxel kills many cancers but causes nerve damage, low blood counts, and allergic reactions, partly from the solvent used to dissolve it. Their version, NK105, tucks the drug inside tiny polymer spheres called micelles.

In animal tests, NK105 kept drug levels in blood about 90 times higher than the free drug, because the spheres leaked little and dodged body filters. Tumor levels ran 25 times higher, thanks to the spheres gathering in tumor tissue. Against human colon cancer grafts, NK105 shrank tumors far better than free paclitaxel. Nerve damage was clearly weaker too, shown by both tissue checks and nerve function tests. The authors said patient trials were warranted.
europmc-pmc2365981:
Schadt and a large team mapped how DNA variation shapes gene activity in human liver in 2008. The liver drives metabolism and is central to obesity, diabetes, and artery disease. Genes linked to illness usually act through such middle steps, so the team measured both DNA and gene activity in the same tissue.

They profiled over 39,000 gene transcripts and about 782,000 DNA variants in more than 400 liver samples. Over 6,000 links between variants and gene activity turned up, many in genes already tied to disease. Merging their data with other human and mouse studies let them test disease genes directly. For a new type 1 diabetes site, their data backed the gene RPS26 over the earlier favourite ERBB3. They also named SORT1 and CELSR2 as likely genes behind a cholesterol and heart disease site.
europmc-pmc2492881:
Statnikov, Wang, and Aliferis compared two leading computer methods for sorting cancers by gene activity in this 2008 paper. The methods are support vector machines and random forests, both used to classify tumors from microarray data, which measure thousands of genes at once. Earlier studies had suggested random forests might be the better tool.

The authors first showed that prior comparisons carried design flaws that favored one method. They then ran a corrected test across 22 diagnostic and prognostic data sets. Support vector machines beat random forests in most data sets, often by a wide margin. The result held both with no gene selection and with several popular gene selection methods applied first.
europmc-pmc2515281:
Koch and colleagues compared T cells, a core part of the immune system, in young and older people in this 2008 study. Immunity weakens with age, and the mix of T cell types in the blood changes. The team used multi-colour flow cytometry, a method that tags cells with several markers at once, to sort the cells in fine detail.

They tracked naive, central memory, and effector memory cells in both CD4 and CD8 groups, adding markers of stimulation and wear. Age shifts were stronger in CD8 cells than in CD4 cells. The results support a step-by-step path from naive cells toward worn-out end-stage effector cells that no longer divide. For CD4 cells, change within each subset mattered more than shifts between subsets.
europmc-pmc2516581:
Zuccato and co-authors tested a new way to track illegal drug use in 2008: analysing city sewage. People excrete drug residues in urine, so wastewater arriving at treatment plants carries a chemical record of what a whole community has taken. The team measured residues of cocaine, opiates, cannabis, and amphetamines by mass spectrometry.

Samples came from treatment plants in Milan, Lugano, and London. Each city showed its own reproducible pattern of drug use, matching national survey estimates. In Milan, cocaine residues rose sharply at weekends, a shift the method caught quickly. The authors argue that sewage analysis can monitor local drug trends almost in real time, far faster than surveys and crime statistics allow.
europmc-pmc2605581:
Grech and a large team of collaborators reviewed in 2008 the methods for solving the EEG inverse problem, locating brain sources from scalp voltage recordings. The problem is mathematically ill-posed: many source arrangements can produce the same scalp pattern. The review organises solutions into two camps. Nonparametric methods spread activity over the whole brain grid. Parametric methods assume a few dipoles.

Surveying published performance, the authors find the LORETA family gives satisfactory results in most cases, while clustered sources favour high-resolution methods such as MUSIC or FINES. Their own Monte-Carlo simulations compared four nonparametric algorithms at varied noise levels and source depths. For a single source, regularised sLORETA gave the best localisation. It produced the fewest ghost sources. A heavier shrinking method added no benefit.
europmc-pmc2642881:
Friston explained in 2009 two ways to study how brain areas talk to each other using brain scans. Scans once showed mainly which areas light up during a task. Newer methods ask a harder question: does activity in one area drive activity in another, for example when attention boosts what we see?

One approach, dynamic causal modelling, builds a model of how areas influence each other and tests whether it fits the scan data. The other, Granger causal modelling, looks for timing patterns in which one area's activity predicts another's a moment later. Friston compares what each method can and cannot show. The piece helps readers judge claims about brain networks, such as whether a signal flows from higher areas down, or from the senses up.
europmc-pmc2718581:
Fazel and co-authors reviewed in 2009 whether schizophrenia and other psychoses raise the risk of violence and violent crime. Public claims and charity campaigns often call any link a myth, while secure hospital numbers have risen in many Western countries. Prior studies gave wildly different estimates, from large increases to none at all.

Pooling population studies, they found a modest raised risk of violence in people with psychosis compared with the general public. Much of that extra risk ran through substance abuse that occurred alongside the illness, not through psychosis alone. People with both psychosis and substance abuse faced risks close to those with substance abuse alone, which reframes where prevention should aim.
europmc-pmc2719581:
Potkin and co-authors ran a genome-wide association study in 2009 using hippocampal shrinkage as a measured trait to hunt Alzheimer's risk genes. Apart from the APOE gene form, common risk genes for late Alzheimer's were unknown. Shrinkage of the hippocampus, a memory center, can be measured on scans. It may track disease genes more directly than diagnosis alone.

In three hundred eighty-one participants in a national imaging study, the usual case-control scan confirmed APOE. It also flagged a new gene, TOMM40, whose risk forms were about twice as common in patients. The shrinkage-based scan added twenty-one candidate areas. Those included genes tied to protein cleanup, cell death, and brain development. All data were made freely public.
europmc-pmc2746281:
Dubreuil and co-authors characterized in 2009 masitinib, a new tyrosine kinase inhibitor drug that targets KIT, a receptor that drives growth in mast cells and some tumors. KIT is a target in cancer, mastocytosis, and inflammatory disease, but the standard inhibitor imatinib has limits. A more selective drug might work as well with fewer side effects.

In lab tests masitinib blocked KIT more strongly and selectively than imatinib, and also hit two related kinases while sparing many others. It blocked mast cell degranulation, cytokine output, and migration more strongly, and worked against KIT mutants that sit near the membrane. In mice it blocked growth of tumors carrying such a mutant, with no heart or gene toxicity seen in animal studies.
europmc-pmc2771281:
Spaulding and co-authors estimated in 2009 the share of the United States HIV and AIDS epidemic borne by inmates and people released from jails and prisons in 2006. Groups at high risk gather in correctional facilities, where infection rates ran high early in the epidemic. They built a new model of population flow through facilities to compare 2006 with 1997.

In 1997, about one in five HIV-infected Americans was among those who left a facility that year. By 2006 the share had fallen to about one in seven, a drop of nearly thirty percent, even as releases rose. For Black and Hispanic men, though, recent releasees still made up about one in five of each group's infected members. Absolute numbers leaving with HIV stayed nearly the same, keeping facilities prime sites for public health work.
europmc-pmc2850381:
Splinter, Akhmanova, Medema, and colleagues traced in 2010 how the cell nucleus gets hauled into position just before cell division begins. As cells enter mitosis, the centrosome, the organizing hub for the cell's skeleton, must split and the nucleus must center correctly. The team searched for partners of Bicaudal D2, an adaptor that links cargo to molecular motors.

Bicaudal D2 latched onto RanBP2, a giant protein of the nuclear pore, the gateway through the nuclear envelope. Through that link it recruited dynein, a minus-end motor, and its counterpart kinesin-1 to the nuclear surface in late G2 phase. Cells missing the adaptor misplaced their centrosomes and nuclei, revealing the missing molecular link between motors and the nucleus.
europmc-pmc2870981:
Rueping and Nachtsheim reviewed in 2010 a decade of progress in the Friedel-Crafts alkylation, a classic reaction that attaches carbon groups to ring-shaped molecules. The old method needed toxic benzyl halides and large amounts of a Lewis acid, a chemical that grabs electron pairs. Newer versions use only a pinch of catalyst, a substance that speeds a reaction without being consumed.

Benign starting materials such as benzyl alcohols and styrenes now replace the toxic halides in many versions of the reaction. Low catalyst amounts still deliver a wide range of products in good yield. The review also highlights the first versions that control which mirror-image or spatial form of the product is made. Those versions point toward cleaner drug and materials chemistry with far less waste.
europmc-pmc2872881:
Gerardo and a consortium of aphid genome researchers reported in 2010 that the pea aphid defends itself with a surprisingly thin immune toolkit. Pea aphids are sap-sucking pests of legume crops, and their genome had just been sequenced. Insects usually recognize germs, signal the alarm, and kill invaders with antimicrobial peptides, small germ-killing proteins.

The aphid genome lacks many genes for each of those steps that other insects rely on, including key recognition and signaling pieces. Some killing peptides are missing entirely. Living with helpful bacteria inside its own cells may have let the aphid shed costly defenses, or its bacteria partners may supply protection instead. Either way, the gaps reshape how scientists think insect immunity must be built and where pest control might strike.
europmc-pmc2885081:
Kumirska and co-authors reviewed in 2010 how light-based laboratory methods reveal the structure of chitin and chitosan, two versatile natural polymers. Chitin is the second most abundant natural polymer on Earth, forming shells of crabs and shrimp and walls of fungi. Its treated derivative chitosan serves medicine, farming, and food production, yet properties vary widely with source and processing.

Spectroscopic methods, which read how a sample absorbs or scatters light and radio waves, can measure chain chemistry without destroying much material. The review covers which method answers which question, from the degree of chemical trimming that turns chitin into chitosan to the makeup of modified versions. Reliable structural checks are what let makers certify a batch for a sensitive use like wound care.
europmc-pmc2888581:
Kinney, Lawn, and the Science in Action working group opened in 2010 a journal series on mother, newborn, and child deaths in sub-Saharan Africa. The region loses about four point four million children, including over a million newborns, plus some two hundred sixty-five thousand mothers every year. That is roughly thirteen thousand deaths a day, half of the world's total for these groups.

Five challenges drive most deaths: complications of pregnancy and birth, newborn illness, childhood infections, malnutrition, and HIV. Proven tools already exist for nearly all of them, from vaccines and treated bed nets to emergency obstetric equipment. The authors argue the core failure is delivery, not knowledge, since governments underuse the interventions science has validated.
europmc-pmc2896381:
Schmid and colleagues built in 2010 a three-dimensional visualization toolkit that plugs into ImageJ, the free image software biologists already use. Modern microscopes and scanners produce 3D stacks that flat viewers handle badly, and writing custom 3D code is slow and specialist work. Their Java framework hides the graphics machinery behind simple high-level calls.

Plug-in authors gain volume rendering, direct editing of 3D volumes, surface extraction from labeled structures, and annotation tools with little extra code. Hardware acceleration keeps big confocal and electron microscopy datasets interactive. Because it rides on ImageJ's vast community library, a lab can move from raw stack to measured 3D structure in one environment. The authors released the source openly so other groups could extend it.
europmc-pmc2908081:
Dayyani and colleagues pooled in 2010 thirty-four studies and over fifty-six hundred patients to define how human papillomavirus changes head and neck cancers. The virus, famous for causing cervical cancer, drives a subset of throat and mouth cancers too. About twenty-two percent of the tumors carried the virus, and nearly nine tenths of those carried type 16, the highest-risk strain.

Virus-positive tumors formed a distinct biological entity: they arose more often in virus carriers, carried far fewer mutations in the guardian gene p53, and answered treatment better. Most strikingly, virus-positive patients died at well under half the rate of virus-negative patients. The authors argue trials should now test whether these patients can be cured with gentler therapy that spares them lasting side effects.
europmc-pmc2939781:
Okusaka and colleagues compared two chemotherapy plans for advanced bile duct cancer in Japanese patients in a 2010 multicentre study. A British trial had hinted that pairing gemcitabine with cisplatin beat gemcitabine on its own.

Eighty-four patients were assigned by chance to the pair or to gemcitabine alone, given in repeating cycles for up to nearly a year. The pair produced modestly longer survival, longer time before the cancer grew, and more tumour shrinkage. Low blood cell counts were the commonest severe side effects, occurring more often with the pairing. The authors judged the pair tolerable and fit as a standard option.
europmc-pmc3002981:
Chan and colleagues used precise mass measurements to watch the chemical decorations on transfer RNA shift during stress in yeast, in a 2010 study. Over a hundred such decorations exist, mostly on the RNAs that carry building blocks to protein factories, yet their collective behaviour was obscure.

Their method measured the decorations with care. It also uncovered fresh routes by which cells build several of them. Different poisons left different signature patterns: peroxide raised three particular decorations, while other agents lowered them or left them alone. Yeast missing the enzymes for those three decorations grew hypersensitive to peroxide.
europmc-pmc3061881:
Reikvam and coauthors refined in 2011 a reliable way to empty a mouse's gut of its bacteria without a germ free facility. Comparing normal mice with microbe free ones reveals what gut microbes do for the body, but germ free colonies are costly and rare. Earlier antibiotic in drinking water protocols proved hard to repeat and sometimes harmed the animals.

Delivering the antibiotics by mouth tube twice a day cleared the growable gut bacteria and cut gut bacterial DNA several hundred fold, while keeping mice healthy. After about two weeks the mice looked much like germ free animals, with enlarged gut pouches and smaller immune tissues. Hundreds of genes changed activity in the colon lining, and gut cell growth slowed. The protocol gives ordinary labs a workable stand in for germ free mice in microbe and host studies.
europmc-pmc3113981:
Jennifer Schumi and Janet Wittes wrote a 2011 guide in Trials to a tricky kind of medical trial. Most trials try to show a new treatment beats an old one, but some only need to show the new option is not unacceptably worse. Their paper explains that design and how regulators in Europe and the United States view it.

The central problem is choosing in advance how much worse counts as too much, since that margin decides the verdict. The authors walk through how sample size, error rates, and confidence ranges work differently when the goal is staying close rather than winning. They stress that a sloppy trial can wrongly pass as good enough, so careful design and honest reading of results matter more here than in standard trials.
europmc-pmc3166781:
Matthew Warman and colleagues issued the 2010 revision of the classification of genetic bone disorders in a 2011 paper in the American Journal of Medical Genetics. These disorders arise from faults in bone development, growth, and upkeep, and their sheer variety makes diagnosis hard. The classification sorts recognised conditions by clinical and X-ray features and, where known, by molecular cause.

The revision lists more than four hundred and fifty conditions in forty groups. Over two thirds now link to mutations in more than two hundred genes, from common recurrent faults to private ones seen in single families. The document thus doubles as both a diagnostic checklist and a gene-to-condition map. It is aimed at genetics, children's medicine, and radiology teams facing the coming flood of sequencing data.
europmc-pmc3168881:
Tatiana Akimova and colleagues tested whether a protein marks a special class of calming immune cells in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Regulatory T cells keep immune responses in check, and a recent report claimed one protein distinguishes those born in the thymus from those converted later in the body. The team tracked the protein across mouse and human T cells at rest and during activation.

Cells lacking the protein were mostly naive, never-activated cells. Switching T cells on and driving them to divide switched the protein on too, in regulatory and ordinary T cells alike, and resting switched it back off. Since the protein simply reports recent activation and division, it cannot separate the two regulatory lineages as claimed. The study corrects a marker the field was beginning to rely on.
europmc-pmc3222181:
Michelle Burns and colleagues built Mobilyze!, a phone-based treatment aid for depression, in this 2011 paper in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. Phones carry sensors that can infer where a person is and what they are doing. The team used that context sensing to deliver help at the moment it might be needed. Eight adults with major depression used the system for eight weeks.

Machine-learning models trained on dozens of sensor readings predicted categorical states such as location with promising accuracy, though mood ratings on scales were hard to predict. The package added feedback graphs, lessons in behavioral activation, and brief clinician contact. Participants liked the app, and their depressive symptoms fell significantly on both self-reports and interviews, with anxiety easing too. The authors present it as a feasible first of its kind.
europmc-pmc3257681:
Emilio Ros reviewed the health benefits of eating nuts in this 2010 article in Nutrients. Tree nuts and peanuts are dense packages of unsaturated fats, quality plant protein, fiber, minerals, and protective plant compounds. Ros asks what that unusual composition means for the people who eat them regularly.

Population studies link nut eating with less coronary heart disease and fewer gallstones in both sexes. They also link it with less diabetes in women. Hints of benefits extend to blood pressure, cancer, and inflammation. Feeding trials consistently show nuts lower cholesterol, even within already healthy diets, and evidence is growing for effects on oxidative stress, blood vessel function, and the metabolic syndrome. Against expectations, regular nut eaters do not gain excess weight and may lose some. The main safety concern is nut allergy in a small number of children.
europmc-pmc3266881:
Daniel Lawson, Garrett Hellenthal, Simon Myers, and Daniel Falush introduced a haplotype-based way to infer population structure, in this 2012 paper in PLoS Genetics. Dense genome-wide data reveal ancestry in unprecedented detail but strain older statistics. Their framework paints each person's chromosomes as a mosaic of chunks copied from other individuals in the sample, summarizing the copying pattern in a coancestry matrix.

That matrix turns out to capture nearly all the information used by standard principal component analysis and by model-based clustering, while squeezing extra signal from the linkage between neighboring markers. Their companion clustering method is faster than rivals, separates more populations, and detects subtler structure. Applied to a worldwide panel of over nine hundred people, it resolved more than two hundred populations, from continental down to family scale, finer than geographic labels suggest.
europmc-pmc3399081:
Jonassen and co-workers explained in 2012 how insulin degludec, an ultra-long-acting insulin, was designed to release slowly after injection. A fatty tail attached to the insulin lets it self-assemble once the injection's helper chemicals fade. The team tested a series of tailed insulins to learn the structural rules.

In the vial, degludec sits as paired six-unit clusters. After injection, as one helper fades, the clusters link into long filament-like chains, then slowly shed single units as a second helper leaves. The shape studies confirmed each stage of that choreography. Weak pairing between shed units means they free themselves quickly once released. The design shows injected depots can be engineered on purpose.
europmc-pmc3400581:
Lovejoy and a consortium team mapped in 2012 how some cancers keep their chromosome ends without the usual enzyme, a route called alternative lengthening of telomeres. This recombination-based path serves a sizable share of human cancers, but what unleashes it was unknown. Mutations in a chromatin complex involving the protein ATRX had recently turned up in such tumors.

Studying twenty-two cell lines using the pathway, the team found loss of ATRX protein or its gene in case after case. The cells also showed scrambled genomes, stray mini-nuclei, a faulty checkpoint before division, and altered repair of broken DNA. Together these hallmarks could help doctors spot and treat cancers that maintain their ends this way.
europmc-pmc3460881:
Liu and colleagues vetted housekeeping genes in 2012 for gene studies in Nicotiana benthamiana, the workhorse plant of virus research. Such studies lean on a steady reference gene for calibration, and infection might wobble the usual choices. Sixteen candidate references were profiled in leaves carrying infections from a panel of five RNA viruses of plants.

Three independent algorithms agreed on the steadiest trio: PP2A, F-BOX, and L23. Together they were enough for accurate calibration, and a demonstration on two immune genes showed clean results. Several traditional favorites proved less steady under infection. The shortlist should serve virus studies directly and guide reference choice for other stresses in this model plant.
europmc-pmc3516581:
Brucellosis makes people miserable in patterned ways, and Anna S. Dean and six colleagues pool the symptom evidence for the World Health Organization in 2012, a companion to their global frequency review. From 2,385 papers on human brucellosis between 1990 and 2010, 57 studies pass quality screening for data extraction.

Fever strikes 78 percent of patients, which makes brucellosis easy to confuse with malaria where both occur. Joint pain affects 65 percent, muscle pain 47 percent, and back pain 45 percent. Severe complications are not rare: about one neurological case and endocarditis at lower rates appear per hundred patients, and one in ten men develops testicle inflammation. The pooled picture feeds disability calculations.
europmc-pmc3519481:
Prostate cancers that stop responding to hormones eventually resist the drug docetaxel too, and Claire Corcoran leads an eleven-author team probing that resistance in 2012. They breed docetaxel-resistant versions of two prostate cancer cell lines and catalogue what changes beyond drug response.

Resistant cells also shrug off doxorubicin, a second drug, and they move, invade, and grow without anchorage differently. More striking, the tiny vesicles called exosomes that resistant cells shed carry the trait with them: sensitive cells exposed to those exosomes gain docetaxel resistance. Early checks of patient serum exosomes are included. Resistance, the study warns, may spread cell to cell like a message.
europmc-pmc3584981:
Yukio Ando and colleagues wrote a clinician's guide to inherited transthyretin amyloidosis in the Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases in 2013. In this disease, a blood protein made in the liver, transthyretin, falls apart, misfolds, and deposits as amyloid in nerves and heart muscle. Damage builds until the disease proves fatal. Its mixed and shifting symptoms, numbness and weakness in one patient, heart failure in another, make it easy to miss for years.

Firm diagnosis needs tissue proof and gene testing, the guide explains, followed by staging of nerve and heart involvement and regular checks as it advances. Care covers symptom relief organ by organ. Liver transplant, which swaps the source of the faulty protein, was the standing treatment, and several drugs then in trials aimed to steady or silence the protein. The authors wrote the guide so ordinary physicians can recognize and manage a disease many never meet.
europmc-pmc3622181:
Minna Balbas and colleagues hunted in advance for ways prostate cancer escapes a new drug, in eLife in 2013. Enzalutamide, a second-generation hormone blocker, had just been approved for castration-resistant prostate cancer, but responses often fade. For older blockers, one escape was mutation of the androgen receptor, the protein the drugs jam. The team deliberately mutated the receptor in a screening system to find changes that defeat the drug before clinics met them.

One change, F876L, did worse than defeat the drug: it turned enzalutamide into a receptor activator, and cells carrying it grew through treatment. Computer simulations of the mutant complex showed the switch reshaping a key helix, explaining the flip. That model then directed a search over existing blocker scaffolds, which found three fresh compounds that shut down both mutant and normal receptors. Advance scouting of resistance is the paper's strategy.
europmc-pmc3654481:
Cell power plants split where they touch the cell's inner net, Murley and six colleagues show in a 2013 eLife study of yeast. The touch points had been seen to mark split sites, but their works were unclear. Two players sit at the centre: a tether complex linking the two structures, and a switch protein called Gem1 in the text.

Gem1 turns out to hold the touch points in check, and that brake is needed so new power plant tips spread out well after a split. The tether complex sits near bundles of power plant DNA that are copying themselves. Most such bundles part before the split, landing in the new tips. Splitting at the net, the authors propose, is how the cell deals out both power plants and their DNA in one move.
europmc-pmc3690481:
Keusekotten and colleagues identified OTULIN, a human enzyme that cuts only one kind of ubiquitin chain. Cells tag proteins with chains of ubiquitin, and chains linked through the first amino acid, called Met1 or linear chains, switch on immune signalling through the LUBAC complex. No dedicated enzyme for removing those chains was known.

OTULIN proved exquisitely specific for Met1 linkages, and crystal structures showed how its binding pockets enforce that choice. Raising or lowering OTULIN changed cell responses to inflammatory signals and altered sensitivity to cell death. The authors position OTULIN as the brake on linear ubiquitin signalling, acting partly through direct contact with LUBAC itself.
europmc-pmc3724681:
Evangelos Kontopantelis, David Springate, and David Reeves published a re-analysis study in PLoS ONE in 2013 on a hidden flaw in meta-analyses. A meta-analysis pools many studies into one result, but studies often differ from each other, a spread called heterogeneity. When tests miss that spread, analysts often assume there is none and use a simpler method.

The team used 57,397 meta-analyses from the Cochrane Library, plus simulated data, to test how methods cope. Hidden heterogeneity looked common, above all in small meta-analyses. A bootstrapped version of a standard method did best, but only slightly. Where spread had been found and then ignored, about 17 to 20 percent of conclusions changed on re-analysis. The authors advise testing how sensitive conclusions are to assumed spread.
europmc-pmc3745981:
Yan Zhao and Baolu Zhao wrote a review in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity in 2013 on oxidative stress in Alzheimer's disease. Alzheimer's is the most common cause of dementia in older people, marked by plaques, tangles, and loss of nerve cells. Oxidative stress means an overload of reactive oxygen species that can damage cells.

Extra reactive oxygen may come from faulty mitochondria or from metals building up in the wrong places. The amyloid and tau proteins that mark the disease seem to worsen that imbalance. In turn, oxidative stress may raise amyloid production and clumping and push tau toward tangles. The authors describe a vicious cycle in which each side feeds the other, driving the disease forward, while noting that the sources of the free radicals are still not settled.
europmc-pmc3747981:
Lisa Funkhouser and Seth Bordenstein wrote an essay in PLoS Biology in 2013 arguing that mothers pass microbes to their offspring across the whole animal kingdom. The old view held that babies develop in a sterile womb and pick up their first bacteria in the birth canal. New sequencing work has unsettled that dogma.

Bacteria have been found in cord blood, amniotic fluid, and fetal membranes from healthy births, and a newborn's first stool is not sterile. The authors widen the meaning of maternal transmission to cover all transfers from mother to young, inside and outside the body. They contend that mothers provision their offspring with needed microbes at birth rather than leaving the task to chance, in animals far beyond the classic studied cases.
europmc-pmc3812781:
Edmund T. Rolls wrote a solo review in Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience in 2013. He sets out how the hippocampus, a brain area key to memory, can both complete and split apart stored patterns. His account rests on the CA3 network and its dense links back onto itself.

Rolls explains how CA3 can store a full memory from a part cue, a skill called pattern completion. He also explains pattern separation, where the dentate gyrus makes like inputs more distinct so they do not blur. Sparse firing, random input wiring, and weak links all help the store hold many memories. The review ties cell-level facts to how recall works as a whole, giving a clear map of the theory.
europmc-pmc3813081:
Afshin Zarghi and Sara Arfaei wrote a review in the Iranian Journal of Pharmaceutical Research, dated 2011 in the record. Their subject is drugs that block the COX-2 enzyme and spare COX-1. Such drugs aim to cut pain and swelling with less harm to the stomach than older pain drugs cause.

The review sorts the drugs by their chemical shape and shows how each shape fits the COX-2 site. Small shape changes can raise or lower both strength and safety. Some early drugs in this class were withdrawn over heart risks, so the search for safer forms goes on. Work also tests these drugs in cancer and brain disease. The review gives chemists a map for new designs.
europmc-pmc3828581:
Christopher P. Howson, Mary V. Kinney, Lori McDougall, and Joy E. Lawn open a journal supplement on preterm birth in Reproductive Health in 2013. Millions of babies are born too soon each year, and rates are rising in most countries with solid data. Their piece sets the global policy scene.

Early birth is now a top block to child survival goals and adds value to mother health work. Babies who live can face lasting disability, which strains families and health systems. Rich countries treat early birth as a clear priority, while poorer ones often overlook it amid myths and weak counts. A 2012 global action report pushed the issue to a tipping point. The authors call for care across the full span from before pregnancy to early childhood.
europmc-pmc3847481:
Jun Wang, Jamie Barstein, Lauren E. Ethridge, Matthew W. Mosconi, Yukari Takarae, and John A. Sweeney review brain wave studies in autism in the Journal of Neurodevelopmental Disorders in 2013. EEG, a scalp read of brain electric waves, offers a cheap way to probe how autistic brains work at rest. The team sum up what resting studies have found.

Power tends to run high at both slow and fast wave bands, a U-shaped pattern across studies. Links between brain areas also look off, and the left side of the brain shows extra power. Such marks could one day split autism into clear subgroups or track new treatments. The authors flag weak spots in past work that may explain clashing results, and they set out steps for stronger studies.
europmc-pmc3866681:
Wolfram Schultz wrote a solo review on dopamine reward signals in Current Opinion in Neurobiology in 2013. Dopamine neurons fire in bursts when a reward beats what the brain expected, a teaching signal called a prediction error. Schultz sums up fresh work on how that signal is shaped.

The signal turns out to draw on model-based knowledge, not just raw surprise, he reports. With proper controls, the neurons show little response to punishers as such, and they do not merely flag how striking an event is. Sound dopamine signaling is needed for learning and for the lasting synaptic changes behind it. The review is a compact update from a leader in the field, sorting which claims about the signal hold firm.
europmc-pmc3874981:
Aaron W. James wrote a solo review on stem cell fate signals in Scientifica in 2013. Mesenchymal stem cells can become fat cells or bone cells, among other types. The two fates trade off: more bone means less fat, a balance set by signal paths inside the cell.

Two master switch factors run the contest, one for fat and one for bone. Many signal paths lean on those switches. Some paths, such as Wnt and Hedgehog signals, push bone and block fat in a steady way. Others, like bone morphogenetic protein signals, can push either fate by context. The review sorts the paths by their lean. Grasping the web matters for bone repair and for diseases where fat crowds out bone in marrow.
europmc-pmc3876981:
Kiichi Nakahira leads a large team in an intensive care marker study in PLoS Medicine in 2013. Doctors in intensive care units need better ways to judge which patients face death. Scores built from standard vital signs help, but blood markers that add real power are few.

The team measure loose mitochondrial DNA in blood. Mitochondria are cell power units with their own small DNA, which spills into blood when cells are badly stressed. In two tracked patient groups, higher levels went with higher death rates in the unit. Adding the marker to standard scores sharpened risk forecasts for medical ICU patients. The authors propose the DNA read as a workable blood sign for the sickest patients, pending wider checks.
europmc-pmc3909981:
Lisa H. Mason, Jordan P. Harp, and Dong Y. Han review the effects of lead on the brain and thinking in BioMed Research International in 2014. Lead is one of the most common heavy-metal exposures in people, and it can cause lasting decline in mental function. The review gathers what is known about how that harm happens and how often it occurs.

The authors walk through lead's effects on intelligence, memory, attention, speed of thinking, language, spatial skills, movement, and mood. They also cover the biology of lead poisoning and who is most at risk. For clinicians who test thinking skills, the paper serves as a single reference linking a patient's exposure history to the pattern of problems that patient may show.
europmc-pmc4011581:
Ulrike M. Litzenburger and a large team of co-authors trace a self-feeding loop that keeps an immune-blocking enzyme active in human cancers, in Oncotarget in 2014. The enzyme, IDO, breaks down an amino acid that immune cells need. Tumours that make IDO can shut down attack, and drugs that block IDO are in trials.

In tumour cells and tissues that make IDO, a signal protein called STAT3 stayed switched on. Blocking a messenger called IL-6, or STAT3 itself, cut IDO output and its chemical product. That product switched on a sensor called AHR, which raised IL-6. The loop thus feeds itself: IDO drives the signals that keep IDO on. Breaking the loop let T cells grow again in mixed cell tests with IDO-making cancer cells. High loop levels tracked with sooner relapse in lung cancer patients, and the loop offers fresh drug targets.
europmc-pmc4011881:
Frency Varghese, Amirali B. Bukhari, Renu Malhotra, Abhijit De, and Syed A. Aziz present a free plugin that scores stained tissue images by computer, in PLoS ONE in 2014. Pathologists use antibody stains to find disease markers in tissue slices. Scoring stain strength by eye is slow and varies with the viewer.

Their tool, IHC Profiler, runs inside the open ImageJ program. It first splits the brown stain from the blue counterstain by colour maths. It then reads the brown channel pixel by pixel and gives a score on a four-step scale. The team tested it on close to seventeen hundred stained images, among them samples from a public human protein atlas. Its scores matched human scoring in close to nine of ten cases. The tool suits markers in the cell body or nucleus, and may cut scoring gaps between labs.
europmc-pmc4218981:
Luis Carretié wrote a solo review of how emotion hijacks attention in Cognitive, Affective and Behavioral Neuroscience in 2014. Attention research mostly used bland, neutral test items, yet in real life emotional sights grab us whether we want them to or not. That automatic pull is called exogenous attention.

Surveying 55 experiments that pitted emotional against neutral distractors during a task, Carretié found emotional items consistently won the contest for attention, in both behaviour and brain measures. The pull varied with the distractor type, the task, and the person. Brain timing and location data let him sketch the stages involved, from first spotting to reorienting and sensory boost, and he offers a model joining them. Several basic questions, he notes, still lack data.
europmc-pmc4336481:
Yong Gan and eleven co-authors updated the evidence on whether depression raises the risk of coronary heart disease. Their meta-analysis appeared in BMC Psychiatry in 2014. Earlier reviews had linked the two, but they carried limits and many new cohort studies had since appeared.

Thirty prospective studies following close to nine hundred thousand people, with nearly sixty thousand heart disease cases, met the entry rules. Depressed participants developed coronary disease at clearly higher rates than non-depressed peers, and the link held across study designs and regions. The authors discuss behavior and biology routes, from smoking and inactivity to inflammation, and argue heart prevention should not ignore mental health.
europmc-pmc4371881:
Jieyuan Zhang and co-authors tested tiny parcels from stem cells as a wound treatment, in the Journal of Translational Medicine in 2015. Mesenchymal stem cells grown from reprogrammed human cells can aid repair, and the small parcels they release, called exosomes, carry much of that effect. No prior work had tried these exosomes on skin wounds. The team injected them around wounds in rats and also tested them on human skin and vessel cells in dishes.

Treated wounds closed faster, re-covered with skin sooner, and formed narrower scars with more mature collagen. New blood vessels formed and matured faster at wound sites. In dishes, the exosomes sped growth and movement of skin fibroblasts and vessel lining cells, and raised collagen output. The results point to a cell-free way to borrow stem cell benefits.
europmc-pmc4425181:
Evelien Neis, Cornelis Dejong, and Sander Rensen reviewed in Nutrients in 2015 how gut microbes handle amino acids, the building blocks of protein, and how that handling affects the host. Changes in gut microbes are increasingly tied to obesity, insulin resistance, and type 2 diabetes, and the products microbes release are part of that link.

Bacteria both take amino acids from food and body proteins and supply amino acids back to the host. Some microbe-made amino acids can also serve as raw material for short-chain fatty acids. Blood levels of certain amino acids, notably the branched-chain and aromatic kinds, run high in insulin resistance. The review weighs evidence that gut microbes help set those levels and may thus shape metabolic disease.
europmc-pmc4493381:
Hanan Ahmed Wahba and Hend Ahmed El-Hadaad reviewed treatment of triple-negative breast cancer in Cancer Biology and Medicine in 2015. These tumors lack estrogen and progesterone receptors and do not overproduce HER2, the three markers that guide most breast cancer therapy. Patients therefore cannot benefit from hormonal treatments or HER2-targeted drugs such as trastuzumab. The disease strikes younger and premenopausal women more often, and African American women especially.

Biologically aggressive, triple-negative cancers can still respond well to chemotherapy at first, in some reports better than other breast cancers. But the disease-free interval after treatment is short, and once spread, the course is rapid, so prognosis stays poor. The review covers current chemotherapy approaches and regimens in early and advanced settings, and the search for new targets in a cancer defined by the targets it lacks.
europmc-pmc4496681:
Adelheid Weidinger, Andrey Kozlov, Peter Eckl, and Michael Breitenbach reconsidered reactive oxygen and nitrogen species in Biomolecules in 2015. These reactive molecules were long cast simply as vandals that damage proteins, fats, and DNA and drive disease. Newer evidence casts some of them as messengers inside cells, an apparent contradiction the review sets out to resolve.

Damage, the authors argue, does not follow from a single primary species such as superoxide or nitric oxide, even at high levels. Harm begins when two primary species react, or meet a transition metal, forming fiercer secondary products such as hydroxyl radical or peroxynitrite, which damage all molecule classes irreversibly. Primary species, by contrast, are tightly controlled by enzymes and react reversibly, making them fit for signaling. The distinction, they propose, explains when the same chemistry heals information flow or causes oxidative stress.
europmc-pmc4540581:
Seth R. Bordenstein and Kevin R. Theis argue that animals and plants cannot be understood apart from their microbes, in PLoS Biology in 2015. Research keeps showing that microbes live on and in every host, shaping health and evolution. The authors call the host-plus-microbes unit a holobiont and its combined gene set a hologenome.

To keep the ideas sharp, they lay out ten principles stating what the concepts do and do not claim. The principles show where the view stretches Darwin's and Mendel's legacy and where it leaves standing theory intact. They also offer a testable framework others can challenge. The paper aims to move zoology and botany toward models that count microbial partners by default.
europmc-pmc4560781:
Chun-Peng Yang and four co-authors tame lithium metal batteries with a sponge-like electrode frame, in Nature Communications in 2015. Lithium metal stores more energy than today's battery anodes, but charging grows needle-like dendrites that waste power and can short the cell. That hazard has stalled lithium metal batteries for decades.

Their current collector is a 3D frame with a submicron skeleton and huge active surface. Lithium plates into the frame's pores evenly instead of spiking outward. Cells ran 600 hours without a short circuit and showed low voltage lag between charge and discharge. The team presents collector design, rather than new chemistry, as a fresh route to long-life lithium metal anodes.
europmc-pmc4566081:
Ratnadeep Mukherjee and five co-authors sort out the true characters of human monocyte subsets, in Scientific Reports in 2015. Monocytes, a blood immune cell type, split into three groups by surface markers CD14 and CD16. Papers disagreed about which group inflames and which engulfs germs, partly because sorting methods themselves changed the cells.

Using multicolor flow cytometry, an automated clustering check, and whole blood stimulated outside the body, the team reached a cleaner verdict. Classical monocytes proved to be the engulfers, with no inflammatory streak. Non-classical monocytes showed the inflammatory behavior and antigen-presenting traits. The intermediate group stayed a tiny share. Validation came from patients with sepsis and lupus.
europmc-pmc4577081:
Jie Liu leads a twelve-author team developing an antibody that strips cancer's invisibility cloak, in PLoS ONE in 2015. CD47 is a surface protein that tells macrophages, the immune system's eaters, not to swallow the cell carrying it. Leukemia stem cells and many tumors display extra CD47 to dodge being eaten. Blocking it in mouse models let macrophages clear several cancers.

The team built a fresh anti-CD47 antibody, 5F9, then humanized it by grafting its gripping loops onto a human antibody frame, producing Hu5F9-G4. The drug bound human CD47 tightly and drove macrophages to engulf cancer cells in tests. Early safety and handling profiles in animals looked favorable, positioning it as a clinical candidate.
europmc-pmc4584981:
Prachi Pandey, Venkategowda Ramegowda, and Muthappa Senthil-Kumar review how plants cope with stress in combination, in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2015. Field plants rarely face one trouble at a time; drought lands with heat, or with germs, and yields fall steeply. Lab studies of single stresses miss how the answers interact.

Evidence now shows combined-stress responses are partly unique, not a sum of single answers, and partly shared across many stresses. The review gives heat with drought pride of place, then drought and heat each paired with pathogens. It maps the molecular cross-talk behind shared and unique responses. That map, the authors argue, can guide breeding crops with broad-spectrum toughness rather than single-stress fixes.
europmc-pmc4630781:
In 2015, a study mapping bacteria across the whole digestive tract of dairy cattle was published by Siyuan Mao and colleagues. Gut microbes affect milk yield and animal health, yet most work samples only the rumen or faeces. The team sampled contents and wall tissue at ten sites in six cattle. The work appeared in Scientific Reports.

They found 542 bacterial genera from 23 phyla, with three phyla dominating. Communities differed sharply by site, in both membership and diversity. Predicted gene profiles also shifted along the tract: carbohydrate use genes were richest in the forestomach contents, while amino acid genes concentrated on gut wall samples. The survey gives cattle researchers a first full-length map of the gut community.
europmc-pmc4698281:
Ann C. McKee, Nigel J. Cairns, Dennis W. Dickson, and a large consensus panel set diagnostic rules for chronic traumatic encephalopathy in Acta Neuropathologica in 2016. CTE is a brain degeneration marked by abnormal tau protein, linked to repeated head impacts, and it can now be confirmed only after death by examining brain tissue. No agreed tissue criteria existed. Seven neuropathologists independently reviewed twenty-five cases spanning several tau diseases, without knowing the diagnoses.

Agreement among the reviewers was good, and agreement with CTE diagnoses was better still. The panel then defined the hallmark lesion: abnormal tau gathered in neurons and astroglia around small blood vessels, deep in the folds of the cortex, in an irregular pattern. Extra supporting features and a standard staining scheme were also set. These first shared criteria give future clinical and lab studies a common language.
europmc-pmc4702781:
Robert Petryszak, Maria Keays, Y. Amy Tang, and a large team updated the Expression Atlas in Nucleic Acids Research in 2016. The Atlas gathers studies that measure which genes are switched on in tissues, cell types, stages of life, and diseases, across animals and plants. Every study is hand-checked, tagged with standard terms, and processed the same way. Since the previous update, the collection had grown sevenfold, reaching 1,572 studies by August 2015.

New data include tissue profiles from the Human Protein Atlas, GTEx, and FANTOM5 projects, plus cancer cell line sets. Plant studies make up a quarter of the whole. The first protein-level dataset now sits beside gene data for the same human tissues. Fresh displays cluster genes by their patterns and enrich comparisons with pathway terms. The Atlas gives biologists one consistent window onto gene activity across the living world.
europmc-pmc4749081:
Ma and nine colleagues reconstruct a decade of fine-particle air pollution across China from satellite data, filling a gap that has hampered health research. Ground monitors arrived only recently, so the team models PM2.5 levels from 2004 to 2013 using satellite aerosol measurements plus weather and land-use data.

The model validates well against ground readings. Winter is the most polluted season and summer the cleanest. Average levels rose by about 1.97 micrograms per cubic metre per year from 2004 to 2007, then eased by 0.46 per year through 2013. The resulting maps reach the fine resolution that long-term health studies need.
europmc-pmc4750281:
Miake-Lye, Hempel, Shanman, and Shekelle review a review method that lacks a standard: the evidence map. Searching ten databases, they find 39 publications presenting evidence maps, and compare how each defines the approach, classifies its data, and displays results.

Definitions differ, but two-thirds describe the purpose as finding knowledge gaps, and over half mention stakeholder engagement or a user-friendly product. Every map uses a systematic search. The outputs split between figures, tables, and online databases. The authors distil an implied definition and argue that standard methods would help researchers and policymakers know what an evidence map promises.
europmc-pmc4890681:
Hilary P. Browne and co-authors grew supposedly unculturable human gut bacteria in Nature in 2016, using a fresh culture approach. A gut holds 100 to 1,000 bacterial species, near unique to each person, and most kinds had never been grown in a lab. DNA surveys name them but cannot test what they do. Patient culturing under gut-like conditions changed that.

A large share of gut species from healthy donors grew, including many new kinds never described. Spore forming proved far more widespread than thought, which explains how gut bacteria survive travel between hosts. Live cultures turn names on a DNA list into organisms that can be tested, stored, and one day dosed as therapy.
europmc-pmc4894981:
Adam D. Wright and co-authors measured how charge carriers couple to lattice shaking in hybrid lead halide perovskites, in Nature Communications in 2016. Such shaking, phonon scattering, caps carrier speed and blurs light emission in these solar materials. The team tracked emission line widening with temperature in four common perovskites, two built on methylammonium and two on formamidinium, with iodide or bromide.

Near room temperature, one coupling route ruled: carriers scatter off lengthwise optical phonons through the Fröhlich interaction. Sound-like phonons mattered less in that range. Knowing the main speed limit tells chemists which lattice traits to stiffen or soften. Sharper emission also helps low-cost lasers built from the same family.
europmc-pmc4915181:
Nino Stocchetti and Elisa R. Zanier reviewed the chronic impact of traumatic brain injury in Critical Care in 2016. A head injury was once framed as a sudden event with brief effects. Death rates have fallen, yet many survivors of severe injury need long rehabilitation and live with lasting body, mind, and mood disorders. Even some mild and moderate cases carry chronic costs.

Judging outcomes is hard, since side injuries such as spinal damage also cut independence. The burden lands on families and on social and health budgets for decades. The review urges care systems to plan for brain injury as a chronic condition, with follow-up that tracks quality of life, not just survival.
europmc-pmc4924581:
Gretchen A. Stevens leads the GATHER Working Group in setting rules for reporting global health estimates. Their statement appeared in PLoS Medicine in 2016, with a matching version in The Lancet. Health numbers for whole populations often rest on patchy data from many sources, mixed by models. Without clear reporting, readers cannot judge how solid an estimate is or compare it with others.

GATHER lists 18 items that authors should report. The items cover the data sources used, how they were combined, and how sure the result is. The scope is broad, from disease rates and deaths to health behaviors and exposures, at global down to local level. A companion document explains each item and why it matters. The authors present the checklist as a floor for honest, usable health estimates.
europmc-pmc4963881:
Mee-Sup Yoon, writing alone, reviews branched-chain amino acids and their tangled link to insulin resistance. Her review appeared in Nutrients in 2016. These amino acids are essential nutrients and also act as signals in the body. Supplements have been reported to aid metabolic health. Yet high blood levels of them predict obesity linked insulin resistance and future type 2 diabetes. Yoon works through that paradox, centering on a nutrient sensing complex called mTORC1.

Branched-chain amino acids switch mTORC1 on. Sustained activation then feeds back on insulin signaling and blunts it. Faulty breakdown of the amino acids in obesity may add toxic intermediates on top of the pileup. Yoon notes fresh doubt about whether normal swings in levels suffice to cause resistance. She presents blood levels as a useful warning marker either way, and she calls for care in how supplements are used.
europmc-pmc5036481:
Wei Wu, Zhaohui Wu, Taekyung Yu, Changzhong Jiang, and Woo-Sik Kim review magnetic iron oxide nanoparticles in Science and Technology of Advanced Materials in 2015. These tiny magnets are cheap, stable, and body-friendly, and medicine wants them for imaging, drug delivery, heat treatment of tumors, and sorting cells. To work in the body, a particle must be strongly magnetic, stable, and safe, with a surface that can be given useful jobs.

The review covers how the particles are made and how their size, shape, and magnetism follow from the recipe. It then surveys surface coats, from polymers and biological molecules to silica and metals, that add targeting and other functions. Applications in MRI contrast, guided drug release, magnetic heating, separation, and sensing are weighed against remaining hurdles such as long-term safety and uniform large-scale production. The authors close with the directions they expect the field to take.
europmc-pmc5116081:
Sergei Svitashev, Christine Schwartz, Brian Lenderts, Joshua K. Young, and A. Mark Cigan reported a DNA-free way to edit maize genes in Nature Communications in 2016. Plant gene editing usually delivers the CRISPR machinery as DNA, which can leave foreign DNA in the crop. Their method sends the machinery in ready-made protein form.

They shot pre-assembled Cas9 protein bound to its guide RNA into maize embryo cells with a gene gun. Plants grown from those cells carried the intended mutations and edits, at high rates, with no DNA or selectable marker inserted. Avoiding DNA delivery can ease regulatory and public concerns, and the team argues the same approach could speed breeding in many other crop species.
europmc-pmc5133381:
Stephen Burgess, Jack Bowden, Tove Fall, Erik Ingelsson, and Simon G. Thompson set out robustness checks for Mendelian randomization in Epidemiology, with the hosted text dated 2017. The method uses gene variants as natural experiments to test whether a risk factor causes a disease, but it leans on strict assumptions about those variants.

When many variants are used at once, some may cheat the assumptions, for instance by affecting the outcome through a side path. The paper explains the logic of instrumental variables and develops sensitivity analyses that probe whether a causal claim survives when some instruments are faulty. Such checks, the authors argue, let researchers spot results driven by bad instruments and report findings that hold up under weaker assumptions.
europmc-pmc5139081:
Anjali Y. Bhagirath, Yanqi Li, Deepti Somayajula, Maryam Dadashi, Sara Badr, and Kangmin Duan reviewed lung infection in cystic fibrosis in BMC Pulmonary Medicine in 2016. Cystic fibrosis airways are thick with mucus and host a distinct microbe mix, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the pathogen that drives most illness and death.

The review connects the chain link by link. The faulty CFTR channel alters lung physiology. Those changes reshape the airway's microbes, and Pseudomonas adapts to thrive there. Diet, environment, and other non-genetic factors add pressure. Because so many forces interact, the authors argue no single target will control the disease. They call for combined, multidisciplinary treatment strategies built on a whole picture of the lung environment.
europmc-pmc516581:
Lale Say, Robert C. Pattinson, and A. Metin Gülmezoglu reviewed near-miss maternal emergencies for the World Health Organization in Reproductive Health in 2004. A near miss means a pregnant or recently delivered woman who nearly died but survived through luck and good care, and counting such cases can teach more than deaths alone.

Their systematic review covered 30 studies, mostly from teaching hospitals. Reported rates swung widely: between 0.80 and 8.23 percent with disease-based definitions, far lower with organ-failure or treatment-based ones. Because each study defined its cases differently, the results could not be pooled, and rates seemed lower in richer countries. The authors call for uniform criteria, favoring an organ-system failure approach as the least biased.
europmc-pmc5186781:
Margit Mahlapuu, Joakim Håkansson, Lovisa Ringstad, and Camilla Björn reviewed antimicrobial peptides in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology in 2016. These short peptides usually carry a positive charge. They occur in nearly all life forms. Many kill microbes outright, while others work by tuning the host's defenses.

With resistance to standard antibiotics rising worldwide, interest in developing the peptides as drugs has quickened. Several are already in clinical trials against germs. Others are being tested to steer immunity and speed wound healing. Still others aim to prevent surgical adhesions. The review covers their biology, classes, and ways of killing, then weighs the hurdles to clinical use. These include how long the peptides last and how they can be given. New mixing tricks meant to overcome those hurdles also get covered.
europmc-pmc5234081:
Erin S. Calipari and ten colleagues traced a sex-specific mechanism of cocaine reward in mice in Nature Communications in 2017. Women move from cocaine use to addiction faster than men and find abstinence harder, a pattern also seen in animals. The work links that gap to the female hormone cycle and to dopamine, the brain's reward signal.

During oestrus, the fertile phase, dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area fired more strongly. That activity changed the dopamine transporter, the protein cocaine blocks, so the drug gripped it harder, an effect driven by the hormone estradiol. Female mice that learned to link cocaine with a place during oestrus later responded more strongly to that place with no drug present. Artificially raising the same neurons' activity with chemogenetic tools reproduced the effect, tying cell firing to the protein change and the stronger reward.
europmc-pmc5297181:
Søren T. Skou and Ewa M. Roos evaluated GLA:D, Denmark's national osteoarthritis program, in BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders in 2017. Guidelines urge education and exercise for knee and hip osteoarthritis, but practice lags. GLA:D, launched in 2013, trains physiotherapists to deliver both, and a national registry tracks patients. The report covers the first three years, with 9,825 participants.

Pain improved by 12.4 points at three months and 13.7 at twelve, on a 100-point scale, while quality of life rose 5.4 and then 9.4 points. Chair-stand and walking tests and weekly activity also improved, and fewer patients took painkillers or were on sick leave a year on. The program runs in all five Danish health regions through 286 units, though only 20 percent of municipalities yet offer it. The authors argue the lifestyle changes largely held at one year, with potential gains for general health and public costs.
europmc-pmc5339881:
Mariaceleste Aragona and co-authors tracked stem cells during skin repair in mouse tails, in Nature Communications in 2017. Skin must heal fast after a cut to keep germs and water loss at bay. Set stem cell pools in the outer skin layer drive that repair. How they juggle growth, travel, and maturing to close a wound was not well mapped.

The team paired growth counts with gene profiling of zones around the wound. Each zone bore its own gene stamp for growth, travel, or maturing. Tests showed the three jobs can split apart and run on their own tracks. Cell family tracing added a surprise. Fast-dividing helper cells burn out and drain away as they speed up. True stem cells wake, spawn fresh helpers, and those expand to mend the wound. The cell ranks stay the same; only the pace changes.
europmc-pmc5344681:
Juan José Bonfiglio and co-authors found the helper behind a new kind of protein tag, in Molecular Cell in 2017. Cells tag proteins with a small unit called ADP-ribose to steer repair and other work. Fresh mapping had found such tags on the amino acid serine in histones, the spools of DNA, after DNA damage. What placed the tag there was unknown.

Their tests showed the tag rests wholly on a partner protein, HPF1. It guides the repair enzyme PARP-1. In cells with no HPF1, serine tags did not form at all. Adding HPF1 to test-tube reactions with PARP enzymes was both needed and enough to place serine tags on histones and on PARP-1 itself. Wide scans found the tag on hundreds more proteins. The pair argue this tag is the key signal in the genome guard work of those enzymes.
europmc-pmc5395581:
Miranda van Bodegom, Judith R. Homberg, and Marloes J. A. G. Henckens review how early life stress reshapes the body's stress system, in a 2017 paper in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience. That system runs from brain to adrenal glands and releases stress hormones. It starts forming before birth and is shielded while young, yet harsh early events can leave marks that last into adult life.

The review covers stress before birth, being parted from the mother, and broken maternal care in animal studies. Most such stress left the adult system over-reactive, much like patterns seen in depression. Effects hinged on when the stress fell, the sex of the young, and the age at testing. The authors also weigh the idea that early stress helps only when adult life matches it.
europmc-pmc5399081:
Hua Su, Chun-Tao Lei, and Chun Zhang review the IL-6 signaling path and its role in kidney disease in a 2017 paper in Frontiers in Immunology. IL-6 is a signal protein that steers immune response, blood cell growth, fuel use, and organ growth. It can push opposite effects at once, because it signals through two routes, a classic route and a trans route that reaches more cell types.

When IL-6 runs off track, it feeds immune and inflamed diseases, fuel disorders, and cancers. The review maps how IL-6 acts on each main kidney cell type, from filter cells to tube-lining cells. It then sums its roles in kidney ills such as IgA disease, lupus kidney harm, diabetic kidney disease, sudden injury, and long-term kidney failure.
europmc-pmc5408681:
Thomas Tu, Magdalena A. Budzinska, Nicholas A. Shackel, and Stephan Urban review how hepatitis B virus DNA joins host DNA, in a 2017 paper in Viruses. Chronic hepatitis B is a major cause of liver harm and death. Infected cells often hold pieces of virus DNA built into their own chromosomes, even though that form is a dead end for the virus, since it cannot copy itself from there.

Why the joining is so common, how it happens, and what it does are still open questions. The review covers the likely joining machinery, which seems to use the cell's own break-repair tools. Joined DNA may still make virus proteins, which could help the virus persist and may play a part in liver cancer. The authors say this odd habit deserves more study for its bearing on cure efforts.
europmc-pmc5441081:
Hippisley-Cox and co-authors build QRISK3, an updated score for ten-year heart and stroke risk. Their cohort study appeared in The BMJ. Doctors use such scores to target prevention. The old QRISK2 score missed some known risk factors. The team drew on English general practice records. Nearly eight million patients formed the building cohort. A separate 2,700,000 patients formed the test cohort.

Follow-up covered about 51 million person years. It yielded 363,565 new cardiovascular cases. The new score adds several clinical factors. They include migraine, lupus, and severe mental illness. Steroid use and blood pressure swings also count. Kidney disease at stage 3 now counts too. For men, erectile dysfunction adds signal. HIV did not meet the entry bar. The score sorted risk well in testing. Its accuracy matched the older version. The authors say the added factors help doctors spot high-risk patients sooner.
europmc-pmc5460881:
Pipkins and co-authors test whether a germ that causes ear and lung disease needs one gene set to stay harmful. Their study appeared in PLoS ONE. The germ is Streptococcus pneumoniae. It lives in the nose and throat. Strains with a sugar coat cause most severe cases, and vaccines target that coat. Coat-free strains escape those vaccines.

Both kinds carry potABCD, a set of genes that pulls in polyamines. The team deleted one gene, potD, from a coat-free strain and a coated strain. The loss changed key proteins and raised biofilm growth in both. But the coat-free strain still settled in mice and caused ear disease. The coated strain grew weaker. The split guides the hunt for new drug targets.
europmc-pmc5466781:
Tremblay and co-authors report a consensus project that fixed shared definitions for research on sitting and inactivity. Their report appeared in The International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity. The field has grown fast in recent years. Its terms, though, meant different things to different teams. That confusion slows comparison across studies. The Sedentary Behavior Research Network set out to settle the language.

The process began with a review of terms in use. A steering committee drafted definitions for the key ones. Network members then judged the drafts through an online survey. In all, 87 members took part and sent feedback. The final list defines terms such as sedentary behavior, stationary behavior, and physical inactivity. It also covers standing, sitting, reclining, and lying. Screen time and patterns such as bouts and breaks are included. The authors hope the shared terms will standardize work across the field.
europmc-pmc5494581:
Sheng and co-authors present a review in Neural Plasticity on depression and chronic pain. The two disorders often occur together and worsen each other. Up to 85 percent of chronic pain patients face severe depression, studies suggest. Why they link so tightly remains unclear. That gap blocks better care for patients who have both.

Pain and mood share several brain regions, the authors note. The insula, prefrontal cortex, and amygdala serve both systems. Both disorders also involve similar changes in brain wiring and chemistry. Monoamine transmitters feature in each condition. The review closes with drug strategies matched to single patients. Pain drugs and antidepressants may need joint planning.
europmc-pmc5514481:
Cannarile and co-authors present a review in the Journal for ImmunoTherapy of Cancer on blocking the CSF1 receptor in cancer. Macrophages inside tumors often shield them from the immune system. These cells depend on signals through the CSF1 receptor to survive. Drugs that block that receptor are now in clinical trials. Early safety data look favorable, the authors report.

One benign tumor type driven by CSF1 shrank impressively on these drugs. Results for malignant cancers, mostly in drug combinations, are still pending. Macrophage behavior varies sharply by tissue and tumor type. That variety may decide where the strategy works best.
europmc-pmc5518881:
Yao and co-authors report a gene-editing study in Cell Research on inserting DNA with CRISPR. Placing a new gene at an exact genome spot is hard in embryos and tissues. The standard route works only while cells divide. The team devised a hybrid route called HMEJ. It pairs long matching arms with cuts in both donor and genome.

In stem cells the new route matched the standard one, they report. In several other cell types it did better. In mouse and monkey embryos it beat all rival routes by far. Liver cells and neurons in living animals took inserts too. The method suits animal models and gene therapy design.
europmc-pmc5524981:
Byrne and co-authors present a sequencing study in Nature Communications on single B cells. Short-read RNA tools chop transcripts into pieces before reading them. Full message variants, called isoforms, get lost in that shuffle. The team read full-length copies instead with a nanopore device. Mouse B1a immune cells served as the test case.

Thousands of unrecorded start and end sites turned up, they report. Hundreds of splicing events appeared as well. Many genes produced several complex isoforms in the same cell type. Surface receptors that define B cells varied richly between cells. Gene level counts stayed accurate alongside the detail.
europmc-pmc5527481:
Yao and co-authors report a liver cancer study in Molecular Oncology on the ZKSCAN1 gene. This gene produces both a standard linear message and a circular RNA. Circular variants are loop-shaped and poorly understood. The team compared tumor and healthy tissue from 102 patients. Both RNA forms ran low inside the tumors.

Restoring either form slowed cancer cell growth and spread, they report. Silencing them sped those traits up instead. The two forms act through separate routes, though. The linear one steers cell metabolism, the circular one cancer signals. The circular form may mark the disease for diagnosis, they suggest.
europmc-pmc5550281:
Takemura and co-authors present a research article in eLife. They mapped the wiring of a learning center in the adult fruit fly brain. That center, the mushroom body, is where flies form associative memories. The map covers one lobe of the structure in full.

Using fine electron microscope images, the team rebuilt all 983 neurons in three units of the lobe. They traced each cell's shape and synaptic links. Kenyon cells, which encode sensory input, connect widely to output neurons. Some output cells sample all inputs, while others favor one sense. The team also found two unexpected synapse classes tied to dopamine cells. Readers get a complete circuit map for studying how memories form.
europmc-pmc5574081:
Watson and co-authors review classroom-based movement programs in the International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity. Many children fall short of daily activity targets. Class time is tight, so teachers fold movement into lessons or add short active breaks. The fear is lost learning time.

The review found 39 studies in primary schools. Sixteen fed the pooled analysis. Movement in class improved on-task behavior and cut off-task behavior. Gains in school achievement showed when progress tools tracked them. No clear effect appeared for thinking skills or total activity levels. Studies varied a lot in design and measures. The authors urge care in picking outcomes and firm activity checks. Readers see movement as a help, not a threat, to class work.
europmc-pmc5622781:
Markowiak and Śliżewska review probiotics, prebiotics, and synbiotics in Nutrients. The gut hosts a dense microbial ecosystem. Its friendly members make nutrients, block pathogens, and tune immunity. Diet can shift that balance on purpose.

Probiotics add live, selected microbes in set doses. Prebiotics feed the resident good microbes instead. Synbiotics combine the two in one product. Sources range from fermented foods to capsules. The review explains how each class is thought to work. It then checks trial results across many conditions. Gut disorders and allergic disease show the firmest gains. Studies also report help with obesity and type 2 diabetes. Fatty liver and immune support appear as well. Effects depend on strain and dose. Readers get a grounded survey of a crowded health aisle.
europmc-pmc5632781:
Kessler and co-authors review trauma and post-traumatic stress disorder in a psychiatry journal. The work draws on the WHO World Mental Health Surveys. Those surveys covered 24 countries and 68,894 respondents. People were asked about 29 kinds of lifetime trauma. PTSD was checked for both the worst trauma and a random one. That design avoids the bias of studying only worst events.

The authors report that 70.4 percent had lived through a trauma. Exposure averaged 3.2 traumas per person. Violent traumas between people carried the highest PTSD risk. Rape and other sexual assault caused a large share of total burden. So did stalking and the sudden death of a loved one. Past trauma also raised the risk of later trauma and PTSD. The findings show how unevenly this burden falls.
europmc-pmc5655781:
Schirrmeister and co-authors test deep neural networks for decoding EEG signals. Their research article appeared in Human Brain Mapping. EEG decoding usually needs handcrafted features. The team trained convolutional networks on raw signals. They varied network designs and training methods. Tasks were imagined or executed movements.

Modern training tricks improved the networks. Batch normalization and cropped training helped most. Mean accuracy reached about 84 percent. That matched or beat a standard filter bank method. New visualization tools showed what networks learned. They used spectral power in key frequency bands. The tools mapped where features mattered. The authors say the approach needs no manual feature design. It also supports EEG-based brain mapping.
europmc-pmc5701281:
