Aghaeepour and co-authors describe an immune clock that tracks human pregnancy. Their research article appeared in Science Immunology. Pregnancy needs finely tuned immune changes. The team measured immune cells in blood samples. Samples came from women across pregnancy. Mass cytometry quantified cell types and responses.

A new regression method modeled the timing. The model captured pregnancy chronology accurately. It was validated on new samples prospectively. Known biology appeared among its parts. New findings emerged as well. One pathway, IL-2 driven STAT5 signaling, stood out. It shapes T cell function in pregnancy. The authors say the clock can flag deviations. Such flags may help predict pregnancy complications.
europmc-pmc5720881:
Steele and co-authors report United States trends in cancers linked to overweight and obesity. The report is a CDC Vital Signs study of national cancer data. It covers the 13 cancer types that a world cancer agency ties to excess body fat.

In 2014, about 631,000 people got one of these cancers. That was 40% of all cancers found that year. Rates were higher in women than men and rose with age. Leaving out colorectal cancer, rates rose for ages 20 to 74 and in 32 states. The authors urge broad action to help people reach a healthy weight. Such steps, they argue, could cut the load of these cancers over time.
europmc-pmc5751581:
Ogden and co-authors report how adult obesity in the United States varied by income and schooling. Their report uses data from a national health survey for 2011 to 2014. Adults were grouped by household income and by highest level of schooling. Measured height and weight set each person's body mass index.

Obesity was less common in the highest income group than in the lower groups. College graduates also showed lower rates than adults with less schooling. The report notes that these patterns did not hold for every sex and racial group. It calls for more progress toward national goals to cut obesity and close gaps.
europmc-pmc5770781:
Ma and co-authors study how autophagy, the cell's recycling system, shapes aging in bone stem cells. These marrow stem cells lose balance with age, making less bone and more fat. The team compared young and aged cells from mice. They also tested drugs that block or boost autophagy.

Autophagy ran far lower in aged cells, they report. Blocking it made young cells act old, with weaker growth and bone making. Boosting it with rapamycin partly restored aged cells. The path runs through reactive oxygen and the protein p53. In live aged mice, boosting autophagy eased bone loss.
europmc-pmc5809481:
Lim and co-authors pool community studies of depression across 30 nations. Depression is the most common mental health condition. Its measured rate shifts with place and method. The team asks how common it truly was from 1994 to 2014.

Their meta-analysis joins 90 studies and over 1.1 million adults. Point prevalence came to 12.9 percent, one-year rates to 7.2 percent, and lifetime rates to 10.8 percent. Rates ran higher in women and in self-report studies. Publication years and response rates also shifted results. Readers get a benchmark for judging depression counts across eras and nations.
europmc-pmc5811581:
Robson and co-authors guide readers through visual electrodiagnostic tests. These painless tests record the eye's electric replies to light. Each test probes a different cell type or layer. Results help doctors pin down where vision fails.

The guide comes from ISCEV, the field's world society. It covers the full-field and pattern electroretinogram. It also covers the multifocal test, the electrooculogram, and evoked potentials. Basic principles come first, then common symptoms and case examples. Suggested work-ups show which test fits which complaint. Readers get a primer on the standard tests of eye function.
europmc-pmc5870681:
Hassani and co-authors review microbial interactions within the plant holobiont. Their article appeared in Microbiome. A holobiont pairs a plant with all its resident microbes. Plants and microbes have evolved together for 450 million years. Host effects alone do not explain these communities. Microbes also compete and cooperate with each other. Those ties shape life in roots, leaves, and inner tissues.

The authors draw on lab studies and whole-community work. They show how microbe-microbe ties set community structure. Such ties also help keep the host healthy and balanced. Simple lab systems revealed tactics of single microbes. Field context remains much less clear, they note. Their framework stresses ties among microbes as a core force.
europmc-pmc5928581:
Farhy-Tselnicker and Allen give a tripartite view of cortical circuit development. Their review appeared in Neural Development. Cortex neurons form layered circuits with precise connections. Correct wiring in development is vital for brain function. Astrocytes, a major glial cell type, guide that process. Synapses begin forming only after astrocytes appear.

The review aligns timelines for neurons and astrocytes in rodents. It covers how astrocyte contact shapes each synapse. Synapse-linked proteins help build distinct circuit types. Astrocytes were once seen as mere support cells. Their active role in formation and function is now clear. Readers get a joint account of all three partners.
europmc-pmc5964481:
Azad and co-authors overview probiotic species used to modulate the gut microbiota. Their review appeared in BioMed Research International. Probiotics are live microbial strains that benefit health. Interest in using them to shape gut microbes has surged. The gut is a complex mix of host cells, microbes, and nutrients. Its microbes guard against many degenerative diseases through immune effects.

The review covers Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species in depth. Other bacteria and Saccharomyces yeasts also feature. Their roles span obesity, diabetes, cancer, and liver disease. Inflammatory bowel disease is covered as well. The authors close with how gut communities might be altered next.
europmc-pmc5979581:
Vurukonda, Giovanardi, and Stefani review Streptomyces germs that live in plants, boost growth, and fight plant disease. Their review was published in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Spraying crops with chemicals takes heavy doses of fungus killers. Germs often learn to resist those sprays in time. Friendly microbes offer a safer path for farming. Streptomyces kinds settle plant tissue from roots to shoots.

These germs make germ-killing drugs and scents, the authors note. That output makes them strong foes of fungi and germs that harm plants. They also help crops grow in many fields. Such traits suit them as living plant food that lifts yields. The review sets out these roles and their promise.
europmc-pmc6003181:
Shimabukuro-Vornhagen and co-authors review cytokine release syndrome, a dangerous side effect of modern cancer immunotherapy. Their review appeared in the Journal for Immunotherapy of Cancer. Potent new treatments have transformed cancer care this decade. Checkpoint drugs and engineered T cells work remarkably well. Yet they can trigger a whole-body inflammatory storm. That storm can prove fatal if missed. The term dates to an early anti-T-cell antibody drug.

The review covers how the syndrome develops mechanistically. Risk factors, symptoms, and look-alike conditions are laid out. Prognostic signs that warn of severe courses are covered. Practical guidance for managing patients follows the evidence.
europmc-pmc6075881:
Rådholm and co-authors examine canagliflozin's effects on heart failure in type 2 diabetes. Their analysis appeared in Circulation. It draws on the CANVAS Program trials. The drug blocks a kidney glucose transporter called SGLT2. Heart failure is a major killer in diabetes.

The drug cut a range of heart failure outcomes. Benefits looked larger in patients with prior heart failure. Those patients showed no extra adverse event burden. Gains appeared on top of standard heart failure care. The authors argue that at-risk patients benefit most. Readers get detailed outcome evidence from a large trial program. It supports planning treatment for diabetic heart risk.
europmc-pmc6090881:
Kerksick and co-authors update the International Society of Sports Nutrition review on exercise and diet. Their update appeared in the society's journal. Sports nutrition papers now number in the thousands each year. The review first appeared in 2004 and was refreshed in 2010. This version centers on muscle growth and performance.

It explains how supplements are defined and regulated in the United States. It teaches readers to judge supplement claims. General fueling and recovery strategies follow. Each common supplement then gets an evidence grade. Grades run from strong support to little or none. Safety is weighed beside effect. Readers get a reference for training and diet choices.
europmc-pmc6099181:
Abel and co-authors review natural killer cells from birth to bedside. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. NK cells are innate lymphocytes that kill tumor and virus-infected cells. They need no prior exposure to act. Special receptors teach them self from non-self.

Common gamma chain cytokines guide their development. IL-2, IL-7, and IL-15 lead that group. Inflammatory cytokines prime their killing programs too. NK cells share more traits with adaptive lymphocytes than once thought. Their unique signaling offers handles for genetic tuning. Donor and engineered NK cells now reach clinics. Readers get a full path from development to therapy.
europmc-pmc6127081:
Ji and co-authors present a research article in Oncogene on a nutrient transporter in lung cancer. Many tumors crave extra glucose, cystine, or glutamine. A transporter called xCT brings cystine into cells. Smoking can raise its levels in mouth cancer cells.

The team found xCT high in non-small cell lung cancer tissue. High levels tracked with late stage and worse five-year survival. A drug that blocks xCT slowed cancer cell growth and invasion. It worked in lab dishes and in animals. Normal airway cells forced to make extra xCT grew hooked on glutamine. The authors name xCT as a treatment target.
europmc-pmc6175981:
Kocaturk and Gozuacik wrote a review in Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology on crosstalk between the cell's two recycling systems. Autophagy and the ubiquitin-proteasome system keep cells clean and balanced. Both use ubiquitin tags to mark cargo for destruction. They were long studied as separate machines.

The review contrasts their usual loads. The proteasome handles short-lived and soluble misfolded proteins. Autophagy clears long-lived proteins, clumps, whole organelles, and even invading bacteria. Recent work shows the two systems regulate each other. Signals pass both ways, and each can compensate when the other falters. The authors gather this evidence into one account of how the systems cooperate.
europmc-pmc6272781:
Shanmugam and co-authors review curcumin's many sided attack on cancer. Their review appeared in Molecules. Cancer deaths have barely moved despite better treatments. Current drugs often carry heavy side effects and high costs. Curcumin, from turmeric, has been studied for decades as a gentler option. Lab work shows it can slow cancer start, growth, and spread.

Curcumin tamps down many cancer driving signals at once. It lowers growth factors, inflammatory signals, and key protein switches. It also stalls cell division and pushes cancer cells toward death. Tumours of many types have been tested. The review maps each target in turn. It notes that human proof still lags behind lab proof. Delivery and dose remain the main hurdles. The authors argue the breadth of action justifies continued trials.
europmc-pmc6273481:
Pulido-Moran and co-authors review curcumin and its effects across many diseases. Their review appeared in Molecules. Curcumin is the main polyphenol in turmeric root. It has been used as a medical herb in Asia for centuries. Modern tests link it to heart, brain, and cancer benefits. It also shows effects in metabolic and liver disorders.

Poor uptake in the body limits what swallowed curcumin can do. New forms and changed molecules aim to fix that gap. The review covers origin, uptake, and recent derivative work. Disease by disease, the evidence is weighed. Cancer, heart disease, and metabolic syndrome get the fullest treatment. Antioxidant and anti-inflammatory actions run through all of them. The authors see curcumin as a strong nutraceutical candidate. Better delivery may turn that promise into real gains.
europmc-pmc6300481:
Cassini and co-authors estimate the health burden of antibiotic-resistant infections in Europe. Their modelling study appeared in The Lancet Infectious Diseases. It covers the EU and European Economic Area in 2015. The team studied 16 resistance and bacterium pairings. Surveillance data came from the EARS-Net network.

They estimate about 672,000 such infections in that year. Most were linked to health care settings. These infections caused an estimated 33,110 deaths. They also cost about 875,000 years of healthy life. Burden was highest in infants and older adults. Italy and Greece carried the largest shares. The authors say the burden has grown since 2007.
europmc-pmc6323981:
Tong and co-authors present TransmiR v2.0, a database of transcription factor and microRNA regulation. The article appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. MicroRNAs tune gene activity after transcription. Their own control often goes wrong in disease. The database maps which factors switch which microRNAs. Curators extracted 3,730 such links from 1,349 reports.

Those reports came from over 8,000 publications surveyed. Chip sequencing data added over 1.7 million tissue-specific links. Coverage spans 19 species in total. A predict module estimates human links from binding motifs. A network module draws the links for any factor. Users can view disease-specific networks too. An enrichment tool finds likely regulators of a microRNA list.
europmc-pmc6386581:
Neurohr and co-authors report a research article in Cell on cell size and aging. Cells of one type keep a tight size range, but why that matters was unclear. The team grew yeast and mammal cells past their normal size and watched what failed.

Oversized cells could not make proteins and nucleic acids fast enough for their volume. Their contents were in effect diluted. Gene responses, cell division, and signals all weakened. DNA became the limiting factor as size grew. Aging cells are large, the authors note. Dilution may thus be one cause of cell senescence.
europmc-pmc6536981:
Rudra and co-authors report outcomes for inoperable pancreatic cancer treated with MRI-guided radiation, writing in Cancer Medicine. The method adapts each dose to daily scans, pushing more dose into the tumor while sparing gut tissue nearby. The team reviewed 44 patients treated at five centers, grouped by the dose they received.

Patients who got escalated doses lived longer. Two-year survival was 49% in the high-dose group against 30% at standard dose, and local control also leaned their way. Distant spread did not differ between groups, though, and the edge faded in deeper statistical checks. Severe gut side effects struck three standard-dose patients and none in the high-dose group. The authors call for a prospective trial.
europmc-pmc6549181:
Shi, Nabar, Huang and Kehrl dissect what one small SARS virus protein does inside cells, writing in Cell Death Discovery. The protein, ORF8b, is an accessory piece of the SARS coronavirus. Earlier work hinted it gathers into clumps. The team traced what those clumps set off.

ORF8b forms stubborn aggregates that hinge on a single valine in its tail. The clumps strain the cell's folding and recycling systems, and wake a master switch for cleanup genes. In lung-type cells they bring death, eased when clumping is blocked. In macrophages, ORF8b binds the sensor NLRP3 directly and fires its inflammasome, releasing IL-1β and causing bursting death. Cells without NLRP3 still die, through stress and failing mitochondria.
europmc-pmc6600381:
Cofano and co-authors review stem cell therapy for spinal cord injury. Their article appears in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. No standard cure exists for the lasting nerve damage that follows such injuries. Mesenchymal stem cells are easy to gather and store. That ease has made them a leading candidate for repair.

The review first explains primary and secondary injury in the cord. Secondary damage spreads through inflammation, vessel changes, and cell death. The authors then survey how mesenchymal stem cells might calm that cascade. Animal studies raised high hopes. Human trials, though, gave weak and mixed results. The review ends with limits to fix and paths for better trials.
europmc-pmc6642581:
Kalil and Thomas review influenza as a cause of critical illness. Their review appears in Critical Care. The virus infects the airway lining directly. Immune responses then add further lung damage. Gas exchange fails through several routes at once. Airway blockage, alveolar loss, and matrix breakdown all contribute. About 30 to 40 percent of hospitalised flu patients develop pneumonia. The very young, the elderly, and the immunocompromised face higher risk.

Secondary bacterial infection often follows the virus. Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pneumoniae lead that list. Flu also predisposes patients to sepsis and ARDS. Pregnancy and obesity raise ARDS risk independently. Vaccination and female sex appear protective. The authors urge broad suspicion in intensive care each winter.
europmc-pmc6700281:
The Genetic Modifiers of Huntington's Disease Consortium reports that CAG repeat length, not polyglutamine length, sets onset timing. Their study appears in Cell. Huntington's onset correlates with the expanded repeat. The field assumed encoded polyglutamine length was to blame. Rare people carry glutamine-encoding CAA interruptions. Their genotyping separates DNA length from protein length. Onset tracked the unbroken CAG tract instead. Genome-wide analysis covered over 9,000 patients. DNA upkeep genes shifted onset timing. Some modifier effects were sex-specific. No link appeared with HTT activity variants.

The key trait looks like a tendency to grow. Repeat growth in tissues likely drives timing. The premise of polyglutamine diseases is questioned. Slowing that growth becomes a treatment target.
europmc-pmc6722781:
Ravindran and co-authors review neutrophil extracellular traps, or NETs. Neutrophils are front-line white blood cells. They can cast out webs of DNA dressed with germ-killing peptides. These traps catch microbes, but they also figure in diseases from cystic fibrosis to cancer.

The review sorts the ways traps form. Some routes need the enzyme NADPH oxidase, others do not, and some let the cell survive. Internal signals, blood acidity, and crowding all steer which path is taken. Mitochondria and gene activity help loosen the DNA for release. Drugs that block these steps are under study. The authors weigh the traps' benefits against their harms.
europmc-pmc6737581:
Hendriksen and co-authors review how genomics tracks antimicrobial resistance worldwide. Cheap, fast DNA sequencing has reshaped how labs detect drug-resistant microbes. Software tools and online databases make that tracking possible. The review counts at least 47 free resources for finding resistance genes in sequence data.

The tools differ in the data they accept and the search method they use. Mapping and alignment approaches each have strengths and limits in sensitivity. Two resources stand out in common use. The authors argue the databases need global harmonization, like general sequence archives. Labs should also join proficiency testing, so resistance calls stay trustworthy for surveillance and care.
europmc-pmc6830681:
Beard and co-authors test a World Health Organization idea about ageing, in BMJ Open. The WHO sums up a person's built-in physical and mental resources as intrinsic capacity. The question is whether that single idea holds together in real data. It should also predict who will later need care.

The team modelled health measures from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing. The study covered 2,560 people aged over 60 years. Their analysis found one general capacity factor, with sensible sub-parts. People with chronic conditions scored lower, and dementia cut scores most. Low capacity also foretold later dependence in daily activities. The authors judge the concept sound and useful.
europmc-pmc6864381:
Williams and co-authors review how discrimination affects health, in Health Services Research. The question is whether being treated unfairly because of race makes people sick. The authors gathered reviews and meta-analyses published from January 2013 to 2019. Twenty-nine studies met their criteria. They span both United States and international data.

Across them, adults who reported more discrimination had worse mental health. They also showed poorer physical markers, including early signs of disease before symptoms start. Health behaviours, use of care, and sticking to treatment all suffered as well. Evidence on stress hormones such as cortisol was mixed. The authors present discrimination as a measurable driver of health gaps.
europmc-pmc6927181:
Hafemeister and Satija present a new way to clean single-cell RNA data. Their methods article appeared in Genome Biology. Cell-to-cell counts vary for technical reasons. Chief among them is sequencing depth per cell. Such noise can mask real biological differences.

Their fix uses regularized negative binomial regression. Cell depth enters the model as a covariate. Pearson residuals then remove the technical influence. Pooling genes of similar abundance steadies the estimates. That step stops the model from overfitting sparse data. The method needs no pseudocounts or log transforms. It improves gene selection, dimension reduction, and expression tests. It ships as sctransform, an R package linked to Seurat.
europmc-pmc7069981:
Choi and co-authors uncover a brain cleanup service in Nature Communications. Microglia keep the brain tidy by removing debris. The protein alpha-synuclein, released by neurons, is a suspect in Parkinson's and related diseases when it misfolds and piles up. Whether microglia can clear the released protein, and how, was the open question behind this study.

Neuron-released alpha-synuclein switches microglia on. The microglia swallow the protein into autophagosomes, self-digesting pouches, and destroy it through a selective form of autophagy the authors name synucleinphagy. The process needs the microglial receptor TLR4, which drives output of p62, a tag that gathers the protein into clusters marked for disposal. In mice expressing human alpha-synuclein, breaking microglial autophagy let misfolded protein build up and killed midbrain dopamine neurons, the very cells lost in Parkinson's disease. The pathway offers a protective mechanism that future therapies might strengthen.
europmc-pmc7074281:
Tang and co-authors estimate the transmission risk of the new coronavirus in the Journal of Clinical Medicine. A basic reproduction number tells planners how far and fast an outbreak can run and how hard interventions must bite. The team built a deterministic compartment model following the disease's clinical stages, people's epidemiological states, and control measures.

Fitted to early data, the model put the control reproduction number as high as 6.47, with a confidence interval from 5.71 to 7.23, implying vigorous spread without action. Sensitivity analysis showed intense contact tracing, quarantine, and isolation can pull that number down. Wuhan's travel restriction, judged by its effect in Beijing, counted about as much as a large increase in quarantine. Under the most restrictive measures the model expected a peak within about two weeks. The authors stress judging the costly Chinese measures on evidence, and deciding carefully how long to sustain them.
europmc-pmc7080981:
Gowen and co-authors examine the hurdles facing a cell-free therapy in Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology. Mesenchymal stem cells are the most studied stem cells in medicine, and much of their benefit seems to come from what they secrete. Chief among them are extracellular vesicles, nano-sized pouches that shuttle biomolecules between cells. Vesicles from these stem cells show regenerative and anti-inflammatory effects.

Swapping cells for vesicles promises advantages: a higher safety profile, lower immune reaction, passage across biological barriers, and no risks of stray tumours, lung entrapment, or rejection that live cells carry. Preclinical results encourage the idea. Clinical use, though, must first settle production, counting and characterising methods, and delivery in the body. The review works through each challenge in turn. Its verdict: the rationale is strong, but manufacturing and measurement discipline will decide whether vesicle therapy reaches patients.
europmc-pmc7096581:
Csapo, Gumpenberger, and Wessner wrote a narrative review on the extracellular matrix of skeletal muscle, in Frontiers in Physiology. Muscle fibers sit in a scaffold of collagens, glycoproteins, proteoglycans, and elastin. That scaffold was long treated as inert packing.

The review covers the makeup and structure of the matrix, and the pathways that remodel it. It explains roles in muscle growth, repair, and force transfer. It also covers harm from aging and diseases such as diabetes, plus changes from training and disuse. Readers get a case for studying this overlooked tissue beside the muscle cells themselves.
europmc-pmc7105881:
Wang and co-authors review subunit vaccines against the emerging human coronaviruses, in Frontiers in Microbiology. Three such viruses, SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and the new 2019-nCoV, have caused severe disease in people. No vaccine against any of them had yet been approved for human use.

Subunit vaccines use single viral proteins rather than the whole virus. Most designs target the spike protein or its receptor-binding domain. Others use spike fragments or different structural proteins. The review sets out the structure and role of each key protein, and the factors that make a subunit vaccine work well. Readers get a design guide meant to speed vaccines against the new virus, and against future coronaviruses with pandemic risk.
europmc-pmc7139981:
Andreeva and co-authors report the 2020 update of the SCOP database, which sorts known protein structures, in Nucleic Acids Research. SCOP groups protein domains into families by their shapes and evolutionary links. This update greatly expands coverage toward sorting nearly all superfamilies that have a known structure.

The sorting is built largely by hand, through expert inspection, and then extended by software to related entries. The team also improved the database design, added a programming interface, and modernised the website. It is the largest coverage jump since SCOP 1.75. Protein scientists use the resource, kept at Cambridge, to find proteins shaped like the ones they study.
europmc-pmc7234781:
Rogers and co-authors review the mental and brain effects of severe coronavirus infections. Their analysis appeared in The Lancet Psychiatry. Two earlier outbreaks frame the work: SARS from 2002 and MERS from 2012. The team searched medical and preprint databases into April 2020. They pooled studies of psychiatric and neuropsychiatric symptoms across all three diseases.

During acute illness, confusion and mood changes were commonly reported. After recovery, post-traumatic stress, depression, and anxiety featured in survivors of SARS and MERS. Female sex raised the odds of post-traumatic stress in one SARS analysis. Early COVID-19 reports suggested a similar pattern forming. The authors urge planners to expect a mental health tail to the pandemic. Their comparison helps services prepare for it.
europmc-pmc7236181:
Guo and co-authors show that an RNA-editing enzyme called ALKBH5 holds back pancreatic cancer. Their study appeared in Molecular Cancer. ALKBH5 removes m6A marks, the most common reversible edit on messenger RNA. Such marks shape how tumors grow. The team measured the enzyme's levels and effects in patient groups and cancer cells.

Raising ALKBH5 slowed cancer cell growth sharply. Cells formed fewer colonies and stalled before division. Removing the enzyme had the opposite effect. In mice, extra ALKBH5 curbed tumor growth in both flank and pancreatic models. The enzyme works by activating a gene called PER1, a clock gene. That activation depends on a reader protein, YTHDF2, spotting the m6A marks. The pathway offers a new angle on a stubborn cancer.
europmc-pmc7240781:
Lightman and co-authors review how the stress hormone system releases ACTH and cortisol in pulses. Their article appeared in Endocrine Reviews. The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis steers the body's stress response. Its main output, cortisol in humans, follows a daily rhythm. That rhythm is not smooth; it is built from pulses of varying size.

A pulse generator below the hypothalamus drives those bursts, recent work shows. The adrenal gland itself holds a regulatory network that shapes the signal. Immune alarm signals can act straight on the gland to raise output. Cortisol then switches off the very genes that raised the alarm. The authors draw out what this timing means for disease. Hormone replacement and drug timing may need to copy the pulses, not flatten them.
europmc-pmc7264181:
Murciano-Goroff, Warner and Wolchok look ahead to combination immunotherapies that reshape the tumor microenvironment. Their review appeared in Cell Research. Immunotherapy can produce lasting responses in cancer, yet only a minority of patients benefit today. Resistance comes from the tumor itself and from the tissue and immune cells around it.

The authors sort new approaches into two groups. One modifies the tumor directly. The other changes the microenvironment around it so immune attack becomes more likely. By working through the known causes of resistance one by one, they identify drug pairings with a clear biological rationale. The goal is to turn more non-responders into responders without guessing at combinations.
europmc-pmc7273381:
Dall'Ora and co-authors review what theory and research say about burnout among nurses. Their theoretical review appeared in Human Resources for Health. Workforce studies often name burnout as an outcome without defining it clearly. The team searched three databases for quantitative studies linking burnout to work factors in nursing.

Ninety-one papers qualified, most of them cross-sectional. High workload, low control over the job, poor social climate, low rewards, and a mismatch between personal and workplace values all predicted burnout, matching Maslach's theory. Long shifts of 12 hours or more, time pressure, role conflict, and low staffing also contributed. Burnout was linked to worse general health and sickness absence. Effects on staff turnover were less clear than theory predicts.
europmc-pmc7285581:
Yin and co-authors review triple-negative breast cancer, a subtype lacking the three receptors most treatments target. Their review appeared in Breast Cancer Research. These tumors express no estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, or HER2. Without those targets, hormone therapy and HER2 drugs do not work, and no standard regimen exists.

The subtype is aggressive, with high invasiveness, strong spread, frequent relapse, and poor prognosis. Researchers have split it into molecular subtypes with different weaknesses. The authors summarize current treatments and drug results subtype by subtype, then review new preclinical work and targeted regimens in development. Their aim is to give clinicians and researchers fresh directions for a disease where new treatment strategies are an urgent need.
europmc-pmc7299281:
Brouwer and co-authors isolate hundreds of antibodies from recovered COVID-19 patients and map where they strike the virus. Their study appeared in Science. From three convalescent patients, the team obtained 403 monoclonal antibodies. The patients had mounted strong responses against the spike protein, the structure the virus uses to bind host cells.

A subset of the antibodies could neutralize the virus. Competition tests and electron microscopy showed they target many different sites, called epitopes, across the spike. The two most potent antibodies aimed at the domain that grips the host receptor. Knowing several vulnerable sites, rather than one, helps designers of antibody drugs and vaccines choose targets the virus cannot easily change.
europmc-pmc7343781:
Song and co-authors compare immune profiles in mild and severe COVID-19 in Nature Communications. Why some patients crash while others stay mild was a pressing early question. The team measured immune cells and inflammatory signals in both groups.

Severe cases showed deeper losses of helper and killer T cells and of natural killer cells. The T cells that remained were overactivated, carried high levels of blocking molecules, and in killer cells loaded up on toxic weapon proteins. Lung tissue from one patient who died held virus RNA plus dense infiltration by T cells and macrophages. The authors argue that this misdirected activation helps drive severe disease, and that immune targets offer a promising treatment route.
europmc-pmc7441381:
Fahed and co-authors test whether broad genetic background changes the risk from single strong gene variants. They studied 80,928 people with variants tied to three tier 1 conditions. The conditions were familial high cholesterol, hereditary breast and ovarian cancer, and Lynch syndrome.

Among variant carriers, polygenic background split risk widely. By age 75 years, coronary artery disease risk ranged from 17% to 78% across background levels. Breast cancer risk ranged from 13% to 76%, and colon cancer from 11% to 80%. One gene variant alone thus gives a rough forecast, not a firm one. The authors argue that adding polygenic scores would sharpen risk estimates. That could guide screening and care for carriers and their families.
europmc-pmc7582481:
Browne and co-authors review the clinical potential of antimicrobial peptides. Drug resistance is a growing threat to global health. The standard antibiotic pipeline has largely run dry.

Peptides occur in all forms of life. They play a key role in innate immunity. Many are conserved through evolution over long spans. Resistance to them appears less likely to develop. Chemical changes can raise activity and stability. They can also cut toxicity for patients. The review covers how peptides kill microbes. Synthetic mimics and their design are discussed. Products on the market and in trials are listed for readers.
europmc-pmc7647981:
Zhao, Song, Liu, Song and Yi review methods for mapping chemical modifications of DNA and RNA. Over 17 types are known in DNA so far. RNA holds over 160 types of such marks.

These marks shape development, aging and cancer risk. New fields study them as epigenomics and epitranscriptomics. Better detection tools have sped work in both fields. The review covers high-throughput methods for finding marks. It also covers the biology those methods revealed. Third-generation sequencing gets its own focus here. Such methods read long molecules one at a time. They can detect marks direct on DNA and RNA. Open questions for the field close the review. The authors stress tool building as the driver of progress.
europmc-pmc7688081:
Schrage and co-authors study a support strategy for patients in cardiogenic shock. The patients were on VA-ECMO, a machine that takes over heart and lung work. This support raises pressure in the left ventricle, which can slow heart recovery. Unloading that chamber with a pump may help.

The study covered 686 patients across many centers worldwide. Use of left ventricular unloading linked to lower death rates. It also linked to more complications, such as severe bleeding and limb blood flow problems. The authors back the approach but call for a randomized trial to prove the benefit and weigh the risks.
europmc-pmc7739981:
Wilson and co-authors report US drug overdose deaths for 2017 and 2018. It uses national death records and splits deaths by drug type. Opioids drove about two thirds of overdose deaths in 2017. The team tracked how each opioid class moved over one year.

Drug overdose deaths fell 4.1% in 2018, to 67,367. Of these, 46,802, or 69.5%, involved an opioid. Deaths from prescription opioids fell 13.5%, and heroin deaths fell 4.1%. But deaths from synthetic opioids rose 10%, likely driven by illicit fentanyl. The authors urge stronger surveillance, naloxone access, and treatment links. In 2017, there were 70,237 drug overdose deaths in the United States in total.
europmc-pmc7900181:
Xiang and co-authors present a review of tumour-associated macrophages as partners for cancer immunotherapy. Immunotherapy has raised hopes for advanced cancers, but responses vary widely between patients. Macrophages that gather in tumours often track with poor outcomes and weak response to treatment. The review examines their role in detail.

The authors summarise how these macrophages shape the response to checkpoint drugs. They also cover tumour vaccines and adoptive cell transfer. In each case, macrophages can help or hinder the therapy. The review then surveys ways to target them. Options include blocking their recruitment, removing them, or reprogramming them to fight the tumour. The authors argue that such steps could lift the reach of current immunotherapies. The review maps a fast-growing route to stronger cancer care.
europmc-pmc7937881:
Dijksteel and co-authors present a review of lessons from clinical trials of antimicrobial peptides. These peptides are part of the body's own defence against yeast, fungi, viruses, and bacteria. They kill microbes by tearing their outer membranes in a broad, non-specific way. That style of attack may explain why resistance to them stays rare. Yet very few have reached clinical use.

The gap between promise and practice frames the review. The authors first set out the case for peptides as stand-ins for antibiotics. They then examine why trials so often fall short. Trial design, dosing, and patient choice all come under review. Strategies to raise the success rate close the account. The authors argue the field can learn from its failures. With antibiotic resistance rising, those lessons carry real weight.
europmc-pmc8167181:
Atcha and co-authors test how the force-sensing channel Piezo1 shapes macrophage behaviour. Macrophages shift roles during immune defence and repair. How tissue stiffness steers them was less clear.

Macrophages lacking Piezo1 showed less inflammation and better wound healing responses. A calcium reporter showed that calcium entry depends on Piezo1. Stiff surfaces raised that calcium flow and changed cell function. Soluble signals tuned the effect further. The study ties a single channel to how immune cells feel their setting. It hints at ways to calm harmful inflammation. The channel also helps macrophages sense how stiff their surroundings are.
europmc-pmc8190181:
Wu and co-authors examine signals in cancer-associated fibroblasts and how to target them. Tumours lean on their surroundings, and these fibroblasts sit at the centre. They reshape matrix, feed tumour growth, and blunt immune attack.

The review maps the signal web between fibroblasts and cancer cells. Paths covered include transforming growth factor-beta, PI3K/AKT, Wnt, and JAK routes. Fibroblasts also drive spread, invasion, and drug resistance. Their mixed nature makes them hard targets. The authors weigh drug strategies aimed at these paths. Better aim could loosen the tumour's support system. Each pathway offers a point where drugs might cut in.
europmc-pmc8265181:
Pang and co-authors introduce MetaboAnalyst 5.0 for metabolomics data analysis. The platform has served the field for over a decade. This release aims to close the gap from raw spectra to insight.

Three new modules carry that aim. A spectra processing module automates settings and can resume stopped runs. A functional analysis module widens the old peaks-to-pathways path. It now serves all organism types the platform covers. High-resolution mass spectrometry data sit at the centre. Lower barriers should let more labs finish full analyses unaided. A third module rounds out the release's coverage.
europmc-pmc8300981:
Đorđević and co-authors survey hurdles that slow nanomedicines on the path to the clinic. Nanomedicine shapes drug delivery, diagnostics, and regenerative care. Its growth now meets unclear, scattered regulation.

The review names the traits a product must prove for safety and effect. It covers physical, chemical, and biological test methods. Key process parameters and preclinical steps follow. Early-stage developers get a map of what regulators will ask. Translation fails often at these seams, not in the lab idea. Clearer guidance could lift the whole field, the authors argue. Guidance gaps are named as a fixable cause.
europmc-pmc8352781:
Rothgangl and co-authors use adenine base editing of PCSK9 to cut cholesterol in primates. Most harmful point mutations swap one letter pair for another. Adenine editors can repair such swaps directly.

Lipid particles carried editor mRNA into the liver. A guide RNA aimed it at PCSK9, a brake on cholesterol clearance. Editing reached up to 67% in mice and 34% in macaques. Blood PCSK9 fell 95% in mice and 32% in macaques. LDL cholesterol fell 58% and 14% in step. The editor cleared fast, and no off-target edits were found. One dose gave lasting change.
europmc-pmc8484581:
Liu and co-authors probe how complete the cell membrane coating on mimic nanoparticles really is. Such coated particles can dodge the immune system and home to set cells. The coating's wholeness is a key quality mark, yet it had gone mostly unchecked.

Their fluorescence test showed that up to 90 percent of the particles were only partly coated. This defies the common faith in perfect coating. Partly coated particles could still enter target cells in lab tests. Computer models joined with lab work revealed the entry routes. Well-coated particles entered one by one. Poorly coated ones had to clump together first. The method aids smarter design.
europmc-pmc8519781:
Payne and co-authors compare standard and extended dosing gaps for the BNT162b2 mRNA vaccine. The United Kingdom stretched the gap to speed first-dose coverage. Trial data for that choice were lacking at the time. A study of UK health workers filled the gap.

The first dose guarded against the Alpha variant over several weeks. In a substudy of 589 people, one dose raised blocking antibodies and lasting B and T cell responses. Antibody levels ran higher after the longer gap of 6 to 14 weeks than after 3 to 4 weeks. Past infection sped and boosted the response. The authors call the extended gap an effective protocol.
europmc-pmc8764781:
Choudhary and Satija compare statistical error models for single-cell RNA sequencing data. Variation in such data mixes real cell differences with technical noise. Count models help split the two, but no consensus picks one model. The team analyzed 59 datasets across technologies, systems, and depths.

A Poisson model fit sparse datasets well. For genes with deeper coverage, counts spread wider than Poisson allows in every system. A negative binomial model was needed there. The extra spread varied a lot by dataset and gene level. The authors advise estimating model settings from the data itself. Their guidance targets teams that build preprocessing workflows.
europmc-pmc9184281:
Mirdita and co-authors present ColabFold, a tool that makes protein folding prediction accessible to all. It combines the fast homology search of MMseqs2 with AlphaFold2 or RoseTTAFold. The search runs 40 to 60 times faster than older methods. A server with one graphics card can predict close to 1,000 structures per day.

Paired with Google Colaboratory, the tool becomes a free platform anyone can use. That matters because folding tools once demanded costly hardware and huge storage. ColabFold matches AlphaFold2 quality on test targets, the authors report. It also predicts protein complexes, not just single chains. The software is open source, and its databases are public.
europmc-pmc9289681:
Nedunchezhiyan and co-authors review how obesity, inflammation, and the immune system drive osteoarthritis. Obesity is the top risk factor for the disease, and joint overload was long blamed. New work shows fat tissue signals, insulin resistance, and immune cells matter as much. Both innate and adaptive immune cells gather in the joint lining.

The review details each immune cell type found in the arthritic joint. Macrophages and their signals are covered most deeply. Neutrophils, dendritic cells, T cells, and B cells get separate treatment. Animal studies and human trials are compared, with gaps flagged. Trials now running are reviewed with their limits. The authors argue the disease is a whole-joint immune disorder.
europmc-pmc9614581:
Perlis and co-authors measure how common long COVID symptoms are among US adults. Long COVID means symptoms that last past two months after infection. Counts for the condition have swung widely by study. The team ran a large cross-sectional survey to pin it down.

The study covered more than 16,000 individuals across the country. Among adults with a prior positive test, 15% reported current long COVID symptoms. Rates varied by age, sex, and other traits. People who finished a vaccine series before infection fared better. They were less likely to report long COVID symptoms than unvaccinated peers. The authors read the pattern as a wide burden with uneven spread. They also flag vaccination as a possible guard against the condition. Full detail on subgroup gaps fills the results.
europmc-pmc9779781:
Butler and co-authors report the PANORAMIC trial of molnupiravir as early home treatment for COVID-19. The oral antiviral had not been tested in vaccinated outpatients. The trial asked whether adding it to usual care helped. Adults at higher risk of bad outcomes took part.

The UK trial assigned 26,411 adults by chance to groups. One group got the drug at 800 mg twice daily for five days. The other group received usual care on its own. Nearly all participants had at least three vaccine doses. Hospital stays or deaths hit about 1% in both groups. The drug did not lower that rate in the results. No subgroup gained a clear edge from the drug. Serious side events were rare and matched across groups. None were judged to be caused by molnupiravir. The authors report faster recovery signals elsewhere in the data.
europmc-pmc9969881:
Wang and co-authors test four blood inflammation indexes as predictors of pneumonia after brain bleeding. Pneumonia is a grave risk after intracerebral hemorrhage. The indexes are the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio and three related composite scores. All four reflect body-wide inflammation after stroke.

Patients were enrolled prospectively at four hospitals. Pneumonia was judged by modified CDC criteria. Index values were taken at admission for each patient. The team compared each index against a clinical lung infection score. A total of 320 patients entered the reported analysis. The aim was early flagging of who would get pneumonia. It also sought clues to how severe it might be. Cheap blood ratios could aid fast triage after hemorrhage.
france-crime-sylvestre-bonnard-1881:
Anatole France published The Crime of Sylvestre Bonnard in 1881, his first novel, Englished here in 1906. The English translation of 1906 gives an elderly scholar's gentle, ironic adventures among books and a young ward. France's limpid irony and love of old Paris announce the master stylist of the next forty years.

Bonnard, a member of the Institute, hunts a rare manuscript to Sicily and into a bookseller's clutches in Paris. He rescues Jeanne, the granddaughter of his lost love, from a cruel guardian and a boarding school's neglect. To give her a dowry he sells his library, and the crime of the title is a kindly theft. The close finds the old scholar content, his books gone and his ward happily wed in Paris. The novel's charm and humane skepticism won France his first wide public in France.
frus-1861-d181:
Carl Schurz wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 October 1861. The dispatch is document 181 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Schurz had now held Madrid through a summer of war. His October report has the ease of a man who knows his court. It told Washington that Spain, for all its pride, showed no haste to aid the South. Spain's pride was real, but its purse and fleet were weak, and Schurz read both facts well. Both facts read well in Washington, where Spain had long been a cause of doubt.
frus-1861-d281:
A State Department letter of 8 July 1861 told Mr. Haldeman what Washington wanted done. Congress received it as Document 281 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d81:
A letter dated 11 September 1861 went from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams in London. The letter is document 81 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Three days of letters to London in a row show a desk that never cooled. Seward drove the effort abroad with his own hand on the pen. This note belongs to the dense September run that kept Adams fully briefed as autumn began. Adams could act on a brief order the day it landed, without waiting for more. Brief orders also left Adams free to spend his days in talks, not in study.
frus-1862-d181:
Document 181 is the second Seward dispatch to Charles Francis Adams dated 3 November 1862, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Adams, the American minister in London, received both letters in the same mail.

When the Department split a day's orders between two letters, each usually took one topic, so the envoy could file and answer them apart. The practice swells the volume but sharpens the record. Read together, the 3 November pair shows Washington's hand at the very moment Britain weighed the French call for a truce in the war. Adams reported home at least once a week, and oftener when the news was hot.
frus-1862-d281:
A Dayton report dated 26 May 1862 stands as Document 281 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

That week, Stonewall Jackson's Valley campaign was alarming Washington itself, a reminder that the war could swing fast. Foreign envoys reported each swing, and ministers at home weighed them. Dayton's letter from Paris in late May is part of the transatlantic conversation by which two governments tried to price a war neither could predict. French public opinion ran warmer for the Union after the emancipation news arrived.
frus-1862-d381:
On 24 January 1862 Cassius Clay wrote again to Secretary of State William H. Seward from St. Petersburg, in a letter printed as Document 381 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Clay was the American minister in Russia.

Clay's Russian service was ending: Simon Cameron had been named to succeed him, though Clay would return to the post in 1863. His January reports closed his first term at a friendly court. For Washington, the Russian channel's value lay in its contrast with Europe's western capitals, where sympathy for the South ran stronger. St. Petersburg's friendship later sent Russian fleets to American ports in 1863, to great cheers.
frus-1862-d481:
James E. Harvey reported from Lisbon to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 3 October 1862. The dispatch is Document 481 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

October reports from the Atlantic posts dealt with a war at sea that was spreading. Confederate raiders were burning American merchant ships. They did so in full view of neutral shores. Portugal's enforcement of its neutrality rules was therefore a live question in Washington. Harvey's account of Lisbon's stance fed the State Department's running brief on the cruisers. Read with Seward's instructions to the same post, his letters show a small legation doing work that touched every American shipowner trading across the Atlantic.
frus-1862-d581:
James Watson Webb received the year's last printed Brazilian order from Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 27 September 1862. It is Document 581 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Seward wrote ten days after Antietam and five days after the emancipation order, though neither fact could shape Webb's conduct in Rio for months. The instruction still mattered. It fixed the Department's line for Brazil on the war. It also fixed the line on slavery's new place in the war. And it stated the neutral rules the Union expected in Brazilian ports. The Brazilian file ends the volume's American missions south of the equator, a thin correspondence stretched by distance over the whole geography of the war.
frus-1862-d681:
William H. Seward wrote to Mr. Blatchford again on 13 October 1862, less than three weeks after his last letter to him. The note is document 681 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. Two letters in quick order point to a matter that needed more than one word from Washington.

Much of a secretary of state's mail never made the papers, yet it was saved all the same. This short run of letters shows Seward tending to a side file in the midst of a war for the Union's life. For the reader, the pair is a reminder that the printed record holds small threads as well as grand ones.
frus-1862-d81:
The mail from abroad brought Seward a letter from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, dated 18 June 1862. Congress received it as Document 81 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1863p1-d181:
The State Department's mail for London dated 4 May 1863 carried this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 181 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

After emancipation became official policy in January 1863, Seward could argue that aiding the South meant aiding slavery. That argument runs under much of the year's diplomacy. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d281:
The American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, wrote this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 5 September 1863. It is document 281 of the 1863 volume of diplomatic papers. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

British yards were building two ironclad rams for the Confederacy in the summer of 1863. The fight to stop those ships reached its peak that autumn, filling the London mail. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d381:
From the British legation in Washington on 3 February 1863, Lord Lyons sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 381 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

London watched for any sign that Washington meant to widen the war. Lyons's job was to read American intentions and report them home faithfully. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d481:
On 27 April 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington wrote to Secretary William H. Seward. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d581:
Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington wrote this official letter to Secretary William H. Seward on 1 July 1863. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d681:
Charles Francis Adams received this dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 5 December 1863. It is printed as document 681 in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States. Adams had held the London post since 1861, the first year of the Civil War.

The London mission was the most vital post the Union had abroad. From it, Adams dealt with British leaders on ships, trade, and the risk of Britain backing the South. Seward's notes told him where Washington stood. A reader gets a feel for the pace of that work. Letters came often, each one short, each one part of a long, careful effort.
frus-1863p1-d81:
While three letters went out from London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote one of his own to Adams, on 13 February 1863. Adams was the American minister there. The letter is document 81 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The two men wrote blind of each other's same-day sheets, since the sea mail took ten days or more. Seward's letter set out the line Adams was to hold on the points then live. It is a neat case of how the exchange worked: not a talk, but two streams of paper that met in the files. This sheet is Washington's half of that crossed day.
frus-1881:
Grief opens the 1881 volume, in Arthur's message on Garfield's death. Foreign governments sent sympathy, he reports, from around the world. The country files then take up their work. Peru fills the longest run by far. Its war with Chile drives the correspondence. Chile itself takes the second-largest section. Venezuela's foreign debt earns a special heading.

A stranger file runs through the German papers. A British consul cabled home a hog cholera scare. He claimed 700,000 swine had died in Ohio alone. Washington answers that the rumor is wholly false. Federal and state officers found no epidemic at all. Switzerland and Mexico both run long. The volume mixes mourning with market defense. A president is buried; pork is protected.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d181: The Most Secret Protocol of the Moscow Conference, dated November 1, 1943, stands as Document 181 of the Cairo and Tehran volume, beside its companion Secret Protocol of the same date. The higher stamp marked the more sensitive of the agreed texts, the one fewest eyes were meant to see. That it is printed at all shows how far time opens wartime files. The protocol appears in the Foreign Relations series, at the close of the Moscow section.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d281:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 404/1 at Cairo on 22 November 1943, answering the American agenda for the Sextant Conference. Signed by Brooke, Portal, and Cunningham, it raises no objection to the American subjects but proposes a simpler order of business.

Five main heads are listed: reaffirming the overall objective and basic undertakings, Southeast Asia operations, Overlord and the Mediterranean, the war against Japan, and progress reports. Southeast Asia is put second, so Chiang Kai-shek and Mountbatten can join the talks at the earliest stage. Detailed points from the American list would be fitted in from day to day, and progress reports left to the end, once the big items were settled.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d381:
A secret report from the Office of Strategic Services gives an account of a visit to Tito's National Army of Liberation in Yugoslavia. It was written at Bari in Italy on 29 October 1943. Its author spent six weeks in the field with the Partisans, from mid-September to late October.

His conclusions run against outside assumptions. The Partisan movement, he writes, is of far greater weight than the world realizes. By their own efforts, ringed by Germans, Italians, Ustasha, and Chetniks, the Partisans have built a free community. In it, Muslims, Christians, Serbs, Croats, Slovenes, and Communists may all speak on how it should be run. The Communist Party failed to organize the movement on party lines and threw every force against the common enemy, though its members work hard to shape the new state's future. Villagers with kin in America greeted the mission with embarrassing faith in American aid.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d481:
On December 5, 1943, in the middle of the Second Cairo Conference, Assistant Secretary of War John J. McCloy again wrote to Harry Hopkins, President Roosevelt's special assistant. McCloy had written to Hopkins the day before as well. The State Department printed this second message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Repeated staff-level messages during a summit usually track problems being worked in real time: questions from the conference floor sent home, answers and material sent back. The McCloy-Hopkins channel was one of the busiest in wartime Washington. Read together, their December messages show the staff machinery that kept the President supplied while he negotiated abroad.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d81: A second Churchill message to Roosevelt dated October 31, 1943 is Document 81 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The prime minister's two notes that day closed out the October correspondence in this series. What divided their business, the record does not say, and a summary should not guess. Both letters are printed in the Foreign Relations volume, at the point where the story turns toward the President's journey east.
frus-1944-quebec-d181:
No participant's official memorandum survives for the dinner meeting of September 13, 1944, so the editors assemble accounts from Leahy's diary, Lord Moran's diary, and later recollections. Shipping was the announced subject, but Moran records that how to prevent another war with Germany was the only subject of conversation all evening. The Americans argued for drastic action against German industry.

Morgenthau wanted the Ruhr closed down, which would help British exports, especially steel. Churchill resisted: "I agree with Burke. You cannot indict a whole nation." He favored disarmament, but insisted Germany be allowed to live decently. Punishment should be swift: "Kill the criminals, but don't carry on the business for years." Cherwell sided with the Americans. Morgenthau later recalled Churchill calling the plan chaining England to a dead body.
frus-1944-quebec-d281:
Roosevelt's message to Chiang Kai-shek of September 16, 1944, is one of the bluntest in the volume. After reading the latest reports from China, he wrote, his chiefs and he were convinced Chiang faced the disaster long feared. The Y Force troops across the Salween had fought with great courage, but unless reinforced and supported with every capacity, their sacrifices would be valueless.

Withdrawal, Roosevelt warned, was exactly what the Japanese were striving to cause. If Chiang failed to man his divisions, the land line to China would never open and the Hump air route would be jeopardized. For that, Chiang must accept the consequences and assume personal responsibility. Stilwell, he noted, still had not been given command of all forces in China.
frus-1944-quebec-d81: Under the number 81, the Quebec 1944 volume prints a short editorial note. Its historians added such notes wherever the paper record needed help. A note may supply context, name a figure, or flag another document. The surrounding papers were prepared for the September 1944 conference. At Quebec, the American and British leaders took up Germany's future and the Pacific war. Treat this note as the editors pausing to orient the reader.
frus-1945-50-intel-d181:
"National Intelligence Authority Directive No. 7" bears the date 2 January 1947. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 181 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The first peace-time setup paired the National Intelligence Authority at the top with the Central Intelligence Group below it.

A numbered directive joined a growing shelf of rules that told the new agencies how to run themselves. Directives set who may do what, what must be reported, and which office has the final say. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d281:
Dated 2 June 1948, this memorandum runs from the Executive Secretary (Souers) to the National Security Council. It is document 281 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The CIA was in its first year, and the Council was taking up covert action for the first time.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. The points are stated once and left to stand; the file around it holds the answer they drew. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d381:
A memorandum dated 15 April 1949 links two senior offices. The sender was the Assistant Director for Policy Coordination, Central Intelligence Agency (Wisner). The reader was the Counselor of the Department of State (Bohlen). It stands as document 381 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. By then the Dulles Report was months old, and the argument had moved to putting its advice into practice.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d81:
Russell, assistant secretary for administration, wrote to Secretary Byrnes on 3 November 1945. Russell's papers in the volume track the money and staffing of the State intelligence office. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

By November the office's first glow had met the house reality: budgets are finite, and other bureaus wanted their share. An administration chief writing to the secretary about the new service marks the moment support had to be argued, not assumed. Readers can watch the mood change across Russell's papers from autumn into winter. The office that arrived in September as a prize was, by year's end, a cost to be justified like any other.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d181:
Italy's cabinet crisis, and a British veto delivered inside it, fill this excerpt from the Secretary of State's briefing of 1 December 1944. The memorandum for the President is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Ambassador Kirk's reports from Rome supply the news.

Kirk has told Premier Bonomi of Washington's concern over the long crisis. The United States will not judge the make-up of a new Italian government, but it must honor Italy's past pledges to the allies. The British ambassador, by contrast, told Bonomi flatly that Count Sforza as foreign minister would be unacceptable. Kirk calls that undue meddling in Italian home affairs. Winant has been told to voice American regret in London, since the move angered the Italian left and drew sharp comment in the American press.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d281:
Ships for soldiers or ships for hungry civilians? McCloy's excerpt of 23 January 1945 states the armed services' hard answer. His memorandum to the Secretary of State, on the shipping situation and the Law Mission, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Hopkins and Justice Byrnes, both bound for the conference, know the Law Mission's story well. Law stated the need for a civilian rebuilding program for Europe, France and Belgium above all, most forcibly; Monnet followed with another appeal. The danger is real, McCloy grants: a great mass of unemployed people, hungry and ill-clothed, threatens politics and even the military position. But while ships are critically needed for operations the heads of state have approved, none may be diverted to separate national import programs.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d381:
Oil and shipping fill the Joint Chiefs' session at Yalta on February 8, 1945, recorded in these minutes. The chiefs first took up levels of supply of petroleum products in all theaters. Then came an overall review of cargo and troop shipping for the rest of 1945. Admiral Leahy noted the report was agreed by the shipping boards.

Leahy observed, dryly, that its essence was an agreement to study the question again when need arose. General Somervell answered that the need had already arisen. Redeployment plans, above all, had outrun the paper. The minutes show the alliance's scarcest asset — hulls — being argued over to the last conference week.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d481:
All three powers have now approved the basic texts for Germany, Ambassador Winant cabled from London on February 6, 1945. The Soviet acting member of the European Advisory Commission had told him that Moscow approved the protocol on zones of occupation. It also approved the agreement on control machinery.

With that word, the three founding texts stood approved without reserve. They were the instrument of unconditional surrender, the zones protocol, and the control machinery agreement. Winant's short cable closes talks that had run in London for over a year. Yalta could build on settled paper; the rulebook for ruling Germany existed before the leaders met.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d81:
Soviet staff kept phoning the American Embassy with questions, Harriman reported on 19 December 1944. His secret cable from Moscow is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It shows the Foreign Office staff puzzling over the sense of Roosevelt's plan for voting in the new world body.

A Soviet aide named Bereshkov had called an embassy secretary more than once. He even asked if some error in the wires had crept into the text. His puzzle was one part of the plan, on settling local disputes through groups of nearby states. Harriman says the embassy staff gave their reading of it. He asks Washington at once: must Moscow accept that part now, or can it wait?
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d181:
Joseph Davies, the former ambassador to Moscow, sent Truman his own tour of the coming agenda in a letter dated July 3, 1945. The letter and its enclosure form document 181 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Davies had spoken with the President that morning and followed up in writing.

The enclosed memorandum sorts the conference business into new matters and unfinished old business from Yalta. Of the eight Yalta agreements, Davies judges that only the joint administration of occupied Germany will need settling at the top political level. Reparations disputes from the Moscow commission may also reach Berlin in principle. The letter itself is warm and personal: Davies tells Truman he stands on the verge of great decisions, and that his high purpose will surely be crowned with success.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d281:
James Riddleberger, chief of the Central European Affairs division, briefed the Secretary on the Austrian zones in a memorandum dated July 4, 1945. The memo is document 281 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The zones had been under negotiation in the European Advisory Commission for eight months.

The tentative plan gives Salzburg and Upper Austria south of the Danube to the United States. It gives Carinthia and Styria to Britain. It gives Upper Austria north of the Danube, Lower Austria, and Burgenland to Russia. And it gives the Tirol and Vorarlberg to France. The main block is airfields near Vienna, which lies inside the Soviet zone though the city is to be held jointly. A telegram going out that day lets Winant accept the Soviet offer of two fields, Tulln and Schwechat, if the United States gets Tulln.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d381:
Control of German assets abroad is urged in a briefing book paper dated July 4, 1945. The United States had lately approached Britain, France, and the Soviet Union with a proposal. The Allied Control Council, as Germany's government, should declare all German external assets, private as well as public, subject to its control.

German official property, including Reich-owned corporations, would at once be taken over by the occupying powers' missions in neutral countries. An emergency in Spain prompted the haste: Madrid might seize, or buy too cheaply, property of a German government corporation. The paper's deeper aim was economic security against German spearhead firms overseas.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d481:
Churchill's Italian anxieties are relayed in Kirk's top secret cable from Caserta of July 12, 1945. Field Marshal Alexander, back from London the night before, reported three conferences with the Prime Minister. Churchill had shown keen interest in the situation in Italy. He promised he would not fail to impress on the President the importance of an active policy toward Italy.

Churchill pointed out a danger. A people in the Fascist camp for over twenty years, he said, might slide almost overnight into the Red camp. That could happen if the allies were not careful. He shared Alexander's concern at the rapid withdrawal of American troops from Italy and Europe, and said the matter would be discussed with Truman.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d581:
Foreign Minister Togo sent a second secret cable to Ambassador Sato in Moscow on July 11, 1945. Sent at 7 p.m. from Tokyo, it is document 581 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It tells Sato what line to give the Soviet leaders.

Togo says Tokyo has decided to state its stance on ending the war more plainly. Sato is to tell Moscow that keeping peace in Asia is one part of keeping world peace. Japan, he is to say, has no wish to annex or hold the lands it took in the war. Japan hopes to end the war so that a lasting world peace can be built. Sato must meet Molotov within a day or two and report back by wire at once.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d681:
A revised briefing paper on the Montreux Convention, dated June 30, 1945, supersedes the June 27 version. It is document 681 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Much of the text carries over, but the statement of U.S. interests is recast.

The paper repeats the history in brief. Moscow voiced discontent at Yalta but withheld its wishes, which were to go to a foreign ministers' meeting. Washington has told London it will discuss the Straits at the coming summit. The United States, though not a signatory, has been drawn fully into the picture by Britain and Russia. Turkey has not been consulted, though it would welcome U.S. interest in the Straits' future. The revised text puts one U.S. interest first: to keep the Dardanelles from becoming an area of international dispute.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d81:
General Jacob Devers, commanding the Sixth Army Group, warned General Marshall on June 20, 1945, that the Berlin survey party was still blocked. His telegram from Frankfurt is document 81 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Every attempt to get Soviet permission for General Parks to enter Berlin had failed.

Antonov in Moscow would not agree to Parks entering before June 28 or 29, Devers reports. He judges it highly unlikely that proper arrangements for the conference could be finished by the scheduled date if work starts that late. He recommends that Washington take the matter up through government channels to win the needed Russian permission. The cable pushed the quarrel over access up to the political level.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1081:
Secretary of State James Byrnes cabled the Acting Secretary of State from Babelsberg on July 28, 1945. The subject is Yugoslavia's protest notes over disturbances on the Greek-Yugoslav frontier. Byrnes agrees the charges are best settled by investigation on the spot. He does not want a special mission sent into the area, though.

Instead, the proposed American reply should offer a commission built from staff already in place. Military and political officers would be drawn from the American, British, and Soviet missions in Belgrade, and the American and British missions in Athens. Moscow would need to name a special group to work with the Athens team. With that change, Byrnes approves quick action.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1181:
President Truman wrote to Prime Minister Churchill on 17 July 1945, the opening day of the Potsdam Conference. The two leaders began the summit already in direct touch, leader to leader. Their exchange set the tone for the British-American side of the talks.

Truman was new to the world stage; Churchill had led Britain through the whole war. Their letters show the younger partnership at work on its first day. A message of this kind could align stands before a session or settle a point after one. This one marks the summit's first day in the principals' own words.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1281:
Admiral King, commander in chief of the United States Fleet and chief of naval operations, wrote to the Navy Department on 26 July 1945. King ran the navy through the whole war. His word to his own department came from the summit's naval side.

The navy's concerns at Potsdam ran from fleets in the Pacific to the ports and coasts of the new Europe. King's message carried his direction home while he served with the team abroad. It shows the sea service's chief running his house by cable, in the same week Britain changed leaders and Japan got its terms.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1381:
