The Combined Chiefs of Staff, the joint British and American military body, addressed President Truman and Prime Minister Churchill together on 24 July 1945. The chiefs advised both governments on the conduct of the war. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

A paper from the Combined Chiefs speaks for the whole Anglo-American war machine. Sent while Churchill still held office, it reached both heads of government at Potsdam at once. Readers should note the weight of the channel: when the chiefs wrote jointly, they settled service disputes before the leaders ever saw them. This message shows the military side of the alliance reporting to its political chiefs in mid-summit.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-81:
Allen, the deputy director of the State Department office for Near Eastern and African affairs, wrote this internal memorandum on July 24, 1945. It was prepared while the Potsdam Conference was in session near Berlin. The paper went into the delegation's working files. It was later printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official series.

Papers of this kind gave senior officials a desk officer's facts and advice in short form. Allen's office tracked a region outside the Big Three's main talks on Germany. Still, its concerns touched the wider war and the peace to come. The memo shows how staff far from the head table fed views into the talks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d781:
On July 25, 1945, Kirk reported from Rome in document 781. The ambassador in Italy wrote to the Acting Secretary in the conference's second week. His reports form a steady thread in the second Potsdam volume. Rome watched Potsdam for signs of its own fate.

A mid-conference report from Italy shows a capital reading the summit's smoke. Kirk had to guess where the talks pointed and advise at home. Readers share that uncertain vantage. The document also shows an embassy's duty to report mood as well as fact. In July 1945, mood in Rome was a fact of its own kind.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d881:
Edwin Pauley, the American representative on the Allied Commission on Reparations, wrote to the Secretary of State from Berlin on July 28, 1945. He encloses a letter from Sir David Waley of the British delegation to Soviet official Ivan Maisky. Waley's letter accepts the American reparations plan with two small changes.

The changes clarify that paying for needed imports ranks as a first charge, and they add the needs of the occupying forces. An attached note defines those needs in detail. Food, fuel, and medical stores for the armies count as German imports. Weapons, vehicles, and soldiers' pay do not.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d981: Emilio Collado sent this brief secret telegram from Babelsberg to Covey Oliver in Washington on July 16, 1945. Collado directed the Office of Financial and Development Policy. His whole request fits in one line. He asks Oliver to bring the delegation up to date on progress in controlling German external assets. Spain is named as a special concern. Collado cites the Department's July 6 telegram to London and Oliver's own memorandum of July 7 as the last word they hold.
frus-1961-63v03-d281:
A telegram from the State Department to Ambassador Lodge in Saigon, sent August 24, 1963, at 9:36 p.m., opens the road to the Diem coup. Nhu, it states, used martial law to smash the pagodas. His forces, not the army's, did the raids.

Washington cannot accept power resting in Nhu's hands. Diem gets a chance to remove the Nhus and free the jailed monks. If he refuses, support ends, and generals may draw direct backing. The cable closes with full support pledged. Its drafting later drew bitter dispute among the men who sent it.
frus-1977-80v08-d281: An editorial note in Volume VIII of the 1977-1980 series draws on President Carter's diary for July 31, 1978. At his weekly foreign affairs breakfast that day, Carter chose to send Secretary Vance to Israel and Egypt. Vance would invite Sadat and Begin to meet Carter at Camp David. Carter wrote that the state of things was growing extreme. He feared Sadat might start a conflict in October, when the 1975 Sinai II accord would lapse. The note marks the birth of the Camp David summit.
gao-gaoreports-b-295781:
In GAO ruling B-295781, dated April 7, 2005, Ben-Mar Enterprises, Inc., was the protester. The Department of Homeland Security had awarded Tech Systems, Inc., a contract for fitting, alteration, and pressing services at the Coast Guard Training Center in Cape May, New Jersey. Ben-Mar attacked the scoring of the winner's far cheaper offer. GAO denied the protest. The digest gives the rule that decided it: where offers are fairly judged technically equal, the agency properly picks the one with the lower price.

Equality on the merits leaves price as the honest tiebreaker. The ruling finds the equality finding itself was sound.
gao-gaoreports-b-298481:
Murray-Benjamin Electric Company, LP protested terms in a Defense Logistics Agency solicitation. The buy sought an open-ended supply of fiber optic cables. The cables support nuclear power plants in the fleet. GAO decided B-298481 on September 7, 2006.

The firm argued that the agency had to order the cables under contracts it already held. GAO split the claim in two. One part raised contract administration, which GAO does not review. The rest failed on the merits. The firm's schedule contract was not mandatory. The agency could seek the best value through open rivalry instead. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298881:
Spacesaver Storage Systems, Inc. protested a Marine Corps purchase order to Staller Enterprises, Inc. The buy covered weapons storage systems. Award rested on best value across six stated factors. GAO decided B-298881 on December 11, 2006.

The protester offered a lower price and a fit product. It said the cheaper bid should have won. The agency, though, judged the rival racks to be the stronger goods. On that view, the higher price bought real added worth. A best-value rule lets an agency pay more for a better product. GAO found that call fair. It denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299381:
LexisNexis protested a National Transportation Safety Board award to West Publishing Corporation. The contract covered online legal research services. The firm attacked its own unfit mark and the path of the award. GAO ruled in B-299381 on April 17, 2007.

The firm claimed the agency softened technical terms to favor the winner. GAO found the dropped terms were already met by other means. The firm had also been let to swap products on linked points. A claim of a missed key amendment failed too. The agency had posted it on the FedBizOpps site through a link. Each claim fell on the record. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299781:
Healthcare Technology Solutions International protested a Veterans Affairs blanket purchase agreement. The deal went to United Audit Systems under a schedule contract. The work covers off-site medical coding services for upstate New York. GAO ruled in B-299781 on July 19, 2007.

The winner's bid scored higher than the firm's. The price gap between the two was tiny. GAO found the pick fair on those facts. When price splits two bids by a hair, merit can rule. The agency's review of both bids stood up. No flaw in the scoring was shown. A best-value pick of the stronger bid can stand. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299981:
Navarro Research and Engineering protested a Department of Energy award to The S.M. Stoller Co. The contract covers support services for the legacy management program. That program tends closed Cold War nuclear weapons sites. GAO ruled in B-299981 and B-299981.3 on September 28, 2007.

The firm faulted the price realism review. The agency had matched bids to its estimate and to each other. It also checked that prices fit the stated labor types and hours. GAO found that check sound for a fixed-price deal. Credit for work past the floor terms was fair too. Prior-holder edges need no discount. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-307681:
The reach of a pay-claim waiver law is set in this GAO opinion, B-307681, dated May 2, 2006. The Secretary of the Senate asked about her power under 2 U.S.C. section 130c. The case grew from bad pay to a past Capitol Police worker. The hire had breached the anti-nepotism law. The pay had gone out through her office or the police Chief.

GAO read the waiver power broadly on one point. It lets her forgive claims for bad nonsalary pay as for bad salary pay. But one door stays shut. Neither she nor the force may grant pay that was never paid. The law forgives debts. It does not create new pay rights.
gao-gaoreports-b-309181:
An office space deal made with no lease power is voidable in this GAO decision, B-309181, dated August 17, 2007. GovWorks helped a Defense spy unit get office space. The space came through a lease with a third party. The lease was wrapped inside a services deal. Neither shop held lease power from the General Services Administration. Neither held its own lease power in law.

GAO held the deal cannot bind the government. It stands only if a proper official ratifies it. Pay made under it counts as improper pay without that step. Yet GAO found no Antideficiency Act breach. Defense had a valid fund for lease costs and stayed inside it.
gao-gaoreports-b-310081:
Five timber firms lost their protest; the GAO decision is B-310081, dated November 13, 2007. Poston Logging and four peers fought terms of eight Forest Service timber sales. Each sale was set aside for small firms. Small buyers face caps on resale of such wood. The firms said price checks for the sales must weigh those caps.

GAO denied the protest. No law or rule makes price checks weigh the resale caps. The check law's clear aim is fair value for the public. That aim does not call for a split method for small-firm sales. A bid to aid small firms does not bend how value is set.
gao-gaoreports-b-310981:
Gift cards as a survey lure are cleared in this GAO decision, B-310981, dated January 25, 2008. The National Telecommunications and Information Administration runs a coupon plan for TV converter boxes. The plan is worth $1.5 billion. A survey would test how the plan lands with the public. Cards would spur folks to fill in and send back the form.

GAO held funds may buy the cards. The facts sought are key to the plan's good start. A tie runs from the cards to those facts. The sum spent is small in scale. The chief gain flows to the government, not to the folks who reply.
gao-gaoreports-b-316381:
Train fare aid for a soldier is cleared in this GAO decision, B-316381, dated July 18, 2008. The Army runs a mass transit aid plan at Aberdeen Proving Ground. The plan rests on 5 U.S.C. section 7905. An Army man asked for aid for his rail trips to work. A pay chief asked if the aid could be paid. She had doubts on short trips and a lone user of the plan.

GAO held the pay may be made. The Army plan in force backs the aid for fit staff. The plan bars posts past the capital zone from tight caps on the aid. Doubts on worth do not trump a plan that grants the aid.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-281:
Financial Audit, GAO-05-281 of February 11, 2005, holds GAO's audit of the bank guard funds for 2004 and 2003. Law makes GAO audit three funds run by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation each year. They are the Bank Insurance Fund, the Savings Association Insurance Fund, and the FSLIC Resolution Fund. The host agency was made in 1933 to back bank deposits and keep faith in banks.

GAO seeks fair proof that the books are shown true in all big respects. It tests the checks on cash reports and the law. It tests the host's tie to set laws and rules. The 1989 law that made the three funds frames the tale.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-381:
DOD Business Systems Modernization, GAO-05-381 of April 29, 2005, warns that the Pentagon pours cash into back-office tech with a loose hand on the reins. The department's books have been a maze for years. Its facts on cash and goods come late or prove false. New systems were to cure that. The spend runs to billions of dollars a year.

GAO counts the fiscal year 2005 sum set for such builds. It asks if firm grip and clear blame hold over the whole set. They do not, the title states in plain terms. With no one map and no gate on new starts, weak builds eat cash that war needs could use.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-681:
Foreign influence over cleared defense contractors is the subject of GAO-05-681, dated July 15, 2005. The Defense Security Service watches over 11,000 sites holding classified work. Its check on foreign-owned firms leans on the firms reporting their own deals. GAO found the service does not gather or study such reports in any steady way. It cannot even list all firms working under protective shields.

One foreign-owned firm held classified access for at least 6 months before a shield was set. Late reports by firms ran to months as well. GAO concludes the service cannot show its watch is strong enough.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-781:
Air crew security training is reviewed in GAO-05-781, issued September 6, 2005. Training crews to face threats on board is a shared task. Airlines carry much of it. The Transportation Security Administration sets the standards. GAO checked how the agency built its guidance. It also checked how the agency makes sure airlines comply, and how its voluntary self-defense course is run.

GAO found the guidance grew stronger after the 2001 attacks. New legal duties were folded in, and the text grew clearer. Some users still saw parts as hard to apply to both flight and cabin crews. The agency set no goals or measures for how well the training works. GAO said better planning and tighter internal checks are needed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-881:
Financial system compliance across agencies is tracked in GAO-05-881, issued September 20, 2005. A 1996 law sets three tests for agency money systems. They must meet system requirements, follow accounting standards, and use the standard ledger. GAO must report each year on how the law is working. This is that yearly report.

Headings in the report state the pattern. System weaknesses still block sound financial management and accountability. Most compliance findings rest on negative assurance, a weaker form of proof. The Defense Department still struggles to lift its financial management. Steady interest from Congress helps hold agencies to account, GAO said. The report closes with agency comments and GAO's take on them. Readers get a government-wide scorecard in one place.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1081:
Can insurers price losses from nuclear, biological, chemical, or radiological attacks? GAO took up that question in GAO-06-1081, released in September 2006. The Terrorism Risk Insurance Act of 2002, extended in 2005, backs coverage for certified terror acts. Yet little was known about insurer exposure to such weapons. GAO met with large insurers, industry groups, and state regulators.

GAO tested these risks against common rules of insurability, such as whether losses can be predicted. It found measurement and prediction very hard for unconventional weapons. Exposure varied widely by line of insurance. Property and casualty firms often dropped such coverage. Workers' compensation, life, and health lines generally could not exclude the risks. Pricing stayed deep in doubt because attack odds defy past data. GAO made no recommendations.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-381:
Moving from a political post into a career job draws close watch. In GAO-06-381, dated May 1, 2006, GAO counts conversions from noncareer to career posts. The count runs from May 1, 2001, through April 30, 2005. Agencies must use proper authority and follow set steps for such moves. A conversion means a worker changes status with no break in service over three days.

GAO tallied the number and traits of conversions in departments and selected agencies. For moves at the GS-12 level and above, it tested authority and procedure. Readers can see how often conversions happened. They can also see where the process was checked most closely.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-781:
Tribal land applications are reviewed in GAO report GAO-06-781, issued on July 28, 2006. When land is taken into trust, the government holds title for a tribe or individual Indians. Trust land is exempt from state and local taxes, which makes each decision weighty. Rules set in 1980 aim for a uniform process at the Bureau of Indian Affairs. GAO checked how the bureau handled applications and how long they took.

GAO found that the bureau generally followed its regulations. Staff told affected state and local governments and took their comments. Required environmental and title reviews were done. After deciding, the bureau normally sent the applicant a decision letter. GAO said new time frames and better data should improve the processing further. Delays had long frustrated tribes and neighbors alike.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-281:
Spare parts that arrive months off schedule throw off budgets and readiness. GAO compared promised and actual delivery times in GAO-07-281, dated March 2, 2007. Lead time estimates guide when the services order parts. GAO checked deliveries across the Army, Navy, Air Force, and the logistics agency. It also judged recent efforts to shrink lead times. Inventory management has sat on GAO's high-risk list since 1990.

Only 5 percent of estimates landed within a week of actual delivery, GAO found. About 44 percent missed by at least 90 days. Late parts tied to weak estimates topped $12 billion in value. Early ordering tied up almost $2 billion more. For the Army, 58 percent of 9,380 reviewed deliveries ran late by 90 days or more. Causes included coding errors and stale data. Recent fix efforts worked less well than those of the 1990s. GAO gave six steps to sharpen the estimates.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-781:
Federal readiness for a flu pandemic is graded in GAO-07-781, dated August 14, 2007. The Homeland Security Council issued a national strategy in 2005. An implementation plan followed in 2006. Congress questioned whether federal leaders know their roles in a crisis. GAO compared the strategy and plan with six marks of an effective national plan. It also checked how clearly leadership roles were set. The report draws on agency plans and official interviews.

The government had set up an information clearinghouse and planning checklists. Health officials gave $350 million in grants to states and cities. They spent over $1 billion more on vaccine technology. Yet leadership roles stay murky, GAO found. The plan does not say how leaders would handle a crisis that strikes many places at once. GAO urged joint drills by the Homeland Security and Health departments. It also urged a deadline to refresh the plan with outside voices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-881:
Protection for large whales off the Atlantic coast fills GAO-07-881, dated July 20, 2007. The National Marine Fisheries Service wrote a plan to cut whale deaths from fishing gear. Right and humpback whales still die tangled in lines and traps. In 2005, the agency proposed stricter gear rules. GAO checked the science behind the changes. It also weighed costs to fishing towns and how success would be judged.

Sinking groundline will almost surely cut entanglements, studies show. The agency cannot say by how much deaths will fall, though. Its cost study for the fishing industry was thin in places. GAO urged a range of possible costs, not one figure. It also urged wider gear marking to trace problem gear. A plan to check industry compliance won the agency's backing. The agency rejected the cost and marking advice. The report lays out the dispute for Congress.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-281:
Bank account fees and fine print are surveyed in GAO report GAO-08-281, issued January 31, 2008. In 2006, consumers paid over $36 billion in checking and savings account fees. Many account holders never see the full terms before they sign up. Congress asked GAO to trace fee trends since 2000 and to test what shoppers can learn upfront.

GAO analyzed fee data and reviewed the rules that govern disclosure. It checked how federal regulators treat fees in their oversight of banks. Its staff also visited institutions across the country to ask for terms in person. Regulators, GAO finds, could better ensure that buyers get the papers first.
geikie-prehistoric-europe-1881:
James Geikie, a Scots rock scholar, wrote this sketch of the ice age and man's place in it in 1881. Its full theme is the rocks of Europe in the time before writ history. Geikie knew the signs of old ice work in the field at first hand.

He reads scraped rocks, stray blocks, and gravel beds to map how far the ice sheets spread. In that cold frame he sets the stone age folk, their tools, and their beasts. The book gave the men of the stone age a firm time scale for the first time.
gibbon-decline-fall-vol-2-1781:
Edward Gibbon published Volume 2 of his Decline and Fall in 1781. This volume moves from Constantine to Julian and the later 300s. Christianity triumphs as the state religion, and Gibbon tells the story with unmatched irony. Councils, heresies, and imperial courts crowd the pages.

Julian the Apostate, who tried to restore the old gods, receives a rich portrait. Gibbon also treats the rise of monastic life and the Goths pressing on the frontiers. His footnotes mix deep learning with dry wit. Readers prized the volume for both narrative and character sketches. The History was becoming the standard against which English histories were judged.
gibbon-decline-fall-vol-3-1781:
Edward Gibbon published Volume 3 of his Decline and Fall in 1781. This volume runs from Theodosius to the fall of the Western Empire in 476. Barbarian invasions, court intrigue, and religious strife fill the story. Attila and the Huns sweep across Europe in famous chapters.

The sack of Rome by Goths and Vandals marks the end of an age. Gibbon treats saints and emperors with the same cool, ironic eye. His account of the last Roman emperors is both sad and scornful. The volume closes the Western story while the East endures. Gibbon's grand design now spans a thousand years. Its scale still awes historians.
giorgio-ferrera-cabalistic-exposition-of:
Giorgio Ferrera presents himself as a scholar of Treviso, sent on embassies across Italy, who came to Milan and found carvings in stone that seemed to speak to him. His subject is the biscione, the great serpent borne as a sign by Milan's ruling house. He reads it, he says, through a hidden tongue, which he calls the language of the Sun and links to Japan. The catalog dates the work to 1481.

The exposition mixes travel notes, wonder tales from old manuscripts, and cabalistic reading of carved signs. Ferrera treats the serpent as a text that hides deep sense for those who can unlock it. The writing is strange and dense, and proud of its secrets. It will suit readers drawn to occult readings of art and arms, and it stands apart from sober history of the sign.
green-making-of-england-1881:
Anglo-Saxon England takes shape in Green's The Making of England, from 1881. English settlers cross the sea and carve kingdoms from Roman Britain's ruins. Missionaries then bring the Christian faith, and Alfred the Great defends the land against Danish invasion.

Green taught Victorian readers where their country truly came from. He writes of plowmen and monks beside kings and war bands. Settlement, conversion, and learning form his triple theme throughout. The book's humane warmth set it apart from drier chronicles of the age. It remains a beloved account of England's birth, written for the people whose story it tells.
hallywell-melampronoea-1681:
Henry Hallywell was a Cambridge scholar and clergyman whose Melampronoea appeared in 1681. The Greek title names his subject: a discourse of the polity and kingdom of darkness. He wrote in reply to John Webster, who had doubted the reality of spirits.

Hallywell defends the reality of spirits against the mechanical philosophy then rising in the Royal Society's circle. If matter and motion explain all, he warns, then soul, providence, and moral rule dissolve with the ghosts. The book catches the moment when England's learned men fought over whether the unseen world existed at all. His fear was pastoral as much as learned: a world without spirits leaves souls unguarded.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol5-1881:
Volume V of the Guiding Symptoms came out in 1881, printed after Hering's death from his stored notes. The series gathers proven signs for hundreds of remedies, and this middle volume keeps the alphabetical march going. Headings split every entry by region, organ, and function.

Small marks beside a symptom carry the real craft of the set. They tell the reader which signs showed up again and again, and which ones cured in practice. Without them the pages would be a flood; with them a working doctor could find a remedy's keynote fast, even mid-consultation.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-from-t:
Chapter fifty of John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands follows Spinola to the Emperor's court. Movements of the Emperor Rudolph open the portion, with the Marquis's reception in imperial circles. The Dutch envoys remember, Motley writes, the appeals the provinces made at imperial diets. Vienna never once answered those appeals with help.

They had not forgotten the famous Cologne negotiations for peace, conducted in the Emperor's presence to no result. The chapter is a reckoning with the Empire's forty years of neutrality. As the truce conferences approach, every old mediation returns to be judged. Motley's Dutch have learned to expect nothing from Vienna. Their diplomacy now runs between the Hague, Paris, London, and Madrid. The Emperor, once their sovereign's lord, has become a spectator of the republic he failed to save or crush.
holmes-common-law-1881:
Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr published The Common Law in 1881, from lectures given in Boston. Holmes, a Civil War veteran soon to be a judge, was not yet forty. The book made his name and began a long shift in American legal thought.

Holmes opened with his famous line: the life of the law has not been logic, it has been experience. He traced crime, torts, and contracts from old Germanic and Roman roots to modern rules, showing law shaped by policy and need. Judges, he argued, make law while claiming only to find it. The book is read as a founding text of American legal realism and of Holmes's own road to the Supreme Court.
jacquier-flagellum-haereticorum-latin-15:
Nicolas Jacquier, a Dominican inquisitor, wrote his Flagellum haereticorum fascinariorum, the Scourge of Heretical Witches, in 1458. This text comes from the edition of 1581, which kept his argument in circulation. Jacquier's target is the old Canon Episcopi, whose skepticism about night flights he sets out to demolish.

He insists that witches truly gather, body and soul, at their assemblies. That claim made the sabbath real for learned theology. Scholars call his book the pivot of fifteenth-century demonology. After Jacquier, doubt needed defending and belief needed only citing. The Latin scourge turned learned opinion toward the burning dogma that shaped the great hunts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-of-neusta: Aaron of Neustadt, surnamed Blumlein, was a Talmudist in Austria at the end of the fourteenth and start of the fifteenth century. With Shallum and Jaekel of Vienna he formed a trio of leading scholars. He was uncle and chief teacher of Isserlein, who often cites his rulings. Aaron died a martyr at Vienna on March 13, 1421. His digest "Hilkot Niddah" survives by mention, and his sermons only in three citations.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abbaye-of-const: Abbaye of Constantinople was a Talmudic scholar of the sixteenth century. He carried on a learned exchange of letters with Samuel di Medina, the rabbi of Salonica. Medina speaks of him in that exchange as the greatest of our teachers. Abbaye also wrote a preface to a book by Moses Nagara. The book, "Leḳaḥ Ṭob," was printed at Constantinople in 1574. No birth or death date for him is given in this entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abigdor-abraham:
Abraham Abigdor was a physician, thinker, and translator, born in Provence, most likely at Arles, in 1350. At the age of seventeen he wrote a work on logic in rimed prose. It was in the main a Hebrew form of Gazzali's book on the aims of the thinkers. He later went to Montpellier to study medicine, taught there by Christian scholars in person.

His life's work was translation, from Latin into Hebrew. He turned works on drugs, on fevers, and on purges into Hebrew, in 1378, 1379, and 1381. He also rendered a logic text of Pierre d'Espagne, and part of Averroes on the "Organon" of Aristotle. In 1399 he helped his son Solomon, then fifteen, turn a Latin work on the judgments of the stars into Hebrew as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-she:
Medical writer Abraham ben Shem-Tob was born in the middle of the thirteenth century, probably at Marseilles. His father, Shem-Tob ben Isaac of Tortosa, practised medicine there. Abraham wrote a medical handbook in ninety-one paragraphs, kept in Paris manuscripts.

He probably studied in Italy, since his last chapter shows the Italian doctor Gentile's sway. He helped translate Serapion on simples, printed in 1473. He also turned chapter twenty-eight of the Liber Practicae into the Liber Servitoris, on making simple medicines. The Latin text, printed at Venice in 1471, credits Simon of Genoa, but Abraham did the real work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-shofet-:
Karaite leader Abraham Shofet lived in Poland at the end of the seventeenth century. He was a favorite of King John Sobieski, who reigned from 1674 to 1696. He played a large part in founding Karaite colonies near Lemberg, in Galicia.

The colony plan was the king's own idea, the entry says. In 1688 Sobieski ordered Abraham to invite Karaite families from Lithuania and the Crimea to settle in Galicia. Many from Troki came, gaining grants, privileges, and communal self-rule. His surname Shofet means Judge. Neubauer guesses the Lithuanian Karaite hakam held court power, which would explain the name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adda-b-hunya-78: Adda b. Hunya is known for one teaching he passed on. It turns on Ecclesiastes i. 4. One line goes, and one line comes, but the earth stands for ever. His gloss runs this way. Hold the present age as good as the age that is gone. Do not say you would have learned from Akiba, Zerah, or Johanan, had they lived. The wise men of your own days count as much as the wise men of old. That single gloss is the whole of the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-afikomen-881: Afiḳomen is a bit of flat bread broken off at the start of the Seder. It comes most often from the middle of three cakes. The head of the house hides it under his pillow. It is eaten at the meal's end, as the last taste. The word is Greek in root, tied to feast song or after-meal sport. Kids are let to snatch it and trade it back for gifts. A kept piece was once held to guard a house from the evil eye.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ahijah-ahiah-ah:
Ahijah, also spelled Ahiah and Ahijahu, is a name borne by several men in Scripture. The entry lists them in turn. One was a youngest son of Jerahmeel. Another was a Benjamite chief. A third, son of Ahitub, was priest at Shiloh. He kept the Ark and stood with Saul at Gibeah. Others include a Pelonite among David's thirty and a Levite over the Temple treasures.

The longest tale concerns Ahijah, son of Shisha, scribe to Solomon. Solomon heard that the Angel of Death must take Ahijah and his brother Elihoreph. He sent them to Luz, a town where death was thought to have no power. They died at its gates, for that was the fated place. The list ends with Ahijah, father of Baasha, and a man who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alberti-conrad-:
Conrad Alberti was the pen name of Conrad Sittenfeld, a German novelist, dramatist, critic, and actor. He was born at Breslau on July 9, 1862. Schooled in his home city, he went to Berlin and took to the stage. After a few years he left acting for study and gave himself wholly to letters.

He was a pioneer of naturalism in Germany. That school brought realism into fiction and social questions into criticism, and it came to a head in Sudermann and Hauptmann. His critical books treat Freytag, Bettina von Arnim, and Ludwig Borne. His novels include "Riesen und Zwerge" of 1887 and the series "Der Kampf ums Dasein," from 1888 to 1894. His plays include "Brot!" of 1888 and "Bluff" of 1893.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alfakar-arabic-:
Alfakar is the name of one of the oldest Spanish-Jewish families. The word is Arabic for "the potter." The family was known for high standing and scholarship, first in Granada, later in Toledo. About 1190 Joseph Alfakar, a Toledo physician, helped suppress the Karaites in Spain. His sons Judah and Abraham were the family's most famous men.

Abraham Alfakar served at the court of Alfonso VIII. of Castile. He was a master of Arabic and a ready poet. He died at Toledo in January of 1231 or 1239. The king sent him on a mission to Morocco's sultan. Judah Alfakar, who died in 1235, was physician to Ferdinand III. In the fight over Maimonides' writings he sided against the philosopher. David Kimhi traveled to win him over, fell ill, and wrote instead. Judah's reply damned the mixing of Greek thought with Judaism. Even his friends condemned that roughness.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-almeida-isaac-1:
Isaac Almeida was a Turkish rabbi and author. He was born in the last half of the seventeenth century. He served as a fellow rabbi in Constantinople. He was still living in 1723. His death fell between 1723 and 1739. His printed work holds new notes and responsa.

That work came out as an added part of a rare book. The larger book came out in Constantinople in 1739. After his death his work was printed again. His son Solomon helped edit the new printing. The entry shows how his dates are fixed. A book named in his pages is dated to 1723.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amemar-ami-mar-:
Amemar is a name shared by two Babylonian teachers. The first taught in the fourth century. He paired law study with close Bible study. He used verses to back rules and sayings of the rabbis. One note of his ranks the sage above the prophet. That rank rests on a verse in Psalms.

The second Amemar was a friend of Rab Ashi. Ashi shaped the Babylonian Talmud as a whole. Amemar rebuilt the college at Nehardea. It had lain in ruins for more than a century. He led that college for more than thirty years. The years were 390 to 422. He also led the court there and spoke for Jews at court.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anatomy-1481:
Anatomy, the science of the structure of living bodies, gets a biblical survey here. The entry warns that the Bible's knowledge of body parts is popular, not technical. It starts with Jacob wrestling the angel, where the touched thigh and the shrunken sinew are read as a nerve.

From Exodus and Leviticus the entry gathers named parts of humans, beasts, and birds, including heart, brow, shoulder, breast, thumb, liver, and kidneys. Priests cutting up sacrifices supply the first Hebrew word for dissecting. The modern Hebrew name for the science grows from that same root. The result is a guide to how far biblical language went in naming the body.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antigonus-of-so:
Antigonus of Soko flourished in the first half of the third century before the common era. Pharisaic tradition, the entry says, preserves both his name and a key teaching. He was the disciple and successor of Simon the Just.

His motto, quoted from the Mishnah, tells people not to serve God like slaves working for daily rations. Serve without thought of pay, he taught, and let the fear of God rest on you. The entry calls this short saying the whole Pharisaic doctrine in seed. Good is to be done for its own sake, not for gain in this life or the next. That stance, the entry argues, grew from the Prophets, not from Greek thought.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arkansas-1781:
Arkansas entered the Union on June 15, 1836, left it on May 6, 1861, and was readmitted on June 22, 1868. About three thousand Jews lived in the state when this entry was written. Their settlement reached back to early days, but shared religious life came late. One sign is an old marriage law of 1838, worded so that Jewish ministers could not perform weddings, left unchanged until 1873.

Only five towns had congregations strong enough to keep a minister: Little Rock, Pine Bluff, Fort Smith, Hot Springs, and Jonesboro. Little Rock, the oldest and largest community, is traced in most detail. Its first traced settlers, the Mitchell brothers from Cracow, came in 1838. A congregation formed in 1866 took the name B'nai Israel, gained a charter in 1867, and dedicated its temple in September 1873.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ascama-plural-a:
Ascama, plural ascamot, is the name Spanish and Portuguese Jewish communities gave to the laws ruling their inner life. Members, called Yehidim, approved these rules and accepted them as binding. Most were framed on ancient models and carry on the self-rule of the old Jewish communities of Spain and Portugal. Written first in Spanish or Portuguese, they were later translated into the tongues of the lands where the communities settled.

England's ascamot, framed in 1664, were turned from Portuguese into English in 1819. They match the tekanot of Ashkenazic communities, though those are narrower in scope. Among Ashkenazim the same word, haskamah, means something else: approval, above all a license to print a book, signed by at least three rabbis. The first such censorship is placed in Italy in 1554.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenazi-meshu:
Meshullam Zalman Ashkenazi was a Polish rabbi and man of letters. Born in the second half of the eighteenth century, he died at Lublin on May 1, 1843. His father, also Meshullam Zalman, of Pomarin, died before the son was born. The family name was Orenstein, and the father was a grandson of Hakam Zebi.

The younger Meshullam held the rabbinate at Cazimir and at Naselsk. From 1826 until his death he served at Lublin. His one named writing is a set of glosses on the Mishnah. Those glosses were printed long after him, in the Wilna edition of the Mishnah in 1869. The entry is short, resting on a single initialed source, and gives his posts and his book without personal detail.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-atheism-2081:
Atheism is a Greek word. It means, at root, disbelief in a god. In its first Greek use it meant failing to honor the god the state owned as supreme. Socrates was charged and convicted on that charge. The Hebrew tongue, the entry notes, has no word of just that sense. Among early Israel, each clan owned its god as a matter of course.

Denying the clan god would have meant leaving the clan itself. So the prophets' fight was never over whether God exists. It was over whether Yhwh alone was Israel's rightful God. Their foes served other gods; they were not atheists in the modern sense. Later prophets mocked idols, yet still framed the quarrel as loyalty, not existence. The entry follows that line through the Psalms and into Greek and Roman times.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-avvites-avva-av:
Avvites is one name with three uses in the Bible, and this entry keeps them apart. First, the Avvites were a people whom the Caphtorim dispossessed, as Deuteronomy tells. Yet Joshua shows Israel failing to conquer them, so the entry dates their fall later. They lived in the Philistine district but were not Philistines. They seem more like Bedouins partway toward settled life.

Second, Avvim was a city in the land of Benjamin, perhaps once theirs. Third, Avva was the place the king of Assyria took people from to settle Samaria. Its people worshiped Nibhaz and Tartak. Elsewhere the name appears as Ivvah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-babinovichi-228: Babinovichi was a town in the district of Orsha, in the government of Mohilev, Russia. The entry is a short census note, and it gives the town in figures only. In 1900 its whole population numbered 1,143 souls. Of those, the Jews numbered about 800. Jews thus made up the larger share of the town. The note adds nothing on the town's history, its trade, or its communal life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baker-2381: Baker, among the Hebrews, was at first not a trade at all. The entry says the daily fresh bread of a house fell to the housewife. Trained bakers appeared only in larger cities, and not at a very early date. Still, bakers are named in Genesis and in Hosea. Jerusalem in Jeremiah's days had a street of bakers, Jer. xxxvii. 21. One tower on its wall bore the odd name "Tower of the Ovens," as Nehemiah records. The entry points readers to the articles on bread and baking for more.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baraita-plural-:
Baraita is an Aramaic word for a tannaite tradition that was not taken into the Mishnah. Later it was applied to collections of such traditions as well. The word means "the outside." One account links it to the phrase for outside books, the Apocrypha, set against the canon. Another ties it to the "bara," the outside schools that prepared pupils for the academies.

In the Babylonian Talmud the term covers the most varied tannaite matter outside the Mishnah: Sifra, Sifre, Mekilta, and Tosefta among them. The entry shows that a Baraita often keeps the old Halakah where the Mishnah gives the later form. Ten Baraitas in one passage supply ten Midrashic reasons for a rule the Mishnah treats as plain. Purely legal Baraita collections were wholly supplanted by the Mishnah and, apart from Talmud citations, have disappeared. The same fate met the haggadic collections.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bazarjik-or-tat:
Bazarjik, also called Tatar Bazarjik, is a small town of eastern Rumelia, twenty-four miles from Philippopolis. Jews there numbered 1,700 in a total of 17,000 people. The community is said to date from 1492 or from a later expulsion under Philip the Second.

Old tombs and Torah scrolls anchor the account. The entry recalls fear under Tatar townsmen and peace made with a Russian general in the war of 1877 and 1878. It closes with two Alliance schools, Jewish tradesmen of many crafts, and a grain trade in firm hands. Each family, the entry says, held its own house and stood in fair comfort for those times.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-behrmann-vasili:
Vasili Lazarovich Behrmann was a Russian lawyer born in Mitau on Sept. 15, 1862. He was a son of Lazar Behrmann and was schooled at his father's St. Petersburg school. He took his law degree there in 1885 and died at Cairo on March 18, 1896.

After riots against Jews in south Russia in 1881, Behrmann became a keen Zionist. He pushed the Palestine movement in Russia and worked for a society spreading schooling among Russian Jews. His books of essays, named Palestine and Zion, appeared in 1884 and 1892. In 1894 he traveled to England to study how that land ran its whole system for emigrants.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-ozer-b: Benjamin Ozer ben Meir, a Polish Talmudist, died at Zolkiev on May 25, 1810. He served as rabbi in Clementow and then as head of the school at Zolkiev. His book Eben Ozer, or Stone of Salvation, came out in 1792 through his grandson. It holds fresh readings on much of the Talmud and on the works of Alfasi and Maimonides. A second set of his notes, under the same title, was later added to editions of the Shulḥan Aruk code.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berkowitz-henry:
Henry Berkowitz, an American rabbi, was born at Pittsburg, in Pennsylvania, on March 18, 1857. He trained at Cornell and at the Hebrew Union College in Cincinnati. He held pulpits at Mobile from 1883 to 1888, at Kansas City to 1892, and at Philadelphia from 1892.

He founded the Jewish Chautauqua Society in 1893 and led it as chancellor. His books run from Bible Ethics in 1883 to a guide for reading the Old Testament and a work on Sabbath feeling in the home. Many papers in Jewish and general journals round out his output. He also sat on the board of governors of his college and on the publication committee of the Jewish Publication Society.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beth-arabah-hou: Beth-Arabah means "house of Arabah." It was a town in the wilderness of Judah. Joshua lists it among Judah's towns. Yet it also appears among Benjamin's towns. The entry explains that it was a border-town. It lay south of Beth-hoglah in the Jericho plain. Robertson Smith proposed a modern site for it. He identified it with 'Ain al-Feshkha. In one Joshua passage the name appears simply as "Arabah."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-biedermann-mich:
Michael Lazar Biedermann was an Austrian jeweler and merchant. He was born at Presburg on August 13, 1769. He died at Vienna on August 24, 1843. At fifteen he apprenticed to an engraver. Prizes for wax modeling and engraving followed. He engraved the imperial seals themselves. By 1800 he opened a jeweler's store.

At the Leipsic fair he entered the wool trade. One English sale in 1807 reached $300,000. His firm became a leading Austrian house. He also led Vienna's Jewish community from 1806. He founded a sick fund and a pension fund. In 1830 he became Jeweler to the Emperor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-borofsky-samuel:
Samuel Hyman Borofsky was born at Wolkovyshki, in Russian Poland, in April, 1865. He was taken to Manchester, England, in 1874 and schooled there. In 1879 he joined his family in Boston.

Borofsky became a justice of the peace in 1891 and a notary in 1894. He sat on the Boston city council in 1898. In 1900 voters sent him to the Massachusetts house. His Five-Cent Ice Bill forced dealers to sell cheap pieces of ice to the poor. In 1899 he founded a temporary home for destitute Jewish children in Boston. He also backed a Sabbath bill that failed in the senate.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bresch-or-bres-: Judah Low ben Moses Naphtali Bresch, called Paulus Milius, turned the Pentateuch into Judaeo-German. He lived in Germany in the sixteenth century. De Rossi credits him with a version printed at Cremona in 1560. That edition also holds the Haftarot and five Megillot with Rashi extracts. Yet its preface names Paulus Aemilius, a converted Jew in Rome, as the maker. The entry thinks Bresch likely took that name at conversion. Steinschneider doubted it, and later writers split on the point here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-buber-solomon-3:
Solomon Buber was a Galician scholar and editor of Hebrew works, born at Lemberg on Feb. 2, 1827. His father taught him Talmudic literature and Jewish philosophy, while hired teachers handled Bible and Talmud. At twenty he married and entered commerce. He rose to audit banks and still held civic and charity posts in 1902.

Alongside business, Buber edited Midrash after Midrash with long introductions and full notes. His 1868 edition of a Pesikta collection won wide scholarly praise. He used every manuscript and print he could obtain, recording variant readings in footnotes. He also edited liturgical and biographical works and wrote on the rabbis of Lemberg. The entry stresses that he paid most publishing costs himself and gave copies away.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bulat-abraham-i: Abraham ibn Bulat was a Talmudic scholar who lived in Spain in the fifteenth century. He was a disciple of Isaac de Leon. In a sharp dispute over a legal ruling, his teacher faced Isaac Gayyal. Bulat took his master's side and wrote a booklet to show the rival ruling broke the law. That booklet was later printed with the arguments of both men. The printing came in a miscellany issued at Leghorn in 1745. The entry gives no birth or death dates for Bulat.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cabret-or-cabri: Jacob Cabret, son of Judah, was a Spanish translator who lived late in the fourteenth century. His surname came, the entry suggests, from a Spanish place called Cabreta or Cabrita. Several people bore the same name. Cabret turned a Latin work by Arnaldus of Villanova into Hebrew and shortened it. The book treated the use of astrology in medicine. He made the translation at Barcelona in 1381. It still survives in manuscript, held in the Bodleian collection. The entry gives no dates for his birth or death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cantarini-kalon: Kalonymus Aaron Clement Cantarini, son of Samuel Simon, was an Italian physician born in 1593 at Padua. He died there on July 30, 1631, of the plague. The entry is only a few lines. It calls him famous as a Talmudist. It also credits him with wide knowledge of the secular sciences of his day. No work by him is named, and no post he held is recorded.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cerf-karl-fried: Karl Friedrich Cerf, a German theatrical manager, was born at Unterreissheim-on-the-Main in 1782. He died at Berlin on Nov. 6, 1845. He took Christianity very young and supported his father's family from age seventeen. After years in the horse trade at Dessau, he rose to chief military agent. He served in the campaign of 1813-15 under Count Wittgenstein. His courage won him a gold medal from Emperor Alexander. At Berlin he gained a lasting grant to build the Königsstädtisches Theater, which he managed until his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chechelnik-4281: Chechelnik is a town in the government of Podolia, in Russia. In 1898 it held about 7,000 people, including 1,967 Jews. Trade was the chief Jewish occupation. Still, 352 Jews worked at handicrafts, 96 as journeymen, about 200 as farm laborers, and 41 in local factories. The town had no charitable organizations, and poverty among its Jews was general. Jewish schooling rested on a private boys' school with 100 pupils and 23 ḥadarim with 367 pupils.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-churriker-abrah: Abraham David Churriker was a Beni-Israel soldier and police officer, born in 1822 and dead at Puna on Nov. 2, 1867. He joined the Third Regiment of the Bombay Native Light Infantry and served in the Punjab in 1848-49. He was present at the siege of Multan and the battle of Gujarat in 1849, earning the Punjab medal with two bars. Promoted subedar in 1853, he later led the Ahmednuggur police, fought in the Mutiny, and rose to assistant superintendent of police at Puna in 1863.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-jacob-rap:
Jacob Raphael Cohen, an American hazzan, was believed born in the Barbary States and died in Philadelphia in September, 1811. He lived in London early in life and was in Quebec and New Orleans in 1777. From 1778 to 1782 he ministered to the Spanish and Portuguese synagogue Shearith Israel in Montreal.

New York's Sephardic congregation then picked him as minister in 1782. Two years later he moved to Philadelphia as hazzan of its Spanish and Portuguese congregation. He married Rebekah Luria, from a family that had lost members to the Spanish Inquisition. He left descendants in Philadelphia, and his son Abraham Hyman Cohen read services for a time after his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-conaniah-4581: Conaniah names two Levites in the book of Chronicles, and the entry treats them as two numbered notices. The first served under King Hezekiah. He held charge of the offerings and tithes brought to the Temple. His brother Shimei worked beside him in that task. II Chronicles xxxi. 12 and 13 are the passages named, where the name is spelled Cononiah. The second Conaniah led the Levites under King Josiah. In that reign he raised flocks. He gave them for the paschal sacrifices of the Levites, as II Chronicles xxxv. 9 records.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cosenza-4681: Cosenza is a city in southern Italy. The entry rests on two documents printed in Ughelli's Italia Sacra. One, from King Ferdinand I. in 1467, restored the archbishop's court power over the Jews of his diocese. A reading of it suggests the archbishop could hand Jewish property to others. The king confirmed such grants in 1469. The entry gives no picture of daily Jewish life in the town. It ends with a hard date: the Jews were expelled from Cosenza, with the rest of Naples, in 1540.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cruceanu-stefan: Stefan Cruceanu was a Rumanian author, born at Jassy on April 25, 1868. He took his bachelor's degree in 1889. He then studied philosophy at Jassy for a year before going to Paris for medicine. His first work, a socialistic story, appeared in April, 1885, in a paper called Rights of Man. He wrote often for political papers in Rumania. His first poem came out in 1891. In 1898 he gathered most of his poems in one volume, titled Lacrime.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-daniel-b-ketina: Daniel b. Ḳeṭina was a Babylonian amora of the second half of the third century. He was a contemporary of Ze'era. Leading teachers of his age cite him in both Talmuds. He mostly passes on rulings he had learned from earlier masters. A legend shows why he was held a saint. Each day he would inspect his garden and mark the beds that needed water. Rain would then fall and moisten just the marked beds. His daughter married a nephew of Rab, the entry adds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-ben-solom:
Solomon ibn Abi Zimra's son David, known as Radbaz, was a Spanish Talmudist and cabalist born in Spain about 1479. He was thirteen when his banished parents settled at Safed. He later moved to Cairo, and in 1517 he became chief rabbi of Egypt, a post he held for forty years. Pupils such as Isaac Luria studied at his school.

At ninety Radbaz resigned, gave most of his fortune to the poor, and settled at Safed, where Joseph Caro held him in great esteem. He died there in 1589, at the reported age of one hundred and ten. His books include decisions on Maimonides' code, a method of Talmud study, and cabalistic works on light and the alphabet.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-demetrius-ii-ni:
Demetrius II Nicator, son of Demetrius Soter, became king of Syria after his father's death. He had been sent to Rome as a hostage and could do nothing there against Alexander Balas. In 147 he marched on Balas with hired troops. At the battle near Antioch in 146, Balas was beaten and killed, and Demetrius took the name Nicator.

Demetrius confirmed Jonathan as high priest for a tribute of 300 talents, with three districts added. When revolting soldiers rose against him, Jonathan sent 3,000 Jewish troops to his aid. Yet Demetrius broke his promise to pull Syrian garrisons out of Judea. A new revolt under Diodotus then drove him from power for a time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dorbolo-or-durb:
Isaac ben Dorbolo was a rabbi of about 1150 who traveled widely. He knew Poland, Russia, Bohemia, France, and Germany from his own journeys. Some time after 1140 he visited Rabbi Tam at Rameru. At Worms he stayed a while and gathered local tradition.

At Worms, Dorbolo saw a responsum from Palestinian rabbis dated to 960. It answered Rhenish questions about a reported coming of the Messiah. Scholars have doubted that document's truth, the entry notes. Additions to the Mahzor Vitry stand in Dorbolo's name, marked by his name or a single letter. The entry clears him of being that prayer's compiler.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dwarf-5381:
Dwarf renders a Hebrew word in Leviticus xxi. 20 for a bodily flaw in priests. The word literally means thin. It names one of the faults that bar a priest from service. Targum and Ibn Ezra take it so, the entry says.

Rabbinic tradition and most modern readers explain the term otherwise. Still, the dwarf is ruled unfit for service in the cited rulings. The entry then turns to lore: all nations tell tales of giants and dwarfs. Bible memory made the land's first peoples giants. Beside them Israel felt like grasshoppers, as Numbers tells it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliseus-or-elis: Eliseus was a learned Jew at a sultan's court. He served Murad the First at Brusa and Adrianople. His time was the late fourteenth century. In time he fell from the sultan's favor. He was disgraced and sent into exile for it. Scholars link him to a Greek Bible work of note. That work is the Graecus Venetus in the sources. A churchman of his day called him an unbeliever. The charge may spring from his bent for philosophy. He taught the famed thinker Pletho in his youth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-enos-5781: Enos was a son of Seth in the Book of Genesis. Seth was the third son of Adam in that tale. In the days of Enos men began to call on God. At ninety years of age he begat a son, Cainan. He died at the age of nine hundred years. The name most likely means man in plain speech. Some new scholars doubt the line of Seth as fact. They call its names a match set for the line of Cain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-etampes-hebr-or:
Etampes, capital of its district in the Seine-et-Oise department of France, had a Jewish community reaching back to the twelfth century. King Louis VII set a provost there who alone could enforce payment of debts owed to Jews. He also barred arresting debtors during the fair. Rabbis of Etampes took part in the Synod of Troyes in 1160.

Philip Augustus expelled the Jews in 1181 and turned their synagogue into the Church of the Holy Cross. On their return, the Count of Etampes was made guardian of their privileges. Toward the end of the twelfth century R. Nathan, son of Meshullam ben Nathan of Melun, lived in the town. The entry rests on royal ordinances and a letter of Pope Innocent III.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ferdinand-iii-t:
Ferdinand III, king of Castile and Leon, was born in 1200, took the throne in 1217, and died in 1252. His reign marks a turn in the fate of Spain's Jews, the entry says. Against clergy pressure he kept his Jewish chief tax farmer, Don Meir, and all the Jewish tax farmers. He upheld the archbishop of Toledo's pact with his diocese's Jews.

As conqueror of Cordova, he confirmed Jewish rights in several cities for services in his campaigns. After Seville fell, Jews shared in the land grants. Don Meir got Valencia del Rio and 1,414 acres. Whole villages near Seville passed to Jews for a time. Seville's Jews kept their synagogue and gained four small mosques to remake as synagogues, and they gave the king a great silver key.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fleckeles-6181:
Fleckeles is one of the oldest Jewish families in Prague. The name was likely Falkeles at first, from Falk, a common Jewish name of the time. Old tombstones in the Prague cemetery show several spellings of it. Rabbi Eleazar Fleckeles built the only known family tree. He traced his line back nine generations, to a Wolf who was a son-in-law of David Gans.

The family was linked by marriage to the house of Rabbi Löw of Prague. It was also linked to Rabbi Heschel of Cracow and other leading houses. Eleazar's daughter married Rabbi Isaac Spitz of Bunzlau. One later member stands out in the entry. Leopold Fleckeles was a physician and medical writer. He was born at Vienna in 1802 and died at Carlsbad in 1879.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-folk-tales-5981:
Folk-tales are stories full of superhuman events, spread by elders or by strangers. They feature dwarfs, giants, fairies, and ghosts. Men turn into beasts, horses fly, and sleepers wake after a hundred years. Traces appear among Jews at every stage of their history. The Bible holds Jotham's fable and the fight of David and Goliath. Haggadic tales of Og, King of Bashan, show the same tall-story marks.

Jews in the Middle Ages helped spread Eastern tales across Europe. Without them, the great story sets of Kalilah wa-Dimnah and Sindbad might never have reached the West. Nearly one-tenth of modern Europe's folk-tales may come from those sources. Yiddish story books gathered tales told in the ghettos. True Jewish legends include the Jewish pope and the golem of Rabbi Löw. Recent gathering found some sixty or seventy tales among living Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frank-mendel-62:
Mendel Frank was a Polish rabbi of the first half of the sixteenth century. He was first rabbi of Posen. A ruling of his there on a divorce case is mentioned by a Lublin rabbi. Later he became rabbi of Brest-Litovsk. On September 4, 1531, King Sigismund I ordered the Jews of Brest to submit to his jurisdiction. A letter from Queen Bona in 1532 barred appeals from his rulings.

That royal backing hints that Frank was not chosen by the community. The entry thinks he was likely forced on it by Michael Esofovich. Esofovich had been made chief of the Jews of Lithuania in 1514. Among his rights from the king was the power to name rabbis. The Jews of Lithuania seem to have disliked the new rabbinical courts. They preferred to take their disputes to the general authorities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-friedlander-mor:
Moritz Friedländer was an Austrian theologian born in Hungary in 1842. By 1903 he lived in Vienna. He was schooled at Prague, where he also heard the Talmud talks of the chief rabbi. His free views kept him from a rabbinical career. For a short time he taught religion in a Vienna gymnasium. In 1875 he became secretary of the Viennese Jewish alliance. In 1881-82 he made many trips to Brody. There he helped Paris delegates move exiled Russian Jews on to the United States.

The sorrow Friedländer saw at Brody went into a book of five weeks there. As alliance secretary he set up the first Jewish public school in Galicia, against strong strict-party anger. His report of a second Galician trip reached Baron de Hirsch. The baron's great fund for schooling and trades grew from it. Friedländer ran that fund and set up fifty schools in Galicia himself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gallego-joseph-: Joseph Shalom Gallego, a poet in the new Hebrew style, died in Palestine on November 25, 1624. He was the first cantor of the first synagogue built in Amsterdam. He held that post for fourteen years and then moved to Palestine. He edited Imre Noam, a book of religious poems, hymns, and laments printed in 1628. He also turned Jonah of Gerona ethical writings from Hebrew into Spanish.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-geneva-6581:
Geneva, capital of the Swiss canton of that name, held about 80,000 people in 1900, of whom 1,076 were Jews. Jews lived there by the fourteenth century. In 1348 lake towns accused Jews of well poisoning, and many were racked and burned. Geneva Jews lived in a set street and were driven out in 1490. A toll then fell on any Jew who passed through.

The modern community dates from 1783, when Lorraine Jews settled at Carouge. Full civic equality came only in 1841. A temple rose in Geneva in 1859, on land the city gave. Joseph Wertheimer became rabbi that year. Most Geneva Jews worked in clock making and in trade.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gikatilla-moses:
Moses ibn Gikatilla, a grammarian and Bible exegete of the late eleventh century, was born at Cordova and later lived at Saragossa. His full name was Moses ben Samuel ha-Kohen. Abraham ibn Ezra calls him the greatest grammarian. Judah ibn Balaam praised his prose and verse in Hebrew and Arabic alike. Weak health alone, he says, held the man back.

Gikatilla wrote a grammar book on masculine and feminine forms, now lost. He rendered Hayyuj two chief works into Hebrew. His comments on Isaiah, the Minor Prophets, and Psalms survive in quotes. He first gave a plain past-based reading of Isaiah prophecy. He set its first part in Hezekiah days and its second in Second Temple times.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ginsburg-saul-m: Saul Moiseyevich Ginsburg, a Russian lawyer and author born at Minsk in 1866, took his law degree at St. Petersburg in 1890. Since 1898 he has served as secretary to the Society for the Promotion of Education Among the Jews of Russia. From 1896 to 1900 he ran the Literary Review of the Voskhod. His own reviews ran under the pen name Ha-Kore. With P. Marek he issued a book of Judaeo-German folk songs in 1901.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gollancz-herman: Hermann Gollancz was an English rabbi. He was born at Bremen on Nov. 30, 1852. Jews' College and University College, London, gave him his schooling. After serving several English synagogues, he followed Dr. Hermann Adler at Bayswater Synagogue. In January 1900 he took the Lit. D. at London. He was the first Jew to win that honor. He also held the Hebrew chair at University College. His books include charms from Syriac manuscripts. He translated the Syriac Sindban and Berachyah's ethical treatises. In 1902 he edited a Bible version for Jewish family use.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-griliches-aveni:
Avenir Girschevich Griliches was a Russian engraver. He was the father of Abraham Avenirovich Griliches. He was born at Wilna in April 1822. He studied Talmud until he was sixteen. He then taught himself engraving with no master's help.

In 1871 the Imperial Mint at St. Petersburg hired him. A rock-crystal portrait of Levensohn won him an academy nomination in 1874. That year he became engraver to the Mint. The entry calls him one of Russia's best engravers. His state seals serve Alexander III and Nicholas II. He held the rank of court councilor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-halayo-david-be: David ben Samuel Ḥalayo was probably a son of the Samuel Ḥalayo of Bersak who wrote to Simon ben Ẓemaḥ Duran. David served as a ḥazzan, or cantor. He was a pupil of Simon Duran, and it was at his urging that Duran wrote his commentary on Isaac Ghayyat's "Baruk Asher Ashash." David praised that commentary in verses. The entry flags its first word with "probably," and it also points to a second David Ḥalayo who flourished about 1363, leaving the link between them unsure.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hananiah-hanina:
Hananiah, also Ḥanina, was a Palestinian amora of the third and fourth centuries, junior to Ḥiyya b. Abba and Ze'era I. He is often called "the comrade of the Rabbis." In debate with Ela he gave as good as he got: "God save us from such opinions," cried Ela, and Hananiah shot back, "Rather may God save us from thy opinions!"

Born in Babylonia, he came young to Palestine with his brother Hoshaiah and settled at Tiberias. The brothers lived by shoemaking on a street of prostitutes, yet kept their modesty so well that the women swore by "the saintly rabbis of Palestine." Johanan meant to ordain them but held back. The brothers consoled him: as sons of Eli's house, no old age in office was promised them. Hananiah died on a semi-festival, and his coffin was made in the public street in his honor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hart-henry-john:
Henry John Hart, born in New York on May 7, 1820, became an Australian magistrate. Trained for the law, he disliked it and sailed for Sydney in 1839. He settled in Melbourne in 1841 and worked in trade. He also took part in the search for gold fields in Victoria.

In 1855 Hart became a territorial magistrate, and Melbourne voters chose him three times as city auditor. The entry credits him with gaining land for a synagogue. He led the East Melbourne congregation for six years. He also served on hospital boards for more than twenty years. He died in 1884.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hayyim-ha-kohen:
Hayyim ha-Kohen, born at Prague late in the sixteenth century, was a German rabbi. His mother was a granddaughter of Low ben Bezaleel, the famed rabbi of Prague. From 1628 to 1630 he served as rabbi at Frankfort on the Main. There he set rules for congregational votes and for Sabbath teaching hours.

In 1630 Hayyim accepted a call to Posen, where people held him in high regard. A pupil of his praised his teaching in print. His new readings on the four codes of the Shulhan Aruk survive in manuscript. A nephew who studied under him wrote them down. Hayyim died at Posen about the middle of the seventeenth century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-health-laws-131:
Health laws in Judaism rest on a clear rule: keeping the body well is a religious duty. Life comes first. In danger, nearly all laws may be set aside, save those against idolatry, adultery, and murder. Neglect of health counts as a sin. Even needless fasting is faulted.

Priests once handled contagious disease for the public. Later, each town kept a doctor among its standing officers. A scholar could not live in a town with no physician. The article gives diet counsel from the rabbis, such as eating only when hungry. It also covers town planning: tanneries, graves, and threshing floors were pushed away from homes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heidenheim-phil:
Philip Heidenheim, born at Bleicherode on June 14, 1814, was a German rabbi and teacher. He was called to Sondershausen in 1834 and rose to principal and preacher there. From 1840 he also taught at the town's modern school, handling many subjects. In 1845 he became state rabbi for Schwarzburg-Sondershausen.

At an 1848 teachers' meeting in Eisenach, Heidenheim won a notable change. A draft line called Christian faith the base of all schooling. His amendment made it moral and religious instead, and four hundred members backed him. At Passover in 1902 he marked sixty-five years since his first sermon in office.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hepner-adolf-75: Adolf Hepner, born at Schmiegel, Posen, on Nov. 24, 1846, was a German-American journalist. Educated at Lissa, Breslau, and Berlin, he became a socialist in 1868. With Liebknecht and Bebel he edited a socialist paper at Leipsic. Tried for high treason, he was acquitted in 1872, then expelled. In 1882 he emigrated to the United States and settled at St. Louis in 1886. There he edited labor papers, including the St. Louis Tageblatt until 1897.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hiyya-al-daudi-: Ḥiyya al-Daudi was a liturgical poet who died in Castile in 1154. He was descended from the Babylonian nasi Hezekiah, the entry says. Many penitential poems bearing the name Ḥiyya appear in prayer books of Tlemçen, Oran, and Avignon, and in the Sephardic prayer book. Whether all are his is not certain, the entry warns. In one poem the surname Al-Daudi is added. Two of his poems were printed by Luzzatto, who mistook him for another Ḥiyya, the collector of Judah ha-Levi's poems.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-horowitz-schmel: Schmelke Horowitz was a rabbi and cabalist born in Poland in 1726. He died at Nikolsburg on April 28, 1778. His father was rabbi of Czortkow, and his brother Phinehas led the Frankfort community. A pupil of Bar of Meseritz, Schmelke loved the Cabala and gained a name for saintliness. That fame brought him to Nikolsburg in 1773. In 1775 he became chief rabbi of Moravia. He set up a Hasidic synagogue at Nikolsburg. His cabalistic sermons appeared later as Dibre Shemu'el.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-ben-josep:
Isaac ben Joseph of Corbeil was a French ritualist of the second half of the thirteenth century. He was the son-in-law of Jehiel ben Joseph of Paris and attended his school. He also studied with the great men of Evreux, above all Samuel, whom he called the Prince of Evreux. His strong piety drew many pupils to him, including Perez ben Elijah of Corbeil.

At his pupils' urging, he published in 1277 a shortened form of the "Sefer Mitzwot Gadol" by Moses of Coucy. His version, the "Ammude ha-Golah," is better known as the "Sefer Mitzwot Katan," or Semak. Communities in France and Germany received it warmly, and it was often edited and annotated. Isaac also published collected notes and small works holding his ritual decisions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-israel-ben-jehi: Israel ben Jehiel Ashkenazi was an Italian rabbi of the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries. He corrected the Talmud edition printed at Pesaro in 1511-13. In 1518 he approved the first edition of Elijah Levita's "Ha-Bahur" at Rome. He sat on Rome's board of rabbis, where he seems to have led his two colleagues in Talmudic knowledge. In 1519 he gave a ruling in a case touching Donina, daughter of Samuel Zarfati. Late in life he emigrated to Palestine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-called-al:
Jacob, called also Israel, was the third patriarch, son of Isaac and Rebekah and ancestor of the Israelites. He was born when his father was sixty, after Rebekah had been barren for twenty years. His name is explained as supplanter or deceiver. He was his mother's favorite, and Genesis shows him as a plain man living in tents, a shepherd's life.

The entry follows the Genesis story. Esau came in faint from hunting and sold his birthright to Jacob for a mess of lentils, sealing the bargain with an oath. Years later, blind Isaac meant to bless Esau. Rebekah dressed Jacob in goatskins and sent him in with the meal first. Isaac blessed him as lord over his brothers, and, learning the trick, confirmed the blessing rather than revoking it, since it matched God's purpose. Esau's hatred followed from that deceit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacobson-heinri:
Heinrich Jacobson, a German physician, was born at Königsberg on Oct. 27, 1826, and took his medical degree at Halle in 1847. He settled in Königsberg, rose to assistant professor there in 1872, and that year became chief physician at the Jewish Hospital in Berlin. He stayed in Berlin for the rest of his life and died there on Dec. 10, 1890.

The entry calls him a great clinicist and lists many essays and books, mostly on experimental pathology. His topics included blood movement in the veins, normal and diseased local temperature, heart sounds, and blood pressure in compressed air.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jelin-aryeh-lob: Aryeh Löb Jelin was rabbi of Byelsk, in the Grodno region of Russia, born in 1820. Leading Russian rabbis often sent him hard points of law for decision. He wrote two books of new readings on Talmud tractates. His chief work gives matching passages across the Babylonian Talmud, the Jerusalem Talmud, the Midrashim, and other old rabbinic books, with sharp notes of great worth to students. That work is printed with the Talmud text in the Romm editions of Wilna. He died on April 2, 1886.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-porat-be: Joseph Porat ben Moses, in French Don Bendit, was a tosafist of the thirteenth century. His surname Porat hints at a verse in Genesis. Gross took him to be the same man as Joseph of Caen, cited by Samuel of Falaise as an authority. He was a pupil, and perhaps a grandson, of Samuel ben Meir, but not his son. He wrote a commentary on the Talmud, parts of which stand in the Tosafot to Shabbat and Yoma.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-ha-darsha: Judah ha-Darshan ben Moses was a French Bible commentator who lived at Toulouse in the first half of the eleventh century. Rashi quotes him often in his notes on the Pentateuch. A prayer book commentary names him twice more, on a verse of Zephaniah and a phrase of the poet Eliezer ha-Kalir. Geiger held that he was a son of Moses ha-Darshan of Narbonne. If so, he may be the Judah ben Moses, a pupil of Rashi, who is said to have taught at Narbonne.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kamenetz-podols:
Kamenetz-Podolsk is a Russian city. It is the capital of the government of Podolia. In 1900 it held 34,483 people, about half of them Jews. Its Jewish groups for charity and learning stood out among its public buildings. In the Cossack rising of 1648-58 the community suffered badly. Cossacks and Crimean Tatars both attacked it.

About the middle of the eighteenth century the city became a center of strife. Talmudic Jews clashed there with the Frankists. Bishop Dembowski took the Frankist side. In 1757 he had the Talmud burned in the public streets. The entry also notes the rich banker Joseph Yozel Günzburg as a resident. Late in the next century many Jews left for the United States.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-klein-philip-93: Philip Klein was an American rabbi. He was born on May 22, 1848, at Baracska, Hungary. He was educated in the Talmudical schools of his native country. He continued his studies at Presburg and at Vienna, Berlin, and Jena. After his ordination he became rabbi at Libau, in Courland, in 1880. In 1890 he emigrated to New York. There he became rabbi of the Hungarian congregation Oheb Zedek. The entry calls it perhaps the leading East Side congregation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levy-emil-9881: Emil Levy, a German philologist, was born at Hamburg on Oct. 23, 1855. He studied at Heidelberg and Berlin and took his Ph.D. in 1880. After two years in Paris and Montpellier, he began teaching at Freiburg in 1883. He became assistant professor in 1887. His chief work is a large Provençal dictionary, begun in 1894 and still unfinished in 1904. It corrects and adds to Raynouard's Roman lexicon. He also wrote on a troubadour and on an Engadine Job.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lightning-bened: Lightning is one of the sights that call for a benediction, by the Mishnah rule quoted here. At shooting stars, lightning, earthquakes, thunder, and storms, a Jew recites a blessing on the One whose power fills the world. At great mountains, seas, and deserts, a second blessing praises the Maker of creation. Alfasi and Maimonides read the Talmud to allow either blessing at lightning. Custom at last split the pair: the power blessing goes to thunder, and the creation blessing to lightning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-loeb-jacques-10: Jacques Loeb was an American biologist born in Germany on April 7, 1859. He studied at Berlin, Munich, and Strasburg and took his medical degree in 1884. He worked at Würzburg and Strasburg and did research at Kiel and Naples. In 1892 he joined the University of Chicago, becoming full professor in 1899. In 1902 he moved to the University of California. His studies covered animal responses to light, forced growth changes, and making eggs develop without fertilization.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lulab-10181:
Lulab, the palm branch waved at the Feast of Tabernacles, is explained in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. The lulab joins with the etrog, or citron, among the four species of the festival. It is made of a folded palm shoot at least three handbreadths long. Three myrtle twigs and two willow branches are tied to its lower end.

The article describes how the lulab was used in the Second Temple. Worshipers waved it during the Hallel psalms, facing east and shaking it in every direction. That act confessed God's rule over nature. Processions circled the altar once each day and seven times on the seventh day. After the Temple fell, Johanan ben Zakkai ordered the rite kept everywhere for seven days. The entry remains a clear period account of the festival custom and its rules.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mantua-10381:
Mantua, the fortified Italian city on the Mincio, receives a Jewish history in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. It held 1,100 Jews in 1901, down from a peak of 2,523 in 1858. The first mention of Jews there comes from the twelfth century. Abraham ibn Ezra finished a grammar work in Mantua in 1145.

The article follows a community favored and squeezed by turns. A special tax of 2,000 ducats in 1459 was beaten down to 600 by protest. Two famous rabbis, Joseph Colon and Messer Leon, feuded and were both expelled in 1475. The Jews won leave to lend at interest, yet the prince ordered them to attend anti-Jewish sermons in 1485. A Jewish badge followed in 1496. Under the dukes a Jewish physician served at court, and an Ashkenazic synagogue was slowly approved. The entry shows Italian Jewish life balanced between princely favor and preachers' pressure.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-of-rothenb:
Meir of Rothenburg was the leading rabbi of Germany in the thirteenth century. Solomon Schechter and Louis Ginzberg profile him at length in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Worms about 1215 and studied at Würzburg and in the great French schools under teachers such as Jehiel of Paris. Back in Germany he drew bands of devoted pupils, some of them married men who left their families to study with him. He served in Kostnitz, Augsburg, Würzburg, Worms, Nuremberg, and Mayence, and, longest, Rothenburg, and died in the fortress of Ensisheim on May 2, 1293.
