Starting with the blocking antibody and switching to the hormone gave denser healing tissue and stronger bones than the reverse order, at equal total exposure. Cartilage lingered longer in the hormone-first groups, a sign of slower progress. Sequence, not just drug choice, may matter in fracture care.
plos-pone-0354681:
Gladys Estheysi Elías Solís and three colleagues published this 2026 review of gut-friendly supplements and childhood anemia. They gathered nineteen trials covering more than four thousand children, testing prebiotics, probiotics, and combined synbiotics against placebos or standard care, and rated how solid each result was.

Overall the supplements produced no meaningful gains in hemoglobin or iron stores, though one trial hinted probiotics might trim anemia rates. No serious side effects appeared. Elías Solís calls for larger, better trials in high-risk children before these products are promoted for anemia.
plos-pone-0354981:
Rudrajit Majumder and co-authors hunted for existing drugs that ultrasound could turn into weapons against glioblastoma. This brain tumour resists treatment partly because the blood-brain barrier blocks medicines. Sound-activated therapy can strike deep tissue without surgery, but proven activator drugs are scarce. Their 2026 pipeline pairs machine learning with printed tumour models.

A classifier trained without reliable negative examples scanned drug libraries for ultrasound-responsive candidates, including drugs first developed for Alzheimer's disease and ovarian cancer. Promising picks were then tested in three-dimensional printed tumour balls that mimic the real tumour's oxygen-starved core. Majumder and colleagues present the combined screen as a faster route to repurposed brain tumour treatments.
plos-pone-0355181:
Murat Akın and Orhan Kahveci compare in 2026 blood levels of a compound linked to vessel health in people with sudden hearing loss in one ear and in healthy peers. Patients were seen at diagnosis and again weeks after treatment, with hearing tested by standard tone methods. The question was whether the compound helps explain the illness or predict recovery.

Levels were higher in patients at the start and stayed high after treatment, even as hearing improved. Higher levels did not predict who recovered, though they did help separate patients from healthy people. The authors read the compound as a risk marker rather than a guide to outcome.
plos-pone-0355281:
Wei Sun and five colleagues published this 2026 pilot study of a possible warning marker for sudden worsenings of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Fifty people took part: patients mid-flare, patients stable, and healthy volunteers. The team measured how many neutrophil white blood cells carried a surface protein called PD-L1, alongside standard blood counts.

That neutrophil share ran higher in patients than in healthy people, and higher still during flares, where it also predicted flare status on its own. Sun calls the marker promising but insists larger multi-center studies must test it before clinical use.
plos-pone-0355381:
Hanan Ibrahim Alsharif led a team of eight authors testing a wild plant against stomach ulcers in animals, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Alcohol can injure the stomach lining and cause ulcers. The team gave an extract of Tragopogon coelesyriacus, a plant with traditional uses, in a live animal model of that injury.

Alsharif's group found the extract reduced the ulcer damage. They linked the effect to calmer oxidative stress, less inflammation, and less cell death in the stomach lining. A plant lead like this needs much more testing before human use. Still, it marks a candidate rooted in traditional knowledge that drug researchers can now examine with care.
plos-pone-0355481:
Khushbu Mishra and co-authors used national survey data from Nepal to test whether mothers' paid work improves young children's nutrition. Child undernutrition traps families in poverty across generations, so any lever matters. Their 2026 study applied matching and instrumental-variable methods to growth measures for children under five.

Maternal employment showed no statistically reliable effect on height, weight, or related growth scores. The authors explain that most mothers' work is informal, so income gains are small. Extra work also cuts time for feeding and care. Limited control by women over household money may further weaken the link. Mishra and colleagues caution against assuming mothers' jobs alone will fix child nutrition.
plos-pone-0355681:
Megumi Sato and colleagues examine in 2026 how baker's yeast turns a gene called YGP1 on and off as sugar runs low or stays plentiful. The gene makes a protein sent out of the cell and rises when food is scarce. Cell cycle timing and stress responses both come into play in the control system the team mapped.

When sugar was plentiful, a binding protein kept the gene active in a rhythm tied to cell division, partly through a second activator. When sugar ran out, two stress factors switched the gene on strongly. The plentiful sugar route also helped cells handle acid and live longer.
plos-pone-0355781:
Johannes Meyer zu Drewer and colleagues puzzled over extra hydrogen appearing in charcoal made with crushed rock. Such rock-enhanced biochar aims to store carbon twice over, by charring biomass and by letting minerals weather. Their 2026 study cooked wood with a silicate rock at two temperatures and many rock shares, then probed the products with advanced instruments.

Most mixtures barely changed carbon yield or char structure. One extreme batch, nearly all rock and cooked hottest, held far more hydrogen than expected. The team traces the surplus to three sources: hydrogen inside the rock itself, hydrogen clinging to mineral surfaces, and a pyrogenic coating over rock grains. The finding refines how such chars should be measured and credited.
plos-pone-0355981:
Ashley Shanahan, Gwenyth Eichfeld, Levi Todd, and Anzela Niraula charted how microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, behave across the stages of a standard laboratory model of multiple sclerosis-like damage. Their 2026 study fed mice a toxin that strips myelin from nerve fibers, then examined the brain's main white matter tract during early damage, peak damage, and early repair.

Microglia multiplied within a week and shifted into debris-clearing mode, eating damaged myelin while dialing down inflammatory signals, a profile tied to two genes involved in cleanup. In the retina, which has no myelin, the toxin still changed microglia directly, proving some effects bypass demyelination entirely. The timeline helps researchers separate helpful cleanup from harmful inflammation when testing therapies.
plos-pone-0356181:
Maia M. Sobejana and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for the Care for Muscle study, on exercise for people whose muscles are weak from rheumatic disease or age-related muscle loss. Endurance training is thought to feed the muscle's energy factories, while strength training builds the contractile machinery, but patients may respond differently depending on what is wrong inside their muscles. The trial randomizes just under seventy patients with rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, or sarcopenia to strength or endurance programs.

Training runs eight weeks, supervised sessions on cable and fitness equipment plus a weekly home session. The main outcome is peak muscle strength on a dynamometer, with ultrasound imaging of thigh muscle, biopsy-based measurement of mitochondrial function, blood inflammation markers, and walking endurance as supporting measures. By matching muscle biology to exercise response, rehabilitation might move toward schedules prescribed by disease mechanism rather than habit.
plos-pone-0356281:
Maheen Sughra, Aisha Irum, Muhammad Ibrahim, and Adnan Ahmad Khan re-tested a classic theory of health behavior against Pakistan's national survey. The survey covered more than fourteen thousand married women. The question was what really drives contraceptive use. Their 2026 study extended the Health Belief Model with fertility preferences and contact with the health system. It estimated the whole structure statistically across three nested versions.

Beliefs mattered, but modestly. Feeling threatened by pregnancy risks and seeing benefits in contraception each nudged use upward slightly. Contact with family planning providers mattered consistently. Fertility desires dominated everything, especially the wish to space births. The authors conclude programs in Pakistan should work through fertility goals and provider contact first. Belief campaigns are supporting players.
plos-pone-0356381:
Renato Luque-Benavides and colleagues reviewed eighteen years of patients with non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising around the eye at a Peruvian referral center, the largest such account from a Hispanic-Latino population. Their 2026 retrospective study covered ninety-eight patients treated between 2000 and 2017 and followed for a median of two decades, relating tumor type, stage, and treatment to survival.

The orbit was the commonest site, and slow-growing marginal zone lymphoma made up half the cases. Slow forms did very well, with roughly nineteen of twenty patients alive at five years, while aggressive forms lost far more ground. Older age independently worsened outlook in the slow group. The long follow-up gives Latin American eye cancer care a rare local benchmark.
plos-pone-0356481:
Joseph Harrison and Matthew Wallace estimate how long immigrants live, and how long they live free of disability, across England and Wales in this 2026 study. Using whole-population death records and three censuses, they built life tables for people born in thirty-seven different countries, measuring outcomes from age fifty. The aim was to test the popular idea of a healthy immigrant effect against both lifespan and healthy lifespan together.

Most migrant groups did outlive the England and Wales-born population and stayed disability-free longer. But several large groups broke the pattern: people born in Scotland and Ireland, and men born in Poland and Lithuania, had shorter lives and fewer healthy years. Women born in Pakistan and Bangladesh lived longer yet carried more disability. The authors stress that migrants are far from one group, and some need targeted public health attention.
plos-pone-0356781:
Yan Jiang and colleagues report a surprising amplifier of bacterial toxin damage in the mouse brain: albumin. Albumin is the commonest protein in blood. Their 2026 study injected mice with bacterial lipopolysaccharide. This molecule triggers fierce inflammation. Some mice got the toxin alone, and some got it pre-mixed with bovine albumin. The team then examined brain blood vessels and barrier leakage. It also examined a fiery form of cell death called pyroptosis.

At the lower toxin dose, the albumin mixture leaked more tracer into brain tissue. It injured more vessel cells. It raised more death and inflammation markers than toxin alone. At a high dose the advantage vanished, swamped by the toxin itself. Tests confirmed albumin physically carries the toxin into the brain. That mechanism may matter whenever infection meets a leaky barrier.
plos-pone-0356881:
Takefumi Yoshida and colleagues surveyed 587 Japanese elementary school students about refusing school, testing whether two strengths, resilience and solution building, the habit of constructing next steps toward goals, soften the behavior. Their 2026 study used self-report questionnaires and modeled the pathways separately for boys and girls.

For boys, resilience calmed refusal directly and also indirectly, by strengthening solution building. For girls, resilience worked only through the indirect route: it built solution skills, which in turn eased refusal. Both paths ended at the same place, children with more of both strengths resisted school less intensely. The authors suggest support programs teach concrete solution building to everyone, since it carries the benefit for both sexes.
plos-pone-0357181:
Shreya Battu and colleagues published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on how COVID-19 treated immunocompromised patients in intensive care as the pandemic changed. Reviewing nearly eight hundred Stanford ICU patients from 2020 to 2022, they split the timeline into pre-Delta, Delta, and Omicron periods and compared survival between immune-weakened patients and the rest.

Across the whole period, immunocompromised patients died more. But the gap reached significance only in the Omicron period, when their ninety-day mortality ran far above the comparison group's. They also made up a growing share of ICU admissions by then. The authors argue the pattern may reflect Omicron-era realities: vaccines and treatments helped the general population more, while the immunocompromised stayed exposed as precautions lifted. Protection strategies, they argue, should be timed to who remains at risk, not declared over for everyone at once.
plos-pone-0357281:
Zhonghui Zhu and colleagues probe whether the sympathetic nerves that support the aorta also protect it from tearing. A tear in the aorta's wall is deadly, and nerve signals help keep the vessel healthy, but their role in early disease was unclear. In mice given a chemical that weakens the aorta, nerve activity markers rose early and tracked with breakdown of the wall's elastic layers.

Removing a nerve hub in the neck did nothing on its own, yet it sharply worsened tearing once the weakening treatment began, raising ruptures and spreading damage. Muscle cells in the wall also showed signs of shifting type after the removal. Zhu and colleagues conclude that intact sympathetic support guards the aorta, and losing it early can hasten disaster.
plos-pone-0357381:
Fatemeh Gholamali Nezhad and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for a pilot trial of an unusual depression treatment: gentle electrical stimulation of the face muscles. Standard treatments fail about a third of people with major depression, so new mechanisms are needed. The idea grows from the notion that activating expression muscles can shift mood from the body upward. Earlier feasibility work suggested practicality, and this registered trial tests it properly.

Sixty participants will receive twenty sessions over four weeks, half with real stimulation and half with a sham version, with neither patients nor assessors told who got which. The trial tracks depressive symptoms, anxiety, quality of life, and sleep, plus dropouts and side effects as measures of tolerability and safety. As a pilot, its real product is design knowledge: effect sizes and practical lessons to shape a large multisite trial.
plos-pone-0357581:
Zelalem Addis and coauthors published a 2026 agronomy study in PLOS ONE on feeding hot pepper, a cornerstone of Ethiopian cooking, in the Amhara Region. Yields lag because soils are tired and losing organic matter. Over two seasons, six feeding regimes mixing liquid bio-slurry, a farm waste product, with standard nitrogen fertilizer in different proportions were compared, measuring soil chemistry and pepper yield in replicated plots.

Blends beat the extremes. Halves of each, and a quarter slurry with three quarters fertilizer, improved soil nutrients and produced the highest yields, above the unfed control, while returning the best profit per investment. The half-and-half blend is the headline recommendation for farmers with enough slurry, the quarter blend suiting those short on it. Farm waste, the study argues, can substitute for a large share of purchased fertilizer without sacrificing the harvest.
plos-pone-0357781: Wu and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on software that grades a citrus fruit used in Chinese medicine. Fructus Aurantii is the dried young fruit. Their system, FAnet, is a light, end-to-end tool that names the fruit and grades its quality. Fast grading by camera could help herb markets sort stock fairly and spot poor or wrong material.
plos-pone-0358481:
Orsolya Csötönyi led a team of eight authors testing a painless way to read pig gut movement, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Stress changes how the gut moves, in pigs as in people, but measuring that usually needs invasive tools. The team tested surface electromyography, which reads electrical signals from the skin surface.

Csötönyi's method detects stress-induced changes in gut motility without surgery or swallowed devices. A painless, continuous window into the stressed gut helps researchers study welfare and feeding with less harm to the animals. Pig studies also inform human gut research, since the systems are alike. Farm science gains a tool that can run during normal housing, not only in a lab.
plos-pone-0358781:
Kimbley Asaso Omwodo leads a team of five testing whether low vitamin D tracks with preeclampsia in Kenyan mothers, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The dangerous blood pressure disorder causes about a fifth of direct maternal deaths in Kenya, and African data on the vitamin link are scarce. At a major referral hospital, the team matched fifty-nine women with the condition to fifty-nine without, pairing them by age, pregnancy stage, and number of previous births.

Blood vitamin D ran significantly lower in the preeclampsia group. Levels classed as suboptimal appeared in about a third of cases but in fewer than one in fourteen controls. Adjusted analysis confirmed higher odds of the condition among women with low levels. The study cannot prove the vitamin shortfall helps cause the disorder, but it strengthens the case for testing whether screening or supplementation in African pregnancies would prevent cases.
plos-pone-0359281:
Michael A Incze leads a team of eight describing a planned trial on hospital discharge for people with substance use disorders, in PLOS ONE in 2026. A hospital stay is a rare chance to start addiction treatment, yet many patients lose contact with care within days of leaving. The IntACT study tests a team based bridge: primary care clinicians meet patients in the hospital and keep following them after discharge.

The pilot will enroll seventy-five admitted patients at one site and assign them by chance to the team or to usual care. The team then supports each patient for four months, working on linkage to follow up medical and addiction care. Researchers will judge reach, acceptability, cost, and early signs of benefit over six months. The protocol lays groundwork for a larger trial if the model proves workable.
plos-pone-0359881:
Natnapa Heebkaew Padchasuwan and colleagues built and checked a new survey in 2026 that measures how well university students in Thailand handle sexual health facts. The skill has a name: sexual health literacy. It means being able to find facts about sexual health, grasp them, and use them well. Thailand had no survey made for this task among its own students.

The team's tool is known by the short name SHL-US. They put it through the standard checks that show a survey is sound: that its questions hang together and that scores stay steady. A sound tool lets schools spot which students are left in the dark. It also shows whether health classes truly raise what students know.
plos-pone-0359981:
Yifan Gu published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies cultural sustainability in Qing dynasty China, between 1644 and 1911. The lens is kinship networks, and the evidence is marriage strategies among literary lineages, families known for producing scholars and writers across generations.

The analysis is quantitative, counting and modeling how these families chose marriage partners. Marriages could spread a family's influence, guard its status, or keep literary culture alive through hard times. Historians of China and of family strategy gain a measured view of how elite culture reproduced itself for nearly three centuries.
plos-pone-0360081:
Mohsen Hesami, Mohammad Rahbari, and Ron Salzman studied in 2026 how maize plants change their gene activity after treatment with a natural biostimulant mixture. The mixture combines quillaja extract, from the bark of a South American tree, with fulvic acid, a substance from decomposed organic matter. Biostimulants are sold to help crops grow and withstand stress without being fertilizers themselves.

The authors track the plant's transcriptional responses, which genes switch on or off, over time and in response to particular stimuli. A time resolved picture shows whether the mixture triggers a quick alarm, a lasting adjustment, or both. Such evidence helps separate biostimulants that genuinely prime the plant from those riding on marketing, a live question in farm supply.
pmc-10364581:
Members of the GBD 2021 Diabetes group report how diabetes spread across the world from 1990 to 2021. Diabetes now ranks among the top causes of death and disability on the planet. It harms people in every country, at every age, and in both sexes.

Using the newest data and methods from the Global Burden of Disease study, the team built estimates for each country and region. They also project how common diabetes may become by the year 2050. Health leaders use such counts to plan care, set budgets, and judge whether prevention work is paying off.
pmc-10703881: Okhovat and co-authors study TADs, the folded blocks that organize DNA inside the cell nucleus. The borders of these blocks, called boundaries, help control which genes switch on. The team compares TAD boundary traits and jobs across mammals to trace how they evolved. Their work shows wide diversity in boundary properties and function, rather than one fixed pattern for all species.
pmc-10707381:
Anna Hrabia and four co-authors report a lab study, published in twenty twenty-three, on how vitamin D3 acts in the egg-laying parts of hens. The team looked at two receptor proteins and two enzymes that build up or break down the vitamin. They checked the ovary, the shell gland, and three other organs.

The group found both receptors in these tissues, with levels that shift as egg follicles grow. The two enzymes were also present, spread across the layers of the follicle wall and the glands of the shell gland. The authors say hen breeding tissues can make and switch off vitamin D3 on their own. That local supply may help run the ovary and the shell gland.
pmc-10738281:
Sheikh Hossain and seven colleagues report a mixed methods pilot study of how veterans with chronic conditions experienced COVID-19. The study ran from December 2021 to January 2023 at two contrasting Veterans Administration settings in New York, one rural and one urban. Forty veterans took part in interviews that included co-created journey maps of their care.

A quarter of the journeys showed an intense COVID-19 reaction, beginning with shock, fear, or extreme distress. Most of that group had a mental health diagnosis, and their paths afterward diverged. Some felt better over time, while others described lasting effects on routines and views of the world. The group also used more outpatient and virtual care, with mixed feelings about virtual visits.
pmc-10738881:
Ethan Siu Leung Cheung studies how neighborhood characteristics relate to sleep problems in older Americans, in twenty twenty-three. Area effects on late-life health are well shown. Sleep quality, though, has got little notice in that past work. Cheung uses longitudinal survey rounds with more than four thousand adults aged sixty-five and older.

Physical disorder in an area went with sleep problems in cross-sectional analysis. Social cohesion was linked to sleep problems both at one time point and over time. Health habits and mental health strongly mediated the cohesion and sleep link. The side effect faded as time passed, however. Findings suggest both area disorder and cohesion shape late-life sleep. Cheung also notes how older adults adapt to adverse settings, next to long-term gains of tight-knit areas.
pmc-10741081:
Jiri Muller and seven co-authors aim to clear up myths about lactate, a molecule long cast as a mere waste product of cells short on oxygen. Lactate was first found in sour milk long ago and later tied to shock states. The article came out in twenty twenty-three.

The authors stress that cells make and use lactate at all times, even with full oxygen, and in large amounts. High blood lactate is a warning sign, yet not all such cases are life threats, and some grave cases show none. Lactate alone does not cause acid build up, is not toxic, and has many helpful roles. Reading high values takes more care than is often shown.
pmc-10743381:
Daniel Dubinski and thirteen co-authors test whether a jaw muscle's thickness on a head scan can flag frailty after brain injury. Temple muscle thickness has been floated as a quick scan sign of a patient's base strength. The team read scans and records of 193 patients admitted with traumatic brain injury. They split patients by thickness and compared injury severity and outcomes.

Patients with thicker muscle had more bleeding inside the skull, yet they scored better at six months. Thin muscle went with falls and poorer scores. The paper backs the measure as an objective frailty sign that may help forecast recovery, though its link to bleeding needs care in reading.
pmc-10743681:
Alexander Kalinin, Ekaterina Zubkova, and Mikhail Menshikov review a stress pathway that may drive cell aging. Their review, from twenty twenty-three, covers the integrated stress response. This ancient network reacts to cell stress by pausing most protein making. A few key proteins still get made, and they steer the cell's next moves.

Senescent cells stop dividing for good and pile up with age. They lack clean markers, which blocks drugs that would clear them. The authors argue the stress pathway sits near the center of that state. It also runs cleanup programs and guards the cell's power units. Its partner proteins and known modulators are mapped in detail.
pmc-10772681:
Ohm, Khwaja, and Karachiwala report three liver cancer patients who got immune therapy before a liver transplant. Their cancer could not be removed by surgery, and transplant was the only cure path. Immune drugs help advanced cases live longer, but data before transplant were scarce.

Patients got one of two drug pairs before their transplants. One patient's tumor load fell by 45 percent, while another stayed stable. No graft rejection or poor wound healing showed up after surgery. All three were transplanted with strong graft function at last check. The authors say such drugs may extend transplant eligibility.
pmc-11571681:
Estela Kobashigawa and eight co-authors compare four tests for chronic wasting disease in white tailed deer, a fatal prion ill of deer kind. Current diagnosis rests on lab stain tests of brain stem or throat glands. The study came out in twenty twenty-four.

The team ran two antibody tests, a seed based test, and a chip based sensor on gland samples from known sick and healthy deer, in equal groups. Both antibody tests called every sample right, though one varied more within runs. The chip sensor also called all samples right and caught sick samples even at strong dilution. The seed test was weighed on the same set.
pmc-11571881:
Mbuh and co-authors mine ten years of drug-resistant tuberculosis records from Cameroon's Littoral region. Drug resistance limits TB cure options and threatens control worldwide. In 2022, resistant cases in Cameroon were 1.4 percent of new cases and 8.3 percent of retreatment cases.

Records from 2013 to 2022 were checked for quality, then sorted into four resistance classes. Classes ran from rifampicin-resistant up to extensively drug-resistant disease. The team tracked trends, patient profiles, and treatment outcomes against an eighty percent success goal. Statistical models hunted risk factors tied to poor outcomes, to guide program fixes.
pmc-11576981:
Lennart Seizer, Estefanía Martínez-Albert, and Johanna Löchner published a psychology study in two thousand twenty-four on body clocks and depression. People differ in whether they peak early or late in the day. Late types are known to report more depression, but the link may bend and vary by symptom.

The team analysed a national United States health survey of over five thousand adults. Depression scores were lowest for a sleep midpoint near three in the morning and rose toward both extremes. Different symptoms tied to body clock in different patterns. A blood inflammation marker did not explain the link. The authors call for long-term studies to sort out cause and effect.
pmc-11603981:
Birye Mekonnen and others pooled maternity care studies from sub-Saharan Africa in 2024. Full mother care spans pregnancy to childhood. It cuts mother and newborn deaths. Completion rates stay low in the region. Whether the pregnancy was planned was the factor tested. Planned and unplanned pregnancies were set side by side.

Intended pregnancy raised completion odds a lot. The pooled effect was clear in the stats. Planning support may lift care completion. Care before pregnancy needs to be stronger, they argue. Birth control advice should expand as well. Fewer unplanned pregnancies would follow. Clinics and policy makers share that task. Listed review methods support the findings.
pmc-11605881:
Mohamed A A Abdella and Gamil E Ibrahim use farm waste to grow an enzyme that breaks down cellulose. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. The enzyme comes from a new strain of a common soil bacterium, found and named by the team. Such enzymes can clear apple juice and raise its yield.

They tune the growth mix with two rounds of planned tests. Corn cob waste serves as the carbon source, which cuts cost and reuses waste. The tuned mix boosts enzyme output many times over. Juice treated with the enzyme gives a much higher yield than plain juice. They also check how the enzyme shifts scent compounds and health-linked traits in the juice.
pmc-11608481:
Amir Jalali and seven co-authors published a scale validation study in twenty twenty-four producing a Persian version of the Coronary Artery Disease Empowerment Scale. Feeling capable of managing one's heart disease matters for outcomes, but Iranian clinicians had no instrument to measure that empowerment. The team translated the scale and tested it in Kermanshah patients.

Forward and backward translation produced the Persian text. Exploratory analysis in one hundred ninety patients and confirmatory analysis in three hundred forty-four more supported a three-factor structure with twenty-five items. Fit statistics were strong, and test-retest and internal consistency checks passed. The authors offer Iranian care teams a validated tool for tracking patient empowerment through treatment.
pmc-11611081:
Himani Shree Pokharel, Julia Morgan, and two co-authors study sex work among transgender women in Nepal. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, mixes a survey with deep interviews. Transgender women face high exposure to sex work and infection risk. One hundred fifty-two women in the Kathmandu Valley took the survey, and seventeen gave interviews.

About two-thirds currently sell sex, the survey finds. Schooling, wealth, housing, and past harm all link to that work. Interview themes sort stigma into silence, shame, and treatment by others. Money need and exclusion from other jobs drive entry. The authors call for support that cuts both poverty and stigma.
pmc-11611481:
Robert Manske and four colleagues wrote a hands-on guide for rehab staff who scan the front of the hip with ultrasound. The iliopsoas, the deep muscle and tendon that lift the thigh, is often to blame in hip pain. It can drive tendon pain, snapping hip, and strains. Its deep spot makes it hard to check by hand or by eye. Sound-wave scans are safe, cheap, and show the tissue while it moves.

The guide walks through the anatomy first, then scan technique step by step. It shows what healthy and sore tissue look like, and how scans can track whether rehab is working. Findings covered include tendon disease and fluid-filled sacs near the joint. For clinics, the twenty twenty-four paper makes the case that a scan at the bedside can sort out front-hip pain fast, without sending the patient off for costlier imaging.
pmc-11614281:
Katherine Marougka and colleagues show that a human cell protein, BST2 or tetherin, can block respiratory syncytial virus, a top cause of severe lung infection in young children. The protein is known for trapping other viruses at the cell surface. The team dialed its levels up and down in infected cells.

Silencing the protein raised virus output, while extra protein cut it. The protein sat with virus coats and threads, as if pinning new virus in place. The virus fights back by lowering the protein, and a strain missing one of its genes, NS1, could not do so and suffered most. The authors name NS1 the virus's counter-weapon.
pmc-11614981:
Honglian Luo and Yun Shen test if a blood mark read from gene-set marks can foretell death. Their study, from two thousand twenty-four, draws on a land-wide health survey.

The mark, a growth factor, rises in many body states, and high blood levels tie to high death risk. But if the mark read off gene switches does the same was dim. The team took survey data from a past span of years. A model gave each one's mark from their gene-set reads. Risk models then weighed death from all causes and from heart ills. Bend tests checked the dose shape, and group splits tested the firmness of the link.
pmc-11618481:
Kenneth Shinozuka and six colleagues combine three large reviews on psychedelic drugs, covering drug action, brain scans, and felt experience, in a twenty twenty-four paper. These drugs show promise for depression and addiction, yet how they work is not settled. The team pooled studies on three classic drugs: LSD, psilocybin, and DMT.

At mid and high doses, LSD scored higher than psilocybin on visionary change scales. Brain scans showed the drugs loosen links inside brain networks while strengthening links between them. At the receptor level, LSD drove one signal more strongly than the others. Each drug left its own fingerprint at each level, but the levels did not line up in a simple way. The authors flag uneven study quality.
pmc-11621581:
Alice Zhao and fourteen co-authors map a molecular switchboard that decides whether starved-of-oxygen cells clean up their mitochondria or die. Removing damaged mitochondria, called mitophagy, is part of adapting to hypoxia. A tagging system based on SUMO proteins turns out to govern the process, generally holding it back.

The team found the de-tagging enzyme SENP3 and the mitochondrial protein FIS1 form the key axis promoting hypoxia-induced mitophagy. When FIS1 carries the SUMO tag it recruits a brake protein, TBC1D17, that suppresses the cleanup. Removing the tag releases that brake. Cells with the axis intact survived oxygen deprivation better. The pathway offers several points where drugs might protect tissue during hypoxic injury.
pmc-11624581:
Virginia Wang and five co-authors track insurance and spending for Americans starting dialysis after the Affordable Care Act. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. Medicare pays for most kidney failure care at any age, but new private options from the Act's marketplace may have slowed Medicare sign-up.

The team followed Colorado patients aged eighteen to sixty-four who were not on Medicare when dialysis began, across twenty twelve to twenty seventeen. Over two thousand patients were included, most in their late forties to early sixties. The study logged which coverage each took in the first year: Medicare, Medicaid, or private plans. It also compared dialysis spending by coverage type. The trends show how a big insurance reform reshaped the start of kidney care.
pmc-11635581:
Jing and co-authors test a scope-based thyroid surgery that can also clear hidden neck nodes. Spread to side neck nodes worsens outlook in papillary thyroid cancer. Scans often miss small hidden deposits before surgery. The team used a route behind the sternocleidomastoid muscle at Beijing Tongren Hospital. They checked 142 patients treated from late 2022 to mid 2024.

After clear cases were set aside, 33 of 134 patients had hidden side node spread. That rate was 24.6 percent of the group. Most of those tumors were small and sat in the mid or upper thyroid. Over a median 17 months of follow-up, the report tracks how the method found and removed disease that scans had missed.
pmc-11641381:
Ya-Lun Yang and colleagues report a 2024 study on training nurse practitioners for emergency care. These nurses often act as first responders when a patient crashes. The team tested a hands-on learning method, where trainees practice real tasks and get one-on-one coaching right after.

The study ran at a teaching hospital in southern Taiwan with ninety-five nurse practitioners and trainees. Each person took a three-minute emergency drill, then got coaching, then repeated the drill at once and again a month later. Skill scores jumped after coaching and stayed well above the starting point a month on. Belief in their own ability also held up. The authors argue that short, guided practice drills can build lasting emergency skill.
pmc-11642681:
Maria Velliou and ten co-authors count a stiff heart protein ill in folks at the ER with sharp heart fail and thick walls. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Of one hundred twenty-seven such folks, ninety-five made the full test run of blood checks and bone scans. Six months of fate checks ran too.

The protein ill sat in near one in twelve folks. Their pump shares spread through all three fail kinds. Blood marks ran high past the rest. Deaths hit the ill pack far more in the span. Plain blood and sound reads can raise the call at the ER door, the team say.
pmc-11643981:
Na-Ra Han and others put out a 2024 lab study of a plant compound that calms swelling. The compound, tryptanthrin, comes from indigo plants. It hit a signaling protein sent out by neutrophils. That protein drives several swelling responses. Two cell systems were used for testing.

Human-like neutrophil cells were triggered by chemicals. Mouse bone marrow neutrophils backed the effect. The compound lowered the protein's output and gene activity. It blocked a three-step signaling chain inside the cells. Less of that signal means possible therapy value. Natural compounds with defined ways deserve work as future drugs.
pmc-11644081:
Jiří Masojídek and colleagues measured algae growth in a pilot pond in 2024. The pond was a shallow raceway inside a greenhouse. The test alga is a common green species used in production. The team tracked photosynthesis directly inside the living culture. Light, temperature, and dissolved oxygen were logged too. Sensors probed several depths in the pond. Fluorescence and oxygen output both gauged active photosynthesis. Lab checks outside the pond added comparison.

Even in thin cultures, light reached only a shallow top layer. Most cells sat below that layer, photosynthetically idle. Cells drifting down faced another problem. Their glare-protection response reacted too slowly to depth changes. Very high oxygen levels built up in the water. Cultures still kept decent efficiency under that stress. The authors offer the data as a design guide. Pond depth and cell density must match light supply. Better mixing regimes could raise yields at scale.
pmc-11645981:
Kuan-Hsien Wu and colleagues associate habitual tea consumption with lower kidney stone prevalence in postmenopausal women. Their 2024 study draws over eleven thousand women from a national biobank with questionnaire data on tea, stones, and comorbidities.

About two thousand women drank tea habitually; the rest did not. Mean age was sixty-one. Stone prevalence was lower in tea drinkers, five percent versus seven percent. After adjustment, habitual tea drinking carried a stone odds ratio of about zero point seven eight. Women drinking two or more cups daily showed a thirty percent lower risk than non-drinkers. The authors suggest habitual tea intake may help postmenopausal women avoid kidney stones.
pmc-11646281:
Guifang Liu and colleagues take a lesson from tree roots to print circuits that hug curved surfaces and refuse to break, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Electronics on freeform shapes, for robots and smart skins, usually fail by tearing, cracking, or peeling in service. Roots solve the same problem underground: they grip.

Their printing method confines ink in a template while adhesive soaks into the functional material, rooting the circuit to its base. Printed lines reached three hundred nanometer resolution, a fineness rare in such printing. The circuits kept conducting through scratching, abrasion, and folding, and even through baking at three hundred fifty degrees. The method suits many inks and any substrate shape. Demonstrations include a body-hugging temperature and humidity sensor and a paper-thin wearable energy store. The authors pitch rooted printing as the reliability fix conformal electronics need.
pmc-11647681:
A research team hunts non covalent blockers of a SARS-CoV-2 enzyme. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with the papain like protease. The enzyme aids virus growth and immune evasion.

A virtual screen ranked compounds from an in house library. Eighty-one hits went to enzyme and binding tests. One modest blocker held a naphthyridine core at its center. Thirty analogs of that core were made and tested. Three stood out as promising non covalent blockers. Their strength sat in a mid range band. Drug like traits were checked in lab assays too.
pmc-11658381:
Mercy Mumba and colleagues lay out a trial of job support for veterans recovering from opioid addiction, in this protocol paper from twenty twenty-four. Work is tightly bound to recovery, yet veterans with opioid use disorder face steep barriers to jobs and to civilian life. The support model, Individual Placement and Support, is proven in severe mental illness but new in addiction care.

The study is a two-arm randomized trial across several veterans' hospitals, comparing the job program against usual care. It will track work outcomes first, and also mental health, substance use, and quality of life. The paper reports who has enrolled so far and their starting profile. The timing matters: the veterans' system has just widened this program to substance use clinics. The authors say the results should decide whether the expansion deserves to stay.
pmc-11662181:
Emmanuelle Bostock and her team read web forums where people with bipolar disorder tell of setting off mania on purpose. Their study from twenty twenty-four digs through posts by people who live with it. Case reports had told of self-induction, but ways and motives were not written down. Forums give a frank view that doctors seldom see.

Forty-four talk threads came up through set search steps. Hundreds of posts by hundreds of site handles filled those threads. Posts were coded for ways to set mania off and for motives told in them. Talk of mania and of its milder form, hypomania, both came up. People told of working their own known triggers on purpose. Motives ran from a wish to know, to getting more done, to pleasure. Doctors may need to ask about this act head-on.
pmc-11671981:
Elly L Sjattar, Rosyidah Arafat, and Lee Wan Ling present a two thousand twenty-four scoping review of self-management interventions for cancer pain in adults. Care increasingly happens at home, leaving patients to manage pain themselves. What programs exist to help them, and in what forms, needed mapping.

Six databases were searched for a decade of English-language studies. Twenty-three studies yielded four intervention types. Education was the commonest approach, with coaching and support variants behind it. The reviewers argue guidance should begin during hospital stays and continue after discharge, since pain control at home decides quality of life between visits.
pmc-11674981:
Anna Christakou and colleagues test whether picturing movements in the mind improves life for older adults with early Alzheimer's dementia. In Athens, 160 people were split three ways: exercise plus mental imagery, exercise only, or neither. The program ran across twenty-four sessions over twelve weeks.

The imagery group pictured the movements in their minds for thirty minutes after each exercise session. Tests found clear differences between groups on walking-while-talking performance, quality of life, depression, and anxiety measures. Most of the people were women, with memory loss as their first symptom. The trial presents guided practice of this kind as a cheap, safe add-on to exercise therapy in early dementia care.
pmc-11676581:
Tanja Bipp, Serena Wee, Marvin Walczok, and Laura Hansal published a meta-analysis in twenty twenty-four on game-based tests of thinking skill. Games are used to assess people, but it is not clear if they tap the same skill as standard tests. The team pooled fifty-two samples from forty-four papers, with over six thousand one hundred adults.

Game scores and test scores were linked, with a raw match of point three zero and a corrected match of point four five. The link was stronger when skill was gauged by more than one test. It did not depend on whether the test was on a computer or on paper. Games built to test skill fared no better than games built for other aims. The authors say game tests tap thinking skill but may also tap other traits.
pmc-11678881:
Nine researchers led by Jin Young Hong review how animal models are used to study diseases of the spinal discs. The review covers disc bulging, disc wear, and narrowing of the spinal canal in the lower back. Animal work lets scientists run controlled tests, watch disease unfold over time, and try new treatments.

The authors weigh clear gains against real limits. Animals differ from humans, study rules vary, lives are short, and ethics matter. New work adds better scans, gene-based models, and force tests to close the gap. Their message is that animal results are useful, but must be read with their limits firmly in mind.
pmc-11688381:
Lu, Xu, and Zhu mine United States drug safety reports for drugs linked to clotting disorders. Coagulopathies can cause dangerous bleeding or clots, and some are triggered by medication. Finding high-risk drugs early helps doctors protect patients who need those treatments.

The team pulled reports tied to coagulopathies from the FDA adverse event system, covering early 2004 to mid-2024. They used signal methods such as the reporting odds ratio and proportional reporting ratio. Strong signals flag drug and event pairs that occur more than expected. The results guide safer prescribing and closer watch on risky drugs.
pmc-11710581:
Hung-Wei Lee, Chia-Fang Cheng, Yi-Hsuan Wang, and Ya-Ning Chang build a speech-based test, published in 2025, to spot Alzheimer disease in Chinese speakers. Speech and language often worsen with the disease. Computer methods that listen to speech could screen people cheaply and might work across languages. The team used a deep learning model already trained on large amounts of speech.

Speech came from a picture description task done by eighty-one native Chinese speakers in Taiwan. The group held healthy controls and patients with early disease. Recordings were cut into six-second clips, and the groups were balanced by sampling. Sound features from the pre-trained model fed a small classifier. Test accuracy passed eighty-one percent, with matched scores for catching cases and avoiding false alarms. The authors say the model is promising and want to learn which sound traits drive its choices.
pmc-11710781:
Tong and co-authors hunt gene spots whose effect on Alzheimer's risk changes with age, across ancestry groups. Age is the largest risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease. Over eighty gene spots are known, but how their effects shift with age was little known beyond APOE.

The study used consortium gene data for nearly fifty thousand people aged sixty and up. Groups covered white, African American, East Asian, and Caribbean Hispanic roots. People were split at age seventy-five into younger and older bands. Models tested each variant's tie to disease times age. Both mixed-group and single-group runs sought new age-linked spots.
pmc-11713181:
Maria Juanita Arbelaez and colleagues reported early trial results in 2025 for a cannabis-derived drug tested in Alzheimer's patients who experience psychosis. About half of Alzheimer's patients develop delusions or hallucinations, yet cannabis is also a known psychosis risk in young people, so safety needed care. The drug, IGC-AD1, combines a low dose of THC with melatonin. Thirteen patients, average age over eighty, joined this first-phase multiple-dose trial.

Three cohorts took the drug once, twice, or three times daily for fourteen days, with washout periods between cohorts. The researchers tracked psychosis symptoms using standard inventory scores for delusions and hallucinations. A phase one trial this small mainly tests tolerability, not effectiveness. Still, any signal on psychosis symptoms in this fragile population draws attention, because current antipsychotics carry heavy risks for dementia patients.
pmc-12208381:
Linfu Zheng and twelve co-authors test if a dental rubber band pull helps trainees learn colon scope cuts. Their trial head is dated twenty twenty-four. The cut, which peels sick pads from the gut wall, is hard and slow to learn. Past work showed band pull cuts case time for trainees and masters alike.

Near one hundred eighty patients were split by lot to trainee-with-band, trainee-plain, or master-plain cuts. Band trainees matched masters on time and beat plain trainees by a lot. Speed, view, and muscle harm marks matched masters too. Harm and full-cut rates tied across groups. Learn bends bent early with the band.
pmc-12692681:
Osmond and coauthors review a cell therapy idea for progressive multiple sclerosis. Illness progression touches many patients, even without a progressive label. Current drugs treat that progression quite poorly. New options are badly due for those patients.

The plan builds regulator T cells with a built receptor. Those cells calm swelling and may aid nerve healing. Their target is a nerve protein called beta-synuclein. A common gene variant in patients presents that target. Built cells would switch on right in inflamed brain tissue. Early proof backs tests, but trials are still due.
pmc-12722481:
Liying Zhu and colleagues tested a classic herbal decoction for constipation in 2025. Functional constipation has no single clear cause. The formula has long clinical use reports. Its mechanism was still unclear though. Patients served as their own controls here.

Symptoms eased after taking the decoction. One harmful gut group shrank clearly. Helpful short-chain fatty acids rose instead. A gut signal pathway was suppressed. That pathway was linked to imbalance. Two helpful species gained ground notably. The authors call results preliminary still. Larger controlled trials are now needed. Gut balance sits at the centre here.
pmc-12731381:
Mirlinda Sopi Krasniqi and colleagues measure inflammatory markers before and after non-surgical gum therapy across periodontitis stages and grades. Their 2025 study uses patient records from a university dentistry centre in Kosovo.

Disease was classified with the twenty eighteen staging and grading system, covering pocket depth, attachment loss, bleeding, plaque, and gum indices. Blood levels of four inflammatory markers, including C-reactive protein and interleukin six, were measured before and after treatment. Patients were spread across stages, with stage three most common, and across grades, with grade B most common. All received standardised scaling and root planing without systemic antibiotics.
pmc-12732981:
Ana Garcia and a large team of colleagues feed whiteleg shrimp a prebiotic extract made from a salt-loving plant and watch their guts respond. The xylooligosaccharide extract from Salicornia ramosissima went into feed at two doses for a fourteen-day trial, followed by a challenge with a pathogenic Vibrio bacterium.

Growth and gene expression barely moved, but the higher dose enriched gut microbial diversity and boosted known shrimp symbionts such as Ruegeria and Leisingera. The extract also shifted gut protein regulation. Stressful challenge conditions altered these effects, the authors caution. They call for longer studies on whether the prebiotic genuinely improves disease resistance in farmed shrimp.
pmc-12733381:
Carlson and co-authors test whether vaccines can protect mice against fungal strains taken from patients in Africa and Asia. Cryptococcus neoformans kills over 100,000 people a year, mostly through meningitis in people with weak immunity. No licensed fungal vaccine exists. Past tests used lab strains, which may not match the strains that sicken people worldwide. The team used six strains from patients in Vietnam, Uganda, and Botswana.

Mice received one of two vaccines, including a weakened live strain. They were then exposed to each clinical strain. The study checks whether protection holds across real-world variety. Broad coverage matters most where the disease burden is highest.
pmc-12738881:
Hiroshi Kameda and colleagues traced a Parkinson's-linked protein in mouse brains in two thousand twenty-five. Clumps of alpha-synuclein spread between neurons. They damage each cell they enter. Whether all neuron types collect clumps equally was unknown. The team injected prepared fibers into one brain region. Staining tracked clumps at set times afterward.

Clumps appeared in several connected regions within weeks. Some sat near the cell nucleus. Striatum cell bodies held far fewer clumps than cortex. Support cells rarely contained clumps at all. Transmitter type seemed to shape accumulation. Selective vulnerability may explain Parkinson's uneven damage pattern. That insight could guide protective strategies.
pmc-12747081:
Sakaorat Petchyim, Supredee Pongrujikorn, Felix Lizarondo, and Woraphong Manuskiatti report an eye tumor arising in a patient with a birthmark type called nevus of Ota. Their case report was published in twenty twenty-five, the first such pairing described in Thai patients.

The patient lost sight slowly and painlessly in the left eye, on the same side as the birthmark. Over seven months the sight worsened until a detached retina was found. A deeper exam and ultrasound then revealed a melanoma in the eye's middle layer. The patient refused removal of the eye. Later the tumor caused a painful pressure crisis as it blocked fluid drainage. Tissue study explained how the tumor drove that secondary glaucoma. The case urges doctors to watch such birthmarks for hidden cancer.
pmc-12749481: A correction notice from twenty twenty-five fixes the author list of a study led by Elizabeth M Kline. The study was about a protein linked to Parkinson's disease and harm in mice. The notice says Fredric P Manfredsson was left off the author list by mistake. It also fixes the section that says who did each part of the work. The name is now added there as well. The notice does not change the results or the claims of the study itself.
pmc-12751481:
Fauste and co-authors study how a low-calorie sweetener affects rat offspring of mothers fed fructose in pregnancy. Maternal fructose intake is known to harm progeny, yet the sugar is not barred during pregnancy. Sweeteners such as tagatose are used more and more as sugar substitutes in foods.

The team fed tagatose or fructose to offspring and tracked fat metabolism. Male offspring of fructose-fed mothers developed features of metabolic syndrome on tagatose. That outcome is a warning against assuming sweeteners are safe swaps. The study shows how maternal diet and later sweetener use can interact.
pmc-12751581:
Henry Abumohor and five co-authors report bowel surgery done while the patient stayed awake, in a case report published in twenty twenty-five. The patient, a seventy-three-year-old man in Palestine, had a twisted sigmoid colon that kept coming back. His heart was weak, his kidneys were failing, and lung problems made general anesthesia very risky.

Doctors from surgery, heart care, and anesthesia chose a steady spinal block instead of putting him to sleep. He stayed conscious and stable while the twisted bowel section was removed. Recovery went well apart from a shallow wound infection treated with simple care. Six months later he ate normally, had no new blockage, and the wound had healed fully. The team calls the approach workable for fragile patients.
pmc-12752781:
Prakika leads a large team comparing lab methods to name a resistant bacterium, in work from twenty twenty-five. The Acinetobacter baumannii complex causes hard to treat infections. Fast, exact naming guides therapy, since drug options are few.

Forty isolates from Thailand, first named by classic biochemical tests, were rechecked. A mass spectrometry method was compared with the biochemical method. Whole genome sequencing served as the reference truth. Retrospective accuracy for each method was then scored. The study shows which routine method labs can trust for this complex, where species level errors can mislead care.
pmc-12756781:
Azizah Aldosari, Awwad Radwan, and Gamal Mahrous lead a team building a color-based assay for the stomach drug famotidine using a charge-transfer partner. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Famotidine treats reflux and ulcers and needs cheap quality checks. Pairing it with bromanil forms a colored complex that light measurements can read.

The team tuned the reaction's timing, temperature, and proportions for stability. The assay read drug amounts linearly with excellent precision across repeats and days. It worked on commercial tablets as well. Quantum chemistry calculations backed the bench results, confirming the charge-transfer bond. Stabilizing factors in the complex were identified. The authors pitch the method as economical and reproducible. It needs only common lab gear. Such assays suit quality control where fancy instruments are scarce.
pmc-12770481:
Amin Zadehnazari and colleagues built light-driven catalyst frameworks in two thousand twenty-five. Their goal was making hydrogen peroxide with sunlight. Peroxide is a clean, valuable oxidant. Metal-free catalysts for its production remain a challenge. The team linked two organic building blocks into crystals. One block donates electrons, and the other accepts them.

Both frameworks produced peroxide at high rates under visible light. One version slightly outperformed the other. Fast spectroscopy showed long-lived excited states. Charge separation inside the framework explains the activity. The materials stayed stable during use. Chemists gain a design rule for solar chemical production. Donor and acceptor pairing does the heavy lifting.
pmc-12776181:
Tongxin Zhang and colleagues published a medical study in 2025 on a rare and fast-growing cancer of the adrenal glands. The team looked back at past patients treated at one hospital in China. They asked whether simple blood counts taken before surgery could help predict how long patients would live.

Inside, the records cover a small group followed over many years. A high ratio of two kinds of white blood cells pointed to shorter survival, even after other risks were counted. High hormone levels from the tumor raised that ratio but did not by themselves predict survival. Readers get a low-cost way to flag higher-risk cases.
pmc-12789881:
Jideofor Okoye and six colleagues systematically reviewed bone grafting for a wrist bone that fails to heal and loses its blood supply. Scaphoid nonunion with avascular necrosis is a surgical challenge because dead bone heals poorly. Graft bone can come from the nearby radius, carrying its own blood vessels, or from the iliac crest of the pelvis. Five studies covering 262 patients compared the two donor sites.

Radius grafts united faster, in roughly eight months, and restored anatomy better. Hip grafts gave strong structural support but cost more pain, gait problems, nerve injury, and scarring. Function ended similar once union was achieved, though radius grafts edged ahead on wrist alignment. The twenty twenty-five review recommends the vascularized radius graft first, reserving hip bone for cases needing bulk.
pmc-12812581:
Hao and co-authors show that dominant TET2 mutations spell worse outlook in a leukemia type. The cohort held 206 adults with cytogenetically normal AML. TET2 faults appeared in 18.9 percent of patients. Those patients were older, with a median age of 55. Fault share by volume did not split survival.

Patients whose TET2 fault was dominant fared worse. Their survival and relapse-free spans ran shorter. The dominant fault stood as an independent risk factor. A chart model from the data scored 0.735 on curve tests. A public Beat AML data set confirmed the pattern.
pmc-12816581:
A large team including Xiaoyun Wang reports a new way to find weak drug-like binders for proteins. Many proteins are thought too hard to drug, and weak binders are easy to miss. The new method tests mirror-image pairs of compounds at once, so it can spot binding, tell which mirror form binds, and confirm the hit in one pass. After trials on known proteins, the team screened thirty-one human proteins against a library of more than eight thousand chiral compounds.

They found sixteen binders across twelve targets, and seven binders favored one mirror form. X-ray work on four targets showed why. The paper offers the method as a fast route to fresh leads.
pmc-12825281:
Nishat Khan and seven co-authors check a hand glucose meter against a lab test in Indian adults at a large hospital. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Self checks of blood sugar are core to diabetes care for their cheap, quick, and home use. Paired finger and vein blood from more than one hundred inpatients were read by both ways.

Meter reads ran a clear span low against lab reads. Just four in ten reads met the strict world mark for truth. Yet near all reads sat in safe zones for care calls on a grid check. Most gaps would not change care, but the team urges care with sick ICU folks. More checks are due.
pmc-12827481:
John Hellgren leads a large team that built a fast screen for drug-caused liver injury, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. Liver harm from new drugs is a top reason drug projects fail late and at great cost. Their tool, called AEGIS, reads how a drug shifts genes that govern cell death in liver cells after short exposure. It then gives each drug and dose a risk score.

The screen sorted drugs by known liver risk with high marks for both catching harm and clearing safe drugs. It worked across human cells, a liver cell line, immune cells, and mice. Cells from patients with fatty liver disease showed worse harm from one test drug, matching what clinics see. The team says early use could cut animal tests and speed safer drugs to patients.
pmc-12853681:
Emmanuel Kumah and six colleagues reviewed what is known about the cost value of mind care for people living with HIV. Drugs for HIV have changed survival, yet stress and social struggles persist. Mind care improves mental health and adherence, and its worth in care is well shown. Whether it is worth its cost had never been pulled together in one place. The team searched medicine, mind science, and money data banks across 2024.

Three reviewers screened studies on their own, with citation tracking to catch strays. No year limits were set. The review weighs the money evidence study by study. Policy points close the paper, aimed at health systems choosing whether to fund joined mental health care. For programs with tight budgets, proof of cost value can be the gap between pilot projects and lasting services.
pmc-12857581:
Raja Bakhsh and ten co-authors wrote a case-based review in 2025 on two self-attack liver ills that can run side by side. A man of fifty-six with high blood sugar and a weak thyroid gland had belly pain, yellow skin, and cholestatic blood tests. He also had a known case of primary Sjögren's syndrome.

Tests showed high immune proteins in his blood, self-attack marks, and much raised IgG4 counts. Scans found a large liver and swollen spit glands. A flesh sample showed the edge-zone liver sore of autoimmune hepatitis plus whorled scars and dense IgG4 plasma cells, so he met the marks for both ills. Steroids with two immune drugs made him well. Rituximab was weighed as a next step up. They stress flesh tests with IgG4 stain in such mixed cases.
pmc-12859381:
Aisha Ahmed Khan, Zaid Azhar, and Muhammad Amer Awan describe a two thousand twenty-five case report of a rare bone-forming tumour inside a child's eye. Choroidal osteoma can sprout abnormal blood vessels that leak fluid and blur vision. Paediatric cases with this complication are uncommon.

Their thirteen-year-old patient showed a yellow-orange mass at the back of the eye on examination. Ultrasound and layered retinal scans confirmed bone-like tissue with fluid and new vessels. Repeated injections of a vessel-blocking drug over nine months shrank the vessels and dried the fluid. Vision and anatomy both improved under continued monitoring.
pmc-12875281:
Alka Christnacht and three colleagues report three cases of ketamine-assisted psychotherapy for postpartum mood and anxiety disorders, in a case series from two thousand twenty-six. New parents face abrupt hormonal, physical, and role upheavals. The drugs in use act at a slow pace. They find it hard to match the compressed distress of that span.

Ketamine therapy is established in other psychiatric conditions. It has also been explored for preventing postpartum disorders. That work was set around cesarean birth in the past. This retrospective series examines three treated cases in the postpartum period itself. A case series cannot prove efficacy for a treatment. But it can document feasibility, timing, and response patterns. It does so in an underserved population of new parents. Faster-acting options count for a lot here. The window of the disorder is gauged in a newborn's first weeks.
pmc-12883381:
Carolina Elizabeth Olaez-Ramos and her team sift the spread and the find of fat liver ill tied to poor power use in the body, in Latin America. Their 2026 review calls the find of this ill a task yet to be met.

The ill hits more than a third of grown-ups in the world. Latin America shows the most high zone rate, at more than forty-four in each hundred. Fat build, type two diabetes, food rich in stored heat, lack of sport, drink use, and gene lean all meet there. Top tests such as flesh cuts and strong scans cost lots, cut into the body, or can not be had. So it stays missed in lots of folk. The team joins zone data, most of all from Mexico. They check screened tools that do not cut into the body and are backed by tests, for an early find.
pmc-12910481:
Tingting Li leads an eleven-author team investigating gut bacteria and their fatty acid products in a severe pancreatitis variant, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Pancreatitis driven by very high blood triglycerides is on the rise. It carries a poor prognosis for the patients it hits. Its mechanisms remain tangled.

Stool and blood from eighteen patients and eighteen healthy volunteers were compared. Gene sequencing profiled the gut microbes in each sample. Mass spectrometry gauged short-chain fatty acids in the serum of each case. Correlations tied microbes, metabolites, and clinical features into one web. Animal experiments probed mechanisms further. These fatty acids are made by gut bacteria from fiber in food. They calm inflammation in other parts of the body. If a lack of them makes this pancreatitis worse, to restore them is a therapeutic idea worth a test.
pmc-13133781:
Pengfei Jin and David Chenoweth design collagen-like peptides that lock into endless fibres. Their study from twenty twenty-six mimics the body's commonest structural protein. Collagen-mimicking peptides usually clump without order. Specific assembly into clean filaments had eluded designers.

A single side-chain change creates bump-and-gap pairing. Peptides then interlock into triple helices with high specificity. The filaments grow micrometres long and very thin. They network into gels when acidity changes. The gels proved stiffer than natural collagen gels. They also thin under shear, suiting injection uses. Programmable assembly opens custom tissue scaffold design.
pmc-13138281:
Ozge Ozen Gokmuharremoglu and Aysel Coban Taskin studied phone restriction and sleep in two thousand twenty-six. Their setting was a male police college. The college imposed a ten-day smartphone restriction. Young men were grouped by addiction risk scores. Sleep measures came before and after the break.

High-risk users reported longer daily phone use at the start. The team tracked sleep quality, hygiene, insomnia, and daytime sleepiness. Changes across the short break showed which sleep areas respond fast. Real-world restriction evidence remains scarce. This natural experiment fills part of that gap. It also highlights heavy users as a priority group.
pmc-13152181:
Akshay Singh and Stuart Hesketh test whether caffeine lifts women's morning muscle performance to evening levels. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. Strength normally dips in the morning, a rhythm effect that can skew training and testing.

Thirteen healthy women completed three trials: evening placebo, morning placebo, and morning caffeine at a set dose per body weight. Each trial measured maximal knee extension force, then repeated holds to failure, then force again. Evening scores beat morning placebo on peak force and endurance. Morning caffeine not only closed the gap; peak force passed the evening mark before and after fatigue. Brain-muscle signals and effort sense were tracked too. The dose used is high, like several strong coffees.
pmc-13153881:
Haowen Jiang and colleagues build a score that needs no invasive test, to predict post-capillary pulmonary hypertension in a multi-ethnic Asian population. This form is driven by left heart pressures, and the norm test for it is catheterization. Past scores were not well checked in Asian populations. The team built it in a past one-center cohort of patients who had had right heart catheterization.

Patients with low ejection fraction or major left valve disease were left out, leaving 266 patients, of whom 110 had raised wedge pressure confirming post-capillary disease. The POISE model that came out joined four items: body mass index, atrial fibrillation, an ultrasound ratio for filling pressure, and left atrial size. Checks inside the group used bootstrapping, and the score was matched against two past scores. Such a score could spare low-risk patients an invasive step, and fast-track likely cases.
pmc-13164281:
Yin Feng and five colleagues isolate a bacterium from fermented soybean paste in Northeast China and test it as a possible probiotic. Whole-genome sequencing named the strain as Bacillus velezensis M4. Its genome carries the gene marks of nattokinase, an enzyme valued for dissolving blood clots. It also holds many genes for handling carbohydrates and cutting proteins.

Safety checks found no activity that destroys blood, and eight common antibiotics still worked on it. No high-risk virulence genes were found. Bench tests showed tolerance of stomach acid and bile, antioxidant activity, and the ability to inhibit other bacteria. With ninety-eight genes unique to this strain, the authors present M4 as a promising food organism. It combines making enzymes with effects that fight other microbes.
pmc-13189781:
Muhammed Çatal and Seda Mesci test salt treatments on Turkish alfalfa varieties. Their study from twenty twenty-six joins plant measurements with gene activity checks. Alfalfa is a major forage crop with high feed value. Salty soils threaten its growth in many regions.

Seven local cultivars received two different salt solutions. Plant height, stem thickness, and leaf traits were measured before harvest. Gene tests tracked known salt stress responses in the plants. The design separates variety effects from treatment effects. Such comparisons help breeders pick tougher local stock. Sustainable forage output depends on varieties matched to local conditions. The study adds Turkish cultivar data to that selection work.
pmc-13191781:
Ashley Toussaint, Om Panda, and Cheryl Graber present a 2026 case series of doctors who are twice exceptional, or 2e. The term means high brain power combined with conditions such as ADHD that can impair performance in standard settings. The idea is known in schooling but little discussed in medicine.

Five doctors at different career stages are profiled. Their conditions include ADHD, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and a nonverbal learning disorder, alongside strong intellect. Themes repeat across cases. High achievement masked disability. Struggles were misread as poor professionalism. Support came late or never. Some thrived with mentors and structure, while others faced isolation and burnout. The authors urge training settings that affirm brain differences.
pmc-13194381:
Xinhui Yuan and five colleagues build a prediction chart for drug resistance in children with a common lung infection, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. The germ, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, often resists a key antibiotic family when a gene mutates. Knowing resistance early guides drug choice. The team combined chest scan features with blood markers from children split into resistant and sensitive groups.

Resistant cases had longer fevers, longer hospital stays, and more breathing trouble. Their scans more often showed a full lobe of lung clouded and fluid around the lung. Blood inflammation markers ran higher too. The chart built from these signs separated the groups with high accuracy, offering doctors a fast risk read.
pmc-13196681:
Bhakti Hansoti and colleagues describe a 2026 framework for national public health institutes. These institutes are state agencies that lead and coordinate public health work. Many form by merging scattered units, yet weak structure can limit their impact.

The framework has a mapping step plus six modules. The modules cover strategy, partnerships, communication, workforce, finance, and governance, meaning how an agency is led and held to account. Each module starts with a check, then guided steps and good practice notes. Teams run each module as a sprint over three to six months. The tools aim to build skill that lasts through funding shifts and new health threats.
pmc-13197281:
Markus Johansson and colleagues present a 2026 sediment trap that reports hourly online. Sediment traps catch sinking particles in lakes to track flux and content. Classic traps gather samples for months and need costly upkeep, so fine timing is lost.

Their trap uses light-based scanning to gauge sediment volume as it settles, hour by hour. Lab tests showed a mean error of well under one milliliter. A trial unit in a Finnish bay caught short sediment pulses from shore building work. The solar unit sends data wirelessly, cutting field trips. Image handling still needs work for extreme sediment loads. The tool suits remote sites and fast-changing waters.
pmc-13198781:
Ouiam Taibi and colleagues present a 2026 case report on trapped air as a hidden cause of belly pain. Spontaneous pneumomediastinum means air collects around the heart and windpipe with no injury. It is rare and usually starts with chest pain, which makes a belly-pain presentation easy to misread.

Their patient was a 28-year-old man, a chronic smoker, with sudden severe upper belly pain. Exam and lung checks were normal. A belly scan ordered to rule out a burst ulcer found no gut problem. Further imaging instead showed the trapped air plus air under the skin of the neck. No trigger was found. The case warns that chest air leaks can pose as belly emergencies.
pmc-13199181:
Sabiha Farooq and colleagues studied a gene variant tied to obesity and blood chemistry in a 2026 case-control study. Large gene scans have linked TMEM18 to obesity, but its job in the body is unclear. The team asked whether one variant in that gene pairs with body measures and blood metabolites, the small chemicals of metabolism.

They enrolled 542 adults in Pakistan, split between overweight or obese cases and normal-weight controls. Blood DNA and serum chemistry were tested for all. The variant tied to five metabolites and to body mass index, body fat share, waist size, and weight. One version of the variant raised obesity risk. Carriers of two copies showed the clearest metabolite shifts.
pmc-13199681:
Abdalla Ahmed Elbashir and Khalid Malik M Hamid developed a 2026 lab method to measure two livestock dewormers at once. Triclabendazole and levamisole treat worms in cattle and sheep and ship as an oral liquid mix. Quality checks need a fast test that still works as drugs break down.

Their liquid chromatography method separates both drugs in minutes with a simple solvent blend. Validation checks covered accuracy, precision, detection limits, and toughness against small setting changes. Calibration lines stayed straight across wide ranges for both drugs. Stress tests showed breakdown products split cleanly from the real drugs, proving the test flags stale stock. The method now serves routine checks of the suspension.
pmc-13199881:
Priya Sharad and colleagues report a preliminary lab study comparing leaf extracts from four medicinal plants grown in a Homa farming environment with the same plants grown elsewhere. Homa is a traditional practice said by its proponents to clean air and restore natural balance. The plants were curry leaf, tulsi, bael, and neem. Writing in twenty twenty-six, the team made extracts from dried leaves collected in both settings. The team tested them on a cervical cancer cell line. It measured cell killing, cell migration, reactive oxygen inside cells, and activity of selected genes.

By the authors measures, extracts from the Homa-grown plants killed cancer cells at lower doses, raised reactive oxygen more, and slowed migration more than control extracts. Three genes were turned down more strongly as well. The authors present the results as preliminary trends suggesting Homa growing may strengthen the plants medical qualities.
pmc-13200181:
Kobeleva and co-authors offer a broader method for reading time-resolved spectroscopy data. This technique tracks fast physical and chemical change, yet its data mix signals from several species evolving at once. Many analysis tools force shaky math or mechanism guesses onto the data, which skews the results.

Their strategy rests on non-negative matrix factorization, widened to suit more cases. It separates the mixed signals with fewer built-in assumptions about the process under study. Cleaner separation should help chemists follow reacting species over time. The method aims at insight drawn from the data, not from preset models.
pmc-13206981:
Seok Beom Lim and five co-authors test if cutting brow fat pads at the nose side lifts looks in brow lift surgery. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Full brow pads at the nose side come from fat that slips past its sheet, and past brow work oft left them be. Near five hundred patients with at least six months of checks were split into cut and no-cut groups by what was done.
