Fullness was graded from photos on a four-point scale. The cut group eased fullness more, and the edge held past checks for start grade. In mild cases too, cut won. Harm rates stayed low and like in both groups. The team backs the cut as a safe add-on.
pmc-13210981:
George Boateng and eight colleagues teach smartwatches to recognize the emotions of couples managing type 2 diabetes together. Thirteen couples wore watches in daily life. The devices captured speech, heart rate, and motion. That yielded eighty-five hours of recordings, paired with self-reported feelings of pleasantness and arousal.

The machine learning models beat chance. They beat earlier laboratory work with similar couples. They even beat the partners' own guesses about each other's emotions. Balanced accuracy reached about seventy-eight percent for pleasantness. The authors frame the system as a step toward tools that help partners monitor emotional well-being. Such tools could time support interventions during the strain of shared disease management.
pmc-13212581:
Junhyeong Yim and a large team report in 2026 the discovery of a chemical handle on a protein found mainly in muscle. Drug-like molecules called PROTACs destroy target proteins by recruiting cellular disposal machinery, yet the two recruiters in common use act in every tissue.

Virtual screening yielded a binder for the muscle-specific recruiter, and the team built degraders from it. One version destroyed a gene-control protein only in muscle, first weakly and then, after a covalent redesign, at very low doses. The handle also worked against a second target. Tissue-limited degradation could cut side effects elsewhere in the body.
pmc-13213081:
Lalitha A. V. Alekya and colleagues report in 2026 a woman whose true diagnosis hid for sixteen years behind a wrong label. At seventeen she was told her absent periods came from a syndrome involving an underdeveloped womb, and she spent years treated for stubborn acne instead.

Referred at thirty-three after a scan found an adrenal mass, she showed signs of excess male hormones, and gene testing confirmed congenital adrenal hyperplasia, an inherited enzyme defect. Treatment with steroids, hormone blockers, and estrogen supplements brought her first period six months later, at thirty-three. The authors urge full hormone workups for absent periods, since a missed cause can be treatable.
pmc-13215181:
Karina Araslanova and colleagues watch in 2026 as live corals build their skeletons, scanning the same colonies again and again with fine X-ray tools. Most past views came from dead, fixed samples, which freeze one moment and hide how growth unfolds.

Growth turned out to be lively, not a plain layering on of stone. Colonies grew up and out in set patterns. They built walls to fend off neighbours. Their edges probed outward, then at times pulled back. Hurt spots healed with fast, rough fills rather than neat work. Each mode mixed fused grains with sheet-like deposits, set down where tissue had marked the plan first. The scheme should fit other animals that build mineral shells and bones.
pmc-13215981:
Isbi Sotelo and Kevin R. Olsen present a 2026 case report on anaesthetic care for a patient with hereditary spastic paraplegia, a rare inherited disorder causing progressive leg weakness and stiffness. Only eight earlier case reports guide anaesthetists facing this condition.

Their patient, a 71-year-old man with the pure form of the disease, needed a kidney tumour freezing procedure while lying face down. The team used standard general anaesthesia with a nondepolarizing muscle relaxant reversed by sugammadex, and the procedure went smoothly. Because the pure form affects upper motor neurons and spares the junction where relaxants act, the authors argue that extensive changes to routine technique are likely unnecessary without other risk factors.
pmc-13216281:
Lexin Ding and co-authors present a 2026 theoretical chemistry paper that rebuilds the idea of a chemical bond from quantum entanglement. Chemists use bonding daily, yet the concept has never had one rigorous definition that covers every case.

The authors define a set of atomic orbitals chosen to be maximally entangled with the rest of the molecule. The entanglement pattern of these orbitals reproduces classic Lewis pair bonds and also multi-centre bonds that Lewis pictures miss, while the strength of multipartite entanglement serves as a bond strength index. The framework holds at transition states during reactions and captures aromaticity. The authors position it as a quantitative companion to existing atom-in-molecule analysis.
pmc-13217181:
Sangita Maji and co-authors present a 2026 chemistry study of two molybdenum complexes that glow when they meet their targets. One is tuned to a textile dye and the other to an amino acid. Both probes work by displacement: the target knocks the built-in ligand off the metal, switching the fluorescence on.

Crystal structures confirmed the two complexes, built from thiophene-bearing amide-imine ligands. The first recognized calcon, a widely used azo dye and pollutant, and the second picked out 2-aminobutyric acid, each with little interference from look-alikes. Detection limits reached about six and five nanomoles per litre respectively. The authors stress that small changes to the ligand platform completely retarget the sensor.
pmc-13217481:
Sumel Ashique and co-authors present a 2026 review of 4D printing for personalized cancer care. Where 3D printing builds a fixed object, the fourth dimension is time. Printed structures made from smart materials reshape themselves or release drugs when they meet a trigger such as heat, light, or acidity.

The review surveys the material toolbox, shape-memory polymers and alloys, responsive hydrogels, ceramics, and liquid crystal elastomers, together with printing methods and the mathematics of programming deformation. Applications in oncology include implants and stents that expand in place, devices for heat-based therapies, and drug carriers that open in the tumour environment. The authors judge the field young but fast-moving, with personalization as its chief promise for cancer treatment.
pmc-13217881:
Saida Hidouri and co-authors present a 2026 paediatric case report of a hidden abdominal wall injury in a four-year-old boy who fell onto a vertical iron bar. Traumatic abdominal wall hernia, where tissue bursts through torn muscle under unbroken skin, is rare in children and easy to miss.

At first the boy had only a small wound and a normal ultrasound, and he went home after stitching. A week later a soft bulge appeared in his right lower abdomen; ultrasound now showed omentum, the fatty abdominal apron, poking through a defect of twenty by ten millimetres. At elective surgery the trapped omentum was freed from adhesions and the defect sewn shut. He recovered fully. The authors urge re-examination after blunt trauma even when first checks are clean.
pmc-13220081:
Kirill V. Chernov and colleagues argue metal drugs are an underused answer to cancer drug resistance in a 2026 review. Resistance causes most relapses, targeted therapies are narrow, and chemotherapy is hard on patients. The authors contend that the next generation of agents must combine precision with versatility, and metal compounds do both.

Metals and their complexes act on cancer cells through routes foreign to organic drugs. They can kill without the standard apoptosis pathway, disrupt critical signaling, and be aimed with unusual precision, while their chemistry suits them to imaging and targeted delivery. The review travels from the role of metals in causing cancer through therapeutic, diagnostic, and delivery strategies built on them. The puzzle the authors keep returning to is translational: despite the advantages, few metal-based drugs have won approval. They close by examining what blocks development, from evaluation to formulation, and where the field's best chances lie.
pmc-13222581:
Mai Thi Tuyet Kieu and co-authors analyze cancer medicine consumption in Vietnam from 2019 to 2023, in a 2026 cross-sectional study of national procurement data. Every bidding package and contract from the Drug Administration of Vietnam fed the analysis. Spending was sorted by technical group, chemical class, procurement level, manufacturing origin, and administration route.

Total consumption reached about 1.4 billion dollars across the five years, dipping sharply to 2022 before peaking in 2023. Targeted therapies took the largest share throughout, followed by chemotherapy, with immunotherapy smaller but growing. Originator and top-tier generic products dominated spending. Mean price per milligram fell over time, and national centralized bidding generally beat regional buying on efficiency.
pmc-13226881:
Li Huang and colleagues hunt a 2026 molecular link between depression and colorectal cancer, two conditions that frequently travel together. A colonoscopy cohort of 2,857 people and a national survey of more than thirty-seven thousand both tied major depression to more precancerous lesions and higher cancer risk. Genetic analysis supported a causal push from depression toward tumour formation.

Layering blood-protein genetics over cancer genome data singled out one shared mediator: nidogen-2, a structural protein of tissue scaffolding. Levels of the protein ran lower in the blood and bowel tissue of affected patients, with matching signals in public gene and protein datasets. The authors propose it as both a warning marker and a candidate treatment target bridging mental and bowel health.
pmc-13231181:
Xiao-Fang Chen and colleagues name in 2026 a new fungus genus found on dead branches of a medicinal plant in China. Material came from Polygonatum plants in Guizhou Province, a region rich in fungi still waiting for description. Microscope work showed upright spore stalks and pear-shaped spores of a kind not matching known genera.

Gene trees built from three markers placed the fungus inside the family Helminthosphaeriaceae, separate from its relatives. The authors named the genus Obovatispora and its first species after the host plant. Only the asexual form is known so far, and some spore-making cells grow odd side chambers. Careful naming work like this maps how fungal diversity ties to the plants of one region.
pmc-13232781:
Nan Jiang and colleagues profile in 2026 the social barriers facing Chinese Americans at risk of diabetes in a New York trial. One hundred fifty adults joined a phone-based prevention program tailored to their language and culture between 2023 and 2024. A fourteen-item survey counted barriers such as housing trouble, unfair treatment, and gaps in schooling.

More than four in five participants reported at least one barrier, with an average above two per person. Needing stronger English or reading skills topped the list, named by about half the group. Experiences of racial discrimination came second, followed by poor housing conditions. Women carried higher barrier scores than men after full adjustment. Prevention delivered by phone still has to reckon with life conditions offline.
pmc-13233181:
Ni Cheng and Jing Zhang published a 2026 study on how generative AI tools affect English learning outside the classroom. College students often practice English informally with chatbots and similar aids, yet losing motivation remains common. Surveying first-year students, the pair modeled how AI-assisted informal learning connects to self-directed study habits, resilience after setbacks, and second language demotivation.

Questionnaire data were analyzed with structural equation modeling. AI-assisted practice was linked to stronger autonomous learning behavior and greater academic buoyancy, meaning students recovered better from everyday academic pressure. Both factors, in sequence, carried part of the link to lower demotivation. The authors suggest designing AI practice activities that support choice and persistence, not just correct answers.
pmc-13233881:
Ebru Yılmaz and colleagues published a 2026 aquaculture feeding trial on European sea bass, testing corn fermented protein as a replacement for corn gluten in the diet. Juvenile fish of about twenty-six grams were fed for sixty days on four diets replacing none, a quarter, half, or all of the corn gluten. All diets carried similar protein and fat levels.

Growth roughly doubled in every group, with no significant differences in weight gain, feed conversion, or growth rate, though the full replacement group scored numerically highest. Blood measures and body composition stayed broadly similar, while gut villi grew taller on the full replacement diet and digestive enzyme activity rose with fermented protein. Diet cost also dipped slightly. The authors judge the swap safe for sea bass production.
pmc-13233981:
Einat Hauzman and colleagues published a 2026 comparative anatomy study of snake eyes. Snakes vary strikingly: daytime species run cone-rich retinas with unusual rod-like cells, while night species pack in true rods. Nobody had examined the inner retinal wiring of snakes before. The team stained retinas from eight nocturnal and thirteen diurnal species across eight families for a standard rod-pathway cell marker.

Nocturnal snakes carried the classic rod bipolar cell that the marker labels in other vertebrates. In diurnal snakes the same stain picked out a different cell altogether, a bipolar cell serving long-wavelength cones. The split mirrors each group's photoreceptor equipment and shows how flexibly the snake visual system has been rebuilt around day and night living.
pmc-13234081:
Mustafa S Alhasan and colleagues published a 2026 commentary on teleradiology and malpractice risk. Remote image reading now underpins round-the-clock hospital cover, but a recent claims analysis found teleradiology cases more often involved death, stroke diagnoses, communication failures, and bigger payouts. An accompanying editorial wondered whether remote reading itself is riskier. The authors push back, arguing the comparison was never adjusted for case mix.

Teleradiology handles a small share of claims yet takes the hardest ones: after-hours emergencies, trauma, and stroke, read at night when communication fragments and fatigue peaks. Stroke diagnoses appeared nearly three times as often among its claims. The authors say severity of caseload, not distance, explains most of the gap, and they caution against policies built on unmatched comparisons.
pmc-13234381:
Yuzhu Chen and co-authors examined in 2026 blood vessel harm linked to three platinum chemotherapy drugs used for solid tumours. The drugs were cisplatin, carboplatin, and oxaliplatin. Reports came from a United States safety database covering two decades of adverse event filings. Laboratory work on human vein cells tested how the drugs changed survival and gene activity.

More than ten thousand vascular events were identified across the three medicines. Low blood pressure, flushing, high blood pressure, and clotting were among the most common reports. Network analysis pointed toward pathways involving oxygen sensing, growth signals, and oxidative stress. In cells, oxaliplatin lowered a protective gene called Nrf2 and reduced viability, while cisplatin raised an adhesion gene. The authors advise early heart and vessel monitoring during treatment.
pmc-13235781:
Tai Meng Chen and co-authors commented in 2026 on a case where a gut disease appeared to inflame the heart muscle during septic shock. Sensitive blood tests and heart imaging now detect myocarditis more often in acute services. Separating true myocarditis from sepsis-related heart weakness or a blocked-artery heart attack changes treatment and prognosis. The case they discuss involved severe shigella disease with failure of several organs.

Chest pain, shifting heart tracing patterns, and raised troponin first suggested a heart attack in that case. A scan excluding blocked arteries redirected focus toward other causes of heart injury. Magnetic resonance imaging of the heart then gave tissue evidence matching myocarditis rather than infarction. The editorial offers a useful diagnostic flow following new European guidance for such presentations. Clinicians are urged to suspect myocarditis whenever troponin rises during systemic inflammation.
pmc-13236881:
Liang Cui and colleagues built a new tool in 2026 for measuring how tightly ArsR proteins grab arsenic. ArsR proteins sense arsenic inside microbes and switch on detox defenses, yet comparing their grip strength had been hard. The team anchored the proteins onto tiny silica spheres using self-assembling protein tags, creating a solid material that pulls arsenic from solution.

Nine ArsR variants from a highly arsenic-resistant bacterium were tested. Two bound arsenic most strongly, and grip strength tracked both sulfur-bearing building blocks and protein shape. One variant also lowered arsenic build-up when used in plants. The method needs no protein purification after early checks and could serve other protein studies or selective cleanup materials.
pmc-13237281:
The editors of Microsystems and Nanoengineering mark their field's rapid growth with an editorial on its ten biggest ground-level challenges. Tiny devices now support smart medical sensing, precision checks in industry, and shrunken hardware for aircraft and spacecraft. They also sit inside the chips planned for the next wave of information technology.

Growth that fast leaves hard problems at ground level: making, measuring, powering, and trusting devices built at near-atomic scales. Naming the worst ten is an agenda-setting move, pointing young researchers and funders at the bottlenecks that matter most. Editorials like this shape a young field by agreeing, in public, on what must be solved next.
pmc-13237681:
Jiayin Cai and team reported in 2026 an orbital solitary fibrous tumor that tormented one woman for eighteen years. She first presented at age 52 with a bulging eye and failing vision. Five operations followed as the thought-to-be slow-growing tumor kept returning, and the fourth recurrence forced removal of the whole eye socket contents.

Five years later the tumor returned again, invading the frontal, ethmoid, and maxillary sinuses. Tissue tests confirmed the same diagnosis, though the newest growth looked more abnormal and divided faster than earlier ones. Endoscopic removal plus radiotherapy followed. The authors blame the hard-to-reach spot, which made clearing the first tumor fully so difficult, and they urge early, complete removal. Lifelong checks, they argue, are a must for this quiet-looking tumor.
pmc-13237981: Abdelhamid and colleagues publish a correction to their study of medication habits among diabetic patients in Upper Egypt. The original paper linked how faithfully patients take their drugs with how they perceive their illness. The correction concerns the passage describing the adherence scale used, the MMAS-8, in the data collection section. It restates the scale's scoring: a total of eight marks high adherence, six or seven mark medium, and below six marks low. Journals record such fixes so later readers score the same tool the same way.
pmc-13239181:
Hao Hou and colleagues surveyed 1,414 caregiver-adolescent pairs twice between 2021 and 2022 in 2026, testing whether low mood flows only from parent to child or in both directions. An actor-partner model separates each person's effect on themselves from their effect on the other member of the pair. Depression and anxiety were measured at both waves.

Adolescents' symptoms at the first wave predicted their caregivers' later depression and anxiety. The return path was narrower: caregivers' anxiety predicted adolescents' later symptoms, but caregiver depression did not show the same reach. Neither caregiver nor adolescent gender changed the patterns. The authors argue that symptoms reinforce each other across generations, and that family-based early help could break the cycle better than treating either generation alone.
pmc-13239381:
Adil Aytaç and colleagues describe a 2026 case of a rare benign nerve tumour in the voice box. A 46-year-old woman came with hoarseness and cough, and examination showed swelling over the right arytenoid cartilage, a small structure that helps the vocal cords move.

Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a small lesion whose features could easily suggest cancer. Tissue examination after removal proved it was a neurofibroma, a growth arising from nerve sheath cells. Surgeons removed it completely with a carbon dioxide laser through the mouth, and her symptoms cleared with no return during follow-up. The authors note this location with spread below the cords has not been reported before.
pmc-13240881:
Zewdie and a large Ethiopia-UK team explored what helps and hinders childhood vaccination across three Ethiopian regions. Ethiopia carries one of the world's largest groups of zero-dose children. The study ran eighteen focus groups, interviews with twenty-three mothers, and forty-two key informant talks. Eight districts in Amhara, Oromia, and Somali regions took part.

Shared barriers included distant services, low awareness, mothers' competing duties, and fear of side effects. Rough or disrespectful care also discouraged return visits. Beliefs differed by region, from delaying shots until after baptism to keeping young infants indoors. Engaging religious leaders and fathers, and timing sessions around local holidays, emerged as promising fixes.
pmc-13240981:
Chew and colleagues in the United Kingdom reanalyzed real-world data from Holly Health, a personalized coaching app for older adults. Users enrolled between August 2022 and January 2023. The secondary analysis tracked well-being, mental and physical health, and attitudes toward food. Acceptability was judged alongside the outcome changes.

After using the app, participants reported better self-confidence, energy, and mindfulness. Health mindset and both short- and long-term outlook also improved. Users rated the personalized tool as acceptable and engaging. The authors say such accessible apps could support healthy aging at scale.
pmc-13241181:
Mattioli and colleagues at the University of Pavia tested how introduced fish change fear reactions in alpine frog tadpoles. Six Western Italian lakes spanned fishless, fish-neighboring, and fish-filled settings. The young frogs faced rising doses of dragonfly predator scent in lab assays. Freezing time gauged how strongly each population sensed danger.

All groups froze more as scent grew stronger, confirming a graded response. Those from fish lakes reacted significantly even at the weakest scent levels. Surprisingly, fishless lakes near stocked waters showed the same raised sensitivity. The invasion's behavioral shadow, Mattioli argues, spills beyond the invaded lakes.
pmc-13241581:
Bueno and Souto in southern Brazil map how curcumin research for food science has evolved. Curcumin, the yellow pigment of turmeric, is held back by poor dissolving and weak uptake. The pair ran a counting study of Web of Science records. They added a focused review of ways to deliver and package it.

Output grew fast, with strong cross-border teamwork across the field. Focus shifted from drug-style action toward keeping curcumin stable and usable in foods. Tiny carriers, coatings, and carrier design lead both the full dataset and the uptake subset. The authors warn that proof stays scattered, and food makers need methods that scale, plus testing in real food matrices.
pmc-13241881:
Uun Triyas Yuni Kurniawan and co-authors present a 2026 open-source test bed for brushless direct current motors, aimed at teaching laboratories. Commercial dynamometers cost more than many programs can afford. Their rig instead combines e-bike parts, a motor controller, and an ESP32 board.

The controller supplies voltage, current, speed, and temperature readings directly, removing much external instrumentation. A low-cost load cell on a calibrated arm measures braking torque. Validation showed small electrical and torque errors, and a mathematical motor model matched measured speed behavior closely. Full build cost stays in the hundreds of dollars. Designs, firmware, wiring diagrams, and data are openly archived for other schools to copy.
pmc-13241981:
Xuan Xu and co-authors present a 2026 theranostic platform for managing inflammation after heart attack. Recovery depends on immune cells called macrophages switching from a damaging mode to a repair mode. Existing scans cannot directly measure how active the damaging cells are.

Their particles hide inside platelet membranes and carry a dye plus an immune-calming drug. The dye lights up in the near-infrared only when it meets nitric oxide, a gas that inflammatory macrophages release in quantity. Acidic conditions around those cells then release the drug, nudging them toward repair. Machine learning turns the glow into maps of inflammatory activity. Animal tests showed better heart function and healing, suggesting a self-adjusting diagnosis-plus-treatment loop.
pmc-13242381:
Kechagia and colleagues in Athens followed two thousand Greek adults for twenty years of eating and diabetes outcomes. The ATTICA cohort began free of diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Validated food questionnaires separated animal from plant protein intake. Waist-hip ratio marked central adiposity throughout the analysis.

About a quarter developed diabetes across the two decades of follow-up. Red meat raised risk in both sexes with every daily serving increment. Animal protein harmed women only, roughly doubling risk among the centrally obese. Plant protein strongly protected younger women carrying excess abdominal fat.
pmc-13242581:
Wisdom Ikezogwo and co-authors built an AI triage system for microscope slides of colon polyps. Their paper appeared in Cancer Informatics in 2026. Colon specimens dominate their pathology service, and screening now starts at age forty-five, which adds volume. The team trained a transformer network on 1,191 slides spanning twelve diagnoses, from harmless polyps to invasive cancer. The authors call for multi-center studies before wider clinical use.
pmc-13242781:
Hongqin Wang and co-authors present a 2026 study of two traditional medicine compounds against heart scarring after heart attack. Four weeks of treatment reduced collagen buildup and cross-linking in injured hearts while preserving pump function. Inside scar-forming cells, the pair lowered copper import machinery, which cut the cross-linking enzyme amount and activity. Restoring the copper pathway reversed the effects in cell tests. The authors propose copper control as the shared mechanism behind the benefit.
pmc-13243181:

The study they discuss, by Gonzalez and colleagues, used the Hospital Frailty Risk Score across surgical specialties and found frailty's heaviest toll in emergency operations. More than ninety percent of the highest-risk patients had undergone emergency surgery, leaving almost no time to strengthen them beforehand.

Because it is built from administrative codes, it can miss fixable problems such as muscle loss and functional decline. Their title states the agenda: from identification to intervention. Naming risk is only step one; hospitals must build care pathways that act on what screening finds. The letter is short, but it presses a large question in surgical care.
pmc-13244081:
Sarah Pangburn and colleagues compared malaria parasites of Caribbean lizards to learn how they eat blood. Their study appeared in Ecology and Evolution in 2026. pmc-13244381:
Tiffany Chang and colleagues report a hernia hiding behind a gynecologic disguise that nearly cost a woman part of her bowel. The surgery widened into an open operation; the starved segment of ileum was removed and the bowel rejoined, and the ligament defect was repaired. The authors warn that internal hernias belong on the list for blocked bowels even without a surgical past. Delay invites strangulation.
pmc-13248081:
Komonski, Jouanneau, and Boureau tested home exercise for frail elders recovering from heart surgery, in this 2026 Journal of Rehabilitation Medicine feasibility study. Of forty-five eligible patients, thirty-eight joined and twenty-nine returned for final testing, completing on average just over half the program. Walking, balance, and grip measures all improved meaningfully, and the most adherent patients ended least frail. The authors judge home-based rehabilitation feasible for this group and worth confirming in larger trials, especially for patients far from specialist centers.
pmc-13248981:
Du and a Chinese team tracked germs growing inside oxygen tubing, in a 2026 study of elderly patients. High-flow nasal cannula therapy delivers humidified oxygen comfortably for long stretches. The researchers sampled the circuits of one hundred two patients whose average age was about ninety-four, checking whether the tubing itself became a germ reservoir.

More than half the circuits grew microbes, including fungi and drug-resistant staph. Patients with colonized tubing developed lung infections far more often. In one case, genome sequencing proved the same Pseudomonas strain lived in the tubing and the patient's lungs. Analysis pointed to replacing tubing around ninety days to cut the risk.
pmc-13249681:
Karataş and a Turkish team asked whether air and weather trigger lung flare-ups differently by blood type, in a 2026 study. Daily pollution and weather records from official monitors were matched to visit dates.

Most attacks were neutrophilic and also the most severe. Overall attack counts showed no environmental pattern, but the eosinophilic type rose on days with more carbon monoxide and sulfur dioxide. Mixed attacks tracked humidity and wind instead. The authors argue flare-up warnings should be tailored by subtype, not issued for COPD as one block.
pmc-13250281:
Congjie He and co-authors test two plant compounds against prostate cancer in this 2026 study. A targeted radiation drug is used for advanced prostate cancer that no longer answers hormone treatment, but uneven tumours and natural radiation resistance limit how well it works.

In mice, the combined treatment shrank tumours by half or more compared with the drug alone, with no clear side effects seen.
pmc-13250381:
Sampaio and co-authors pool trial evidence on simulation training for obstetric emergencies among health care students. Seven trials, with a few hundred students in total, fed the combined analysis, and simulation produced clearly larger knowledge gains after training. Some trials also reported better teamwork and critical thinking among the simulation students. Results varied a lot between settings, and the range of plausible effects crossed zero, so benefits may depend on context. The authors call for studies on how long the skills last and whether patients fare better.
pmc-13250881:

Some early surveys undercounted the risk for children and for lower-income countries.

Later antibody studies that reached the right groups, plus corrections for known biases, lined up with the early modeling results. The authors say this agreement vindicates the models that guided policy at the time. They urge health authorities to tell the public plainly about that success and about the limits of early survey work. Clearer lessons, they argue, will help the public judge risks in future pandemics.
pmc-13251781:
Heena Arshad and co-authors review trastuzumab deruxtecan, a targeted cancer drug, in gynecological cancers in 2026. The review gives special weight to interstitial lung disease, a serious lung inflammation linked to the drug that demands early detection and fast action. Careful HER2 testing before treatment is presented as essential. The authors also survey ongoing trials that may move the drug into earlier treatment lines.
pmc-13253081:
Matthew R. Jones leads a large multicentre audit of 3D printed plastic objects used in radiotherapy, reported in 2026. Because dose calculations assume tissue behaves like water, printed substitutes must match water closely and hold their printed dimensions.

Centers printed three standard test blocks of graded sizes using fused deposition printers, the type that lays down melted plastic layer by layer. The audit measured how accurately the blocks matched their designs. It also tracked how density and radiation behavior varied with the printer's infill setting, which controls how much of the interior is plastic versus air. The authors designed the audit to test whether relationships found in single-center studies hold across many hospitals. Their goal is shared benchmarks that let clinics adopt printing with consistent, verifiable quality.
pmc-13253381:
Maen Abdelrahim and colleagues review immune checkpoint inhibitors around liver transplantation for liver cancer in a 2026 transplant oncology article. pmc-13253981:
Xueting Wu and colleagues describe a hard airway emergency in a 2026 case report. A 22-year-old man had acute epiglottitis, a fast swelling of the flap over the windpipe, with neck swelling and noisy breathing. Several tries to place a breathing tube failed because swelling hid the airway opening.

A mask still delivered air well, a state the team calls can ventilate but cannot intubate. Following airway guidelines, they stopped further tube tries and did a planned tracheostomy, an opening in the neck, at the bedside. His oxygen rose fast and he recovered with no complications, which the authors credit to early teamwork.
pmc-13254081:
Dirk Bauer and colleagues test how immune cells stick to an eye implant in a 2026 lab study. The PreserFlo MicroShunt is a tiny tube that drains fluid to treat glaucoma, made from a rubber-like material called SIBS. Human macrophages, immune cells that react to foreign materials, were grown on the shunts for 35 days.

Far more macrophages stuck to the SIBS shunts than to two common lens materials used as controls. The authors say surface traits of SIBS invite this sticking, which could affect long-term implant success, mainly in eyes with uveitis, an eye inflammation. Live studies are still needed.
pmc-13254681:
The EFSA Panel on Food Enzymes gives a safety verdict on a food enzyme in a 2026 opinion. pmc-13255581:

pmc-13257581:

pmc-13258381:

pmc-13258481:

pmc-13259281:

pmc-13259381:

pmc-13259581:

pmc-13261081:

pmc-13261581:

pmc-13261681:

pmc-13261981:

pmc-13263481:

pmc-13263681:

pmc-13263881:

pmc-13264081:

pmc-13264581:

pmc-13264781:

pmc-13264981:

pmc-13265881:

pmc-13266181:

pmc-13269381:

pmc-13272081:

pmc-13272381:

pmc-13273981:

pmc-13274481:

pmc-13275381:

pmc-13275481:

pmc-13278981:

pmc-13279081:

pmc-13279481:
Francesco Bertoldo and colleagues report a 2026 survey of fragility fracture care in Italian emergency departments. Fragility fractures are breaks from small falls in weak bone, and they are often missed in busy emergency rooms. Missed breaks lose the chance to start bone strength care and stop the next break. The team surveyed staff on how they spot and handle such breaks.

Thirty four health workers took part: ten emergency doctors, eleven radiologists and thirteen emergency nurses from many regions. A panel of experts built the survey on break checks, risk facts, records and referrals. Answers showed patchy checks of key risk facts across roles. Gaps stood out between what staff know and what they do each day. Set routines for spotting, writing and referral could close the gap.
pmc-13279681:
Kazuki Aihara and colleagues published a 2026 validation study comparing three imaging methods for judging whether stent struts in leg arteries have been covered by new vessel lining. Delayed coverage matters because uncovered struts can trigger clots that block the stent. In a swine model, 22 arteries were examined one month after stenting. Each method was checked against tissue histology, the reference standard, in segments where the lining was thin.

Of 112 matched image sets, 62 had thin lining. Histology confirmed true endothelial coverage in only 8 of those segments. Angioscopy reading by color achieved perfect sensitivity with 92 percent specificity. The ultrasound and optical methods called nearly everything covered, scoring zero specificity, because they could not tell endothelium from fibrin deposits. The authors conclude angioscopy reads healing more truthfully in thin layers. That could help clinicians decide how long a patient needs anti-clotting therapy after leg stenting.
pmc-13280581:
Alexis Aomreore and colleagues present a 2026 cross sectional survey of patient portal use in primary care in Ontario, Canada. Patient portals are digital programs that give patients access to their electronic health records and care tools. Portals are now widely used, yet desirability of their features is less known. The survey ran from December 2022 to March 2023 and captured use and anticipated use of five feature types, from messaging the practice to scheduling appointments.

A total of nine hundred seventy responses were obtained: seven hundred forty three patients and two hundred twenty seven caregivers. Portal access sat at fifty seven percent for patients and sixty two percent for caregivers. Features held communicating with the practice, viewing records, entering record information, receiving practice information and scheduling. Associations between socio demographic data and current use of features were tested. The profile of who uses what can guide portal design for equity.
pmc-13281281:
Amrita K Johal reviewed how hospitals pick adults for a last-resort heart and lung machine in a 2026 paper. The machine does the work of the heart and lungs for the sickest patients. It costs a lot, and who gets it shapes who lives. The review found few hospitals use firm written rules for the choice. Most studies on the topic were small and used unlike methods.

One scoring tool stood out as the best guide for most cases. A tweaked version, which adds a blood marker of strain, fit two hard groups better. Teams that decided as a full group, not by one or two doctors, saw better survival. The author calls for more proof tests of the scores. Fair, shared rules, the review argues, would help hospitals choose well.
pmc-13281881:
Ying-Xing Xiang and colleagues probed whether a common arthritis drug can drive lung disease in a 2026 study. The drug, methotrexate, calms the immune system and is used for joint and skin disease. COPD is a long-term lung disease that narrows airways and worsens over time. Past reports hint the drug might affect the lungs, but cause was unclear. The team worked two ways. Network maps predicted the drug's targets and paths. Gene data then tested for a cause-style link.

The maps tied the drug to nine proteins with strong binding fits. Those proteins steer swelling, stress response, and cell growth. The gene test found a clear positive link between drug use markers and COPD risk. The authors say the pair of methods points the same way. They frame it as a warning for long-term users. More direct clinical study is needed, they add.
pmc-13282081:
Parth Patel and co-authors tell of a 2026 case where a vein, not an artery, squeezed the gut. A sixty-year-old woman arrived with belly pain, nausea, and vomiting. Scans first raised concern for a rare syndrome in which the duodenum, the first part of the small gut, is pinched between the aorta and a major artery. Her images instead pointed to pressure at the level of the superior mesenteric vein, a large vein from the gut.

A camera exam down the throat showed outside pressure on the duodenum, with a pulsing mass and widening above the block. Surgeons then used robotic tools through small cuts to inspect the belly and free stuck bowel loops. They joined the duodenum to the next gut section, bypassing the squeezed spot. The authors highlight how this vein-based mimic can mislead even careful imaging, so direct inspection may be needed.
pmc-13282381:
Chengbin Liu and co-authors wrote a 2026 perspective on reading chemical tags in environmental DNA to monitor ecosystems more deeply. Environmental DNA, shed by organisms into water and soil, usually tells which species are present. It also keeps methylation tags, chemical marks that help control gene activity. The authors call this meth-eDNA and argue it could reveal traits of whole populations without catching any animals.

Three topics structure the piece: detecting the signals, how stable they stay in water, and uses as ecological indicators. Trait clues from tags could show stress, age structure, or adaptation that species lists miss. The authors expect that combining tag reading with other molecular layers and newer sequencing will sharpen precision. They frame the approach as a future tool for conservation and ecosystem management. Practical hurdles, such as signal decay outdoors, still need solving before routine use.
pmc-13282681:
Neyon Loku Gamage and co-authors present a 2026 study of heartworm-type parasites in dogs in Colombo District, Sri Lanka, and the bacteria living inside them. The parasites, Dirofilaria, spread by mosquitoes and can also infect people. The bacteria, Wolbachia, help the parasites survive and breed, making them a control target. Blood was collected from three hundred sixty-eight dogs between May and December 2025.

Only thirty-five samples showed parasite larvae under the microscope. Gene tests confirmed Dirofilaria in eighteen of those, and Wolbachia in just three. Most identified parasites were one species, Dirofilaria repens, with a few of two others. One dog carried two species at once. Sequencing gave Sri Lanka's first molecular proof of the heartworm species Dirofilaria immitis there, and the first molecular detection of Wolbachia in these parasites in the country. The authors urge gene-based diagnosis and worm control aimed at the bacteria.
pmc-13282981:
Macrophages that shelter liver tumors receive a full 2026 mapping from Yuhao Su and partners, from origins to treatment targets. These immune cells are the most common myeloid cells inside liver tumors. They help tumors grow, spread, and hide from immune attack in many settings.

Macrophages come from liver-resident cells and from blood cells that enter the tumor. Tumor signals push them toward a state that aids tumor growth. They release factors that build vessels and drive spread traits. They also damp immune attack through suppressive signals and partner cells. High macrophage counts predict early return and poor outlook. The review maps treatment ideas that target these cells.
pmc-13283381:
Protein gas bubbles grown by microbes could carry ultrasound imaging into molecular territory, Ailin Cui and co-reviewers survey in 2026. Gas vesicles are tiny protein shells filled with gas from microbes. They can reflect ultrasound in ways that reveal tagged cells and tissues.

Formats range from cleaned vesicles to genes that let cells make their own vesicles. Each format differs in dose, route, and proof level reached so far. Strong proof covers collapse under pressure and surface tweaks for targeting. Fully designed protein shells remain a future aim, not a clinic-ready tool. Barriers include shell strength, body fate, and safe exposure limits. Careful clinician-led safety rules frame the path forward.
pmc-13283681:
Lauren Butler and colleagues surveyed dancers in 2026 about weight training habits and hurdles. Fitness work with resistance is advised for dancers because it lifts performance and cuts injury risk, yet views on it vary in the dance world. Eighty-nine dancers aged twelve to twenty-five, almost all female, answered an online survey on training outside and inside dance, drive, and barriers.

Dancers averaged about three days a week of outside resistance training, in sessions of roughly half an hour at fairly hard effort. Training inside dance class ran a little less often and a little shorter. Bodyweight work was the most common form in both settings. Only about six in ten used bands or dumbbells for added load. Drive scores suggested dancers broadly agreed with training, while ranked barriers showed what still holds them back.
pmc-13283981:
Hui Yang and colleagues explored in 2026 whether hepcidin, the body's iron control hormone, relates to retinopathy of prematurity, an eye disease of early-born babies where abnormal vessels grow in the retina. Current care targets a growth signal called VEGF but not the oxidative injury upstream. The team measured blood hepcidin in 35 preterm infants and tested hepcidin on human retinal vessel cells under low oxygen.

Babies with the eye disease were born earlier and smaller, and their hepcidin signals ran numerically lower without a clear stage pattern. In the dish, low oxygen raised stress signals and harmful oxygen byproducts, and hepcidin cut VEGF output, lowered those byproducts, and curbed excess tube growth by vessel cells. Gene profiling pointed to shifts in several metabolic pathways.
pmc-13284181:
A tiny tunable filter for heat-vision cameras is built by Tengfei Xu and colleagues in a 2026 device study. Long-wave infrared light suits passive imaging and material fingerprinting without added light. Filters in this band suffer from material absorption and few low-loss film choices.

Reflective stacks of germanium and zinc sulfide passed a high reflectivity bar. A three-armed ring suspension moved the filter gap with electric force. Tuning ran continuously across a broad long-wave range in lab tests. Filter sharpness reached strong values for this device class. A dual-channel demo paired spectral sensing with vision for object recognition. Hybrid sensing beat vision alone.
pmc-13284281: A 2026 correction notice in General Psychiatry fixes sample counts in an earlier study of brain connectivity, tobacco smoking, and psychosis risk, and carries no author byline. Four passages are corrected, spanning the abstract methods and the results demographics text. The baseline analysis is narrowed to participants with baseline MRI data: 364 high-risk non-smokers, 94 high-risk smokers, and 67 controls. Wording around the summary table is also corrected. Only the corrections themselves are given, so coverage stays brief.
pmc-13284881:
Zhouyi Song and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, how gut and brain signals shape chronic pain in both directions. Pain is now seen as more than tissue harm, with mood and thought involved. The gut-brain axis links gut microbes, bowel lining, and the central nervous system through nerve, hormone, immune, and chemical routes.

Microbe products such as short-chain fatty acids, plus gut-brain peptides, can tune pain sensitivity in body and brain, the review reports. Inflammatory signals from microbes may stir brain immune cells and loosen the blood-brain barrier. Gut lining cells also send active signals, not just form a wall. The authors map gaps for conditions such as bowel pain, migraine, and fibromyalgia.
pmc-13285081:
Lisa T. Porschen and co-authors report a 2026 study linking low blood levels of a vessel lipid to brain vessel activation in ischemic stroke. The lipid, sphingosine-1-phosphate, helps vessels stay sound and calms immune action, and its blood levels drop in stroke. Whether brain vessels shift in step was unclear, so the team joined patient blood tests with mouse and cell work.

Blood levels were lower in fifty acute stroke patients than in matched controls and rose again by ninety days, the authors report. Mouse stroke models showed like patterns. Brain vessel gene work and cell tests under low oxygen tracked pathway changes and barrier stress. The results tie blood loss of the lipid to vessel strain.
pmc-13285681:
Blocking one chemokine may rescue immune therapy in kidney cancer, Ryuta Sobu and co-authors test in a 2026 study. Checkpoint drugs help many kidney patients, yet resistance is common and forecast marks are weak. Tissue and blood from fifty-one patients on anti-PD-1 therapy were mined for what splits responders from the rest.

Tumor tissue traits failed to split the groups, but blood told a story: suppressor white cells stayed high in those who gained nothing. A new mouse model, grafted with a patient tumor plus that same patient immune cells, mirrored personal clashes. Adding an IL-8 blocker, which cuts suppressor cell calls, tended to slow tumor growth beside PD-1 blockade.
pmc-13285981:
Connor R Volpi and colleagues asked men in Abuja, Nigeria, who live with HIV and are drawn to men, what would make HPV vaccination work for them. The 2026 study responds to high rates of HPV disease in this group and low vaccine uptake, shaped by cost, stigma, and service design. Two hundred fifty men attending a supportive clinic completed a choice exercise.

Each man compared pairs of made-up vaccination offers that varied in setting, price, travel time, and benefits. Free services and welcoming settings mattered most, each near a fifth of the decision weight. Protection against warts and clear information also counted. The authors say removing fees and affirming care are essential steps for fairer vaccine access.
pmc-13286081:
Sohaib Shujaat and colleagues draw policy lessons for national virtual hospitals in a 2026 viewpoint anchored on Saudi Arabia's Seha Virtual Hospital. Aging populations and packed wards push countries to move hospital care onto screens, yet whole-nation virtual hospitals stay rare. The authors gather world proof from remote intensive care, hospital-at-home, and stroke networks to judge what a national model must get right.

Across settings, virtual care matched in-person results when staff picked patients well, set clear rescue paths, and wove remote teams into local work. Saudi Arabia's hub, launched in 2022, now links hospitals across the kingdom for urgent consults, clinics, and case talks at national scale. Hard proof of its effect on deaths, costs, and fairness still lags behind its fast growth, the authors note. They urge built-in testing, sound funding, and care for access gaps as such systems spread.
pmc-13286281:
Farzin Tahvili, Martin Vinck, and Matteo Di Volo build a math model of brain rhythms in a 2026 theory study. Cortex gamma waves were long explained by a two-crowd dance of excitatory cells and generic blockers. Real circuits, though, split the blockers into fast PV cells and slower SOM cells with separate jobs. Their model folds all three crowds into one averaged system drawn from actual wiring.

The three-crowd system sings gamma on its own and matches lab quirks, including how light-pulse tricks on one cell type bend the rhythm. Trimming the math down shows the wiring pattern itself breeds the wave, no extra mechanism required. PV activity runs ahead of SOM activity, just as recordings show, because of who connects to whom. Modelers gain a firmer base for building large, cell-aware brain simulations.
pmc-13286781:
Rakesh Kanth Andugala and co-authors train machine learning models to spot glioma, an aggressive brain tumor, from tiny RNA molecules in body fluids. Their 2026 study pools four public datasets of microRNA readings. Current diagnosis leans on scans and tissue sampling, which are costly and invasive, so a fluid-based test would be valuable.

Five ways of picking useful features fed six classification algorithms. Models separating glioma from healthy controls reached perfect accuracy in the best runs, and three-way sorting with another tumor type also scored at the top for two methods. Seven microRNAs emerged as candidate markers and held up in a separate validation dataset. The authors present the pipeline as a step toward blood-based brain tumor screening.
pmc-13287081:
Narsimha Rao Keetha and co-authors pool studies on hidden celiac disease inside fatty liver clinics in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Both conditions are rising and may share immune and gut-driven roots, yet how often they overlap was unclear. The team searched four databases for studies reporting celiac diagnoses among patients with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.

Across the pooled studies, celiac disease appeared in about 3.8% of fatty liver patients, higher than general population expectations. Studies that confirmed the diagnosis with both blood tests and biopsies found more of it. Lower body mass, higher liver enzyme readings, lower hemoglobin, and lower platelet counts each leaned toward the overlap group. Disagreement between studies was extreme, so the authors urge selective screening and bigger, standardized prospective work rather than firm rules.
pmc-13287281:
Samuel Tundealao and colleagues built and piloted a talking digital guide in 2026 to help cancer survivors learn about inherited cancer risk and decide on genetic testing. Patients and at-risk relatives from varied backgrounds helped shape wording, layout, and privacy messages before a small feasibility trial.

Users rated the guide as easy to accept, with a usability score the authors report as 70.3. Testing uptake reached 73.3% with the guide, against 7.7% under enhanced usual care. Guide users also reported less conflict and regret about their choices. No guide user asked for pre-test counselling, against one in the comparison group. A larger randomised trial is proposed.
pmc-13287481:
Derk-Jan Dijk wrote a perspective in 2026 looking back over forty years of human experiments testing a classic two-part account of sleep control. In that account, a build-up of sleep pressure during waking interacts with a daily body clock to set when and how deeply people sleep.

Dijk sorts findings into those that fit the account and those that strain it. Points of tension include how the two parts truly interact and what they imply for brain recovery. His own doctoral work in Groningen during the 1980s helped test early predictions. The piece invites fresh work on how clock timing and sleep need jointly guard brain function.
pmc-13287681:
Qixiang Chen and co-authors used computer inverse design in 2026 to build a layered photonic surface that hides objects in visible light and in heat cameras at the same time. The structure draws on a material that flips state with temperature, vanadium dioxide, to change how it gives off infrared energy.

Colour across a wide band can be tuned over much of the print colour range without disturbing heat behaviour. Heat emission switches between two paired states in the two infrared bands. Precise heating also lets the surface send coded messages in infrared that ordinary cameras cannot see. Tests confirmed both hiding and signalling in one platform.
pmc-13288681:
Miriam Fornells-Ambrojo and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a feasibility trial of narrative exposure therapy inside early psychosis services in England. Repeated personal trauma raises the chance of psychosis and slows recovery, yet trauma therapy rarely reaches first-episode patients, partly because services lack time and trained staff.

Fifty patients with first-episode psychosis and multiple traumas, cared for by two NHS trusts, will be assigned by chance to fifteen therapy sessions plus usual care or to usual care alone. Masked assessors will measure outcomes at the start, at four months, and at eight months, focusing on recruitment, retention, and completion. Interviews with patients and clinicians will probe acceptability, obstacles, and any harms, guiding a later full trial.
pmc-13288881:
Emsea Akers and co-authors plan a scoping review on injured children going home in 2026. Their piece is a protocol. Accidental injury fills children's wards worldwide. Families can hit a second crisis after discharge. Recovery at home can prove harder than expected. The team will gather caregiver views.

Four databases will be searched. English studies from 2000 to 2025 count. Patients must be under eighteen. Discharge views and improvement projects both count. Findings will sort through an access framework. Tables and summaries will expose challenges. Promising fixes will be named. Fairness checks will also be tracked.
pmc-13289081:
Alfonso Lagares and colleagues publish a 2026 study plan in Madrid, Spain. The IMPACTS-BRAINI study deals with mild brain injury. Two blood markers can rule out bleeds on scans. The markers are called GFAP and UCH-L1. Past work tested them in labs.

One hospital will run the study. Staff will log care before the test starts. They will log care after it starts too. Blood must be drawn within 12 hours of injury. Patients must meet set clinical marks. The team will count CT scans ordered. ER stay time will also be counted. Past patient data will serve as the contrast.
pmc-13289181:
Marta Simonetti and colleagues study nurse workloads and patient deaths in Chile in 2026. Their study covers public hospitals nationwide. Of 45 large hospitals, 43 took part. Nurses filled an online survey. Patient outcomes came from 2023 discharge data.

The data held 344,567 adult patients. Each ICU nurse covered 3.0 patients at once on average. Ward nurses cared for 10.1 at a time. Loads swung widely by hospital. Each extra patient raised the odds of death. That held in ICU and ward units. Ward stays also grew longer with load. Cutting loads could save lives, the authors say.
pmc-13289781:
Lisa Birzle and colleagues share a 2026 case series on endoscopic intermuscular dissection for early rectal cancers thought to invade deeply. The method cuts between muscle layers to remove lesions whole, fitting risk-based strategies that spare major surgery when safe. Sixteen patients at university hospitals in Augsburg and Bochum underwent the procedure with pre-procedure assessment guiding selection.

Every lesion came out in one piece without major complications in the series. Tissue review found a mix: deep or shallow invasive cancers with low-risk traits, pretreated cancer, one deeper cancer, benign growths with varied grades, a hormone-type tumor, and a vessel malformation. Margins were clear in fourteen cases overall. Two cases had deep margin concerns needing added care.
pmc-13290081:
Chrysanti Murad and coauthors test a 2026 lab question on whether a gum disease germ helps lung pneumococcal germs stick to airway cells by serotype. Porphyromonas gingivalis can raise a host receptor that pneumococci exploit, called PAFR. Lung lining cells were primed for 24 hours with fluid from the W83 strain, then exposed to four pneumococcal serotypes for adhesion counts.

Priming raised receptor gene activity clearly in the cell model. Adhesion jumped significantly for serotypes 4 and 7F after priming in the counts. Thick-coated serotypes 3 and 6A rose only slightly without statistical firmness overall. The mouth-lung partnership thus favors select pneumococcal types, shaping pneumonia risk by strain.
pmc-13290781:
A plant compound fed to pregnant mice protected their daughters from a fat-rich diet's metabolic fallout, Xueran Mei and colleagues report in an animal study from 2026. Mothers on a high-fat diet pass metabolic syndrome risk to offspring, and the team tested whether perinatal phlorizin could blunt that inheritance in females.

Daughters of high-fat-fed mothers showed disturbed sugar and fat handling at weaning and, as adults, gut imbalance, insulin resistance, and a leaky gut barrier despite no plain obesity. When mothers also received phlorizin, the daughters kept a healthier microbiome richer in SCFA-producing bacteria, made more short-chain fatty acids, and resisted obesity better. Transplanting gut microbes from protected daughters into antibiotic-treated males transferred much of the benefit. Mei and colleagues pitch phlorizin as a functional food candidate with effects across generations.
pmc-13291281:
Salt can coax a sea fungus to make new chemicals. Minh Van Nguyen leads a 2026 study of a marine Trichoderma strain. One strain can yield many compounds under changed growth. Bromide salt in the broth was the switch used here.

Salt-grown cultures turned darker in color. Their chemical mix grew richer as well. Extracts fought a key plant disease bacterium better. Fourteen compounds were pulled from the mix. Two were new to science, in the viridin family. Some compounds fought fungi, others fought bacteria. Fire blight signs on plants eased under treatment. Changing broth salts is a cheap discovery trick.
pmc-13291481:
A Chinese herbal mix may fight lung scarring disease. Yifan Ren leads a 2026 computer and lab study of Jingfang Granule. The disease, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, kills slowly. Few drug options exist for patients today.

Public gene data on the disease were mined first. Thousands of genes shifted in sick lung tissue. Network tools linked herb targets to disease targets. Five learning methods hunted for marker genes. Two genes, SPP1 and MMP1, stood out as key. Docking tests checked how herb parts bind them. Tissue stains backed the computer findings. The pair may guide new drug design for this disease.
pmc-13291781: Rosario Amato and co-authors put out a 2026 correction to their article on whether Lisosan G might serve as a glaucoma treatment. The notice says a preliminary version of panel A in Figure 4 was published by mistake. It supplies the corrected figure, showing retinal ganglion cell staining and density analysis in mouse retinas. The original article has been updated. Only this short correction is available here, so the underlying study's design and findings cannot be described from it.
pmc-13292381:
María José Ferreira Díaz tests a structured observation exercise for nursing students in a 2026 mixed-methods study. Students on placement often focus on tasks and miss the wider system around care. The exercise gave 125 students a ten-item tool covering clinical management and safety culture. Sites spanned three hospitals and nine primary care centers. Scores were compared across settings, and open reflections were analyzed for themes.

Students rated organizational functioning and safety culture positively overall. Primary care scored higher than hospitals on patient and family information and participation. Student notes showed them spotting strengths, pressures, and realistic fixes in teamwork, communication, workflow, and leadership. The author presents structured observation as a cheap way to build systems awareness. Guided looking, she argues, grows judgment beyond task checklists. Placement learning could borrow the tool widely.
pmc-13292981:
Mei-Mei Kuan and Javad Sarvestan build, in 2026, a forecast tool for hospital load from enterovirus in Taiwan. The virus sickens many children, and a post-pandemic rebound in 2023 and 2024 made planning harder for wards.

Weekly health data covered clinic, emergency, and hospital counts split into five age groups, plus past weeks and seasonal terms. A random forest model trained on most of the period gave one-week-ahead forecasts for late 2024. Visits by the youngest children, ages 0 to 2 and 3 to 4, were the strongest clues. Weekly errors stayed modest, suggesting the tool could help plan beds and staff.
pmc-13293481:
Kinner L. Flaglor and colleagues report how one American medical school is weaving generative artificial intelligence into its curriculum, in a 2026 update from East Tennessee State University. The team tracked student attitudes with a repeated survey and built a training program to bring faculty up to speed. Questions covered both how learners use the tools and whether they still build core clinical skills without them.

Newer students showed growing awareness of the technology, paired with stronger resolve to master examination skills on their own. Rising third-year students used the tools more for active study, such as generating practice questions and self-testing. Faculty workshops raised confidence and hands-on engagement, while a session on ethics left participants more cautious. Teachers asked for practical, role-specific training that does not depend on any single product.
pmc-13293681:
Ameni Mehrez, Edouard Machery, and Valerio Capraro compare, in a 2026 study, how everyday Christians and Muslims view free will next to God's knowledge and power. Faith traditions have answered the tension in unlike ways for centuries, yet everyday belief may not follow doctrine.

Across denominations, Christians answered alike on abstract questions and on concrete cases about control, blame, and punishment, suggesting doctrine leaves lay views much alike. Muslims differed: in abstract terms they held both free will and divine rule together, matching Qur'an teaching. In concrete cases, though, they played down free will. Lay faith thus blends doctrine with situation in complex ways.
pmc-13293781:
Yoko Takahashi and co-authors survey, in a 2026 study, local nurses 13 months after the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake, asking whether losing their workplace harmed mental health apart from personal losses. Disaster research has centered on home and family loss, not workplace ruin.

A total of 414 nurses in coastal Miyagi Prefecture replied, giving rates of probable post-traumatic stress at 11.7% and depression at 24.6%, shares the authors report. Nurses from tsunami-wrecked hospitals looked worse in raw counts, yet the workplace link faded once personal burdens were counted. Death or loss of a family member stayed the strongest tie to severe stress symptoms.
pmc-13293881:
Tanuja Kistwal and colleagues report in 2026 that light can create quantum friction between carbon nanotubes and water. Quantum friction means momentum passes directly between a liquid and electrons in a solid, an effect that is hard to catch. The team tracked glowing single-walled nanotubes moving in water and varied light power, exciton levels, and surface defects.

Stronger light cut diffusion by about 50%, and chemical tweaks that raised or lowered exciton numbers shifted diffusion up to twofold. When excitons were pinned by defects, the effect vanished. Spectroscopy and simulations point to exciton dipoles dragging on water, a route to steering tiny motion with light.
pmc-13293981:
Haobo Wang and colleagues present HiCapR in 2026, a protocol for mapping how viral RNA strands touch each other across a whole genome. RNA viruses fold into shapes that control infection and immune evasion. Older ligation methods map contacts broadly but miss rare targets in mixed samples, so capture steps were added to enrich viral pieces.

Workflow covers psoralen crosslinking in live virus and infected cells, cutting, joining close pieces, capture, sequencing, and computer analysis of joined reads. Applied to HIV-1, the method resolved the full genome layout, including pairing regions and long-range contacts. Prior validation on SARS-CoV-2 supports use for antiviral design.
pmc-13294681:
Yasemin Özdemir presents a 2026 dataset on birds at Karataş Lake in Burdur, Turkey, covering fieldwork from 2021 to 2022. The lake has held Wildlife Development Area status since 2006 but is shrinking under low rainfall, drying inflows, and heavy farm use. Bird records are paired with vegetation and climate data.

Surveys used point counts, vegetation greenness came from Sentinel-2 images for 2017 to 2024, and climate figures came from TerraClimate. Observers recorded 46 species, including a near threatened lapwing and a vulnerable pochard. Summer brought the most species and individuals, and the combined data are offered to guide wetland restoration, farm practice, and water management.
pmc-13295481:
Wen Li and co-authors feed laying hens extra folic acid to learn what lands in the egg and what changes on the way, in a 2026 study. Over half the world's people get too little folate, the B vitamin that guards against birth defects, and eggs are a rich, well-taken-up source. Past work tracked mainly one active form of the vitamin.

The trial gauged laying output, egg quality, taste-linked traits, and the full family of folate forms stored in yolk. That wider count matters, since heavy doses of the factory-made form raise their own questions, among them masking a lack of vitamin B12. A form that many people convert poorly, owing to common gene variants, also enters the tally. The authors frame fortified eggs as a handy delivery route, if each form is watched.
pmc-13295781:
Chenchen Hao, Zeguo Wang, and Ping Wang ask what draws preschool teachers to use generative artificial intelligence, in a 2026 mixed-methods study. Young-child teaching has been slow to take up such tools, and the reasons were little mapped. The team built a model on a known adoption framework and ran a workshop for 434 teachers, gathering 399 sound surveys and fifteen deep talks.

Hope of better work results, peer pull, and tech skill each tied to a stronger wish to use the tools, while fear of risk pulled the other way. Ease of use and support at hand showed no clear link. Talks with teachers backed the survey pattern. The authors warn that tangled measures make the results a first sketch, and they call for firmer tests in other settings.
pmc-13295981:
Yamin Han and colleagues teach software to read beef cattle behavior from night farm video, in a 2026 study. Round-the-clock watch over cattle helps welfare and farm output, yet night footage is dark, blurry, and weak in motion cues, so reading it well is hard. Key night acts, such as heat signs tied to breeding, can be missed and cost farms money.

Their method sharpens space and time cues in the footage and blends features in a dynamic way that adapts to poor light. In the team's tests the approach read behavior with strong accuracy and held up across lighting changes. The authors offer it as a path to steady night watch on real farms, catching health and breeding events that daylight-only systems miss.
pmc-13296181:
Stella Vosniadou reviews how teachers can grow self-regulated learning in the classroom, in a 2026 article. The term covers how learners set goals, watch their own understanding, steer feelings and drive, and judge results. Skilled self-regulators keep attention, reflect, and persist, while weaker ones lean on teachers for structure and give up early when tasks turn hard.

Proof gathered over years shows that coaching in thinking habits and strategy use lifts learning and achievement. Yet many students still lack core skills, above all the habit of checking what they truly grasp, and loosely run settings expose the gap. New digital tools promise tailored support while asking more of the learner. Vosniadou sets out what classroom practice can do to build these skills on purpose.
pmc-13296481:
Weikang Xian and co-authors use computer simulation to link particle networks inside filled polymers to the material's stiffness over time, in a 2026 study. Nanoparticles strengthen plastics and rubbers, yet the microscopic reason for the bulk effect has stayed murky. Their mesoscale model treats chains bridging particles as dynamic bonds within a simplified polymer background.

The framework gives materials scientists a way to test how filler structure shapes the feel and durability of nanocomposites.
pmc-13296781:
Jaunius Urbonavičius, Augusta Ivaškė, and Daiva Tauraitė work out how E. coli bacteria recycle methylated RNA building blocks in a 2026 study. Modified bases appear in RNA across life, but how bacteria strip the methyl groups and reuse the pieces was unknown. Mutant strains unable to make their own purines were fed modified bases in a minimal diet.

One methylated base supported growth of one mutant, showing the cells could convert it back to a usable form. The doubly methylated version supported no growth at all. Purified enzyme tests identified which deaminase performs the conversion, and which related enzyme cannot. The authors propose pathways that return these modified pieces to normal metabolism.
pmc-13297381:
Metastatic prostate cancer care now favors early drug combinations over hormone treatment alone, and Takatoshi Somoto with co-authors mapped that shift in a 2026 review. Their account follows how landmark trials reshaped management of hormone-sensitive and castration-resistant disease.

Readers get guidance on who gains from upfront intensification, why DNA repair testing belongs early in the pathway, and how PSMA PET scans flag candidates for targeted radioligand therapy. The authors also explain why one androgen receptor blocker can blunt response to the next, citing receptor reactivation, lineage change, and uneven PSMA expression. Practical sequencing advice weighs blood reserve, other illnesses, and local access to monitoring.
pmc-13298181:
Why do buyers in Brazil call a bag of fine coffee worth its price? Ari Melo Mariano and his team model that call in a 2026 study. Their frame links what a product has, to the good it does the buyer, to the worth the buyer feels.

Survey replies came from 88 people, and the team fit the frame with a path model. The model made sense of 29.4% of the spread in felt worth. The traits of the coffee did most of their work through the middle step: gains that felt handy, useful, and smart. The team says this chain can guide how farms and brands pitch, talk up, and stand apart with green, top-grade coffee.
pmc-13298981:
Entropy, the mathematics of uncertainty, can grade how tamper-proof a blockchain really is, propose Lanlan Li and co-authors in a 2026 theoretical study. They model ledger states as probability distributions and track Shannon entropy on-chain, off-chain, and inside the virtual machines that run smart contracts.

Simulations showed on-chain entropy decaying almost exponentially as honest consensus piles up, while off-chain entropy stayed flat, exposing the weakness of conventional storage. The team also argues the virtual machine's computation entropy mirrors arbitrary Turing machines. Their framework is pitched as a practical instrument for watching ledger integrity, spotting tampering, and sizing up protocol resilience under attack.
pmc-13299081:
Gulsum Ozturk Emiral and a team measure health literacy among emergency department patients at a university hospital, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. A two-part questionnaire gathered social details, visit history, and short screening questions for inadequate literacy. More than four hundred adults took part, with a young average age.

Nearly half showed inadequate health literacy. Rates ran higher in people over forty and in those with eight or fewer years of schooling. Repeat emergency visits were common overall, yet visit patterns showed no significant link to literacy level in this group. The authors call for larger longitudinal studies with adjusted analyses to untangle the relationship.
pmc-13299281:
One drug shielded healthy cells from radiation while making bone cancer cells more vulnerable to it, report Artem Ermakov and colleagues in a 2026 in vitro study. They tested sodium aminodihydrophthalazinedione, sold as Tameron, on human mesenchymal stem cells and osteosarcoma cells exposed to X-rays.

The compound mopped up radiation-generated hydrogen peroxide in solution. In stem cells at 0.25 mM and above, it lowered reactive oxygen, reduced cell death, sped DNA break repair, and preserved colony growth. In the cancer line it did the reverse, raising cell death and slowing break repair. Gene activity profiling backed the split response, and the authors propose the drug as a selective radiation modulator.
pmc-13299381:
Shingles reached both the brain and the bladder in an unusual case described by Jordan Pyatt and colleagues in 2026. A healthy 66-year-old man developed fever, severe headache, and light sensitivity, and only later did the telltale blistering rash appear over his sacrum.

pmc-13299881:
U K Khanolkar and a team fuse heart tracing waveforms with clinical data to predict new atrial fibrillation during hospital stays, in a 2026 modelling study. New rhythm problems during acute illness predict poor outcomes, and simple clinical scores miss cases. Their system trains one network on raw tracings and another on structured variables such as age, heart rate, laboratory values, and medicines.

The fused model beat either single-source model on held-out test data. Threshold tuning trades sensitivity against false alarms: one setting catches most future cases for wide screening, while a stricter setting cuts false alarms sharply when follow-up resources are scarce, the authors report.
pmc-13299981:
I Deisenhofer and colleagues trace five years of ablation workflow change across Europe and India through a device registry, reported in 2026. Just over three thousand patients treated for atrial fibrillation, supraventricular rhythms, or ventricular arrhythmia were enrolled between 2020 and 2024. Patient profiles stayed broadly similar across the period.

Total procedure times held steady, while energy delivery times, lesion patterns, power levels, and sedation choices shifted by indication. Conscious sedation rose sharply for ventricular cases. Safety stayed constant overall, recurrence fell for one rhythm group, and acute success climbed for ventricular ablation. New catheters and high-power techniques drove much of the change.
pmc-13300281:
L Donisi and co-authors examine premature battery depletion in subcutaneous defibrillators using the French HONEST cohort, reported in 2026. These devices avoid leads inside veins, yet a manufacturer advisory flagged batteries draining early in certain EMBLEM models. The analysis covered 4,924 patients implanted between 2012 and 2019 and compared patients whose batteries depleted early with those showing normal depletion.

Premature depletion affected 462 patients, about one in ten, over a mean follow-up a little above four years. Diagnosis came at a mean of 4.8 years after implant, and replacement followed roughly fifty-four days later, with no sudden deaths in that interval. Newer device generations were heavily over-represented among affected patients. Local complications and reintervention rates matched the normal group, so the authors judge timely generator replacement safe while confirming the problem's scale.
pmc-13300381:
Staying active in old age tracks with feeling healthier, Keon Woo and two colleagues report from Korean survey data in a 2026 study. They drew on the eighth Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey and scored older adults with the HINT-8 quality-of-life tool. Active aging was split into health, participation, and security domains for regression analysis.

The health domain carried the strongest link to quality of life, and security also mattered. Participation showed only a weak, non-significant tie, which the authors partly blame on how it was measured. Older adults with less schooling and those in rural areas scored lower on both scales. The authors ask for longitudinal work to test cause and effect.
pmc-13300681:
Water near abandoned uranium mines on the Navajo Nation still carries cancer-linked metals, Christine Samuel-Nakamura and Abdul-Mehdi S. Ali report in a 2026 study from northwestern New Mexico. More than 500 unreclaimed mines dot the region. The pair measured nine metal(loid)s in local water with plasma mass spectrometry.
