pmc-13390181:
Margareta Morrissette and co-authors ask, in 2026, whether the face's retaining ligaments steer how basal cell carcinoma spreads in the midface and around the eye. These ligaments are best known for holding facial soft tissue in place during ageing and facelift surgery.

The team reviewed 163 patients treated with Mohs surgery and used the final surgical defects as a stand-in for tumour size and shape. Each defect was classed as near, far from, or crossing a ligament, and its shape was measured relative to the ligament line. Skin surgeons gain evidence on whether ligaments act as barriers that channel tumour growth, knowledge that can sharpen surgical planning in a cosmetically sensitive region.
pmc-13391481:
Ziqi Ren and colleagues present, in 2026, a solid-state osmotic power source inspired by the resting voltage of living cells. Osmotic power harvests energy where salt levels differ, but liquid designs risk leakage and drying out.

Using a layered material called MXene, whose ion and electron behaviour can be coupled, the team built an integrated electrode design needing only three building blocks for a compact device. The solid architecture raises power per volume and removes liquid handling problems. Arrays of the devices powered commercial electronics in demonstrations. Energy researchers gain a portable, responsive power concept drawn from cell biology rather than river-mouth engineering.
pmc-13391981:
Xiaohan Zheng and co-authors test, in 2026, whether fat around neck arteries, read on spectral scanning, can flag the plaques that cause symptoms. Carotid atherosclerosis threatens stroke, and identifying symptomatic plaques early guides preventive treatment.

The team analysed 306 consecutive patients whose carotid disease was confirmed on angiographic scanning and who also had spectral scans of the head and neck. Plaque size data and fat signal data were pulled from each scan. The team checked how the two sets moved as a pair. They then built models to find which fat signs flag a plaque on their own. Scan doctors gain a new sign to test. It comes from tissue that most scans catch now but few teams take the time to gauge.
pmc-13392081:
Alaa M Khalil and colleagues test, in 2026, whether pulsed electromagnetic fields can boost or blunt an antibiotic carried in chitosan nanoparticles. The approach aims at severe bacterial infections without relying solely on high antibiotic doses, as multidrug resistance escalates.

Ciprofloxacin was packed into chitosan beads, tiny balls of a shell-based sugar. The beads held a high share of the drug fed into them. Beads and fields then faced three germ types, alone and paired. The study checks with care for both help and harm. The fields might boost the drug, or they might blunt it. A booster that blunts the drug at times would not be safe to use. Care teams gain a clear map of how the pair acts.
pmc-13392281:
Weisi Ma, Zhiwei Zhao, Jinshuo Zhang, and Mengyao Xun map, in 2026, how ecosystem services in the Yellow River Basin trade off against or reinforce each other. Managing land well requires knowing these interactions and their drivers, yet past work often ignored service pairs with no effect and the role of two-way land change.

Using the InVEST model and spatial methods, the team tracked carbon storage, soil retention, water yield, food production, habitat quality, and landscape aesthetics from 2003 to 2023. Changes from land cover transitions were quantified and drivers analysed with attention to spatial variation. Basin managers gain a twenty-year interaction map for one of China's great river systems.
pmc-13393281:
Thomas Quail and Sina Wittmann argue that the many descriptions of transcription compartments in the cell nucleus are not rivals. They range from tidy small complexes to sprawling droplet-like condensates, but they are points on one continuum. Gene transcription gathers its machinery into dynamic, membrane-free assemblies, and the field lacks a shared frame. The authors propose transcriptional compartment as an umbrella term covering the whole range.

Surveying what such assemblies have actually been shown to do, they find the firmest functional evidence where cells need switch-like responses: fate choices, stress reactions, environmental sensing, and disease states. Most everyday biology likely runs on the small, fleeting middle forms, which are also the hardest to study, sitting below microscope resolution and built from interactions that double as their function. The piece maps the available toolkit and the methodological gaps that remain.
pmc-13393481:
Volkan Kizilkaya and Sefa Erdem Karapinar study advanced bone death in the hip after COVID-19 in a 2026 five-year retrospective cohort paper. Some patients develop avascular necrosis of the femoral head after infection, and severe cases reach Ficat stage III or IV, where the bone structure collapses.

The single-center study followed patients with at least five years of clinical and imaging records, recording illness severity, hospital and intensive care stays, steroid type and duration, and antiviral treatment. Logistic models tested which factors predicted advanced disease. Clinicians gain clues about who needs closer hip monitoring after severe COVID-19 illness.
pmc-13393581:
Marc T Cantwell, Marwa O El-Derany, Raja Gopal Reddy Mooli, Sadeesh K Ramakrishnan, and Yatrik M Shah traced how low oxygen inside liver cells shuts down the urea cycle. That pathway detoxifies ammonia into urea. Fatty liver disease involves chronic oxygen shortage, and the oxygen sensor HIF2-alpha drives severe inflammation and scarring in mouse models. Working in mouse hepatocytes and in liver tissue from mice bred for chronic low oxygen, the team hunted for nitrogen handling faults.

The urea cycle proved significantly depressed in a HIF2-alpha-dependent manner, and ammonia duly climbed. Control sits with HNF4-alpha, the master regulator of mature liver identity, which HIF2-alpha suppresses. With the master switch dimmed, several liver-specific pathways falter together. The authors suggest blocking HIF2-alpha could preserve full hepatocyte function, while noting that exactly how it represses its target remains an open investigation.
pmc-13393881:
Dou-dou Li and others report blood washing for severe pancreas swelling with fat overload in a 2026 case write-up plus a look back at past cases. Both high-fat pancreas swelling and fat overload from vein-fed fat fluid are rare, and the pair together is rarer still.

A 78-year-old woman with gullet cancer fell ill with severe pancreas swelling after about three weeks of fat fluid with no fat checks in her blood. Plain care failed as pain and defense markers rose, so blood washing began at once to pull fat from her blood. The case backs fast blood washing when fat-driven pancreas swelling spurns plain care.
pmc-13394081:
Xu, Nan, and Yu review, in 2026, recent progress on graphitic carbon nitride photocatalysts for making hydrogen peroxide with sunlight, water, and oxygen. Hydrogen peroxide is a widely used green oxidant, with annual production of 5.5 million tons, yet over 95 percent comes from the energy-hungry anthraquinone process. Carbon nitride, a metal-free semiconductor, can drive the reaction under light, but its efficiency needs improvement before industry switches.

The review explains the reaction principles, then surveys seven families of fixes used on the catalyst. These include doping with other atoms, engineering defects into the crystal, joining it with other materials, loading metal cocatalysts, anchoring single metal atoms, and adding chemical functional groups. Each strategy aims to harvest more light, separate electric charges better, or steer the chemistry toward peroxide instead of water. The authors close with the field's challenges, including efficiency at scale and long-term catalyst stability.
pmc-13394181:
Mathilde Liffran leads a fourteen-author team linking damage along the spinal motor pathway to disability patterns in multiple sclerosis, in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. The corticospinal tract carries movement commands; its lesions are common in MS, yet symptoms vary widely.

One hundred patients were prospectively scanned and grouped. Some had only brisk reflexes; some had leg weakness; some had arm and leg deficits. Lesions were segmented on brain and spinal cord images. Quantitative imaging gauged microstructural damage severity. The hypothesis: wider deficits mean more extensive tract damage. Ninety-two patients entered the final analysis. Mapping lesion load to limb patterns could sharpen prognosis and rehabilitation targeting.
pmc-13394381:
Jaehyun Lee and colleagues describe, in 2026, a friendly gut germ reshaped to fight pancreatic cancer in mice. The germ settles in tumours, where oxygen is low, and makes a tuned form of interleukin-2. That signal wakes up killer T cells more than the cells that calm them down. Plain interleukin-2 fades fast and can harm the whole body, so local delivery matters.

Given to mice, the germ slowed both skin tumours and tumours grown in the pancreas. It also worked better when paired with chemo, radiation, or other immune drugs. The authors offer the approach as a route into cancers that shrug off standard care.
pmc-13394681:
Akihiro Sunaga and co-authors reply, in 2026, to critics of their heart ablation sub-study. The work tested extra burning of low-voltage patches in the left atrium during care for lasting atrial fibrillation. Critics raised doubts about the win ratio method and about who was left out. The reply thanks them and walks through each point.

The authors agree the method has limits, such as how ties and outcome order shape results. They note that patients with tiny low-voltage patches were excluded. In the main group, extra ablation showed no clear gain. A stricter pick of patients hinted at benefit. The reply calls for care in reading patch size as a target.
pmc-13396081:
Olamazadeh and team explore, in 2026, how stimulation frequency affects force steadiness in Parkinson's patients with deep brain stimulators implanted in the subthalamic nucleus. Keeping a pinch force steady is a fine test of motor control. Ten patients did a precision pinch tracking task at 10 and 20 percent of their maximum strength under high-frequency stimulation at 130 hertz, low frequency at 50 hertz, and stimulation switched off.

Patients with worse motor scores, above 25 on the standard UPDRS-III scale, showed shakier force control than less impaired patients at both effort levels. Within that more impaired subgroup, 130-hertz stimulation cut force variability versus stimulation off, while 50-hertz responses varied widely between individuals. In less impaired patients, no meaningful difference between frequencies emerged for steadiness. The authors suggest stimulation settings should be tailored to disease severity rather than set the same way for every patient.
pmc-13396381:
Citro and colleagues compare, in 2026, the frontal aslant tract, a frontal-lobe wiring bundle central to speech, across monkeys, chimpanzees, and humans. All three groups share frontal regions for vocalization, yet only humans talk. Using diffusion tractography, the team measured the tract's size and layout in each species, then correlated degeneration of its subsegments with language deficits in patients with primary progressive aphasia.

The human tract is left-lateralized and enlarged, mostly in its anterior, prefrontal part. That prefrontal segment measured four times the monkey size in chimpanzees and eleven times the monkey size in humans, a striking divergence, while the precentral segment shrank in both apes and humans. Species differences in total tract volume were large, with an effect size of 0.71 in the analysis. In patients, posterior tract damage tracked impaired verbal fluency, while anterior damage disrupted syntax, supporting a speech-sequencing role.
pmc-13396981:
Morie Vandi and co-authors ran a year of surveillance on babies admitted with chest infections to Kenema Government Hospital in Sierra Leone. Their 2026 study enrolled children under two years old between October 2020 and October 2021, within two days of admission, all with at least one breathing symptom.

Nose and throat swabs from 502 children were tested with a panel that detects many viruses at once. At least one virus turned up in 376 children, 74.9 percent of those enrolled. Younger age linked with more severe illness in the analysis, which also hunted maternal, infant, and household factors behind severity, data meant to guide vaccine and care priorities in a high-burden country.
pmc-13398081:
Vanessa Dalla Costa and Raffaella Filippini grow avocado cells in the lab as a greener source of the fruit's healthy compounds. Their 2026 study responds to the costs of orchard avocado: heavy water use, seasonal swings and fruit lost after harvest. Cell cultures of the Hass variety offer a controlled, year-round supply grown from a small start of plant tissue.

Colour tests across growth stages found 14-day-old callus richest in phenolic compounds and antioxidant power, so that batch went forward for deep profiling. Chemical scans revealed flavonoids, proanthocyanidins and galloyl compounds among a phenolic-heavy mix. The authors frame lab-grown callus as a candidate production route, while noting that yield and scale still need work.
pmc-13398481:
Jianbo Qing and co-authors build a cell-level atlas of kidney diseases that attack the podocyte, the cell wrapping the kidney's filters. Their 2026 study combines single-nucleus gene sequencing with high-resolution spatial mapping across five major podocytopathy types. Podocyte injury drives these diseases toward kidney failure, yet its molecular and spatial mechanics were poorly charted.

Each disease type carried its own molecular signature, with shared signs of skeleton damage inside podocytes and neighbourhood features tied to outcomes. One protein, PDE4DIP, emerged as an unrecognised keeper of the podocyte skeleton, bracing it through partner proteins and growth signals. Gene editing in cells and animals confirmed the role, and its levels tracked kidney function in patients.
pmc-13398681:
Kerryn Brown and colleagues check a dose snag when breast radiotherapy is delivered face-down on an MR-Linac machine. Their 2026 technical note covers three patients with left-sided breast cancer treated prone, where the breast unavoidably touched the couch. Partial breast treatment gives a higher dose to a smaller volume, and the magnetic scanner-linac sees soft tissue superbly, but its narrow bore forces the contact in question.

Plans delivered 30 Gy in five fractions and were recalculated with and without the magnetic field to isolate its effect. Dose to the whole skin layer ran consistently higher with the field on, and the contact patch of skin was scored separately. All plans still met target and safety limits, giving planners numbers for a quirk of the prone setup.
pmc-13399281:
Caitlin F. Canfield and co-authors set out the protocol for a randomized trial, published in 2026, that blends two early-childhood programs inside pediatric primary care. HealthySteps already embeds child-development specialists in clinics. PlayReadVIP coaches parents in reading and play through video feedback. The trial asks whether delivering both together strengthens parent-child relationships more than HealthySteps alone for families with low incomes.

The design enrolls 355 parent-child pairs, starting with 35 in an implementation phase and then 320 in an effectiveness phase, assigned at random to the combined program or to HealthySteps alone. Support arrives at every well-child visit from birth to age two. Assessments at enrollment and at 12 and 24 months cover relationship quality, parents' cognitive stimulation, and children's social and emotional development. Because the report is a protocol, it describes the plan and its reasoning rather than results, which will come once the trial finishes.
pmc-13400481:
Kazuaki Hasegawa and colleagues review, in 2026, the infraorbital vein, a small vein beneath the eye socket that anatomy texts often skip. It links the midface, the eye socket and a deep vein network near the skull base. Its course varies beside the nerve and artery of the same name.

The review pulls together what is known about its development, tissue structure and many variants: a single trunk, paired channels or a web-like plexus. Extra openings in the bone add further variety. Clinically, the vein matters for repairing eye socket and cheek fractures, placing implants, tracking spread of dental infection and cosmetic work. Knowing its variants helps surgeons plan and dodge complications.
pmc-13400581:
Randeep Wadhawan leads a team estimating, in 2026, the economic benefits of robot-assisted repair for abdominal wall hernias in India. The analysis uses patient-level data from a prospective multicenter study and compares robotic with standard keyhole surgery. Health gains were converted to quality-adjusted life years over 30 days.

Simulations scaled results to a yearly cohort of 300,000 operations. Total benefit ran to roughly 2.8 billion rupees at the standard value threshold, with a wide uncertainty range. Time saved in the recovery unit after anesthesia made up about two thirds of the benefit, followed by patient and caregiver productivity gains. The authors offer the figures as a basis for policy and purchasing choices.
pmc-13400681:
Bruno Calsa and co-authors show, in 2026, that feeding pregnant mice a low-protein diet leaves their offspring with weaker bones in old age. Poor nutrition before birth is known to shape later health, but effects on bone aging were not well mapped. Osteoporosis stems from failed bone renewal and crumbling internal structure.

Male offspring were examined at 12 and 18 months. Those from protein-restricted pregnancies had less spongy bone, lower mineral density and thinner outer bone by old age, and their thigh bones broke under less force. Microscopy showed more porous bone and disordered collagen fibers. Gene data pointed to a lasting shift in the bone immune environment, with more macrophage-linked signals and more bone-eating cell activity.
pmc-13400981:
Thuy Hao Nguyen and co-authors report, in 2026, a woman in her seventies whose heart valve infection and strokes traced back to a mouth bacterium, alongside a hidden bowel tumor. Infective endocarditis is a dangerous infection of the hearts inner lining, usually seeded by bacteria entering the blood. Sometimes no entry source is ever found.

Blood cultures grew Streptococcus mitis, and heart imaging showed a mobile growth on her mitral valve. Brain scans revealed multiple strokes thrown off from the heart. Persistent abdominal symptoms then led doctors to severe fecal impaction and a previously unknown neuroendocrine tumor in her small intestine with liver spread. The authors suggest gut pathology may seed such infections and deserves evaluation when no source is clear.
pmc-13401581:
Adrian-Valentin Potârniche and co-authors describe a 2026 case of chronic proliferative rhinitis in a sheep in Romania, linked to an unusual Salmonella strain. It is reported as the first noted case of its kind in southeastern Europe. The patient was a three-year-old ewe at a university teaching farm in Transylvania.

A check found discharge from both nostrils and visible growths filling both nasal cavities. Heat imaging showed extra warmth over the nose, matching active inflammation, and CT scans revealed wide growth invading the ventral nasal turbinates. Tissue analysis showed chronic proliferative rhinitis, with fibrous blood-vessel tissue, thickened surface cells, and a mixed inflammatory infiltrate rich in lymphocytes, plasma cells, and macrophages. Salmonella enterica subspecies diarizonae was the only microbe found in nasal swabs, confirmed by serotyping, PCR, and immunostaining.
pmc-13401681:
Maryam Nasimi and colleagues published a 2026 retrospective analysis of 54 cases of lupus erythematosus panniculitis, a rare form of cutaneous lupus that inflames the fat layer under the skin. The condition is hard to diagnose and treat because its clinical and tissue features are poorly documented.

All cases were biopsy-proven and evaluated at a dermatology referral centre between 2016 and 2022, with records mined for demographic, clinical, laboratory, and treatment details and slides re-examined where needed. Women outnumbered men five to one, and the mean age was just under 39 years. About a quarter of patients also had systemic lupus. Delayed diagnosis was strongly tied to lipoatrophy, the permanent loss of fat that deforms the skin. Under the microscope, lymphocytic vasculitis appeared in about 72 percent of cases and discoid lupus features in about 69 percent.
pmc-13401781:
Fang Yan and co-authors examined whether giving dexamethasone through the liver's artery during chemoembolization improves long-term survival in liver cancer, in a 2026 retrospective study. Chemoembolization, called TACE, delivers chemotherapy into the tumour's blood supply, and the steroid's survival effect in this setting was uncertain.

The team reviewed patients who got TACE as their first treatment between January 2014 and December 2016, dividing them into those who got arterial dexamethasone and those who did not. Propensity matching, weighting, and score adjustment all tried to equalize the groups. In weighted analysis, the dexamethasone group lived longer without progression and longer overall, with risk reductions of roughly a third on both measures. Matched analyses showed similar trends, and pre-specified subgroup checks explored where the association held.
pmc-13401881:
Mengyuan Cen and a large team of co-authors built a lung-targeted nanomedicine carrying bilirubin to treat paraquat poisoning, in a 2026 study. Paraquat, a widely used herbicide, kills through acute lung injury driven by reactive oxygen species attacking the lung's microvascular lining.

Their particle, called BR@Lipo-CerTP, wraps bilirubin in liposomes decorated with a peptide that binds C16 ceramide, steering the cargo to pulmonary endothelial cells. Under the microscope the particles were uniform spheres of about 120 nanometres with a narrow size spread and good stability, and lung lining cells took them up better than untargeted versions. In cell tests they blunted paraquat's killing, cell suicide, and oxidant build-up while restoring antioxidant defences. Multi-omics work traced the mechanisms, and a mouse model of paraquat lung injury tested survival, tissue damage, swelling, and safety.
pmc-13402581:
Mahdee Jodayree and colleagues designed an explainable transformer system to detect zero-day attacks on medical Internet of Things networks. Their 2026 paper tackles intrusion detection under severe class imbalance, unseen attacks, and deployment limits, where older methods rely on heavy feature work and fail on new datasets. A protocol-aware model could generalize better.

The team built a transformer with protocol-state masking at multiple scales that embeds protocol rules into attention, plus auxiliary heads and an energy-based open-set module. Trained on one IoMT benchmark and tested on a fully separate testbed, it reached about 99.6 percent accuracy on the unseen data and strong zero-day detection, with an AUROC of 0.975. The paper supports protocol-aware modeling for hospital networks, while live deployment testing remains ahead.
pmc-13402681:
Victoria A. Fuchs and colleagues measured drug interactions for direct oral anticoagulants in Belgian primary care for atrial fibrillation. Their 2026 retrospective study uses the THIN database for 2022 to 2023, covering patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat that raises stroke risk. Blood thinners prevent clots, but interacting drugs can raise bleeding or clotting risk.

Among 5,637 patients and 13,334 prescriptions, 22.9 percent of patients had at least one interaction during the year, and 17.8 percent of prescriptions involved one, mostly pharmacodynamic, meaning additive effects rather than altered drug levels. Antidepressants, antiplatelets, and anti-inflammatory drugs led the list. Higher stroke-risk scores and multiple anticoagulant types raised interaction odds. The paper urges routine review of bleeding-risk combinations in primary care.
pmc-13402881:
Cláudia Agostinho and colleagues report two rare cases of urothelial carcinoma reaching the pericardium, the sac around the heart, and review what is known about the pattern. Bladder-type cancers usually spread to lymph nodes, bone, lung, and liver; heart involvement shows in only about 1.8 percent of cancer cases tied to the heart, and pericardial spread often stays silent until autopsy.

The first case follows a man in his late 50s with stage IV disease diagnosed in July 2022 who answered fully to cisplatin and gemcitabine, then held on maintenance avelumab. In March 2023 he arrived breathless with a dry cough and fast pulse, the turn that exposed pericardial disease. The authors use both cases to argue that new breathlessness in advanced urothelial cancer should prompt a look at the heart sac, not only the lungs.
pmc-13403381:
Jeong Jae Han and co-authors unveiled Polychip in 2026, a droplet chip that tests how microbes affect each other at very large scale. Six chip steps run in one device, so tiny drops can be made, mixed, grown, and sorted with little hands-on work. The team says the setup works far faster than robot liquid handling.

They screened over two million soil microbes against a drug-proof lung germ. About twenty thousand drops showed killing action, and three soil strains stood out for broad power. Liquid from those strains also slowed two major hospital germs. Gene and chemical tests pointed to one secreted compound behind the effect.
pmc-13403681:
Rafal P. Piprek, Izabela Rams-Pociecha, and Paulina C. Mizia surveyed in 2026 the headgear of cud-chewing mammals, the only living mammals with bony head growths. Cattle horns, deer antlers, pronghorn sheaths, and giraffe knobs differ in form and growth pattern. One view holds they share a single origin, while another says they arose apart.

The review weighs body structure, growth, fossils, family trees, and gene clues for both views. Headgear first appeared more than 20 million years ago in this group. Settling its origin could also teach doctors about regrowing tissue, since antlers regrow each year in a way few mammal parts can.
pmc-13404381:
Danae Goetze led a 2026 study that tested outcome forecasting after cardiac arrest in patients kept on life support for at least four weeks. Withholding care can make grim forecasts come true, which clouds older data. The team enrolled coma patients at eight German hospitals and kept 101 for review after set exclusions.

Poor outcome at one year struck about 67.3 percent of the group. Single markers rarely cried wolf yet missed many poor cases. Two or more poor markers together gave no false alarms at all in the window studied. Adding a coma recovery score sharpened the sorting further. Repeated checks beat one-off reads, the team concludes.
pmc-13405781:
Yuankun Qi and co-authors pair magnetic heart recordings with a neural network to detect pulmonary hypertension, in a 2026 study. Magnetocardiography senses the heart's magnetic field with high detail, but reading it needs machine help. Patients had the diagnosis confirmed by catheter testing or were low-probability controls.

A temporal convolutional network learned from 64-channel recordings plus age, sex and body mass. Discrimination reached an AUC of 0.939 in internal checks and 0.974 on held-out patients in the reported results, beating standard machine learning models. Decision curve analysis supported clinical usefulness at sensible thresholds. Which signal features drove the verdicts is explored through attribution analysis.
pmc-13406681:
Remigiusz Olędzki and Kristi Kerner review a friendly gut bacterium as a candidate ally against allergy and cancer, in a 2026 narrative article. Lactobacillus acidophilus lives in the gut and is widely used as a probiotic. Literature mainly from 2019 to 2026 covers live bacteria, killed preparations and the liquid they grow in.

Studies report anti-allergy effects and the ability to slow cancer cell growth and trigger their death in dishes and animal models. The bacterium spurs protective compounds, including short-chain fatty acids and surface sugars, and steadies the gut wall. Immune signalling changes thread through most findings. The authors place the microbe inside modern natural and functional medicine, with human proof still developing.
pmc-13407081:
Annika Bender and colleagues, writing in 2026, ask whether chemical tagging of a stress-related gene in blood differs among adults with mental disorders who endured difficult childhoods. They focused on SIAH3, a gene linked to stress response and cell energy structures, in people with borderline personality disorder, major depression, or social anxiety, plus healthy controls.

Both diagnosis and heavy childhood adversity leaned toward lower tagging of the gene, and the two factors interacted significantly across the whole group. Disorder-level looks told messier stories. Borderline cases leaned the opposite way before adjustment. Depression results weakened once other factors were counted. In social anxiety, lower tagging with adversity appeared only in healthy controls. The authors read this as disorder-specific biology rather than one shared mark.
pmc-13407581:
Guojun Li and co-authors test, in 2026, whether calibrating surgical navigation in real time sharpens screw placement in spines deformed by neurofibromatosis type 1. The genetic condition twists the spine and distorts the bony posts that screws must thread. The team compared standard navigation with a recalibrated version. Sixty-three patients were operated on between 2023 and 2025.

Surgeons placed 1,228 screws in total. The calibration group seated more screws perfectly. This held across most pedicle types on the curve's concave side, and most on the convex side. Fewer screws broke the bone wall overall. Operating time, blood loss, and complications did not differ between groups. The authors present real-time calibration as a practical add-on for complex deformity surgery.
pmc-13407681:
Partha S. Kundu and co-authors map, in a 2026 scoping review, how psychiatry is taught to undergraduate medical students in India. Future doctors must spot and manage common mental illness. Yet psychiatry teaching has been brief and low-stakes. The review gathered curricula, studies, and policy papers on the subject up to April 2026.

Fifty-five reports qualified. Teaching has shifted from a fixed time-based syllabus toward a structured competency framework under the national regulator, and short clinical postings with interactive methods improved knowledge, attitudes, and confidence. Persistent problems include stigma among students, a hidden curriculum that undervalues the subject, scarce faculty, and psychiatry's near-absence from high-stakes final examinations, which leaves a certification gap. Local innovations and faculty development offered the brightest facilitators.
pmc-13407881:
Xin Wen, Runjia Wang, Li Zhang, and Minghua Liu show, in 2026, that mixing left- and right-handed molecules unevenly can outshine using either one purely. Mixed-handed systems usually follow the majority handedness. They glow more weakly in twist-sensitive optical tests than single-handed ones. The team set out to break that rule. Their tool was a glutamic-acid-derived pair of mirror molecules.

Fine-tuning the imbalance between the two forms triggered a structural reshuffle, and at particular ratios both circular dichroism and circularly polarised light emission exceeded the pure single-handed assemblies. Simulations explained why. Minority units slot into mixed-handed oligomers that align the light-active units at an optimal pitch, amplifying the signal instead of diluting it. A design principle for high-performance chiral optical materials follows.
pmc-13408181:
Rongming Guo and team present a sub-second method to gauge electrical impedance of epithelial cell layers. Their 2026 work introduces Time-domain Epithelial Impedance Measurement, which swaps slow frequency sweeps for step current pulses and time-domain voltage study, skipping Fourier transforms. Standard impedance spectroscopy takes tens of seconds per reading, too slow for fast cell events.

The method gauges resistance, capacitance, and linked traits every 0.3 seconds, a 100-fold time detail gain, with errors benchmarked against standard methods in circuits and human bronchial and colorectal cell lines. Applied to colorectal cells exposed to saponin, it revealed smoothly gated double-exponential resistance and capacitance shifts too rapid for standard methods. The work offers a high-detail tool for dynamic barrier and drug assays.
pmc-13408481:
Alisher Sherov and co-authors present in 2026 a three-layer optimisation scheme for running a small power grid that is disconnected from any national network. Such off-grid systems must balance cheap generation, stable voltage, and happy customers at once, while demand itself can be managed. Their test case is a standard 33-node grid with a hydrogen system acting as central storage.

The top layers reshape demand by clipping peaks at offered prices and shifting flexible loads to better hours. The bottom layer then optimises generation against all three goals together, using entropy weighting and a constraint method to choose among trade-offs. Case comparisons reported satisfaction up by about nine percent, voltage quality up by about seven and a half percent, and production cost down by about nine percent.
pmc-13408881:
Junzhuo Cai and colleagues compress one of nature's slowest recycling processes into an hour in 2026. In soil, dead biomass matures into humic substances over days to years, building fertility as it goes. Their electrochemical version drives the same transformation with electrodes: reactive fragments born at the anode and hydrogen species at the cathode stitch the breakdown products back into large humic-like molecules.

The artificial product resembles natural humus in composition and behaviour, and it shows promise as a slow-release fertiliser, as an oxidising helper, and for treating salty, alkaline soils and polluted water. Economic and life-cycle comparisons favoured the method over landfilling and composting on land use, transport distance, greenhouse effect, and acidification. The authors pitch it especially at land-scarce megacities drowning in organic waste.
pmc-13409081:
Fulvia Ceccarelli and colleagues report in 2026 the first use of a lupus drug against the autoimmune anaemia that strikes a minority of lupus patients. In this complication the immune system destroys red blood cells, raising damage and mortality risk, and treatment guidance is borrowed from blood medicine rather than written for lupus. Seven patients with active haemolysis received anifrolumab, which blocks the type I interferon receptor.

Every patient entered with a positive direct Coombs test and laboratory proof of ongoing haemolysis. Haemoglobin climbed progressively during treatment, reaching a statistically significant gain over baseline by three months, and overall lupus activity was tracked with a standard index in parallel. The authors present the series as a proof of concept that interferon blockade can quiet this manifestation, while the tiny, uncontrolled sample demands confirmation before practice changes.
pmc-13409281:
Ryuto Yashiro, Masataka Sawayama, Ayumu Yamashita, and Kaoru Amano probe in 2026 what the brain's body-selective patch actually knows about a scene. This region, the extrastriate body area, fires for human bodies, but recent work hints it encodes richer meaning. Rather than decoding raw brain patterns, the team predicted the region's response from written captions of natural scenes, then asked which object pairings drove the predictions.

Bodies photographed alongside sports equipment produced the strongest predicted responses of any category, with vehicles and accessories also potent partners. Digging further, three features carried the effect: the speed of body motion implied by a still image mattered most, with the number of people and their size contributing secondarily. The caption-plus-co-occurrence framework gives neuroscientists an interpretable way to ask what selective brain regions represent.
pmc-13412381:
Carolyn C Foster and colleagues survey American pediatricians in 2026 about caring for children with disabilities. Little nationally representative data existed on these doctors' attitudes and confidence. The American Academy of Pediatrics 2023 Periodic Survey drew 463 weighted responses covering whether practices welcome such patients and how fairly the wider system treats them.

Nearly every respondent, 98 percent, said their practice welcomed patients with disability. Yet 81 percent agreed the health care system often treats these patients unfairly. Only 27 percent felt very confident they could match the quality of care given to children without disabilities. The most confident doctors were over twice as likely to welcome disabled patients, linking training to openness.
pmc-13413681:
Kairat Ruslanuly and colleagues describe in 2026 what kinds of cataracts bring Kazakh children to surgery, using three years of records from two national eye centres. Their retrospective cohort included every child aged seventeen or younger operated on in Astana and Almaty between 2022 and 2024, totalling 528 children and 782 eyes. Causes were grouped as congenital, traumatic, lens displacement, or complicated by other disease.

Congenital cataract dominated, accounting for 78 percent of children and over half of them affected in both eyes. Trauma caused 12.9 percent of cases, always in one eye and mostly in boys, who made up 77.9 percent of that group. The middle age at surgery was 6.5 years across the cohort. The authors show how cause patterns shift with age, sex, and one-sided versus two-sided disease.
pmc-13415281:
Neil Hawkins and colleagues compared two long-acting HIV prevention shots in 2026 without a direct trial between them. Injectable cabotegravir and lenacapavir each beat older options in their own trials. No study has pitted them head to head, so the team linked the trials through shared controls of no prevention and daily oral pills.

Both network methods found high and comparable protection, with wide uncertainty bands that reflect the indirect design. The paper gives prevention programs a careful reading of two strong options, while noting that only a direct trial could settle which shot edges ahead.
pmc-13415781:
Eva Arino-Mateo and colleagues tracked telework in Spain from 2021 to 2022 in a 2026 study of 4606 teleworkers from national statistics. As emergency remote work settled into hybrid routines, the team asked whether people worked remotely more or less often, how they judged the experience, and what they actually wanted.

Remote days fell even as ratings of the experience improved, widening the gap between wanted and actual remote days, with younger and better-educated workers wanting the most. The paper frames telework as a negotiation between staff hopes and employer control, with stakes for motivation and well-being.
pmc-13415881:
Ashley N. Hutchinson, Robert J. Brummer, and Julia Rode check whether probiotic effects on the brain outlast the pills, in a 2026 randomized trial follow-up. Thirty-two healthy older adults in Örebro, Sweden took one of two forms of a Lacticaseibacillus strain or placebo for six weeks. Brain imaging and questionnaires were repeated four to six weeks after stopping.

Some earlier changes persisted at follow-up while others had faded. Brain connectivity between a parietal region and visual areas differed by formulation at follow-up. Anxiety scores also showed group by time patterns between week six and weeks ten to twelve. Gut to brain effects may linger longer than assumed.
pmc-13418481:
Ghulam Murtaza and colleagues pair a plant hormone with biochar made from dog manure to help common beans tolerate salty soil, in a 2026 glasshouse study. Pots ran over two seasons with three salt levels, three hormone doses, and raw or chemically treated biochars. Salt stunted shoots and roots, disturbed hormones, and raised oxidative damage in untreated plants.

Combined treatments rebalanced growth hormones, lifted antioxidant enzyme activity, and improved water status and root traits. Raw biochar with the higher hormone dose gave the strongest protection against damage under moderate salt. Acid treated biochar with the lower dose maximised one key enzyme. Field and molecular validation are still needed.
pmc-13418781:
Xianwen Hu and colleagues tested whether early PET/CT scans predict outcomes in adult Hodgkin lymphoma in a 2026 study of 116 patients. Scans at diagnosis and after four chemotherapy cycles yield measures of tumor uptake, volume, and total glycolysis, yet which ones truly forecast survival needed a head-to-head test.

Interim tumor volume and total lesion glycolysis predicted overall survival best, while baseline volume, interim volume, and Deauville response score independently predicted progression-free survival. Clinicians gain a leaner set of scan markers for judging who needs stronger or gentler treatment when risk allows.
pmc-13419081:
Belachew Tefera and colleagues run a national quality check on animal antibiotics sold in Ethiopia, hunting for unregistered, weak, or fake products. Bad veterinary drugs threaten animal health, farm output, and food safety at once. Inspectors gathered 142 product samples and put each through three checks: registration status, visual screening, and official lab testing.

Most of the products, some 95.7 percent of the set, were imported, chiefly from China and India. A full 17.9 percent of samples, 25 products in total, had no registration at all. Among registered goods, visual screening still flagged about a quarter as below standard on paperwork or packaging grounds. The findings give regulators a concrete target list for tighter market control.
pmc-13419181:
Erin C. Blankenship-Sefczek and colleagues ask whether hard times in early life leave a mark on the shape of the first upper molars. Teeth keep a lasting record, since enamel defects form when growth is stressed in childhood. The team focused on one defect type, shallow grooves called linear enamel hypoplasia, often used to flag early stress in past populations.

Shape measures for the molars were set beside defect records for the same teeth. Statistical models, including methods that shrink complex shape data into main patterns, tested the links. Marks of disruption did track with altered tooth form in the results. For researchers who read skeletons, the link means tooth shape itself may carry a quiet record of childhood hardship.
pmc-13419681:
Teruyuki Nomura and Shunsuke Kanou argue that crisis care plans built on patient preferences fail when the system behind them is never checked. Joint crisis plans and advance choice documents let people state treatment wishes before a mental health crisis hits. Trial results for such tools have been read as proof that they do not work.

The authors say that verdict is premature, since the trials rarely verified that wishes could reach the team at the moment of crisis. A major evidence review found low confidence in most shared decision results and did not cover these plans at all. For Japan, they urge testing advance documents as measurable infrastructure, with delivery tracked, rather than as paperwork. The shift reframes a negative record into a building task.
pmc-13420281:
Finsterer reported in 2026 a single patient who developed four rare immune diseases in sequence, a combination never described before. The woman developed relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis at 31 and took an immune-calming drug for over seven years. A thymoma, a tumor of the thymus gland, followed and was treated with chemotherapy and surgery.

Finsterer recounts that a year later she was diagnosed with myasthenia gravis, the muscle weakness disease, treated with steroids and other immune therapies. After a sclerosis relapse at 40 she received a stronger antibody drug for two and a half years, and then developed T-cell lymphoma, a blood cancer. The lymphoma answered chemotherapy only partly, so she received a transplant of her own stem cells. Whether the immune drugs, an underlying immune fault, cancer therapy, or pure chance linked the chain stays unclear, and the author calls for deep studies of such cases.
pmc-13420381:
Madison F Muehl and colleagues test a food web theory in Lake Turkana, the great desert lake of East Africa. The theory holds that large, wide-ranging eaters link the fast open-water and slow shore food chains, steadying the whole web. The team traced the feeding niches of five major fish species across their life stages.

Chemical isotope records in fish tissue, joined through a statistical mixing model, showed which species truly link the two channels. Small mid-level fish, not the giants, did the vital linking work in this lake. That flip challenges a theory built largely on other waters. Lake managers who protect only trophy species may miss the small fish holding the web together.
pmc-13420481:
Hassan Chamseddine and colleagues describe a front-of-belly route, passing below the pancreas, to reach the upper aorta for complex repair. Standard routes to this aorta segment split the working field and block access to right-side vessels. Their patient was a 73-year-old man whose leg arteries were so narrowed by disease that walking 50 yards was his limit, after eight years of worsening claudication.

Scans showed heavy disease around the organ branches and down through the pelvis, with both thigh pulses absent on exam. The operation combined clearing the aorta itself with a bypass graft to both legs. The midline route kept the whole field in one view, the advantage the authors stress. Vascular surgeons facing hostile upper abdomens gain a described path with its steps laid out.
pmc-13421281:
Paladino and colleagues report a 2026 study from Spain's SENDO project on ultra-processed food and young children's daily movement.  The team measured diet at ages four to five in 586 children, then checked two years later who still met all three guidelines.

Most children met at least one guideline, but only about four in ten met all three. Children in the highest third of ultra-processed food intake were more likely to fall short later than the lowest third, with a steady trend across intake levels. The clearest gap was recreational screen time, where the highest-intake group had nearly double the rate of missing the limit. Cutting ultra-processed food in preschool years may help protect sleep, play, and screen habits.
pmc-13421681:
Reda A. Ali, Heba E. Aboulqasem and Dalia Elzahraa F. Mostafa document, in a 2026 study, how two common plasticisers damage the testes of young mice. Dibutyl phthalate and its relative DEHP, used to soften plastics, are tied to male reproductive harm, and the team tracked dose and timing carefully.

Immature mice received three dose levels for fifteen days and were examined at four ages. Chemical measures showed depleted protective glutathione alongside more nitric oxide and fat oxidation, signalling oxidative stress. Tissue damage grew with dose: at the top dose every sperm-producing tubule was damaged in the youngest animals. Recovery between fifty and seventy days was substantial at low doses but incomplete at high ones. Cell-death and inflammation markers rose with injury.
pmc-13423081:
Uchenna Cosmas Ugwu and five co-authors measure how common depressive symptoms are among older Nigerians with type 2 diabetes in the rural southeast. Diabetes raises the risk of depression in later life, yet rural communities there had rarely been surveyed, so the team visited 25 communities across five states between September 2025 and February 2026.

Using staged random sampling, they recruited 683 adults aged 60 or older with confirmed diabetes and screened mood with a short geriatric scale adapted to local culture. A striking 83.3% showed depressive symptoms, and 39.7% scored in the severe range. Being male, being older than 71, and living with family each tracked with severe symptoms, while some schooling appeared protective. The authors urge joint diabetes and mood screening.
pmc-13424281:
Ethan Waisberg and nine colleagues review red and near-infrared light therapy, called photobiomodulation, as a gentle add-on treatment for ageing and diseased eyes. The eye is a natural target, since light reaches it easily. The retina and optic nerve also burn energy heavily. Their decline with age involves the mitochondria that light is thought to stimulate.

Their evidence-weighted survey separates the stronger findings from the weaker. It stresses that results depend heavily on device and dose. It also distinguishes multi-wavelength therapy from repeated low-level red-light treatments used in children. Proposed mechanisms run through a mitochondrial enzyme that responds to light, with anti-inflammatory effects downstream. Safety questions and the gap to routine clinic use get frank treatment.
pmc-13424381:
Ying Liu leads a fourteen-author mouse study pinpointing which inner switch carries the insulin-boosting signal of gut hormone receptors in pancreatic beta cells. Protein kinase A does the carrying, and the team suspected one specific form, type IIB, because beta cells express it distinctively.

Mice lacking that form handled glucose poorly and answered weakly to liraglutide, a GLP-1 mimic, in both whole-animal tests and isolated islets. Gene profiling, electrical recordings of ion channels, and microscopy of insulin granules filled in the picture: the switch coordinates channel behaviour and the look and readiness of granules. Hormones such as glucagon and FSH fed into the same route. The authors name type IIB PKA the primary effector of this pathway.
pmc-13425081:
Sirikorn Densrisereekul and colleagues report a 2026 case of a middle-aged man with progressive facial swelling and widespread violaceous plaques. Testing revealed AIDS-related angiomatous Kaposi sarcoma, a rare tissue subtype that can resemble benign haemangiomas under the microscope and in clinic. No earlier history pointed toward HIV infection, which made the diagnosis harder to reach.

Facial lymphoedema had not previously been linked with this subtype, yet the authors argue it reflects the stepwise tumor growth seen in Kaposi sarcoma. They warn that tumor-related swelling signals a poorer outlook and may call for chemotherapy alongside antiretroviral therapy.
pmc-13426981:
Benedetta Mariani and coauthors study how whisker stimulation strengthens resting brain networks in the rat barrel cortex in a 2026 neuroscience article. Even without input, cortex shows restless collective activity, including synchronized oscillations and power-law avalanches thought to support readiness and efficient processing. Simultaneous multi-electrode recordings covered barrel cortex and thalamus, the relay for whisker signals, during spontaneous activity.

Oscillations near 11 hertz appeared alongside slow waves below 4 hertz, with avalanche activity nested between them. Whisker input reinforced this resting network structure, suggesting sensory experience tunes the brain's idle dynamics for faster future responses. The rat whisker map is neat and well known, which makes it a strong test bed for how rest states form and how they shift with touch. The touch of a whisker is slight, yet the brain marks it with care.
pmc-13427081:
Cian Ó Móráin reflects on caring for a dying patient in Canada's North in a 2026 narrative essay. His patient Peter was a 75-year-old Inuk man from Nunavut with advanced pancreatic cancer, flown three hours south to hospital near Great Slave Lake for care. Morning rounds began with polite clinical exchange, yet conversation soon turned to stories Peter chose to share with his physician.

Late-winter light, thawing wool jackets, and a deeply lined face frame an encounter about distance, culture, and end-of-life care far from home. The essay honors what a patient teaches when medicine can offer presence more than cure.
pmc-13427381:
Michael Ingber and colleagues measured patient satisfaction with a new postcoital fluid-absorbing vaginal device in a 2026 study. Postcoital discharge, semen leakage, odor, and residual fluid discomfort are common yet under-studied quality-of-life concerns for sexually active women, rarely assessed in routine care. The evaluated device reportedly reduced patient-reported discharge and odor and sped normalization of vaginal pH after intercourse in the work described.

Formal epidemiologic data on postcoital hygiene worries remain thin despite extensive research on libido, arousal, and painful sex. Satisfaction data give clinicians a starting point for discussing a topic patients often raise only when asked.
pmc-13427781:
Zhengyu Lin and colleagues share fifteen years of experience with baclofen pumps placed into the spinal fluid in China, for regions where the treatment is still new. One surgeon at Ruijin Hospital in Shanghai treated every patient in the review, from January 2011 to October 2025.

Sixty-eight people, with 44 men, gave 214.3 pump-years of follow-up. Cerebral palsy led the brain-level causes at 10 of 68, while traumatic spinal cord injury led spinal causes at 23 of 68. Goals counted as achieved for 87.2 percent of people, and the paper pairs complication lessons with a wider nerve-stimulation plan.
pmc-13428181:
Tim Van Langenhove and a panel of Belgian experts set out how Alzheimer's disease should be diagnosed now that disease-modifying treatments exist. Their 2026 consensus statement, coordinated by the Belgian Dementia Council, responds to rules requiring biomarker proof of amyloid pathology before treatment.

Thirty-one experts from neurology, geriatrics, neuropsychology, imaging, laboratory medicine, and primary care developed the recommendations through multidisciplinary discussion of current evidence. The statement lays out a stepwise pathway combining clinical assessment with confirmatory tests: spinal fluid analysis, amyloid brain scans, and emerging blood tests. It weighs the strengths and limits of each option across clinical situations. Using Belgium as an example, the panel highlights shared European problems such as limited reimbursement, uneven access to expertise, and too little diagnostic capacity, and proposes practical fixes.
pmc-13430181:
Dan Wang and co-authors examine, in a 2026 study, how a fat-cell hormone changes lipid handling in chicken liver cells. Adiponectin guides fat metabolism in mammals, yet its role in birds, whose livers do most fat making, was unclear. The team treated primary chicken liver cells with lab-made adiponectin, with and without a fatty acid preload that mimics overload. Cell fat content, exported fats, and gene activity were all measured.

Adiponectin cut the fat stored inside cells under both conditions. It raised the receptor that receives its own signal and pushed more triglycerides and fat-carrying particles out of the cells. A key energy-sensing pathway switched on briefly. Curiously, cells also took up more sugar and fat while quieting their fat-burning genes, a feedback pattern the authors note. Export, they conclude, is the main drain the hormone opens.
pmc-13430781:
Vid Duplančić and colleagues measure life quality among Croatian women of working age living with breast cancer, against national norms. Survivorship outcomes matter, yet population-referenced data for women aged 18 to 65 in Central and Eastern Europe were scarce.

Outpatients at two tertiary cancer centres in Croatia completed a five-dimension health questionnaire plus a breast-cancer module in a 2024 cross-sectional study. Utility scores used a Slovenian value set and were set beside age-matched Croatian female norms from 2022, with non-parametric tests for group gaps. Clinicians get a benchmark for where cancer dents daily life most for working-age women.
pmc-13433681:
Nima Afshar Moghaddam and colleagues review how HPV, vaginal germs, and body defences interact in cervical cancer. Lasting infection with high-risk HPV drives most cervical cancer, yet whether the virus stays put rests on more than the virus alone.

When vaginal germs fall out of balance, with fewer Lactobacillus germs and more Gardnerella, Sneathia, Prevotella, and Atopobium, the body clears HPV less well. Long-term inflammation then grows, and early cell changes can turn into invasive cancer. The review points to germ tuning, immune drugs, and gene editing as future tools. Doctors get a three-way view of prevention that goes past tests and shots alone.
pmc-13433881:
Lynn Cheaito and co-authors surveyed adults in Lebanon in 2026 on what they know and feel about organ donation, and what tips their will to give. An online form spread by chain sharing from late 2024 to mid 2025 and drew 830 adults, three fifths of them women. Set scales graded facts, views, and a joined will score.

Near all had heard of donation, yet only a fifth held good facts. Two thirds held warm views, while under half held a firm joined will, and only a third would sign up now. High degrees, health jobs, and private work each lifted will. Blocks named span kin and crowd pull, fear of death talk, thin facts, and faith qualms. Hypothetical aids lifted will, which hints at levers for drives.
pmc-13434381:
Jun Young Kim and colleagues used Korean health insurance records to test whether removing children's tonsils and adenoids cuts later chest and airway infections. Adenotonsillectomy means surgery that takes out both the tonsils and the adenoids, often done for snoring or repeated throat infections.

The study matched 6,848 children who had the surgery with 34,240 children who did not, then tracked hospital visits for three years after surgery. The surgery group had higher odds of hospital visits for upper and lower airway infections, while pneumonia rates showed no clear gap. Increases appeared first in younger children and later in older ones, and were stronger in children with no past infections. Kim concludes the surgery should not be done just to prevent such infections.
pmc-13434481:
Marion Lecorguillé and colleagues study what shapes toddlers' diets in a French birth cohort, from family social position to migration background. Diet-linked chronic disease shows stark social gaps, yet few studies have weighed family factors in full, including fathers' traits.

A long-term socio-ecological model was used, with diet patterns found by principal component analysis as outcomes in multivariable linear regression. Models added maternal immigrant status, schooling, older siblings, single motherhood, and age first, then job, then household income, with matching analyses for fathers. Health teams get a family-wide map of how social position and migration shape what young children eat.
pmc-13434581:
Huan Nguyen Pham's team set out in 2026 to improve iron checks for women in early pregnancy, working with patients at a hospital in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. Standard ferritin cutoffs were built to catch anemia, so low iron without anemia often slipped past routine screening. Their cross-sectional study focused on healthy women in the first trimester who were not yet anemic.

The team modeled ferritin against red blood cell measures to find a level that marked early iron shortage, then tested it in 452 women with full records. A cutoff near 59 gave a four-zone scale, from clear shortage through a middle zone to enough iron, and it flagged more cases than older cutoffs. Readers get a practical case for earlier, finer screening before anemia sets in.
pmc-13435581:
Chen and colleagues used patient-derived midbrain organoids, small lab-grown brain tissues, in 2026 to study POLG disease, a severe inherited disorder of the mitochondria, the cell's energy producers. Mutations in the POLG gene destabilize mitochondrial DNA, and dopamine-making neurons suffer most. Single-cell gene sequencing let the team inspect neuron subtypes one by one.

Mutations jointly turned down genes for energy production and for synaptic signaling, hitting fully matured dopamine neurons hardest. Two subtypes, called DA2 and ventral midbrain neurons, showed the strongest changes, suggesting maturity itself brings vulnerability. Chronic treatment with nicotinamide riboside, a vitamin-like compound that feeds the NAD pathway, shifted gene activity back toward normal in part. The authors say tuning NAD metabolism may be a route worth testing for this disease.
pmc-13435981:
Sitohang and colleagues gathered in 2026 what systematic reviews say about how far clinical practice guidelines take sex and gender into account. Guidelines shape standard care, and ignoring sex and gender can bake unfairness into it. This umbrella review combined seven reviews that together appraised 784 guidelines published across two and a half decades.

Sex or gender was mentioned in about seven in ten guidelines, yet only about fifteen percent let it shape a diagnosis or treatment recommendation. The rest treated it as decoration, with muddy terms and thin follow-through. Barriers named include too few women in the underlying studies, few sex and gender experts on guideline panels, and weak methods for turning sex-specific evidence into advice. The authors list fixes for each stage of guideline writing, from drafting to review.
pmc-13437081:
Virkud and a large team revisit two famous trials that disagreed about preventing repeat preterm birth. Their 2026 paper concerns 17-alpha-hydroxyprogesterone caproate, a hormone drug: the Meis trial found it cut recurrence substantially, while the PROLONG trial found no benefit. The leading explanation blames different baseline risks between the trial populations, and the authors test that with transportability methods built on doubly debiased machine learning.

Transporting the Meis effect onto the PROLONG population kept the protective point estimate, though with a wide uncertainty range. Transporting PROLONG onto the Meis population did not recover the Meis benefit, yielding a small harmful-leaning estimate instead. Because measured population differences could not reconcile the trials, the authors suspect a hidden problem, such as unmeasured factors that modify the drug's effect. They call for direct study of how treatment effects vary by preterm birth history.
pmc-13437181:
Ashish Suresh and Sunny Priyatham Tirupathi compared two numbing drugs for children's dental work in a blinded trial. Half received buffered 4 percent articaine, adjusted with bicarbonate to body-like acidity, and half received standard 2 percent lidocaine.

Buffered articaine hurt less at injection and during the procedure, the 2026 report finds. It also took effect much faster, in about seventy-two seconds against about one hundred fifteen, and dentists rated it easier to give. Numbness in soft tissue lasted longer, and heart rate rose less during the shot. Success in numbing the tooth pulp was nearly equal, at 84 percent against 82 percent, and side effects a week later did not differ. The authors judge the buffered drug the more comfortable choice for young patients, with a similar safety picture.
pmc-13437581:
Renata Zajączkowska's team tested mirogabalin with mood drugs in 2026 in mice with nerve injury pain. After sciatic nerve injury, mice got single or repeat doses of mirogabalin, amitriptyline, or duloxetine, alone and paired, with touch and cold sensitivity measured.

Each drug alone eased hypersensitivity, the new drug longest at up to six hours, and repeat new-drug doses plus a daily mood drug strengthened relief beyond single-drug effects. Pain teams get a combination lead grounded in a standard nerve injury model. Human dosing, safety, and long-term benefit remain untested, so clinical translation is still early.
pmc-13437981:
Wangshu Tu's team built MDBiomarkers in 2026, a searchable database for Duchenne muscular dystrophy markers drawn from blood and muscle studies. An interactive web app now offers exportable summaries and supports fresh meta-analysis beyond single-study p-values, with plans for living updates as new work lands. Duchenne teams get a time-saving starting point that should cut duplicate discovery studies. Users must still weigh study quality, since the database gathers published evidence rather than re-validating it.
pmc-13439281:
Li and colleagues presented a quiz case in 2026 about a rare stomach growth in a woman aged 52. She had upper belly pain for several years, yet exams and blood tests were normal. A camera exam found a small doughnut-shaped raised area, about one centimetre wide, under the stomach lining. Ultrasound probing and biopsy first suggested a common harmless polyp, but a CT scan showed a dense spot hinting at bone or calcium.

Doctors removed the growth in one piece using endoscopic submucosal dissection, a method that cuts under the lining through a scope. Lab study of the removed tissue showed a fundic gland polyp containing mature bone, a rare change called osseous metaplasia. They advise doctors to consider this rare change when scans show dense spots in stomach growths.
pmc-13439481:
Xiaotian Liao and Ben Lehner ask how often distant-site effects, called allostery, explain why gene variants break proteins, reporting in 2026. A mutation far from a protein's working site can still silence it by shifting its shape, yet such cases are usually lumped with simple unfolding damage. The pair built a comparison method that separates true activity loss from loss of protein amount. They applied it across paired laboratory measures of abundance and activity, plus proteome-wide evolution and stability data.

Across those datasets, allosteric damage emerged as a common route to loss-of-function disease variants. Harm from mutations also faded with distance from the active site in a steady, shared pattern. The authors argue that mapping allosteric links across human proteins would sharpen predictions of which variants cause disease.
pmc-13440281:
Bin Yan and colleagues review magnetic hyperthermia as a cell-level immune tool against cancer, writing in 2026. Recent work recasts the warmth as a precise stress signal inside cells, gentle enough to spare much healthy tissue while reshaping tumour immunity.

The review covers three linked fronts. One is designing particles that turn field energy into heat efficiently. Another pairs field-controlled heating with drug delivery for combined cell regulation. A third explains how treatment provokes immune-visible cell death and activates immune cells. Links to tumour vaccines and standard immunotherapy receive close attention. The authors present magnetic hyperthermia as a flexible platform for precision cancer immunotherapy rather than a stand-alone heat cure.
pmc-13440681:
Santos and colleagues report a 2026 longitudinal study of disability in people with hearing loss before and after a year of hearing aid use. The schedule scores six life domains, from thinking and moving to social participation.

Average disability scores fell by about twelve percent after a year with hearing aids. Thinking, self-care, and participation domains improved significantly, while some physical domains moved less, as expected from a hearing device. The change was not just in hearing tests but in lived function, which is the outcome patients care about. The domain pattern helps set honest expectations for patients.
pmc-13441881:
Zakharova-Luneva and colleagues audited outcomes for 61 people with spinal cord injury or disorder. These spanned demographics, surgery, rehabilitation management, and the full range of complications after repair.

By discharge, 95 percent of patients could sit for at least four hours. Half tolerated more than eight hours of sitting daily. Setbacks were common though: 15 percent had reduced transfer ability. And 27 percent needed more personal care support than before surgery. Being overweight raised total complications by 54 percent in the adjusted analysis. Diabetes alone showed no such link to overall counts. Local wound complications tracked with more pressure injuries at admission, prior flap surgery, osteomyelitis, and longer waits before sitting.
pmc-13442881:
Song Ding and colleagues describe a 2026 machining study that brings nonlinear model predictive control into the shaping of Wolter-I mirrors, curved X-ray optics used in extreme ultraviolet collection systems. The team replaced the usual PID controller in a computer-controlled surfacing process, modeling the mirror shape and the grinding process for both rough and fine stages.

Simulations found the best removal when the spindle feed ran at 25 millimeters per second with a removal pressure of 9 newtons and a mid-range abrasive size. Experiments then showed the new control improved surface accuracy and efficiency while cutting production cost. The work offers optics shops a steadier route to the fine surfaces these mirrors demand, with the usual caveat that shop conditions vary.
pmc-13443281:
Ezequiel Antorán and colleagues test which plant traits steer who lives beside whom in a 2026 field study. Their plot held more than 45,500 plants from 45 species in a dry annual community. Teams tracked pairs from seedling to adult across two years of unlike weather, on whole or torn soil crust.

Trait gaps mostly pushed species apart in the models. Leaf build, seed mass, and fruit-to-leaf mass shares drove the splits most, above all in wet years and among seedlings. Crust tears reshaped trait effects in unlike ways at fine and broad scales. The authors read coexistence as a moving balance of habitat filters and rivalry. Forecasts that freeze trait roles will miss those shifts, they warn.
pmc-13444181:
Oh, Hong, and Shim reviewed in 2026 slow-release local anaesthetics, designed to stretch pain relief after surgery from a single injection. Three carrier families lead the field.

Oh describes fat-bubble preparations that leak drug slowly at the injection site. Polymer systems pair the drug with anti-inflammatory agents to calm the tissue. Gel networks hold and release the drug while limiting spread into the blood. Gains are real but uneven: early burst release, variable timing, high cost, and thin trial proof slow adoption. The authors expect these systems to grow into catheter-free pain control as delivery tech and validation improve.
pmc-13445181:
Yukun Mei and colleagues recast Confucian self-cultivation as a practice of the body, arguing that ritual form trains mind and conduct over time, in a 2026 theory paper. The authors work within psychology of philosophy and culture rather than lab research. Their model draws on close readings of classic texts and on ritual life in late imperial China.

Five linked parts make up the model, among them moral agency held in the body and attention shaped by repeated rite. Ancestral rites in Huizhou lineages serve as the worked case, not as a stand-in for all Confucian practice. The paper closes with claims that later studies could test, widening views of selfhood past models that center on lone thought and belief.
pmc-13445381:
Xiaolu Liu and colleagues report a trial of a traditional Chinese herbal granule for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, a fatal disease that wastes muscle, tested against the standard drug riluzole, published in 2026. No cure exists for the disease, so any safe way to slow decline draws close interest. The trial ran at eleven centers in China with blinded treatment.
