One pre-set analysis showed a small edge for the granule that fell short of firm proof, while a second model favored by the authors showed a clear edge. They call for a larger final-stage trial to settle the claim.
pmc-13446181:
Maurizio Marogna and colleagues revisit patients with dust mite allergy fifteen years on, asking whether under-the-tongue immunotherapy kept asthma at bay, in a 2026 follow-up study. The therapy is known to calm nose allergy and asthma symptoms, yet its power to prevent asthma over the long haul was less sure. All patients began with nose allergy alone plus twitchy airways.

Seventy-eight patients enrolled, and fifty-nine finished the fifteen-year span, split among drug care alone and three, four, or five years of the therapy. New allergies appeared in every drug-only patient but in under a quarter of treated ones. Asthma, marked by a set drop in lung power, struck over half the drug-only group and only about one in fifteen treated patients, at any therapy length.
pmc-13447181:
Minju Han and Jeehoon Kang ask in a 2026 commentary whether every person with new heart failure needs routine testing for blocked heart arteries. Guidelines back testing when disease is suspected and treatment could change, not as an automatic step for all. A large Danish study in the same journal issue gives the discussion fresh numbers to weigh.

Among more than sixty-one thousand people with new heart failure and no known artery disease, only one in five had such testing within ninety days. Tested patients were younger and healthier at the start. After weighting, testing linked to slightly lower long-term death risk overall, with no gain past age eighty-five. Han and Kang note that testing itself was tracked, not what it found or what treatment followed, so selection effects may explain much of the gap.
pmc-13447381:
Shaojie Lin and Guang Zeng introduce a neural framework for encoding musical sequences in 2026 work on music cognition and composition tools. Music involves curved, non-flat structure, timing patterns and uncertainty that standard sequence models handle poorly. A model that respects musical geometry could serve analysis, recommendation and automatic composition alike.

Their encoder joins three parts, covering curved-space mapping of sequences, a planning module for timing and rhythm, and a filter that measures uncertainty to harden predictions. Training aligns internal representations with the input and refines outputs using the uncertainty estimates. Experiments report clear gains in accuracy and robustness over existing methods, though the summary gives few hard numbers. The authors frame the system as a principled step toward machines that encode music in a more human-like way.
pmc-13448681:
Dandan Li and coauthors unravel a 2026 finding: thrombospondin-1 from smooth-muscle-like cancer-linked support cells recruits tumor-linked white-cells in gastric cancer. Mixing single-cell reading with tissue staining, the team mapped THBS1 output, its link to worsening and outlook, and its spatial overlap with white-cells.

THBS1-marked support cells grew in tumors, and higher THBS1 tracked deadly worsening, poor outlook, and heavier white-cell entry. Cutting or blocking THBS1 cut white-cell call-in and slowed tumor growth in models, partly by cutting call signals CXCL1, CXCL5, and CXCL6. The support-cell-white-cell axis emerges as an immune therapy target.
pmc-13448781:
Weiwei Wang and co-authors present a 2026 case report of retinal inflammation caused by the Epstein-Barr virus in a man with no clear immune weakness. The 33-year-old patient arrived with a month of blurred vision, redness, and light sensitivity in his left eye. Scans showed inflamed vitreous gel, a swollen optic disc, and yellow-white patches on the retina.

Cultures from the vitreous fluid grew nothing, so the team turned to genetic testing of that fluid. The test found Epstein-Barr virus DNA at 123 copies per milliliter, while three related herpesviruses tested negative. Antiviral and steroid treatment calmed the inflammation, and later surgery cleared lingering opacity and traction. At four months the retinal patches had largely faded and vision had improved.
pmc-13448881:
Karina Martins and colleagues ask in 2026 whether poor function of tiny blood vessels forecasts who will develop diabetes, using the ELSA-Brasil cohort. They studied 1,268 adults free of diabetes at the start whose vessel function was measured by a fingertip pulse device. Two readings mattered: basal pulse amplitude, reflecting resting vessel tone, and a dilation ratio after blood flow restriction.

Over an average follow-up of 8.8 years, 159 participants developed diabetes. Those in the worst quarter for basal pulse amplitude faced more than double the risk, with a hazard ratio of 2.13 after adjustment for lifestyle and body size. The dilation ratio pointed the same way but more weakly. Obesity did not change the strength of either link. The authors argue vessel dysfunction is part of how cardiometabolic disease begins, not only a consequence of high blood sugar.
pmc-13449481:
Wang and colleagues report a 2026 study that predicts whether clear cell kidney cancer will return after treatment, using a machine learning model that fuses clinic data with scan patterns. The scan side uses a deep learning signature, image traits learned by a three-dimensional vision model. The team tested the best design on outside patients.

The three-dimensional vision model beat the rival designs, scoring strongly on outside patients, and the combined model that added clinical features reached an even higher agreement score for ranking who stays cancer-free. It also beat two established clinical scoring systems used for this cancer. Multi-year predictions of recurrence-free survival held up well. A tool that sorts patients by return risk more sharply can guide how closely each patient is watched and who should get added treatment, instead of treating all the same.
pmc-13449581:
Bixi Gao and colleagues mapped the shared genetics of schizophrenia and suicide attempt in a 2026 statistical study. The two conditions co-occur more often than chance, but the genetic overlap and any causal direction were unclear. The team drew on genome-wide association data from people of European ancestry.

Local and global genetic correlation methods found a significant positive correlation, with a correlation estimate of 0.48 and thirteen regions linked to both traits. Cross-trait analysis turned up thousands of shared variants, and bidirectional Mendelian randomization tested causality in both directions. The results give researchers shared loci and pathways to probe for biology that links psychosis risk with suicide risk.
pmc-13449781:
Abang Ulrich Akwo, Julius Luvanga, and Ketonze Valademy Ketu review in 2026 how DNA recovered from ancient remains turned the study of the past into a time-lapse science. Instead of inferring history from a single snapshot of living genomes, researchers now sample genes century by century. The review synthesizes the paleogenomic era from 2010 to 2025 across four themes. They are human migration and mixing, adaptation during domestication and selection, the history of pathogens and microbiomes, and ecosystem change read from sedimentary DNA.

The authors stress that the field's power carries obligations. Sampling destroys culturally significant remains, so rigor and ethical stewardship, including real partnership with descendant communities, are preconditions for trustworthy conclusions. They argue the next advances will come from weaving genomes together with archaeology, isotope chemistry, and ancient proteins. The past should be treated as moving processes rather than frozen events, with lessons for conservation, health, and social justice today.
pmc-13450581:
Mette Lange and co-authors set out in 2026 a new add-on approach for a painful skin disease marked by boils and tunnels. The disease, hidradenitis suppurativa, favors the armpits, groin, and the area under the breasts, and pain is its chief burden. Surgery plays a large role once tunnels and scars form.

The plan adds shots of a person's own fresh fat tissue near the sores, an idea borrowed from fistula care near the anus. Fat tissue may calm swelling, grow new blood vessels, and help skin rebuild, though the full path is not yet known. The authors frame the shots as a support to surgery, not a swap for it, for sore sites that resist standard care.
pmc-13451081:
Fogg and colleagues release robustocs, a Python package that helps breeders pick parents when the scores behind their choices carry error bars. Classic optimal contribution selection balances gain against inbreeding using estimated breeding values, but it treats those estimates as exact. Their 2026 package rebuilds the method with robust optimization, a math approach that plans against the uncertainty itself. It ships two solvers, one conic and one sequential quadratic programming, wired to free and commercial engines.

Tests favored the quadratic programming route with the free HiGHS solver. Classic truncation selection and classic optimal selection turn out to be special cases of the robust forms, which eases comparison. On an example, the robust picks trimmed the uncertainty in expected gain and group relatedness, at the cost of some gain. For breeding programs betting decades ahead, the authors argue, a smaller but surer step beats a bold one built on sand.
pmc-13452181:
Yanzhao Mao and colleagues combined machine learning with single-cell and tissue mapping data to find genes that drive pancreatic cancer. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is among the deadliest cancers, with only about 13 percent of patients alive five years on.

Their screening of large gene datasets flagged four candidate genes, with DKK1 the strongest marker of poor outlook. A second gene, S100P, proved steady at telling cancer from healthy tissue and partly tracked survival too. Cell-level maps showed the two genes mark different cancer cell states rather than one single cell type. Lab tests confirmed both genes push cancer cells to grow and move, supporting them as targets and markers.
pmc-13452581:
Xiaodong You and eleven co-authors train a computer model to warn early when kidney injury in sepsis patients is about to get worse. Sepsis is a body wide response to infection, and kidney injury is one of its deadliest turns. Their 2026 study defines worsening as a jump to the most severe kidney stage within seven days of the first injury.

Records came from four intensive care databases, with over 9,000 patients in the main training set alone. Twelve measures fed the final model, among them weight, blood pressure, urine output, and blood urea nitrogen. A random forest model, which averages many decision trees, beat five rival methods in checks inside and outside its home data. The team also built a simple web tool so doctors can enter the measures and get a risk score at the bedside.
pmc-13452981:
Grace E Steward, Adam J Culbreth, Fernando S Goes, and Vikram S Chib test whether fatigue, more than low mood, drives people with depression to avoid hard mental work. Their 2026 study gave 26 healthy adults and 18 adults with major depression a set of choices. Each choice paired a simple task for a small reward with a harder task for a larger reward.

The depression group reported far stronger fatigue than the healthy group on a standard scale. Across everyone, stronger fatigue meant fewer picks of the harder task, most clearly when the effort gap was large. Fatigue scores predicted choices better than either the diagnosis itself or a mood score. The authors suggest that care for depression should target fatigue head on when drive and follow through fade.
pmc-13453681:
Xiaofang Zhu, Zhenghui Ge, Zhou Wang, Xuejie Fu, and Zhan-ao Wu make magnetic nanoparticles that soak up methyl blue dye from wastewater at a huge scale. Dye laden water from factories threatens health and ecosystems worldwide. Their 2026 method uses rapid combustion to form mixed metal oxide particles of nickel, magnesium, copper, and iron.

The best mix held mostly magnesium, with particles averaging 17.4 nanometres wide, baked at 400 degrees for two hours. In tests with dye levels from 800 to 1,100 milligrams per litre, uptake fit a pattern that points to chemical binding as the slow step. The surface took the dye in many layers rather than one neat coat. After five rounds of use and cleaning, the particles kept about 90.7 percent of their first capacity, a mark of sturdy reuse.
pmc-13453981:
N. C. Wieland and others built a body model for the bug-killer acetamiprid in 2026, from pee, blood, and stool data, to work back from body levels to dose. This bug-killer is widely used and can harm nerves, and Euro chiefs cut its safe daily dose. Past body models lacked good human rate data for the drug and its break-down form.

Four folk took a mouth dose at ninety percent of the safe dose and a skin dose on a separate day, with drug levels tracked over time in all three body fluids. A body model built from those rates was checked against past human data. The drug was soaked up fast and mostly broken down, gone from pee after a day while its break-down form lasted four days. Rule-makers gain a model to infer dose from body signs.
pmc-13454281:
Jiahao Zhou, Ruiyang Han, and Tianshu Gao review, in 2026, how targeted immune drugs used for skin disease may affect the thyroid. Autoimmune thyroid disease, mainly Hashimoto thyroiditis and Graves disease, affects about two to five percent of people. Such thyroid problems often occur alongside skin conditions such as psoriasis, eczema, hair loss, and hives.

The review weighs thyroid evidence drug class by drug class. Checkpoint inhibitors show the clearest link to thyroid harm, while reports for dupilumab and ustekinumab rest on rare cases. Drugs blocking interleukin-17 or interleukin-23 might calm thyroid inflammation in theory, though trials have not confirmed that hope. The authors close by proposing thyroid checks matched to each drug's risk level.
pmc-13454781:
Butterbach-Bahl and colleagues review thirty years of research on nitrous oxide released from farm soils, a potent greenhouse gas that traps far more heat than carbon dioxide. The 2026 review traces work from the 1990s to today. It covers four areas: how emissions are measured, how soil processes make the gas, which microbes drive it, and how computer models predict it for national climate counts.

New tools such as fast sensors, laser based gas measures, and isotope tracing showed that emissions spike in brief hot moments and small hotspots, which sparse sampling missed. Gene based tools also revealed microbes that make or consume the gas through paths once overlooked. Yet big gaps remain. Lab findings still link poorly to whole fields, prediction error stays high, and insight seldom becomes farm practice that cuts emissions without harming food output.
pmc-13455281:
Adam Stachowski and colleagues review Polish rules for preventive breast removal in a 2026 paper from Szczecin. Poland funds such surgery for women with strong family history or BRCA1 and BRCA2 gene faults, yet newer gene findings have left other high risk women outside the rules. The review weighs evidence on four further genes, TP53, PTEN, PALB2 and CHEK2, and counts how many extra operations a wider rule would bring.

Evidence backed preventive surgery for all carriers of faults in TP53, PTEN or PALB2, while for CHEK2 only carriers of a truncating fault plus a family history qualified. Widening the rules would add about 122 two-sided operations and 25 one-sided operations each year in the estimate. The paper thus argues for a broader, gene-based rule, while leaving each woman to weigh surgery against watchful screening with her own doctors.
pmc-13455381:
Adedayo Oluwadamilola Adesida and colleagues measure how often two blood fluke species infect the same person in sub-Saharan Africa in a 2026 review. Schistosomiasis burdens the region, yet most counts cover each species alone, leaving joint infection poorly sized despite its treatment implications. The team searched four sources for studies from 1980 to 2025 reporting joint Schistosoma haematobium and Schistosoma mansoni infection, pooling rates with a random-effects model and splitting by place and age.

Twenty-six studies with 33,121 people across 11 countries gave a pooled joint infection rate of 19.1 percent, highest in West Africa at 26.9 percent and lowest in East Africa at 4.8 percent, with no clear gap across age groups. Variation between studies was very high, so the pooled rate should be read with care. Control programmes gain a first region-wide size for joint infection, with West Africa standing out for combined treatment planning.
pmc-13457381:
Haotian Wu and colleagues reframe MXenes, flat metal carbides and nitrides, as coordination chemistry platforms rather than mere sheets that conduct. Every MXene flake ends in a dense skin of terminal groups such as oxygen, hydroxyl, or fluorine, plus vacancies and interlayer ions, and that skin is where reactions happen. Their 2026 review organizes the field around the local metal-ligand settings those features create.

Worked examples span hydrogen evolution, oxygen electrocatalysis, surface-anchored single-atom catalysts for small-molecule redox chemistry, and metal-air and lithium-oxygen batteries. Across them, terminal groups, metal vacancies, swapped-in heteroatoms, and anchored single atoms each tune how molecules adsorb, how charge moves, and which products form. The authors warn that hybrid materials piled with extra parts obscure which site does the work. Progress, they argue, depends on naming which inorganic site does the work and tracking how it changes under working voltages.
pmc-13457481:
Artak Heboyan, Afsheen Maqsood, and Naseer Ahmed introduce a 2026 journal collection on prosthodontics, the dentistry branch that rebuilds and replaces teeth. Writing as editors, they frame the specialty's concerns: choosing among tooth- and implant-supported restorations, removable and fixed prostheses, ceramics, resins, and glass ionomer cements, each with trade-offs in strength, looks, and durability.

The piece previews studies inside it. One tested how bleaching routines strip enamel minerals and roughen enamel, finding the McInnes solution harshest, a modified version gentler, and artificial saliva partly healing. Another examined the sandwich technique, layering glass ionomer under composite resin, and found bond strength hinged on the cement, composite, and adhesive pairing, with resin-modified cement plus etch-and-rinse adhesive best. The editors argue that materials and digital tools, from CAD/CAM to artificial intelligence, need checking for biological safety and long-term behavior over first-day performance.
pmc-13457781:
Oh and colleagues report a 2026 study of hidden lymph node spread in papillary thyroid cancer.  Using a common data model database, the team studied 1,020 patients whose preoperative ultrasound and CT showed no suspicious nodes, hunting for everyday clinical factors tied to hidden spread.

Knowing which clean-scan patients actually harbor spread decides a hard surgical question. The choice is whether to remove the central nodes preventively, which risks voice and calcium complications, or to spare them and risk leaving cancer. Factors available before surgery, such as tumor features and lab values, were tested in statistical models for independent links. A reliable risk profile would let surgeons individualize that choice instead of applying one rule to a thousand necks.
pmc-13457881:
Tae Jin Yun and colleagues test an AI aid for spotting acute stroke on plain brain CT in a 2026 multi-reader study. Plain CT is the fastest first scan in stroke, yet small or subtle infarcts elude even skilled readers, delaying treatment. Nine readers, three non-radiologist physicians, three radiologists and three neuroradiologists, reviewed 917 cases with and without AI help in a crossover design.

Alone, the AI reached an area under the curve of about 0.81 with about 74 percent accuracy, about 76 percent sensitivity and about 73 percent specificity. With AI help, reader accuracy rose from about 72 to about 76 percent, with the largest gain for non-radiologists, from about 70 to about 75 percent. Emergency teams gain evidence that AI support narrows the expertise gap for stroke CT, though real-world timing and treatment gains still need prospective proof.
pmc-13458381:
Guus R. M. van den Heuvel and colleagues document what happens to early-stage lung cancer patients receiving no curative treatment. Median overall survival was 5.9 months across the supportive-care group and 9.6 months for those who chose it themselves, against 54.1 months for curatively treated patients. pmc-13458681:
Sandra G. Velleman and Krystyna Pierzchala-Koziec present the third Women in Avian Physiology topic, a 2025 Frontiers collection built to spotlight bird research led by women early in their careers. Nine papers span the microbiome and immunity, muscle satellite cells and their matrix, eggshell production and skeletal integrity, stress, and avian influenza.

Bardoxolone methyl steadied metabolism and stress handling in the turkey hen's sperm-storing tract, microbial variety left alone. pmc-13458981:
Ndumba and colleagues searched for enterovirus D68 in Zambian children hospitalized with severe respiratory infections in this 2026 study. The virus can cause serious breathing illness. It has also been linked to sudden limb weakness in children. Yet African data are scarce, even though such infections are a leading cause of child illness and death there. The team retested stored samples collected between 2018 and 2020.

Eight samples tested positive, all from 2020, and sequencing showed every one belonged to the A2 subclade, a genetic branch of the virus. No positives appeared in the earlier years' samples covered by the analysis. The authors argue that ongoing surveillance is essential, because a single retrospective check cannot show how widely the virus circulates in Africa or how its local strains change over time.
pmc-13459381:
Kanjanaporn Tantrongphak and co-authors talked with older Bangkok residents who worry about falling, to learn how they build a sense of control over falling. It used semi structured talks about fall stories, ageing, and daily life, grouping themes to trace how felt control is built and renegotiated over time.

Five connected themes emerged. People blamed falls on internal or external causes, and early fear often turned into adaptive awareness rather than paralysis. Acceptance of ageing and practical adaptation let some feel control beyond their physical limits. Life history, peers, and social expectations shaped how resilient individuals felt about risk. Control itself kept shifting, negotiated day by day, shaping whether participants stayed active and used prevention strategies.
pmc-13459681:
Lufianti and co-authors carried out a 2026 qualitative study of tuberculosis control barriers in rural Indonesia, where stigma and weak systems stall progress. Their title quotes the finding that patients hide because they fear being judged. The PRECEDE-PROCEED planning model sorted factors into predisposing, enabling, and reinforcing groups for closer analysis.

Nine themes emerged, led by lasting misconceptions and stigma marked by fear, shame, and shunning of patients. Access barriers covered poor housing and ventilation, staff shortages, low preventive therapy reach, and strained community health workers. Support gaps covered patchy treatment follow-up and little role for schools. The authors champion young people as unused agents of change.
pmc-13459781:
Yagna Oza and Katherine Borkovich mapped which internal signal proteins control the enzymes a bread mold fungus uses to digest cellulose, work with direct relevance to biofuel production. Neurospora crassa breaks plant fiber into sugar using three enzyme classes that cooperate, and earlier genetics showed G protein signals, the cell's relay switches, are required. Two G alpha subunits together proved needed for the first enzyme class, and the signal enzyme cr-1 was essential for action. Another subunit pair jointly regulated the second class, while the third was swayed by many signal genes but essential to none. Adding the messenger molecule cAMP rescued action most strongly. One regulator mutant lost action across all three classes, matching a permanently on mutant, a clue for tuning factory strains.
pmc-13460181:
Li Yan and colleagues studied in 2026 whether four blood tumor markers can forecast survival in small cell lung cancer, an aggressive cancer where earlier marker studies disagreed. Records from 160 untreated patients at a Tianjin hospital between 2019 and 2022 supplied marker levels measured before treatment, with survival checked by telephone follow-up. Statistical models weighed the markers together and adjusted for cancer stage.

All four markers rose in a straight line with worse survival, each carrying roughly half again the hazard at high concentrations. Only one, CYFRA 21-1, a fragment of a structural protein, stayed independently tied to survival once stage was considered. Predictive accuracy was modest overall, around the level the authors report for the combined curves, so markers support rather than replace clinical judgment.
pmc-13461081:
Aishwar Dixit and colleagues analyzed in 2026 whether rising childhood obesity tracks with acute lymphoblastic leukemia burden across 204 countries and territories. Using Global Burden of Disease 2021 estimates from 1990 to 2021, they compared age-standardized rates of this childhood blood cancer attributed to high body mass. National obesity prevalence was checked against incidence with correlation and trend methods.

The global rate of leukemia attributed to high body mass rose about fourteen percent across the three decades, reaching just under one case per hundred thousand. North America and Western Europe carried the highest burden, while middle-income regions climbed fastest, and national obesity prevalence correlated strongly with incidence. The authors caution that ecological data built on modeled estimates cannot prove that obesity causes leukemia in individual children.
pmc-13461181:
Tersur Theophilus Akpensuen and colleagues propose a hub-and-spoke model for African forage biodiversity in a 2026 paper. Native grasses, legumes and fodder trees could strengthen livestock nutrition, soil health and climate resilience, yet feed shortages and degraded grasslands limit productivity. Weak seed systems, limited extension support and scarce climate finance block adoption, so the authors call for forage strategies inside national policies. Policymakers and researchers gain a scaling pathway from proven forage innovations to continent-wide livestock transformation.
pmc-13461281:
Seong-Beom Koh comments in 2026 on research into how thinking problems reshape walking in Parkinson disease, focusing on a study by Wong and colleagues in the same journal issue. Falls and gait trouble disable many patients, especially those with mild cognitive impairment, yet how the brain adapts during long stretches of obstacle walking was unexplored. The featured study combined brain oxygen imaging with continuous gait measurement while patients negotiated repeated obstacles.

Both cognitively impaired and unimpaired groups engaged the brain more strongly early in the task. Impaired patients, however, showed a steeper fade in activity across the supplementary motor and premotor areas as walking continued, suggesting their neural adaptation tires faster and works less efficiently. Koh highlights the design's realism, since daily walking demands exactly this sustained adjustment.
pmc-13461481:
Aaron Ackerman and colleagues asked whether extra chemotherapy before transplant helps children with high-risk leukaemia already in deep remission. The patients had acute myeloid leukaemia, a fast blood cancer, and all reached transplant with no measurable disease left.

The single-centre review covered 40 children transplanted between 2011 and 2023, split by one-to-two versus three-to-four prior chemo rounds. Two-year relapse-free survival was nearly identical, about 66 to 68 percent, whichever group children fell in. Overall survival and relapse rates also showed no clear difference between the groups. Non-relapse deaths ran higher after fewer rounds, but Ackerman stresses the study was too small to settle the question. The authors back testing a leaner path: transplant soon after deep remission, guided by risk and response.
pmc-13461681:
Frederik J. de Lange and colleagues issue agreed guidance on carotid sinus massage for unexplained fainting in a 2026 document. Carotid sinus massage alone identifies heart-slowing reflex fainting, yet it is sidelined outside special fainting units and done with no set pattern. A world expert panel sets out uses, no-go cases and step-by-step method for general clinics, special fainting units and A&E wards.

Guidelines advise the test for patients over 40 with fainting of unknown origin fitting a reflex route, and pacing when heart-slowing syndrome with repeat sudden fainting is brought back. Tilt test with non-stop blood pressure watching best captures both heart-slowing and pressure-drop answers. Doctors gain handy steps to restore an ignored test tool and deliver cause-based treatment.
pmc-13462281:
Langxiong Chen leads a 2026 study of the protein TRIM32 in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, a cancer of the lining cells of the mouth and throat. TRIM32 had been linked to tumor growth in other cancers, yet its role was unmapped. The team profiled its levels in samples, checked them against patient records, and silenced the gene in two cell lines. Protein tests traced its partner chain.

TRIM32 ran high in tumor tissue, and high levels tracked with poor outlook. TRIM32-rich tumors showed active self-eating and p53 signaling in gene scans. Silencing TRIM32 slowed growth and invasion. It holds down TP53, the guardian tumor suppressor, and disturbs lysosomes, the cell's recycling centers, along with the self-eating flow they support. Immune cell patterns in tumors shifted with TRIM32 level. The authors name TRIM32 a harmful marker and a treatment target in this cancer.
pmc-13462381:
Khan authored a 2026 systematic review on the bodily costs of prolonged desk sitting for corporate employees, with attention to India. The review followed PRISMA reporting rules across four databases.

Eleven peer reviewed sources from 2012 to 2025 met the criteria Khan set for inclusion in the synthesis. Reported muscle and joint disorder rates reached about eighty-one percent among office workers in the included evidence. Blood vessel function in the leg fell sharply after three hours of unbroken sitting in one laboratory study. Sitting beyond roughly ten hours daily linked to forty to sixty percent higher cardiovascular death risk, even in people active outside work.
pmc-13462681:
Shengxin Zhang and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether a chemical signal in lung wash fluid can predict twitchy, overreactive airways after Mycoplasma pneumonia in children. The signal, leukotriene C4, is a known airway constrictor. The team reviewed 158 children treated for this pneumonia between 2023 and 2024, with 20 children scoped for foreign objects as controls. Lung fluid levels were measured, and airway reactivity was checked two weeks later in 87 children.

Fluid levels ran far higher in pneumonia cases than in matched controls, and higher still in children who later showed reactive airways. Higher levels went with worse lung function at follow-up, a link standard blood markers did not show. Nine machine learning models were compared; the best used two inputs, the lung signal plus a blood enzyme, and sorted cases with good accuracy. The authors propose the pair as an early warning aid.
pmc-13464281:
Asaad Nakhle leads a team that reports pulling a deployed heart stent out through a leg artery. An eighty-nine-year-old woman came for a valve replacement, yet an old coronary stent jutted from her right artery mouth into the aorta. The overhang risked clashing with the new valve hardware.

A snare loop threaded from the leg artery caught the jutting end and drew the whole stent free. The team then placed a fresh stent at the artery mouth under ultrasound guidance from inside the vessel. Few such removals are reported, since most cases go to open surgery. The save shows a snare can spare frail patients that larger operation.
pmc-13464881:
Claudia Ariadna Acero-Ortega and five colleagues published this 2026 study on whether calling a product 'gluten-free' in English rather than 'libre de gluten' in Spanish changes how Mexican consumers represent it. Celiac consumers split: the Spanish label evoked a restrictive eating experience and cost, while the English loanword tilted perception toward health and aspirational dimensions. The authors conclude that label language works as a cultural vehicle, signalling status to lifestyle buyers. For celiac patients, it may soften the sense of dietary restriction that their required diet imposes.
pmc-13465781:
Mustafa Öz and Enes Üstüner published a 2026 review of nano-scale immune boosters for fish farming. Farmed fish suffer frequent disease outbreaks. Antibiotics fill the gap, driving resistance. Tiny engineered carriers could deliver immune stimulants better. The review weighs mechanisms, benefits, and safety.

Four carrier families were compared in detail. Polymer carriers showed the strongest practical promise. They improved survival against major fish pathogens. Metal and carbon options raised more safety questions. Environmental effects received careful attention. The authors chart a path from laboratory to farm. Eco-friendlier disease control matters as aquaculture keeps growing worldwide.
pmc-13466081:
Chung and co-authors audited in 2026 how completely pilot trials in hip and knee replacement report their methods. Pilot trials test whether a full trial can run, and a special CONSORT checklist extension governs their reporting. The team searched PubMed for such trials from 2017 to 2023. Of 278 eligible papers, a random sample of 147 was scored in detail. Fourteen extra feasibility elements were checked too.

Reporting fell well short. Studies covered only about 55 percent of the checklist items that applied to them. Pilot-specific aims and what the pilot means for a future trial were often missing. Papers also skipped about seven in ten of the key feasibility elements. Citing reporting guidelines in the text tracked with better completeness. Failing to state funding sources tracked with worse reporting. The authors urge journals and authors to enforce the checklist, since weak pilot reports waste the trials they are meant to de-risk.
pmc-13466781:
Cunha and colleagues report real-world gene testing results for colorectal cancer in this 2026 single-center study. Next-generation sequencing, which reads many genes at once, guides modern cancer care, but how it performs in everyday practice is less clear. The team reviewed 97 patients chosen for routine targeted testing on two sequencing platforms and linked the results to their clinical records.

Ninety-one patients, about 94 percent, carried at least one reportable gene change, with 198 changes found in total. The most often altered genes were TP53 in about 56 percent of patients, KRAS in about 40 percent, PIK3CA, and BRAF. About 19 percent of tumors showed microsatellite instability, a sign of faulty DNA repair. Links between mutations and clinical features were weak, and none survived statistical correction for multiple testing.
pmc-13467381:
Klaudia Marek, Joanna Piwnik and Elżbieta Miller published this 2026 study of radial shockwave therapy for stiff, spastic arm muscles after stroke. Spasticity develops in roughly 43 percent of stroke patients and can lock the wrist and hand. The treatment sends pressure pulses into muscle without surgery. The authors tested whether adding four sessions to standard rehabilitation would loosen the wrist flexors and improve hand use.

The study involved 62 stroke patients with marked upper-limb spasticity. The treatment group received four shockwave sessions to the wrist flexor muscles, spaced six days apart, alongside usual rehabilitation, while the comparison group had rehabilitation alone. The treated group improved more in arm motor function and daily-living independence, and their wrist extension range grew. Spasticity scores also fell clearly in the treated group. The authors note the gains in movement and stiffness appeared independently of any change in pain.
pmc-13467481:
Mi-Kyoung Kang and colleagues report a retrospective study, published in 2026. It screens for sleep apnea in people with cluster headache. Cluster headache is severe one-sided head pain. It often follows daily and seasonal rhythms. Both conditions raise cardiovascular risk. The team tested the standard STOP-Bang questionnaire in these patients. They also tested whether adding headache-specific details helps.

Fifty-two patients had overnight sleep studies. Nearly half had sleep apnea severe enough to warrant treatment. The standard questionnaire performed only modestly. Adding the age at which cluster headache began improved screening. This held even during headache remission. Prospective multicentre validation is needed before clinical use, the authors say.
pmc-13467981:
Pan and co-authors scan the brains of young adults in this 2026 study to find neural signatures of internet addiction, compulsive online use that disrupts daily life. They focused on the hippocampus, a memory structure, and measured both its steady connections with other regions and how those connections fluctuate over time using resting-state brain imaging.

Forty-five young adults with internet addiction were compared with 29 healthy controls. The addiction group showed stronger steady coupling between the left front hippocampus and default mode network regions involved in self-directed thought, plus unstable, flickering connections between the hippocampus and visual areas. Both abnormalities grew with addiction severity and with difficulty regulating emotions. Further analysis showed emotion dysregulation partly carried the effect. It linked the altered wiring to symptom severity. The authors suggest emotion training as a treatment lever.
pmc-13468781:
Supriya Amanna and colleagues present a narrative review, published in 2026. It covers muscle and joint disorders among women who roll beedis. Beedis are thin Indian cigarettes made by hand at home. Rolling tobacco in leaves takes long hours. The posture is fixed and seated. It is a main income source for millions of poor women. The authors gather the evidence on its physical costs.

The reviewed studies report persistent pain and disorders. They concentrate in the neck, shoulders, and back. The upper limbs are also affected. Repetitive hand work drives the harm. Floor sitting and no ergonomic support add to it. The work is home-based and poorly regulated. Problems are recognised late. The authors recommend low-cost workstation changes and stretching. Links with primary care are also recommended.
pmc-13468981:
Ong and colleagues grew human stem cells on a collagen scaffold from treated cow heart lining in 2026, asking whether the material nudges cells toward unwanted fates. The scaffold, CardioCel, already patches children's hearts. The cells were mesenchymal stromal cells, versatile repair cells taken from fat and bone marrow. The team checked whether they stuck, multiplied, and could still mature into different tissues on demand. Gene activity was profiled across the whole genome.

The scaffold proved a neutral host. Cells adhered, grew, and differentiated normally when given the right cues. Of thousands of genes, only 57 changed activity on the scaffold, touching adhesion, oxygen response, and reactions to internal signals. Genes for the healing factors these cells secrete stayed switched on. The authors conclude the material supports cells without steering them. They propose such stem cell assays as a screening test for whether new scaffolds suit the body's own repair cells.
pmc-13469081:
Yuqian Sang, Yanan Wu, Huifang Bai, and Ling Yang report a randomised clinical study, published in 2026. It covers anaesthesia for bronchoscopy in older patients. Bronchoscopy is a camera inspection of the airways. The patients had coronary heart disease. Ninety-nine patients were split among three regimens. The regimens combined a sedative with a nerve block. The sedative was remimazolam or propofol. The block numbs the upper airway. Ultrasound guided it.

The remimazolam-plus-block group did best. Circulation stayed steadier during the procedure. Less extra painkiller was used. Patients coughed less. Low-oxygen episodes were fewer than in the remimazolam-only group. Satisfaction was better for patients and operators. The authors call the combination feasible for this fragile group. They ask for larger multicentre confirmation.
pmc-13469281:
Kim and colleagues build a classification system for park prescribing in Korea, the practice of doctors recommending park visits to prevent chronic disease, in 2026 health planning research. Programs are expanding internationally, yet Korea lacks an institutional base and any structured way to describe what a park offers as a health service. The team drafted items from international programs and park assessment tools, then refined them through expert rounds.

Two rounds of a modified Delphi survey, a structured method for reaching expert consensus, involved 20 panelists: ten park specialists and ten healthcare specialists. The final classification has three domains covering park characteristics, spatial components, and activities. Inside sit 11 major items, 36 middle-level items, and 101 sub-items in the framework. Accessibility and user convenience ranked as key characteristics, while pedestrian space and rest space led the spatial list. Kim presents the system as groundwork for prescribing parks like other health resources.
pmc-13470181:
Luo and co-authors review how tiny parcels shed by cells may drive joint harm in rheumatoid arthritis. These parcels are called extracellular vesicles, and they carry proteins, fats, and small bits of RNA. In a sore joint, they are shed by joint lining cells, white blood cells, and bone cells. Their load tends to mirror the state of the cell that shed them. The 2026 review traces how the parcels form, cross the joint lining, and enter new cells.

Once inside, parcel loads can switch on signals that drive swelling and pain. They can also spur joint lining cells to invade and bone cells to break down bone. The team weighs two hopes for care. Parcels in blood or joint fluid might serve as signs of disease, and parcels might carry drugs to the joint. Both hopes face hard limits: lab methods vary, and proof in patients is still thin.
pmc-13470481:
Solomon Ferede Ezez built a self-tuning sliding-mode driver in 2026 for an air fake muscle leg rehab arm. Air fake muscles copy human muscle give, but their curved pressure-force-squeeze ways, friction, and bumps defeat precise tracking. A self-tuning finite-time super-twisting driver drives hip and knee flexion-bends on a planar two-degree-of-freedom leg model.

Euler-Lagrange motion with viscous-Coulomb friction and paired muscle torque support the design, with self-tuning gains handling unknowns without preset bounds. Lyapunov analysis proved finite-time settling, and MATLAB runs beat standard sliding-mode drivers on fit and toughness. Reduced shaking improves patient comfort and safety for robotic nerve rehab.
pmc-13470581:
Ying Zhan and a large team report a stem cell study, published in 2026. It identifies a protein that shields tissue stem cells from cell death. The death form is ferroptosis, driven by iron. The protein is NSUN2. It adds a chemical tag to RNA. The team asked how it keeps stem cells alive across several organs.

Deleting NSUN2 lowered the protective enzyme GPX4. An antioxidant was drained. Iron and fat damage built up. Stem cells died and tissue repair suffered. The team traced the chain through the KLF4 gene switch. Restoring KLF4 in animals rescued the stem cell defects. NSUN2 gene therapy boosted repair. The team proposes it for regenerative medicine.
pmc-13471081:
Farwa Baber, Jana Jaklová Dytrtová, Michal Jakl and Noor ul An Babar published this 2026 review asking whether menstrual cycle phase changes how women respond to exercise-induced muscle damage. Hormone swings across the cycle could alter damage and inflammation markers, but studies disagree. The authors searched three databases to June 2026 for studies of menstruating women not on hormonal contraception. They measured biomarkers or recovery across two or more cycle phases, and weighed methods as as results.

Eighteen studies qualified. Muscle damage and inflammation markers such as creatine kinase and interleukin-6 responded predictably to the exercise itself and to when blood was sampled. Phase-related differences appeared inconsistently, flipping with exercise type, hormone contrast and how phase was verified. Many studies skipped hormone confirmation or used incompatible phase definitions. The authors conclude there is no uniform menstrual phase effect, and they set out design standards for cycle-aware exercise research.
pmc-13471181:
Marthe Le Prevost leads a ten author team examining in 2026 how British newspapers portrayed mpox during the 2022 outbreak. That outbreak was the first with sustained spread outside the regions where the virus is endemic. It fell hardest on gay and bisexual men, and on other men who also have sex with men. News coverage shapes what the public fears and does during such events, so the team analyzed five national newspapers across reading habits and political leanings.

They found 746 headline articles from May to December 2022, with coverage peaking in May and then fading even as cases climbed through June and July. Seventy nine pieces were read closely for themes. Stories explained the disease, carried health promotion messages, and anchored mpox to familiar illnesses such as COVID-19 and chickenpox to help readers place it.
pmc-13471281:
Hossein Abbasi leads a thirteen author mini review in 2026 on joining many layers of biology to understand mental illness. Psychiatric disorders grow out of interactions among genes, gene regulation, proteins, metabolism, and gut microbes, and any single layer explains only a slice. The review surveys how researchers combine those layers, with emphasis on weaving genetic risk scores, gene activity networks, and brain imaging for conditions such as depression, schizophrenia, and Alzheimer disease.

Practical needs get equal attention: standard sample banking, lab information systems, shared data rules, and privacy preserving methods that let centers analyze data without moving it. The authors also flag a fairness gap, since most datasets come from wealthy, largely white populations. African led consortia are held up as models for building capacity and keeping data sovereignty local.
pmc-13471381:
Qing Qin tested ambient fine dust in 2026 for bowel cancer outlook among patients in China. Dirty air worsens cancer results, yet its effects on spread shifts and go-between pathways in patients were unclear. A look-back cohort followed 3,357 non-spread bowel cancer patients after curing surgery at Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center from 2012 to 2017.

Each mid-spread rise in PM2.5 raised bowel cancer death risk 35%, with ammonia and sulfate parts showing the strongest links. Multi-state models tied contact to all three spread shifts, most strongly from disease-free living event to death. Swelling and rust stress signs carried 1.7% to 8.9% of the effect, led by mono-to-lymph ratio at 8.9%.
pmc-13471481:
Yang and colleagues asked whether simple blood markers measured before knee replacement surgery can forecast how long a patient stays in hospital. Their 2026 retrospective study covered 464 patients who had a first total knee replacement for osteoarthritis at one institution during 2023.

A higher prognostic nutritional index, a score built from albumin and lymphocyte counts, came with shorter stays: the primary model linked it to a stay shorter by 0.42 days per unit rise, and to lower odds of a stay beyond eight days. Inflammation markers performed worse: high-sensitivity C-reactive protein showed only a modest link to longer stays, with a coefficient of 0.17 in the model, and the CRP-to-albumin ratio was inconsistent. The authors float pre-surgery nutrition checks as a planning aid.
pmc-13471581:
Siann Hirani, Lance Grove, Adrian Furnham, and Alastair McClelland survey in 2026 how ordinary people would ration a scarce donor liver. British transplant policy weighs sickness, outlook, and waiting time, and pointedly not age, yet younger patients reportedly wait longer. Four hundred lay participants, younger and older, rated sixteen hypothetical patients for transplant priority using only four facts about each.

Sickest first, judged by life expectancy without a transplant, carried the most weight in the ratings. Outlook after transplant came second, then youngest first, with waiting time last. Both age groups favored younger patients, though they differed in degree. The authors use the pattern to probe where public instinct and official policy diverge, especially on the age question that policy currently refuses to ask.
pmc-13471681:
Huang and co-authors irradiated mustard seeds with gamma rays to map where useful mutation breeding ends and genomic wreckage begins. Their 2026 dose-response study treated Shuidong mustard seeds with cobalt-60 radiation from 0 to 4,000 gray and measured germination, seedling vigor, and genome-wide mutation patterns.

The response bent in two: below the LD50 dose of 971 gray, seeds took manageable damage, mostly single-letter DNA substitutions, with only moderate germination effects. At 2,000 gray and above, viability collapsed, with seedling fresh weight down 51.5% against controls and large deleted fragments appearing across the genome. Mutations clustered at stable hotspots, notably chromosome AA_Chr09, and enriched in DNA-repair and metabolism genes. Baseline germination above 90% validated the seed lot.
pmc-13473081:
Evangelia Delli and ten colleagues reported in 2026 on growing gallium antimonide, a material for mid-infrared light devices, directly on silicon. Silicon photonics moves data as light on chips, and would gain new uses if this material could be grown on silicon. The two crystals fit together poorly, so threading dislocations, line defects through the crystal, riddle the layer. Cutting that defect density is the main hurdle for workable devices.

The team grew layers by molecular beam epitaxy, depositing atoms one layer at a time in vacuum, reaching a defect density of six million per square centimetre. Their recipe combined an aluminium antimonide interface layer, a two-step temperature schedule, and strained superlattices that block defects from climbing upward. Stronger light emission confirmed the improved crystal quality, marking a step toward infrared lasers and sensors on ordinary silicon chips.
pmc-13473181:
Jia and a team in China fed in 2026 a gut germ, Lactiplantibacillus plantarum AS21, to old mice for six months, and found its help split by sex. Old males slid into poor sugar control, the pre stage of diabetes, far more than old females. Their blood had run low on citrulline, an amino acid that helps sugar work, while female blood had more than youth marks. Germ maps of the gut wall split the same way.

The fed germ fixed the males and left the females near as they were. In males it reshaped gut wall germs, raised two genes that build citrulline, and filled the blood pool back up. Sugar tests then ran near youth marks. Plain citrulline in feed copied the whole gain, with sharper insulin release after sugar. The team pitches the germ as a male aimed tool for age linked sugar slide.
pmc-13473281:
Ioannidis and colleagues report a 2026 clinical study of a combined treatment for chronic wounds that will not close. The treatment joins two known helpers: micrografts of the patient's own skin and fat, minced and spread on the wound, and a collagen-elastin scaffold that gives new tissue a frame. Thirty-four of forty-four screened patients received the combination after surgical cleaning of the wound.

Because every patient got the treatment, the study judges feasibility and safety first, with healing as an early signal rather than proof.  Chronic wounds stall through inflammation and failed rebuilding, so a living graft on a structural frame attacks both faults at once. The series is groundwork for a controlled trial.
pmc-13473481:
Yang and co-authors profiled small molecules in the cells and fluid around human eggs and found adenosine, a signaling nucleoside, out of balance in poor-quality cycles. Their 2026 metabolomics study compared 112 metabolites between cycles above and below a 40% high-quality embryo threshold, then validated the signal in two mouse models.

Adenosine ran high inside cumulus cells when embryo quality was low, discriminating quality with an ROC area of 0.75 on the standard scale, yet ran low in the surrounding follicular fluid of the same cycles. The mismatch tracked with lower expression of the ENT1 and ENT2 adenosine transporters and the gap-junction part CX37. Adding adenosine back rescued early development of low-quality mouse eggs, cutting oxidative stress and chromosome errors.
pmc-13473981:
Joowon Lee revisits safety questions in 2026 for a chickenpox vaccine made in Korea and sold as SKYVaricella. The vaccine uses a weakened live virus and won national approval in 2018, then global prequalification a year later. After a child died from spread of the vaccine virus, Korean agencies reviewed the case in 2024. They cleared the vaccine of causing the death and kept it in the national program.

The review notes a higher rate of shingles seen in children who got this vaccine. The maker updated its risk plan in 2024 to list shingles as a key possible risk. Lee argues that detailed follow-up steps have yet to be shared in public. Parents and doctors gain a clear record of what is known and what remains open.
pmc-13474381:
Mohammed Sarhan Alzahrani examined in 2026 the root canal anatomy of permanent canines in people from the Al-Baha region of Saudi Arabia, using cone-beam computed tomography. Canines are often assumed simple, but their internal anatomy varies, and missed canals doom root canal treatment.

All 120 scanned teeth had a single root, and the simplest canal pattern predominated overall. Mandibular canines, however, showed significantly greater complexity in the middle third, including Class III patterns in 8.5 percent of cases. Canal shape most often shifted from oval at the neck to round near the tip. Dentists should image carefully and adapt cleaning to these mandibular variations.
pmc-13474481:
Amiri and colleagues proposed in 2026 a single model that links brain circuits, self-monitoring, and emotion control in attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder. ADHD is often framed as a fault of attention alone, yet poor emotion control is common across life and adds much of the harm. Past frameworks rarely tied circuits to thinking and feeling in one account.

Drawing on three decades of studies, the model starts with weak control from front brain areas that oversee thought. When that oversight fades, self-monitoring slips, and lower emotion centers such as the amygdala react more strongly with less restraint. The result is the mix of impulsivity, restlessness, and emotional swings that marks the disorder. The authors present ADHD as a breakdown of layered self-regulation and suggest that treatments aimed at those layers may work better than symptom-by-symptom care.
pmc-13474781:
Cuiwen Li and colleagues report anesthesia care in 2026 for a 28-year-old man needing surgery on a narrowed windpipe. His airway gap measured about four millimeters after past arrest and long tube breathing. He also had heart artery narrowing, which raised the stakes. Standard tubes, masks, and a neck airway were all judged unsafe for this case.

Neck nerve blocks plus a calming drug kept him breathing on his own through the whole repair. Oxygen was fed locally once the windpipe was opened for the fix. Surgery finished without machine support for heart or lungs. Careful block-based plans can give a safe path where tubes cannot go.
pmc-13474881:
Nakashima and colleagues asked whether adding a second antibiotic helps patients with severe belly infections in a 2026 review of nine years of hospital cases. Meropenem already covers most gut bacteria, but the anaerobe Bacteroides fragilis, a germ that grows without oxygen, is growing resistant to it. The team compared 114 patients treated with meropenem alone against patients who also got metronidazole, a drug aimed squarely at anaerobes.

Cure rates were nearly identical, at 91.2 percent for meropenem alone and 91.3 percent for the two-drug group in the unmatched comparison. Deaths within 28 days and hospital stay lengths also matched closely, and a matched analysis of 20 patients per group again showed no clear advantage for the extra drug. The authors conclude that adding metronidazole brought no measurable benefit once the infection source was controlled by surgery or drainage in these cases.
pmc-13474981:
Jiyong Kim and colleagues report in 2026 a first known case of an eye vessel disease arising in Usher syndrome type 2. Usher syndrome pairs hearing loss with slow vision loss from retina decay. A 63-year-old man with gene-confirmed disease saw his left eye vision drop over six years after diagnosis. Layered eye scans confirmed polypoidal vessel growth, a leaky network under the retina.

A pale mole-like spot on the deep eye layer was also found by scan. Five injections of a vessel-blocking drug lifted his vision from poor to near normal range. Fluid under the retina cleared fully, and the raised pocket shrank by three quarters. Even thinned retinas can hide this treatable disease.
pmc-13480081:
Beste Uncu and Idil Yavuz present a 2026 method for grouping single cells by their gene activity. Each clustering tool for such data wins on some sets and fails on others, so picking one tool feels like a gamble. Their framework, called ScEnsemble, runs many tools and merges results through a weighted network, giving more say to groupings that score well on quality checks.

Tests across five datasets showed the best merged setup matched or beat the best single tool in nearly all comparisons. Weighting by quality beat plain merging in most cases as well. On breast tumour data the merged groups lined up with known cell types confirmed by outside gene scores. Users can tune the merge toward tidy maths or toward clear biology. The approach turns a hard tool choice into a combined answer.
pmc-13480181:
Merijn H. Rijk and colleagues present a 2026 study of heart and vessel events after chest infections seen in family practice. Records came from a Dutch GP network for patients aged forty and above who sought care for lower airway infections between 2016 and 2019. The group counted 11,065 patients with 16,497 infection episodes and tracked events for ninety days after each visit.

New rhythm problems were the most common event, followed by major heart and brain events, then vein clots. Risk ratios spiked most in the first week after infection, with vein clot risk near seven times the usual level across the window. Overall, about five to nine extra acute events arose per thousand infection patients. The authors suggest targeted prevention steps and stronger seasonal vaccine drives, since even small per-case risk adds up during winter outbreaks.
pmc-13480281:
Jia Sun and co-authors describe a 2026 case billed as the first pairing of two inherited fat disorders in one patient. A 35-year-old man had stubborn high cholesterol with lumps of fat at his joints and heavy calcium build-up in his arteries. Gene testing found faults in the receptor that clears cholesterol from blood and in a gene that pumps plant sterols out of the body, the second fault being new to science.

Single drugs failed him, as did a statin paired with a newer injected agent. A four-part plan finally cut his lipids sharply: a statin, the injected agent, a gut absorption blocker, and a diet low in plant sterols. The case argues for gene testing whenever standard care fails badly, since hidden second disorders can block progress.
pmc-13481781:
Wang and colleagues studied an insurance reform in China in 2026 that pooled outpatient costs so patients could claim more care outside hospital, expecting this to ease pressure on inpatient wards. Drawing on county service records from Sichuan from 2010 to 2020 and a national aging survey, they used a staggered difference-in-differences design, comparing places as the reform reached them at varied times.

Admissions rose after the reform, the opposite of the intent. Outpatient and inpatient care behaved as complements, not substitutes: more clinic use went hand in hand with more hospital care. Two channels drove the effect. Expanded primary care visits fed some patients upward into hospital as induced admissions, and hospitals shifted tests into outpatient accounts, freeing inpatient capacity and efficiency. The authors say payment design must reckon with this linkage or reforms will keep backfiring.
pmc-13483381:
Shaqul Qamar Wani and co-authors present a 2026 study of palliative care gains among people with life-limiting illness in Kashmir, a conflict-scarred region of India. The team read records for 881 patients who joined a Srinagar pain and palliative clinic between late 2023 and early 2025. They scored symptoms at sign-up and one week later with a standard scale.

Nearly all patients carried cancer, and three quarters lived below the poverty line. Median pain scores plunged from seven to two within the week. Total symptom scores fell from twenty-nine to twenty as well-being lifted. Gains showed no tilt by age, sex, wealth band, or diagnosis. One week of basic palliative care thus delivered wide relief even amid scarce services and household strain, with sons serving as lead caregivers in half the homes.
pmc-13483581:
Erkan Durar and Serap Yildirim ask whether dirty outdoor air affects the mental health of university students in Türkiye. Their 2026 repeated-measures study followed 365 students at a university in a region with poor air quality during the 2023 to 2024 academic year. Students completed a standard symptom inventory once when pollution was moderate and again when it was unhealthy.

Depression scores, anxiety scores, and overall distress were all higher at the second measurement, when the air had worsened. Each difference reached statistical significance. The authors conclude that periods of unhealthy air coincided with measurably worse student mental health on campus. Longer follow-up work is still needed to show whether the effect fades when air clears or builds with repeated exposure.
pmc-13483681:
Haiying Tang, Wenjie Jiang, Yulong Ma, and Dongguang Wang test a paired soil fix for antimony harm in rice. Antimony is a toxic metal-like element that stunts rice and seeps into the grain. Their 2026 pot study sets up eight groups. Some pots get char, some get zinc oxide nano grains, some get antimony stress, and some get mixes of all three.

Antimony alone raised cell damage signs and cut soil food levels. The paired fix cut much of that harm. Soil antimony that plants could take up fell sharply, and roots grew a stronger iron coat. Defense genes in the rice switched on, while genes that move antimony switched down. The pair may let farms grow safe rice on tainted land.
pmc-13484881:
Trevena and colleagues in Australia built in 2026 risk models to flag kidney injury after lung transplant surgery. Sharp kidney harm is common after this operation and raises the risk of death. The team read records of 534 adults treated at one center from 2016 to 2025. They built one model from facts known before surgery, and one that also used facts from the first hours after.

About two in five patients went on to suffer kidney injury, and near one in eleven needed dialysis, a machine that cleans the blood. The after surgery model sorted patients far better than the before surgery one. Key added clues were how long the operation ran, blood oxygen levels, and the total dose of a blood pressure drug. The authors say such split timing models can guide care that shields the kidneys.
pmc-13487581:
Muramatsu, writing as an expert by experience, examines his own mental health recovery as a social process. The 2026 autoethnography analyses a personal diary kept over 85 days from April 2024, broken into 2,142 textual units and coded thematically. Rather than treating recovery as a private journey, the study asks how relationships and surroundings constitute it day by day.

Four themes emerged: interpersonal relationships during recovery, the felt sensations of the process, environmental influences, and how the process itself is understood. Recovery proved deeply relational, shaped by supportive and difficult interactions alike, and decidedly non-linear. Progress was not steady: flat stretches returned, along with mixed feelings where positive and negative experiences sit side by side. Muramatsu argues recovery frameworks should build in this intersubjective, uneven character, and that professionals should respect the experiential knowledge of those living it.
pmc-13488181:
Tianwei Wang and Xi Jiang compare two immune drug pairings for advanced bladder and urinary tract cancer in a 2026 real-world study. Both regimens join disitamab vedotin, an antibody-drug that delivers a cell-killing payload, with a PD-1 blocker that frees the immune system. One pairing uses toripalimab and the other uses tislelizumab. Records covered patients treated between 2021 and 2025, with survival, tumor response, and side effects compared.

Survival and overall response looked similar between the pairings in this retrospective comparison. The toripalimab group showed less disease progression and higher disease control, while the tislelizumab group had more skin inflammation, low potassium, anemia, and low calcium reported. The authors ask for prospective multicenter trials to settle the choice.
pmc-13488281:
Yunyan Luo and co-authors catalog disease-causing variants in medically important genes across eleven ethnic groups in southwest China in a 2026 genome study. The gene list comes from the American College of Medical Genetics, covering genes where a finding should be reported because care can act on it. Whole genomes from 476 people in a Guizhou multi-ethnic database were classified under international guidelines for how harmful each variant likely is.

After filtering, 521 variants remained, and only a small share counted as pathogenic or likely pathogenic with high confidence. Variants in a copper-handling gene linked to Wilson disease were most common, with clear differences between groups. Three variants were absent from major global databases. The authors offer the frequencies as a base for genomic medicine in the region.
pmc-13491581:
Elisabeth Kac and four colleagues present a 2026 records analysis of gender and grading in medical school clerkships, the supervised rotations where students train in hospitals. Earlier work on bias in trainee evaluations gave mixed answers across specialties. The group studied thousands of evaluations from one United States osteopathic medical school.

The data held 6,855 evaluations written by 2,425 preceptors for the classes of 2022 through 2024 across six required rotations. Female preceptors gave slightly lower overall and clinical competence scores than male preceptors. Female students scored a little higher on overall average and professionalism, with no combined effect of both genders. Rotation mattered most, since family medicine and pediatrics graded higher than surgery and internal medicine.
pmc-13491781:
Yumeng Liu, Zhongguang Yang, and Yulin Yin follow in 2026 how cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome, a staged measure of intertwined heart, kidney, and metabolic trouble, relates to death among American cancer survivors. National survey data from 1988 through 2018 yielded 2,598 survivors aged twenty and older, whose syndrome stage was graded from zero to four. Deaths were tracked for a median of about eight years.

More than eleven hundred participants died during follow-up. Survivors at stage four faced roughly three and a half times the overall death risk of stage zero survivors after full adjustment. Their risk of dying from cardiovascular causes was nearly eightfold higher, and cancer death risk was also elevated. The authors argue that staging this syndrome should become part of routine survivorship care.
pmc-13491881:
Melesse and co-authors report a 2026 validation study of an Amharic translation of the RCADS-25, a 25-item questionnaire that screens children for anxiety and depression. The team gave the translated scale to 142 children aged 8 to 18 who were receiving cancer care in Ethiopia. They checked whether the questions held together consistently, whether scores stayed stable over time, and whether results matched a separate quality-of-life measure.

Internal consistency was very high, with alpha values around 0.95 for the anxiety items and slightly higher for the full scale when the authors combined both parts. Repeat testing also proved stable, and scores correlated strongly, in the expected negative direction, with the quality-of-life inventory. Statistical modelling supported the original two-part structure, with anxiety and depression as separate factors. The authors recommend wider testing in larger and more varied Ethiopian samples before routine use.
pmc-13493981:
Yu and colleagues searched the genomes of Taiwanese arthritis patients for clues to who benefits from methotrexate, the standard first drug for rheumatoid arthritis, and who suffers side effects. Pulling hospital records from 2009 to 2022, their 2026 study covered 1,948 patients on the drug. The 872 who later needed stronger biologic medicines counted as non-responders, while 1,076 managed without them. The team tested 82 candidate gene variants drawn from earlier literature.

One variant in a drug-transporter gene predicted better response to methotrexate, while two variants in a related transporter gene predicted poorer response in the adjusted models. pmc-13494181:

One by one, mice flipped tween act and no-act states at that dose. The flips were chance-like but bore a hold: beasts stuck a while in each state. Hold marks for the two tests did not tell each other. Dose reads as a live span, not a point.
pmc-13495381:
Mahshad Maadani and colleagues count, in a 2026 study, the extra birth defects found in children with anorectal malformations at a Tehran children's hospital. pmc-13495481:
Giuseppe Accurso leads a large expert panel setting out, in a 2026 consensus article, when helicopter ambulances should fly patients between hospitals in Italy. A helicopter earns its cost, the panel held, when it meaningfully cuts time to final care or brings advanced care during the flight. pmc-13495581:
Nugroho and colleagues built EmoTweetID in 2026, a large open dataset of Indonesian tweets for teaching computers to read emotion in text. From those, about 2,200 tweets were labeled by hand and by word lists, with three student raters agreeing well. A neural network paired with one embedding scored well on the labeled set, and the dataset is free on Mendeley Data.
pmc-13495981:
Ziqi Xie, Tan Bahar, and Keith Karoly introduce in 2026 a free software tool that tells two similar oaks apart from leaf shape alone. Leaves from herbarium collections were measured with digital tools, and a statistical model learned which traits separate the species. The new plug-in, built for the widely used ImageJ program, measures leaves on its own and predicts the species. It reached high accuracy on stored specimens and caught every European oak sampled in Portland, though native oaks proved harder.
pmc-13496381:
Daniel Liu and colleagues compare in 2026 hospital outcomes for shinbone shaft fractures caused by skiing or snowboarding against fractures from all other causes. The shinbone is a common site for long-bone breaks, and winter sports load the leg in unusual ways. Little prior work had separated these injuries out, so the authors used a national trauma registry to fill the gap.

From 2017 to 2018 they found 12,996 patients, of whom 232 were hurt in winter sports, and they matched groups on age, health, and injury features. Winter-sport patients left hospital sooner in several adjusted models, although that edge vanished once added health factors entered the final model. Older age, severe injury, open fractures, diabetes, and a pressure complication in the leg each lengthened stays.
pmc-13499381:
Benjamin and colleagues present a 2026 concept analysis of the cognitive work of acute care nurses, the mental labor behind nursing that stays hidden and hard to describe. Thinking work, such as tracking many patients, spotting decline early, and coordinating care, shapes safety and quality. The team used a hybrid analysis method: a literature phase, then fieldwork observations in real hospital units.

A clear concept lets managers count the invisible half of nursing when they plan staffing and safety.
pmc-13500081:
Mohammed Aharmim and colleagues report in 2026 an immune deficiency diagnosed only in late middle age after years of chest trouble. Common variable immunodeficiency is the most frequent inherited antibody shortfall in adults, marked by low antibody levels and repeated chest infections, yet its varied face delays diagnosis. pmc-13500681:
Kai Wei and co-authors build in 2026 a quantitative method for predicting when a logging cable will stick inside an oil or gas well. Such accidents halt operations and risk losing expensive instruments downhole. Their approach rests on a soft string model of the cable's mechanics. The model derives the adhesion forces that build as the tool is jacked through the borehole and converts them into a sticking risk probability. A real well served as the test case for validation.

The assessed well showed signs of sticking, matching what crews actually observed in the field in the reported comparison. Sensitivity analysis found risk most responsive to borehole inclination and drilling fluid density among the factors tested. Managing the main sensitive factors together cut overall sticking risk by roughly a third in their calculations. Engineers planning wells gain a pre-run risk check rather than learning about adhesion the hard way.
pmc-13501781:
Carmela Rapino and others evaluate a public health-led pre-exposure prophylaxis clinic reaching suburban and rural Ontario. In 2026, the implementation study uses the RE-AIM plan and electronic records from 2018 to 2024 for a mixed in-person and remote interdisciplinary clinic in Southeastern Ontario. HIV findings rose sharply in Canada while PrEP remained underused outside cities.

Median engagement lasted eight months with no new HIV findings, though over half disengaged, often early or after a year. Flexible public health models appear scalable for equitable access.
pmc-13501881:
Miranda and Varella calculated how a radiosensitizer molecule behaves when it captures low-energy electrons, in a 2026 theoretical chemistry study. Radiosensitizers are drugs meant to make radiation kill tumor cells more effectively, in low-oxygen tumor regions that resist treatment. One route is capturing the electrons radiation generates, then shattering into reactive fragments that damage DNA. Their molecule, a chlorinated nitropyrimidine, is a model for this drug class.

Miranda mapped the molecule's negative-ion states using quantum methods plus scattering calculations. They assigned the fragmentation seen in experiments, loss of nitrogen oxide fragments and the anion formed at zero electron energy, to one resonance perched above threshold. A state sits too bound to drive the process through an alternative route, so the breakup flows through coupling between the resonance and the bound states. Such dual behavior is proposed as a design target for sensitizers.
pmc-13504081:
Fumitaka SHITAMORI leads a team testing a red-cell-boosting drug in healthy cats, in a 2026 study. The drug, roxadustat, tricks the body into making its own blood hormone and is used for anemia tied to kidney disease in people. A sister drug already helps anemic cats, but this one lasts longer in the body.

Single doses up to a set level caused no clear harm, while a very high dose brought vomiting and death. Treated cats made more young red cells and more of the blood hormone, which shows the drug works in cats. Six weeks of low daily doses were tolerated well, with clean blood counts. The authors name that dose range as a candidate for trials in cats with kidney disease.
pmc-13504281:
Raro and colleagues gave the first full lab profile of PAC-1, an antibiotic-destroying enzyme carried by the bacterium Pseudomonas aeruginosa, in a 2026 study. Older blockers such as avibactam failed fully against it, whereas two newer ones, zidebactam and xeruborbactam, blocked it potently at low doses, making cefiderocol plus zidebactam the most active pairing. The same mobile element appeared in unrelated lineages, prompting closer watching.
pmc-13504981:
Ying Yuan and others develop risk prediction algorithms for low biological width using fused dental imaging. In 2026, the one-time study studies 4,420 sites from 740 teeth in fifty-five adults with good oral hygiene, joining cone beam computed tomography, intraoral scanning, and gum probing. Biological width protects the gum ligament and air sac bone, and reduced width invites troubles.

Predictors included tooth kind, tooth place, gum edge to cementum-enamel junction distance, junction to ridge crest distance, and gingival thickness, with low width defined below 1.13 mm. The raw model discriminated well with area under the curve 0.867, while external testing reached 0.68. A visual nomogram lets doctors estimate site-level risk and detect threatened gum tissue.
pmc-13505081:
Boyu Li leads a team showing that a rhubarb compound can fight lung scarring by restoring a neglected enzyme, in a 2026 study. The disease, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, stiffens lungs with scar tissue and kills within years. Few drugs slow it, so new targets are prized.

In mice given a scarring chemical, the compound danthron cut collagen build-up and scar scores. It also calmed scar markers in human lung slices kept alive in the lab. At cell level it stopped scar cells from switching to their aggressive form and even reversed some that had. The path ran through an enzyme, CES3, which lifted the cells' energy factories and their cleanup of worn parts. Blocking CES3 erased the gains, and patient lungs showed the enzyme low. The authors name CES3 a candidate target.
pmc-13505181:
