Brains from people with Alzheimer's also showed faster chemical ageing than brains from unimpaired donors. One site, near a gene called AZU1, linked with later decline in a separate living cohort. The work frames ageing marks as a large part of the chemical ageing seen in Alzheimer's.
pmc-13507081:
Panpan Zhang, Wenbin Gao, Zhenning Si, Zongjie Mu, and Yawen Tan model, in 2026 work, heat-based gas production from sea-floor gas hydrates in the Shenhu area of the South China Sea. pmc-13507481:
Ingrid E. Adriaans and others show how ATP-driven skin binding and chaining of germ actin MreB loosens skins locally. In 2026, the study looks at MreB from Geobacillus stearothermophilus using one-way glow, fat bubble binding, atomic force scope work, and solid-state NMR. Single units made edge charge skin contacts, while Mg-ATP-made threads sank into the bilayer without breaking its layered phase and clearly loosened local skin. pmc-13508281:
Haile Dean Figueiredo Chagas leads an eleven-author team checking whether a tick drug still works after a season of use on Brazilian cattle, in 2026 work. Pasture larvae were sampled monthly with a dragging cloth. Lab immersion tests on larvae and adult ticks measured drug sensitivity before and after the program. Cattle on fluralaner carried lower tick counts than controls on nearly every weekly check. The before-and-after lab tests let the team judge whether use had dulled the drug's punch. Such checks help farms keep control programs effective without breeding resistant ticks.
pmc-13508381:

Urinary side effects peaked at treatment's end, led by bladder irritation symptoms, frequency, and painful urination, each affecting a substantial minority at moderate grade. They faded to a percent or two by three months. Bowel effects stayed at the mildest grade throughout the acute window in the report. Patient-reported symptom trajectories were favourable overall in the mixed-effects models.
pmc-13510181:
da Silva and co-authors measured psychological distress among older adults in Northeast Brazil in 2026, a region where rapid aging meets persistent poverty and most existing evidence comes from wealthier countries. Older adults facing food insecurity scored higher on distress than food-secure peers, and the link survived statistical adjustment for other factors. Lower income, lower schooling, and medication use also tracked with more distress, while physical activity and life satisfaction tracked with less. The authors urge pairing food security support with mental health care.
pmc-13511381:

A blocker drug pushed diffusion the other way, while recovery tests showed more receptors stuck immobile after activation. pmc-13513481:

pmc-13517181:

pmc-13517581:

pmc-13518681:

Links appeared with immune cells, checkpoint genes, and RNA-modifying genes. pmc-13518781:

pmc-13520181:

pmc-13520381:

pmc-13521481:

pmc-13522281:

A guard enzyme moved onto mitochondria under the switch. Human heart cells rich in the switch beat chemical oxidative stress better. Shared paths across models back the claim.
pmc-13523281:

Central incisors first tipped one way and then the other as angle rose, while side incisors kept a steadier pattern and switched earlier. pmc-13523481:

pmc-13524681:

pmc-13524881:

pmc-13525081:
Linda-Marie Lavenburg and six co-authors study who accepts a weight program referral among kidney transplant hopefuls, and who then makes contact. Obesity is a big barrier to transplant, yet follow through on referrals was unknown. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

Those who accepted had higher body mass and lived much closer to the center. Each added mile cut acceptance odds a bit, while each body mass unit raised them. Among accepters, older age cut the odds of making contact.
pmc-13526281:

It mixed neck numbing, light sedation, and full sleep in stages. He woke on the table and healed with no mishaps. Shared airway cases need such care.
pmc-13526881:
Joseph and colleagues reported plasma wave observations in 2026 from NASA's Juno spacecraft at Jupiter's bow shock, the standing shock wave where the solar wind slams into the planet's magnetic shield. The drift instability runs intense, as if compensating for the stronger shock, while magnetic readings hint the shock surface reforms itself. The authors say dissipation physics at giant planet shocks mirrors Earth's with local twists.
pmc-13527481:

Standard scales scored app quality and functions. Match between raters was worked out for trust.

Others held only some parts of therapy. Symptom tracking ranged from daily to minimal tracking. Some apps gave users no feedback at all. Doctors need clearer quality signals for choosing apps.
pmc-13527881:

One pair is backed by solid data in muscle models. For two pairs, direct pairing is unproven or shown only outside muscle. One pair has no direct interaction reported at all. The pair framework is promising, but most of its joints still await proof.
pmc-13528081:

The map shows a typical order of events. ECG changes and thickening tend to come first. Blood markers rise later, and scarring follows. The authors offer the four-part map for routine clinic use.
pmc-13530081:

pmc-13530581:

pmc-13531781:
Shuaishuai Xue and co-authors nominate in 2026 a metabolic gene as a drug target for the most aggressive childhood brain tumor group. Medulloblastoma outside the two calmer families often spreads and resists care, especially with extra copies of the MYC growth gene. Public gene datasets were mined along a spectrum between tumor subtypes.

One energy-pathway gene, PCK2, tracked that spectrum most tightly. Silencing it in tumor cells slowed growth, movement, invasion, and sugar burning, while shifting immune macrophages away from a tumor-friendly state. The findings tie tumor metabolism to its immune surroundings and offer a precision target.
pmc-13532281:
Narumi Ueda, Jun Inoue, and Kazuyuki Okuda combine in 2026 two gene methods to diagnose prosthetic joint infection more reliably. Broad bacterial gene screening first measures how much bacterial material a sample holds, then sequencing names the germs only when levels pass a safe threshold. Samples came from loosened joint fluid and surgical tissue.

Screening agreed with itself almost perfectly and matched culture results with fair sensitivity and specificity. Sequencing confirmed most culture-positive infections and caught three culture-negative ones, including a case whose flagged germ caused a real infection two years later. Threshold-first testing filters contamination noise.
pmc-13532781:
Lianne H E Wieske, Gintare Lygnugaryte, and Mate Erdelyi compare in 2026 six common NMR pulse programmes for measuring distances inside molecules. Such distances help work out shape and folding for small molecules and proteins. Small errors in the setup can shift the distances a lot.

The team counted usable signals and checked distance errors for each programme, plus two ways to suppress solvent signals. Dropping spectra from build-up curves raised errors sharply, and one solvent method biased distances low. Readers learn that careful choice of programme is required for trustworthy distance work.
pmc-13535681:
George Samyo Stephenson and six co-authors test two fills for wisdom tooth sockets in a split-mouth trial. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Jaw wisdom tooth cuts bring pain, swell, tight mouth, slow heal, and slow bone growth. One side got a blood fibrin fill, and the other got the same fill plus a bone graft grain.

One hundred patients had both back jaw teeth out, one per side plan. The graft side bled less, swelled less, opened wider, and grew bone more. The plain fill side healed skin fast and hurt less. The team backs the graft mix as the best all-round pick for socket care.
pmc-13536481:
In Young Lee, Doo-Hee Lee, Ju Hong Park, and Nami Joo report a two thousand twenty-six study of dried edible plants from a Korean island. Ulleungdo's wild greens are traditionally blanched and sun-dried. How that handling changes their chemistry was poorly understood.

Three related species were profiled with sensitive chemical instruments. Over one hundred compounds were identified across freeze-dried and sun-dried samples. Species identity drove the biggest differences. Traditional drying cut fragile flavonoid compounds, while coffee-like acid compounds survived well. Machine learning picked out marker chemicals for each drying style, useful for quality checks.
pmc-13536581:
Olivier Hermine and colleagues analyse in 2026 outcomes for systemic mastocytosis with an added myeloid neoplasm in a large international registry. This combined form is the most common advanced subtype, yet solid outcome data were thin. The registry held 3,925 patients from 35 centres across Europe and the United States.

About one in nine patients had the combined form, most often with chronic blood disorders of mixed type. Survival was far shorter than in mastocytosis alone, and worse still when parts were advanced or acute leukaemia was present. The data sharpen risk grouping for care planning.
pmc-13536781:
Ali O Ali leads a 2026 field study of outdoor malaria risk on Pemba Island, Zanzibar, where indoor spraying and bed nets have driven cases very low. Remaining spread may occur outdoors, where the main mosquito bites outside and people spend evenings outside. Over a full year, collectors caught biting mosquitoes indoors and outdoors while observers logged hourly where people were, what they did, and whether nets were in use.

Nearly all collected mosquitoes were the outdoor-biting type, and most bites landed outdoors, peaking in the early evening. Most unprotected exposure also occurred outdoors while people were awake. Young children still gained strong net protection indoors, while older children and adults faced mostly outdoor risk. The authors call for added outdoor measures alongside indoor tools.
pmc-13537381:
He Huang, Zifei Ni, Shujun Yan, and Heyuan Tian studied how copper loading affects a catalyst that cleans diesel exhaust. Ammonia-based selective catalytic reduction is the leading way to remove nitrogen oxides from exhaust. Their catalyst uses copper loaded into SAPO-34, a molecular sieve material. The twenty twenty-six study prepared catalysts by a two-step ion-exchange method with varying copper amounts. Performance was measured on a dedicated evaluation setup.

A battery of characterization tools probed the catalysts' structure and chemistry. First-principles calculations modeled how copper changes the support structure and active sites. Together the experiments trace how copper content shapes reaction pathways. Finding the right loading matters because too little or too much copper can hurt conversion. The results guide design of cleaner diesel after-treatment systems.
pmc-13537481:
Ibrahim Alkatout and colleagues followed a surgical team's move to a new robot system. Published in 2026, the months-long survey study ran from November 2022 to April 2023 with 63 staff across four roles: surgeons, anesthesiologists, residents, and theatre nurses. The clinic's old robot had passed its learning curve, raising the ethics of switching while a trusted low-risk option stood ready.

Surgeons and theatre nurses began with the deepest doubts about the Dexter robot and patient safety, and surgeons' doubts eased as Dexter cases mounted. Theatre nurses stayed wary, their ratings flat as case counts rose. Trainees rated the new robot best of all four groups. The authors call for a standard required training course for the whole team, clear patient facts, and rules that clinics now lack.
pmc-13538481:
Yanxia Lu and co-authors hunt a blood pattern for future memory decline in a 2026 community study from Singapore. Protein and small-molecule panels plus standard blood tests measured nearly 1,900 molecules in stored blood. Baseline links to existing mild impairment and dementia were screened first. A trained model then predicted who developed fresh impairment or dementia over three to five years of follow-up.

Hundreds of molecules linked to baseline states of impairment. The best model for future prediction used just ten measures spanning gene control proteins, one immune alarm signal, one growth signal, and hard fats. Listed roles cover immune trouble, body-wide swelling, fat handling, gene switching, and nerve growth. The authors hope the compact blood pattern sharpens early detection without invasive tests.
pmc-13539881:
Yasamin Zahedi and five colleagues explore, in a 2026 cross-sectional study from Iran, whether diets that promote inflammation in the body are linked to female infertility. A scoring system called the Dietary Inflammatory Index turns food records into a single number for how inflammatory a diet looks.

Within the Fasa Adults Cohort, 2,036 women aged 35 to 45 completed a long food questionnaire, and nearly three in ten reported a history of infertility. Women with infertility averaged higher diet scores. After adjustment for age, body size, smoking, schooling, and energy intake, each extra point on the index came with higher odds of infertility. The authors call for prospective work to test cause and effect.
pmc-13540881:
Yiming Zhang and colleagues tested a tiny RNA signal as a heart-risk marker in Anderson-Fabry disease. Published in 2026, the study set 60 patients with the rare passed-down disorder beside 60 healthy controls. The disorder stems from a faulty gene that lets fatty waste pile up in nerves, heart, kidneys, and skin, driving organ damage.

Just over half the patients showed heart damage with clear shape changes. The RNA signal ran lower in patients and in those with heart muscle disease, spotting both the disorder and its heart injury with high hit rates. Higher injury tracked lower signal levels, and the signal stood out on its own as a shield against heart damage. The authors propose it as a strong marker choice for heart risk in this illness.
pmc-13541781:
Mary Isabel Villacís and colleagues study microplastics in a 2026 paper. They asked whether the plastics change a water flea's work. The flea, Daphnia magna, pulls zinc out of water. That job may help polish treated wastewater. The particles were ground from real commercial items. Three polymers and two size ranges were used. Some particles were aged under ultraviolet light.

Microscopy located the particles inside the animals. Plasma analysis measured zinc in water and tissue. The plastics did not change how much zinc left the water. Polymer type did change zinc build-up inside the fleas. Ageing state mattered too. Particle size mattered little in the range tested.
pmc-13542081:
Hugo Corval and colleagues found that stored genetic variety holds the key to barn owl climate coping. Published in 2026, the study paired habitat mapping with genome scans for the Western Palearctic barn owl. Owls now range across a wider climate band than at the Last Glacial Maximum, yet how past shifts point to future adjustment power was unclear.

Genome scans showed ongoing natural picking tied to local settings in every population, with local tuning driving change across groups. That local tuning let owls settle new homes and shaped how stay-at-home groups meet climate change. The authors stress that standing variety, not just new gene changes, fuels adjustment to past, present, and coming shifts. Readers get a case for guarding diverse groups as climate backup.
pmc-13542281:
Jonas Afful and colleagues published a 2026 cross-sectional study of abnormal blood fats among people being treated for high blood pressure at Effia Nkwanta Regional Hospital in Ghana. The pair of conditions often occurs together and each raises cardiovascular risk. The team enrolled 347 adults with diagnosed hypertension, gathered social, lifestyle, and body measurements through a structured questionnaire, and measured fasting blood lipids in the laboratory.

Nearly three in five participants, 58.5 percent, had dyslipidaemia. Where a person lived, their income, smoking history, body mass index, and waist-to-hip ratio all showed significant links to lipid status, and occupation related to particular lipid fractions. Early morning headaches and irregular heart rhythms were the most reported symptoms, though neither differed between those with and without lipid problems. The authors recommend routine lipid screening as part of hypertension care at the hospital.
pmc-13543381:
Natalie Getreu and colleagues published a 2026 cross-sectional study linking vaping and smoking to lower markers of ovarian reserve, the remaining egg supply suggested by hormone levels. Data came from 16,087 women aged eighteen to forty-five using a private hormone testing service, excluding reproductive conditions or hormonal contraception. Blood levels of anti-Müllerian hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone were compared across never, former, occasional, and current users of each product.

Current vapers had about 5.6 percent lower anti-Müllerian hormone than never-vapers, with no clear difference in the second hormone. Current smokers fared worse: roughly 9.4 percent lower on the first marker and 7.7 percent higher on the second, a pattern pointing the same way. Occasional and former use showed no associations, and results held after removing dual users. E-cigarettes are marketed as safer than smoking, yet these data tie current use to reduced reserve markers.
pmc-13544281:
Miguel Martins and colleagues published a 2026 multicentre study of an artificial intelligence model that reads high-resolution anoscopy images to screen for anal cancer precursors. This examination is the reference standard for HPV-related anal lesions, but readings vary between observers. Their network was trained and tested on nearly 192,000 frames from 107 procedures. The frames came from five imaging devices at five centres on several continents, with every lesion confirmed by tissue diagnosis.

The model sorts each finding into high-grade lesion, low-grade lesion, or non-dysplastic change. Recall reached about ninety-eight percent for both lesion grades, and precision stayed in the mid-to-high nineties, with overall test accuracy of 88.1 percent. Because it worked across devices and centres, the authors present it as the first interoperable tool of its kind. They say it could steady a notoriously subjective examination and extend expert-level reading to more clinics.
pmc-13544381:
Hyundam Gu and colleagues published a 2026 study updating the Alcohol Preparedness Index, a scorecard of national alcohol control policy, for 141 countries between 2010 and 2019. Policy data from the World Health Organization were scored across five domains, from national frameworks and pricing to drink-driving measures and monitoring. The team summarised regional trends and tested which national traits explained the changes.

The median index rose from 57.0 in 2010 to 67.8 in 2019, peaking mid-decade. Pricing, production, and taxation improved most dramatically, while fewer than a quarter of countries had a strong national plan by 2019 and forty percent had none at all. Larger population size predicted smaller gains; wealth and drinking levels did not. Having policies on paper, the authors conclude, still outruns putting them into practice, and they urge alignment with the international SAFER package of proven measures.
pmc-13544681:
Mutian Cao and eight colleagues identify a fat-processing enzyme as vital to acute myeloid leukemia, in a study from twenty twenty-six. The enzyme, LPCAT3, remodels membrane lipids. Patient data showed too much of it in leukemia, with high levels tracking worse survival. The team held it down in leukemia cell lines.

Knocking the enzyme down stalled cell growth and triggered cell death. Cell cycles stopped at the resting phase. Forcing extra enzyme, in turn, helped cells survive. In mouse xenografts, loss of it shrank the leukemic burden. Gene activity after loss shifted toward pathways that attract granulocytes. That hints the enzyme also shapes cell maturing and the tumor surroundings. The authors name LPCAT3 as a therapy target worth pursuing.
pmc-13546581:
Akihiro Dejima and co-authors asked in 2026 whether a standard drug combination for advanced liver cancer works equally well in every organ the cancer has reached. The pairing of atezolizumab and bevacizumab is a first-line treatment, yet the liver's immune environment might blunt responses there. Records covered 42 patients treated at one Japanese hospital between 2020 and 2024 who had spread beyond the liver.

Overall, about a third of patients responded, and responses appeared in liver, lung, lymph nodes, and the abdominal lining, though not in the small bone and adrenal groups. Measured shrinkage and time to progression did not differ significantly between organs, but the groups were small. The authors describe the results as exploratory evidence of fairly even activity across sites.
pmc-13547681:
Saroja Devi Geetha and colleagues checked how often TERT gene changes appear in unclear thyroid nodules. Published in 2026, the case series looked back at 567 thyroid samples sent for gene testing from 2019 to 2022. TERT changes were tied to thyroid cancers, yet their spread across unclear nodules was little known.

Only 12 samples, about 2 percent, carried TERT changes, four alone and eight with extra changes, in patients aged 69 on average. Of eight with surgery follow-up, half were cancer, a quarter benign, and a quarter of unclear cancer potential, with most nodules oncocytic. All checked patients were alive without return or spread at last contact. The authors stress a wider range than past reports, which tied TERT to cancers alone.
pmc-13548581:
Mert Aytaç and Elif Erol survey 520 Syrian refugee adults about the mental resources that held up during the COVID-19 pandemic, in a 2026 study. Refugees faced displacement and then a pandemic, and the pair wanted to know which inner factors tracked with psychological well-being. Participants aged twenty-five to fifty, mostly men, completed scales for well-being, resilience, difficulty managing emotions, perceived stress, and their sense of a life project.

Well-being rose alongside resilience, hopeful views of one's life project, and healthier aims in handling emotions. Regret and several forms of emotion difficulty pulled it down, as did perceived stress. Because the survey captured one moment, the authors avoid causal claims. They suggest that programs building resilience and a meaningful life direction may support refugee mental health, and they frame their findings as groundwork for intervention research.
pmc-13549981:
Madalin Damoc and colleagues make gold compounds that behave as ionic liquids and then transform into a rare paired form of gold, in a 2026 chemistry study. Starting from ring-shaped sulfur ligands fitted with flexible tails, the team reacted them with a gold chloride acid. The products were salts pairing a protonated ligand with a gold chloride anion, their ionic character confirmed by crystal structures and spectroscopy.

One salt melts near fifty-five degrees Celsius, while the other is already liquid at room temperature, and electrical measurements showed the ions move and trade electrons like a true ionic liquid electrolyte. Adding water coaxed out something rarer: twin gold centers locked in the unusual plus-two oxidation state, sitting close together. The authors highlight the compounds as electroactive materials bridging liquid salts and exotic gold chemistry.
pmc-13550481:
Ali S Ahmed and colleagues bake demolition waste into high-performance fiber-reinforced concrete, in a 2026 materials study. Brick waste sand replaced part of the river sand, and ceramic waste powder replaced part of the cement. Polyethylene glycol was added as an internal curing agent. It releases water as the concrete hardens, compensating for the thirsty, angular brick particles.

The optimized mix swapped half the sand for brick waste and a tenth of the cement for ceramic powder. One and a half percent glycol completed the recipe. The mix reached compressive strength of sixty-three megapascals, with strong bending and tensile results and low water absorption. Microscopy showed a denser matrix with better bonding at the interfaces. The authors present the trio as a workable recipe for strong, durable composites that consume construction waste instead of landfilling it.
pmc-13551381:
Giorgia Sbarra, leading five colleagues, published a 2026 case report of a skin allergy that mimicked erythema multiforme, a more serious reaction pattern. The patient, a 22-year-old female student with atopic dermatitis, applied a cream containing isoconazole nitrate for ringworm. A plaque formed where the cream touched, then spread over fourteen days into widespread target-shaped and blistering lesions.

Fungal tests were negative at presentation and after recovery. Patch testing with a standard Italian series plus the cream itself produced a reaction to isoconazole nitrate, tying the eruption to contact sensitization rather than true erythema multiforme. The authors note that such polymorphous eruptions usually spare the mucous membranes, a clue that can separate the two conditions at the bedside.
pmc-13551681:
Jia Fu's team tested whether a simple calcium score from chest scans can flag narrowed heart arteries in people with end-stage kidney disease, in a 2026 study. Heart vessel disease is a leading killer in this group, yet the standard angiogram is invasive, so a scan-based screening aid would help. The team reviewed chest CT scans from 105 patients who had also had angiography between 2021 and 2025.

Scoring calcium in the four main heart vessels tracked the degree of narrowing. The combined score predicted major blockage well, and a cutoff of 5 caught two-thirds of cases while wrongly flagging none. The score worked best for the left main artery and least well for the right heart vessel. The authors present it as a first screen, with angiography still needed for a firm diagnosis.
pmc-13551781:
Yuan-Yuan Yang, leading six colleagues, published a 2026 sequencing study of the mitochondrial genome of Dactylogyrus wunderi, a flatworm parasite of fish. Codon usage bias, the uneven use of equivalent genetic code words, was unexplored in its class. The team sequenced the complete mitochondrial genome and compared composition and codon patterns across six Dactylogyrus species and 35 relatives.

The genome formed a typical circle of 14,920 base pairs in the reported assembly. Its group carried markedly less AT bias than the wider class, and most genes used codons in a relatively unbiased way by the measures applied. Family trees mostly recovered single-origin families, with one exception noted. The authors conclude natural selection, more than mutation drift, shapes codon use in these parasites.
pmc-13551981:
Kübra Yurtseven, with four colleagues, published a 2026 study of diet in women with polycystic ovary syndrome. The syndrome is a hormone disorder often paired with metabolic problems. Records covered 420 women aged eighteen to fifty. All had nutrition therapy between December 2023 and June 2024. A fourteen-item screener scored adherence to the Mediterranean diet. Body measures and blood tests came from the same records.

Mean diet adherence was low. Scores tied weakly to many measures, in mixed directions. They fell as body mass, body fat, and an inflammation marker rose. They rose with some glucose and insulin readings, which the team reports plainly. The inflammation marker tracked body fat fairly closely. The team calls for larger studies that follow women over time.
pmc-13552181:
Jialong Wang and five co-authors link a blood sugar score to kidney stones. Their study from twenty twenty-six uses health check data from China. The score, called eGDR, stands in for how the body handles sugar.

The group split a large set of adults by score range. Low scores went with more stones, even after checks for other traits. Curves and group tests probed if the link changed by subgroup. The score also beat some other marks at spotting stone cases. The link may help flag risk early for care.
pmc-13552581:
Emelie Andersson, with Nicole Mpatsiaris Riboe and Kajsa Järvholm, shares a 2026 Swedish interview study on bullying tied to body weight at school. Thirteen teens aged twelve to nineteen, most met through obesity clinics, spoke about being picked on. The authors sort their accounts into three themes using a reflective form of theme analysis. Talk took place between April and October 2025.

One theme shows teens blaming their own bodies after hearing their worth mocked each day. Another shows schools looking away, or even adding to the harm. A third shows lasting damage to trust, self-belief, and hope for adult life. The authors urge health staff to ask about such bullying, and schools to act without blaming the teen who was hurt.
pmc-13555881:
Redi Aditama leads an eleven-author team building a graph-shaped pan-genome for oil palm in a 2026 study. Oil palm yields more oil per hectare than any rival crop, yet narrow genetics limit breeding. Single reference genomes miss much of the species' variation. Their graph weaves thirty assemblies from wild, semi-tamed, and commercial palms into one shared map.

The map exposed wide structural variation and genes present in only some palms. A conserved core sat beside shell and unique gene sets rich in stress and defence roles. Semi-tamed palms varied most of all. Resistance gene families split in behaviour: one class stayed stable while another churned through duplication. The resource supports future trait hunts and breeding for resilience.
pmc-13555981:
Junhui Zhu and four colleagues published a 2026 study of how body mass index relates to physical fitness in young schoolchildren. They used routine fitness records for 1,572 pupils in grades one to six at a single primary school in the Tianfu New Area of Sichuan, China. Tests covered lung capacity, a short sprint, sit-and-reach flexibility, and one minute of rope skipping.

Rather than assuming a straight-line link, the authors fitted curved models that let fitness rise or fall unevenly as body mass index changes. They present the work as a methods demonstration from one school rather than a survey of all children. Readers get a clear example of how flexible statistical models can reveal patterns that simple averages would hide.
pmc-13556981:
Wenjie Shi and colleagues investigate a worm protein that calms allergic disease, in a 2026 study. Parasitic worms release proteins that quiet the host's immune system, and these proteins might treat allergies without the risks of live infection. One class, called serpins, blocks cutting enzymes. The team asked whether that blocking action is what delivers the immune benefit.

They engineered a changed version of a serpin from the worm Trichinella spiralis, altering one key building block. The changed protein blocked its target enzymes far more weakly. In a mouse allergy model, it also failed to calm lung inflammation as the natural protein did. The blocking action steered immune cells, including macrophages and regulatory T cells, toward tolerance. The study pins the benefit to a single chemical skill of the protein. That clarity helps designers build allergy treatments from worm biology.
pmc-13557881:
Lee and colleagues hunt for preoperative predictors in this 2026 study of stage II to III lung cancer treated with immunotherapy before surgery. Pathologic complete response, no viable tumor left in the removed tissue, predicts lasting benefit but is only known after the operation. The team combined metabolic PET imaging with immune profiling of biopsy samples to look for signs visible beforehand.

Thirteen patients were analyzed, and eight, 62 percent, achieved complete response. Responders showed a lower tumor-to-liver uptake ratio after treatment, a median of 1.51 against 2.14 in non-responders, and a steeper relative fall in that ratio. Their pre-treatment biopsies also carried more CD4 T cells and more of the checkpoint molecule TIGIT on both CD8 and CD4 cells. Only one patient recurred during follow-up. The authors propose pairing scans with immune profiling for perioperative decisions, pending larger validation.
pmc-13558681:
Arundhasa Chandrabalan and eight colleagues showed in 2026 that a human protein, annexin A5, grabs both the coronavirus spike and its doorway receptor, jamming viral entry from two sides. New variants keep eroding existing defences, so multi-action blockers are prized. The team made the pure proteins and probed their binding with four biophysical methods, including nuclear magnetic resonance and light scattering.

Annexin bound the spike's receptor-binding region most strongly exactly where the receptor docks, while also binding the receptor itself. In cell tests with a pseudovirus carrying the spike, annexin cut entry, lowered viral burden, and improved infected cell survival. Its known anti-inflammatory record adds a second, calming dimension. The authors argue for developing this two-handed grip into a treatment that variants cannot easily escape, since the drug targets the host receptor as well as the virus.
pmc-13559981:
Eszter Rimányi and colleagues frame American firearm harm as a market-driven epidemic, borrowing lessons from tobacco and prescription opioids. Their 2026 analysis uses peer-reviewed literature, government documents, and media reports to test firearms against a five-phase epidemic framework. Firearm deaths hit a record 48,830 in 2021, and rates vary tenfold between states.

The authors argue the industry marketed ownership through fear and emphasis on lethality while stalling public health research for decades. Classic market-driven epidemics shrank only when governments, nonprofits, academics, media, and sometimes companies acted together over long periods. A robust shelf of mitigation tools already exists, from safety laws to hospital-based and community programs. State experience shows large sustained reductions are possible where measures take hold. The authors call for applying those lessons with far more active engagement from every stakeholder group.
pmc-13560081:
Didier Sornette and colleagues published a 2026 study proposing a new way to rank influence in networks. Classic ranking tools treat networks as frozen snapshots. Real influence rises and falls with events. The authors model activity as bursts that trigger more bursts. Outside shocks and internal echo both count.

Their method scores importance from live event intensity. Old measures like PageRank appear as special steady cases. Tests used simulations and online emotion data. Rankings adapted quickly after sudden shocks. The framework could serve science, economics, and public health. It ties importance to observable activity, not guesswork.
pmc-13560181:
Romana Erblich and colleagues compare survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in children across the arrest's different causes. Their 2026 multicentre retrospective study draws on a nationwide helicopter emergency service that treated 9,018 arrest patients, of whom 247 were children and 200 entered the analysis. External and traumatic causes dominated the pediatric cases.

Trauma was the single commonest cause, followed by drowning. Survival differed sharply by cause at every horizon measured. Drowning led the table, with over half the children alive at thirty days and half at one year in the reported rates. Sudden infant death syndrome fared worst, with only one child in twenty surviving. Non-cardiac internal causes and asphyxiation sat between those poles. Adjusted models kept cause independently tied to circulation return and to survival. The authors underline how strongly prognosis in pediatric arrest depends on what caused it.
pmc-13560381:
Kutlay Gür and four colleagues test how switching growth charts reclassifies tiny preterm babies as small for gestational age or growth restricted after birth. Their 2026 retrospective single-center study covers 272 infants born between twenty-four and thirty-two weeks. Three charts, the new Fenton-2025, INTERGROWTH-21st, and Fenton-2013, were applied to the same babies.

Classification swung widely by chart. The new Fenton curves labeled 24.3 percent of babies small at birth and 40.8 percent growth restricted at discharge, the highest shares of the three in both cases. The charts nested, with each broader one swallowing the narrower one's cases plus more. Babies flagged as growth restricted under any chart carried higher adjusted odds of serious intestinal disease, necrotizing enterocolitis. The authors call Fenton-2025 more inclusionary and ask for outcome-linked validation before its wider net guides care.
pmc-13560481:
Sarah Hamersma and Mitchell McFarlane examine whether losing food assistance before pregnancy harms babies, exploiting county-level waivers of SNAP work requirements. Their 2026 policy study links near-complete US birth records from 2004 to 2018 with waiver status in the year before each pregnancy. Childless adults normally lose benefits after three months unless they meet work rules.

When waivers were withdrawn and requirements reimposed, participation among childless women fell. Their later babies paid a measurable price. Among first-time mothers, very low birth weight rose about fourteen percent and very preterm birth about ten percent relative to baseline rates in the reported estimates. Waiver introductions, by contrast, changed little. Maternal outcomes mostly held steady, with an unexpected drop in eclampsia after removals. The authors warn that work requirements aimed at childless adults can echo into the next generation's health.
pmc-13560681:
Junxiu Yu and three colleagues review short-chain fatty acids, the fermentation products of gut bacteria, as immune tuners with anti-infective promise. Their 2026 article works through the acids' dealings with eleven key germs spanning bacteria, a fungus, and four viruses. Acetate, propionate, and butyrate arise from fiber fermentation at roughly sixty, twenty, and twenty percent.

Against most gut microbes the acids act as foes, holding back growth by blocking enzymes and receptor signals. One germ, Campylobacter jejuni, breaks the pattern by using them to aid its own spread. Effects on lung viruses and the gut fungus Candida muddy any simple story of protection. The authors argue the microbiota-fatty acid axis deserves deeper study before therapies follow. Their review aims to give infection research a working map of these daily metabolites.
pmc-13560981:
Abdur Razzaque Sarker, Rasedul Islam, and An Tran-Duy measure how health bills push families in Bangladesh into poverty. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, uses a national survey from twenty twenty-two. More than fourteen thousand households took part across all eight regions. The team counts care costs paid straight from the pocket.

Near eighteen percent of households spent over a tenth of their budget on care. At a higher bar, the share was about seven percent. Some families fell below the poverty line only because of medical bills. The authors use a standard method to find which traits raise the risk. Their work aims to guide stronger cost protection in health policy.
pmc-13563481:
Marloes L. C. Spekman and Eva-Maria Merz survey how blood services across 17 European countries recruit and keep plasma donors. Plasma feeds the manufacture of medicines that many patients cannot live without, and supply is fragile. The 2026 report draws on a survey sent to collection organisations in 2023. Seventeen responded: ten state bodies, five non-profit organisations, and two hospital services. All collected whole blood, twelve collected plasma, and nine admitted they fall short of national demand and lean on imports.

Every organisation runs recruitment campaigns, with separate pitches for blood and plasma, and most court both first-time and repeat donors with gestures of thanks. Retention work for plasma donors lags behind, and about half the organisations check whether any of it works. Staff shortages, thin budgets, and weak computer systems hamper the effort. The authors call for evaluation so scarce outreach money lands where it changes behaviour.
pmc-13563781:
Gülşah Çelik and four colleagues let doctors and parents grade ChatGPT's answers to the questions families of boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy ask most. The disease weakens muscle, and parents hunt for guidance on its course and care. Their 2026 study fed ten real family questions to ChatGPT-4o. Specialists in rehabilitation and child neurology scored the answers for accuracy, currency, completeness, usefulness, and clarity. Parents scored separately for satisfaction, empathy, completeness, and clarity.

Accuracy led the scores at 4.3 out of five, with over ninety percent of ratings at four or better. Every expert category cleared four. Parents marked clarity highest at 4.5 and empathy lowest at 4.2, the soft spot both groups could feel. The authors conclude the chatbot gives sound, usable information that can support, never replace, the clinical team. They call for work on warmth and on the ethics of machine advice before its role grows.
pmc-13563881:
Yin and co-authors show how a Chinese hospital stopped throwing away CT contrast dye. Their 2026 retrospective study at Tongji Hospital in Wuhan covers a year of contrast prescriptions across nine products. A multidisciplinary team redesigned the scan workflow. It also switched billing from one vial per patient to shared vials. Leftover dye in an opened vial now serves the next patient instead of the bin.

Under vial-sharing, the hospital saved about 2.9 million millilitres of contrast agent in a year. That translated to roughly 9.2 million yuan in avoided drug cost, and each patient's prescription bill fell by an average of about 67 yuan. The authors credit the process redesign, not just the billing change. They frame the gains as economic and environmental. Less pharmaceutical waste is incinerated or washed into wastewater, and a costly resource goes further.
pmc-13567781:

pmc-13572381:

pmc-13572481:

pmc-13573381:

pmc-13573481:

pmc-13574381:

pmc-13574881:

pmc-13575181:

pmc-13575981:

pmc-13576281:

pmc-13577381:

pmc-13578281:

pmc-13578381:

pmc-13579481:

pmc-13580181:

pmc-13582081:

pmc-13582781:
Ramona L. Martinez, Annie Regan, and Sonja Lyubomirsky ran a 2026 experiment on two ways of being kind to oneself. pmc-13583581:

pmc-13584481:

pmc-13585081:
Jessica Salam, Inder Kumar Pandit, Neeraj Gugnani, and Monika Gupta test two fluoride varnishes in young children. pmc-13585581:

pmc-13587881:

pmc-13588681:

pmc-13589381:

pmc-13590081:

pmc-13591281:

pmc-13591781:

pmc-13592081:

pmc-13592481:

pmc-13595781:

pmc-13598481:

pmc-13600681:

pmc-13601581:

pmc-13606581:

pmc-13608781:

pmc-13611681:

pmc-13614681:

pmc-13614981:

pmc-13615481:

pmc-13615781:

pmc-13616381:

pmc-13616581:

pmc-13618981:

pmc-13619181:
