The authors urge doctors to keep parasitic infection in mind even after cancer is found.
pmc-13619281:
Jonathan A Hermel and five colleagues reply to a letter about their project on timely team debriefs after cardiac arrests and airway procedures in a pediatric emergency department. They thank the commenter and agree that patient outcomes, debrief quality, and staff well-being deserve study. Their reply explains why the project itself focused first on getting structured debriefs into routine practice.

The form they used followed an established plus-delta pattern, with a facilitation script meant to keep discussion safe and focused. Sessions were designed to last about seven minutes, balancing a standard structure with room for each team's needs. The authors say proving that debriefs could happen reliably, without disrupting care, had to come before testing downstream effects. They present adoption as a necessary first step, not the final evidence.
pmc-13619681:
Julian Wolfes and seven colleagues probed the rhythm effects of omecamtiv mecarbil, a heart-muscle activator hoped to treat heart failure, using isolated rabbit hearts kept beating in the lab. Forty-eight hearts were split between a lower-chamber setup and an upper-chamber setup. The team varied the drug dose and paced the tissue at several rates while recording electrical recovery times.

On its own in the lower chambers, the drug shortened electrical recovery yet widened its spread across the tissue and raised dangerous rhythm episodes. Paired with another drug that already strained recovery, it added still more rhythm risk. In the upper chambers the picture flipped by context: the drug raised fibrillation risk in healthy tissue, yet strongly suppressed fibrillation in tissue primed by two stimulating chemicals. The authors call the profile substrate-dependent, helpful or harmful depending on the heart's starting state.
pmc-13620181:
Wookjin Yang reviews how low blood cholesterol targets should guide prevention of ischemic stroke, a 2026 neurologist's perspective on a fast-moving evidence base. Lowering low-density lipoprotein cholesterol is central to preventing artery disease, and guideline targets have tightened as trials of statins, ezetimibe, and PCSK9 blockers showed benefit at ever lower levels. Stroke-specific trials on aggressive lowering after atherosclerotic stroke have added direct support for intensive treatment.

The review also weighs early intensive lowering right after a stroke and traces how stroke guidelines shifted from borrowing heart-trial evidence to standing on stroke-specific data. A major gap remains for non-atherosclerotic strokes, such as small-vessel disease and cardioembolism, where ideal targets are poorly defined and current guidance stays focused on atherosclerotic cases. Clinicians get a clear synthesis of what is settled, what is emerging, and where large ongoing trials should sharpen tailored targets.
pmc-13620281:
Muhammet Fatih Şahin wrote a letter to the editor questioning a trial that used glycated albumin to guide early diabetes treatment. Glycated albumin reflects blood sugar over a shorter window than the standard HbA1c test, so the trial let doctors act sooner in newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes. The letter praises the multicenter randomized design, then presses on weak points in how the results were read.

The main target, reaching the standard HbA1c goal at twelve weeks, came out identical in both groups. A stricter goal looked better only under a secondary analysis that drops the protection of randomization, and many secondary comparisons went unadjusted. Şahin's sharpest point is mechanical: the guided group simply received far more combination therapy, so gains may credit earlier intensification rather than the biomarker itself. The letter asks for trials that separate the marker's value from the treatment push it triggers.
pmc-13623381:
Enrique Lanzarini and co-authors test a new way to light up lymph nodes during stomach cancer surgery. Removing the right nodes, a step called D2 lymphadenectomy, is central to curing the cancer, and a glowing dye called indocyanine green can show where lymph drains. Standard practice injects the dye a day earlier by scope; this team injected it during the operation itself.

The pilot study ran at two institutions with twenty patients having keyhole stomach removal with curative intent. The dye went into the stomach wall in two small injections after the surgeons first looked inside. Every case finished the full node clearance without technical trouble or dye side effects, and the median harvest reached thirty-nine nodes. Glow appeared reliably in the main drainage stations and never in one distant station. The authors call the method feasible, safe, and repeatable without a separate pre-op procedure.
pmc-13623781:
Tomohiro Kikuchi and colleagues published a 2026 study building reference charts for abdominal organ sizes across Japan. Doctors judging whether a liver or kidney looks enlarged need to know what is normal for a person's age, sex, and build, and large reference data were lacking. The team mined a national medical image database for non-contrast CT scans from 2024.

Nearly fifty thousand examinations from nine institutions were measured by an automated outlining program. Men carried larger organs than women across the board, from liver and kidneys down to the small adrenal glands. Adjusted for body size, liver, pancreas, and kidney volumes curved with age, rising then falling, while spleen and a key hip muscle shrank steadily in older groups. The prostate and women's adrenal glands grew with age instead. The authors offer the percentiles as a yardstick for clinics and for imaging research.
pmc-13624781:
Gisli G Einarsson and colleagues write to the editor with deeper results from the CFMATTERS trial in cystic fibrosis. During lung flare-ups, patients usually get two intravenous antibiotics, and the trial added a third drug chosen from gene-sequencing profiles of each patient's sputum germs. The main trial had already shown no clinical gain, so the team asked whether the extra drug at least cut germ levels or airway inflammation further.

Sputum gathered before treatment, at its start, and on day fourteen showed no extra drop in microbe measures or inflammation markers from the added drug. The usual pair did the measurable work. The letter tempers hopes that sequencing-guided add-ons help during flare-ups, at least with the drugs and timing this trial used.
pmc-13627281:
Raphaëlle Giac and co-authors follow Canadian mothers from pregnancy to their babies' first birthdays to trace how prenatal mood reaches infant temperament. The Quebec pandemic-era study enrolled over fourteen hundred mothers and measured depression and anxiety late in pregnancy, again at three months, and rated babies' difficult temperament at twelve months. Partner support, as the mothers felt it, was tracked along the same path.

Heavier prenatal symptoms did predict fussier, harder-to-soothe infants, yet the effect traveled entirely through two middle steps: the mother's symptoms after birth, and how supported she felt by her partner. The same held for anxiety as for depression, and boys and girls showed no difference. Screening after birth and shoring up partner support, the authors suggest, are practical places to break the chain.
pmc-13627881:
Zhiqiang Ma and four colleagues review how thyroid problems can damage memory and thinking, and whether a training method called neurofeedback could help repair that damage. Their paper pulls together published research on the link between thyroid dysfunction and cognitive impairment, the brain mechanisms behind it, and the treatments now being tried.

The review argues that the brain pathways behind thyroid-related decline are still poorly mapped, and that this gap slows the search for targeted treatments. It presents neurofeedback, a non-invasive method that trains people to shift their own brain activity, as a candidate for rehabilitation. The authors close by setting out research directions meant to turn a scattered field into a clearer program.
pmc-13627981:
Tingting Liu and nine colleagues tested whether total glucosides of paeony, a plant-derived mixture, can protect kidneys from damage caused by the chemotherapy drug cisplatin. Acute kidney injury was triggered in mice with a single cisplatin dose, and the researchers then measured kidney tissue damage, organ function, and immune cell behaviour.

Treatment reduced tissue injury and calmed the immune response inside the kidney. Dendritic cells, which normally alert T cells to attack, became less mature and less mobile, while calming regulatory T cells grew in number and aggressive killer T cells were restrained. Two inflammatory signaling routes were dampened at once, leading the authors to present the mixture as a candidate for future kidney-protective drugs.
pmc-13628281:
Zhicheng Gong and seven colleagues tested a staged treatment for dense, stubborn keloid scars. Keloids are overgrown scars that resist single treatments and often grow back. The team treated 87 patients holding 285 keloid lesions. The work ran from September 2023 to April 2024 at one centre.

Stage one paired a punch removal method, done with drug help, with shallow radiation. Stage two added repeated shots of two drugs into the scars. At twelve months, nearly nine in ten patients scored far better on standard scar scales. Side effects stayed mild. Dark skin patches were common for a time. A few ulcers and skin reactions appeared, and all settled. The team calls the sequence a practical, gentle option for a hard caseload.
pmc-13629281:
Cristina Thompson and colleagues explored nurses' experiences running a social-prescribing scheme for lonely older adults in Australian general practice. Social connection is a growing public-health concern, and nurses in health-connector roles were new territory. Their qualitative study interviewed eight practice nurses at scheme end and five again a year later, plus two focus groups during delivery.

Nurses found the connector role aligned with their scope and care philosophy, and their primary-care skills prepared them, though extra training and resources proved essential. Older patients gained, motivating nurses to keep elements alive despite sustainability struggles. Thompson and colleagues argue nurse-led social prescribing benefits nurses and patients alike.
pmc-13631281:
Jiawen Wang and eight colleagues pool the genetics of six pelvic floor conditions. They hunt for the shared inherited roots of these disorders. Their study appeared in 2026. Prolapse, incontinence, and kin disorders affect roughly a quarter of adult women. They frequently arrive together. That points to common roots that single-condition studies keep missing.

Combining genome-wide data with structural modelling split the shared genetics into two strands. One is structural, tied to prolapse anatomy. One is functional, tied to bladder and bowel control. Gene-level analysis flagged 267 strong genes. They cluster in connective tissue organisation and urogenital growth. A network-aware machine learning step sharpened the priority list beyond a plain baseline. Key signals also held direction in a separate ancestry group.
pmc-13631381: The authors of a 2026 study of dual targeted therapy for hard-to-treat psoriatic arthritis issued this correction. One results table had been calculated from an early analysis including patients with incomplete follow-up, against the study's own methods. All values were recomputed using complete cases only. Two physician-rated measures were dropped, as too few patients had full data. Two skin measures were added in their place. One results passage was rewritten to show joint swelling eased later than first stated. The abstract, safety findings, and conclusions are unchanged.
pmc-13635081:
Zachary Ells and colleagues measured how much radiation tumors and healthy organs absorb during a targeted prostate cancer therapy. Their data come from a randomized phase 2 trial comparing two doses of a lutetium-labeled drug homing to prostate cancer cells. Forty-eight patients had complete imaging sets. The team combined repeated whole-body scans with one detailed three-dimensional scan after the first cycle building dose estimates for kidneys, salivary glands, liver, and tumors.

Healthy organ doses per unit injected were low and did not differ between the two dose sizes. Bone tumors, the commonest site, absorbed moderate doses, varying widely between lesions. Lymph node tumors absorbed more on average in the lower-dose group, a quirk of small numbers. Deeper marker responses tracked with tumor dose in a direction the team reports carefully. The work shows routine imaging can yield patient-specific dose maps for this therapy.
pmc-13635181:
Xinjin Liu and eight colleagues published this 2026 systematic review of digital health tools for skin disease patients. Skin conditions burden over a third of the world's people, harming mood, sleep, and self-image alongside the skin itself. Clinic visits are brief and far apart, which leaves daily struggles unsupported. The review gathered fourteen studies and grouped them into four tool types: remote consultations, targeted messages to patients, personal health tracking, and patient-to-patient communication.

Remote care matched or beat in-person care on quality of life in most of its studies. Targeted messages gave mixed quality-of-life results yet improved mental health and confidence in managing illness. The single tracking study showed no clear life-quality gain, while the peer communication study offered emotional support. Weak methods, bias risk, and short follow-up limit the whole field. The authors recommend shared outcome standards and fair, adaptive digital support.
pmc-13638981:
Qingqing Li and five colleagues present a 2026 study that maps three kinds of chemical marks on DNA in papillary thyroid cancer. This common thyroid cancer is well described genetically, yet the added marks that switch genes on or off had not been charted together.

The team compared tumor and normal tissue from six patients who had not yet received treatment. Distinct mark patterns emerged, and a selection process narrowed thousands of changed regions to a panel of 187 locations that separated tumor from normal tissue reliably. Tumors with BRAF mutations behaved differently from those with RAS mutations, linking marks to drivers.
pmc-13647381:
Attila Ábrahám and eight colleagues compare three ways to make glass shed water while staying clear. One route treats the surface directly with a silicon chemical, while two lay down thin silica coatings made by a sol-gel process, one of them further modified. The team measured water angles, surface energy, light transmission, and pore structure for each. A designed experiment then stressed the coatings with heat and chemistry together.

Every treatment turned the glass water-repellent with smooth, even behavior. Both coatings actually passed more light than bare glass, a bonus for windows and optics. Their inner pore networks differed sharply, one fine and vast, the other more open. Acidity and alkalinity proved the main killers of the effect, with heat and time speeding the damage. Chemical fingerprints blamed loss of methyl groups. The comparison gives coating designers a clear map of which recipe suits which demand.
pmc-13648081:
Tatsuya Iwashina and five colleagues synthesise zinc complexes using a blue azulene-based ligand shortened to DEHA, and they characterise what forms under different conditions. Azulene is unusual because it glows from a higher excited state than most molecules, which makes its metal complexes interesting for light-based materials.

Changing the zinc salt and the alkali metal carbonate base produced several distinct complexes, with three or four ligands around the zinc and sodium, potassium, or rubidium acting as counter ions. Structures were confirmed by X-ray analysis and several spectroscopies. All the complexes emitted light from the same first excited state, and the team also cast them into plastic films for material testing.
pmc-13649381:
Tong Feng and four colleagues chart breast cancer deaths among Americans aged sixty-five and older from 1999 to 2020, asking whether national improvements were shared fairly. Using a federal mortality database, they calculated age-adjusted rates and modelled trends across sex, race, region, and state.

More than half a million such deaths occurred over the period, overwhelmingly among women, whose rates were highest at older ages and among Black women. Overall mortality fell substantially, although the decline slowed after the middle of the following decade, and wide geographic and social gaps persisted. The authors call for targeted efforts on screening access, timely diagnosis, and geriatric cancer care to close those gaps.
pmc-13649481:
Lingping Ding and two colleagues report a 52-year-old man who lost his hearing in both ears after a severe brain infection from a pig-linked germ. He worked with swine and drank heavily for years. Gene-based tests on blood and spinal fluid found the pig germ in the spinal fluid and a second germ in the blood alone.

Strong drug care cleared the brain infection but could not restore his hearing. Scans hinted that scar tissue had grown inside the inner ear. Surgeons placed a hearing implant in his left ear, slid the full wire set in place, and got stable nerve responses in spite of dense scar tissue. The case shows such implants can still work after this kind of damage.
pmc-13649981:
Zhiyue Jiang and seven colleagues study older adults in a rural Chinese community and ask how mouth health, social weakness, and memory and thinking skills fit together. Oral frailty covers problems such as tooth loss and weak chewing, while social frailty covers going out less, rarely seeing friends, and living or spending days alone.

Data came from a 2022 follow-up survey of rural older adults, using a standard mental test, an eight-item oral frailty index, and a five-item social frailty check. Both forms of frailty were tied to lower cognitive scores. Much of the oral frailty link ran through social frailty, which accounted for about three quarters of the total association in the pooled result. Patterns differed for men and women. Because everyone was measured once, the authors call for follow-up studies over time to test the pathway.
pmc-13650681:
Mutasim Binidris and six colleagues review surgery planning for patients with chronic myeloid leukemia who take tyrosine kinase inhibitors, the targeted pills that have turned this blood cancer into a long-term condition. More patients now live long enough to need operations, and their drugs complicate anesthesia, bleeding risk, and healing in drug-specific ways.

One drug stood out for impairing platelet function and lowering blood counts, while two others raised arterial and heart risk. A swollen spleen, obesity, weight-loss surgery, and pregnancy each shifted drug handling and operative risk further. No validated schedule exists for pausing the pills before surgery, so the review advises case-by-case decisions weighing drug toxicity, disease control, and procedural stakes. Common anesthetic and pain medicines also interact through a shared liver enzyme route, favoring alternatives that bypass it. The authors call for genuinely multidisciplinary planning.
pmc-13651481:
Maryam Alheddi and six colleagues report a 60-year-old woman whose aggressive lymphoma returned in her breast after nearly twenty quiet years. Her original disease, plasmablastic lymphoma, had sat in the nose and sinuses and stayed in long remission. This rare lymphoma usually appears outside lymph nodes and can imitate a primary breast cancer on scans almost perfectly.

Imaging flagged the fast-growing lump as highly suspicious, and a needle biopsy confirmed recurrence of the same disease. A month later, follow-up imaging unexpectedly showed the lump partly shrinking on its own, a twist that could have misled the team. Whole-body metabolic imaging then revealed widespread disease elsewhere, overturning any comfort from the local shrinkage. The authors stress precise tissue subtyping for prognosis and the need to combine functional with structural imaging, since a single shrinking lesion can disguise a body-wide relapse.
pmc-13652081:
Larske Soepnel and colleagues compare gut microbes and type 2 diabetes across five populations of African origin. Their study covers middle-aged adults in Ghana, South Africa, Jamaica, Seychelles, and the United States. Places that sit at very different points in the shift from fiber-rich traditional diets to processed foods. Stool samples were sequenced and tested for short chain fatty acids, alongside blood measures of glucose and insulin.

Microbial diversity and fatty acid levels ran highest in Ghana and lowest in the United States. Diabetes came with lower diversity overall, though that link faded once location was taken into account, and certain microbes stayed tied to the disease after adjustment. The results show that findings from Western cohorts do not transfer neatly, and that diet transition leaves a measurable mark on the gut.
pmc-13652881:
Family life after a young person's psychiatric hospital stay is mapped by Friedrich and colleagues. Up to a third of children and adolescents return to inpatient psychiatric care within a year, usually within three months. Reviews have struggled to synthesise family factors because studies define them so differently. The team reviewed eighty-three reports, mostly retrospective record-based studies from the United States, covering caregiving setting, family psychiatric history, and involvement in treatment.

Readmission linked most consistently to disrupted or burdened caregiving, including foster or institutional care, to psychiatric problems within the family, and to patterns of treatment involvement. By contrast, research on specific family processes, such as communication or conflict, remains sparse despite its known importance in adult psychiatry. Friedrich and colleagues conclude that family factors matter for youth readmission, while calling for forward-looking studies that capture family processes and short-term risks more directly.
pmc-13653581:
Elisa D'Arrigo and four colleagues image living three-dimensional cell clusters with a hybrid microscopy that sees beneath the surface. Spheroids mimic real tissue better than flat cultures, but conventional electrochemiluminescence only reports events at the electrode surface. Their confocal approach breaks that limit, mapping spheroids up to one hundred fifty micrometers deep while following changes over time.

Slow electron-transfer chemistry lets the light-generating reactions propagate into the cluster's interior. The spheroid itself acts as a reaction-diffusion chamber, concentrating intermediates and brightening internal regions. The method reaches single-cell resolution and is non-invasive. The authors present it as a tool for probing permeability and redox metabolism inside tissue-engineered models.
pmc-13669381:
Alex Rodriguez-Palacios and colleagues tested coconut oil in gut disease in 2026. Health guidance warns against saturated fats, coconut oil included. Yet coconut oil is common where bowel inflammation rates stay low. Many patients also believe it helps them. The oil is rich in medium-chain fats, notably myristic acid. The team fed the oil to mice bred to develop Crohn's-like gut inflammation. They varied dose, timing, and pairing with steroids.

Early feeding prevented gut inflammation in many young mice. Lower doses, closer to human use, also protected. The oil did not reverse disease once it was established. Paired with steroids, it lengthened the quiet period after treatment. Protection tracked with myristic acid in the diet. Gut microbe shifts and stronger regulatory T cells came with it. No clear harms appeared in the model. The authors urge a fresh look at coconut oil guidance.
pmc-13673781:
Tommaso Cambiaghi describes a 2026 surgical technique that runs heart-lung bypass and an Impella 5.5 heart pump through a single aortic opening using a direct Y-graft. Normally, starting bypass and placing the pump need separate aortic access points, adding incisions and complexity to an already high-stakes setup. The report gives step-by-step placement and removal instructions, noting it varies an established approach, uses no patient-specific data, and needed no ethics approval.

A ten-millimeter woven Dacron graft is formed into a Y shape. It is tunneled from a neck incision between the sternocleidomastoid muscle heads, and joined to the aorta through one opening under partial clamping. The graft is cleared of air through the pump sheath, the pump is placed before weaning from bypass, and the graft is later cut, shortened, and secured with slack for safe removal.
pmc-13677281:
Ben Buttle, Daniel Verdon, and Hilary Sheppard review the hard problem of inserting large DNA stretches into human T cells with CRISPR. Their review was published in twenty twenty-six. Big inserts power the next wave of cell therapies, yet knock-in stays the bottleneck.

Small edits are routine; large ones are not. The most efficient delivery, electric pulses with ready-made enzyme bundles, also kills many cells. Gentler options like cell-penetrating peptides and fat particles spare cells but edit fewer. Target site choice, guide design, and the local DNA landscape all sway success. Template formats from bare strands to virus carriers trade efficiency against toxicity. The review weighs each route toward safer engineered cells.
pmc-13682481:
Aimal Fatima, Duncan Lambie, and Genevieve Casey reported a case in 2026. A ten-year-old girl had a slow-growing facial nodule. It had been present for about two years. The tumor type is trichoblastoma, a benign growth. It arises from hair follicle germ cells. Such tumors are rare in children overall. They usually appear in adults on face or scalp. The growth can closely mimic skin cancer clinically. Even under magnification it resembles basal cell carcinoma.

Tissue examination is essential to separate the two. Cell patterns and special stains guide the diagnosis. One marker especially helps distinguish the tumor types. Complete surgical removal is the recommended treatment. Rare malignant change makes removal prudent anyway. Early biopsy protects children from misdiagnosis harm.
pmc-13683481:
Joanna Sender and Monika Różańska-Boczula survey invasive alien plants along two lowland rivers in eastern Poland, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. River valleys are rich in species but open to invasion through water links and frequent disturbance. The team read 150 vegetation plots at ten sites on the Biala Lada and Czarna Lada rivers. Plant indicator scores rated each site's nutrient and warmth conditions.

Invasive species favored richer, warmer spots more than native ones. Sites thick with invaders showed flatter species balance, more weedy plants, and more alike plant mixes. A biotic integrity index graded each site's health. The authors tie invasion control to nutrient and land care along rivers.
pmc-1552081:
Zamora, Abraira, Muriel, and co-authors introduce Meta-DiSc, software for pooling diagnostic test accuracy studies. Reviews that combine such studies increasingly guide doctors in practice. Yet at the time, no dedicated and complete program existed for this kind of pooling.

Meta-DiSc fills that gap for studies of how well a test spots disease. It lets reviewers gather sensitivity and related measures across many trials in one workflow. Better pooled estimates help clinicians choose tests with open eyes, knowing how often each misses cases or raises false alarms.  It remains a reference point whenever reviewers combine sensitivity results across studies.
pmc-5133381:
Burgess, Bowden, Fall, and their colleagues wrote in 2017 about sensitivity analyses for Mendelian randomization. Mendelian randomization uses genetic variants to test whether a risk factor truly causes a disease. Studies increasingly use many variants at once, which raises the chance that some variants break the method's assumptions.

Sensitivity analyses are extra checks that ask whether a causal conclusion survives when those assumptions are relaxed. Different checks probe different kinds of violation, such as variants that act through other pathways. Robust causal inference matters because these results guide prevention and drug development. The paper supports analysts who must defend a causal claim built on genetic data.
pmc-5466781:
Tremblay, Aubert, Barnes, and their team led a consensus project in 2017 on sedentary behavior terms. Work on sitting and low-activity time had grown fast in health science. Growth brought a mess: fields used the same words in unlike ways, so studies were hard to compare.

The Sedentary Behavior Research Network ran a formal process to agree on clear terms and definitions. Experts from many fields took part, which made agreement hard but more valuable. Shared words let studies be pooled and guidelines be written in plain terms. The agreed set now anchors work on how long sitting time shapes the risk of chronic disease.
pmc-6300481:
Alessandro Cassini and colleagues estimated the burden of antibiotic-resistant infections in Europe in 2019. Drug-resistant bacteria threaten modern care, from surgery to cancer treatment. Counting the deaths and disability they cause is hard but vital.

Focusing on the European Union and nearby countries, the team modeled infections with key resistant bacteria. They estimate tens of thousands of deaths each year trace to these infections. Much of the burden falls on infants and older adults, and on hospitals. The numbers support stronger infection control and careful antibiotic use across the region.
pmc-6927181:
Christoph Hafemeister and Rahul Satija presented a normalization method for single-cell RNA data in 2019. Cells in such data vary in how many molecules get captured. That technical swing can masquerade as real biological difference.

Their framework models counts with a regularized negative binomial model and uses the residuals for analysis. This steadies variance across genes with very different average levels. Clustering and marker finding sharpen as a result. The method ships inside the widely used Seurat toolkit, so it reached thousands of labs quickly. The approach ships with clear guidance on when the model assumptions are likely to break down.
pmc-7234781:
Jonathan Rogers and colleagues published a systematic review and meta-analysis in 2020 on the mind and brain effects of severe coronavirus infections. They gathered studies from the earlier SARS outbreak, which began in 2002, and the MERS outbreak, which began in 2012. They then compared those older findings with early reports from the COVID-19 pandemic.

The review pulls together what doctors saw in patients during and after these infections, from confusion and agitation to longer lasting mood and thinking problems. By placing the new virus beside its two closest relatives, the authors give clinicians a grounded sense of which mental health problems to watch for. It remains a useful early map of a side of coronavirus illness that received less attention than lung damage.
pmc-7285581:
Li Yin and colleagues reviewed in 2020 the biology and treatment of triple-negative breast cancer, one of the hardest forms of the disease to treat. This subtype lacks three targets that guide therapy in other breast cancers: the estrogen receptor, the progesterone receptor, and a growth factor receptor called HER2. It tends to grow fast, spread early, and return after treatment.

The authors explain how this cancer is now split into smaller molecular subtypes, each with its own behavior and weak points. They then survey treatment progress, from chemotherapy backbones to newer targeted drugs and immune based approaches matched to those subtypes. For clinicians and patients, the review maps where real progress is being made against a cancer long short on options.
pmc-8265181:
Zhiqiang Pang and co-authors unveiled MetaboAnalyst 5.0 in 2021, a major update of a web platform for metabolomics, the study of the small molecules in a sample. Since its first release more than a decade earlier, the platform had become a standard way to analyze such data. The fifth version aims to close the gap between raw instrument readings and biological meaning.

The authors describe the new modules and workflows, which carry a dataset from processing through statistics to interpretation in one place. They also show example analyses that highlight the added power. By keeping the platform free and browser based, the team keeps advanced metabolite analysis open to labs without dedicated computing staff.
pmc-9184281:
Milot Mirdita and colleagues built ColabFold in 2022 to make protein structure prediction fast and open to everyone. Their tool combines the quick similarity search of MMseqs2 with the AlphaFold2 and RoseTTAFold prediction systems. The pairing makes the search step far faster and uses the prediction models more efficiently.

The authors report speeds that allow close to a thousand structures or complexes to be predicted in a day on modest hardware. Because ColabFold runs in a free browser notebook, a student with no computing cluster can fold a protein in minutes. That openness spread advanced structure prediction far beyond well funded labs, and the tool became a default in teaching and research alike.
pothier-traite-contrat-de-vente-1781:
Robert Joseph Pothier's Treatise on the Contract of Sale, printed in French in this 1781 edition, is a classic of French private law. Pothier, a judge at Orléans, wrote a series of treatises that ordered the whole law of obligations. The sale contract, the most common deal in daily life, got his fullest care.

He defines what a sale is, what may be sold, the duties of buyer and seller, and the remedies when goods or payment fail. His clarity is the marvel: hard cases dissolve under his plain distinctions. When the drafters of Napoleon's Civil Code needed a guide, they drew on Pothier more than on any other writer. The treatise thus taught France its private law, and its influence reached Louisiana and Quebec as well.
reminiscences-of-dr-spurzheim-and-george: Reminiscences of Dr. Spurzheim and George Combe, 1881. The reminiscences. This book preserves that memoir. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. The archive guards it with care for all readers.
rossetti-ballads-sonnets-1881:
Dante Gabriel Rossetti was a painter as well as a poet, a founder of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood. Ballads and Sonnets, published in 1881, was his last book, appearing a year before his death. It completes the long sonnet sequence he had worked on for decades.

The House of Life here reaches its full 101 sonnets, tracing love, loss, and memory across a lifetime. The ballads include The King's Tragedy, a dark tale of James I of Scotland's murder, told with dramatic force. Rossetti's language is rich, musical, and steeped in medieval color. The volume sealed his place as the central poet of the Pre-Raphaelite circle.
sbe-10-dhammapada-suttanipata-1881:
F. Max Muller built the Sacred Books of the East as a vast set of fifty books. Book Ten of the set came out in 1881. It holds two of the best loved texts of the Buddhist faith. V. Fausboll made the English dress used here.

The Dhammapada is a book of short verses on the mind, on pain, and on the path. Its lines are said to hold the core teach of the Buddha in brief form. The Sutta-Nipata holds some of the most old talks of the faith. The book is a sound first step into Buddhist texts in English.
sbe-11-buddhist-suttas-1881:
T. W. Rhys Davids gave the Buddhist Suttas English dress in 1881. The book is Book Eleven of the Sacred Books of the East. Rhys Davids was the great Pali man of his age in Britain. The texts here are talks said to come from the Buddha himself.

The Mahaparinibbana Sutta tells of the last days and death of the Buddha. The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta is his first preach, the turn of the wheel of law. More talks deal with marks of a true priest and the snares of false views. The book is a core set of texts for the faith.
sbe-13-vinaya-texts-1-1881:
T. W. Rhys Davids and Hermann Oldenberg gave the Vinaya Texts English dress in 1881. The work is Book Thirteen of the Sacred Books of the East. Part One of the Vinaya holds the core rules for monks of the Buddha. The Vinaya is the rule book of the monk host.

The Patimokkha lists the rules a monk must own to, month by month. The Mahavagga, Books One to Four, tells how the order was formed and how new monks join. Tales of the first monks frame the dry lists of rules. The book shows the monk life as the faith first set it down.
schiller-robbers-1781:
Friedrich Schiller was twenty-one when The Robbers burst onto the German stage in 1781. Alexander Fraser Tytler translated the play into English in 1792. Karl Moor, cheated of his inheritance by his brother Franz, takes to the forest as captain of a robber band.

Karl's rage at a corrupt world drives him to crimes he cannot undo. Franz, cold and scheming, plots to seize the estate and their father's love. The old count and the faithful Amalia stand between the brothers' storm. Schiller wrote with the heat of the Sturm und Drang movement behind him. The play made him famous overnight and set a pattern for European melodrama.
scientific-american-supplement-no-275-ap: Dated New York, April 9, 1881, Supplement No. 275 appears as Volume XI, Number 275, priced at five dollars a year alone or seven dollars with the weekly paper. Its contents open with Arthur Archard of Geneva on the various modes of transmitting power to a distance, continued from Number 274, covering compressed air, pressure water, and electricity. A Hotchkiss revolving gun and a floating pontoon dock follow. A technology section then gives H.
scientific-american-supplement-no-286-ju: Supplement No. 286, dated New York, June 25, 1881, and headed Volume XI, leads with a one thousand horse power Corliss engine by Hitch, Hargreaves and Company, shown in five figures to scale. Next comes the opening of the new workshop of the Stevens Institute of Technology, with speeches by Professor R. W. Raymond and Mr. Horatio Allen.
scientific-american-supplement-no-288-ju: A dry air refrigerating machine, shown in five figures with plan and diagrams, leads Supplement No. 288, dated New York, July 9, 1881, in Volume XI. Thomas's improved steam wheel follows, then an address by President Francis to the American Society of Civil Engineers at Montreal and a piece on the water power of the United States.
scientific-american-supplement-no-299-se: Volume XII, Number 299, dated New York, September 24, 1881, opens its contents with progress and development of the marine engine. Sub-heads cover marine boilers, steel boilers, corrosion, fuel use, screw propellers, and how the marine engine may be improved. Steam ferry boats of the port of Marseilles, shown in section drawings, come next.
scientific-american-supplement-no-303-oc: A new eighty-ton steam hammer at the Saint Chamond works in France, shown in seven figures with foundation and forging mill plans, leads the contents of Supplement No. 303, dated New York, October 22, 1881, in Volume XII. Great steamers follow, comparing the Servia, the City of Rome, the Alaska, and the Great Eastern. An improved road locomotive, Albert Hoppin on American milling methods over ten years, and a machine for dotting tulles and other light fabrics round out the first section.
scientific-american-supplement-no-312-de: Dated New York, December 24, 1881, Supplement No. 312 in Volume XII opens with an improved fifteen ton traveling crane designed for building Port Alfred Harbor in South Africa, shown in three figures. An improved steam boiler and the elevated railways of New York follow. Sir Frederick Bramwell's paper for the British Association covers fifty years of growth in engine work. His list runs from steam engines, ships, and brakes to motors and power transmission. It ends with iron and steel making, bridges, and machine tools.
sinnett-the-occult-world-1881:
A. P. Sinnett stunned the West with The Occult World, his book of 1881. Sinnett was a news man in India. He said wise Masters in the far hills sent him notes by strange means. He prints their words and tells of marvels he saw at first hand.

Crowds seized on the book at once. It gave the new creed of Blavatsky a loud launch in the West. Doubts rose just as fast, and rows dogged the claims for years. True or not, the book changed what the West sought in the East. Sinnett kept his faith in the notes long past the first doubts. His calm tone in print helped win the claims a fair first hearing.
stanton-history-woman-suffrage-vol-1-188:
Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Susan B Anthony, and Matilda Joslyn Gage edited Volume 1 of History of Woman Suffrage, published in 1881. The leaders of the movement wrote its history themselves, from records they had kept. Volume 1 covers the years from 1848 to 1861.

Speeches, letters, convention reports, and newspaper accounts trace the movement from the Seneca Falls convention of 1848 to the Civil War. The editors printed documents at length so later readers could judge the record directly. Their version favors their own wing of the movement, a point later historians note. Still, the volume is the documentary record of the American women's movement by the women who led it, and a basic source ever since.
the-magic-wand-and-medical-guide-the-mos: Only a bookplate and a garbled title page are present here, so the guide's contents do not appear. A bookplate names the National Library of Medicine as recipient, from James Harvey Young. What can be read of the title page names The Magic Wand and Medical Guide, edited by R. F. Yungs and published by the Eureka Medical Institute at 29 Broadway in 1881. It promises disclosures and hints for love, courtship, and marriage, methods of curing and preventing disease, and secrets of natural and celestial magic, alchemy, and transmutation.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
The Mirror's number for Saturday, October 4, 1828, No. 334, illustrates the United Service Club-House in London. Modern club-houses, the article begins, show what luxury and good living have attained in this country. To the public their interest lies in the architectural embellishment they add to the streets. The club serves army and navy officers, who in peacetime may read the history of the war from quarto to the latest Foreign Office dispatches.

This house, at the angle of Charles Street and Regent Street, is judged a meagre specimen of its architect, Mr. Smirke. Apart from a bas-relief of Britannia distributing laurels, it carries no characteristic decoration of either service. Its columns are rigid, its whole architecture cold and unfeeling, the critic complains. A luxurious private club, he argues, admitted far more florid embellishment. Readers get clubland assessed as street scenery first and comfort second.

The Mirror's number for Saturday, April 16, 1831, No. 485, illustrates Mocha, the Red Sea port in Arabia Felix from which the finest coffee is exported. A young Princess Esterhazy, sent to bed without dinner, called her punishment good for digestion; the editors say the same of coffee. Lord Valentia's description, from which the engraving is copied, is called the fullest and most minute. From the sea the whitewashed town looks cheerful, its flat roofs broken by domes and three mosques' minarets.

A pier serves the trade, and a lofty cannon-mounted tower protects the sea gate. Inside the gates, though, the pleasing ideas flee before the filth abounding in every street and open space. The roadstead lies almost open, guarded only by two narrow sand spits with a round castle and an insignificant fort. Readers taste the coffee trade's geography: glamour at anchorage distance, squalor at street level.
tob-10481:
Israel Abrahams wandered off the main roads of Hebrew literature in By-paths in Hebraic Bookland. Standard histories follow famous books and authors. Abrahams, a scholar of Judaism with a collector's curiosity, went looking for overlooked books, curious authors, and odd corners that those histories skip.

Each essay rescues some forgotten corner of Jewish reading life, treating old volumes, inscriptions, and marginal figures with affection and wit. The pleasure is in the detours: what people actually read, kept, and argued over. For readers who love books about books, Abrahams offers a learned companion happy to leave the highway and explore side streets.
tob-10781:
An unknown author published the Arbatel, Of the Magic of the Ancients, in Latin in 1575. It is a short Renaissance grimoire, far gentler than most books of its kind. Its author frames magic as wisdom given by God to the worthy.

The book names seven Olympian spirits who rule the ages of the world and gives their seals and the provinces under each. Aphorisms teach the magician to live cleanly, keep secrets, and seek knowledge rather than gold. Brief and humane, the Arbatel shaped later occult writers and still serves as many readers' first grimoire.
tob-4081:
Abu Nasr al-Farabi, the great philosopher of medieval Islam, asked how words join onto things in his Kitab al-Huruf, the Book of Letters. Language, logic, and grammar meet in his inquiry. Arabic philosophy of language begins, in large part, with his distinctions.

Farabi traces how terms pass from daily speech into science and philosophy, changing sense as they go. He sorts letters, particles, and names with a logician's patience. The result is precise, dry, and foundational for readers of Arabic thought. The entry rests on a verified 1919 public-domain edition. Few medieval books reward slow reading more than this study of how meaning is built.
tob-4181:
Firdausi spent some thirty years on the Shahnama, the Book of Kings, Persia's national epic. Arthur George Warner and Edmond Warner turned it into English in a monumental Trubner series. Volume one opens the long chronicle with the mythic first kings and the ordering of the world.

Heroes are born, demons are bound, and the royal glory passes from line to line. Rustam, the epic's mightiest champion, makes his first deeds here, though his tragedies wait for later volumes. The Warners keep the Persian couplets in steady English verse. A thousand years after Firdausi, his kings still anchor how Persians tell their own past.
tylor-anthropology-1881:
Edward Burnett Tylor's Anthropology, published in 1881, was the first general textbook of the field he had founded. His subtitle promises an introduction to the study of man and civilization. Tylor wrote it for the general reader, and it served as the standard primer for a generation.

The book ranges over the races of mankind, the rise of language, the arts of life, and the growth of custom and belief. Stone tools, fire, counting, myth, and marriage customs each get their clear, brief chapter. Its judgments on peoples reflect Victorian assumptions that readers now question. As a map of what the young science claimed to know, it has no rival.
tyndall-floating-matter-air-1881:
John Tyndall, an Irish man of physics who worked in London, set out these essays in 1881. His theme is the fine dust that floats in the air around us. The work grew from his clash with Henry Bastian over the birth of life.

With a beam of light, Tyndall could see dust in air and tell when air was pure. He showed that pure air starts no rot and no growth in sealed broths at all. His proof backed Pasteur in England and shut the case on life from rot.
un-ga-res-181:
Palestine's fate was set on a new course by Resolution 181, adopted by the General Assembly on 29 November 1947. Britain, which ruled the land under a League mandate, had asked for a UN study of its future rule. A special team toured the land and heard all sides. Its main plan, backed by most of the team, was partition with a shared trade union.

The Assembly urges Britain and all member states to adopt and carry out that plan. Palestine would split into two states, one Jewish and one Arab, linked in trade. Jerusalem would stand apart, under world rule. Britain's pull-out was set for 1 August 1948. The plan lit the war of 1948, and its two-state frame still shapes the debate.
un-ga-res-a-69-81:
A full ban on nuclear tests is pressed toward force in Resolution A/69/81, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The halt of all test blasts, the text holds, is a real step toward disarmament and against the spread of such arms. The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty was adopted in 1996 and opened for signing that same month. After more than fifteen years, its entry into force is called more urgent than ever.

The counts are laid out with pride. One hundred eighty-three states had signed the pact, among them 41 of the 44 whose assent is needed to bring it to life. One hundred sixty-three had ratified it, three of them nuclear-armed states. The holdouts are named by their absence, not by blame.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 181 (II), adopted on 29 November 1947, recommended the partition of Palestine. Britain planned to end its mandate by 1 August 1948. The Assembly, acting on its Special Committee's report, proposed the Plan of Partition with Economic Union. It proposed it as the way to settle the land's future government.

The plan called for separate Arab and Jewish states, joined in an economic union. Jerusalem was to be under a special world regime run for the United Nations. A five-state commission was to take over rule step by step and set borders. It was to set up temporary councils leading to elections and democratic constitutions, with equal rights for all.

Resolution 69/81, adopted by the General Assembly at its sixty-ninth session in 2014, presses for entry into force of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty. It notes that 183 states had signed and 163 had ratified. But only 36 of the 44 states whose ratification is required had done so. It urges those states to ratify without delay or conditions. It calls on all states to keep their test moratoriums while the verification regime is completed.
un-sc-res-1181:
Sierra Leone drew a formal Council decision in Resolution 1181, adopted on 13 July 1998. The elected government had been restored with West African help. Former junta fighters and rebels still resisted and attacked civilians. A disarmament plan had been agreed with donors and now needed watching on the ground.

The Council creates the United Nations Observer Mission in Sierra Leone, called UNOMSIL, for six months until 13 January 1999. Up to 70 military observers deploy, about 40 of them first to areas held by the West African force. They track security, watch disarmament camps, and check respect for humanitarian law. Civilian staff advise on police reform and report on human rights abuse.
un-sc-res-1381: With a catalog date of 2001, Resolution 1381 records a decision of the UN Security Council. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-1481: Resolution 1481 dates to 2003, when the Security Council issued it as part of its regular business on peace and security. Wikisource's transcription of the official record is the source of the text kept here. Readers find the Council's standard architecture inside: recitals first, then decisions written to be quoted word for word by diplomats.
un-sc-res-1581:
Trials at the Yugoslavia war crimes court were running past the terms of the short-term judges hearing them in 2005. Six judges sat on cases that had not finished. The Secretary-General had asked the Council to act, in a letter dated 6 January 2005. The court's president had restated its plan to complete all work on schedule. Resolution 1581 was adopted unanimously on 18 January 2005.

The Council decided that the judges named in the text would stay on after their terms ended. Once replaced as short-term judges, they would keep serving until the trials they had begun were done. The cases included the Hadžihasanović, Orić, Limaj, Krajišnik, and Halilović trials. Letting a judge vanish mid-trial would have stalled those cases, or forced them to start again. The decision kept the trials moving, and it served the court's wider plan to finish its work on time.
un-sc-res-1681: Under number 1681, the fifteen-member Security Council filed a formal decision, preserved here via a Wikisource transcription of the UN record. The document's two movements are easy to spot: the Council first tells the world what it sees, then tells it what will be done. The entry preserves both movements in full.
un-sc-res-1781:
Georgia and Abkhazia are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1781, adopted in October 2007. Armed incidents had hurt the peace process, and some had cost lives. A rocket attack in the upper Kodori valley in March 2007 remained under joint investigation. Trust between the two sides stayed low.

The text extends the United Nations Observer Mission in Georgia, called UNOMIG, until 15 April 2008. It asks that the mission's watching capacity be strengthened. Both sides must finish papers on the non-use of violence and on refugee return without delay. Georgia must keep the Kodori valley in line with the 1994 Moscow cease-fire deal. Refugees keep their right to go home, starting with the Gali region.
un-sc-res-181:
South Africa's apartheid system faced the Council in the summer of 1963. Thirty-two African states had brought the question forward. On 7 August 1963 the Council strongly condemned South Africa's racial policies. Apartheid, it said, clashed with the Charter and with South Africa's duties as a member. A special committee's reports had documented the system. World opinion, voiced in the General Assembly, ran the same way.

South Africa had to abandon apartheid and discrimination at once. It had to free everyone jailed or restricted for opposing those policies. All states were called on to stop selling arms to South Africa. Guns, ammunition, and military vehicles were covered. The Secretary-General had to report by 30 October 1963. The text began the long sanctions campaign against apartheid.
un-sc-res-1881: Security Council Resolution 1881 is held here as a transcription of the United Nations official record from English Wikisource. The Council's authority is collective, and the text is where that collectivity becomes visible: fifteen positions merged into one set of findings and decisions. The merged result is preserved entire in this entry.
un-sc-res-281:
Mid-1970 found the Cyprus peacekeeping force due for another term. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 1 June, said the force was still needed to maintain peace on the island. Cyprus's government agreed it should continue beyond 15 June 1970. Resolution 281 was adopted unanimously on 9 June 1970.

The Council reaffirmed its Cyprus resolutions, from Resolution 186 of 1964 onward. The parties were urged to act with the utmost restraint. They also had to make good use of the favorable climate and keep working together toward the Council's goals. The force's stationing was extended for a further period, ending on 15 December 1970. The text follows the settled form of these renewals, which kept the mission in place through years of slow diplomacy.
un-sc-res-381:
The Golan Heights observer force was renewed by the Security Council on 30 November 1975. The Secretary-General had reported on the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force and had talked with all parties about the Middle East. The Council voiced concern over the continued tension in the area. It also looked beyond the force to the wider Arab-Israeli dispute.

The Council renewed the observer force's mandate for six more months. It decided to reconvene on 12 January 1976 to continue the debate on the Middle East problem, including the Palestinian question. All relevant United Nations resolutions were to be taken into account at that session. The Secretary-General was asked to keep the Council informed of further developments. The pairing of a routine renewal with a set date for a broad debate shows the Council treating the Golan posting as one part of an unsettled regional question.
un-sc-res-681: Security Council business produced Resolution 681, catalogued in this library as a 1949 record in the DECLASSIFIED group. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-81: First rules for its own acts were noted by the Security Council in Resolution 81, passed on 24 May 1950. The Secretary-General had sent the Council a note of May 1949 on the point. The Council takes note of an Assembly text of 28 April 1949 on the same ground. It rules that, should a fit chance arise, it will base its acts on the rules held in that text. The vote passed with all in favor, the Soviet member being absent from the hall.
un-sc-res-981:
Croatia gained its own United Nations operation in the spring of 1995. On 31 March 1995 the Security Council established UNCRO. The name means United Nations Confidence Restoration Operation. The Secretary-General's report of 22 March supplied the design. The mission would run until 30 November 1995. It replaced the Croatia part of the wider UNPROFOR force.

The Council restated its search for a negotiated end to the Yugoslav wars. It stressed respect for the borders of all states in the region. It also stressed mutual recognition among them. The Secretary-General had to keep consulting on the details of the mandate. He would report on the talks as the mission deployed. UNCRO's life proved short and stormy.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
A UN observer mission for Sierra Leone is created in Resolution 1181, adopted on 13 July 1998. The restored government was rebuilding under a disarmament plan agreed with international donors, ECOMOG provided security and ran arms collection, and rebel remnants kept attacking civilians.

The Council establishes the United Nations Observer Mission in Sierra Leone, UNOMSIL, for six months until 13 January 1999, with up to 70 military observers and a small medical unit. UNOMSIL must monitor the security situation. It must watch the disarmament and demobilization of former combatants in secure areas and ECOMOG's role there. It must monitor respect for international humanitarian law. It must follow the Civil Defence Forces' voluntary disarmament. About 40 observers deploy first to ECOMOG-secured areas, the rest as security allows, once security arrangements and a status of mission agreement are confirmed. Its civilian staff advise on police reform and report human rights violations.

On the Golan Heights, the force that watches the separation between Israeli and Syrian troops is renewed on 27 November 2001. UNDOF, the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force, stays in place for six months, until 31 May 2002. The Council called on the parties to carry out resolution 338 of 1973 at once, and asked for a report on developments at the end of the period.

What short-term judges may do at the Yugoslavia war crimes tribunal is widened on 19 May 2003. The tribunal's president had raised the point in letters. Ad litem judges were called in for a single trial, and their powers stopped there, even when other work sat waiting.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council amended article 13 quater of the tribunal's Statute. While appointed to a trial, an ad litem judge may now also handle pre-trial work in other cases, where the need arises and the judge is able to take it on. The replacement article is annexed. The small change aimed to speed the tribunal's crowded trial schedule.

Part-heard war crimes trials in The Hague needed a rule fix in 2005. On 18 January, the Council adopted Resolution 1581 without dissent. The Yugoslavia court was racing to finish trials on a set schedule. Several stand-in judges sat on big cases as their terms ran out. Losing them mid-trial would waste years of work.

The text rules that named judges will finish the cases they began. The list covers five trials. Names include the Hadžihasanović, Orić, and Limaj cases. The Krajišnik and Halilović cases are there too. The fix spared the court from restarting long trials with fresh panels. It also guarded each accused person's right to a timely trial.

Four months, with cuts, are granted to UNMEE on 31 May 2006. The Ethiopia-Eritrea mission is extended while being reshaped smaller. The parties had not met the Council's demands, and the border remained unmarked. The Temporary Security Zone between the two armies still had to be respected.

A reconfiguration of UNMEE's military component to a smaller size, matched to the stalled process, is authorized. Full compliance with resolution 1640 is demanded, including free access and support for the mission. Both parties are called on to cooperate fully with the Boundary Commission so demarcation can move forward. They are also to create the conditions for the commission's ruling to be carried out on the ground.

Armed incidents strain Georgia's ceasefire in Resolution 1781, adopted in October 2007. A rocket-firing incident in the upper Kodori Valley on 11 March 2007 and a further incident on 20 September had been investigated by the Joint Fact-Finding Group. Trust between the Georgian and Abkhaz sides stayed low, and documents on the non-use of violence and on refugee return remained unfinished.

The Council extends the UN Observer Mission in Georgia, UNOMIG, to 15 April 2008. It calls for a stronger observation capacity for the mission and urges Georgia to bring the upper Kodori Valley in line with the 1994 Moscow Agreement, while the Abkhaz side shows restraint. Both sides must sign the two pending documents without delay, resume regular quadripartite meetings, and protect the right of all refugees and displaced persons to return, starting with the Gali region. It welcomes UNOMIG police deployment in Gali and urges deeper cooperation there.

South Africa's race laws drew a world arms call in 1963. Thirty-two African states brought the case to the Council. Pretoria had jailed men for fighting its apartheid rule. It was piling up arms, some used to crush dissent. It had spurned a call to send a man to be heard. Resolution 181 passed on 7 August 1963 by nine votes to none. France and Britain held back.

Apartheid was damned as a breach of the Charter's word. South Africa had to drop its race laws at once. All held for fighting them had to walk free. Then came the sharp edge. All states were called, in grave terms, to halt arms sales to Pretoria at once. Guns, shells, and war trucks were named. Word on the scene was due from the chief by 30 October.

UNAMID, the joint African Union-United Nations mission in Darfur, is extended for twelve months on 30 July 2009, to 31 July 2010. The mission had taken over from the African Union force at the start of 2008. Violence against civilians, peacekeepers, and aid workers in Darfur continued, and no lasting ceasefire held.

All parties are demanded to end violence and attacks at once, meet their duties under human rights and humanitarian law, and commit to a sustained ceasefire. The Secretary-General is asked to develop a better ceasefire monitoring mechanism with the parties. UNAMID is told to report major violations and to use its full mandate to protect civilians across Darfur, while political talks toward a lasting settlement are pressed forward.

Into the 1970s, the Cyprus force rolled on by six-month steps. On 9 June 1970, the Council adopted Resolution 281 without dissent. The Secretary-General reported that the force was still needed to keep peace. Cyprus agreed it should stay past mid-June.

The text restates the whole Cyprus series back to 1964. It urges the parties to use the hopeful climate for joint work. It then extends the posting to 15 December 1970. The standing hope appears once more. Progress toward a final deal might by then let the force shrink or leave. That phrase had become the mission's refrain by 1970.

Resolution 381, adopted on 30 November 1975 by thirteen votes to none, renews the peacekeeping force stationed between Israel and Syria. The United Nations Disengagement Observer Force had watched the Golan separation lines since 1974. The Secretary-General's report on the force and his talks with all parties were before the Council, which voiced concern at continuing tension.

Three decisions follow. The Council set 12 January 1976 to resume debate on the Middle East, the Palestinian question included, in light of all past rulings. It renewed the observer force's mandate for another six months. And it asked the Secretary-General to keep it informed on further developments, the standard leash on a force renewed in short cycles.

Civilians in the lands held by Israel were the subject of Resolution 681, adopted in December 1990. The Secretary-General had reported on ways to keep Palestinian civilians safe there. Israel had rejected Resolutions 672 and 673, which concerned a fact-finding mission. It had also decided to resume deportations of Palestinians. 

The Council expressed grave concern at Israel's rejection of the two resolutions. It deplored the renewed decision to deport Palestinians. Israel was urged to accept that the Fourth Geneva Convention applies in law to all the lands held since 1967. It had to obey that pact fully and carefully. The Secretary-General was asked to develop one idea from his report. The states that signed the pact might meet to discuss protection. With the Red Cross, he also had to watch the situation of civilians there and report every four months.

A short procedural decision from the early United Nations was taken on 24 May 1950. The Council had before it a note from the Secretary-General, dated 13 May 1949. The note concerned a General Assembly resolution of 28 April 1949. Resolution 81, adopted unanimously, does two things only. The Council took note of the Assembly's resolution. It then decided that, if a suitable occasion arose, it would base its own action on the principles set out in that text. That pledge is the whole content of the resolution.

Croatia demanded a smaller, reshaped UN presence in 1995. The old protection force was being split into separate missions. Resolution 981, adopted unanimously on 31 March 1995, created UNCRO, the UN Confidence Restoration Operation in Croatia. It followed the Secretary-General's report of 22 March. Its mandate ran to 30 November 1995.

UNCRO would watch the 1994 ceasefire between Croatia and local Serb forces. It would track arms crossing from Bosnia and Yugoslavia. It would help aid reach Bosnia across Croatian land. It would also watch demilitarization on the Prevlaka peninsula. The Council even allowed air support to defend UNCRO staff. The hope was that confidence might grow into a negotiated settlement.
uslaw-usc-t2-s2181:
Section 2181 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers the assignment of space for meetings of joint committees. It sits in Chapter 30 of that title, on the operation of the Capitol complex, among its general rules. The President pro tempore of the Senate and the Speaker of the House are to cause a survey to be made. The survey is of space at hand within the Capitol.

The space must be such as could be used for joint committee meetings and for meetings of conference committees. It must also serve other meetings that call for both Senators and Members of the House to be present, as the text goes on to state. The text is current through Public Law 119-134.
